How to Use This

The clinical content is downstream of the method. Read this section once, then let the briefs reinforce it.

Method guide — the three habits, question verbs & the trap speciestap to expand

The three habits

  1. The assassin scan. For each answer choice, find the sentence in the stem that makes it impossible. When every option but one has an assassin, the question is finished — no forward reasoning required. A stem's "normal" findings are eliminations, not filler.
  2. The switch rule. Change an answer only when rereading reveals a misread fact — never when it reveals a new possibility. A detail that is merely compatible with another diagnosis is flavor. Incompatibility, not plausibility.
  3. Store the discriminator, not the outcome. Learn "limping child → score Kocher," never "limping child → aspirate." Rules stored as outcomes fire on the benign mirror-twin stem and get you twice.

Read the verb before the choices

  1. "Most likely diagnosis" → the diagnosis that explains all findings, not the most findings.
  2. "Most sensitive / screening" → lowest detection threshold. "Most accurate / definitive / confirms" → tissue, or the gold-standard test.
  3. "Next step in management" → the next rung on the ladder. "Next step in diagnosis" → the test whose result changes what you do tonight.
  4. "Most beneficial / reduces mortality" → match the intervention's time-to-benefit to the outcome's time horizon. Lipids = years. BP, volume, GDMT = weeks to months.
  5. "Underlying cause" → the trunk of the causal tree, not a branch.
The ten trap species
SpeciesHow it worksAntidote
Salient decoyA vivid, concrete detail — occupation, travel, family history — that is compatible with the right answer but suggests a wrong one. Camping in Georgia → Lyme, when the answer is rheumatic fever.Ask what job the detail is doing. If it's making you nervous rather than deciding anything, it's bait.
Treat-the-numberAn abnormal lab planted so you medicate the value instead of the outcome. Low HDL → niacin. High A1c → metformin. High Hct → phlebotomy.Ask which intervention changes the outcome named in the question.
Trump-card inversionA risk calculator offered when a categorical indication already decides it. 10-year risk 4.9% in a diabetic — diabetes already earned the statin.Check trump cards before calculators: prior event, LDL ≥190, diabetes 40–75.
True-fact-wrong-slotA real association placed where the timeline or findings forbid it. Post-URI in a 12-month history. Fibroids causing postmenopausal bleeding.Verify the interval and the physiologic state before you use the association.
Mirror twinThe benign version of a stem you just learned the dangerous version of. Transient synovitis right after septic arthritis.Store the scoring rule, not the action.
Sequencing trapA correct action offered one step out of order. MRI before conservative therapy. Antibiotics before aspiration. Imaging before airway.Name the ladder out loud before choosing a rung.
Uniform-answer doubtAn "all yes" or "no further testing" option rejected because it feels too easy. HIV vaccine grid — the answer really was yes to all four.Reject it only with a named disqualifying criterion you can say out loud.
Test-overrides-findingsA normal or discordant test offered against classic findings. Negative scaphoid film. Negative nitrite. Negative Phalen. Normal creatinine in early nephropathy. A nonfocal neuro exam in brain abscess.A negative result lowers probability according to the test's performance. It supports ruling out disease only when the remaining probability is sufficiently low for the decision.
Unchecked attributeThe right category is retrieved and then never checked against the one attribute that separates its members — direction, age, duration, grade, timing, or kind. The option is the correct disease family with the wrong value on the deciding axis.Name the attribute the stem specified, out loud, before choosing: which direction, at what age, over how long, at which grade.
Class-vs-memberThe right drug class represented by the wrong member, making a keyed answer look like it contradicts a guideline. "NSAIDs are first-line for OA" — but the only NSAID offered is ketorolac, a 5-day drug, so acetaminophen wins.Read which specific agent represents each class before rejecting the class.
The recurring failure mode Fast-and-wrong misses cluster where the deciding fact lives in the background — the past medical history, the gestational age, the menopausal status, the duration — rather than in the foreground finding. Recognition speed is not the problem; the missing step is a deliberate 10-second completion pass: read the entire lab panel and the entire PMH before locking.
NBME blueprint: coverage by system and how questions are wordedtap to expand

Counts and ranges follow the shelf you are viewing: each clerkship shows its own NBME subject exam outline, and Step 2 shows the USMLE Step 2 CK outline. A low NBME count means not yet seen on a form you have logged, not untested.

How NBME words questions

Patterns seen on the NBME form questions logged so far. Each line gives one paraphrased example and the brief that shows it.

Using the trap lines: each trap line in a brief names one wrong option, why it tempts, and the finding in the stem that rules it out.

  1. The diagnosis is given as its mechanism. A toddler with hip dysplasia found late is keyed as a poorly developed acetabulum, and a newborn with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency as an enzyme deficiency. The Limping Child
  2. The organism is asked as a class. A painless genital ulcer is keyed as a spirochete, with obligate intracellular bacterium and gram-negative diplococcus beside it. Genital Ulcers
  3. A disease appears under a formal or older name. Kawasaki disease is listed as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, usually as a decoy. Acute Rheumatic Fever
  4. A decoy shares a name with a disease that would fit. Fanconi syndrome, a kidney tubule disorder, is offered among marrow failures; Fanconi anemia is the disease that would fit. Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function
  5. The genetic defect and the parent of origin replace the syndrome. Angelman syndrome is keyed as a chromosome 15 deletion inherited from the mother, with the same deletion from the father as the next option. Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi
  6. The key is a procedure or a way of measuring. Protein on a routine dipstick in a well adolescent is keyed as a repeat urinalysis at bedtime and on waking; a high automated blood pressure is keyed as a measurement by auscultation. Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child
  7. An exposure is planted as bait. Cat scratches sit beside a cat-scratch disease option when the key is an infected thyroglossal duct cyst, and mosquito bites sit in a spotted fever stem. A refugee camp is different: it is a real risk factor for rheumatic fever, and it also invites travel-fever decoys. Lymphadenopathy
  8. Development comes as a grid. Each option is a row of delayed or normal for gross motor, fine motor and language, so every domain in the stem has to be read on its own. Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth
  9. The lead-in grants part of the answer. A bleeding newborn is asked what to give in addition to vitamin K, which leaves only the blood product to choose. Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies
  10. A definition may be dated. Older sources, including this NBME explanation, set adolescent hypertension at the 95th percentile at every age. The current 2017 American Academy of Pediatrics guideline uses a fixed cutoff of 130/80 mm Hg from age 13. High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent
  11. Every wrong option is the treatment of a look-alike. A slipped capital femoral epiphysis is keyed as internal fixation, beside abduction bracing and spica casting (hip dysplasia), traction (fracture) and physical therapy (strain). Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis
  12. The finding is described, never named. A boy with a red, tender foot 3 weeks after a nail went through his shoe has osteomyelitis, but the word never appears; the question asks only for the organism. Foot Puncture Infection
  13. Each negative in the stem closes one decoy. In a newborn with two flank masses, an uncomplicated pregnancy, good Apgar scores and a normal hematocrit close renal vein thrombosis, which leaves polycystic kidney disease. Abdominal Mass in a Young Child
  14. One noun at different sites makes a location question. A virilized 10-year-old girl is offered adrenal, ovarian and pituitary adenoma. A high dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate (DHEAS) with a normal testosterone and a normal pelvic ultrasound places the source in the adrenal. Precocious Puberty
  15. A disease usually taught in its severe form appears mild. Posterior urethral valves appear in a well, feeding newborn with no Potter features, among four other causes of prenatal hydronephrosis. The thick bladder wall and a dribbling stream place the level. Posterior Urethral Valves
  16. The key is an umbrella term. A soft newborn murmur spreading to the lung fields and axilla is peripheral pulmonary stenosis, keyed as pulmonary stenosis because the specific name is not offered. Heart Murmurs in a Child
  17. The common answer is left off, and a planted sign fits a decoy. A 16-year-old smoker with past asthma admissions and severe hyperinflation is keyed as alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency because asthma is not an option. Clubbing and yellow sputum pull toward Kartagener syndrome. Obstructive Lung Disease
  18. A prevention lead-in skips the diagnosis. A recent immigrant with a rash that starts on the face is asked which vaccine would have prevented it. Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine prevents both measles and rubella, so the two need not be separated. When the stem reads as rubella and the explanation teaches measles, the stem sets the facts. Fever and Rash in a Child
  19. The options are an age ladder, and the date is a cue. A 4-month-old seen in October is offered rotavirus, influenza, MMR, chickenpox and shingles. October fits influenza, but only rotavirus among the options is due at 4 months. Chickenpox and shingles are one virus listed twice. Vaccines at the Infant Visits
  20. The clue sits in a relative. A boy with recurrent abscesses, osteomyelitis and pneumonia has a maternal uncle who died of fungal pneumonia, which points to X-linked chronic granulomatous disease. The key is written as impaired microbicidal activity. Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function
  21. Nine options form a lab grid. An 18-month-old with poor growth, no vomiting or diarrhea, a normal blood pressure, low potassium, a normal-gap acidosis and an alkaline urine is offered nine causes of a potassium problem. Each option sits in one cell of potassium (high or low), acid-base (acidosis or alkalosis) and blood pressure (high or normal); only renal tubular acidosis fills the low-potassium, acidosis, normal-pressure cell. Bartter syndrome appears under its tissue name, juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia. Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child

Musculoskeletal & Rheumatology 17 topics + 3 board-style + 1 Aquifer

The shelf's densest system. Nearly every stem is decided by a maneuver, a time course, or a red flag hiding in the past medical history.

Polymyalgia Rheumatica

Elderly · proximal stiffness · ESR

The decision point

Polymyalgia rheumatica presents at age >50 with bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness, systemic symptoms and ESR ≥50 (erythrocyte sedimentation rate). There is no true weakness and no muscle tenderness. "Can't get out of bed" here reflects pain and stiffness, not weakness; weakness points to myositis. Treatment is low-dose prednisone ~15 mg. A dramatic response within days is nearly diagnostic.

Defining criteria Diagnosis — age >50, bilateral proximal girdle aching with morning stiffness, ESR ≥50, with normal strength and no muscle tenderness · Response criterion — dramatic improvement on prednisone ~15 mg within days is nearly diagnostic · Rules out polymyositis — PMR is pain with normal CK; polymyositis is weakness with elevated CK
Proximal pain & stiffness — the differential
DiagnosisKey discriminatorLabsTreatment
Polymyalgia rheumaticaProximal pain/stiffness, strength normalESR/CRP ↑, CK normalLow-dose prednisone
Giant cell arteritis EmergencyHeadache, jaw claudication, vision loss; coexists with PMR in ~50%ESR often >50–100High-dose prednisone; don't wait for biopsy if vision is threatened
PolymyositisProximal weakness > painCK ↑, anti-Jo-1High-dose steroids
Elderly-onset RASmall-joint synovitis (MCP/PIP), erosionsRF / anti-CCP +Methotrexate
FibromyalgiaDiffuse tender points, younger womenNormal ESR/CRPExercise, duloxetine, amitriptyline
Hypothyroid myopathyFatigue, weight gain, bradycardiaTSH ↑, CK ↑Levothyroxine
Statin myopathyStatin exposureCK ↑Stop the statin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
ESR and CRPFirstESR elevated, typically 50 or higherSupports PMR in the right clinical picture; normal values point toward fibromyalgia or another cause
CKFirstNormal CKPain without muscle injury; excludes polymyositis and statin myopathy
TSHFirstNormal TSHExcludes hypothyroid myopathy, which can mimic proximal aching
RF and anti-CCPBy branchNegative in PMRSwollen MCPs or PIPs: consider elderly-onset RA
Temporal artery biopsyBy branchGranulomatous arteritisHeadache, jaw claudication or vision change: GCA; start high-dose prednisone before biopsy
Response to prednisone about 15 mg (clinical diagnosis)ConfirmsDramatic improvement within daysPMR; no response after a week means reconsider the diagnosis
EMG and muscle biopsySkipNormal in PMR; strength is 5/5Reserved for true weakness with high CK (polymyositis)
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo F, bilateral shoulder and hip girdle aching, morning stiffness 90 min, ESR 62, strength 5/5 → Polymyalgia rheumatica → prednisone 15 mg daily
  2. 72 yo F with known PMR, new jaw claudication and temporal tenderness → Giant cell arteritis → high-dose prednisone immediately, biopsy after
  3. 68 yo M, progressive proximal weakness, CK 4,000, normal ESR → Polymyositis → EMG and muscle biopsy
  4. 70 yo F on atorvastatin, proximal aching, CK 900 → Statin myopathy → stop the statin and recheck CK
  5. 66 yo F, proximal aching, ESR 12, TSH 14 → Hypothyroid myopathy → levothyroxine
  6. 74 yo F with presumed PMR, no response after a week of prednisone 15 mg → Reconsider the diagnosis — PMR responds within days
  7. 63 yo F, widespread pain, non-restorative sleep, normal ESR and CK → Fibromyalgia
Pearls PMR (polymyalgia rheumatica) = pain with normal CK (creatine kinase); polymyositis = weakness with high CK · PMR responds to low-dose steroids, GCA (giant cell arteritis) needs high dose · every PMR diagnosis gets a GCA symptom screen, and ~50% of GCA patients have PMR · NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) fail in PMR; they are a close but inadequate therapy.
Sequencing trapTreat-the-number

Wrist and Hand Pain and Numbness

snuffbox vs styloid vs thumb base · occult scaphoid fracture · carpal tunnel and its mimics · when not to imageWhere exactly is the tenderness or numbness, and would a negative test change anything?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Locate the finding first:

  • Anatomic snuffbox after a fall on the outstretched hand: scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise. A negative film does not rule it out (up to 20 to 25% are occult in week one): thumb spica cast, then re-image in 2 to 3 weeks or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) now.
  • Radial styloid with a positive Finkelstein test: de Quervain tendinopathy, a clinical diagnosis; no imaging and no labs.
  • Thumb to half the ring finger numb at night, thenar sensation spared (the median nerve's palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the tunnel): carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS); numbness that includes the thenar eminence is a proximal lesion.

A negative test cannot rule out disease when pretest probability is high; when the diagnosis is clinical, a provocative test is positive and there are no red flags, extra testing adds only incidental findings.

Diagnosis
Numbness by distribution: which nerve or root
LesionDistributionThe tell
Carpal tunnelFirst 3.5 digits, volarNocturnal, relieved by shaking; thenar spared
Pronator teres syndromeSame digits plus thenar eminenceForearm pain with pronation; not nocturnal
Anterior interosseous nerveNone: pure motorCannot make the OK sign
C6 (sixth cervical) radiculopathyThumb and index, with neck painDiminished brachioradialis reflex: cervical spine MRI
C7 (seventh cervical) radiculopathyMiddle fingerDiminished triceps reflex
Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel4th and 5th digitsWorse with elbow flexion; Froment sign, claw hand
Ulnar nerve at Guyon canal4th and 5th digits, volar onlyCyclists; hook of hamate fracture
Radial nerve at the spiral grooveDorsal web spaceWrist drop (Saturday night palsy)
Pancoast tumor (cannot miss)C8 (eighth cervical) to T1 (first thoracic), medial armHorner syndrome, shoulder pain, weight loss: chest CT
Other wrist and hand findings First carpometacarpal (CMC) osteoarthritis – thumb base pain, positive grind test, squared joint, older · Colles fracture – distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation (dinner fork) after a fall · Intersection syndrome – crepitus about 4 cm proximal to the wrist, dorsal; rowers, weightlifters · Trigger finger – catching or locking with a nodule at the A1 (first annular) pulley · Ganglion cyst – soft dorsal wrist mass that transilluminates and fluctuates · Dupuytren contracture – palmar cord and contracture of the 4th and 5th digits; alcohol, diabetes · Disseminated gonococcal infection (cannot miss) – fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis of several sheaths, pustules: NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) and ceftriaxone · Hand arthritis – rheumatoid spares the DIP (distal interphalangeal) joints and hits MCP (metacarpophalangeal) and PIP (proximal interphalangeal) symmetrically; osteoarthritis hits DIP (Heberden) and PIP (Bouchard); psoriatic hits DIP with dactylitis, nail pitting and pencil-in-cup erosions
Management and treatment
Management ladders
ConditionFirstEscalate to
Scaphoid fracture, presumed (negative film)Thumb spica castDisplaced waist or proximal pole fracture: surgical fixation
De Quervain tendinopathy: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, first dorsal compartmentThumb spica splint and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug)Corticosteroid injection, then first dorsal compartment release
Carpal tunnel syndromeNocturnal neutral wrist splintThenar atrophy: surgical release (motor loss is late: lumbricals 1 and 2, opponens, abductor and flexor pollicis brevis)
Why cast on suspicion Retrograde blood supply – enters distally and runs back to the proximal pole; a missed fracture ends in avascular necrosis and nonunion, worst at the proximal pole · Same risk – femoral head, talus and humeral head (retrograde or tenuous supply)
Practice
  1. 22-year-old man fell on his outstretched hand playing basketball tender in the anatomic snuffbox wrist radiographs with a scaphoid view are negative Pain on gripping; no deformity Afebrile · radial pulse normal · sensation intact → Thumb spica cast and re-image in 2–3 weeks → snuffbox tenderness after a fall is a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise; up to 20 to 25% are occult in week one: thumb spica cast and re-image in 2 to 3 weeks
  2. 22-year-old man, a professional goalkeeper, has snuffbox tenderness after a fall radiographs negative needs a definitive answer before a match next week Thumb spica cast in place Afebrile · sensation intact → MRI of the wrist → MRI shows an occult fracture immediately when a 2-week wait for repeat films is not acceptable
  3. 22-year-old man has 6 months of wrist pain fell on an outstretched hand last winter, not imaged then tender in the anatomic snuffbox Grip weak and painful Afebrile · radiograph: sclerotic proximal scaphoid with a fracture gap → Avascular necrosis and nonunion → the blood supply runs retrograde to the proximal pole, so a missed fracture ends in avascular necrosis and nonunion
  4. 68-year-old woman fell on her outstretched hand on ice tender over the distal radius, not the snuffbox wrist looks like a dinner fork Radiograph: distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation Afebrile · radial pulse normal → Colles fracture → dorsal angulation of a distal radius fracture after a fall is a Colles fracture; snuffbox tenderness would point to the scaphoid
  5. 24-year-old woman was diagnosed with a scaphoid fracture on MRI fracture line near the end closest to the forearm nondisplaced She asks about the risk of the bone dying Afebrile · sensation intact → Proximal pole → the proximal pole carries the highest avascular necrosis risk: its blood supply arrives last, retrograde from the distal end
  6. 22-year-old man fell from his skateboard onto his outstretched hand tender in the anatomic snuffbox radiograph: displaced fracture through the scaphoid waist No other injury; pain on gripping Afebrile · radial pulse normal → Surgical fixation → a displaced waist or proximal pole fracture goes to surgical fixation; casting is for the presumed fracture with a negative film
  7. 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks of gestation has numb hands tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers shakes her hands to relieve it Thenar sensation spared; no neck pain BP 118/72 mm Hg · mild hand and ankle edema → CTS of pregnancy → numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers relieved by shaking, with thenar sparing and no neck pain at 34 weeks, is carpal tunnel syndrome of pregnancy: nocturnal splint; it usually resolves after delivery
  8. 48-year-old man has new numbness in both hands at night his rings no longer fit coarse facial features and large hands Shoe size has increased BP 148/92 mm Hg · glucose 168 mg/dL → Acromegaly → bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome with enlarging hands and coarse features is acromegaly: IGF-1 (insulin-like growth factor 1)
  9. 52-year-old woman has numbness in both hands at night fatigue and 6 kg of weight gain cold intolerance, dry skin Delayed relaxation of ankle reflexes HR 56/min · BP 128/84 mm Hg → Hypothyroidism → bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome with fatigue and weight gain is hypothyroidism: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)
  10. 60-year-old man on long-term hemodialysis for 12 years has numb hands at night both hands, thumb to middle finger, for months shoulder pain and stiffness No diabetes Afebrile · BP 138/80 mm Hg → β2-microglobulin amyloidosis → long-term hemodialysis with carpal tunnel syndrome is beta-2 microglobulin amyloidosis
  11. 58-year-old woman has 2 years of numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers thenar atrophy weak thumb abduction Nerve conduction: severe median slowing at the wrist Afebrile · TSH normal → Carpal tunnel release → thenar atrophy means the nerve is losing motor fibers: skip conservative therapy and release the carpal tunnel
  12. 32-year-old woman, a new mother, has 4 weeks of radial wrist pain worse lifting her baby out of the crib tender over the radial styloid Finkelstein test positive Afebrile · no snuffbox tenderness → De Quervain tendinopathy → radial styloid tenderness with a positive Finkelstein test is de Quervain tendinopathy: a clinical diagnosis; thumb spica splint and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug)
  13. 65-year-old woman has thumb base pain when opening jars squared appearance of the thumb base grind test positive Radiograph: joint space narrowing at the base of the thumb Afebrile · Finkelstein test negative → First CMC osteoarthritis → thumb base pain with a positive grind test in an older patient is first carpometacarpal (CMC) osteoarthritis
  14. 24-year-old woman, sexually active, has wrist tenosynovitis: painful swelling over both wrists migratory joint pains for 4 days a pustular rash: a few pustules on her forearms New partner last month T 38.4 °C · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Disseminated gonococcal infection → tenosynovitis, migratory arthralgia and pustules is disseminated gonococcal infection: nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), blood cultures and ceftriaxone
  15. 32-year-old woman was diagnosed with de Quervain tendinopathy and is still in pain 6 weeks of a thumb spica splint and an NSAID Finkelstein test still positive No numbness Afebrile · no swelling over the snuffbox → Corticosteroid injection → after splint and NSAID fail, the next rung is a corticosteroid injection; release of the first dorsal compartment comes after that
  16. 40-year-old man, a competitive rower, has dorsal forearm pain worse with repetitive wrist extension crepitus a few centimeters proximal to the wrist with motion Radial styloid not tender Afebrile · Finkelstein test negative → Intersection syndrome → pain with crepitus about 4 cm proximal to the wrist in a rower is intersection syndrome
Transferable rule

A negative test cannot rule out disease when pretest probability is high, as with a D-dimer in high-probability pulmonary embolism; and when the diagnosis is clinical with a positive provocative test and no red flags, restraint is the answer.

Low Back Pain in an Adult

red flags and when to image · acute pain with no red flags · inflammatory back pain and spondyloarthritisIs there a red flag or a neurologic deficit, and does the pain improve when the patient moves?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Acute low back pain (under 4 weeks) with no red flag and a normal neurologic exam: no imaging. Treat with an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and tell the patient to stay active.

Read the past medical history before the population rule:

  • Prior cancer: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) with contrast; early vertebral metastasis is neurologically silent, so a normal neurologic exam does not remove the concern.
  • Urinary retention or saddle anesthesia: emergent MRI and decompression.
  • Upper motor neuron signs with known or suspected cancer (cord compression): dexamethasone first, then emergent whole-spine MRI.

Night pain that improves once the patient gets up is inflammatory; night pain unrelieved by moving, with age over 50, prior cancer or weight loss, is malignant.

Diagnosis
Red flags by category
CategoryRed flagsImaging
MalignancyPrior cancer, over 50, weight loss, night or rest pain, pain over 4 to 6 weeksMRI with contrast; radiograph plus ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) or CRP (C-reactive protein) if suspicion is moderate
InfectionFever, injection drug use, recent bacteremia, immunosuppression, recent spinal procedureMRI with contrast plus blood cultures
FractureOver 70, osteoporosis, chronic steroids, traumaRadiograph first
Cauda equina (emergency)Urinary retention (most sensitive), saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, reduced anal toneEmergent MRI and decompression
Cord compression (emergency)Upper motor neuron signs, hyperreflexia, sensory levelEmergent whole-spine MRI; dexamethasone first only when cancer is known or suspected
InflammatoryUnder 40, over 3 months, better with exercise, worse with rest, HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen B27)Sacroiliac (SI) joint radiograph, then MRI
Abdominal aortic aneurysmOver 60, atherosclerosis, pulsatile mass, tearing painUltrasound or CT (computed tomography) angiography
Inflammatory versus mechanical
InflammatoryMechanical
OnsetUnder 40, insidious, over 3 monthsAny age, often acute after an event
Night painSecond half of the nightUsually absent
Morning stiffnessOver 30 minutesUnder 30 minutes
Rest and activityWorse with rest, better with movementBetter with rest, worse with activity
NSAID responseDramaticVariable
Defining findings Inflammatory back pain – enthesitis, where tendons and ligaments insert into bone (rheumatoid arthritis causes synovitis instead) · Spondyloarthritis (PAIR) – psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease-associated, reactive; seronegative (rheumatoid factor negative), HLA-B27 associated; enthesitis, dactylitis, uveitis · Ankylosing spondylitis – young men; HLA-B27 in about 90% (supportive, not diagnostic); sacroiliitis first; reduced Schober test and chest expansion, lost lumbar lordosis, late bamboo spine · Its complications – anterior uveitis (25 to 40%), aortitis with aortic regurgitation, AV (atrioventricular) block, apical pulmonary fibrosis, immunoglobulin A nephropathy, a rigid spine that fractures with minor trauma · Vertebral metastasis – seeds the vertebral body through the valveless Batson plexus; pedicle loss gives the winking owl sign; bone-seeking primaries “BLT (breast, lung, thyroid) with a Kosher (kidney) Pickle (prostate)”; plain films miss 30 to 50% of bone loss
Management and treatment
Management ladder: acute low back pain
TierInterventionEscalate when
1NSAID and stay active, no bed rest; heat or a short muscle relaxant optionalNo better at 4 to 6 weeks, or a red flag appears
2Physical therapy (PT); MRI if radicular symptoms persistRadicular symptoms 6 weeks or more
3Epidural steroid injectionFailed conservative therapy
4Surgical referralProgressive deficit, cauda equina, refractory pain
By diagnosis Ankylosing spondylitis – NSAID and exercise, then a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) or interleukin-17 inhibitor; methotrexate and sulfasalazine help peripheral, not axial, disease; screen for latent tuberculosis before a TNF inhibitor · Malignant cord compression with deficits – dexamethasone before imaging, the one place treatment precedes diagnosis · Unstable aneurysm – straight to surgery
Why no imaging Early imaging brings more surgery without better outcomes. Asymptomatic disc bulges and degenerative change are near-universal by middle age, so a scan mostly finds incidental lesions that invite intervention. About 90% of acute low back pain and of sciatica resolves within 6 weeks.
Practice
  1. 40-year-old man has 1 week of low back pain began 1 day after moving furniture tender over the paraspinal muscles, not the spine No fever, chills, constipation or urinary incontinence Afebrile · reflexes, strength and sensation normal → No imaging → acute pain with a mechanical cause and a history full of pertinent negatives needs no imaging: an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and stay active
  2. 47-year-old woman has 5 days of low back pain after gardening chronic kidney disease, stage 3 bleeding gastric ulcer last year No fever, weight loss or bladder change Creatinine 1.9 mg/dL · neurologic exam normal → Acetaminophen or a topical NSAID → same tier, a different agent: kidney disease and a prior bleed rule out an oral NSAID, so acetaminophen or a topical NSAID
  3. 47-year-old woman has 8 weeks of low back pain pain shoots down the lateral leg to the top of the foot no better with an NSAID No bladder change Afebrile · strength normal · left straight-leg raise positive → MRI, PT, consider epidural → radicular symptoms past 6 weeks: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) and physical therapy (PT), with an epidural steroid injection if conservative care keeps failing
  4. 47-year-old woman has 3 weeks of low back and left leg pain now cannot lift the front of her left foot foot slaps on walking No bladder or bowel change Afebrile · left ankle dorsiflexion 3/5 · saddle sensation normal → Urgent MRI → a new foot drop is a progressive deficit: urgent MRI, without the bladder or saddle signs that make it an emergency
  5. 47-year-old woman has 2 days of low back pain now pain down both legs cannot pass urine since this morning Numb over the buttocks and inner thighs Afebrile · bladder scan 800 mL · anal tone reduced → Emergent MRI + decompression → urinary retention and saddle anesthesia are cauda equina syndrome: emergent MRI and decompression
  6. 62-year-old woman has 6 weeks of low back pain treated for breast cancer 4 years ago worse at night, not relieved by rest Neurologic exam normal Afebrile · no weight loss → MRI for metastasis → prior cancer with night pain needs MRI with contrast even with a normal neurologic exam; plain films miss 30 to 50% of bone loss
  7. 55-year-old woman has 2 months of back pain that wakes her at night not relieved by getting up and moving lost 6 kg without trying Treated for breast cancer 3 years ago Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Metastasis → night pain unrelieved by moving, with prior cancer and weight loss, is metastasis, not inflammatory back pain: MRI
  8. 34-year-old man who injects drugs has 1 week of back pain fever and chills focal tenderness over one lumbar spinous process No leg weakness T 38.9 °C · erythrocyte sedimentation rate 98 mm/h → Vertebral osteomyelitis → fever with focal spinal tenderness in injection drug use is vertebral osteomyelitis: MRI with contrast plus blood cultures
  9. 72-year-old woman on chronic prednisone has sudden back pain began after a minor fall point tenderness over one midline lumbar vertebra No leg pain, numbness or weakness Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Vertebral compression fracture → age over 70, chronic steroids and a minor fall point to a vertebral compression fracture: lumbar radiograph first
  10. 72-year-old man has 1 hour of sudden severe back pain pulsatile, tender mass above the umbilicus pale and light-headed Smoker with peripheral arterial disease and hypertension BP 82/50 mm Hg · HR 124/min → Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm → back pain with a pulsatile mass and hypotension is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: straight to surgery; do not delay for CT
  11. 68-year-old man has 1 year of buttock and leg pain when walking relieved by sitting or leaning forward on a shopping cart cycles without pain No back pain at rest Afebrile · pedal pulses normal · strength normal → Spinal stenosis → leg pain on walking relieved by flexing forward, with normal pulses, is spinal stenosis
  12. 38-year-old man has 2 weeks of low back pain pain shoots below the right knee into the foot right straight-leg raise positive Began while lifting a sofa Afebrile · strength normal → Radiculopathy → pain radiating below the knee with a positive straight-leg raise is radiculopathy
  13. 34-year-old man has 4 months of low back pain better with activity, worse with rest morning stiffness over 30 minutes Wakes in the second half of the night Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Inflammatory back pain → under 40, over 3 months, better with movement: inflammatory back pain; sacroiliac joint radiographs and HLA-B27
  14. 26-year-old man has 6 months of low back pain improves with exercise, worse after sitting morning stiffness for an hour Sacroiliac joint radiographs are normal Afebrile · reduced Schober test · chest expansion reduced → MRI of the SI joints → radiographs normal with suspicion still high: MRI of the sacroiliac joints shows active sacroiliitis first; HLA-B27 is supportive only
  15. 30-year-old man with HLA-B27-positive sacroiliitis has a red, painful left eye began yesterday photophobia and blurred vision No discharge or itching Afebrile · small left pupil · redness greatest around the cornea → Anterior uveitis → the eye complication of spondyloarthritis is anterior uveitis: topical steroid and a cycloplegic
  16. 45-year-old man with a fused, bamboo-like spine for 15 years new exertional dyspnea diastolic murmur at the left sternal border No chest pain or syncope BP 150/50 mm Hg · HR 76/min → Aortic regurgitation from aortitis → aortitis widens the aortic root: aortic regurgitation
  17. 52-year-old man with HLA-B27-positive sacroiliitis for 20 years new neck pain after a minor fall pain on any neck movement Old radiographs show a fused spine Afebrile · strength and sensation normal → Spinal fracture → a rigid spine is brittle: fracture after minor trauma, so CT (computed tomography) of the spine
  18. 24-year-old man has 1 week of a swollen right knee and left ankle bloody diarrhea 2 weeks ago red eyes and burning on urination No rash or nail changes T 37.8 °C · rheumatoid factor negative → Reactive arthritis → asymmetric lower-limb arthritis weeks after dysentery, with conjunctivitis and urethritis, is reactive arthritis
  19. 68-year-old man with diabetes has back stiffness radiograph: flowing ossification along the front of 4 or more vertebrae sacroiliac joints normal No morning stiffness over 30 minutes Afebrile · HLA-B27 negative → Diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis → flowing anterior ossification with spared sacroiliac joints in an older man with diabetes is diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis, not spondyloarthritis
Common wrong answers Bed rest: harmful, delays recovery. CT of the lumbosacral spine: not indicated at 1 week, and MRI is the modality for disc and nerve root. Epidural injection: only after 4 to 6 weeks of failed conservative care. Oral prednisone: does not improve acute sciatica.
Transferable rule

When most patients do not need a test, ask whether this patient is the exception. A dense list of pertinent negatives supports doing less. When a symptom fits two categories, its behavior separates them: here, what happens when the patient gets up.

Hip Injury in an Adult

Hip fracture versus posterior dislocation: leg positions are often confused

The decision point

Shortened + externally rotated + abducted = hip fracture (femoral neck / intertrochanteric). Shortened + internally rotated + adducted + flexed = posterior hip dislocation. It is the dashboard injury, accounts for ~90% of hip dislocations, and puts the sciatic nerve at risk.

Mnemonic and the shoulder mirror Fracture = Falls outward (external). Posterior dislocation = Points inward (internal). The shoulder mirrors it: anterior dislocation (95%) = abducted + externally rotated; posterior dislocation (seizures, electrocution) = adducted + internally rotated. In both joints the common and rare forms are mirror images.
Scenario bank
  1. 78 yo F after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated → Femoral neck fracture → X-ray, then arthroplasty
  2. 28 yo M after a head-on collision, leg shortened, internally rotated, adducted and flexed → Posterior hip dislocation → reduction within 6 hours
  3. 28 yo M with foot drop after a posterior hip dislocation → Sciatic nerve injury
  4. 78 yo F with a displaced femoral neck fracture → Arthroplasty → retinacular vessel disruption risks AVN
  5. 28 yo M whose hip dislocation was reduced at 10 hours → Increased risk of femoral head osteonecrosis
  6. 70 yo M after a fall, leg shortened and externally rotated but abducted, groin pain → Intertrochanteric fracture
Time-critical Posterior dislocation needs reduction within ~6 hours to avoid femoral head AVN (avascular necrosis). In the elderly, femoral neck fracture carries AVN risk from retinacular vessel disruption; treat it with arthroplasty.

Hip and Thigh Pain and Numbness

groin vs lateral vs buttock · tendon vs nerve · which nerves have motor fibers · when to imageWhere is the pain, and is there tenderness, weakness or only numbness?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sort by location, then trust findings over descriptors:

  • Groin: the joint itself (osteoarthritis, avascular necrosis, fracture, labral tear).
  • Lateral hip: trochanter and its tendons, greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS), or the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.
  • Buttock: spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis.

Point tenderness over the trochanter with a normal neurologic exam is GTPS, however burning the pain sounds.

The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory: a numb upper lateral thigh with normal strength is meralgia paresthetica, and normal strength confirms it.

Diagnosis
Defining findings GTPS – overuse tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus at the greater trochanter (trochanteric bursitis is a misnomer); point tenderness, normal range of motion; worse lying on that side, stairs, uphill, getting out of a car; age 50 or more, women, obesity, lower-limb or low-back disorders · Meralgia paresthetica – lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, from the L2 (second lumbar) and L3 (third lumbar) roots, compressed under the inguinal ligament near the ASIS (anterior superior iliac spine); upper lateral thigh patch, no bony tenderness, no motor loss; tight belts, straining, obesity, pregnancy
Hip and thigh: the mimics
DiagnosisWhere and whatThe tell
Hip osteoarthritis (OA)Groin or medial, to thigh or knee; internal rotation reduced, groin pain on FABER (flexion, abduction, external rotation)Crepitus; morning stiffness under 30 minutes
Femoral neck stress fractureGroin or anterior; pain with hopping and log-rollRunner or recruit; female athlete triad: MRI
Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral headGroin; motion reduced in all planesSteroids, alcohol, sickle cell: MRI
Gluteal tendon tearLateral hip; abductor weakness, Trendelenburg gaitSevere end of GTPS: MRI
Osteoid osteomaProximal femur; often no focal finding in adultsNight pain dramatically relieved by an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug); children and young adults
Iliotibial (IT) band syndromeLateral knee at the femoral condyle; Noble testA knee diagnosis, not a hip one
L2 to L3 radiculopathyDermatomal with back pain; hip flexion weaknessFemoral stretch test positive
Femoral neuropathyAnterior thigh and medial leg; quadriceps weaknessReduced patellar reflex
Diabetic amyotrophyProximal weakness, wasting; asymmetricSevere pain and weight loss
Piriformis syndromeButtock, down the back of the thigh; worse sittingPiriformis tenderness, normal neurologic exam
Diabetic polyneuropathyStocking-glove, feet first; motor lateBilateral, symmetric; vibration lost first
Management and treatment
Management ladder: GTPS
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Activity modification, an NSAID and physical therapy (abductor strengthening)Refractory
2Corticosteroid injectionRefractory to injection: reassess the diagnosis ⚠︎
Any tierAbductor weakness or Trendelenburg gaitMRI for a gluteal tendon tear
By diagnosis Meralgia paresthetica – weight loss, loosen restrictive belts; conservative care resolves over 90% · Metformin neuropathy – vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency over years gives a distal symmetric neuropathy, never a focal thigh patch · Peroneal palsy – foot drop after leg-crossing or rapid weight loss, at the fibular head · Other sensory-only nerves – sural (lateral foot), superficial peroneal (foot dorsum), saphenous (medial leg), digital (Morton neuroma, third interspace between the third and fourth toes, Mulder click)
Practice
  1. 54-year-old woman has 3 months of lateral hip pain she calls burning worse lying on that side and on stairs point tenderness over the greater trochanter Hip range of motion full; neurologic exam normal Afebrile · body mass index 33 → Greater trochanteric pain syndrome → tenderness over the trochanter with a normal neurologic exam outweighs the word burning: greater trochanteric pain syndrome (GTPS); activity modification, an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and physical therapy
  2. 58-year-old woman was diagnosed with greater trochanteric pain syndrome 2 months ago still tender over the trochanter 8 weeks of an NSAID and abductor-strengthening therapy No weakness or limp Afebrile · hip range of motion full → Corticosteroid injection → refractory to an NSAID and physical therapy: corticosteroid injection; MRI is for suspected tendon tear
  3. 66-year-old woman has 6 months of lateral hip pain weak hip abduction Trendelenburg gait Tender over the greater trochanter; worse lying on that side Afebrile · no back pain · sensation and reflexes normal · hip internal rotation full → Gluteus medius tendon tear → abductor weakness with a Trendelenburg gait is the severe end of the GTPS spectrum, a gluteus medius tendon tear: MRI; weakness separates a tear from uncomplicated GTPS, which has normal strength
  4. 67-year-old man has 2 years of groin pain pain radiates to the knee, worse after walking internal rotation reduced, with crepitus Morning stiffness under 30 minutes Afebrile · body mass index 29 · no trochanteric tenderness → Hip OA → groin pain with reduced internal rotation and crepitus is the joint itself, hip osteoarthritis: radiograph
  5. 26-year-old woman training for a marathon has groin pain pain when she hops on that leg log-roll of the leg reproduces the groin pain Hip radiograph normal; irregular periods Afebrile · body mass index 18 → Femoral neck stress fracture → groin pain on hopping in a runner with a normal film is a femoral neck stress fracture: MRI; irregular periods and low weight suggest the female athlete triad
  6. 30-year-old man, a cyclist, has lateral knee pain tender over the lateral femoral condyle Noble test reproduces it Hip examination normal; rides 200 km a week Afebrile · BP 118/70 mm Hg · no knee effusion → IT band syndrome → lateral knee pain at the femoral condyle with a positive Noble test is iliotibial (IT) band syndrome, a knee diagnosis, not a hip one
  7. 40-year-old man has numbness over the upper lateral thigh a patch that burns when he wears a tight belt no tenderness over the trochanter; no back pain Strength normal; reflexes normal Afebrile · body mass index 36 → Meralgia paresthetica → a sensory-only patch on the upper lateral thigh with normal strength is meralgia paresthetica; a radiculopathy usually brings back pain, a dermatomal pattern or weakness
  8. 16-year-old boy has 3 months of thigh pain pain wakes him at night ibuprofen relieves it dramatically No trauma; no weight loss Afebrile · radiograph: small lucency with sclerosis in the proximal femur → Osteoid osteoma → night pain dramatically relieved by NSAIDs in a young patient is an osteoid osteoma; CT (computed tomography) shows the nidus
  9. 45-year-old man on prednisone for 2 years has progressive groin pain drinks heavily range of motion reduced in all planes Hip radiograph normal; no trauma Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin normal → AVN → steroids or alcohol with groin pain and a normal film is avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging)
  10. 38-year-old woman has 2 months of right buttock pain pain runs down the back of the thigh worse sitting, tender over the piriformis No back pain; straight-leg raise negative Afebrile · strength, reflexes and sensation normal → Piriformis syndrome → buttock pain sorts to the spine, sacroiliac joint or piriformis; worse sitting with piriformis tenderness and a normal neurologic exam fits piriformis syndrome
  11. 44-year-old man, obese, has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh wears a tight work belt every day no back pain Strength 5/5 throughout Afebrile · BP 136/86 mm Hg · reflexes normal · body mass index 37 → Meralgia paresthetica → the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory, so full strength confirms meralgia paresthetica: weight loss and loosening restrictive belts
  12. 44-year-old man has numbness over the anterior thigh and medial leg weak knee extension reduced patellar reflex Began after a long procedure in the lithotomy position; no back pain Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg → Femoral neuropathy → anterior thigh and medial leg numbness with quadriceps weakness and a reduced patellar reflex is a femoral neuropathy
  13. 60-year-old man with diabetes has severe right thigh pain proximal leg weakness and thigh wasting lost 7 kg in 2 months Asymmetric; the left leg is spared Afebrile · hemoglobin A1c 9.1% → Diabetic amyotrophy → severe asymmetric thigh pain, proximal weakness and weight loss in diabetes is diabetic amyotrophy; polyneuropathy is symmetric and starts in the feet
  14. 44-year-old man has 2 months of lateral thigh numbness back pain radiating to the knee reduced patellar reflex, weak hip flexion Femoral stretch test positive; no bladder symptoms Afebrile · BP 132/84 mm Hg → L2–L3 radiculopathy → back pain with weakness, a reduced reflex and a positive femoral stretch test is an L2 to L3 radiculopathy; meralgia has no motor or reflex loss
  15. 56-year-old woman has 2 months of lateral hip pain point tenderness over the greater trochanter no numbness Worse lying on that side and climbing stairs Afebrile · strength normal · knee examination normal → Trochanteric bursitis → trochanteric tenderness without numbness is trochanteric bursitis, the older, misnamed label for greater trochanteric pain syndrome; the exam may still use it
  16. 44-year-old man has burning numbness over the upper lateral thigh since he started wearing a tool belt strength and reflexes normal No back pain Afebrile · sensory loss in a patch on the upper lateral thigh → No testing; it is a clinical diagnosis → meralgia paresthetica is a clinical diagnosis; no imaging or electrodiagnostic testing is needed
Transferable rule

When the pain quality and the findings disagree, rely on the findings. A nerve's motor content sets what its lesion can look like: if it has no motor fibers, a normal motor exam confirms rather than refutes.

Osteoarthritis

Class vs. member

The decision point

A drug class can be correct while the offered member is wrong. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) is first-line for knee OA (osteoarthritis). The NSAID ketorolac has a hard 5-day maximum because of GI (gastrointestinal), renal and bleeding risk. If it is the only NSAID offered, it is ruled out for a 6-month condition in a 72-year-old, and acetaminophen is the default choice.

Guideline currency The ACR/Arthritis Foundation 2019 (ACR: American College of Rheumatology) guideline strongly recommends topical NSAIDs for knee OA (upgraded from conditional in 2012). It also strongly recommends oral NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs). In the same guideline, acetaminophen was downgraded to conditional. It is framed for patients unable to take NSAIDs, and its effect sizes in trials are small. Older NBME (National Board of Medical Examiners) items still key acetaminophen. This patient's factors also favor it: age 72, with its GI (gastrointestinal), renal and CV (cardiovascular) risk, and pain rated 3/10.
Osteoarthritis pharmacotherapy ladder
TierIntervention
AlwaysExercise (strongly recommended) · weight loss — with BMI 35, the highest-value intervention · self-management programs
First-line drug, kneeTopical NSAIDs — preferred in the elderly, minimal systemic exposure
NextOral NSAIDs — lowest effective dose, add a PPI if GI risk
ConditionalAcetaminophen (limited efficacy) · duloxetine · topical capsaicin
AdjunctIntra-articular glucocorticoid injection
Recommended againstOpioids · hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate (strongly against) · glucosamine · oral glucocorticoids (strongly against)
DefinitiveJoint replacement for refractory disease
Excluding inflammatory arthritis No fever, no morning stiffness, no synovitis, crepitus present: this pattern is mechanical, not inflammatory. It excludes hydroxychloroquine and prednisone. Oral steroids are strongly recommended against in OA (osteoarthritis); the accepted steroid route is intra-articular.
Scenario bank
  1. 68 yo F with knee osteoarthritis still limited by pain despite exercise and weight loss → Topical diclofenac → the first-line drug for knee OA
  2. Knee OA with CKD or prior GI bleed → Topical NSAID or acetaminophen, avoid systemic NSAIDs
  3. Refractory pain despite NSAIDs and PT → Intra-articular glucocorticoid
  4. Morning stiffness >1 hour with symmetric MCP/PIP synovitis → Rheumatoid arthritis → RF/anti-CCP, DMARDs
  5. Acute monoarticular knee with warmth and effusion → Arthrocentesis before any pharmacotherapy
  6. End-stage disease, failed all conservative measures → Joint replacement
Transferable rule When choosing initial pharmacotherapy, read which specific agent represents each class. A class can be right while the offered member is wrong: ketorolac for chronic OA (osteoarthritis), gentamicin for simple cystitis, chloramphenicol for otitis. Check the offered drug rather than rejecting the guideline.
Class-vs-member

Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult

septic arthritis, crystal arthritis and septic bursitis · synovial fluid thresholds · prosthetic joint and gonococcal branches · post-injection flareIs joint motion preserved, and has the fluid been sampled before any treatment?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Aspirate before you treat. Nothing on exam excludes infection, and a missed septic joint destroys cartilage in days.

Passive range of motion picks the space:

  • Preserved, swelling over the bursa: the bursa is aspirated when infection is plausible (redness, warmth, fever, or pain worsening days after an injection).
  • Pain with any passive motion, diffuse effusion: the joint is aspirated.

No antibiotics, colchicine, steroid or repeat injection before the fluid is sampled.

Diabetes and joint space narrowing raise septic risk even when the history suggests gout.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Septic bursitis – localized bursal swelling with redness and warmth, joint motion preserved; fever in only about 40% and absent in most patients 65 or older; usually Staphylococcus aureus, also Streptococcus pyogenes · Septic arthritis – hot, swollen joint, severe pain on passive motion, fever; joint fluid white cells over 50,000 (often over 100,000), neutrophils over 75% · Gout – negatively birefringent needles (monosodium urate) · Pseudogout – positively birefringent rhomboids of CPPD (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate), chondrocalcinosis on radiograph · Post-injection steroid flare – starts within hours and settles within 48 hours; infection worsens over several days; timing separates them, not severity
Risk factors Bursa – cellulitis, abrasions, penetrating trauma, bursal injection or instrumentation; diabetes and immunocompromise · Joint – diabetes; preexisting joint disease (joint space narrowing on radiograph)
Synovial fluid
FluidWhite cells/mm³Neutrophils
Noninflammatory (osteoarthritis)200 to 2,000 ⚠︎Under 25%
Inflammatory (crystal, rheumatoid arthritis)2,000 to 50,000 ⚠︎Over 50%
SepticOver 50,000, often over 100,000Over 75%
Prosthetic joint infectionAbout 3,000Over 70%
Management and treatment
Management ladder: the hot joint
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Arthrocentesis: cell count and differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals; through clean skin or image-guided, never through cellulitisAlways, for any acute hot joint
2Empiric intravenous antibiotics after cultures: vancomycin with or without ceftriaxone or cefepime; add Salmonella coverage in sickle cell diseasePurulent fluid or white cells over 50,000; do not wait for culture
3Joint drainage: serial aspiration, arthroscopic or open washoutConfirmed septic arthritis
By diagnosis Septic bursitis – systemic antibiotics; incision and drainage if not improving after about 2 days · Gout – NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or colchicine, once infection is excluded · Suspected infection – no corticosteroid injection, into a joint or a bursa · Subacromial bursa – can communicate with the glenohumeral joint, so its infection can become septic arthritis
Practice
  1. 54-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen, red right knee severe pain on passive range of motion obesity, hypertension and diabetes Radiograph: joint space narrowing T 38.5 °C · HR 102/min · no rash → Arthrocentesis → nothing on exam excludes infection, and diabetes and joint space narrowing are risk factors for it: aspirate before any treatment
  2. 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate: 68,000 white cells/mm³, 85% neutrophils No crystals seen under polarized light T 38.6 °C · Gram stain pending → Septic arthritis → over 50,000 white cells with over 75% neutrophils and no crystals is septic arthritis: vancomycin after cultures, then drainage
  3. 47-year-old woman has 2 days of a hot, swollen right knee aspirate shows negatively birefringent needle crystals and 60,000 white cells/mm³ Gram stain shows no organisms T 38.2 °C · culture pending → Treat as septic → crystals do not exclude coexisting infection: over 50,000 white cells is treated as septic until culture says otherwise
  4. 55-year-old man woke with severe pain at the base of the big toe red, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint began after a steak dinner Aspirate: 12,000 white cells/mm³ T 37.6 °C · negatively birefringent needles → Gout → an inflammatory count with negatively birefringent needles is gout: an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) or colchicine
  5. 72-year-old woman has 1 day of a hot, swollen right knee radiograph shows chondrocalcinosis aspirate: positively birefringent rhomboid crystals Gram stain shows no organisms T 37.8 °C · aspirate 18,000 white cells/mm³ → Pseudogout → positively birefringent rhomboids with chondrocalcinosis are calcium pyrophosphate crystals: pseudogout
  6. 68-year-old man has 3 weeks of right knee pain had a knee replacement 2 years ago aspirate: 3,200 white cells/mm³, 82% neutrophils No crystals seen T 37.4 °C · radiograph: no loosening seen → Prosthetic joint infection → around a prosthesis the 50,000 threshold does not apply: about 3,000 white cells with over 70% neutrophils is prosthetic joint infection
  7. 24-year-old woman has 4 days of joint pain moving from knee to wrist tenosynovitis over the wrist extensors a few pustules on the hands Sexually active, inconsistent condom use T 38.1 °C · no back pain or conjunctivitis → Disseminated gonococcal infection → migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and pustules are disseminated gonococcal infection: NAAT and cultures of cervix, urethra, pharynx and rectum
  8. 47-year-old woman has a hot, swollen left knee and fever red, warm cellulitis over the front of the knee the joint must be sampled Diabetes, on metformin T 38.4 °C · pain with passive motion · knee effusion → Arthrocentesis straight through the cellulitis → a needle through cellulitis seeds the joint: aspirate through clean skin or under image guidance
  9. 60-year-old man with sickle cell disease has a hot, swollen left knee pain with any passive motion aspirate cloudy, cultures drawn Empiric antibiotics are being chosen T 38.7 °C · aspirate 90,000 white cells/mm³ → Add Salmonella to coverage → sickle cell disease adds Salmonella to the organisms to cover
  10. 70-year-old man has 2 days of a diffusely swollen right knee severe pain with any passive motion fever and chills No swelling localized over the kneecap T 38.8 °C · large knee effusion → Septic arthritis → pain with any passive motion and a diffuse effusion is the joint, not the bursa: aspirate the joint
  11. 52-year-old man has a red, hot, tender swelling over the kneecap fever since yesterday full, painless passive knee motion Kneels on concrete at work T 38.6 °C · no knee effusion → Septic prepatellar bursitis → preserved joint motion with swelling over the bursa is extraarticular: septic prepatellar bursitis, aspirate the bursa
  12. 45-year-old man, a floor installer, has 3 days of knee swelling boggy swelling over the kneecap, red and warm knee range of motion intact Serum uric acid not yet drawn T 37.4 °C · no knee effusion → Aspirate the bursal fluid → redness and warmth make infection plausible: aspirate the bursal fluid before presuming crystals or overuse
  13. 49-year-old man was diagnosed with septic prepatellar bursitis no improvement after 3 days of antibiotics swelling and redness unchanged Culture grew Staphylococcus aureus T 38.0 °C · knee motion still full → Incision and drainage of the bursa → failure to improve after about 2 days of antibiotics is the drainage gate: incision and drainage of the bursa
  14. 58-year-old woman has worsening right shoulder pain began 4 days after a subacromial corticosteroid injection fever and myalgias Pain was mild the day after the injection T 38.4 °C · white cells 14,000/mm³ → Image-guided aspiration of the bursa → pain worsening days after an injection is iatrogenic inoculation of skin flora: image-guided aspiration of the deep bursa
  15. 60-year-old man has severe right shoulder pain began 6 hours after a corticosteroid injection already easing by the next morning No chills or redness at the injection site Afebrile · white cells normal · no swelling → Post-injection steroid flare → pain within hours that settles within 48 hours is a post-injection steroid flare; infection worsens over days
Distractors Naproxen: skips a tier; treats a diagnosis not yet made and delays drainage. Serum uric acid: wrong parameter; neither rules gout in nor infection out.
Pairs with Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: in adults every acute hot joint is aspirated at tier 1; only in children does tier 1 depend on toxicity and inflammatory signs, not on the presence of fluid.
Transferable rule

When a test is both diagnostic and therapeutic and the disease it excludes is time-destructive, the test comes before every treatment, even one right for the more likely diagnosis. Aspirate the space that is infected, because infection cannot be excluded.

Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child

Aspirate, or treat and recheck? · Count the Kocher criteria before the needle

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A septic hip is a surgical emergency: aspirate before antibiotics.

Count the Kocher criteria:

  • Fever over 38.5 °C
  • Refuses to bear weight
  • ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) over 40 mm/h
  • WBC (white blood cell count) over 12,000/mm³
  • CRP (C-reactive protein) over 2.0 mg/dL is often added as a fifth

3 or more: blood culture and ultrasound-guided aspiration. 0 or 1: transient synovitis; NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) and a recheck.

An effusion, and the flexed, abducted, externally rotated hip it causes, occurs in both septic arthritis and transient synovitis; effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis.

Septic fluid (over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant) means surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics.

Diagnosis
Kocher criteria Fever – over 38.5 °C · Weight bearing – refuses · ESR – over 40 mm/h · WBC – over 12,000/mm³ · Score – one point each, unweighted
Kocher criteria ladderProbability of septic arthritis by criteria count
Kocher criteria presentProbability of septic arthritisAction
0under 0.2%Treat as transient synovitis; recheck
1about 3%Observe with close follow-up
2about 40%Gray zone: 2 alone is below the gate; aspirate if toxic
3about 93%Arthrocentesis
4about 99.6%Arthrocentesis; surgical urgency Kocher, J Bone Joint Surg Am 1999 derivation (n=282)
Management and treatment
Management ladder: the painful hip
TierInterventionEscalate when
Kocher 0 to 1Rest and NSAIDs; activity as toleratedFever, refuses to bear weight, or no improvement in 24 to 48 hours
RecheckRepeat CBC, ESR, CRP; re-examine and rescore3 or more criteria, a toxic child with an effusion, or worse
AspirateBlood culture, then ultrasound-guided aspiration, before antibioticsFluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³ or purulent
SepticSurgical drainage plus IV antibioticsTop rung
Before you treat Organisms – S aureus overall; Kingella under 4 years; gonococcus in adolescents; Salmonella in sickle cell disease · Delay – femoral head osteonecrosis and growth arrest · Bone, not joint – fever with point tenderness over the metaphysis, motion preserved: osteomyelitis · On methotrexate – one hot joint out of step with the rest is infection until the fluid says otherwise
Practice
  1. 3-year-old boy with 1 day of right hip pain refuses to bear weight on the right leg cries with any passive movement of the hip No trauma; no recent illness T 39.1 °C · WBC 15,000/mm³ · ESR 62 mm/h → Arthrocentesis → 4 of 4 Kocher criteria (about 99%); draw a blood culture and aspirate before antibiotics
  2. 4-year-old boy limping since a cold 10 days ago today he refuses to bear weight on the left leg holds the left hip flexed and turned outward T 39.2 °C · ESR 78 mm/h · WBC pending → Arthrocentesis before antibiotics → fever, refusal to bear weight and an ESR over 40 are 3 of 4 with the WBC still pending; a recent cold does not make it benign
  3. 7-year-old boy with 2 days of left hip pain will not walk; lies with the hip flexed, abducted and externally rotated screams with gentle passive rotation No point tenderness over the femur T 39.0 °C · WBC 14,000/mm³ · ESR 90 mm/h → Septic arthritis of the hip → Kocher 4 of 4; the position only shows an effusion (it occurs in transient synovitis too); motion this painful is the joint, not the bone
  4. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of a limp after a cold 10 days ago walks, favoring the right leg; well appearing T 37.9 °C · WBC 11,500/mm³ · ESR 18 mm/h · CRP 0.8 mg/dL (normal under 1) · ultrasound: effusions in both hips → Transient synovitis → Kocher 0 of 4; an effusion occurs in both diseases, but effusions in both hips favor transient synovitis (septic arthritis is usually one-sided): NSAIDs and a recheck
  5. 6-year-old girl with 4 days of right knee soreness and a limp began after gymnastics practice right knee: full, painless motion, no swelling or tenderness right hip: internal rotation limited and painful Afebrile · bears weight → Ultrasound of both hips → a normal knee exam sends you to the hip, which refers pain to the knee; ultrasound of both hips looks for effusions
  6. 6-year-old girl with 3 days of a left-sided limp well appearing; walks and bears weight mild pain at the end of hip rotation T 37.4 °C · WBC 8,900/mm³ · ESR 12 mm/h · CRP normal · ultrasound: small effusions in both hips → Arthrocentesis of both hips → Kocher 0 of 4: the needle is for 3 or more; treat and recheck
  7. 4-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk ultrasound-guided hip aspiration: cloudy fluid 80,000 WBC/mm³, 90% neutrophils; Gram stain pending Blood culture drawn before the tap T 39.4 °C · BP 98/60 mm Hg → Surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics → fluid over 50,000 WBC/mm³, neutrophil-predominant: a septic hip is a surgical emergency, and antibiotics alone cannot decompress the joint
  8. 2-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of fever and refusal to bear weight on the left leg screams when the left hip is moved Ultrasound shows a left hip effusion; aspiration is planned T 39.4 °C · WBC 18,000/mm³ → Salmonella → sickle cell disease adds Salmonella to S aureus; Kingella also fits his age, and gonococcus is the adolescent's
  9. 3-year-old boy with 2 days of fever and refusal to walk hip aspirate: purulent, 95,000 WBC/mm³, mostly neutrophils the operating room is not free until tomorrow Started on IV antibiotics after cultures T 39.2 °C · ESR 70 mm/h → Femoral head osteonecrosis → pus under pressure inside the capsule cuts off blood to the femoral head; delay also risks growth arrest
  10. 4-year-old boy with 4 days of a limp and left thigh pain point tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis passive hip and knee motion nearly full and only mildly painful Well appearing T 38.6 °C · CRP 6 mg/dL · radiographs normal → Osteomyelitis → fever with point bone tenderness and preserved motion is bone, not joint: MRI; radiographs are normal early
  11. 5-year-old boy treated with ibuprofen for a post-viral limp 4 weeks later he still limps, worse after play hip abduction and internal rotation now limited No fever, night pain or weight loss T 37.0 °C · WBC and ESR normal → Radiographs of both hips → most transient synovitis resolves within 2 weeks; a limp past that needs hip radiographs for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
  12. 11-year-old girl with polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis on methotrexate wrists, knees and ankles improving 4 days of right shoulder pain, now waking her at night will not move the shoulder T 38.5 °C · synovial fluid 55,000 WBC/mm³, 80% neutrophils → Begin antibiotic therapy → one joint out of step with the rest, with fever and septic fluid on an immunosuppressant: infection, not a flare: antibiotics, then drain the joint; steroid into the joint or more methotrexate would feed it
  13. 4-year-old boy with 1 day of hip pain and a limp cold 10 days ago; no trauma appears well; no bony tenderness hip motion limited by pain Vital signs normal · ultrasound: small right hip effusion · CBC and ESR pending → Ibuprofen and a recheck → afebrile and walking: at most 2 of 4 even if both pending labs return high, and he looks well, so treat and recheck; read the labs when they return; the ultrasound already answered the imaging question, and his pain needs treatment
Pairs with The Limping Child: no hot hip, so match the age and the time. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: the adolescent who cannot rotate the hip inward.
Transferable rule

A limp alone is not a reason to aspirate: score Kocher first.

Before ordering another test, name the question it answers that the last one did not.

The Limping Child

Sick or well, then age and time · Is the hip hot, how old is the child, and how long has it been?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sick first: fever or refusal to bear weight means scoring Kocher and aspirating at 3 or more.

A limp with night pain that wakes the child, weight loss or bruising: CBC (complete blood count) with smear before calling anything benign.

Then match the age:

  • Infant, or a new walker: DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip)
  • 1 to 3 years: toddler's fracture
  • About 3 to 10: transient synovitis; about 4 to 10: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease
  • 10 to 15: SCFE (slipped capital femoral epiphysis)

Then time it: days point to infection, synovitis or fracture; weeks to months point to Perthes disease, SCFE, JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) or tumor.

Knee pain with a normal knee exam: examine and image the hip.

Diagnosis
Exam tells DDH – Barlow and Ortolani in infants; once walking, a painless limp, a shorter leg and limited abduction · Perthes disease – abduction and internal rotation lost · SCFE – internal rotation lost; the hip rotates outward on flexion · Osgood-Schlatter disease – knee pain with a tender tibial tubercle and a normal hip · Psoas abscess or appendicitis – hip pain on extension (psoas sign) with a normal hip joint
Management and treatment
By diagnosis DDH – Pavlik harness under 6 months; closed reduction and spica cast at 6 to 18 months; untreated, early osteoarthritis · Perthes disease – avoid high-impact activity; NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); physical therapy · SCFE – no weight bearing; urgent pinning in situ · JIA – slit-lamp exam for uveitis; highest risk when ANA (antinuclear antibody) is positive · Rheumatic fever – ASO (antistreptolysin O) titer and the Jones criteria
Practice
  1. 13-month-old girl, walking for 1 month, with a painless limp born breech asymmetric thigh skin folds left leg shorter; left hip abduction limited Her mother wore a hip harness as an infant Afebrile · no bruising or tenderness → Developmental dysplasia of the hip → breech, female, a family history, a short leg and limited abduction in a new walker: missed DDH; past 4 to 6 months, image with a radiograph
  2. 2-year-old girl with a painless limp since she began walking right leg shorter than the left right hip abduction limited Born at term; no trauma; growth normal Afebrile · knees and ankles normal → Radiograph of the pelvis → missed DDH in a walker: the femoral head has ossified, so a radiograph; ultrasound is for infants under about 4 to 6 months
  3. 2-year-old boy who will not put weight on his right leg began yesterday after a fall at daycare that no one saw tender over the distal right tibia Well appearing Afebrile · CRP normal · hip and knee motion full → Toddler's fracture → a new limp after a minor, unwitnessed fall with tibial tenderness: tibia radiographs for a spiral fracture; corner or bucket-handle fractures suggest abuse
  4. 6-year-old boy with a limp for 2 months, worse after play intermittent groin and knee pain hip abduction and internal rotation limited No fever, trauma or night pain Afebrile · CBC and ESR normal · radiograph: flattened, fragmented femoral head → Legg-Calvé-Perthes → an insidious limp over weeks with normal labs at about 4 to 10 years; early films can be normal, so MRI when they are
  5. 13-year-old boy with 3 weeks of left thigh and knee pain and a limp 95th percentile for height, 50th for weight left hip internal rotation lost; the hip rotates outward when flexed Knee examination normal Afebrile · white cell count normal → Slipped capital femoral epiphysis → lost internal rotation with obligate external rotation at the growth spurt, whatever the build: AP and frog-leg radiographs of both hips
  6. 10-year-old boy with 8 weeks of a swollen right knee and a limp stiff each morning, easing by midday no diarrhea, urethritis or rash beforehand Lives in a city; no tick bites T 37.2 °C · ESR 28 mm/h → Juvenile idiopathic arthritis → arthritis for 6 weeks or more with morning stiffness and no other cause; a slit-lamp eye exam screens for uveitis
  7. 8-year-old boy with 5 days of painful joints and a limp left knee, then right ankle, then left elbow, one after another sore throat 3 weeks ago, untreated New soft apical murmur T 38.4 °C · ESR 60 mm/h → Acute rheumatic fever → migratory large-joint arthritis 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis: check an ASO titer and apply the Jones criteria; the murmur is carditis
  8. 5-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a limp leg pain that wakes him at night tired; bruises easily pale; lost weight this month T 37.8 °C · hip and knee motion full → CBC with smear → a limp with night pain, bruising, fatigue or weight loss: CBC with smear for leukemia before calling anything benign
  9. 14-year-old boy with 3 months of anterior knee pain worse with running and jumping in basketball tender, prominent tibial tubercle hip motion full and painless Afebrile · no night pain or weight loss → Osgood-Schlatter disease → the hip is cleared and the tibial tubercle is tender in an active adolescent: activity modification and NSAIDs
How NBME framed it: question 1

Healthy 16-month-old girl with a painless right-sided limp since she began walking 4 months ago term; cesarean delivery for breech presentation no family history of musculoskeletal disorders left leg shorter than the right left hip abduction limited to 30 degrees; right hip normal Sensation, circulation and strength normal

Most likely underlying mechanism?

Competing answers
  • Acute epiphyseal fracture: a toddler's limp; but it needs trauma, with pain, bruising and guarding; this limp is painless and 4 months old.
  • Acute suppurative arthritis: limited hip motion; but it brings fever and pain; she is healthy and painless.
  • Avulsion of muscle origin: a limp; but it follows an injury and hurts, often with a defect or mass.
  • Displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis: limited hip motion and a limp; but that is the adolescent slip, which limits internal rotation.
  • Failure of osteoid to mineralize: a toddler's leg problem; but rickets bows both legs; it does not shorten one or limit one hip.

Down to two: poorly developed acetabulum or displacement of the capital femoral epiphysis. Poorly developed acetabulum: a breech girl with a painless limp from her first steps, a short leg and limited abduction has DDH missed in infancy. Every option was a disease written as its mechanism. (The stem puts the limp on the right and the signs on the left; carried as written.)

Pairs with Septic Arthritis in a Child: the hot hip. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: the adolescent. Leg Pain in a Child: the gait is normal. Suspected Child Abuse: corner and femur fractures in a child who cannot walk; could he have generated the force? Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: a breech baby also needs a hip exam.
Transferable rule

Ask sick or well, then how old, then how long; a limp with night pain is a blood count first.

Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis

Count the joints, chart the fever · Six weeks of arthritis, then joints and fever set the subtype

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Arthritis for 6 weeks or more, before age 16, with no other cause is JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis). The diagnosis is clinical.

Set the subtype by the first 6 months:

  • Systemic: any joints, plus daily fever spikes for 2 weeks or more, with an evanescent salmon rash, nodes, big liver or spleen, or serositis
  • Polyarticular: 5 or more joints, symmetric; no fever or rash
  • Oligoarticular: 4 or fewer, usually a knee or ankle

Treat with an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) first, such as naproxen; weekly methotrexate when arthritis persists. Systemic: NSAID and steroids, then a biologic.

Slit lamp every 3 months if oligoarticular or RF (rheumatoid factor) negative polyarticular, ANA (antinuclear antibody) positive, onset before 7 and within 4 years of onset; otherwise every 6 to 12 months.

Low counts in two or more cell lines in a child labelled systemic JIA: bone marrow before any steroid.

Diagnosis
JIA subtypes All – true swelling, morning stiffness that eases, 6 weeks, no other cause · Systemic – fever 2 weeks or more plus rash, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or serositis; boys and girls equally · Polyarticular – 5 or more joints; peaks at 2 to 5 and 10 to 14; girls more · Oligoarticular – 4 or fewer joints; ages 2 to 4; girls more
Mimics: what the stem shows instead
MimicThe tellTreat
Gonococcal arthritissexually active; one joint or a few, asymmetric; tenosynovitis; vesiculopustulesCeftriaxone
Lyme arthritisone large joint, usually the knee, after erythema migrans in an endemic areaDoxycycline
Hypothyroidismaches and fatigue, no true swelling; height velocity fallsLevothyroxine
Vitamin D deficiencydiffuse bone pain, same all day; no swellingVitamin D and calcium
Leukemiacytopenias, bone painBone marrow first
Dengue, malariaacute fever after travel; dengue lowers the counts and bruises; malaria has no rashInfection workup, not JIA therapy
Management and treatment
Management ladder: JIA
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineNSAID such as naproxen; steroid injection into a few jointsArthritis persists on the NSAID
PersistentWeekly methotrexateMethotrexate fails
RheumatologyA biologicTop rung
By situation Systemic – NSAIDs and steroids, then a biologic · MAS – ferritin in the thousands, high triglycerides, falling ESR and fibrinogen, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation): high-dose steroids, after a marrow if two lines are low · Uveitis – oligoarticular highest, polyarticular too, systemic lowest; enthesitis-related (older boys, HLA-B27 (human leukocyte antigen type B-27)) gives a red, painful eye · One hot joint – in a child on methotrexate it is septic until the fluid says otherwise
Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl with 6 weeks of swollen knees and wrists 3 weeks of fever to 39.5 °C each evening, normal by morning salmon-pink rash with each spike that fades hepatosplenomegaly WBC 21,000/mm³ · platelets 610,000/mm³ · ANA low-titer positive · RF negative → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → quotidian fever with an evanescent rash and 6 weeks of arthritis, with high counts: systemic JIA; a low-titer ANA does not exclude it, lupus lowers counts, and rheumatic fever's fever is persistent with a rash whose margin expands
  2. 5-year-old girl with 2 weeks of daily fever and 3 weeks of a swollen right knee parents' log: spikes to 39.8 °C each evening rash with each spike Seen in the afternoon, well appearing T 37.0 °C · ESR 64 mm/h → Continue the evaluation for systemic JIA → quotidian fever returns to normal between spikes, so a normal clinic temperature excludes nothing; no focus and well between spikes is not a bacterial infection
