  3. 6-year-old boy diagnosed with systemic JIA a year ago, now persistently febrile oozing at venipuncture sites hepatosplenomegaly WBC 6,000/mm³ · platelets 92,000/mm³ · ferritin 18,000 ng/mL · fibrinogen 110 mg/dL · ESR 6 mm/h (70 last month) · AST 220 U/L · triglycerides 380 mg/dL → Macrophage activation syndrome → in systemic JIA, persistent fever with ESR and fibrinogen falling as ferritin, triglycerides and AST climb, and oozing from consumed clotting factors: macrophage activation syndrome; with only platelets low, high-dose steroids
  4. 4-year-old girl diagnosed 1 month ago with arthritis of the left knee and right ankle ANA positive no eye pain, redness or blurred vision Knee swelling improving on naproxen Afebrile · visual acuity 20/30 both eyes → Slit-lamp exam for asymptomatic uveitis → young, ANA positive and few joints carries the highest uveitis risk, and it is silent: slit-lamp exams every 3 months
  5. 4-year-old boy with 6 weeks of evening fever spikes since a trip to Costa Rica pink rash with each spike, gone by morning right knee swollen 6 weeks; spleen tip palpable Well between spikes hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL · platelets 640,000/mm³ → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis → weeks of quotidian fever with an evanescent rash, mild anemia and high platelets: systemic JIA; dengue and malaria are acute and usually lower platelets, and malaria has no rash
  6. 7-year-old boy with 4 weeks of daily evening fevers to 39.6 °C normal temperature each morning salmon rash during fevers; both knees and the left wrist swollen for 7 weeks pericardial rub Afebrile in clinic → High WBC and platelets, high ferritin; ANA and RF negative → systemic JIA is inflammation without autoantibodies: high WBC, platelets, ESR and ferritin; ANA and RF usually negative
  7. 3-year-old girl with 8 weeks of a swollen, warm left knee limps after waking, better by afternoon right ankle also swollen No fever or rash; lives in a nonendemic area; no tick bites Afebrile · ANA positive → Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis → 4 or fewer joints for 8 weeks with morning stiffness: oligoarticular JIA; nonendemic with no tick bite argues against Lyme; ANA positive and young: slit-lamp exams
  8. 13-year-old girl with 2 months of aching legs, hips and back pain the same all day; no morning stiffness no joint swelling; tibias tender to pressure Strict vegan diet without fortified foods Afebrile · height and weight steady → Vitamin D deficiency → diffuse bone pain that never eases and no swollen joints, on an unfortified vegan diet: vitamin D and calcium
  9. 14-year-old girl, ankles aching 3 months since starting daily walks this month knees, elbows, wrists; all swollen bilaterally stiff mornings that ease Tired despite 9 hours' sleep; new plant-based diet Afebrile · weight 95th to 90th percentile · height steady · chest normal → Naproxen → 5 or more joints within months, symmetric, stiff in the morning and easing: polyarticular JIA; naproxen first, methotrexate if it persists; deficiency pain never eases or swells joints, and falling weight with steady height is not hypothyroidism
  10. 4-year-old girl labeled systemic JIA 6 weeks ago, joints improving on naproxen now pale, with petechiae on her trunk and legs lymph nodes enlarged in the neck and groin T 39.4 °C · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · WBC 2,100/mm³ · platelets 38,000/mm³ → Bone marrow aspiration → low counts in two or more cell lines in a child labeled systemic JIA: bone marrow first; leukemia mimics JIA, and a steroid can mask it and change the marrow
  11. 9-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a swollen right knee stiff after waking, better by noon no preceding diarrhea, urethritis or rash; nonendemic area No injury; walks with a slight limp Afebrile · WBC normal · ESR 32 mm/h → Naproxen and reassess at 6 weeks → JIA needs 6 weeks of arthritis with no other cause: treat the pain and reassess before labeling it or starting methotrexate
Pairs with Acute Leukemia in a Child: the marrow comes before the steroid. Septic Arthritis in a Child: one hot joint on methotrexate. The Limping Child: sick or well, then age and time.
Transferable rule

Before naming JIA, time the arthritis, chart the fever and look at every cell line.

Arm Injury in a Young Child

A pull with a normal elbow is reduced; anything else is imaged

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A pull on the arm at 1 to 4 years, an arm held extended and pronated, and no swelling, deformity or bony point tenderness: radial head subluxation (nursemaid's elbow). Reduce without imaging.

Reduce:

  • Hyperpronation (more first-attempt success), or supination with flexion
  • Uses the arm within minutes (most by 10, 90% by 30): done; no radiograph or sling; counsel against pulling the arm

Image first with swelling, deformity or point tenderness, a fall rather than a pull, or age over 5; image if the arm stays unused after reduction.

An exam line describing the maneuver and a child reaching for toys afterward is the treatment already done: nothing further.

A mechanism that does not fit, no mechanism at all, or a fracture before walking: suspect abuse; skeletal survey under 2 years, and report.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Nursemaid's elbow – axial traction on an extended, pronated arm slips the annular ligament over the radial head · Exam – arm extended and pronated; no swelling, bruising, deformity or bony point tenderness · Supracondylar fracture – fall on an outstretched hand (extension type); swelling; posterior fat pad sign
Management and treatment
Management ladder: the unused arm
TierInterventionEscalate when
ReduceHyperpronation or supination with flexionArm still unused after reduction attempts
ImageElbow radiographsFracture, or a normal film with the arm still unused
ReferImmobilize; orthopedicsTop rung
By situation Recurrence – about 1 in 5; counsel against pulling the arm · Displaced supracondylar – closed reduction and pinning; a pale, pulseless hand is urgent
Practice
  1. 3-year-old girl who will not use her left arm pulled up by the wrist as she stumbled holds the arm extended and pronated at her side No swelling, bruising or deformity; no bony point tenderness Afebrile → Radial head subluxation → a pull on an extended, pronated arm at 1 to 4 years, with no swelling, deformity or point tenderness: a clinical diagnosis; reduce without imaging
  2. 3-year-old girl not using her right arm after being swung by her hands no swelling, deformity or point tenderness her elbow was supinated and flexed 15 minutes later she reaches for toys with that arm Afebrile → No further intervention → the maneuver was the treatment, and using the arm confirms the reduction: no radiograph or sling; counsel against pulling the arm
  3. 6-year-old boy who fell off monkey bars onto his outstretched hand elbow swollen and tender above the joint will not bend or straighten it Fingers warm; radial pulse present Afebrile · lateral radiograph: posterior fat pad sign → Supracondylar fracture → a fall on an outstretched hand with elbow swelling and a posterior fat pad: supracondylar fracture; check the anterior interosseous nerve and the brachial artery
  4. 6-year-old boy with a displaced supracondylar fracture of the right humerus right hand cool and pale no palpable radial pulse Makes an OK sign; forearm compartments soft T 37.0 °C · capillary refill 5 seconds → Brachial artery injury → a pale, cool, pulseless hand after a supracondylar fracture is brachial artery injury: urgent orthopedic reduction and vascular assessment; the intact OK sign spares the anterior interosseous nerve
  5. 3-year-old girl with her second pulled elbow this year, reduced today both times her brother lifted her by one hand using the arm normally within minutes Growth and development normal; no bruises or other injuries Afebrile → Counsel the family to avoid pulling the arm → recurrence is common (about 1 in 5) until the ligament strengthens after age 5; a fitting mechanism in a well child needs counseling, not an abuse workup
  6. 10-month-old boy who will not move his left arm mother says he rolled off the sofa yesterday not yet crawling; no prior fractures Bruise on the left upper arm; white sclerae Afebrile · radiograph: spiral fracture of the humeral shaft → Non-accidental trauma → a spiral fracture in a child who cannot generate the twist, a delay in care and a history that does not fit: suspected abuse; skeletal survey (under 2 years) and report; white sclerae make osteogenesis imperfecta less likely
  7. 2-year-old girl not using her arm after her mother pulled her from a puddle arm held extended and pronated; no swelling two reduction attempts, no click Still not reaching 30 minutes later Afebrile · no bony point tenderness → Radiographs of the elbow → most children use the arm within 10 minutes and 90% by 30; still not using it after reduction attempts: radiographs for an occult fracture, and if normal, immobilize and refer to orthopedics
Pairs with Suspected Child Abuse: corner, rib and multiple healing fractures. Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth: the newborn who does not move an arm.
Transferable rule

Read the exam section for the treatment already given, and image only when the mechanism or the elbow says fracture.

Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis

Keep off it and pin it · Lost internal rotation at the growth spurt, whatever the build

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Stop weight bearing now (crutches or a wheelchair) and refer for urgent in situ screw fixation. Never force a reduction.

Suspect it at 10 to 15 years with hip, thigh or knee pain and a limp:

  • Internal rotation lost
  • The hip rotates outward on passive flexion
  • Knee pain with a normal knee exam

Obesity raises the risk but is not required: tall, thin adolescents slip during the growth spurt too.

Image both hips: AP (anteroposterior) and frog-leg lateral, or cross-table lateral if it may be unstable.

Atypical (under 8 or over 15, underweight, or short): look for an endocrine cause (hypothyroidism, GH (growth hormone) deficiency, panhypopituitarism, hypogonadism) or renal osteodystrophy.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Age – 10 to 15, the growth spurt; girls slip earlier than boys · Exam – lost internal rotation; obligate external rotation on passive flexion · Film – Klein line along the top of the femoral neck misses the epiphysis, or a widened, irregular physis · Slip – the epiphysis moves posteriorly and inferiorly through the hypertrophic zone
Two decoys Recent cold – the age and a weeks-long course rule out transient synovitis · Minor fall – it prompts the visit or tips a chronic slip into an unstable one; the slip came first. A femoral neck fracture needs high-energy trauma
Management and treatment
Management ladder: a slipped epiphysis
TierInterventionEscalate when
TodayNon-weight-bearing: crutches or a wheelchair; urgent orthopedic referralSlip confirmed on films
SurgeryIn situ fixation across the physis; never force a reductionNew groin pain or a narrowing joint space after fixation
ComplicationImage for osteonecrosis or chondrolysisTop rung
Around the fixation Other hip – bilateral in 20 to 40%; image it even when painless · Prophylactic pinning – considered for high risk: obesity, male sex, a first slip under age 10, an endocrine disorder · Does not stop the slip – bracing, casting, traction or physical therapy · Late – avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head, chondrolysis, early osteoarthritis
Practice
  1. 14-year-old boy with 4 weeks of intermittent left groin pain tripped on a stair this morning; now cannot bear weight at all, even with crutches left leg lies externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: left femoral epiphysis displaced posteriorly → Unstable slipped capital femoral epiphysis → unable to bear weight even with crutches defines an unstable slip: osteonecrosis risk up to about half; keep him off it and pin urgently, without reduction
  2. 9-year-old girl was diagnosed today with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis below the 5th percentile for height and the 10th for weight growth slowed over the past 2 years Fatigue and constipation HR 62/min · BP 100/64 mm Hg → Screen for hypothyroidism, GH deficiency, panhypopituitarism, renal osteodystrophy → short and underweight is atypical at any age: look for an endocrine or renal cause alongside fixation
  3. 12-year-old boy was diagnosed with a left slipped capital femoral epiphysis today pinning is scheduled right hip: no pain, full internal rotation Body mass index above the 95th percentile Afebrile · radiographs were taken of the left hip only → Radiographs of the right hip now → both hips are imaged at diagnosis: 20 to 40% of slips are bilateral, often silent at first
  4. 13-year-old boy with 3 weeks of aching right knee pain and a limp knee: no effusion, no tenderness, full painless motion ligament tests normal Plays football; no specific injury Afebrile · knee radiographs normal → Examine the hip → a normal knee exam sends you to the hip: a slip refers pain to the knee through the obturator nerve
  5. 14-year-old girl 5 months after screw fixation of a slipped left capital femoral epiphysis new left groin pain and stiffness hip motion now limited in all directions Afebrile · radiograph: narrowed joint space; screw position unchanged → Chondrolysis or AVN → joint space narrowing after fixation is cartilage loss (chondrolysis) or collapse of the head (osteonecrosis); an unchanged screw argues against hardware failure
  6. 16-year-old girl, a cross-country runner, with 3 weeks of right groin pain worse with each run; now hurts to hop on the right leg recently doubled her weekly mileage Afebrile · radiographs of both hips normal → Femoral neck stress fracture → groin pain on hopping with normal films after a training increase: MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) for a femoral neck stress fracture
  7. 12-year-old girl with 3 weeks of right thigh pain since a minor fall today she cannot bear weight on the right leg right leg held externally rotated Afebrile · radiograph: right femoral epiphysis displaced off the neck → Forceful closed reduction of the slip → forcing the epiphysis back raises the risk of osteonecrosis: keep her off the leg and pin it where it lies
How NBME framed it: question 1

Previously healthy 13-year-old boy with 4 weeks of intermittent left groin pain and a limp no fever; not in acute distress height 50th percentile, weight 97th, body mass index above the 97th left hip: internal rotation and abduction limited; rotation to 75 degrees hurts; externally rotates on passive flexion Right hip and both knees normal T 37 °C · pulse 90/min · RR 20/min · BP 116/75 mm Hg AP and cross-table lateral films: irregular widening of the left femoral physis; mild osteopenia of the left femoral head and neck

Analgesia and weight-loss counseling given; next step?

Competing answers
  • Physical therapy: weeks of pain and stiffness; but it treats a strain after an injury, and there was none.
  • Abduction bracing: limited abduction; but it treats DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip) in infants.
  • Traction: a painful hip and a limp; but it pulls a fractured bone to length; there was no trauma.
  • Spica cast immobilization: holding the hip still; but it holds an infant hip reduced for DDH.

Down to two: internal fixation or spica cast immobilization. Internal fixation: groin pain, lost internal rotation and a widened, irregular physis are a slip even before the epiphysis visibly moves; every other option treats another hip problem.

Pairs with The Limping Child: age and time for every limp. The Post-Traumatic Limb Mass: the adolescent thigh mass that dates to an injury.
Transferable rule

A stereotype is a prior, not a rule: when the exam fits and the patient does not, trust the exam and ask why.

Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans

Did the pain resolve and come back? · Heterotopic bone weeks after a contusion; does passive stretch reproduce the pain?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A contusion whose pain clears, then returns weeks later with a firm, mobile intramuscular mass, is myositis ossificans: bone forming inside the muscle (quadriceps and brachialis most often).

The exam decides it:

  • Pain on passive stretch of the muscle (knee flexion for the quadriceps)
  • Strength and sensation intact
  • No fever, erythema or limb-wide swelling

Early films are often normal; calcification appears at about 4 to 8 weeks. Never biopsy an early lesion: it can mimic osteosarcoma.

Treat with range of motion and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) such as indomethacin; excise only a mature lesion that stays symptomatic.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Lesion – lamellar bone in muscle (heterotopic ossification) · Trigger – muscle injury, fracture or surgery such as arthroplasty; or neurologic: stroke, brain or spinal cord injury · Labs – alkaline phosphatase, ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and CRP (C-reactive protein) may rise, so they do not exclude infection
Mimics the stem rules out Quadriceps tendon tear – knee extension lost, gap above the patella · Venous thrombosis – whole thigh and calf swollen; 2 cm more thigh girth alone is not enough · Osteoid osteoma – night pain relieved by NSAIDs, no mass
Management and treatment
Management ladder: myositis ossificans
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineRange of motion and an NSAID; no forceful stretching or deep massageStill painful and limited with a mature lesion after at least 6 to 12 months
SurgeryExcise the mature lesion completely; early excision recursTop rung
Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy, football thigh contusion 4 weeks ago pain gone by 2 weeks, back last week indurated, mobile 3-cm anterior mass; no erythema passive knee flexion hurts; strength, sensation normal Vital signs normal · thigh girth +2 cm · pulses, calves normal → Myositis ossificans → injury, recovery, then pain with a mobile intramuscular mass weeks later, hurt by stretching the muscle: heterotopic bone; no fever or erythema rules out infection, and a tumor progresses with night pain and never clears first
  2. 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with myositis ossificans of the quadriceps today kicked in the thigh 4 weeks ago firm mass; knee flexion limited to 90 degrees Pain limits running Afebrile · radiograph: peripheral calcification → Range-of-motion exercise with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug → range of motion and an NSAID such as indomethacin; excision only for a mature lesion that stays symptomatic
  3. 15-year-old girl with a firm thigh mass 3 weeks after a soccer collision mass unchanged in size over 1 week pain on passive knee flexion No night pain, weight loss or fever Vital signs normal · radiograph of the thigh normal → Repeat imaging in 2 to 4 weeks → early films are often normal; repeat in 2 to 4 weeks to see peripheral calcification, since a biopsy of an immature lesion can mimic osteosarcoma
  4. 16-year-old boy with 1 day of severe thigh pain after a minor scrape spreading erythema and swelling pain out of proportion to the examination Confused and ill appearing T 39.0 °C · HR 128/min · BP 92/54 mm Hg → Emergency surgical exploration with broad-spectrum antibiotics → fever, spreading erythema and pain out of proportion within a day: necrotizing infection; operate now with broad antibiotics
  5. 45-year-old man who stumbled on stairs, landing on a flexed knee cannot extend the knee against gravity palpable gap just above the patella No induration or mass Sensation normal · knee radiograph: low-lying patella → Orthopedic referral for surgical repair → lost knee extension with a gap above the patella is a complete quadriceps tendon tear: surgical repair; a heterotopic mass leaves strength intact
  6. 24-year-old man 8 weeks after a traumatic brain injury stiff, painful right hip hard mass near the joint No fall or new injury since admission Afebrile · white cell count normal · alkaline phosphatase elevated → Neurogenic heterotopic ossification → the same heterotopic bone with a neurologic trigger (brain or spinal cord injury, stroke) and no trauma to the joint
  7. 18-year-old man with quadriceps myositis ossificans diagnosed 12 months ago still painful; knee flexion limited despite range-of-motion therapy and NSAIDs Mass unchanged for 6 months Afebrile · radiograph: mature, well-defined bone → Surgical excision → a mature lesion that stays symptomatic is excised; excising it before it matures invites recurrence
  8. 15-year-old boy was diagnosed with quadriceps myositis ossificans this week thigh contusion 3 weeks ago firm, tender anterior mass Asks how to speed recovery before the season Afebrile · knee flexion to 100 degrees → Aggressive passive stretching and deep massage of the lesion → aggressive passive stretching and deep massage of the lesion worsen the ossification; keep gentle active motion and an NSAID
Pairs with Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis and The Limping Child: other adolescent hip and thigh complaints, sorted by age and tempo. Bone Lesions in a Child: osteosarcoma and osteoid osteoma in depth.
Transferable rule

When a mass follows an injury, ask whether the pain cleared and came back, and what provokes it: stretch points to muscle, night pain to bone.

Leg Pain in a Child

A normal exam is growing pains; tender calves after influenza are myositis

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Bilateral leg pain in a child: examine before you test.

  • Normal exam, episodic evening or night pain with pain-free days, age 3 to 12: growing pains. Reassure; no labs or films.
  • Tender calves days after an influenza-like illness: benign acute childhood myositis (influenza-induced myositis). CK (creatine kinase) is high and reflexes are preserved.
  • Ascending weakness with absent reflexes: Guillain-Barré syndrome.
  • Bone tenderness with pallor, bruising, fever or weight loss: CBC (complete blood count) with smear for leukemia.
  • One side, a focal tender spot or a mass: radiograph, even when night pain responds to NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).

Night pain alone is not the flag; laterality, a limp, tenderness and systemic signs are.

Myositis can cause weakness (the NBME explanation: mild weakness to quadriparesis), so strength does not separate it from Guillain-Barré syndrome; preserved reflexes do, with calf tenderness and a high CK in support.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Growing pains – age 3 to 12; both legs (thighs, shins, calves), evenings or nights, worse after active days; pain-free days; pain in muscles, not joints; normal exam and gait; no systemic signs or activity limits · Myositis – influenza A or B, during or just after the illness; tender calves; tiptoe gait or refusal to walk; more often boys · Confirm – CK elevated; a positive influenza test names the cause
How NBME framed it: question 1

12-year-old boy with 2 days of severe pain in both calves a week ago: dry cough, sore throat, headache and fever all resolved on ibuprofen after 5 days; no medications now Marked tenderness of both calves T 37 °C

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Dermatomyositis: a myositis; but it brings proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules; the stem describes no rash and no weakness.
  • Mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome (Kawasaki disease): the fever may have just reached its 5-day threshold; but it has resolved, with no conjunctivitis, rash, node, hand, foot or lip change. NBME used the formal name.
  • Parvovirus B19-induced arthritis: a post-viral ache; but it is symmetric arthritis of the small joints of the hands, wrists and feet; this tenderness is in muscle.
  • Rheumatic fever: a sore throat came first; but it follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis and is diagnosed by the Jones criteria (carditis, arthritis, nodules, erythema marginatum, chorea); calf tenderness is none of them.

Down to two: influenza-induced myositis or dermatomyositis. Influenza-induced myositis: tender calves a few days after a flu-like illness, with no rash or proximal weakness. The stem never names influenza, and the key names the cause rather than the syndrome.

Management and treatment
By situation Growing pains – explain the benign course; massage, heat, analgesics or stretching; no activity restriction or braces; recurrence is expected · Myositis – analgesia, fluids and rest; never aspirin with influenza (Reye syndrome) · Dark urine – heme on the dipstick, few red cells, high CK: rhabdomyolysis; admit for IV fluids; check creatinine and potassium
Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy, 3 months of pain in both thighs and shins only at night; worse after running days pain-free days; not worsening massage and ibuprofen help Walks, runs and plays normally Afebrile · no weight loss · hip and knee exam normal → Observation and reassurance → both legs, episodic night pain with pain-free days, a normal exam and no systemic signs: growing pains, a clinical diagnosis with no film or blood count
  2. 8-year-old boy with 2 months of right thigh pain at night wakes him; ibuprofen relieves it dramatically the left leg never hurts No mass or limp Afebrile · exam otherwise normal → Order plain radiographs → night pain on one side needs a film even when ibuprofen relieves it: osteoid osteoma also hurts at night and answers to NSAIDs
  3. 7-year-old girl with 3 weeks of leg pain that wakes her at night intermittent fevers pale, with scattered bruises Tender to palpation over both tibias T 38.1 °C · hip and knee motion full → Order a complete blood count with peripheral smear → bone tenderness with pallor, bruising and fever is not growing pains, which needs a normal exam: CBC with smear for leukemia
  4. 7-year-old boy was diagnosed with growing pains 2 weeks ago night leg pain after soccer days exam and gait normal Parents ask about stopping soccer or buying knee braces Afebrile · no weight loss → Continue normal activity without restriction → growing pains do not limit activity, and restriction and bracing are not recommended; reassure, and offer massage, heat, analgesics or stretching
  5. 9-year-old girl was diagnosed with growing pains 1 year ago still has night pain in both shins a few nights a month, with pain-free weeks Growing normally; plays sports Afebrile · joints and gait normal → Continued reassurance and supportive care → growing pains wax and wane for months to years and resolve by adolescence; recurrence with a normal exam is expected, not a reason to escalate
  6. 10-year-old boy with night leg pain his parents read that night pain means a tumor both shins hurt, worse after sports pain-free days; ibuprofen helps Exam and gait normal Afebrile · no weight loss → Osteoid osteoma is also nocturnal and also relieved by NSAIDs, so laterality is the discriminator → night pain and relief from NSAIDs are shared by growing pains and osteoid osteoma, so check the side, not the hour
  7. 7-year-old boy was diagnosed with influenza B 3 days ago now afebrile; woke refusing to walk walks on his toes both calves tender Strength normal when encouraged Knee and ankle reflexes normal · T 37.0 °C → Serum creatine kinase → tender calves with reflexes intact days into influenza: benign acute childhood myositis; an elevated CK places the problem in muscle
  8. 6-year-old boy on day 4 of influenza B, now afebrile pain in both calves; walks on tiptoe calves tender; strength and reflexes normal CK (creatine kinase) elevated T 37.2 °C · urinalysis normal → Analgesics, fluids and reassurance → myositis with a normal urinalysis: analgesia, fluids and rest at home; recovery within about a week
  9. 8-year-old girl with influenza A and 2 days of severe leg pain both calves tender tea-colored urine Urine dipstick strongly positive for blood T 37.4 °C · 0 to 2 red cells per high-power field · CK markedly elevated → Admission for intravenous fluids and renal monitoring → a heme-positive dipstick with almost no red cells and a markedly high CK is myoglobin: rhabdomyolysis; admit for intravenous fluids and follow creatinine and potassium
  10. 9-year-old boy with influenza, now afebrile pain in both calves for 2 days calves tender; strength and reflexes normal Parents ask what to give for the pain CK elevated · urinalysis normal → Aspirin → aspirin in a child with influenza risks Reye syndrome; give ibuprofen or acetaminophen
  11. 6-year-old boy with 2 days of leg pain upper respiratory infection 10 days ago trouble climbing stairs, now spreading upward symmetric leg weakness; no calf tenderness No sensory level; bladder normal Knee and ankle reflexes absent · T 37.0 °C → Guillain-Barré syndrome → ascending symmetric weakness with lost reflexes after an infection is Guillain-Barré syndrome: lumbar puncture and watch breathing; myositis keeps reflexes and hurts to touch
  12. 8-year-old girl with 2 months of trouble climbing stairs struggles to rise from the floor violaceous rash on both upper eyelids Scaly red papules over the knuckles CK elevated · T 37.0 °C → Juvenile dermatomyositis → weeks of proximal weakness with a heliotrope rash and Gottron papules is juvenile dermatomyositis: systemic glucocorticoids plus methotrexate
  13. 7-year-old girl with 4 months of aching in both calves evenings only, worse after active days pain-free days; no recent illness No calf tenderness; joints and gait normal Afebrile · no weight loss → Growing pains → episodic evening leg pain with pain-free days and a normal exam is growing pains; myositis follows influenza with tender calves, and arthritis swells joints
Pairs with The Limping Child: the gait is abnormal. Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis: one-sided hip, thigh or knee pain in an adolescent. Acute Leukemia in a Child: the systemic picture. Dark Urine: Hemoglobin, Myoglobin or Blood: heme on the dipstick, no red cells.
Transferable rule

A frightening symptom shared by benign and serious causes is not the flag; find the feature that separates them. In leg pain, it is the exam and the side, not the hour.

Bone Lesions in a Child

Name the lesion from its site, age and film, then predict its course

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Read the plain film by site and periosteum; then recall what that lesion does next.

  • Painless hard bump near a joint, spur continuous with the cortex and medulla: osteochondroma. It grows until the physes close, then stops. Observe; no biopsy. About 1% of solitary lesions turn malignant.
  • Night pain relieved by NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), small lucent nidus: osteoid osteoma. It involutes over years.
  • Central metaphyseal lucency, no periosteal reaction: unicameral bone cyst. Observe with serial films; the risk is fracture.
  • Sunburst periosteum, often with a Codman triangle, in a metaphysis: osteosarcoma. Onion skin in the shaft, pelvis or spine, sometimes with fever: Ewing sarcoma.

Night pain that wakes the child, with fever or weight loss, points to malignancy, not a benign lesion.

An aggressive film gets MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) before biopsy; chest CT (computed tomography) stages the lungs. Fever does not exclude a tumor: Ewing sarcoma can raise the ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), CRP (C-reactive protein) and WBC (white blood cell count).

Diagnosis
Where it sits, and the clue
LesionSiteAge and clue
ChondroblastomaEpiphysisTeens, physes open; well-defined lucency, thin sclerotic rim
Giant cell tumorEpiphysisOver 20, mature; soap bubble
OsteochondromaMetaphysisTeens; most common benign; painless spur; multiple if hereditary
Unicameral bone cystMetaphysis (humerus, femur)Physes open; painless, incidental; central lucency, no periosteal reaction
OsteosarcomaMetaphysisTeens; sunburst; high ALP (alkaline phosphatase); rarely febrile
Osteoid osteomaLong bone (often proximal femur) or spineTeens; night pain gone with NSAIDs; nidus
Ewing sarcomaShaft, pelvis, axialPeak 10 to 15; may be febrile; onion skin
ChondrosarcomaPelvis, proximal femur or humerusAdults over 40 to 50
Ewing sarcoma or osteomyelitis Ewing – weeks; shaft, pelvis or spine; small round blue cells · Osteomyelitis – days; long-bone metaphysis; trauma or immunodeficiency support it when present; inflammatory cells and necrotic bone
Management and treatment
By lesion Observe – osteochondroma; unicameral bone cyst with serial films; osteoid osteoma with NSAIDs · Curettage – chondroblastoma and giant cell tumor, both locally aggressive; giant cell tumor has high local recurrence · Malignant – osteosarcoma: chemotherapy plus resection; Ewing sarcoma: chemotherapy plus resection, radiation or both
Practice
  1. 13-year-old girl, painless hard bump above the left knee 3 weeks; unchanged no trauma, fever or weight loss Firm, nontender distal femoral mass Vital signs normal · film: metaphyseal spur pointing away from the joint, continuous with cortex and medulla → Grows until the growth plates close, then stops → a spur continuous with the cortex and medulla is an osteochondroma, the most common benign bone tumor: it grows with the skeleton until physeal closure, then stops; transformation is about 1% and involution belongs to osteoid osteoma
  2. 15-year-old boy with 2 months of right thigh pain worst at night; unrelated to activity ibuprofen relieves it completely No weight loss or limp Afebrile · film: small round lucency with a sclerotic rim, proximal femur → Osteoid osteoma → night pain relieved by NSAIDs with a small lucent nidus in a sclerotic rim is osteoid osteoma, most often in the proximal femur
  3. 16-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the femur 2 months ago night pain controlled by ibuprofen no other complaints Parents ask what happens if nothing more is done Afebrile · repeat film unchanged → Spontaneous involution → osteoid osteoma involutes on its own over years, so NSAIDs and serial films are reasonable
  4. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with osteoid osteoma of the tibia last week pain wakes him at night one ibuprofen dose stops it within an hour Parents ask why the medicine works so well Afebrile · nidus under 2 cm on film → Prostaglandin production by the nidus → the nidus makes prostaglandins, which NSAIDs block, so the response is nearly diagnostic
  5. 13-year-old girl with 6 weeks of worsening pain below the knee firm mass over the proximal tibia no trauma Pain now present at rest Afebrile · film: mixed lytic and dense metaphyseal lesion, sunburst periosteal reaction → Osteosarcoma → a metaphyseal mixed lesion with a sunburst reaction in a teenager is osteosarcoma, the most common primary bone malignancy of childhood; prior radiation and hereditary retinoblastoma raise the risk
  6. 15-year-old boy with 6 weeks of progressive pain above the right knee now wakes him at night firm, tender distal thigh swelling Film: ill-defined mixed lytic-sclerotic distal femoral metaphysis Afebrile · sunburst reaction, Codman triangle · ALP elevated → MRI of the right femur → an aggressive film gets MRI of the affected bone before biopsy: it maps soft tissue and vessels and plans the biopsy; chest CT stages the lungs
  7. 12-year-old boy with 6 weeks of worsening thigh pain wakes him at night intermittent fevers; lost 2 kg; no trauma or recent infection Film: moth-eaten mid-shaft femoral lysis, onion-skin periosteum T 38.2 °C · ESR 55 mm/h → Ewing sarcoma → a permeative diaphyseal lesion with onion-skin layers over weeks, with weight loss, is Ewing sarcoma; the shaft and the 6-week course argue against osteomyelitis; fever, when present, often means it has spread
  8. 14-year-old girl, 5 weeks of worsening left hip pain stairs hard intermittent fever, fatigue; no trauma or chronic illness Warm, tender left iliac crest swelling T 38.3 °C, other vitals normal · lucent ilium, layered periosteum · biopsy: small round blue cells → Ewing sarcoma → a pelvic lytic lesion over weeks with layered periosteum is Ewing sarcoma: MRI maps it, and biopsy shows uniform small round blue cells in sheets, little cytoplasm, fibrous septa; osteomyelitis favors long bones over days, and osteosarcoma is metaphyseal, rarely pelvic and rarely febrile
  9. 7-year-old boy, febrile 4 days won't bear weight on left leg warm, point-tender distal femoral metaphysis; full, painless knee motion MRI: marrow edema, small subperiosteal collection T 39.2 °C · WBC 16,000/mm³, neutrophils · hemoglobin, platelets normal · CRP markedly high · film normal → Osteomyelitis → days of fever with metaphyseal point tenderness and an early normal film is osteomyelitis: blood culture, intravenous antibiotics, drain the abscess; Ewing sarcoma runs for weeks
  10. 9-year-old boy with arm pain after a minor fall no pain before the fall tender upper arm Fracture through a well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency Afebrile · thin sclerotic margin; no periosteal reaction → Unicameral bone cyst → a central metaphyseal lucency with no periosteal reaction that fractures is a unicameral bone cyst; medullary expansion thins the cortex; chondroblastoma is also a lucency with a sclerotic rim, but it sits in the epiphysis
  11. 10-year-old girl, mild shoulder pain after a fall on an outstretched hand full range of motion no weight loss No fracture on film Afebrile · incidental well-defined central proximal humeral metaphyseal lucency · thin cortex; narrow transition; no periosteal reaction → Observation with serial radiographs → an incidental unicameral bone cyst is observed with serial films; it resolves by physeal closure, and the risk is pathologic fracture
  12. 28-year-old woman with 4 months of knee pain and swelling skeletally mature no trauma, fever or weight loss Eccentric expansile lytic lesion of the distal femoral epiphysis Afebrile · soap-bubble appearance on film → Giant cell tumor of bone → an expansile soap-bubble epiphyseal lesion after skeletal maturity is giant cell tumor: locally destructive, curettage or excision, high local recurrence
  13. 16-year-old boy with 3 months of constant knee pain physes still open; no weight loss mild joint swelling Well-circumscribed epiphyseal lucency, thin sclerotic rim, crossing the physis Afebrile · no periosteal reaction → Chondroblastoma → an epiphyseal lucency before skeletal maturity is chondroblastoma; age separates it from giant cell tumor; curettage
Pairs with Leg Pain in a Child: one-sided night pain needs a film. Muscle Contusion and Myositis Ossificans: the post-injury mass. Acute Leukemia in a Child: bone pain from marrow. The Limping Child: the febrile limp.
Transferable rule

To predict a lesion's course, name it first, then recall what it does. To name it, check site, age and fever before reading the film.

Adolescent Kyphosis

Does the curve correct? · Run the correction test before naming it postural or Scheuermann

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A teenager with thoracic roundback: lie the patient prone or ask for active extension.

  • Corrects fully: postural kyphosis. Exercises and reassurance; a film, if taken, shows a smooth curve without wedging.
  • Stays rigid, often with activity-related mid-back pain: standing lateral film. Wedging of 5 degrees or more in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae is Scheuermann disease, most often in boys aged 12 to 17.

Treat by curve size and growth: observe and exercise a mild curve; brace a moderate curve (about 50 to 75 degrees; one source gives 60 to 80) or one that progresses, while growth remains; fuse a severe curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain, even with growth remaining.

Diagnosis
Defining findings Rigid – over 40 degrees (normal 20 to 40); does not correct prone or in extension · Film – anterior wedging of 5 degrees or more in 3 or more consecutive vertebrae (Sorensen) · Schmorl nodes – disc herniation through the endplate; dramatic on film, not an emergency; support, not required
Mimics Compression fracture – trauma or osteoporosis; acute focal pain; height loss at one level, not three · Ankylosing spondylitis – young adult; sacroiliac pain, morning stiffness; not isolated thoracic wedging
Management and treatment
Management ladder: Scheuermann kyphosis
TierInterventionEscalate when
Mild curveObserve; exercise and stretchingCurve reaches the brace range or progresses, growth remaining
Moderate or progressing, still growingBrace until skeletal maturity; it halts progression, rarely correctsSevere curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain
Severe or refractory painPosterior spinal fusionTop rung
Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy with 1 year of worsening thoracic roundback aching mid-back pain curve does not correct prone or in extension No morning stiffness or buttock pain Afebrile · lateral film: 8-degree anterior wedging of 3 consecutive mid-thoracic vertebrae, Schmorl nodes → Scheuermann disease → a rigid kyphosis with 5 degrees or more of wedging in 3 consecutive vertebrae is Scheuermann disease; Schmorl nodes support it
  2. 15-year-old girl whose parents worry about her posture round shoulders for 2 years curve fully corrects lying prone and on active extension No back pain Afebrile · lateral film: smooth curve, no vertebral wedging → Postural kyphosis → a curve that fully corrects is postural kyphosis, the most common cause of adolescent roundback: postural exercises and reassurance; no structural vertebral change
  3. 16-year-old boy with 8 months of increasing thoracic roundback mild mid-back ache after sports curve does not correct in hyperextension No pain that wakes him from sleep or weight loss Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Standing lateral thoracic spine radiograph → a rigid kyphosis gets a standing lateral spine film first to measure the wedging and the Cobb angle; MRI is for pain that wakes from sleep, weight loss or neurologic signs
  4. 14-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease 1 year ago Cobb angle now 65 degrees, up from 52 about 2 years of growth remaining Doing his extension exercises Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Brace until skeletal maturity → a 65-degree curve sits in the brace range and is progressing; with growth remaining it is braced to halt progression until maturity; fusion is for a severe curve, over about 75 degrees, or refractory pain
  5. 17-year-old boy was diagnosed with Scheuermann disease at 13 Cobb angle 80 degrees skeletally mature; physes closed on film Back pain limits school despite a year of physical therapy Afebrile · neurologic exam normal → Posterior spinal fusion → a severe curve (over about 75 degrees) or refractory pain at skeletal maturity goes to posterior spinal fusion; a brace no longer works once growth ends
Transferable rule

One bedside maneuver, whether the curve corrects, separates structural from postural kyphosis; the film confirms, it does not decide.

5 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Musculoskeletal & Rheumatology

Foot Puncture Wounds and Osteomyelitis

A nail through a shoe and a foot still sore weeks later is Pseudomonas

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

After a foot puncture, the exposure and the clock name the organism:

  • First 1 to 4 days, spreading redness: cellulitis from Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci.
  • Nail through a shoe, pain and redness persisting a week or more, little fever, often a normal WBC (white blood cell count): osteomyelitis or osteochondritis (bone or cartilage infection) from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, carried in from the shoe's foam sole.
  • Wound soaked in fresh water at injury (NBME adds soil), then a fast-spreading infection: Aeromonas hydrophila. Salt water: Vibrio vulnificus.

A normal film does not exclude bone infection; MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) does better. Treat with debridement and bone culture, covering Pseudomonas and S. aureus.

Diagnosis
How NBME framed it: question 1

7-year-old boy, follow-up 3 weeks after a nail went through his shoe into the right foot wound thoroughly cleaned and bandaged; moderate pain persists tetanus vaccine at age 5; otherwise healthy Red, warm skin over the wound, tender to touch T 37.2 °C · other vital signs normal

Most likely causal organism?

Competing answers
  • Aeromonas hydrophila: a wound pathogen that also causes diarrhea and infections in immunocompromised hosts; but it needs fresh water or soil in the wound at injury; this stem gives a shoe and a 3-week course.
  • Group A streptococcus: causes cellulitis; but as a fast-spreading skin infection in the first days, not a deep infection weeks after a puncture.
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae: a gram-negative rod like the key; but it causes aspiration pneumonia, not puncture-wound bone infection.
  • Staphylococcus aureus: the most common cause of osteomyelitis; but a nail through a shoe with a deep infection weeks later points to Pseudomonas.

Down to two: Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus. Pseudomonas aeruginosa: a nail through a shoe, then pain, redness and warmth still present at 3 weeks with a near-normal temperature, is osteomyelitis by direct inoculation. The stem never names osteomyelitis. NBME calls Pseudomonas the puncture-wound organism; that holds for the deep infection weeks after a shoe puncture, while the first days are S. aureus or streptococci. Tetanus at age 5 is 2 years ago: no booster, and no organism.

Management and treatment
By situation Osteomyelitis – surgical debridement, bone cultures, empiric antibiotics covering Pseudomonas and S. aureus · Through a shoe – past 72 hours with signs of infection, add Pseudomonas coverage · Tetanus – a puncture is tetanus-prone: booster if the last dose was over 5 years ago; it names no organism · Fever – a near-normal temperature does not argue against bone infection after a puncture
Practice
  1. 10-year-old boy, 10 days after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel improved at first; heel pain now returning limps; mild swelling and tenderness No water exposure Afebrile · WBC normal · MRI: calcaneal marrow edema → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → a deep infection 1 to 2 weeks after a nail through a sneaker, often afebrile with a normal white count, is Pseudomonas osteomyelitis; S. aureus and streptococci cause the early cellulitis
  2. 9-year-old girl stepped barefoot on a tack on the kitchen floor 2 days ago spreading redness around the puncture warm and tender No water or soil exposure T 38.1 °C · foot radiograph normal → Staphylococcus aureus → a puncture infection in the first days is cellulitis, most often Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci; through a sneaker, a deep infection that appears 1 to 2 weeks later points to Pseudomonas
  3. 15-year-old boy cut his sole on a branch while wading barefoot in a lake 1 day later: rapidly spreading painful redness foot swollen Fresh water, not the sea T 38.9 °C · HR 112/min → Aeromonas hydrophila → a fast-spreading wound infection soon after fresh-water exposure is Aeromonas hydrophila; salt water or raw shellfish points to Vibrio vulnificus
  4. 8-year-old boy, 2 weeks after a nail went through his sneaker into the heel worsening heel pain and swelling tender over the calcaneus Walks on his toes T 37.4 °C · foot radiographs normal → MRI of the foot → early radiographs are often normal in osteomyelitis; MRI is more sensitive and shows marrow edema
  5. 11-year-old girl was diagnosed with calcaneal osteomyelitis by MRI today a nail went through her sneaker 3 weeks ago heel pain and swelling persist Afebrile and otherwise well T 37.3 °C · foot film normal → Surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics → osteomyelitis after a puncture through a shoe needs surgical debridement with bone cultures and antipseudomonal antibiotics, plus S. aureus coverage until cultures return
Pairs with The Limping Child: a limp after a nail through a shoe routes here. Septic Arthritis and Transient Synovitis in a Child: joint organisms by host. Diabetic Foot Ulcer: diabetes also carries a high risk of Pseudomonas osteomyelitis.
Transferable rule

Name the organism from the exposure and the clock: a shoe and weeks mean Pseudomonas; the first days mean S. aureus or streptococci.

Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant

The tilt names the tight muscle; the ear names the flat head

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line
  • Head tilts toward a firm sternocleidomastoid mass that appears at 1 to 4 weeks and does not transilluminate, chin turned away: congenital muscular torticollis; the muscle bends the head toward itself and turns the chin away. Clinical diagnosis; stretching, repositioning, tummy time and physical therapy. Late treatment leaves permanent craniofacial asymmetry.
  • Flat occiput, ear on that side forward (parallelogram): positional plagiocephaly, from supine sleep, a neck that turns one way or prematurity. Reposition; no imaging.
  • Flat occiput, ear pushed back with a ridge (trapezoid): lambdoid craniosynostosis. Head CT (computed tomography) and craniofacial referral.

Breech, oligohydramnios or twins (intrauterine crowding): examine the hips and feet; hip dysplasia, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot travel with torticollis.

A new tilt in an older child with any neurologic sign is a posterior fossa tumor until MRI (magnetic resonance imaging).

Diagnosis
Flat back of the head: look down from above and find the ear on the flat side
DiagnosisEar on the flat sideHead seen from above, and the clue
Positional plagiocephalyPushed forwardParallelogram: the flat back and the same-side forehead both shift forward; no ridge
Lambdoid craniosynostosisPulled backTrapezoid: no forehead shift; a hard ridge over the fused suture
Torticollis with positional flatteningPushed forwardParallelogram, flat on the side the chin turns to (opposite the tight muscle); head tilts toward a firm neck-muscle mass
Neck-mass mimics Cystic hygroma – lymphatic malformation, linked to aneuploidy; soft, fluctuant, posterior triangle, transilluminates · Cervical lymphadenitis – tender, warm node outside the muscle, often with fever · Clavicle fracture – after shoulder dystocia; crepitus and an arm not moving, not a tilt
Management and treatment
Management ladder: torticollis and flat head
TrackInterventionEscalate when
Flat headRepositioning and tummy timeNot better in 4 to 8 weeks: image the sutures; if open, a helmet for severe flattening
Tight muscleStretching and physical therapyNo improvement by 6 months of age: pediatric orthopedics; release, usually after 12 months, in the 5 to 10% that fail
Practice
  1. 2-month-old girl, born breech, with a flat right occiput neck mass first felt at 3 weeks; right ear forward head tilts left; chin turns right Firm, painless left sternocleidomastoid mass; does not transilluminate T 37.0 °C · hips stable → Congenital muscular torticollis → tilt toward a firm sternocleidomastoid mass with the chin turned away is congenital muscular torticollis; the flat head with the ear forward is positional, from lying one way; stretching, repositioning, tummy time
  2. 3-month-old girl with a flat right occiput right ear and forehead sit forward sleeps on her back; full neck rotation No neck mass or ridge T 36.9 °C · head circumference 50th percentile → Positional plagiocephaly → a flat occiput with the ear and forehead forward (a parallelogram) is positional plagiocephaly: repositioning and tummy time, no imaging
  3. 4-month-old boy with a flat right occiput right ear sits behind the left palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture No neck mass; full neck rotation T 37.0 °C · head circumference 40th percentile → Craniosynostosis → a flat occiput with the ear pushed back and a ridge (a trapezoid) is lambdoid craniosynostosis: head CT and craniofacial referral
  4. Newborn girl with a neck mass noted at birth soft, fluctuant, in the posterior triangle the mass transilluminates Head held midline; no tilt T 36.8 °C · feeding and breathing normally → Cystic hygroma → a soft posterior-triangle mass that transilluminates is a cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation), linked to aneuploidy; the torticollis mass is firm and does not transilluminate
  5. 8-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a new head tilt morning headaches; vomits on waking papilledema on fundoscopy Left sixth nerve palsy: cannot abduct the left eye T 37.0 °C · no neck mass or fever → Posterior fossa tumor → an acquired head tilt with any neurologic sign in an older child is a posterior fossa tumor until imaged: MRI of the brain
  6. 2-month-old girl was diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis today born breech at term head tilts right; chin turns left; firm right sternocleidomastoid mass Feet look normal T 37.0 °C · hip exam equivocal → Hip ultrasound → torticollis and breech both come from intrauterine crowding, which also causes hip dysplasia: screen the hips with ultrasound (a Melbourne children's hospital guideline recommends it for torticollis; breech alone also qualifies)
  7. 2-month-old girl with a head tilt to the right since birth born breech; firm right sternocleidomastoid mass left hip clunks on Barlow, reduces on Ortolani Left thigh folds asymmetric T 37.0 °C · no hip swelling or warmth → Developmental dysplasia of the hip → a dislocatable hip that reduces in an infant is developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), part of the crowding picture: Pavlik harness; the tilt and mass are the torticollis
  8. 6-month-old girl was diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis at 2 months 3 months of daily stretching and physical therapy tilt and limited rotation unchanged Sternocleidomastoid still tight T 37.0 °C · no neurologic signs → Refer to pediatric orthopedics → most torticollis resolves with stretching; no significant improvement by 6 months of age goes to pediatric orthopedics for evaluation, rather than 6 more months of the same; release, usually after 12 months, is for the 5 to 10% that fail
Pairs with Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth: the newborn who will not move an arm. Posterior Fossa Localization: the acquired tilt with cranial nerve signs. Posterior Urethral Valves: the same constraint physiology.
Transferable rule

The underlying cause explains every finding: crowding gives the tilt and the hip, and the tilt gives the flat head; reject a diagnosis that leaves one out.

Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth

Absent grasp with Horner · which of Moro, biceps and grasp is lost?

Source vignette Pt — 1-day-old boy, 4.4 kg, 39 wk forceps delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia, mother with insulin-treated gestational diabetes and obesity; right hand barely moves, held with the wrist extended, MCP joints hyperextended and IP joints flexed; grasp absent, Moro and biceps reflexes intact; no crepitus; slight right ptosis and a smaller right pupil · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned clavicle fracture, humerus fracture, C5-C6 injury, C8-T1 injury, perinatal asphyxia and perinatal ischemic stroke
The decision point

Three reflexes localize a weak newborn arm. The Moro reflex needs shoulder abduction and elbow extension (C5-C6) and a pain-free arm. The biceps reflex runs through C5-C6, and the grasp runs through C8-T1. Here the grasp is absent while Moro and biceps are intact. The hand is clawed, and the same side has ptosis and miosis. This is a lower plexus (Klumpke, C8-T1) injury. Horner syndrome occurs because the sympathetic fibers to the eye leave the cord with T1.

Erb palsy (C5-C6) is the most common birth palsy and shows the reverse pattern: Moro and biceps lost, grasp kept. A clavicle or humerus fracture lowers the Moro only through pain. It keeps biceps and grasp and has crepitus.

Newborn arm weakness: reflexes by lesion
MoroBicepsGraspPosture and other tellInjury
Decreased (pain)IntactIntactCrepitus or a bony step over the clavicle; a callus lump laterClavicle fracture
Decreased (pain)IntactIntactCrepitus and swelling of the upper armHumerus fracture
DecreasedDecreasedIntactWaiter's tip: arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated, wrist and fingers flexedErb-Duchenne palsy, upper plexus (C5-C6)
IntactIntactAbsentClaw hand (wrist extended, MCP hyperextended, IP flexed) with ipsilateral Horner (ptosis, miosis)Klumpke palsy, lower plexus (C8-T1)
AbsentAbsentAbsentFlail arm, often with HornerTotal plexus palsy (C5-T1)
VariablePreserved or briskPreservedFocal seizures and later upper motor neuron signsPerinatal ischemic stroke
Depressed on both sidesDepressed on both sidesDepressed on both sidesAltered mental status, poor tone, poor feeding or breathing, seizuresPerinatal asphyxia
Scenario bank
  1. 1-day-old boy, 4.4 kg, delivered with forceps after shoulder dystocia; mother has insulin-treated gestational diabetes; the right hand is held with the wrist extended, MCP joints hyperextended and IP joints flexed; grasp absent; Moro and biceps reflexes intact; no crepitus; mild right ptosis and a smaller right pupil → Lower brachial plexus (C8-T1) injury → Klumpke palsy
  2. 1-day-old girl, 4.6 kg, after shoulder dystocia; the left arm lies adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended, forearm pronated and wrist flexed; left Moro and biceps reflexes absent; left grasp strong; no crepitus; pupils equal → Erb-Duchenne palsy → Physical therapy with gentle range of motion
  3. 2-day-old boy, 4.2 kg, after shoulder dystocia, moves the right arm less; right Moro diminished and he cries when the arm is moved; biceps reflex and grasp present on both sides; crepitus over the midshaft of the right clavicle → Clavicle fracture → Gentle handling and pain control
  4. 3-week-old girl with an Erb palsy from a shoulder dystocia delivery; she has begun to flex the elbow a little; no crepitus; radiographs of the clavicle and humerus are normal → Range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury
  5. 7-month-old boy with a left upper brachial plexus injury from birth who has had physical therapy since the first weeks; he still has no elbow flexion or shoulder abduction on the left → Referral for surgical nerve repair → Upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury without recovery
  6. 3-day-old girl with weakness of the right arm after a difficult vaginal delivery → Ipsilateral ptosis and miosis → Horner syndrome from a T1 injury
Management and prognosis Gentle massage and range-of-motion exercises with physical therapy to prevent contractures; most infants recover within months. No improvement by 3 to 9 months: refer for surgical nerve repair. Horner syndrome marks a T1 injury and predicts a poorer outcome. A clavicle fracture needs only gentle handling and pain control.
Pearls Risk factors: macrosomia, shoulder dystocia and maternal diabetes, with obesity and instrumented delivery adding to them · Traction on the head and neck during shoulder dystocia stretches the upper roots (Erb); traction on a raised arm, as in delivering the posterior arm, stretches C8-T1 (Klumpke) · An intact, symmetric Moro does not exclude a plexus injury, because Klumpke spares the shoulder; check the grasp
Pairs with Arm Injury in a Young Child: its pediatric elbow neighbors line names these palsies; this brief covers the reflex split. Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant: the other birth-position injury; it lists clavicle fracture only as a neck-mass mimic, and the clavicle question is in this brief. Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: perinatal stroke presents with focal seizures and upper motor neuron signs, not a limp arm with one lost reflex. Ask: are the signs upper or lower motor neuron?
Transferable rule When a newborn will not move one arm, read three reflexes before the posture. A lower Moro alone with crepitus is a fracture. Lost Moro and biceps with a kept grasp is C5-C6. A lost grasp with Moro and biceps kept is C8-T1. In C8-T1 injury, ptosis and miosis confirm T1 and predict slower recovery.
Mirror twinC5-C6 injury is the commonest birth palsy and shares the shoulder dystocia, but it loses Moro and biceps and keeps grasp, the reverse of this infant.
Salient decoyClavicle fracture: suggested by a 4.4 kg infant after shoulder dystocia. It lowers the Moro from pain, keeps the grasp and gives crepitus; none of these is present.
True-fact-wrong-slotPerinatal ischemic stroke causes one-sided weakness, but with seizures and upper motor neuron signs, not a clawed hand with Horner.
Unchecked attributePerinatal asphyxia is global and bilateral, with altered mental status and poor tone; this infant has one weak hand.
