High-risk stress findings → cath ST depression ≥2 mm at low workload · ST elevation · hypotension with exercise · ventricular arrhythmia · large or multiple perfusion defects · drop in EF (ejection fraction).
SLE as a cardiac risk factor SLE (systemic lupus erythematosus) causes accelerated atherosclerosis. Lupus mortality is bimodal: early deaths come from disease activity and infection, and late deaths from cardiovascular disease. Chronic prednisone compounds the risk, and antiphospholipid antibodies add thrombosis. Framingham and the PCE (Pooled Cohort Equations) underestimate risk in SLE. When traditional risk factors are absent, look for one in the past medical history.
Transferable rule For chest or epigastric symptoms, the trigger and the reliever localize disease better than the location does. Pain on exertion that is relieved by rest is cardiac, wherever the patient points. Pain with meals that is relieved by antacids is GI (gastrointestinal). Pain with position or breathing is pleural or pericardial. Pain reproducible on palpation is musculoskeletal.
True-fact-wrong-slot

Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis

Both a high-risk cardiac condition and a high-risk procedure are required

The decision point

Prophylaxis requires a high-risk cardiac condition AND a high-risk procedure. MVP (mitral valve prolapse) with regurgitation, bicuspid valve, rheumatic valve disease and HCM (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) all came off the list in 2007. A patient with MVP having a dental visit needs no prophylaxis.

Gate 1 — high-risk cardiac conditions (the whole list)
  • Prosthetic valve or prosthetic material used in valve repair
  • Prior infective endocarditis
  • Unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; repaired with residual defect near prosthetic material; or fully repaired with prosthetic material for the first 6 months
  • Cardiac transplant with valvulopathy
Gate 2 — high-risk procedures
  • Dental work with gingival manipulation or mucosal perforation
  • Respiratory procedures breaching mucosa; procedures on infected skin or tissue
  • Not routine GI/GU procedures — that indication died in 2007 too
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo F with mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis
  2. 45 yo M with a prosthetic aortic valve, due for a dental extraction → Amoxicillin 2 g one hour before
  3. 45 yo M with prior infective endocarditis and penicillin allergy, dental cleaning → Cephalexin, azithromycin or doxycycline
  4. 45 yo M with a prosthetic valve undergoing screening colonoscopy → No prophylaxis → GI and GU procedures are no longer covered
  5. 45 yo M with unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease, due for dental work → Prophylaxis is indicated
  6. 45 yo M with a bicuspid aortic valve, due for a dental cleaning → No prophylaxis → bicuspid aortic valve was removed from the list in 2007
If both gates open Give amoxicillin 2 g PO (by mouth) 30–60 min before the procedure. If the patient is penicillin-allergic, give a macrolide or doxycycline. If the patient cannot take oral drugs, give IV (intravenous) cefazolin or ceftriaxone. Clindamycin is out because of C. difficile risk. Its removal is the newest edit.
Transferable rule When a case details a patient-specific factor that only matters if the intervention is indicated (an allergy, a dose adjustment), verify the indication. The detail does not confirm the indication.
Trump-card inversion

Venous Thromboembolism

Pretest probability governs the test

The decision point

Pretest probability picks the testing branch, and stability picks the test. With high probability, skip the D-dimer and go to imaging. Use D-dimer only as a rule-out in low-probability patients. It is elevated in infection, malignancy, pregnancy and post-op states, so it can never rule anything in.

Defining criteria Anticoagulation duration — provoked DVT 3 months; unprovoked ≥3–6 months · D-dimer role — rule-out in low pretest probability only; never rules in · IVC filter — only when anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails
VTE testing by pretest probability
SituationNext stepConfirms, then
Low pretest probability (PE)D-dimer; negative excludes. Low + PERC negative → no testing at allA positive D-dimer confirms nothing; go to CT pulmonary angiography
High probability, or obvious DVT with PE symptomsCT pulmonary angiographyA filling defect confirms PE; anticoagulate
CTA contraindicated (renal failure, contrast allergy, pregnancy)V/Q scanA high-probability scan confirms and a normal scan excludes; a nondiagnostic scan needs leg duplex
Hemodynamically unstableBedside echo (RV strain) ± empiric anticoagulation — treat firstRV strain with hypotension: thrombolysis; CT angiography once stable
Unilateral leg swelling, moderate/high probabilityDuplex ultrasoundNoncompressible vein confirms DVT; low probability starts with D-dimer instead
The swollen leg differential
ConditionThe tell
DVTStasis/hypercoagulable risk, diffuse swelling, calf tenderness, low-grade temp
CellulitisFever, sharply demarcated spreading erythema, skin break or tinea
Ruptured Baker cystSudden calf pain with knee OA/RA; "pseudo-DVT," crescent bruise at the malleolus
Superficial thrombophlebitisPalpable tender cord along a superficial vein
Chronic venous insufficiencyHemosiderin staining, worse standing, bilateral-ish
LymphedemaPainless, non-pitting, dorsal foot, Stemmer sign
Mnemonic Virchow triad names the three routes to venous thrombosis. They are stasis (immobility, long travel), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma, a line) and hypercoagulability (cancer, pregnancy, estrogen, inherited thrombophilia).
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo F, unilateral leg swelling with a high Wells score → Compression ultrasound → skip the D-dimer
  2. 34 yo F with pleuritic chest pain and low pretest probability → D-dimer to rule out
  3. 62 yo F with suspected PE and creatinine 3.2 → V/Q scan
  4. 62 yo F with suspected PE, hypotensive with right ventricular strain → Thrombolysis
  5. 62 yo F with a warm erythematous calf, fever, and no swelling gradient → Cellulitis
  6. 62 yo F with sudden calf pain and ecchymosis below the malleolus → Ruptured Baker cyst
Pearls The ECG (electrocardiogram) in PE (pulmonary embolism) is usually just sinus tachycardia; S1Q3T3 neither confirms nor excludes it · treatment: DOAC (direct oral anticoagulant) or heparin bridge; thrombolytics only if hypotensive/massive · provoked DVT (deep vein thrombosis) 3 months, unprovoked ≥3–6 months · IVC (inferior vena cava) filter only if anticoagulation is contraindicated or fails · the named emergencies: phlegmasia and PE · smokers ≥35 cannot use estrogen-containing OCPs (oral contraceptive pills); WHO (World Health Organization) category 4.
Test-overrides-findings

Heart Murmurs in a Child

Pediatric murmurs · one pathologic feature buys the echo

The decision point

Innocent murmurs are turbulent flow through a structurally normal heart. They are grade 1–2, early or midsystolic, musical or vibratory, and softer with standing or Valsalva. Order ECG (electrocardiogram) and echocardiography for any single pathologic feature. Pathologic features are grade ≥3, holosystolic or diastolic timing, harsh quality, persistence upright, abnormal S2, weak femoral pulses, or symptoms. A murmur that gets louder on standing or Valsalva is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until proven otherwise.

Defining criteria Benign profile — grade 1–2, early/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, decreases with standing/Valsalva, normal vitals, S1/S2, and growth · Evaluation gate — any single pathologic feature → ECG + echocardiography · The reversal — intensity that increases with standing/Valsalva = hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
Benign vs pathologic murmurs — the screening exam
AxisBenignPathologic
HistoryAsymptomatic, normal growthInfants: poor weight gain, feeding difficulty, respiratory distress; older: chest pain, syncope, exertional intolerance
MurmurEarly/midsystolic, musical or vibratory, grade 1–2, decreases uprightHolosystolic or diastolic, harsh, grade ≥3, persists upright
Other findingsNormal vitals, normal S1 & S2, symmetric pulsesCentral cyanosis, loud/fixed/single S2, weak femoral pulses, hepatomegaly
ManagementReassuranceECG & echocardiography
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Auscultation lying and standingFirstFull benign profile: grade 1 to 2, early systolic, softer standingInnocent murmur: reassurance, no testing
Murmur louder on standing or ValsalvaHypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded: hold sports, ECG and echo
Femoral pulses and four-extremity blood pressuresBy branchWeak femoral pulses with arm hypertensionCoarctation
ECGNextHypertrophy or conduction abnormalityPaired with echo whenever any pathologic feature is present
EchocardiographyConfirmsStructural lesion namedAny single pathologic feature, or a benign murmur outliving its window
Echocardiography for the full benign profileSkipNormal heartReassurance alone once every benign feature is named
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, grade 2 vibratory murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder supine, vanishes on standing → Still murmur → reassurance
  2. 14 yo athlete, systolic murmur that grows louder with standing and Valsalva → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → echocardiography before sports
  3. 6 yo F, continuous infraclavicular hum that disappears with neck rotation → Venous hum → reassurance
  4. 3 yo M, harsh grade 3 holosystolic murmur, otherwise well → ECG and echocardiography → one pathologic feature is enough
  5. Infant with weak femoral pulses and upper-extremity hypertension, continuous murmur over the back → Aortic coarctation → collateral flow murmur
  6. Well 4 yo, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border radiating to the axilla, normal S2 → Pulmonic flow murmur → innocent; a wide fixed split or ejection click would change the answer
  7. 4 yo with a soft continuous murmur under the right clavicle that fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine → Turbulent flow through the curved jugular and subclavian veins → venous hum, and why it is usually right-sided
  8. 3 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur under the left clavicle that does not change with head position or posture → Patent ductus arteriosus → echocardiography
  9. 9 yo with a continuous murmur heard best over the back, upper-extremity hypertension and diminished femoral pulses → Coarctation with intercostal collateral flow → echocardiography and four-extremity pressures
  10. 6-week-old with a large VSD and tachypnea with feeds, the chamber that receives the increased preload → Left atrium → left-to-right shunt increases pulmonary venous return
  11. 2 yo with a continuous machine-like murmur below the left clavicle that runs through S2, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure → Patent ductus arteriosus → the machine-like continuous murmur, with a wide pulse pressure
  12. 6 do M, well and thriving, a soft 2/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, normal apical impulse, 2+ equal femoral pulses, saturation 98% → A large ventricular septal defect → soft because a wide defect creates little turbulence
  13. 3 wk old, well and feeding normally, grade 2 midsystolic murmur at the upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, normal S2 with symmetric pulses → Peripheral pulmonary stenosis → resolves by 6 to 12 months
  14. 5 yo F with a continuous grade 2 hum below the right clavicle that is louder when she sits up and disappears when she lies down → Venous hum → the one benign murmur that increases upright
  15. Why a venous hum is typically louder on the right than the left → The right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical → more turbulent flow into the superior vena cava
  16. 18 mo old whose neonatal murmur radiating to the axillae and back is unchanged, with normal growth and no symptoms → Echocardiography → peripheral pulmonary stenosis should have resolved by 12 months
  17. 7 yo F, well and growing normally, with a grade 2 vibratory midsystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that softens on standing; normal S2 and pulses → Reassurance → the full benign profile is present
  18. 15 yo soccer player, asymptomatic, with a grade 2 systolic murmur that grows louder when he stands from a squat → Hold sports pending ECG and echo → louder on standing is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy until excluded
The three innocent murmurs Still murmur — vibratory, lower left sternal border, louder supine · Pulmonic flow murmur — systolic ejection, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla · Venous hum — continuous, supra/infraclavicular, usually right-sided because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical, so flow velocity into the superior vena cava is higher; disappears with neck rotation or compression and when supine.
The continuous murmur A continuous murmur in a child has three causes, separated by location: Right infraclavicular and positional — venous hum, benign, fades with ipsilateral head rotation and when supine · Left infraclavicular and fixed — patent ductus arteriosus, machine-like, unchanged by head position or posture; runs through S2, with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure · Over the back with weak femoral pulses — coarctation collateral flow, with upper-extremity hypertension · Normally split S2 — a fixed split is the atrial septal defect sign, so an S2 split that moves with respiration excludes atrial septal defect.
Pairs with Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers the cyanosis and single S2 of the pathologic column. Heart Murmurs in an Adult covers the pathologic counterpart of the innocent pulmonic flow murmur. Ask: "what does standing do to it?"
The four benign murmurs Still murmur — younger children, left lower sternal border, midsystolic, vibratory or musical, louder supine and softer standing; resolves by adolescence · Pulmonic flow murmur — childhood through adolescence, left upper sternal border, may radiate to the axilla; appears or intensifies in high-output states such as fever, anemia and anxiety · Venous hum — continuous, supra- or infraclavicular, right louder than left because the right jugular and brachiocephalic veins are shorter and more vertical; the one benign murmur that increases sitting up, and it disappears supine or with ipsilateral head rotation · Peripheral pulmonary stenosis — the neonatal benign murmur, upper sternal borders radiating to both axillae and the back, from physiologically narrow proximal pulmonary arteries while fetal resistance is still falling; resolves by 6 to 12 months · Persistence past the expected age — a benign murmur that outlives its window is itself a pathologic feature · Intensity and defect size — a small ventricular septal defect is loud and a large one is soft or silent, because turbulence falls as the orifice widens
How NBME framed it A murmur new on day 3 after a normal birth examination pulls toward a ventricular septal defect or patent ductus arteriosus; its soft grade and spread to the axilla mark peripheral pulmonary stenosis. The options were the five common acyanotic lesions, so the key was the umbrella term, pulmonary stenosis.
Transferable rule In screening, reassurance requires the entire benign profile. One pathologic feature on exam, in the vitals or in the history is sufficient to start the workup.
Unchecked attributePatent ductus arteriosus: it is the right category for a continuous murmur near a clavicle. Check the side and the positional change; a ductus murmur does not change with head turning.
Unchecked attributeAtrial septal defect: the split S2 here moves with respiration, the opposite of the fixed split it requires.
Mirror twinHypertrophic cardiomyopathy: it is the dangerous mimic of the innocent murmur; the direction the murmur moves on standing separates them.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance: accept it only after naming the full benign profile.

Congenital Heart Disease

cyanotic lesions · left-to-right shunts · their timing: weeks for shunts, days for the ductusWhen did it declare, and which structure makes the murmur?

WorkupCyanotic lesionsShuntsPractice
Bottom line

Sort by when it declares (birth, infancy, spells) and the murmur (present or absent, and its source).

  • A murmur needs a pressure gradient: when one appears or fades, the gradient changed.
  • Left-to-right shunts declare over weeks, as pulmonary vascular resistance falls.
  • Ductal-dependent lesions declare over days, as the ductus closes.
  • Silent cyanosis: total anomalous pulmonary venous return or hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
  • Tet spell: the outflow obstruction is partly dynamic; crying or dehydration can tighten it (the trigger is not fully understood), or a drop in systemic vascular resistance (SVR) lets more blood shunt right to left; squatting or knee-chest raises SVR and aborts it.
Workup
Cyanotic lesions
Mechanism, then the tell
LesionMechanismThe tell
Total anomalous pulmonary venous returnPulmonary veins drain to the right heartBirth; no murmur, at most soft pulmonic flow
Hypoplastic left heart syndromeTiny left ventricle, absent mitral and aortic valves; lives on the ductus and atrial defectBirth; no murmur
Tricuspid atresiaNo right atrium to right ventricle path; atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductusBirth; ventricular defect or ductal murmur, or both
Truncus arteriosusOne arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defectTypically infancy, not birth; holosystolic murmur
Tetralogy of FallotOutflow narrowing pushes blood right to left across a large ventricular septal defectHarsh systolic, left upper sternal border; fades in a spell
Ebstein anomalyTricuspid valve displaced apically; atrialized right ventricleTricuspid regurgitation, widely split S1 (first heart sound), sail sound; severe: birth
Tetralogy PROVe – Pulmonic stenosis (right ventricular (RV) outflow obstruction), RV hypertrophy, Overriding aorta, VSD (ventricular septal defect) · Murmur – from the narrowed outflow tract; the defect is too large to make one · Spectrum – severe narrowing, cyanotic at birth; milder, spells in infancy · 5 Ts – Truncus, Transposition, Tricuspid atresia, Tetralogy, Total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Left-to-right shunts and the transitional clock
Acyanotic lesions
LesionThe tellThen
Ventricular septal defectHolosystolic, lower sternal border; louder means smallerDiurese and feed; close if failure persists
Atrial septal defectFixed split S2 (second heart sound), soft pulmonic flow murmurOften silent into childhood; no cyanosis
Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous machine-like, bounding pulses, wide pulse pressurePreterm: indomethacin or ibuprofen closes it; murmur disappears
Coarctation of the aortaArm-leg pressure gap, weak femoral pulsesDays: PGE1 reopens the ductus
Prostaglandin opens, indomethacin closes Ductal-dependent – coarctation, pulmonary atresia, transposition, hypoplastic left heart decompensate as the ductus closes: reopen it · Preterm ductus – shunting into the lungs is the problem: close it · Softening murmur – in an unrepaired large shunt, a warning, not an improvement
Practice
  1. 5-week-old boy, born at term, had a normal 2-week visit now feeds poorly and breathes fast new holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min · acyanotic → Pulmonary vascular resistance has fallen → at birth pulmonary vascular resistance is near systemic, so almost nothing crosses the defect; as it falls, the gradient opens, the murmur appears at 2 to 4 weeks, and the same overcirculation causes the tachypnea and poor feeding. The ductus was already closed by the normal 2-week visit, and its closure removes a continuous murmur rather than creating a holosystolic one; rising pulmonary pressure would soften the murmur
  2. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows the pulmonary veins draining to the right atrium Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 80% on room air · HR 160/min → Total anomalous pulmonary venous return → pulmonary veins draining to the right heart give cyanosis at birth with no murmur, at most a soft pulmonic flow murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur, and truncus arteriosus has a holosystolic murmur with cyanosis typically arriving in infancy
  3. 6-week-old boy was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks poor weight gain liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Feeds tire him Afebrile · respiratory rate 70/min → Diuretics, afterload reduction and caloric fortification → heart failure from a left-to-right shunt arrives at 4 to 6 weeks; failure to thrive is the infant form of exercise intolerance. Diurese and feed first, and close the defect if failure persists: observation leaves the failure untreated, and surgery comes after medical therapy fails
  4. 4-month-old boy has episodes of deep cyanosis while crying episodes resolve when he is held with knees to chest harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · oxygen saturation 84% between episodes → Tetralogy of Fallot → right ventricular outflow tract obstruction drives right-to-left flow across a large ventricular septal defect, and knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance to reverse it; truncus arteriosus gives a holosystolic murmur without spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  5. 1-day-old girl has a normal examination before discharge fails her pulse oximetry screen at 24 hours Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding well Afebrile · HR 140/min · BP 70/42 mm Hg → Echocardiography → a failed screen means possible critical congenital heart disease, and only echocardiography names the anatomy; a chest radiograph only supports, and repeating a failed screen delays the study
  6. 1-day-old girl has been cyanotic since birth no murmur echocardiogram shows a severely underdeveloped left ventricle Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 82% on room air · HR 166/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → the ductus and the atrial defect are the only route to the systemic circulation, so the shunts must stay open: prostaglandin E1 keeps the ductus open; indomethacin closes it, and oxygen alone leaves it to close over days
  7. 3-week-old girl is seen for a weight check fixed splitting of S2 soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border Thriving and gaining weight Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air → Atrial septal defect → a fixed split S2 with a soft pulmonic flow murmur and no cyanosis is an atrial septal defect; the atrial gradient stays low, so it is often silent into childhood. A ventricular septal defect is holosystolic at the lower sternal border, and a patent ductus is continuous and machine-like
  8. 2-month-old boy was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth deeply cyanotic while crying improves when his mother holds his knees to his chest Afebrile · oxygen saturation 62% while crying, 84% after → Increased systemic vascular resistance reduces right-to-left shunting → knee-chest raises systemic vascular resistance, which reverses the right-to-left shunt; the lever is systemic vascular resistance, not venous return or the coronary circulation
  9. 2-month-old girl is evaluated for a murmur holosystolic tricuspid regurgitation murmur at the left lower sternal border widely split S1 early systolic sail sound Feeding and growing well Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on room air → Ebstein anomaly → apical displacement of the tricuspid valve atrializes the right ventricle and makes the regurgitation murmur, the widely split S1 and the sail sound; tricuspid atresia has no right atrium to right ventricle path, and pulmonic stenosis makes an outflow murmur
  10. 4-month-old girl was diagnosed with a large ventricular septal defect at 1 month never repaired murmur has softened now desaturates with crying Parents say the quieter murmur means it is closing Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% at rest → Urgent cardiology referral → a softening murmur in an unrepaired large shunt is a warning, not an improvement: pulmonary vascular resistance is rising and the shunt is starting to reverse, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome ⚠︎; refer urgently while repair is still possible. Reassurance reads it as closure; an afterload reducer with a 3-month recheck treats overcirculation that is already reversing and delays repair
  11. 1-day-old boy has been cyanotic since birth holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border ECG shows left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces No spells with crying Afebrile · oxygen saturation 78% on room air → Tricuspid atresia → with no right atrium to right ventricle path, flow depends on the atrial defect plus a ventricular defect or ductus, whose murmur is heard; left axis deviation with small right ventricular forces is its ECG. Tetralogy has right ventricular hypertrophy and an outflow murmur. Ebstein, cyanotic at birth when severe, also gives a regurgitation murmur, but adds a widely split S1, a sail sound and a massive box-shaped heart; left axis with small right ventricular forces is the tricuspid atresia ECG
  12. 2-day-old boy is pale and mottled weak femoral pulses right arm blood pressure 30 mm Hg above the leg In shock on arrival Afebrile · BP 86/50 mm Hg in the right arm · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 → coarctation declares in days, as the ductus closes: prostaglandin E1 reopens it. Diuretics and a fluid bolus leave the closing ductus untouched
  13. 2-month-old boy has cyanosis that began in recent weeks holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a single arterial trunk over a large defect in the ventricular septum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 86% → Truncus arteriosus → a single shared arterial trunk over a ventricular septal defect gives cyanosis characteristically in infancy, not at birth, with a holosystolic murmur; tetralogy has a harsh outflow murmur and spells, and total anomalous pulmonary venous return has no murmur
  14. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with a ventricular septal defect at 2 weeks loud grade 4/6 holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border echocardiogram shows a small defect Afebrile · weight at the 50th percentile → A small defect produces high-velocity turbulent flow → a small defect makes high-velocity turbulent flow; large defects are quieter and shunt more, so murmur intensity runs opposite to severity. A loud murmur reflects a high gradient, not a high right ventricular pressure, which would soften it
  15. 3-month-old girl has episodes of deeper cyanosis with crying episodes resolve when she is calm harsh systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border Afebrile · baseline oxygen saturation 86% → Echocardiography → echocardiography confirms the ventricular septal defect, overriding aorta and narrowed outflow tract; a chest radiograph (boot-shaped heart) and an ECG only support
  16. 3-day-old preterm boy born at 28 weeks continuous murmur below the left clavicle bounding pulses widened pulse pressure Murmur first heard today on rounds Afebrile · BP 58/24 mm Hg · respiratory rate 64/min → Indomethacin or ibuprofen → a hemodynamically significant preterm ductus (bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, tachypnea) shunting into the lungs is the problem, so close it with indomethacin or ibuprofen; prostaglandin E1 keeps a ductus open, and observation alone leaves the shunt in place
  17. 1-day-old boy with Down syndrome has mild cyanosis with feeds fixed split S2 grade 3/6 systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Born at term after an uncomplicated delivery Afebrile · oxygen saturation 90% during feeds → Complete atrioventricular canal defect → an atrial sign (fixed split S2) and a lower-sternal-border murmur, with cyanosis, in Down syndrome: echocardiography defines it. An isolated ventricular or atrial septal defect shunts left to right and causes no cyanosis. On day 1 pulmonary vascular resistance is still near systemic, so little crosses left to right yet
  18. 3-day-old girl has cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen single S2 now weak pulses with poor perfusion Born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy; feeding poorly today Afebrile · oxygen saturation 70% on 100% oxygen · HR 190/min → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → unchanged saturation on 100% oxygen is a fixed shunt, not lung disease; weak pulses mean the ductus is closing, so instability licenses prostaglandin E1 before the picture; waiting for echocardiography or adding oxygen lets it close
  19. 3-month-old girl was diagnosed with tetralogy of Fallot at birth harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border echocardiogram shows a large ventricular septal defect and an overriding aorta Afebrile · oxygen saturation 88% → Flow through the narrowed RV outflow tract → the ventricular septal defect is real anatomy but too large to generate a murmur; the murmur comes from the narrowed right ventricular (RV) outflow tract, and the overriding aorta adds none
  20. 6-week-old boy has fed poorly for 1 week tachypneic and acyanotic holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border Murmur absent on the newborn examination; born at term Afebrile · respiratory rate 68/min · oxygen saturation 98% → Ventricular septal defect → a holosystolic lower-sternal-border murmur in an acyanotic infant is a ventricular septal defect, appearing as pulmonary vascular resistance falls; an atrial septal defect gives a fixed split S2 and is often silent into childhood, and a patent ductus is continuous
How NBME framed it: question 1

3-month-old boy brought to the emergency department with 3 days of pallor, low-grade fever, vomiting, occasional diarrhea and poor feeding Mildly dehydrated and cyanotic; perfusion and muscle tone normal T 37.8 °C · pulse 165/min · respirations 35/min · BP 80/48 mm Hg · oxygen saturation 85% on room air harsh grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur over the whole precordium cries and becomes agitated as an intravenous catheter is attempted saturation then drops to 60% and the murmur is barely audible Supplemental oxygen is given

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Atrial septal defect: a common defect with a systolic murmur; but it shunts left to right with a fixed split S2 and causes no cyanosis.
  • Coarctation of the aorta: a can't-miss lesion in an ill infant; but it gives arm hypertension, weak leg pulses and lower leg pressures, not cyanotic spells.
  • Ventricular septal defect: a harsh murmur in an infant; but an isolated defect is holosystolic and acyanotic; a murmur that fades as cyanosis develops over months means rising resistance reversing the shunt, the road to Eisenmenger syndrome ⚠︎, not an acute spell with crying.

Down to two: tetralogy of Fallot or pulmonary stenosis. Tetralogy of Fallot: isolated pulmonary stenosis makes a similar outflow murmur, but with no ventricular septal defect it causes no cyanotic spells with crying. Crying tightens the outflow obstruction (the trigger is not fully understood), pulmonary flow drops, and less flow makes a softer murmur. The stem reads like a febrile stomach illness; the witnessed spell names the lesion, and the oxygen given treats the number, not the shunt.

Common wrong answers Give oxygen in a spell: the shunt is anatomic; SVR, not inspired oxygen, is the lever. Flow across the ventricular septal defect: real anatomy, wrong source of the tetralogy murmur. Ductal closure: removes a continuous murmur, cannot create a holosystolic one. Rising pulmonary pressure: the opposite direction; it would soften the murmur.
Pairs with Part I Heart Murmurs in a Child: central cyanosis and a single or fixed S2 are pathologic; ask, cyanosis at birth, and is there a murmur? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the sort to finish first. Part II Heart Murmurs in an Adult: murmur shape and location. Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant: lung versus heart.
Transferable rule

Time it, then hear it: when did cyanosis or the murmur arrive, and which structure makes the sound? A murmur that appears or fades means the gradient changed, not the heart.

Heart Murmurs in an Adult

shape first, then breathing · the click and the second heart sound (S2) decide · a repaired congenital lesion in a young adult is the causeWhat is the shape, which side does breathing point to, and what are the click and S2 doing?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Fix phase and side before you name a valve; the click, S2 and the response to breathing or standing carry the diagnosis.

  • RILE (right inspiration, left expiration): inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure and fills the right heart, so right-sided murmurs grow (as with leg raise or hepatic compression); left-sided on expiration.
  • Pulmonic stenosis: ejection click, crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace, widened S2 split; usually congenital and isolated (rarely carcinoid or rheumatic), often silent until adult exertional dyspnea.
  • Tricuspid regurgitation: holosystolic at the left lower sternal border, with right heart failure: distended jugular veins with v waves, pulsatile, tender, enlarged liver, ascites, edema, right ventricular heave.
  • Pulmonic regurgitation: decrescendo diastolic off S2, louder on inspiration; classically after tetralogy of Fallot repair (disrupted pulmonic annulus); with a loud P2 (pulmonic component of S2), pulmonary hypertension.
  • Atrial septal defect: wide, fixed S2 split, no click.
  • Functional flow murmur: no click, normal S2, in a high-output state (anemia, fever): treat the cause.
Diagnosis
Murmur Man: the shape places the murmur, breathing names the valve
ShapeTenantsWhat separates them
Diamond head: crescendo-decrescendo ejectionAortic stenosis, pulmonic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathyHypertrophic cardiomyopathy louder with Valsalva and standing, aortic stenosis softer; pulmonic stenosis louder on inspiration
Flat body: holosystolic, S1 (first heart sound) to S2Mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, ventricular septal defectTricuspid louder on inspiration; mitral radiates to the axilla; septal defect harsh at the lower sternal border
Left arm: late diastolic rumble into S1Mitral and tricuspid stenosisTricuspid louder on inspiration; mitral on expiration, with an opening snap at the apex
Right arm: early diastolic decrescendo off S2Aortic and pulmonic regurgitationPulmonic louder on inspiration; aortic on expiration, with a wide pulse pressure
Late systolic with a clickMitral valve prolapseClick moves earlier with standing and Valsalva
Crossing S2Patent ductus arteriosusContinuous, machine-like: runs through S2
Reading S2 Widened, varies – pulmonic stenosis, after an ejection click · Wide, fixed – atrial septal defect: more right-sided flow across a normal pulmonic valve · Narrowed, or paradoxical when severe – aortic stenosis (a bicuspid valve calcifies early, 40s to 50s); paradoxical also in left bundle branch block · Single – severe pulmonic regurgitation, pulmonary atresia, severe aortic stenosis, transposition, truncus · Loud P2 – pulmonary hypertension; with a decrescendo diastolic murmur, Graham Steell
Management
Treatment Congenital pulmonic stenosis – percutaneous balloon valvulotomy preferred, if severe and symptomatic · Pulmonic regurgitation after repair – serial echocardiography; pulmonic valve replacement when severe, with progressive right ventricular dilation and symptoms · Tricuspid regurgitation – usually functional: find the cause · Graham Steell – treat the pulmonary hypertension
After congenital heart repair In a young adult the repair is the etiology, not the background. Tetralogy of Fallot repair: pulmonic regurgitation, right ventricular dilation, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death; palpitations and syncope: ECG (electrocardiogram), Holter and electrophysiology referral. Aortic valvotomy: aortic regurgitation. Coarctation repair: re-coarctation, persistent hypertension. Fontan: protein-losing enteropathy, arrhythmia. Mustard or Senning: baffle obstruction, systemic right ventricular failure.
Practice
  1. 30-year-old man has exertional dyspnea tetralogy of Fallot repaired at age 3 decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, louder with inspiration single S2; parasternal heave Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Pulmonic regurgitation → a decrescendo diastolic murmur off S2 sits on the right arm, and louder on inspiration puts it on the right heart; P2 is lost (single S2), the heave is the dilated right ventricle carrying the volume load, and the repair enlarged the outflow tract and disrupted the pulmonic annulus. Aortic regurgitation is the same arm, wrong side; tricuspid regurgitation is the right side, wrong phase. Next, echocardiography to grade the regurgitation and right ventricular size; severe regurgitation with symptoms and progressive right ventricular dilation goes to valve replacement
  2. 18-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur ejection click, then a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace widely split S2 that varies with respiration Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Pulmonic valve stenosis → an ejection click and a widened split that varies with breathing are pulmonic stenosis; an atrial septal defect splits S2 wide but fixed, with no click, and the innocent pulmonic flow murmur has no click and a normal S2; confirm with echocardiography
  3. 38-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap loud S1 ECG shows atrial fibrillation Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 112/min, irregularly irregular → Mitral stenosis → a diastolic rumble into S1 is the left arm, mitral or tricuspid stenosis; the opening snap at the apex marks the mitral valve, while tricuspid stenosis grows louder on inspiration; a myxoma rumble varies with body position
  4. 17-year-old boy is evaluated for a murmur harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left mid-sternal border louder with Valsalva and on standing Family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 120/74 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → a diamond-shaped murmur that grows with Valsalva and standing (reduced preload) is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a dynamic left ventricular outflow obstruction at the left mid-sternal border; aortic stenosis, bicuspid or not, gets softer, and pulmonic stenosis grows louder on inspiration; confirm with echocardiography
  5. 64-year-old man has leg edema and ascites distended jugular veins with large v waves pulsatile, tender, enlarged liver holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Tricuspid regurgitation → a holosystolic murmur is the flat body; louder on inspiration puts it on the right, and a pulsatile liver with large v waves belongs to tricuspid regurgitation, usually functional from right ventricular dilation. Mitral regurgitation radiates to the axilla; a ventricular septal defect is harsh at the lower sternal border but does not grow on inspiration or bring a pulsatile liver and v waves
  6. 45-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur that decreases with inspiration bounding pulses No history of heart surgery or lung disease Afebrile · BP 158/52 mm Hg, a wide pulse pressure · HR 76/min → Aortic regurgitation → a decrescendo diastolic murmur off S2 is the right arm; softer on inspiration puts it on the left, and a wide pulse pressure with bounding pulses marks aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic regurgitation grows louder on inspiration, and mitral stenosis is a rumble into S1; confirm with echocardiography
  7. 20-year-old woman has 6 months of heavy menstrual periods soft midsystolic murmur normal S2; no click No syncope or chest pain on exertion Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 8 g/dL → Functional flow murmur → no click and a normal S2 exonerate the valve and the septum: a flow murmur of a high-output state, here anemia; treat the anemia. Pulmonic stenosis brings an ejection click and a widened split, and an atrial septal defect a wide, fixed split
  8. 55-year-old woman has dyspnea that changes with body position a plop and a rumble that vary with body position fever and weight loss T 38.1 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 92/min → Left atrial myxoma → a plop and a rumble that shift with position, with fever and weight loss, are a left atrial myxoma; mitral stenosis gives an apical rumble with an opening snap, and fever with weight loss also fit endocarditis, but a plop and rumble that shift with position point to a mass ⚠︎
  9. 20-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border S2 split widely, and fixed with breathing; no click Lungs clear; no edema Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Atrial septal defect → a wide, fixed split with no click is an atrial septal defect, more right-sided flow across a normal pulmonic valve; pulmonic stenosis splits S2 widely but the split varies, after an ejection click, and tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic at the lower border
  10. 78-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of syncope crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids softer with Valsalva delayed carotid upstroke No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 128/84 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Aortic stenosis → a diamond-shaped murmur to the carotids that softens with Valsalva, with a delayed upstroke, is aortic stenosis; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy grows louder with Valsalva, and mitral regurgitation is holosystolic and radiates to the axilla; confirm with echocardiography
  11. 28-year-old man has 2 weeks of palpitations and one episode of syncope repaired tetralogy of Fallot No chest pain, fever or seizure activity Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 92/min → Ventricular arrhythmia → a repaired lesion is the etiology: tetralogy repair gives pulmonic regurgitation, right ventricular dilation, ventricular arrhythmia and sudden death, and palpitations with syncope point to the arrhythmia: ECG, Holter and electrophysiology referral. Pulmonic regurgitation dilates the right ventricle and sets up the arrhythmia, but by itself brings dyspnea and a heave, not palpitations with syncope; a residual ventricular septal defect is a holosystolic murmur
  12. 30-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border loud P2 echocardiogram shows pulmonary hypertension No prior heart surgery Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 80/min → Graham Steell murmur → Graham Steell is pulmonic regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension: a loud P2, not the absent one (single S2) after repair, and there was no surgery; aortic regurgitation brings a wide pulse pressure, and this one is normal; treat the pulmonary hypertension
  13. 28-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur the click moves earlier on standing No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Mitral valve prolapse → a click that moves earlier with standing (reduced preload) is mitral valve prolapse; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also grows louder with reduced preload but is a harsh diamond-shaped murmur, and aortic stenosis has no mid-systolic click and gets softer with reduced preload
  14. 22-year-old woman has exertional dyspnea ejection click and a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace echocardiogram shows a doming pulmonic valve with a severe gradient Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Percutaneous balloon valvulotomy → congenital pulmonic stenosis, often silent until adult exertional dyspnea, now severe and symptomatic: percutaneous balloon valvulotomy is preferred over surgical replacement, and a severe, symptomatic valve is past observation
  15. 52-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur systolic murmur at the right 2nd interspace S2 splits paradoxically ECG shows no bundle branch block Afebrile · BP 134/82 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valve → a right 2nd interspace murmur with a narrowed split, or a paradoxical one when severe, is aortic stenosis; a bicuspid valve calcifies prematurely and presents in the 40s to 50s, the most common congenital defect found in adults. Pulmonic stenosis sits at the left 2nd interspace with a widened split, and a flow murmur keeps a normal S2
  16. 30-year-old man has worsening exertional dyspnea repaired tetralogy of Fallot echocardiogram shows a severely regurgitant pulmonic valve right ventricle more dilated than a year ago Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 86/min → Pulmonic valve replacement → severe pulmonic regurgitation after repair with progressive right ventricular dilation and symptoms needs pulmonic valve replacement; serial echocardiography is surveillance, and diuretics with a recheck in a year leave the dilating ventricle untreated ⚠︎
Common wrong answers Tricuspid regurgitation: against pulmonic stenosis it also grows on inspiration, so the click and the split decide; against pulmonic regurgitation it is the right side, wrong phase. Aortic regurgitation: the other tenant of the right arm, right shape, wrong side. Atrial septal defect: fixed splitting, when the stem says single. Anemia flow murmur: the benign look-alike; a normal S2 and no click exonerate it.
Pairs with Part I Heart Murmurs in a Child: the innocent pulmonic flow murmur, the benign counterpart of pulmonic stenosis; ask: is there a click, and what is S2 doing? Part II Congenital Heart Disease: when a murmur appears and why; this brief covers what the murmur is.
Transferable rule

Fix phase and side before you name a valve, and check inspiration in every murmur. Then separate look-alikes by the accompanying findings, not the sound.

Hypertension in an Adult

baseline panel · end-organ injury starts the drug · comorbidity picks it · secondary causes and how renin separates themIs there end-organ injury or a comorbidity that picks the drug, and is the patient resistant, young or hypokalemic?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Confirmed hypertension gets one baseline panel: it looks for end-organ injury and the comorbidity that picks the drug.

  • End-organ injury, such as LVH (left ventricular hypertrophy) on ECG (electrocardiogram): start treatment at that visit; echo or stress testing never delays it.
  • No comorbidity: an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker), thiazide or dihydropyridine CCB (calcium channel blocker), interchangeable first-line.
  • A comorbidity: match the drug to it. Gout takes losartan (mildly uricosuric); thiazides are avoided because they raise urate.
  • Resistant, young or hypokalemic: hunt a secondary cause. In a young patient, hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis and normal renal function is mineralocorticoid excess.
  • Renin separates the look-alikes: suppressed in primary hyperaldosteronism, high in renal artery stenosis.
Diagnosis
Secondary hypertension: what to test for
DiagnosisThe stem showsFirst testConfirms, then
Primary hyperaldosteronismHypokalemia and alkalosisAldosterone-to-renin ratioAldosterone fails to suppress with salt loading; then adrenal CT (computed tomography) and adrenal venous sampling to lateralize
Fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, media of the artery)Young woman, abdominal bruitRenal artery duplex or CT angiographyCT or MR (magnetic resonance) angiography; catheter angiography is the reference standard
PheochromocytomaEpisodic hypertension, headache, sweatingPlasma or urine metanephrinesMetanephrines several-fold high; then adrenal CT or MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) to locate the tumor
Obstructive sleep apneaSnoring, obesity, daytime sleepinessPolysomnographyPolysomnography is itself confirmatory; a home study can screen
Coarctation of the aortaWeak femoral pulses, rib notchingEcho or CTArm-leg pressure gradient first at the bedside; CT or MR angiography defines the narrowing
Cushing syndromeStriae, moon facies, hyperglycemiaLow-dose dexamethasone or 24-hour cortisolA second, different screening test abnormal (late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urine cortisol, 1 mg dexamethasone); then ACTH (adrenocorticotropic hormone) to localize
Mechanism Aldosterone – raises ENaC (epithelial sodium channel) in the collecting duct; sodium reabsorption leaves the lumen electronegative, which drives potassium and hydrogen ion secretion: hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis · Aldosterone escape – through ANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) and pressure natriuresis, sodium plateaus and there is no edema; a normal sodium does not argue against the diagnosis · Bilateral renal artery stenosis – classically flash pulmonary edema with severe hypertension in an elderly patient with vascular disease
Management and treatment
Antihypertensive choice by comorbidity
ComorbidityPreferred agents
Coronary diseaseAngina: β-blocker, CCB; after myocardial infarction: ACE inhibitor or ARB plus β-blocker
Heart failure with reduced ejection fractionACE inhibitor or ARB, β-blocker, diuretic, aldosterone antagonist
Atrial fibrillation or flutterβ-blocker, nondihydropyridine CCB
Chronic kidney diseaseACE inhibitor or ARB
GoutLosartan, other ARB, CCB; avoid diuretics
OsteoporosisThiazide diuretic
Migraineβ-blocker, CCB
Calcium kidney stonesThiazide diuretic
By situation Two drugs – stage 2 hypertension (BP 140/90 mm Hg or more): most adults start two first-line drugs from different classes, preferably as one single-pill combination · LVH – regresses on an ARB or ACE inhibitor · Atrial fibrillation – a β-blocker or a nondihydropyridine CCB controls rate and treats the pressure; avoid combining them (bradycardia, heart block, depressed contractility) · Bilateral renal artery stenosis – an ACE inhibitor causes AKI (acute kidney injury): the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR (glomerular filtration rate)
Practice
  1. 48-year-old man has hypertension confirmed on 3 separate visits gout, no flares in a year on allopurinol ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy No chest pain or dyspnea BP 136/86 mm Hg · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL · uric acid 8.4 mg/dL → Losartan → gout picks losartan, which is mildly uricosuric; a thiazide raises urate, and stopping allopurinol treats neither the pressure nor the hypertrophy and invites a flare
  2. 62-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated office readings osteoporosis, with a hip T-score of -2.7 BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or migraine BP 134/84 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide reduces urinary calcium loss, so one drug treats both the pressure and the osteoporosis; losartan and a dihydropyridine CCB treat only the pressure
  3. 60-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings chronic kidney disease, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 420 mg/g No diabetes, gout or heart failure; takes no medications BP 138/86 mm Hg · potassium 4.6 mEq/L → ACE inhibitor → albuminuric chronic kidney disease takes an ACE inhibitor or ARB; a thiazide or a nondihydropyridine CCB treats only the pressure
  4. 45-year-old woman has hypertension on repeated readings migraine headaches 6 times a month BP unchanged after 6 months of lifestyle changes No gout, kidney disease or osteoporosis BP 136/84 mm Hg · HR 78/min → Β-blocker → a beta-blocker treats both the pressure and the migraine, one drug for both diagnoses; a thiazide treats only the pressure, and hydralazine is not a first-line class
  5. 58-year-old man has hypertension on repeated readings 3 calcium kidney stones in 4 years urine calcium high on a 24-hour collection No gout or kidney disease BP 134/86 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Thiazide diuretic → a thiazide reduces urinary calcium and treats both; a loop diuretic increases urinary calcium, and losartan treats only the pressure
  6. 55-year-old man has hypertension newly confirmed on home readings ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy no chest pain, exertional dyspnea or syncope Baseline electrolytes, creatinine and urinalysis normal BP 138/88 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Start an antihypertensive now → left ventricular hypertrophy is end-organ injury, the treatment gate; echo or stress testing only characterizes it and never delays the first drug
  7. 29-year-old man has hypertension found at a work physical potassium 2.8 mEq/L bicarbonate 32 mEq/L, metabolic alkalosis No headaches, sweating or abdominal bruit BP 168/102 mm Hg · sodium 142 mEq/L · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Aldosterone-to-renin ratio → hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with normal renal function are mineralocorticoid excess; a suppressed renin separates primary hyperaldosteronism from renovascular disease, and a normal sodium (aldosterone escape) does not argue against it. Duplex fits a bruit, metanephrines fit spells
  8. 32-year-old woman has new hypertension found at a routine visit abdominal bruit lateral to the umbilicus plasma renin activity elevated Femoral pulses normal and equal to radial pulses BP 166/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.0 mEq/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Fibromuscular dysplasia → a young woman with an abdominal bruit and high renin has fibromuscular dysplasia (“string of beads”, a disease of the media): CT angiography. Primary hyperaldosteronism suppresses renin; coarctation weakens the femoral pulses
  9. 38-year-old man has spells of pounding headache palpitations and drenching sweats during spells hypertension during spells, normal pressure between Thyroid-stimulating hormone normal BP 188/110 mm Hg during a spell · HR 124/min → Pheochromocytoma → episodic hypertension with headache, palpitations and sweating is pheochromocytoma: plasma free metanephrines, several-fold high, then adrenal CT or MRI. A normal thyroid-stimulating hormone argues against hyperthyroidism, and with hypertension during the spells, metanephrines come before a panic disorder diagnosis ⚠︎
  10. 16-year-old boy has headaches and hypertension at a sports physical weak, delayed femoral pulses chest radiograph shows rib notching No palpitations, sweating or snoring right arm BP 162/94 mm Hg · leg BP 118/70 mm Hg → Coarctation of the aorta → weak femoral pulses, rib notching and an arm-leg pressure gradient are coarctation of the aorta; CT or MR angiography defines the narrowing. The arm-leg gradient places the lesion in the aorta, not the renal artery or the adrenal ⚠︎
  11. 48-year-old man has hypertension resistant to 3 medications loud snoring and daytime sleepiness body mass index 38 kg/m², obese No striae; neck circumference 46 cm BP 158/98 mm Hg · potassium 4.3 mEq/L → Obstructive sleep apnea → snoring, daytime sleepiness and obesity with resistant hypertension are obstructive sleep apnea: polysomnography, itself the confirmatory test. Snoring, sleepiness and a thick neck point to the airway first, and there are no striae to suggest Cushing syndrome
  12. 42-year-old woman has new hypertension and 6 months of weight gain wide purple abdominal striae round, full face Snoring absent; no episodic headache, palpitations or sweating BP 158/96 mm Hg · fasting glucose 168 mg/dL → Cushing syndrome → striae, moon facies and hyperglycemia are Cushing syndrome: an overnight dexamethasone suppression test, then a second, different screening test, then ACTH to localize
  13. 44-year-old woman has hypertension and potassium 3.0 mEq/L was diagnosed with primary hyperaldosteronism after salt loading CT shows a 1.5-cm left adrenal nodule She is willing to undergo surgery BP 162/98 mm Hg · renin suppressed → Adrenal venous sampling → bilateral adrenal hyperplasia is more common than adenoma, so adrenal venous sampling lateralizes before any adrenalectomy; another CT shows the anatomy again, not which gland secretes
  14. 74-year-old man has severe hypertension peripheral vascular disease with claudication was diagnosed with bilateral renal artery stenosis on CT angiography A new antihypertensive is being chosen BP 186/104 mm Hg · creatinine 1.4 mg/dL → An ACE inhibitor → the efferent arteriole needs angiotensin II to maintain GFR, so an ACE inhibitor causes AKI; a calcium channel blocker and a thiazide do not remove that support ⚠︎
  15. 66-year-old man has hypertension that has worsened over a year abdominal bruit and high plasma renin CT angiography: 80% narrowing of the left renal artery BP 174/100 mm Hg · potassium 3.3 mEq/L · creatinine 1.2 mg/dL → Angiotensin II → renin initiates the cascade and aldosterone causes the hypokalemia, but angiotensin II directly mediates the vasoconstriction
Common wrong answers Discontinue the allopurinol: the uric acid level baits it, but it lowers nothing that matters; it treats neither the pressure nor the LVH and invites a flare. Echo or stress testing first: characterization never delays treatment.
Pairs with Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the hypertension is one organ in a heritable pattern. Part II Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: fibromuscular dysplasia versus Takayasu arteritis, the inflammatory cause of renal artery stenosis in a young patient. Part II Hypokalemia and Acid-Base Disorders in a Child: low potassium without hypertension, sorted by acid-base status.
Transferable rule

Store the pairings, never a favorite drug: the same agent is preferred with one comorbidity and avoided with another. Name what the evidence proves: labs prove the physiology (hyperaldosteronism), imaging or pathology proves the lesion (adrenal adenoma).

Cyanosis in the Newborn

Sort lung, heart or airway before naming a lesion · Is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing?

Source vignette Pt — 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen · Imaging — ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned respiratory distress syndrome, d-transposition of the great arteries and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
The decision point

Three bedside findings settle the sort before any lesion is considered. He is working to breathe (grunting, flaring and retracting); cyanotic heart disease produces comfortable tachypnea, not distress. His saturation rises from 65% to 92% on oxygen. That cannot happen in d-transposition, where systemic flow bypasses the lungs entirely. The two limbs read the same, so nothing is shunting right-to-left across the duct. That leaves parenchymal disease. A 32-week infant with ground-glass opacification and air bronchograms has surfactant deficiency: respiratory distress syndrome.

Sometimes the examination is instead a list of normals: no murmur, symmetric pulses, equal four-extremity pressures, clear lungs, no retractions, no stridor. These normals already exclude lung and heart. The remaining finding is temporal. Ask: What brings the cyanosis on, and what relieves it? Cyanosis on latching that clears with crying is nasal obstruction, because neonates are obligate nasal breathers and crying opens the oral airway. The inverse pattern, cyanosis worsened by crying, is a tet spell.

Defining criteria Oxygen responsiveness — saturation rises substantially with supplemental oxygen in alveolar disease; it does not in d-transposition, because most systemic flow bypasses the pulmonary vasculature · Preductal vs. postductal — the right upper extremity is preductal and the lower extremities postductal; a higher preductal saturation means right-to-left ductal shunting · Ductal closure clock — the ductus arteriosus begins to constrict as early as 12 hours after birth, so ductal-dependent lesions declare after that, not at minutes · RDS risk — inversely related to gestational age, highest at ≤28 weeks; antenatal glucocorticoids reduce but do not eliminate it · Bilateral choanal atresia — incomplete canalization of the posterior nasal passage; cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, with noisy breathing (stertor), symptomatic shortly after birth · Why crying relieves it — neonates are obligate nasal breathers; hypoxia and hypercapnia trigger crying, which opens the oral airway and temporarily bypasses the obstruction · The bedside test — inability to pass a catheter through the nares into the oropharynx, confirmed by CT or nasal endoscopy · The stability gate — a cyanotic newborn whose hypoxemia does not correct on oxygen gets echocardiography, and prostaglandin E1 is added when the infant is hemodynamically unstable, because instability is what raises concern for a ductal-dependent lesion
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting, flaring, retractions — work of breathing; this is lung disease, and it excludes the two structural cardiac options, which give tachypnea without distress · 65% → 92% on oxygen — the alveoli can be recruited; excludes d-transposition outright · Right upper and left lower extremity both 65% — no ductal gradient; argues against persistent pulmonary hypertension and against a coarctation presentation · Cyanosis at minutes of life — too early for ductal closure, which begins at about 12 hours; coarctation cannot yet have declared · 32 weeks, 1.7 kg — the base rate for surfactant deficiency; RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) incidence is inversely related to gestational age · Ground-glass with air bronchograms and low lung volumes — RDS; transient tachypnea gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures, and pulmonary hypertension a clear or oligemic film · Grade 1/6 systolic murmur — soft and non-specific, consistent with a physiologically open duct rather than a structural lesion · A dose of antenatal glucocorticoids — lowers the risk but never excludes the diagnosis · PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) with intrapartum penicillin — sets up group B streptococcal pneumonia, whose film is indistinguishable from RDS ⚠︎ · Acrocyanosis — peripheral cyanosis of hands, feet, and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes is a normal finding in the first 24–48 hours of life; central cyanosis (mucous membranes blue) requires workup
Cyanosis in the newborn — sorting by physiology
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by

Cyanosis with a normal examination — sorting by trigger
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Bilateral choanal atresiaPosterior nasal passage fails to canalize; the obligate nasal breather obstructs whenever his mouth closesWorse with feeding, better with crying; stertor; catheter will not pass— (the answer)
Tetralogy of FallotRight ventricular outflow obstruction; a spell when systemic resistance fallsCyanosis worse with crying and agitation — the inverted trigger — plus a murmur ⚠︎Crying makes him pink; there is no murmur
Transposition of the great arteriesParallel circulations; deoxygenated blood to the bodyConstant cyanosis unchanged by feeding or crying, unimproved by oxygenThe cyanosis comes and goes with what he is doing
Tracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresiaAspiration through a fistula or from a blind pouchCoughing and choking with feeds, respiratory distress, a tube that coilsHe fed well without coughing; lungs are clear
LaryngomalaciaSupraglottic collapse on inspirationInspiratory stridor worse supine and with exertion; cyanosis uncommonNo stridor at all
Transient tachypnea of the newbornRetained fetal lung fluid after deliveryTachypnea with flaring, retractions and grunting in the first hoursNo respiratory distress of any kind
MethemoglobinemiaOxidized hemoglobin iron cannot carry oxygenPersistent cyanosis that does not improve with crying or with oxygenHis cyanosis clears every time he cries
Neonatal sepsisBacterial infection with varied, nonspecific signsTemperature instability, lethargy, poor feedingNormal temperature; vigorous; blue only at the breast
Intraventricular hemorrhageGerminal matrix bleed, mainly in preterm infantsLethargy, hypotonia, apnea, seizures; found on head ultrasoundTerm infant with a normal neurologic picture
Management, in one line Support RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) with CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure). Reserve mechanical ventilation and exogenous surfactant for severe or failing cases. In the heart branch, management is instead a prostaglandin infusion to hold the duct open; in the pulmonary-hypertension branch, it is inhaled nitric oxide ⚠︎. For the nasal obstruction, the first step is an oral airway with orogastric feeding to bypass the obstruction, and definitive treatment is surgical repair.
Decision spine Is he working to breathe? — Grunting, flaring, retracting → lung, not heart · Does oxygen help? — 65% to 92% → not a fixed right-to-left shunt, so not transposition · Do the limbs differ? — No → nothing is shunting across the duct · How old is he? — Thirty minutes → the duct is still open; ductal-dependent lesions have not declared · What does the film show? — Ground-glass with air bronchograms in a 32-weeker → surfactant deficiency · If every examination finding is normal — sort by the trigger: worse with feeding and better with crying is nasal obstruction; worse with crying is a tet spell; unchanged by either is a fixed shunt.
FigureApproach to neonatal cyanosisshow

Redrawn rather than reproduced. The one deliberate change from the usual published version: echocardiography and prostaglandin are shown as separate steps with the stability gate between them, because bundling them is what makes the sequencing question hard.

Scenario bank
  1. 32 wk, 30 minutes old, grunting and retracting, saturation 65% correcting to 92% on oxygen, ground-glass with air bronchograms → Respiratory distress syndrome → Surfactant deficiency
  2. 32 wk with respiratory distress syndrome at 30 minutes of life, breathing spontaneously → Start CPAP → Surfactant and intubation are reserved for severe disease
  3. 32 wk on CPAP with a rising oxygen requirement and worsening retractions at 6 hours → Intubate and give exogenous surfactant → CPAP has failed
  4. Term newborn at 14 hours, cyanosis with comfortable tachypnea and no retractions, clear lungs, a loud single S2, equal pulses, saturation unchanged on 100% oxygen → Obtain echocardiography → an anatomic right-to-left shunt; prostaglandin is added only if the infant is unstable
  5. Term after meconium-stained fluid, distress, right hand 95% and foot 78%, film clear with decreased vascularity → Inhaled nitric oxide → Persistent pulmonary hypertension
  6. Why an infant with respiratory distress syndrome grunts → To generate end-expiratory pressure and keep alveoli open → Flaring lowers airway resistance
  7. 2-hour-old, cyanotic when latched at the breast, pink when crying, no murmur, clear lungs, normal four-extremity pressures → Bilateral choanal atresia → Obligate nasal breathing
  8. Newborn with cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying → Pass a catheter through each naris→ CT or nasal endoscopy confirms it
  9. 6-month-old with tetralogy of Fallot, sudden deep cyanosis and inconsolable crying → Knee-to-chest positioning with supplemental oxygen → A tet spell, triggered by crying
  10. Why crying temporarily relieves the cyanosis of bilateral choanal atresia → Crying bypasses the obstructed nose→ by opening the oral airway; Neonates are obligate nasal breathers
  11. Term newborn with cyanosis unimproved on 100% oxygen and a single S2, now with weak pulses, poor perfusion and a falling blood pressure → Start prostaglandin E1 and obtain echocardiography → instability licenses the drug before the picture
  12. Why supplemental oxygen fails to raise the saturation in transposition of the great arteries → Parallel circulations bypass the lungs→ systemic blood bypasses the lungs entirely; a fixed anatomic right-to-left shunt
  13. Term newborn cyanotic from the first hours with a loud single S2 and no murmur, unimproved on oxygen → Transposition of the great arteries → mixing flow is too low-velocity to make a murmur
  14. 1-day-old F, pulse oximetry 99% right hand and 91% right foot, well appearing, no cyanosis, femoral and brachial pulses 2+ → Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn → inhaled nitric oxide if severe
  15. Newborn at 5 minutes of life, HR 120, RR 50, vigorous cry, flexing extremities, cyanosis of hands feet and circumoral area with pink mucous membranes → Reassurance and routine care → acrocyanosis
  16. 6-day-old breastfed M, unconjugated bilirubin 14, weight 11% below birth weight, 3 wet diapers on day 5, nursing every 4 hours, mother milk just came in → Breastfeed every 2 to 3 hours and follow up in 1 day → lactation failure jaundice
  17. 10-day-old breastfed F, unconjugated bilirubin 16, weight appropriate, 8 wet diapers daily, nursing well every 2 to 3 hours → Breast milk jaundice → continue breastfeeding and monitor
  18. 1-day-old term boy whose face turns blue within a minute of every feed and pinks up when he cries; normal heart and lung exam, pulse oximetry 97% in the right hand and 96% in the foot; a catheter cannot be passed through either naris beyond the nasopharynx → Oral airway and orogastric feeding → Bilateral choanal atresia; confirm with CT or nasal endoscopy, then surgical repair
Decoy note Antenatal glucocorticoids are genuinely protective, but they only lower the risk of RDS (respiratory distress syndrome); they do not treat it away. A grade 1/6 murmur is soft and non-specific. In a 30-minute-old it is almost certainly a physiologically open duct rather than a lesion. PPROM (preterm prelabor rupture of membranes) with intrapartum penicillin points to group B streptococcal pneumonia, whose film is indistinguishable from RDS. In practice the ambiguity remains ⚠︎. In the normal-examination case, six normal findings each exclude one diagnosis, and the only positive finding is the timing. A primigravida with an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery, and an infant who voided and passed meconium, are inert findings. They only establish that the baby is well, which is the precondition for the sort.
Pearls Grunting with retractions that improves on oxygen is lung disease; in a preterm infant with ground-glass and air bronchograms that is surfactant deficiency. · Work of breathing is the first sort: grunting, flaring and retractions mean lung; comfortable tachypnea with cyanosis means heart. · Oxygen is diagnostic and therapeutic: it separates alveolar disease from a fixed shunt and treats RDS (respiratory distress syndrome). It is occasionally harmful, because it constricts the duct a ductal-dependent lesion needs ⚠︎. · A lesion that depends on the duct presents when the duct closes, from about 12 hours onward. Cyanosis in the delivery room is lung disease, failed transition or transposition. · Antenatal glucocorticoids stimulate fetal surfactant synthesis and lower the risk of RDS; a dosed 32-week infant can still have it. · Hypoxia in RDS is self-amplifying. Collapse causes hypoxia, hypoxia constricts the pulmonary vasculature, and the resulting right-to-left shunt deepens the cyanosis. Shunt physiology can therefore be present without a shunt lesion. · Newborns are obligate nasal breathers. Nasal obstruction therefore gives cyanosis that worsens when the mouth is occluded by feeding and improves when it opens with crying. · The inverse pattern is the tet spell: cyanosis worsens with crying and agitation and is relieved by knee-to-chest positioning ⚠︎. · Pass a catheter through each naris first. It is a free bedside test, and imaging only confirms what the catheter suggested. · Choanal atresia may belong to CHARGE (coloboma, heart defects, atresia choanae, retardation of growth, genital and ear abnormalities). Unilateral disease often goes unrecognized until childhood, when it presents as chronic unilateral nasal discharge. · Tachypnea without distress points to the heart: fast breathing with no flaring, grunting or retractions, and clear lungs. Work of breathing points to the lung. · A loud single S2 with no murmur is characteristic of transposition. The absent murmur is a positive finding rather than a missing one, because flow through the mixing shunts is too low-velocity to generate sound.
Pairs with Part II Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the film-based sort among the parenchymal causes. Part I Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesion catalog once the sort points to the heart. Part II Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia covers the newborn clock (which diagnosis belongs at which hour) and includes choanal atresia in its minutes-to-hours group. Ask: is he working to breathe, does oxygen help, do the limbs differ, and does the cyanosis change with what he is doing? Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers the step after a positive catheter test: which syndrome includes the choanal atresia. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers acrocyanosis as the decoy beside a trisomy 18 murmur; ask: are the lips and tongue pink?
Transferable rule When a finding has both a lung and a heart cause, sort by physiology before naming a disease. The bedside triad of work of breathing, oxygen response and a pre-to-postductal difference decides which group of diagnoses to consider. When the sort finds nothing abnormal, the pattern in time is the key finding. A trigger that runs the opposite way excludes the lesion it resembles.
Unchecked attributeContinuous positive airway pressure: a respiratory rate of 66 reads as distress, but the stem negates flaring, grunting and retractions and reports clear lungs. The rate was checked and the work of breathing was not.
Salient decoyd-Transposition of the great arteries: Transposition gives cyanosis without grunting or retractions, and oxygen does not improve it; the stem shows both the retractions and a rise to 92%
True-fact-wrong-slotPersistent pulmonary hypertension: That is a consequence of the atelectasis, not the primary disease; PPHN (persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn) gives a preductal-postductal gradient and a clear film, and neither is present
Mirror twinTransient tachypnea of the newborn: it is mild and gives perihilar streaking with fluid in the fissures; this infant has severe distress and a ground-glass film
Unchecked attributeCoarctation of the aorta: The duct does not begin to constrict until about 12 hours; at 30 minutes it is open, and coarctation would show a lower postductal saturation, not equal ones
True-fact-wrong-slotTetralogy of Fallot: its trigger is inverted. Tet spells come with crying and agitation, which is what turns this baby pink, and a murmur would be expected
Class-vs-memberTracheoesophageal fistula with esophageal atresia: Aspiration through a fistula brings coughing, choking and respiratory distress; this infant latched, sucked well, and has clear lungs
Class-vs-memberLaryngomalacia: It obstructs at the larynx and announces itself with inspiratory stridor, which is explicitly absent; cyanosis is uncommon

Kawasaki Disease

Medium-vessel vasculitis · a 10-day clock · fever for 5 days plus 4 criteria: treat now?

ScriptStem cuesDiagnosisManagementPreventionComplicationsPractice
Bottom line

Diagnosis is clinical: fever for 5 days or more plus at least 4 of 5 CRASH criteria. IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) must be given within 10 days of fever onset, with aspirin, and an echocardiogram is obtained at diagnosis. Treat now; do not delay it for a workup. Sterile pyuria is a feature of Kawasaki disease. Kawasaki disease causes urethritis, giving urinary white blood cells with no bacteria.

Exception: with only 2 or 3 criteria (incomplete disease, especially in infants under 6 months), use CRP (C-reactive protein) and ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate), supplemental labs and echocardiography, and treat if they are supportive.

Illness script
Kawasaki disease
What it isMedium-vessel vasculitis that targets the coronary arteries
DriverImmune-mediated arteritis; the cause is unknown
TriggersNone proven; age under 5 and Asian ancestry, especially Japanese, raise risk (non-modifiable)
WhoYoung children; infants under 6 months have the most atypical presentations
LooksFever for 5 days or more with the CRASH findings; irritable
LabsAnemia, low albumin, high ALT (alanine aminotransferase), sterile pyuria; platelets high after day 7
CourseUntreated, coronary aneurysm risk is ~20–25%; IVIG within 10 days lowers it to ~3–5%
Chain: Kawasaki disease

Vasculitis

→ an immune response inflames medium-sized arteries

→ the coronary arteries are the main target

Structural

→ the inflamed coronary wall dilates into an aneurysm

→ the aneurysm can expand, rupture or clot

Clinical

→ myocardial ischemia or infarction

→ heart failure: fast breathing, fast pulse, low blood pressure, big heart

How it hides in a stem
