Cardiovascular

1 briefAquifer · Case-Based Briefs

Cardiovascular

High Blood Pressure in a Child or Adolescent

High automated reading at a sports physical · confirm by auscultation, then stage

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo M at a pre-participation examination for football; feels well; no illnesses, medications or family history; BMI 29; automated oscillometric reading 138/88 mm Hg, stated as the 95th percentile for age and height, then 140/89 mm Hg on the same device; rest of the examination normal · Q — the most appropriate next step in diagnosis; options spanned auscultatory measurement, echocardiography, 24-hour ambulatory monitoring and repeat device readings daily for 3 days or in 2 weeks
The decision point

Automated oscillometric devices tend to read higher than auscultation for both systolic and diastolic pressure. A high device reading needs confirmation by auscultation, even after the same device has repeated it. Take at least two auscultatory readings at that visit and average them. The averaged auscultatory value sets the category and the recheck interval.

From age 13, the 2017 AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) guideline uses fixed cutoffs that match the adult categories. By those cutoffs, 138/88 mm Hg falls in stage 1 and 140/89 mm Hg in stage 2. Device readings are not staged until auscultation confirms them. Ambulatory monitoring, echocardiography and drug therapy all come after that confirmation.

Defining criteria, age 13 and older Confirming a high reading — repeat by auscultation at the same visit and average the readings; a device reading alone is not staged · Elevated blood pressure — systolic 120 to 129 mm Hg with diastolic below 80 mm Hg · Stage 1 hypertension — 130/80 to 139/89 mm Hg · Stage 2 hypertension — 140/90 mm Hg or higher · Hypertension diagnosis — auscultatory-confirmed readings of 130/80 mm Hg or higher at 3 separate visits
Management ladder — high blood pressure in an adolescent
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Screening reading at a routine visit; an oscillometric device is acceptable. Yearly from age 3, and at every visit with obesity, kidney disease, diabetes, prior coarctation or a drug that raises blood pressureReading of 120/80 mm Hg or higher
2Repeat by auscultation at the same visit, at least 2 readings, and average themAveraged auscultatory value in the elevated or hypertensive range; that value sets the stage
3Recheck by auscultation on a schedule set by stage: elevated, lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 months; stage 1, lifestyle advice and recheck in 1 to 2 weeks; stage 2, lifestyle advice and specialty referral within 1 weekElevated readings for 1 year, or stage 1 readings at 3 visits
424-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to confirm hypertensionHypertension confirmed: evaluate for secondary causes and end-organ damage
5Lifestyle change first: the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet and moderate to vigorous activity 3 to 5 days a week. Echocardiography for left ventricular hypertrophy when drug therapy is consideredLifestyle change fails, especially with left ventricular hypertrophy, symptoms or stage 2 without a modifiable cause: start a drug
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo M at a football pre-participation examination, well, BMI 29, automated oscillometric blood pressure 138/88 mm Hg and 140/89 mm Hg on repeat with the same device, otherwise normal examination → Blood pressure measurement by auscultation → the averaged auscultatory readings set the stage
  2. 15 yo F at a well visit with an automated reading of 136/82 mm Hg; two auscultatory readings at the same visit average 132/78 mm Hg → Stage 1 hypertension → a systolic of 130 to 139 mm Hg sets stage 1 even with a diastolic below 80
  3. 14 yo M at a well visit whose auscultatory readings average 124/76 mm Hg, with a normal examination → Lifestyle advice and recheck in 6 months → elevated blood pressure
  4. 16 yo F with obesity whose auscultatory averages are 134/84, 132/82 and 136/86 mm Hg at three visits over 3 months → 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring → confirms hypertension before workup and treatment
  5. 17 yo M, asymptomatic with a normal examination, whose auscultatory readings at one visit average 146/94 mm Hg → Lifestyle advice and referral within 1 week → stage 2 hypertension
  6. 16 yo M with obesity and hypertension confirmed by ambulatory monitoring whose blood pressure stays high after a trial of diet and exercise, so drug therapy is planned → Echocardiography → measures left ventricular mass before drug therapy
Guideline history The 2004 Fourth Report defined hypertension as a reading at or above the 95th percentile at every age, and older questions still use that definition. The 2017 AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) guideline set fixed adult cutoffs from age 13 and kept percentiles only for children under 13. Under 13, stage 1 starts at the 95th percentile for sex, age and height, or at 130/80 mm Hg if that is lower. From age 13, stage 1 starts at 130/80 mm Hg regardless of percentile.
Exit ramps A symptomatic adolescent, or a reading above 180/120 mm Hg, goes to the emergency department · Stage 1 or stage 2 readings call for a leg blood pressure; an arm reading higher than the leg suggests coarctation of the aorta · Confirmed hypertension opens a search for secondary causes and end-organ damage
Pearls Electrocardiography is not used to look for left ventricular hypertrophy in a hypertensive child; echocardiography is · Lifestyle change aimed at obesity is the first treatment for most adolescent hypertension · How NBME framed it: with the device reading already repeated, the key is a measurement method, not a diagnosis, heart test or later recheck
Pairs with Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers confirmation, baseline tests and drug choice in adults. Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers the causes to test for once hypertension is confirmed.
Transferable rule A high blood pressure from an automated device is confirmed by averaged auscultatory readings before it is staged, monitored, imaged or treated.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography looks for left ventricular hypertrophy once drug therapy is considered, and this reading is not yet confirmed.
Sequencing trapAmbulatory monitoring is accurate, but it follows auscultatory office readings that stay elevated for 1 year or in stage 1 across 3 visits.
Unchecked attributeDaily device readings for 3 days repeat the same overestimate; the method must change, not the number of readings.
True-fact-wrong-slotA 1 to 2 week recheck follows stage 1 confirmed by auscultation, but a repeat device reading in 2 weeks confirms nothing.

Pulmonary 11 topics + 0 Aquifer

Occupational and exposure histories dominate here — and they are as often bait as they are the answer. Check the lobe and the pleura before trusting the resume.

Obstructive Lung Disease

asthma vs COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) by spirometry · alpha-1 antitrypsin · what lowers COPD mortality · long-term oxygenIs the obstruction reversible, and does the intervention change survival or only symptoms?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Reversibility is a measurement: spirometry before and after a bronchodilator separates asthma from COPD; relief after albuterol does not.

  • Asthma: FEV1 (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) rises 12% or more and 200 mL or more; the ratio often normalizes.
  • COPD: post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC (forced vital capacity) below 0.70; obstruction persists despite some improvement.
  • Asthma-COPD overlap: long-standing asthma, smoking, fixed obstruction; include an inhaled corticosteroid (ICS).

In COPD, rank interventions by outcome. These lower mortality:

  • Smoking cessation: first-line while the patient still smokes.
  • Long-term oxygen: for resting hypoxemia that meets the criteria below.
  • Others: annual influenza vaccination; lung volume reduction surgery in severe upper-lobe emphysema with low exercise capacity; nocturnal noninvasive ventilation for chronic daytime hypercapnia.

Bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, macrolides and roflumilast reduce symptoms or exacerbations, with no survival benefit shown as single additions; the Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) cites triple-therapy data, not verified here ⚠︎. Pulmonary rehabilitation improves dyspnea, fatigue and quality of life.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Asthma – onset in childhood or early adulthood; episodic, variable, trigger-driven, often atopic; reversible obstruction · COPD – progressive, usually after 40 and years of smoking; post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 · Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency – emphysema in the young or minimal smoker, panlobular and worst at the bases; liver disease from misfolded protein: neonatal cholestasis, later cirrhosis
Management and treatment
Long-term oxygen: who qualifies
ThresholdApplies whenThen
PaO2 (arterial oxygen pressure) 55 mm Hg or less, or SaO2 (arterial oxygen saturation) 88% or lessAt rest; not for exertional or nocturnal hypoxemia aloneOxygen 15 hours a day or more, titrated to SaO2 90 to 94%
PaO2 59 mm Hg or less, or SaO2 89% or lessWith cor pulmonale or secondary polycythemia (hematocrit over 55%)Oxygen; reversing hypoxic vasoconstriction protects the right heart
By diagnosis Asthma – inhaled corticosteroid, with or without a long-acting beta-agonist · COPD – long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta-agonist; add an inhaled corticosteroid for frequent exacerbations with eosinophils of 300/μL or more · Secondary polycythemia – treat the hypoxemia, not the number; phlebotomy only for symptomatic hyperviscosity, typically hematocrit over 65% · Polycythemia vera – all three cell lines up, low erythropoietin, a JAK2 (Janus kinase 2) mutation
Practice
  1. 68-year-old man with COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) is seen for follow-up former smoker, quit 2 years ago already on a long-acting bronchodilator pair No ankle edema PaO2 52 mm Hg at rest on room air · hematocrit 46% → Long-term oxygen therapy → a resting PaO2 of 55 mm Hg or less meets the standard criterion: long-term oxygen, which lowers mortality
  2. 68-year-old man with COPD asks what else reduces mortality stopped smoking 3 years ago already completed pulmonary rehabilitation and is vaccinated Dyspnea on one flight of stairs SaO2 87% at rest on room air · hematocrit 49% → Long-term oxygen if hypoxemic → with cessation already done, long-term oxygen for resting hypoxemia is a remaining intervention that lowers mortality; bronchodilators and roflumilast treat symptoms
  3. 68-year-old man with stable COPD has ankle edema from cor pulmonale jugular venous distension, loud pulmonic second sound ruddy, plethoric face PaO2 57 mm Hg at rest · SaO2 89% · hematocrit 57% · white cells and platelets normal → Start long-term oxygen → cor pulmonale or a hematocrit over 55% lowers the gate to PaO2 59 mm Hg or SaO2 89%: start oxygen now
  4. 68-year-old man with COPD still smokes a pack a day two exacerbations this year asks which single step most improves survival No oxygen requirement SaO2 93% at rest · FEV1 48% of predicted → Smoking cessation → smoking cessation gives the largest mortality benefit available; oxygen is for resting hypoxemia, which he lacks
  5. 68-year-old man with COPD is referred to pulmonary rehabilitation asks what it will achieve breathless walking to the mailbox Stopped smoking last year SaO2 92% at rest · FEV1 45% of predicted → Improved symptoms and quality of life → rehabilitation improves dyspnea, fatigue and quality of life; it does not raise lung function
  6. 68-year-old man with COPD has had 3 exacerbations this year on a long-acting bronchodilator pair for 2 years inhaler technique and adherence checked Former smoker SaO2 93% at rest · blood eosinophils 340/μL → Add an inhaled corticosteroid → eosinophils of 300/μL or more with frequent exacerbations: adding an inhaled corticosteroid reduces exacerbations
  7. 24-year-old woman has 6 months of episodic wheeze and cough worse with exercise and cold air symptom-free between episodes Spirometry today is normal Afebrile · SaO2 98% · lungs clear on exam → Methacholine challenge → suspected asthma with normal spirometry: methacholine challenge; a negative test rules out asthma
  8. 62-year-old man has 3 years of progressive exertional dyspnea 40 pack-years of smoking daily cough with sputum No childhood wheeze or allergies Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.62 · FEV1 up 6% after albuterol → COPD → a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 with little reversibility is COPD: a long-acting muscarinic antagonist and beta-agonist
  9. 30-year-old woman has episodic wheeze and chest tightness each spring eczema as a child; hay fever never smoked Symptom-free between episodes Afebrile · pre-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.66 · post 0.78, FEV1 up 18% and 350 mL → Asthma → a 12% and 200 mL rise with a normalized ratio is reversible obstruction: asthma, treated with an inhaled corticosteroid
  10. 40-year-old man has 2 years of progressive exertional dyspnea minimal smoking history: 5 pack-years, quit at 25 CT: emphysema worst in the lower lobes Mildly raised liver enzymes Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58 → Alpha-1 antitrypsin level → emphysema under about 45, little smoking, lower lobes, and liver involvement: alpha-1 antitrypsin level
  11. 34-year-old woman with asthma has worsening control despite high-dose inhalers coughs up brown mucus plugs most mornings CT: central bronchiectasis Aspergillus precipitins positive; skin test to Aspergillus positive Afebrile · eosinophils 1,400/μL · IgE 2,600 international units per mL → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → refractory asthma with brown plugs and central bronchiectasis is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA): oral steroids and itraconazole
  12. 70-year-old woman with COPD has had 2 hospitalized exacerbations this year on a long-acting bronchodilator pair uses her inhalers correctly Quit smoking 10 years ago SaO2 92% at rest · blood eosinophils 360/μL → Add ICS → frequent exacerbations with eosinophils of 300/μL or more: add an inhaled corticosteroid
  13. 29-year-old man has 3 months of dry cough worse at night and when he runs in cold air no heartburn; takes no medications Never smoked; no postnasal drip Afebrile · spirometry normal · chest x-ray normal → Cough-variant asthma → isolated cough worse at night and with cold air and normal spirometry is cough-variant asthma
  14. 55-year-old woman, a long-standing asthmatic who smokes, is breathless breathless on most days for a year, not only in attacks obstruction no longer fully reverses Prior inhaled corticosteroid response Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.64 · FEV1 up 9% → Asthma-COPD overlap → long-standing asthma with smoking and fixed obstruction is asthma-COPD overlap; the regimen must include an inhaled corticosteroid
  15. 60-year-old man, a smoker, has chronic airflow obstruction productive cough for years and progressive dyspnea barrel chest The team must decide between emphysema and chronic bronchitis as the main process Afebrile · post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.60 → DLCO → the diffusing capacity (DLCO) is low in emphysema, normal in chronic bronchitis, and normal or high in asthma
  16. 15-year-old boy has had a wet cough since infancy recurrent sinusitis and two pneumonias digital clubbing; weight below the 5th percentile Never smoked; eats well but stays thin Afebrile · SaO2 94% · chest x-ray: hyperinflation → Cystic fibrosis → clubbing with a lifelong wet cough and poor growth points to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride test; clubbing is not a feature of COPD or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
How NBME framed it: question 1

16-year-old girl in the emergency department with 3 days of cough with thick yellowish sputum and 1 day of shortness of breath No fever. Asthma on albuterol and inhaled corticosteroids, hospitalized 10 times between ages 8 and 10 Smokes 1.5 packs a day for 4 years T 37 °C · pulse 102/min · respirations 42/min · BP 108/80 mm Hg mild clubbing; increased anteroposterior chest diameter; occasional end-expiratory wheezes chest x-ray: severe bilateral hyperinflation, nothing else

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Congenital lobar emphysema: emphysema and hyperinflation; but it overinflates one lobe, not both lungs diffusely, and alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is more common.
  • Kartagener syndrome: thick sputum and clubbing; but there is no situs inversus, chronic sinusitis or lifelong wet cough.
  • Pulmonary sequestration: a congenital lung lesion; but it gives recurrent pneumonia in one region, and this film shows only hyperinflation.
  • Sarcoidosis: chronic lung disease in the young; but there is no hilar adenopathy or infiltrate.

Down to two: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency or Kartagener syndrome. Emphysema this young, with barrel chest and diffuse hyperinflation, points to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency: unopposed neutrophil elastase, panlobular and basal; misfolded protein in the liver causes cirrhosis. The common answer (severe asthma in a smoker) is not offered, the childhood asthma admissions pull toward it, and the clubbing is a planted pull toward Kartagener syndrome. Confirm with a serum alpha-1 antitrypsin level.

Pairs with Asthma covers severity and step therapy once asthma is confirmed. Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease covers ABPA and the structural lung. Ask: which test measures the defining variable?
Transferable rule

When two choices test the same variable, pick the one that yields a number. An association is not a discriminator, and an intervention is ranked by the outcome the question names.

Chronic Cough

Failed empiric trials eliminate causes

The decision point

Chronic cough (>8 weeks) with a normal chest X-ray comes down to three causes: upper airway cough syndrome, asthma, and GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease). A completed empiric trial is a diagnostic test. Antihistamines and decongestants are the diagnostic trial for upper airway cough syndrome. Failure of that trial ("did not respond to antihistamines and decongestants") effectively excludes it.

Chronic cough — cause → clue → diagnostic move
CauseCluesDiagnostic moveConfirms, then
UACSupper airway cough syndrome / postnasal dripThroat clearing, drainage, cobblestoningEmpiric antihistamine/decongestant — response is the diagnosisResponse to the trial confirms; no response effectively excludes it
Cough-variant asthmaNocturnal + triggers (cold, exercise), ± wheezeSpirometry → methacholine challenge; empiric ICSPositive methacholine challenge when spirometry is normal; cough resolves on ICS
GERDWorse supine/after meals; often silent — no heartburn in 40–75%Empiric PPI × 8 weeks; pH monitoring if refractoryCough resolves on the PPI; if all three trials fail, refer for further testing
ACE inhibitorCheck the med list — onset days to months after startingStop the drug (resolves in 1–4 weeks)Cough resolves off the drug; switch to an ARB if needed
PostinfectiousRecent URI, self-limited<8 weeks by definitionResolves by 8 weeks; if not, work up as chronic cough
Lung cancer / TB Can't missWeight loss, hemoptysis, risk factorsCXR first in all chronic coughAbnormal film or red flags: chest CT, then biopsy; sputum for acid-fast bacilli if TB
Scenario bank
  1. 45 yo F, 3 months of cough, normal chest X-ray, post-nasal drip and throat clearing → Upper airway cough syndrome → first-generation antihistamine trial
  2. 45 yo F on lisinopril with 3 months of dry cough → ACE-inhibitor cough → stop the drug
  3. 45 yo F whose cough is worse at night and with cold air, spirometry normal → Cough-variant asthma → methacholine challenge
  4. 45 yo F with cough and heartburn after failed antihistamine and inhaled steroid trials → Gastroesophageal reflux → proton pump inhibitor trial
  5. 45 yo F, smoker, cough with hemoptysis and 6 kg weight loss → Malignancy → chest CT
  6. 45 yo F with cough for 5 weeks after a viral illness, normal chest X-ray → Postinfectious cough → observation
  7. 55 yo M with 10 weeks of cough and no imaging yet → Chest X-ray → first in all chronic cough, before any empiric trial
  8. 45 yo F on lisinopril with 3 months of dry cough and a normal chest X-ray → Stop lisinopril → ACE-inhibitor cough resolves in 1 to 4 weeks
  9. 30 yo M with chronic cough at night and with exercise and cold air; normal exam and normal spirometry → Methacholine challenge → normal spirometry does not exclude cough-variant asthma
  10. 45 yo F with 3 months of dry cough, normal chest X-ray and no heartburn, after failed antihistamine-decongestant and inhaled corticosteroid trials → Proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks → GERD cough is often silent; the failed trials have eliminated the other two
Transferable rule When a stem says "did not respond to X," it is not giving history; it eliminates the cause X treats. Read treatment failures as eliminations. Nocturnal dry cough with a normal exam and everything else normal is GERD (gastroesophageal reflux disease) until proven otherwise.

Occupational Lung Disease

Matching occupational exposure to lung disease

The decision point

The occupation identifies the dust, and the lobe distribution and pleural involvement confirm it. Asbestosis is the exception: it affects the lower lobes and involves the pleura. Everything else with a mining/quarry history affects the upper lobes.

Occupational lung diseases
DiseaseExposureLobesThe tellAssociation
AsbestosisBrake linings, shipyard, insulation, plumbing, roofingLOWERPleural plaques; ferruginous bodiesBronchogenic CA > mesothelioma; smoking multiplies bronchogenic only
SilicosisSandblasting, mining, foundry, stone countertopsUPPEREggshell calcification of hilar nodes↑ TB risk — annual PPD
Coal workers'Coal miningUPPERCoal macules → progressive massive fibrosisCaplan syndrome (+ RA nodules)
BerylliosisAerospace, nuclearDiffuseNoncaseating granulomas — sarcoid mimicResponds to steroids
ByssinosisCotton / textile mills—"Monday fever" — worse at the start of the work weekObstructive
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisMoldy hay, birds—Episodic fever/cough hours after exposureAvoidance cures
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Chest X-rayFirstUpper versus lower zones; pleural plaques; eggshell hilar nodesUpper: silica or coal; lower with plaques: asbestos
High-resolution CT of the chestSupportsFibrosis pattern with or without pleural plaquesDefines distribution; plaques alone mark exposure and are benign
Pulmonary function testsStagingRestrictive pattern with a low DLCOSeverity of fibrosis; byssinosis is obstructive instead
None: exposure history plus imagingConfirmsNamed dust, typical distribution, latency of decadesBiopsy only when the picture is atypical
Beryllium lymphocyte proliferation testBy branchPositive in a granulomatous pictureBerylliosis rather than sarcoidosis
Tuberculin skin test, yearlyBy branchPositive in a patient with silicosisLatent TB, which silicosis makes more likely
CT and pleural biopsyBy branchPleural mass with an effusionMesothelioma after asbestos exposure
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M shipyard insulator with lower-lobe fibrosis and pleural plaques → Asbestosis
  2. 55 yo M sandblaster with upper-lobe nodules and eggshell-calcified hilar nodes → Silicosis
  3. 58 yo M coal miner with upper-lobe nodules and black sputum → Coal workers' pneumoconiosis
  4. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with noncaseating granulomas on biopsy → Berylliosis
  5. 45 yo F cotton mill worker with chest tightness worst on the first day back at work → Byssinosis
  6. 40 yo M pigeon breeder with fever and dyspnea 6 hours after exposure → Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
  7. 62 yo M with asbestos exposure, a pleural mass and an effusion → Mesothelioma
  8. 55 yo M sandblaster and never smoker with silicosis → Annual tuberculin skin test → silicosis raises tuberculosis risk
  9. 66 yo M, retired shipyard worker, asymptomatic, with calcified pleural plaques and normal lung parenchyma on imaging → No treatment → plaques alone mark exposure and are benign
  10. 62 yo M with decades of asbestos exposure who also smokes heavily → Bronchogenic carcinoma → smoking multiplies bronchogenic risk only, not mesothelioma
  11. 50 yo M aerospace machinist with progressive dyspnea and noncaseating granulomas on biopsy, now removed from exposure → Oral corticosteroids → berylliosis responds to steroids
Mnemonic and timing Asbestos comes from the roof but affects the base; silica and coal come from the ground but affect the top. Latency is typically 20–30 years, so exposure that ended decades ago still counts. Pleural plaques alone are a marker of exposure, benign, and need no treatment.
Transferable rule Answering a long stem in under 40 seconds means one cue was pattern-matched and the verification pass was skipped. This costs the most in occupational stems. The lobe distribution usually decides the diagnosis, and it comes at the end of the stem.

Rhinitis

Step-up therapy in the right order

The decision point

For moderate-to-severe seasonal rhinitis that has failed antihistamines, step up to an intranasal corticosteroid. It is the single most effective drug class for allergic rhinitis. A visit in "late winter" points to prophylaxis: start it ~2 weeks before pollen season. The steroid suppresses the mucosal inflammatory response and needs lead time.

Option analysis — why each fails
ChoiceWhy it fails
Minimize outdoor activitiesImpractical for pollen (unlike dust mites or pets); inadequate once disease is complicated
Continue OTC antihistaminesAlready failing — and first-generation agents bring sedation and anticholinergic effects
Desensitization (immunotherapy)The real bait — the only disease-modifying option, but reserved for failure of maximal pharmacotherapy. He has never tried a nasal steroid
MontelukastLess effective than intranasal steroids; carries an FDA boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects
Oral prednisoneSystemic steroids for a benign chronic condition — never the answer
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F with moderate seasonal rhinitis failing OTC antihistamines → Intranasal corticosteroid
  2. 28 yo F seeking durable control after several drug classes have failed → Allergen immunotherapy
  3. 28 yo F advised to minimize outdoor activity for her pollen allergy → Impractical for pollen, unlike dust-mite control
  4. 28 yo F with rhinitis and asthma who wants a single oral agent → Montelukast — with neuropsychiatric counseling
  5. 28 yo F using oxymetazoline for 10 days with worsening congestion → Rhinitis medicamentosa → stop the spray
  6. 28 yo F with clear rhinorrhea, no itch or sneezing, triggered by temperature change → Vasomotor rhinitis
The ladder Start with allergen avoidance (when practical), then an intranasal corticosteroid. Next, add a second-generation oral or intranasal antihistamine. Use immunotherapy only after pharmacotherapy fails. Any first-generation antihistamine in a stem is usually there to be replaced, not continued.
Sequencing trap

Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease

cystic fibrosis · primary ciliary dyskinesia · antibody deficiency · foreign body · allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis when antibiotics failWhich exam finding could no immune defect produce, and when an adequate antibiotic course fails, are the eosinophils and immunoglobulin E (IgE) up?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Frequency shows that something is wrong; anatomy shows what. Antibiotic-requiring bacterial sinusitis and pneumonia crosses the gate; up to 12 self-limited viral illnesses a year is normal.

  • Heart on the right: the point of maximal impulse in the right chest is situs inversus; only a ciliary defect moves the heart: primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Kartagener syndrome is PCD with situs inversus, recurrent sinusitis and bronchiectasis.
  • Poor growth or greasy stools: cystic fibrosis; sweat chloride.
  • Focal and abrupt after choking: a retained foreign body; bronchoscopy.
  • Normal anatomy with absent tonsils or adolescent or adult onset: an antibody defect; quantitative immunoglobulins.
  • Antibiotics fail in a damaged airway: no improvement after a week of adequate antibiotics or unexplained lung-function decline, with eosinophilia and IgE usually above 1,000 international units (IU)/mL, is allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), an immune response.
  • Bronchiectasis: the endpoint of any retained secretions, never the cause.
Diagnosis
Recurrent infection: the finding that picks the cause
DiagnosisThe stem showsSets it apart
PCD (autosomal recessive dynein-arm defect)Wet cough, otitis and sinusitis from infancy; distress as a term newborn ⚠︎Heart on the right, in about half ⚠︎
Cystic fibrosis (autosomal recessive CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) defect)Inspissated secretions, repeated infection, bronchiectasisFailure to thrive, greasy stools, meconium ileus, nasal polyps; heart on the left
Retained foreign bodyToddler, abrupt choking episodeFocal wheeze; unilateral hyperinflation on expiratory or decubitus film
Antibody deficiencyEncapsulated sinopulmonary infection, normal airway anatomyXLA: absent tonsils and adenoids; common variable immunodeficiency (CVID): adolescent or adult onset
Heterotaxy (situs ambiguus)Congenital heart disease, midline liverAsplenia or polysplenia ⚠︎
When antibiotics fail in a structural lung
DiagnosisThe stem showsSets it apart
Hypersensitivity pneumonitisOrganic antigen; fever, malaise, airspace infiltratesImproves in hospital; no eosinophilia, normal IgE
StrongyloidiasisRural tropics or subtropics; eosinophilia, high IgERoaming urticaria, gastrointestinal symptoms
Granulomatosis with polyangiitisNecrotizing bronchiectasis mimicking refractory pneumoniaOlder men; sinus destruction, hemoptysis, glomerulonephritis; no eosinophilia
Nontuberculous mycobacteriaMycobacterium avium complex in cystic fibrosis bronchiectasisMonths to years; nodular, then cavitary; no eosinophilia or IgE rise
Mechanism Dynein arms – the defect makes airway cilia dysmotile and leaves embryonic nodal cilia unable to set left-right asymmetry, so laterality is randomized · Aspergillus – everyone inhales the spores and the mucociliary escalator clears them; a damaged airway (asthma or cystic fibrosis) traps them, and chronic colonization becomes Th2 hypersensitization
Management
By diagnosis PCD – daily airway clearance · ABPA – systemic glucocorticoid first-line; an antifungal such as voriconazole is added to reduce spore burden; an antifungal alone treats the antigen, not the response · Eosinophilia with tropical exposure – exclude or empirically treat strongyloidiasis before systemic steroids, which convert it to hyperinfection ⚠︎ · Heterotaxy with asplenia – encapsulated-organism prophylaxis ⚠︎ · Cystic fibrosis – annual total IgE screens for ABPA
Practice
  1. 11-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has a week of fever and productive cough no improvement after a week of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia IgE 3,225 IU/mL No travel, rash or gastrointestinal symptoms T 38.4°C · bilateral crackles → Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis → antibiotic failure plus eosinophilia and an IgE more than triple the usual threshold make it allergic, not bacterial. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis improves in hospital and gives no eosinophilia and a normal IgE; granulomatosis with polyangiitis affects older adults, without eosinophilia
  2. 3-year-old girl has had a chronic wet cough since infancy recurrent otitis media since infancy chest film: cardiac silhouette on the right stomach bubble on the right Growth normal for age Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% → Primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) → a heart on the right fits only a ciliary defect: the dynein-arm defect leaves nodal cilia unable to set left-right asymmetry. Cystic fibrosis never moves the heart; heterotaxy is situs ambiguus with asplenia or polysplenia and heart disease ⚠︎. Confirm with nasal nitric oxide, then ciliary electron microscopy
  3. 15-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis has an exacerbation that fails initial therapy sputum grows Pseudomonas resistant to the current antibiotic eosinophil count normal IgE normal T 38.3°C · oxygen saturation 93% → Adjust antibiotics according to culture sensitivities → a resistant organism with normal eosinophils and IgE is still a bacterial exacerbation: adjust to culture sensitivities. Without the allergic markers, neither glucocorticoids nor repeat Aspergillus serology fits
  4. 2-year-old boy has his third pneumonia this year chronic loose, greasy stools weight below the 3rd percentile point of maximal impulse in the left chest No choking episode; tonsils present T 38.6°C · oxygen saturation 95% → Sweat chloride testing → with the heart on the left, poor growth and greasy stools open the cystic fibrosis axis: sweat chloride, 60 mmol/L or more. Immunoglobulins fit normal anatomy without tonsils; nasal nitric oxide fits a ciliary picture with normal growth
  5. 16-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis this week Aspergillus-specific IgE positive CT: mucoid impaction, finger-in-glove opacities Productive cough despite a week of antibiotics T 37.9°C · total IgE 2,600 IU/mL → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → the pathology is allergic inflammation: a systemic glucocorticoid first-line, with an antifungal added to reduce spore burden. Voriconazole alone treats the antigen, not the response; more antibacterial coverage treats an infection that is not there
  6. 14-month-old boy choked while eating nuts 3 weeks ago now a focal right-sided wheeze second right lower lobe pneumonia film: right-sided hyperinflation Well before the choking episode T 38.2°C · oxygen saturation 95% → Rigid bronchoscopy → abrupt onset after choking, focal wheeze and unilateral hyperinflation are a retained foreign body: rigid bronchoscopy finds and removes it. Another antibiotic course or a CT leaves the obstruction in place
  7. 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis comes for her routine annual review feels well baseline cough unchanged No wheeze or new sputum Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% · lung function at her baseline → Total serum IgE → cystic fibrosis earns an annual total serum IgE, one of the few purely serologic screening intervals; CT and skin testing are not the yearly screen
  8. 5-year-old boy has had recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia since 9 months of age no palpable tonsils no cervical lymphadenopathy Heart sounds loudest in the left chest; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Quantitative serum immunoglobulins with B-cell flow cytometry → normal anatomy with absent lymphoid tissue is the antibody axis; all immunoglobulins low with B cells absent is X-linked agammaglobulinemia. Sweat chloride needs poor growth or greasy stools, and ciliary biopsy needs a ciliary picture
  9. 45-year-old man with cystic fibrosis has several months of cough and weight loss CT: nodular and cavitary opacities No hemoptysis; no recent travel eosinophils 2% · IgE 90 IU/mL · oxygen saturation 94% → Nontuberculous mycobacterial lung disease → cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis is colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria such as Mycobacterium avium complex, rather than Mycobacterium tuberculosis: chronic over months to years, nodular then cavitary. No eosinophilia or IgE rise removes the allergic cause
  10. 8-year-old boy has a year-round wet cough unexplained respiratory distress as a term newborn chronic otitis media point of maximal impulse in the left chest Growth and stools normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Nasal nitric oxide measurement → situs inversus appears in only about half of PCD ⚠︎, so a heart on the left does not exclude it; low nasal nitric oxide supports PCD with normal situs. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and a repeat film adds nothing
  11. 34-year-old woman has asthma that is difficult to control recurrent brown mucus plugs central bronchiectasis on CT IgE 2,400 IU/mL Aspergillus skin test positive T 37.2°C · peripheral eosinophilia · oxygen saturation 95% → Systemic glucocorticoids with an antifungal agent → same disease, different structural host: asthma, like cystic fibrosis, traps the spores. A systemic glucocorticoid with an antifungal; more inhaled steroid or antibacterial therapy leaves the allergic response untreated
  12. 3-year-old girl in daycare has had 9 upper respiratory illnesses this year each self-limited without antibiotics normal examination between illnesses Older brother is well growth at the 50th percentile · Afebrile → Normal frequency of childhood viral infection → up to 12 viral illnesses a year is normal in daycare or with older siblings: reassure, no immune workup. Ciliary disease and antibody defects give antibiotic-requiring bacterial infection, not colds that clear alone
  13. 52-year-old man who farms has fever, malaise and airspace infiltrates no response to a week of antibiotics symptoms improve over 3 days in hospital No travel or rash IgE 40 IU/mL · eosinophils 1% → Identify and eliminate the inciting antigen exposure → improvement in hospital, away from the exposure, with a normal IgE and no eosinophilia is hypersensitivity pneumonitis: identify and eliminate the antigen, since removal from the exposure is what brings improvement. The allergic fungal disease needs eosinophilia and a high IgE, and the improvement already explains the picture without a biopsy
  14. 18-month-old boy has had 8 antibiotic courses for sinusitis and pneumonia older brother has the same illness mildly enlarged tonsils point of maximal impulse in the right chest Delivered vaginally without complications oxygen saturation 99% · bilateral rales and rhonchi → Primary ciliary dyskinesia → the heart on the right decides: no antibody defect displaces it. Tonsils exclude X-linked agammaglobulinemia, and 18 months excludes CVID; bilateral rales with a normal saturation argue against a foreign body; the affected brother alone separates none of them
  15. 40-year-old man from the rural tropics has refractory pulmonary infiltrates migratory urticaria abdominal pain IgE 4,100 IU/mL Infiltrates persist after 10 days of antibiotics T 37.8°C · eosinophils 18% · oxygen saturation 94% → Treat for strongyloidiasis before giving systemic glucocorticoids → eosinophilia and a high IgE with roaming urticaria, gut symptoms and tropical exposure are strongyloidiasis: treat it before any systemic glucocorticoid, which risks disseminated hyperinfection ⚠︎. Antituberculous therapy explains neither the eosinophilia nor the urticaria
  16. 4-year-old boy adopted at 6 months has 6 months of nasal obstruction recurrent nosebleeds repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia bilateral nasal polyps; digital clubbing Diffuse coarse crackles weight 3rd, height 5th percentile · oxygen saturation 93% → Cystic fibrosis → nasal polyps, clubbing and poor growth with recurrent infection point to cystic fibrosis: sweat chloride testing; newborn screening misses rarer CFTR mutations. Allergic rhinitis causes neither poor growth nor clubbing, and a vasculitis explains neither in a 4-year-old with recurrent sinopulmonary infection
  17. 15-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 2 weeks of productive cough no improvement after 10 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics peripheral eosinophilia total IgE 1,850 IU/mL No travel or rash Afebrile · oxygen saturation 95% → Aspergillus-specific IgE or Aspergillus skin testing → total IgE suggests; Aspergillus-specific IgE or a skin test confirms sensitization. A sputum culture or galactomannan looks for the fungus, but everyone inhales it: the disease is the immune response
  18. 17-year-old boy has had sinusitis all his life chronic productive cough infertility evaluation with his partner semen analysis: normal sperm count, absent motility No greasy stools; growth normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% → Electron microscopy of respiratory cilia for dynein-arm defects → a normal count with absent motility is the ciliary pattern, and electron microscopy shows the dynein-arm defect. Cystic fibrosis gives obstructive azoospermia from congenital absence of the vas deferens ⚠︎, which a normal count excludes. Klinefelter syndrome typically gives small testes with reduced testosterone, not a normal count with immotile sperm, and no sinusitis
  19. 13-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis was diagnosed with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis sputum has grown Aspergillus repeatedly IgE 2,900 IU/mL Neutrophil count normal; no cavity on CT Afebrile · eosinophils 12% · oxygen saturation 96% → Mucus trapping defeats mucociliary clearance, allowing colonization and Th2 sensitization → everyone inhales the spores, and the mucociliary escalator clears them; trapped mucus allows colonization, then Th2 sensitization. A normal neutrophil count and no cavity remove the other two
  20. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with primary ciliary dyskinesia at age 4 daily purulent sputum high-resolution CT: lower-lobe bronchiectasis crackles at both lung bases Takes no maintenance therapy Afebrile · oxygen saturation 96% → Begin daily airway clearance therapy → the bronchiectasis comes from failed mucociliary clearance, so start daily airway clearance; antibiotics only during exacerbations leave the secretions in place, and resection removes one lobe of a disease of the whole airway
  21. 10-year-old girl has had two pneumococcal bacteremias midline liver complex congenital heart disease no spleen on abdominal imaging Growth normal; no chronic wet cough Afebrile · HR 96/min · oxygen saturation 96% → Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccination plus daily antibiotic prophylaxis → situs ambiguus with no spleen is the functional asplenia of heterotaxy: protect against encapsulated organisms with vaccination and daily prophylaxis ⚠︎. Intravenous immunoglobulin treats an antibody defect, and airway clearance a ciliary one
  22. 4-year-old boy has a chronic wet cough recurrent otitis media recurrent sinusitis since infancy chest film: situs inversus totalis Growth normal; tonsils present; stools normal Afebrile · HR 104/min · oxygen saturation 97% → Dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme → dynein arms power ciliary beating; their defect impairs mucociliary clearance and randomizes laterality. CFTR and Bruton tyrosine kinase defects cause infection but never move the heart
  23. 6-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has recurrent nosebleeds greasy, foul-smelling stools weight below the 3rd percentile repeated antibiotics for sinusitis and pneumonia Bruises easily on the shins platelets 280,000/mm³ · prothrombin time prolonged → Pancreatic insufficiency with vitamin K malabsorption → pancreatic insufficiency causes malabsorption of the fat-soluble vitamins, and vitamin K deficiency causes the bleeding; neither sinus inflammation nor platelet dysfunction prolongs the prothrombin time
Common wrong answers XLA with tonsils present: it has no tonsillar or adenoidal tissue. CVID at 18 months: it presents in adolescence or adulthood. Normal childhood infection: those are viral and need no antibiotics; eight antibiotic courses are a disease pattern. Fever as proof of infection: fever, malaise and blood-streaked sputum are common in ABPA. Broader antibiotics: antibiotic failure is a finding, not a dosing problem; change the category (allergic, mycobacterial, vasculitic) before the spectrum. Tuberculosis: cystic fibrosis airways are colonized by nontuberculous mycobacteria.
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies: the airway is structurally normal, so immunoglobulin levels and the B-cell count decide. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies: what pancreatic insufficiency does to vitamins A, D, E and K; is the prothrombin time long? Part I Obstructive Lung Disease: the adult with brown mucus plugs.
Transferable rule

A physical finding that no immune defect could produce decides the cause of recurrent infection. When a treatment that should work fails, the failure is the finding: change the category of disease, most often infection to hypersensitivity, rather than intensifying treatment.

Hypoxemia

sort by A-a gradient and the oxygen response · Is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia correct when you raise inspired oxygen?

Source vignette Pt — 28 wk preterm, 1 hour old, cyanosis with grunting and increased work of breathing, bilaterally decreased breath sounds · Q — the mechanism of the hypoxemia; options spanned five mechanisms — intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, hypoventilation, diffusion limitation and low inspired oxygen
The decision point

Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds at one hour of life in a 28-weeker indicates diffuse alveolar collapse. Surfactant deficiency raises alveolar surface tension, and the alveoli close. Those units stay perfused while their ventilation falls to zero, so blood crossing them reaches the left heart unoxygenated. This is intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt. Of the five mechanisms listed, it is the only one that produces cyanosis with increased work of breathing and bilaterally reduced air entry.

Defining criteria A-a gradient — alveolar minus arterial PO2. Widened in shunt, V/Q mismatch, and diffusion limitation; normal in hypoventilation and in low inspired PO2. Normal value approximately (age/4) + 4 · Shunt vs V/Q mismatch — shunt is the limiting case of mismatch (V/Q = 0). The gate is the oxygen response: mismatch corrects with modest supplemental oxygen; true shunt barely moves, because blood bypassing ventilated alveoli never sees the higher FiO2 ⚠︎ · Saturation gap — pulse oximetry far below what the measured PaO2 predicts → the hemoglobin is the problem (methemoglobin pins the reading near 85% regardless of the methemoglobin level, and it does not move on 100% oxygen; carboxyhemoglobin is read as oxygenated, so the pulse oximeter is falsely reassuring ⚠︎)
Pertinent positives & negatives Grunting with bilaterally decreased breath sounds — auto-PEEP against closed alveoli; locates the lesion in the parenchyma and excludes both cardiac shunt and central hypoventilation · Increased work of breathing at 1 hour — excludes apnea of prematurity, which appears days later with apnea and bradycardia and no respiratory effort · No murmur, regular rhythm — does not by itself exclude cyanotic heart disease, but with loud parenchymal findings it makes an intracardiac cause the second explanation, not the first · Normal CBC — no anemia to lower content, no leukocytosis. The sepsis workup already running does not explain the hypoxemia; the CBC is typically normal in RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) · Still hypoxemic on 30% oxygen by CPAP — the shunt fraction is large enough that a modest FiO2 cannot overcome it; recruit alveoli rather than raise the oxygen concentration
Hypoxemia — sorting by A&ndash;a gradient and oxygen response
MechanismIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt (V/Q = 0)Alveoli perfused but unventilated — RDS, lobar atelectasis/mucus plug, pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edemaWidened A-a, hypoxemia refractory to raising FiO2, corrected by recruitment (CPAP, PEEP, surfactant)— (the answer)
V/Q mismatch (low but non-zero)Asthma, COPD, early pneumonia, atelectasis in evolutionWidened A-a that corrects on a few liters of oxygen — the commonest mechanism in adult medicineThe question keys the extreme: collapsed alveoli with zero ventilation
Right-to-left shunt outside the lungCyanotic CHD; hepatopulmonary syndrome; PFO opened by high right-sided pressuresNo rise in PaO2 on 100% oxygen; lungs clear, work of breathing normal or minimalGrunting and bilaterally decreased breath sounds — the lungs are abnormal
Dead space (ventilated, not perfused)Pulmonary embolism, low cardiac outputSudden dyspnea with a clear chest; hypercapnia is the primary consequenceBilateral decreased breath sounds; PE is vanishingly rare in young children
Normal-A-a hypoxemia: hypoventilation or low inspired PO2Opioids, neuromuscular disease, obesity hypoventilation, apnea of prematurity · altitude, hypoxic gas mixtureNormal A-a gradient; hypoventilation adds a high PaCO2, altitude does not; both fully correct with a little oxygenTachypnea and grunting — effort is increased, not depressed; he is already receiving 30% oxygen
Abnormal hemoglobin affinity or carryingCO poisoning, methemoglobinemia, fetal hemoglobinNormal PaO2 with cyanosis or a saturation gap; cyanosis unmoved by oxygenNormal Hb, no exposure; fetal hemoglobin's left shift is physiologic and does not cause distress
Management, in one line Diffusion limitation is a seventh category and has no row in the table. It is a chronic, exertional finding (interstitial disease, emphysema) with a low DLCO (diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide). The resting saturation is often normal. The typical patient desaturates only on the walk down the hall. Shunt from collapsed alveoli is treated by reopening them with surfactant plus CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), not by turning the oxygen up.
Decision spine Is the PaO2 low, or only the saturation? — Saturation-only → hemoglobin problem (carbon monoxide, methemoglobin) · Is the A-a gradient normal? — Normal → hypoventilation (high PaCO2) or low inspired PO2 (normal PaCO2) · Widened: what happens on oxygen? — Corrects → V/Q mismatch. Refractory → shunt · Shunt: are the lungs abnormal? — Grunting, decreased breath sounds, infiltrate → intrapulmonary. Clear lungs, no distress → intracardiac or intravascular · Any reason to think dead space? — Sudden onset, clear chest, risk factors; without them, embolus is unlikely
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Arterial blood gas with pulse oximetryFirstSaturation low but PaO2 normalHemoglobin problem, not the lungs
Co-oximetryConfirmsMethemoglobin or carboxyhemoglobin raisedMethemoglobinemia or carbon monoxide poisoning
A-a gradient from the blood gasNextNormal gradientHypoventilation if PaCO2 high; low inspired PO2 if PaCO2 low
Response to supplemental oxygenBy branchWidened gradient that corrects on modest oxygenV/Q mismatch; little change means shunt
Chest X-rayBy branchClear lungs with oxygen-refractory hypoxemiaIntracardiac shunt or embolism: echocardiogram or CT angiography
DLCO with a walk testBy branchLow DLCO, desaturation only on exertionDiffusion limitation: interstitial disease or emphysema
Pulse oximetry alone in suspected CO poisoningSkipReads falsely normalCarboxyhemoglobin is counted as oxygenated; get co-oximetry
Scenario bank
  1. 27 wk preterm M, 3 h old, grunting, ground-glass film with air bronchograms, SpO2 85% on CPAP FiO2 0.6 and rising → Intubate and give intratracheal surfactant → Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome
  2. 24 yo M, POD 1, RR 6, pinpoint pupils, PaO2 55, PaCO2 68, normal A-a gradient → Naloxone → Opioid-induced hypoventilation
  3. 4 mo F, cyanosis after topical teething gel, chocolate-brown blood, SpO2 fixed at 85% on 100% oxygen, PaO2 96 → Methylene blue IV → Methemoglobinemia
  4. 34 yo F and two housemates with headache and nausea after a furnace failure, COHb 18%, no syncope, normal neurologic exam → High-flow 100% oxygen by nonrebreather → Carbon monoxide poisoning
  5. 58 yo M with ARDS, PaO2 58 on FiO2 0.8 with PEEP 8, diffuse bilateral opacities → Increase PEEP → Refractory intrapulmonary shunt
  6. 68 yo M, COPD exacerbation, baseline PaCO2 62, now receiving oxygen → Titrating oxygen to a saturation of 100% → Oxygen-induced hypercapnia
  7. 62 yo F, 8 months of exertional dyspnea, resting SpO2 96% falling to 86% with ambulation, clear lungs, normal chest film → Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide → Diffusion limitation
  8. 44 yo F, POD 5 from knee arthroplasty, sudden dyspnea, clear lungs, normal film, widened A-a gradient → CT pulmonary angiography → Pulmonary embolism
  9. 29 yo M trekker at 4,500 m, dyspnea with SpO2 84%, clear lungs, PaCO2 30, normal A-a gradient → Reduced inspired oxygen tension → Descent; acetazolamide
  10. 72 yo F, POD 2 laparotomy, febrile, SpO2 88%, absent breath sounds at the left base, film shows left lower lobe collapse → Intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt → Incentive spirometry and mobilization
Decoy note The umbilical line and the started antibiotics reflect a sepsis workup. They do not explain the hypoxemia: the CBC (complete blood count) is normal and no fever or instability is reported. Apgar 7 at both marks argues against perinatal depression, which would present as hypoventilation. The absent murmur does not exclude cyanotic heart disease on its own; the parenchymal findings do.
Pearls Normal A-a means hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen; widened and oxygen-responsive means V/Q mismatch; widened and oxygen-refractory means shunt. · Shunt is the hypoxemia that oxygen will not fix. When the FiO2 goes up and the saturation does not follow, stop titrating and start recruiting. Recruit with PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure), CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure), surfactant, drainage, or a diuretic for the edema behind it. · RDS (respiratory distress syndrome) hypoxemia is clinically responsive to oxygen administration. The reason is that partially collapsed alveoli are recruitable by the CPAP delivering that oxygen, not that shunted blood responds to FiO2. · Hypoventilation is the one hypoxemia with a normal A-a gradient and a high PaCO2; low inspired PO2 is the one with a normal gradient and a low PaCO2 from the compensatory hyperventilation. · A normal or high PaO2 in a cyanotic patient means the hemoglobin cannot carry or release oxygen. Causes are methemoglobin, carbon monoxide, or cyanide (where the tissue, not the blood, is the problem). · Boundary: refractory hypoxemia with clear lungs and no cardiac history can still be an embolus. If it raises right-sided pressures enough to open a PFO (patent foramen ovale), a dead-space disease presents as a right-to-left shunt. Look for the cause of the raised pressure, not just the shunt.
Pairs with Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant covers the parenchymal differential by chest film (ground glass and air bronchograms versus retained fluid, meconium, or air leak). Congenital Heart Disease covers the lesions themselves. Cyanosis in the Newborn covers sorting at-rest physiology in the delivery room. This brief covers the mechanism categories above all three. Ask: is the A-a gradient widened, and does the hypoxemia respond to oxygen?
Transferable rule Treat hypoxemia as a physiology question. Compute the A-a gradient, then check what happens on supplemental oxygen. Those two answers name the mechanism before the illness is named.
True-fact-wrong-slotUnderdeveloped medullary respiratory center: Apnea of prematurity appears days later as apnea with bradycardia and no respiratory effort; this infant is grunting and tachypneic at one hour
Salient decoyObstructed pulmonary arterial blood flow: Obstruction creates dead space, not bilaterally reduced breath sounds; embolus is nearly nonexistent in neonates
True-fact-wrong-slotGreater red blood cell oxygen affinity: It is the normal neonatal state; it is physiologic and does not cause respiratory distress
Class-vs-memberIncreased intracardiac left-to-right shunting: Left-to-right recirculates already-oxygenated blood; systemic saturation is unaffected, so it cannot desaturate a newborn

Sickle Cell Disease and Trait

trait or disease: read the electrophoresis first · what each causes · chronic dyspnea: the timing pattern picks the testIs any adult hemoglobin (HbA) present, and are the symptoms nocturnal and intermittent, or exertional and progressive?

Trait or diseaseComplicationsChronic dyspneaPractice
Bottom line
  • Sickle cell trait: HbA about 60% exceeding sickle hemoglobin (HbS) about 40%, with a completely normal complete blood count (CBC).
  • Sickle cell anemia: HbA absent; any HbA at all excludes homozygous disease (HbSS).
  • Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia: HbA present but S exceeds A, with a low mean corpuscular volume (MCV).
  • Newborn screen: FAS (fetal, adult, sickle) is trait, FS (fetal, sickle) is disease; F leads because fetal hemoglobin (HbF) predominates at birth.
  • Chronic dyspnea: nocturnal and intermittent means airway; exertional and progressive means vascular or interstitial.
  • Asthma: a common comorbidity in children and adolescents with sickle cell disease; spirometry with bronchodilator response is the first test.
Trait or disease
Hemoglobin electrophoresis: reading the pattern
ConditionElectrophoresis and CBCThe tell
NormalHbA about 97%, HbA2 (the minor adult hemoglobin) about 2.5%, HbF under 2%; normal CBCReference
Sickle cell traitHbA about 60% over HbS about 40%; completely normal CBCA exceeds S, and no anemia
Sickle cell anemiaHbA 0%, HbS about 90%; anemia, reticulocytes 10 to 20%Absent HbA is the finding
Hemoglobin SCHbA 0%, HbS about equal to hemoglobin C (HbC); milder anemiaRetinopathy and avascular necrosis out of proportion to the anemia
Sickle-beta-zero thalassemiaHbA 0%, HbS high, HbA2 elevated; low MCVLooks like HbSS but microcytic
Sickle-beta-plus thalassemiaHbA present but low, S exceeds A; low MCVThe sharpest mimic of trait
Reading it The inequality – in trait HbA always exceeds HbS, because alpha chains bind normal beta chains with higher affinity; memorize the inequality, not the numbers · HbF after infancy – under 2% by 6 months and 0 to 2% from age 2; a raised HbF later suggests hydroxyurea, a beta-thalassemia or hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin
What each one causes
Trait Painless hematuria – the most common complication: the renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic, the one microenvironment that polymerizes HbS at the 40% a carrier has; spleen, lungs and bones are spared, the vasa recta are not · Splenic infarction – real, at altitude, but uncommon · Renal medullary carcinoma – rare but nearly pathognomonic · Extreme exertion – a real risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis and sudden death, which is why trait matters in athletes and recruits
Disease only Complications – acute chest syndrome, dactylitis, stroke and osteomyelitis; none belongs to a carrier · Sepsis – pneumococcus is the leading cause despite vaccination (non-vaccine serotypes) · Osteomyelitis – Salmonella is the leading cause
Chronic dyspnea in sickle cell disease
Chronic respiratory symptoms in sickle cell disease: the differential
CauseMechanism and tellAgainst it in the night-cough case
AsthmaAirway hyperreactivity; wheeze, tightness or cough, often worse at night, with exercise or with an upper respiratory infection; normal filmThe answer: obstruction that reverses
Pulmonary hypertensionChronic hemolysis and vasculopathy; exertional dyspnea, jugular venous distension, edema, enlarged pulmonary arteriesNo edema, undisplaced apex, nocturnal rather than exertional
Pulmonary fibrosisRepeated vasoocclusive lung injury; progressive exertional dyspnea, reticular markings, honeycombing, restrictive functionNormal film; intermittent nocturnal symptoms
Pulmonary embolism (can't miss)Thrombotic risk; acute, persistent pleuritic pain and cough, tachycardia, hypoxia, raised D-dimerFour weeks, intermittent, normal vital signs
Acute chest syndrome (can't miss)Pulmonary vasoocclusion, often with infection; fever, hypoxia, chest pain, new infiltrateAfebrile, normal saturation, normal film
SarcoidosisNoncaseating granulomas, not associated with sickle cell disease; bilateral hilar adenopathyNo adenopathy; a family history is not a risk transfer
Asthma in sickle cell disease Treatment – as in anyone else: inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids · Bidirectional – acute chest syndrome drives airway hyperreactivity, and asthma raises the risk of the next acute chest syndrome, so treating it is also prevention · Clear lungs – wheezing is often absent when symptoms are mild or intermittent; spirometry with reversibility, not auscultation, is the test
Practice
  1. 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night Prior acute chest syndrome; family sarcoid history Normal vital signs · lungs clear · no edema · normal chest x-ray → Spirometry with bronchodilator testing → nocturnal and intermittent means airway, so the first test is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, looking for obstruction that reverses; clear lungs do not argue against it, since wheezing is often absent when symptoms are mild or intermittent. The angiogram answers an embolism, acute and persistent with tachycardia and hypoxia; the echocardiogram answers exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs. The prior acute chest syndrome makes asthma more likely, and a family history of sarcoid is not a risk transfer
  2. 1-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 60%, HbS 40% complete blood count normal Asymptomatic; her older sister has sickle cell anemia Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile → Sickle cell trait → HbA exceeding HbS with a completely normal blood count is trait, not disease. Sickle cell anemia has no HbA at all; sickle-beta-plus thalassemia has HbA but S exceeds A, with a low MCV. The affected sister makes the disease complications look plausible; the most common complication of trait is painless hematuria
  3. 16-year-old boy with sickle cell disease 1 day of pleuritic chest pain chest x-ray shows a new left lower lobe infiltrate T 38.9 °C · oxygen saturation 88% on room air · HR 118/min → Transfusion with antibiotic therapy → fever, hypoxia, chest pain and a new infiltrate are acute chest syndrome, pulmonary vasoocclusion often with infection: transfuse and give antibiotics. Spirometry is for chronic, nocturnal airway symptoms, and echocardiography for exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs
  4. 20-year-old man with sickle cell trait nocturia and polyuria Otherwise healthy; takes no medications or diuretics urinalysis shows no glucose and no protein Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · serum creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Hyposthenuria → the renal medulla is hypoxic, acidic and hypertonic, the one site that sickles a carrier's cells, so trait impairs urinary concentrating ability: hyposthenuria. Central diabetes insipidus is a pituitary defect; trait alone explains a medullary concentrating defect, and a normal creatinine with no protein argues against chronic kidney disease
  5. 19-year-old man with sickle cell disease exertional dyspnea jugular venous distension and pedal edema loud pulmonic component of the second heart sound No nocturnal cough or chest tightness Afebrile · HR 98/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air → Echocardiography → exertional dyspnea with right-sided failure signs is pulmonary hypertension from chronic hemolysis and vasculopathy: echocardiography shows tricuspid regurgitation with a raised estimated pulmonary pressure, and catheterization confirms. Spirometry answers nocturnal, intermittent airway symptoms, and chest computed tomography answers progressive fibrosis
  6. 1-year-old girl has laboratory results reviewed at a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 90% hemoglobin 7.5 g/dL reticulocytes 14% Parents ask what her results mean Afebrile · growth at the 25th percentile → Sickle cell anemia → no HbA with about 90% HbS, anemia and reticulocytes of 10 to 20% is sickle cell anemia: ensure penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination. Trait keeps HbA above HbS with a normal blood count, and hemoglobin SC has HbS about equal to HbC with no HbA and a milder anemia
  7. 9-month-old boy has painful swelling of the hands and feet Previously well; no recent trauma; family history unknown fingers and toes diffusely swollen and tender Afebrile · hemoglobin 7 g/dL · reticulocytes 12% → Dactylitis → painful swelling of the hands and feet is dactylitis, often the first presentation of sickle cell disease; trait carries no anemia and none of the disease complications, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis does not explain a hemoglobin of 7 with a high reticulocyte count
  8. 24-year-old woman with sickle cell disease 1 year of progressive dyspnea on exertion chest x-ray shows increased reticular markings No edema; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 93% on room air → CT scan of the chest → progressive exertional dyspnea with reticular markings is fibrosis from repeated vasoocclusive lung injury; chest computed tomography shows honeycombing, and pulmonary function testing is restrictive. Spirometry with bronchodilator testing answers nocturnal, intermittent airway symptoms, and the pulmonary angiogram answers an acute, persistent embolism with tachycardia and hypoxia
  9. 2-year-old boy is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 15%, HbS 70% mean corpuscular volume 68 fL Parents ask whether he has sickle cell trait Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL → Sickle-beta-plus thalassemia → HbA present but S exceeding A, with a low MCV, is sickle-beta-plus thalassemia, the sharpest mimic of trait. In trait HbA exceeds HbS with a normal blood count, and sickle-beta-zero has no HbA at all
  10. 22-year-old man with sickle cell trait collapses during military basic training diffuse muscle pain and weakness dark urine Lungs clear on examination T 37.4 °C · HR 116/min · creatine kinase 48,000 U/L → Exertional rhabdomyolysis → trait carries a real risk of exertional rhabdomyolysis and sudden death under extreme exertion, which is why it matters in recruits. Acute chest syndrome belongs to disease, not to a carrier, and the lungs are clear; heat stroke alone does not fit a normal temperature
  11. 17-year-old girl with homozygous sickle cell disease 4 weeks of intermittent chest tightness and dry cough worse in the middle of the night spirometry shows airway obstruction that improves after albuterol Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% on room air → Inhaled corticosteroid with a short-acting bronchodilator → asthma in sickle cell disease is treated as asthma is in anyone else, with inhaled bronchodilators and corticosteroids, and control also lowers the risk of the next acute chest syndrome. Chronic transfusion does not treat reversible airway obstruction, and an oral glucocorticoid taper alone leaves out the inhaled treatment
  12. 3-year-old boy with sickle cell anemia has a high fever hypotension and tachycardia leukocytosis with bandemia Vaccinations up to date; no bone pain T 39.5 °C · BP 70/40 mm Hg · HR 168/min · leukocytes 24,000/mm3 → Streptococcus pneumoniae → pneumococcus remains the leading cause of sepsis in sickle cell disease despite vaccination (non-vaccine serotypes): start empiric ceftriaxone. Salmonella is the leading cause of osteomyelitis, and there is no bone pain; Staphylococcus aureus is not the leading septic organism
  13. 16-year-old boy has 3 months of right hip pain radiograph shows avascular necrosis of the femoral head retinopathy on dilated eye examination hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 50%, HbC 48% Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL → Hemoglobin SC disease → no HbA with HbS about equal to HbC and a milder anemia is hemoglobin SC disease, whose retinopathy and avascular necrosis run out of proportion to the anemia. Sickle cell anemia and sickle-beta-zero thalassemia both have high HbS with no HbC; the 48% HbC decides
  14. 20-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has sudden pleuritic chest pain tachycardic and short of breath at rest Chest x-ray clear; no new infiltrate Afebrile · HR 124/min · oxygen saturation 89% on room air → CT pulmonary angiogram → acute, persistent pleuritic pain with tachycardia and hypoxia and a clear film is embolism, and sickle cell disease raises thrombotic risk: computed tomography angiography shows the filling defect. Spirometry answers chronic nocturnal airway symptoms, and serum ACE answers sarcoidosis, which is not associated with sickle cell disease
  15. 19-year-old woman with sickle cell trait left upper quadrant pain began after a high-altitude flight yesterday Lungs clear; no chest pain Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL · oxygen saturation 98% → Splenic infarction → splenic infarction is real in trait, at altitude, though uncommon. Acute chest syndrome belongs to disease, not to a carrier, and the lungs are clear; a normal hemoglobin argues against sequestration
  16. 13-year-old boy with sickle cell disease was diagnosed with asthma last year His mother asks why his asthma and his acute chest syndrome episodes each seem to raise the risk of the other Afebrile → Parenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculature → parenchymal hypoxia promotes inflammation and sickling within the pulmonary vasculature, and acute chest syndrome in turn worsens airway hyperreactivity, so treating the asthma is also acute chest syndrome prevention. Hydroxyurea bronchial irritation and transfusional iron in the pulmonary vessels are not the link
  17. 2-week-old boy is seen for a weight check newborn screen reported as FAS Parents ask what the result means and whether he needs treatment Born at term; feeding well Afebrile · examination normal → Sickle cell trait → FAS is trait and FS is disease; F leads because fetal hemoglobin predominates at birth, and the A shows HbA is present, which excludes sickle cell anemia; hemoglobin SC has no HbA. Counsel the parents; no treatment
  18. 22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease has a cough chest x-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy anterior uveitis and hypercalcemia No exertional dyspnea; symptoms not worse at night Afebrile · oxygen saturation 97% → Sarcoidosis → bilateral hilar adenopathy with uveitis and hypercalcemia points to sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas); the chest film makes the diagnosis, and it is not associated with sickle cell disease, so the film decides, not the sickle history. Fibrosis shows reticular markings and honeycombing rather than hilar nodes, and asthma leaves the film normal
  19. 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has sudden pallor reticulocyte count 0.2% spleen not palpable Tired for 3 days; no jaundice or dark urine Afebrile · HR 124/min · hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL → Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis → a reticulocyte count near zero means the marrow has stopped: parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis. Splenic sequestration would bring an enlarging spleen, and hyperhemolysis would bring jaundice and dark urine with a responding marrow
  20. 28-year-old man with sickle cell trait has 2 weeks of painless hematuria imaging shows a mass in the right kidney No flank pain or fever Afebrile · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Renal medullary carcinoma → renal medullary carcinoma is rare but nearly pathognomonic for trait; painless hematuria in a carrier is usually medullary sickling, and imaging is what excludes the carcinoma. Clear cell carcinoma is not the trait-linked tumor, and papillary necrosis makes no mass
  21. 15-year-old boy with sickle cell disease intermittent chest tightness and cough worse at night and with exercise no wheezing on examination Pulmonary function testing is ordered Afebrile · oxygen saturation 98% · chest x-ray normal → Airway obstruction that reverses after bronchodilator administration → asthma is confirmed by pulmonary function testing showing airway obstruction that reverses with a bronchodilator; absent wheeze does not exclude it. A restrictive pattern belongs to fibrosis, and a low diffusing capacity with normal spirometry shows no obstruction to reverse
  22. 3-year-old girl is seen for a well visit hemoglobin electrophoresis: HbA 0%, HbS 88%, HbA2 elevated mean corpuscular volume 64 fL Painful swelling of the hands at 10 months Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.1 g/dL · reticulocytes 11% → Sickle-beta-zero thalassemia → no HbA, high HbS and a raised HbA2 with a low MCV is sickle-beta-zero thalassemia: it looks like HbSS but is microcytic. Sickle cell anemia shares the absent HbA but is not microcytic, and sickle-beta-plus keeps some HbA; the raised HbA2 decides
  23. 14-year-old boy with sickle cell disease has chest pain chest x-ray shows a new infiltrate Cough began yesterday; no leg swelling T 38.6 °C · oxygen saturation 87% on room air · HR 120/min → Acute chest syndrome → chest pain, hypoxia and a new infiltrate in sickle cell disease is acute chest syndrome, pulmonary vasoocclusion often with infection, treated with transfusion and antibiotics. Calling it pneumonia alone leaves out the transfusion, and embolism gives a clear film with a filling defect on angiography
  24. 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait asks about future children her partner also carries sickle cell trait Neither has anemia; both have normal blood counts They plan their first pregnancy next year → 25% Disease, 50% trait, 25% unaffected → two carriers each pass a sickle gene half the time, so each pregnancy carries 25% disease, 50% trait and 25% unaffected; 50% disease overstates the risk, and not every child carries trait
  25. 14-year-old girl with sickle cell disease intermittent dry nocturnal cough for several weeks Family history of sarcoidosis; no exertional dyspnea Her parents ask which tests she needs Afebrile · lungs clear · no film yet → Serum ACE activity → serum ACE has poor sensitivity and specificity, sarcoidosis is not associated with sickle cell disease, and nothing suggests hilar adenopathy, so it should not be ordered first. The chest x-ray comes first and is expected to be normal in asthma; spirometry with bronchodilator testing then confirms
  26. 7-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops sudden hemiparesis right arm and leg weaker than left no headache before onset Noncontrast computed tomography of the head shows no bleeding Afebrile · BP 104/62 mm Hg · glucose 92 mg/dL → Ischemic stroke → sudden hemiparesis in sickle cell disease is an ischemic stroke, a disease complication no carrier gets: treat with exchange transfusion. A scan without blood argues against hemorrhage, and no headache argues against a complicated migraine
  27. 26-year-old woman with sickle cell trait is 24 weeks pregnant 2 days of dysuria No flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase and nitrites Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Urinary tract infection → dysuria in a pregnant carrier is a urinary tract infection. Hematuria is the commonest trait complication but is painless, and pyelonephritis would bring fever and flank pain
Common wrong answers Prior acute chest syndrome, transfusions, hydroxyurea: none separates the causes of chronic dyspnea, and the prior episode makes asthma more likely, not less. Family history of sarcoidosis: no association with sickle cell disease, and no hilar nodes. Echocardiography: needs exertional dyspnea and right-sided signs; a normal point of maximal impulse and no edema argue against it. D-dimer: as with the angiogram, the picture is not embolism, so no step of that pathway applies. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy: invasive, and it answers fibrosis, already excluded. Splenic infarction as the most common trait complication: real but uncommon. An affected sibling: makes every disease complication look plausible; read the panel. Dactylitis: the disease version of the carrier stem.
Pairs with Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome: painless hematuria, the commonest trait complication. Part II Stroke in a Child or Adolescent: the sickle cell stroke among the other pediatric causes. Part I Asthma: what follows once spirometry confirms. Part I Obstructive Lung Disease: the adult version of the which-test question.
Transferable rule

Read a supplied lab panel first; it usually excludes most of the differential in one line. A dramatic chronic disease sets the prior for its own complications but does not suspend the base rate of common disease. Ask what the timing of the complaint means before asking what the known diagnosis predisposes to.

Noisy Breathing in a Child

Stridor vs. wheeze · toxic vs. well

Pediatric noisy breathing — the differential
DiagnosisThe pictureThe tellCause & next step
Croup6 mo–3 yrBarky seal cough, hoarse, inspiratory stridor, worse at night, nontoxicSteeple signParainfluenza · dexamethasone for all; racemic epi if stridor at rest
Epiglottitis Emergency2–7 yr, unvaccinatedAbrupt, high fever, toxic, drooling, tripod, muffled voiceThumbprint sign — but never delay the airway for X-ray; don't examine the throatH. influenzae b · secure airway in the OR → ceftriaxone + vanc
Bacterial tracheitis"Croup that got worse" — sudden toxicity, purulent secretionsNo response to racemic epiS. aureus · airway + IV antibiotics

Retropharyngeal abscess<5 yrFever, drooling, refusal to extend the neckWidened prevertebral spacePolymicrobial · CT + IV abx ± drainage

TracheomalaciainfantChronic noisy breathing on expiration with a brassy cough; common after tracheoesophageal fistula repairExpiratory stridor; no change with position or albuterolFloppy intrathoracic trachea collapses on expiration · bronchoscopy confirms; most outgrow it

The phase of the noise localizes the lesion
SoundWhere the narrowing isWhy that phaseCauses
Inspiratory stridorExtrathoracic, collapsible (supraglottis, glottis)Fast inspiratory flow lowers pressure inside the airway, pulling floppy tissue inwardLaryngomalacia, croup, epiglottitis, vocal cord dysfunction
Expiratory stridorIntrathoracic tracheaExpiration raises intrathoracic pressure and compresses a soft trachea; inspiration widens itTracheomalacia, tracheal compression by a vascular ring (often biphasic when tight)
Biphasic stridorFixed narrowing, usually subglotticThe complete cricoid ring cannot change caliber, so noise sounds in both phasesSubglottic stenosis, severe croup, a foreign body in the trachea
Expiratory wheezeSmall intrathoracic airwaysBronchioles narrow further on expirationAsthma, bronchiolitis
RhonchiLarger airways with secretionsCoarse sound that may clear with coughPneumonia, bronchitis
