Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M, barky cough, inspiratory stridor, low-grade fever, steeple sign → Croup → dexamethasone
  2. 4 yo M, unvaccinated, drooling and tripoding with high fever and no cough → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  3. 2 yo M with sudden choking while eating peanuts and a unilateral wheeze → Foreign body aspiration → bronchoscopy
  4. 3 yo M, toxic with high fever and thick purulent tracheal secretions after a viral prodrome → Bacterial tracheitis
  5. 6 mo M in winter with wheeze and crackles following a URI → Bronchiolitis → supportive care
  6. 3 wk M with inspiratory stridor worse supine and better prone, well-appearing → Laryngomalacia → reassurance
  7. 4 mo M with paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting and lymphocytosis → Pertussis → azithromycin
  8. 4 wk F, noisy breathing since birth, inspiratory vibratory sound louder supine and quieter prone, feeding well, no cyanosis → Laryngeal collapse on inspiration → Laryngomalacia — position-dependent, the commonest cause of neonatal stridor
  9. 14 yo F, episodic stridor she calls wheezing, normal voice between episodes, saturation 99% during an attack, no response to albuterol → Vocal cord dysfunction → Paradoxical vocal cord motion — inspiratory and expiratory stridor, not wheeze
  10. Adolescent with recurrent stridor unresponsive to albuterol and a normal saturation → Laryngoscopy during a symptomatic episode → Cords must be seen moving abnormally while symptomatic
  11. 2 yo M, barky cough and inspiratory stridor 3 days after coryza, low-grade fever → Subglottic narrowing from mucosal edema → Croup — the obstruction sits below the cords
  12. 4 yo M, unimmunized, 2 days of fever and rhinorrhea, now severe sore throat and refusing food, temperature 39.4 °C, leaning forward with the chin thrust out, tonsils only mildly erythematous, submandibular space soft → Absent Haemophilus influenzae type b immunization → the risk factor, not the finding
  13. 4 yo M, unimmunized, toxic and tripoding with drooling and a normal-looking pharynx → Intubation in the operating room → visualization happens where the airway can be secured; take him there with anesthesia and ENT present
  14. The organism still isolated most often from pediatric epiglottitis despite universal vaccination → Haemophilus influenzae type b → rates fell sharply but the ranking did not change
  15. Preventing epiglottitis in a healthy infant → Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine → immunization is the whole of prevention here; the conjugate series, from 2 months
  16. Agitated 4 yo with suspected epiglottitis in the emergency department → Depressing the tongue to inspect the pharynx → anything that agitates him can complete the obstruction
  17. 3 mo girl with 2 weeks of squeaky noisy breathing when lying on her back, louder and more persistent over time, quieter when prone; gaining weight and breastfeeding well; no labored breathing or cyanosis; laryngoscopy shows patent nasal passages, small adenoids and tonsils, a normal palate, and arytenoid tissue that intermittently falls into the airway, worse with crying; both vocal cords move normally → Inspiratory stridor → laryngomalacia: inspiration lowers pressure in the collapsible extrathoracic airway
  18. 4 mo boy with noisy breathing since 1 month of age, a low-pitched sound heard mainly on expiration over the central chest, and a brassy cough; worse with crying and during colds; no change with position or with albuterol; feeding well without choking or vomiting; normal growth; afebrile → Tracheomalacia → expiratory stridor from a floppy intrathoracic trachea; bronchoscopy confirms
  19. 7 mo boy born at 26 weeks who was intubated for 6 weeks in the neonatal ICU; now noisy breathing on both inspiration and expiration that is constant and worse with colds; no change with position; afebrile, feeding well → Subglottic stenosis → fixed subglottic narrowing after prolonged intubation gives biphasic stridor
  20. 5 mo girl with inspiratory stridor since 2 weeks of age, worse supine and with feeding; weight has fallen from the 50th to below the 5th percentile, with suprasternal retractions at rest and two episodes of perioral cyanosis during feeds; flexible laryngoscopy shows supraglottic collapse on inspiration with normal vocal cord movement → Referral for airway surgery → laryngomalacia with failure to thrive, distress and cyanosis
Decision spine 1. Stridor (upper) or wheeze (lower)? Then which phase: inspiratory is extrathoracic, expiratory is the intrathoracic trachea, biphasic is fixed and usually subglottic. 2. Sudden + afebrile → foreign body; the absence of fever is a key clue. 3. Toxic + drooling + tripod → epiglottitis, airway first in the OR (operating room). Getting a throat exam or X-ray first is an error. 4. Barky + nontoxic → croup. 5. Croup that is not behaving like croup → bacterial tracheitis. 6. Vaccination status always matters.
Risk factors, and the ones that are not Absent Hib immunisation is the strongest risk factor for epiglottitis in a child · Immune deficiency raises the risk, but far less strongly · Diabetes mellitus raises the rate of epiglottitis in adults, not in children · Obesity raises postoperative and nosocomial infection risk and brings sleep apnoea, but is not associated with epiglottitis · Secondhand smoke causes middle ear disease, dental caries and lower respiratory infection, but not epiglottitis · Poor dental hygiene points instead at Ludwig angina, which needs tender bilateral submandibular induration and an elevated floor of mouth; a soft submandibular space excludes it
Paired pearls Croup improves with racemic epi, tracheitis doesn't · laryngomalacia better prone, croup worse at night · bronchiolitis gets nothing · expiratory film for foreign body because the trapped lung stays inflated.
Pairs with Part II Deep Neck Infections covers Ludwig angina and the retropharyngeal space. These are the two deep-neck mimics of a toxic child with a sore throat. Ask: is the submandibular space soft?
Sequencing trapThroat exam or lateral neck film in a toxic, drooling child: the airway is secured in the operating room first
Unchecked attributeExpiratory stridor: the sound of the floppy intrathoracic trachea (tracheomalacia); laryngomalacia is above the thoracic inlet, so it collapses on inspiration
Unchecked attributeBiphasic stridor: needs a fixed lesion such as subglottic stenosis; the arytenoid tissue in laryngomalacia is mobile and position-dependent

Respiratory Infection in a Child

green mucus is not a bacterial sign · one side is a foreign body · typical vs atypical pneumoniaWhich side, how long and how sick, and does the illness span the upper and lower airway?

Upper airwayPneumoniaPractice
Bottom line

Purulent or colored discharge does not mean bacterial: the green is myeloperoxidase from neutrophils recruited by any inflammation, viral included. Read the side before the color.

  • Viral upper respiratory infection (URI): afebrile and well, 2 days of symptoms, clear mobile tympanic membranes, no exudate, clear lungs; supportive care.
  • Nasal foreign body: unilateral, foul, purulent discharge in a well, afebrile toddler; the other naris normal, no systemic signs.
  • Acute bacterial sinusitis: bilateral, usually with fever and cough, and it must still pass one door: 10 days or more without improvement, or high fever with purulence for 3 to 4 consecutive days or more, or double worsening. Clinical diagnosis, no imaging.
  • Strep pharyngitis: test before treating; treatment prevents rheumatic fever, not poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Centor criteria: fever, exudate, tender anterior nodes, no cough.
  • Acute otitis media: bulging, immobile, erythematous tympanic membrane; mobility on pneumatic otoscopy is the discriminator.
  • Atypical pneumonia: a child who looks “tired but not ill” with 2 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough, low-grade fever, bilateral diffuse findings and normal saturation; at school age, Mycoplasma pneumoniae.
Upper airway: nasal discharge
Nasal discharge in a child: the differential
DiagnosisPictureKey discriminatorNext step
Nasal foreign body, 1 to 6 yearsWell, playful, afebrile; insertion usually unobserved; food items give the worst dischargeUnilateral, foul, purulent, sometimes bloody; that side's mucosa red and swollen, the other side normalRemove it: positive pressure, then instruments; ear, nose and throat (ENT) endoscopy if not visible
Acute bacterial sinusitisFollows a viral URIBilateral discharge with fever and cough, through one of the three doorsAmoxicillin-clavulanate; no imaging
Allergic rhinitisSneezing and itch; smoke and pets raise riskBilateral clear rhinorrhea; pale or bluish, boggy turbinatesIntranasal corticosteroid
Adenoid hypertrophyMouth breathing, snoring, nasal voiceBilateral chronic obstructionObserve, or refer to ENT if sleep is disturbed
Mucormycosis (emergency)Diabetic ketoacidosis or severe immune compromise (CD4 (helper T-cell) count under 50, neutropenia)White (ischemic) or black (necrotic) turbinates or palateSurgical debridement and amphotericin B
Nasal foreign body: remove it, do not image it Positive pressure first: the parent's kiss (a parent seals the child's mouth and gives a short puff while pressing the clear naris closed), or forceful exhalation with the other naris occluded in an older child · Then office instruments; ENT endoscopy if not visible or penetrating · No imaging: most objects are radiolucent · Do not wait: sinusitis, periorbital cellulitis and aspiration follow · Button battery or paired magnets: emergency removal; pressure and current necrose the mucosa and perforate the septum; epistaxis or black discharge is the tell
Pneumonia: typical or atypical
Typical vs atypical pneumonia
Typical (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae)Atypical (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila)
OnsetAbruptGradual, over 1 to 2 weeks
Fever, coughHigh with rigors; productiveLow-grade; dry, persistent
AppearanceIll, chest pain, more work of breathingWalking around, functional
Exam, filmFocal lobar consolidationBilateral crackles, with or without wheeze; diffuse interstitial
TreatmentAmoxicillinMacrolide; doxycycline if over 8 years
Organism by age Neonate: group B streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria · 1 to 3 months: Chlamydia trachomatis: staccato cough, afebrile, conjunctivitis, eosinophilia · Under 5: viruses: RSV (respiratory syncytial virus), parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus · 5 or older: Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, S. pneumoniae
Atypical organisms: settings and features
OrganismSettingSets it apart
MycoplasmaYoung; dorms or barracks; fall to winterIndolent dry cough, nonexudative pharyngitis, macular rash, cold agglutinins, normal white count, bullous myringitis
Chlamydophila pneumoniaeYoung adultsSimilar; hoarseness prominent, often biphasic
LegionellaOlder, smokers, immunosuppressed; water systems, air conditioning, cruise ships, hotelsHigh fever with diarrhea or vomiting and confusion; hyponatremia, raised liver enzymes, relative bradycardia; urine antigen
Chlamydophila psittaciBird exposureSevere headache, splenomegaly
Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)Farm animals, sheep, parturient catsNo rash; hepatitis; culture-negative endocarditis later
Mycoplasma: the organism and its complications No cell wall, so beta-lactams fail and Gram stain misses it; grows on Eaton agar · Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia: immunoglobulin M (IgM) against the I antigen, Coombs-positive, with or without Raynaud · Erythema multiforme or Mycoplasma pneumoniae-induced rash and mucositis (MIRM): the leading infectious cause of erythema multiforme after herpes simplex virus · Bullous myringitis; Guillain-Barré syndrome, encephalitis, transverse myelitis · Effusion: a small serous pleural effusion occurs in about 25%, so it is not evidence for pneumococcus
Practice
  1. 3-year-old boy has had 2 days of green nasal discharge playful and eating well tympanic membranes clear and mobile on pneumatic otoscopy no pharyngeal exudate; lungs clear Discharge from both nostrils Afebrile · HR 110/min · oxygen saturation 99% → Viral upper respiratory infection → the green comes from neutrophil myeloperoxidase in any inflammation, so 2 days of colored discharge in a well, afebrile child is viral: supportive care. Sinusitis must pass a door (10 days, 3 to 4 consecutive days or more of high fever with purulence, or double worsening); otitis media needs a bulging, immobile membrane
  2. 6-year-old boy has a sudden onset of high fever with shaking chills cough productive of rust-colored sputum chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation Ill appearing; right-sided chest pain T 39.8°C · HR 140/min → Streptococcus pneumoniae → abrupt onset, rigors, rusty sputum, lobar consolidation and an ill appearance separate pneumococcus from Mycoplasma, which is gradual and diffuse; Legionella brings diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia in an older smoker
  3. 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of foul-smelling, purulent discharge from the left naris only white bead visible just inside the left naris right naris normal Active, eating well, calm and cooperative; no cough Afebrile → Positive-pressure expulsion → a visible bead in a calm child comes out first with positive pressure (the parent's kiss, or blowing with the other naris closed); instruments if it fails, ENT endoscopy if not visible. No imaging, since most objects are radiolucent, and antibiotics leave the object in place
  4. 9-year-old girl is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia now jaundiced and pale hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test positive for C3 Fingers turn white in the cold T 37.9°C · HR 118/min → Cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia → Mycoplasma triggers IgM against the I antigen: a Coombs-positive cold agglutinin hemolytic anemia, sometimes with Raynaud. Fingers that blanch in the cold and a C3-positive direct antiglobulin test pick the cold type over warm autoimmune hemolysis or glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
  5. 4-year-old girl has had 2 days of runny nose with green discharge her mother asks whether the green color means she needs an antibiotic Playful; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · lungs clear → No; neutrophils color it in any inflammation → the green is myeloperoxidase in neutrophils recruited by any inflammation, viral included, so color never proves bacteria; duration, fever and double worsening decide
  6. 35-year-old woman who breeds parrots at home has 1 week of dry cough and fever severe headache spleen tip palpable chest x-ray: patchy infiltrate, no hilar adenopathy No farm animal contact; no travel T 39.0°C · HR 96/min → Chlamydophila psittaci → a pet parrot with severe headache and splenomegaly is psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci). Histoplasma comes from soil rich in bird or bat droppings and typically enlarges the hilar or mediastinal nodes, which this film lacks; Coxiella needs farm animals, sheep or parturient cats
  7. 3-year-old boy has had 12 days of nasal discharge without improvement thick purulent discharge from both nostrils daytime cough No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.1°C · HR 112/min · tympanic membranes mobile → Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → 10 days or more without improvement is the first door to acute bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate, with no imaging. The persistence, not the color, is what separates it from a viral cold; allergy gives clear discharge with sneezing and itch
  8. 10-year-old boy has had 2 weeks of gradually worsening dry cough no improvement after 4 days of amoxicillin bilateral crackles; diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest x-ray Walking around and attending school T 37.9°C · white blood cell count 7,800/mm³ → Mycoplasma has no cell wall → a gradual, diffuse picture in a school-aged child is Mycoplasma, which has no cell wall, so beta-lactams cannot work: switch to a macrolide. Resistant H. influenzae or pneumococcus would still be a typical, focal pneumonia
  9. 3-year-old boy has clear rhinorrhea and frequent sneezing itchy, watery eyes seasonal recurrence each spring for 2 years pale, boggy nasal turbinates Father smokes; a cat at home Afebrile · HR 100/min → Allergic rhinitis → bilateral clear discharge, itch and pale, boggy turbinates are allergic rhinitis, and smoke and pets raise its risk: an intranasal corticosteroid. Sinusitis is purulent and must pass a door; the itch and the seasonal pattern point to allergy over a vasomotor cause
  10. 2-year-old girl pushed something from the television remote into her nose 2 hours ago her brother saw it now right-sided nosebleed and dark discharge smooth, gray, coin-shaped object deep in the right naris Afebrile · breathing comfortably · oxygen saturation 99% → Immediate removal in the emergency department → a coin-shaped object from a remote is a button battery: pressure and current necrose the mucosa and can perforate the septum, and a nosebleed or dark discharge is the tell, so remove it now. An outpatient endoscopy or an antibiotic recheck lets the injury progress
  11. 2-year-old boy has 3 days of cough, runny nose and wheeze diffuse wheezes and crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial pattern, no consolidation Attends daycare T 38.3°C · respiratory rate 44/min · oxygen saturation 95% → Viral pneumonia → under 5, viruses lead: RSV, parainfluenza, adenovirus, human metapneumovirus. Mycoplasma belongs to age 5 and older, and lobar bacterial pneumonia gives a focal consolidation
  12. 5-year-old girl had an upper respiratory illness that improved over 5 days on day 8, new fever worsening purulent nasal discharge Tympanic membranes mobile; lungs clear; eating less T 39.5°C · HR 124/min → Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate → an illness that improves and then worsens with new fever is double worsening: acute bacterial sinusitis, treated with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate. Supportive care alone ignores a door already crossed; the diagnosis is clinical, so no sinus computed tomography (CT)
  13. 28-year-old woman who works on a sheep farm has 10 days of fever and dry cough helped with lambing and a cat's delivery last month No rash, joint pain or bird contact T 39.2°C · alanine aminotransferase 140 U/L → Coxiella burnetii → farm animals, sheep and parturient cats with hepatitis and no rash are Q fever (Coxiella burnetii), which can cause culture-negative endocarditis later. Brucella also spreads to people in contact with livestock, but it brings cyclical fever with migratory arthralgia or sacroiliitis, often from unpasteurized dairy; psittacosis needs bird exposure, which she denies
  14. 3-year-old boy: 2 weeks of nasal discharge, first clear, now thick, foul right naris: pus, red swollen mucosa and turbinates; left normal Human immunodeficiency virus since birth, treated; CD4 520/mm³ Father smokes; pet dog Afebrile · playful · no cough → Nasal foreign body → one-sided foul pus in a well, afebrile toddler is a nasal foreign body: remove it with positive pressure or instruments. Sinusitis is bilateral and usually brings fever and cough; the smoking father and the pet dog raise allergy risk, but allergy is bilateral and clear; human immunodeficiency virus invites mucormycosis, but a CD4 count of 520 and red, not white or black, turbinates leave mucormycosis out. Afebrile, playful and without cough, he has no systemic signs
  15. 11-year-old girl had a dry cough and low-grade fever 3 weeks ago weakness rising from feet to thighs over 4 days absent ankle and knee reflexes sensation normal, no sensory level Pupils and bladder function normal HR 98/min → Guillain-Barré syndrome → ascending weakness weeks after a respiratory illness is a postinfectious complication: Guillain-Barré syndrome. Mycoplasma can also cause encephalitis and transverse myelitis, but normal sensation with no sensory level and normal bladder function argue against a cord lesion, and normal pupils argue against botulism
  16. 7-year-old boy has had 3 days of runny nose and cough mild maxillary pain profuse yellow-green nasal discharge tender upper cheeks Well appearing; no fever for the past 48 hours T 37.2°C · HR 96/min → Saline irrigation and analgesics → 3 days of symptoms, afebrile for 48 hours, meets no door, so this is viral rhinosinusitis despite the colored discharge: supportive care with saline irrigation and analgesics. Amoxicillin-clavulanate waits for a door; an antihistamine treats allergy, which gives clear discharge with itch
  17. 8-year-old boy is being treated for presumed Mycoplasma pneumoniae pneumonia target lesions on the hands and feet painful oral mucositis with crusted lips raised three-ring targets; no skin sloughing Cough improving over the past week T 38.2°C · HR 110/min → Erythema multiforme / MIRM → target lesions with mucositis during Mycoplasma infection are erythema multiforme or MIRM; Mycoplasma is the leading infectious cause of erythema multiforme after herpes simplex virus. Raised, typical targets with three rings and no epidermal detachment pick erythema multiforme over Stevens-Johnson syndrome, whose target-like lesions are atypical, with two zones. The Mycoplasma link to targets and mucositis is what this stem shows; nothing in it builds a Kawasaki picture
  18. 4-year-old boy has had 5 days of a viral upper respiratory illness green nasal discharge from both nostrils improving each day Eating and sleeping normally; tympanic membranes clear Afebrile · HR 104/min → Prescribe antibiotics → an improving viral illness meets no door; antibiotics do not shorten it and carry adverse effects. Supportive care and intranasal saline are both appropriate
  19. 12-year-old girl has had 2 weeks of dry cough and headache scattered crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: bilateral interstitial infiltrates Well appearing; eating normally T 38.0°C · oxygen saturation 97% on room air → Oral azithromycin → presumed Mycoplasma pneumonia in a well child is treated as an outpatient with a macrolide, or doxycycline over age 8; it lacks a cell wall, so amoxicillin and intravenous ceftriaxone fail
  20. 3-year-old boy has had fever and a runny nose for 3 days and is irritable right tympanic membrane bulging and erythematous no movement on pneumatic otoscopy External canal normal T 38.9°C · HR 128/min → Acute otitis media → a bulging, immobile, erythematous membrane is acute otitis media; mobility on pneumatic otoscopy is the discriminator. With fever and a bulging red membrane this is acute infection rather than effusion alone, and the normal canal leaves otitis externa out
  21. 64-year-old man who smokes has 2 days of high fever and confusion watery diarrhea crackles at the right base Returned from a cruise last week T 40.1°C · sodium 128 mEq/L → Legionella pneumophila → high fever, diarrhea, confusion and hyponatremia in an older smoker after a cruise is Legionella: the urine antigen confirms. Mycoplasma is indolent in the young, and pneumococcus is the rigors and rusty sputum picture
  22. 3-year-old boy had a cold that was improving by day 5 on day 7, new fever nasal discharge worsening again, from both nostrils No sneezing or itchy eyes T 38.8°C · HR 120/min · tympanic membranes mobile → Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → improvement, then new fever and worse discharge, is double worsening, the third door to acute bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate. The turn, not the day count or the color, crosses the door; allergy gives clear discharge with sneezing and itch
How NBME framed it: question 1

Previously healthy 10-year-old boy with 10 days of worsening cough a low-grade fever mild dyspnea on exertion diffuse crackles in both lungs chest x-ray: diffuse perihilar infiltrate

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Pneumonia due to respiratory syncytial virus: viral, with diffuse bilateral findings; but it causes wheezy lower respiratory disease in infants and children under 2, not at 10.
  • Congestive heart failure: a diffuse perihilar infiltrate with bilateral crackles also describes pulmonary edema; but in children it usually follows congenital heart disease, an arteriovenous fistula or severe malnutrition, and this child was previously healthy and febrile.
  • Tuberculosis: the cough is subacute; but there is no exposure, weight loss or night sweats, and the film shows no hilar adenopathy or cavitation.

Down to two: Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Streptococcus pneumoniae. Mycoplasma over pneumococcus: pneumococcus brings a productive cough, pleuritic chest pain and a single-lobe consolidation, not a gradual 10-day course with a diffuse film. A film that looks worse than the child is the Mycoplasma pattern. The stem never says atypical; age, onset and film carry the answer, and a macrolide treats it.

Common wrong answers Acute bacterial sinusitis for one-sided pus: purulence fits, but sinusitis is bilateral and usually febrile with cough; one-sided discharge in a playful, afebrile toddler is a foreign body. Allergic rhinitis because of a smoking father and a pet dog: risk factors, but allergy gives bilateral clear discharge with pale turbinates, not unilateral foul pus. Mucormycosis because of his human immunodeficiency virus infection: a CD4 count of 520/mm³ and red, swollen turbinates, not white or black, rule it out.
Pairs with Part I Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis: the cold-agglutinin hemolysis Mycoplasma causes and the direct antiglobulin pattern that identifies it. Part I Tuberculosis: the child with a subacute cough and a known contact; is there weight loss, night sweats or hilar adenopathy?
Transferable rule

For each striking detail, ask what it adds to the diagnosis; a detail that only raises alarm is a distractor. When symptoms involve two compartments at once (upper and lower airway, as pharyngitis with an interstitial pneumonia in adults), ask which organisms span both: typical bacterial pneumonia does not cause pharyngitis.

Asthma

Exam answer vs. current guideline

The decision point

NBME tests the NAEPP/EPR-3 severity ladder (National Asthma Education and Prevention Program, Expert Panel Report 3). Intermittent asthma means symptoms ≤2 days/wk, ≤2 nights/mo, normal FEV₁ (forced expiratory volume in 1 second) and no activity limits. Treat it with SABA PRN alone (short-acting beta-agonist, as needed). Mild persistent → add low-dose ICS (inhaled corticosteroid). Moderate → low-dose ICS+LABA (long-acting beta-agonist) or medium ICS. Severe → high-dose ICS+LABA.

Defining criteria Intermittent — ≤2 days/wk symptoms, ≤2 nights/mo, normal FEV₁, no activity limits → SABA PRN alone · Mild persistent — add low-dose ICS · Moderate persistent — low-dose ICS+LABA or medium-dose ICS · Severe persistent — high-dose ICS+LABA
Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M, symptoms 1 day per week, night waking once a month, normal FEV₁ → Intermittent → SABA as needed
  2. 9 yo M, symptoms 4 days per week, 3 nights a month, FEV₁ 85% → Mild persistent → low-dose inhaled corticosteroid
  3. 9 yo M with daily symptoms, weekly night waking, FEV₁ 70% → Moderate persistent → low-dose ICS plus LABA
  4. 9 yo M with symptoms throughout the day, nightly waking, FEV₁ 55% → Severe persistent
  5. 9 yo M using his rescue inhaler four times a week → Step up to a daily controller — this is not intermittent asthma
  6. 9 yo M with symptoms only on exertion, otherwise well → SABA before exercise
Guideline currency GINA now states SABA monotherapy is not supported at any step, any severity, any age (GINA, Global Initiative for Asthma; SABA, short-acting beta-agonist). Even intermittent asthma gets therapy containing an ICS (inhaled corticosteroid): as-needed ICS-formoterol, or an ICS-SABA combination reliever. This is because intermittent symptoms do not mean intermittent inflammation. Use NAEPP (National Asthma Education and Prevention Program) on the exam and GINA in clinic. An answer ladder running "nothing extra / montelukast / low-dose ICS / ICS+LABA" (LABA, long-acting beta-agonist) signals that the question is keyed to NAEPP.
Numbers that key the answer 2 per week · 2 nights per month · daily · nightly. Classify severity by these frequency counts.
Pairs with Part I Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers which test to order before this classification in a patient with sickle cell disease.

Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant

neonatal respiratory distress causes · bronchopulmonary dysplasiaHow preterm, did labor occur, when did it start, and what does the film show?

WorkupDistress at birthPreterm clockPractice
Bottom line

Time it first. At birth, four facts decide before any pathophysiology: gestational age, whether labor occurred, when distress began and what the film shows; the oxygen response then separates lung from shunt. In the preterm infant each complication has its own window: check the timing before the findings.

  • Transient tachypnea of the newborn: retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs; fluid in the fissures; onset within 2 hours, gone within 24 to 72.
  • Respiratory distress syndrome (RDS): preterm surfactant deficiency; distress at birth, ground glass with air bronchograms.
  • Apnea of prematurity: the immature brainstem does not sustain breathing; central pauses, with no obstruction and no lung disease, in an infant well between episodes.
  • Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD): a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days of life or more; arrested alveolar development, not fibrotic ventilator injury and not air leak.
Workup
Distress at birth
Gestational age, labor, onset, film
DiagnosisSettingThe tell
Transient tachypneaTerm or late preterm; cesarean without labor, macrosomia, maternal diabetes or asthmaFluid in the fissures, perihilar streaking; resolves in 24 to 72 hours
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiency, worsening over 48 to 72 hoursLow lung volumes, diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms
Meconium aspirationTerm or post-term, meconium-stained fluid, fetal distressCoarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation
Group B streptococcal pneumoniaRupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxisFilm mimics RDS exactly; temperature instability, neutropenia
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaViscera crush the developing lungScaphoid abdomen, shifted heart sounds; bowel loops in the chest with a displaced heart
Persistent pulmonary hypertension Can't missFailed transition, often after asphyxia or aspirationPre- to postductal gap above 10%, poorly oxygen-responsive
PolycythemiaIntrauterine hypoxia or placental transfusionPlethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film; venous hematocrit above 65% in a term neonate
Exit ramps Diaphragmatic hernia – never bag-mask (it inflates bowel inside the chest): intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma ⚠︎), decompress with a nasogastric tube; the lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists · Displaced heart sounds – scaphoid abdomen with absent breath sounds on the defect side: hernia; distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant: tension pneumothorax, needle decompression; well, heart on the right, no distress: dextrocardia · Diabetic mother – raises the risk of transient tachypnea and delays surfactant maturation, so RDS can appear at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe
The preterm clock
Apnea of prematurity Definition – a pause over 20 seconds, or a shorter one with bradycardia or desaturation · Diagnosis – clinical, after the mimics are checked: anemia, infection and intraventricular hemorrhage, plus glucose and electrolytes (seizure and reflux are the other usual mimics) · Versus hemorrhage – lethargy, a tense fontanelle, a growing head or seizures; cranial ultrasound · Management – caffeine, a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia Severity – graded by support required at 36 weeks postmenstrual age · Prevention – antenatal steroids plus surfactant turned it from fibrotic injury into developmental arrest; caffeine and vitamin A each reduce it · Management – supportive: oxygen, nutrition, fluid restriction; alveoli keep forming over months · Complications – pulmonary hypertension, systemic hypertension, recurrent respiratory infections, neurodevelopmental delay · Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) – first season, under 8 months: nirsevimab or clesrovimab; second season, 8 to 19 months: nirsevimab only, for BPD that needed oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids in the 6 months before the season; palivizumab is no longer available after December 31, 2025 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance)
Practice
  1. 1-hour-old boy born at 40 weeks by cesarean without labor is tachypneic chest x-ray shows fluid in the interlobar fissures Afebrile · birth weight 4200 g · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 88% on room air, 98% on oxygen → Transient tachypnea of the newborn → retained fetal lung fluid in structurally normal term lungs: fluid in the fissures appears in no competing diagnosis, and saturation correcting from 88% to 98% on oxygen is alveolar fluid, not a shunt. Cesarean without labor misses the catecholamine surge that switches the epithelium to absorbing fluid; macrosomia adds risk. Respiratory distress syndrome is the right category but a preterm member, and group B streptococcal pneumonia needs risk factors the stem never supplies. Supportive care: onset within 2 hours, and it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so an infant breathing normally by 48 hours fits
  2. 6-week-old boy born at 26 weeks still needs supplemental oxygen on nasal cannula oxygen every day since birth enteral feeds introduced today Weight gain appropriate on total parenteral nutrition Afebrile · oxygen saturation 92% on 0.5 L/min → Arrested alveolar development → a preterm infant still on supplemental oxygen at 28 days or more has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and since antenatal steroids and surfactant it is arrested alveolar development: fewer alveoli, less septation, disrupted vasculogenesis. Fibrotic ventilator injury is the old form, and air leak belongs to the first days on high pressures, weeks before this. Feeds introduced today suggest refeeding syndrome, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition
  3. 6-hour-old girl born at term has tachypnea and grunting membranes ruptured 24 hours before delivery maternal fever 38.5 °C in labor; no intrapartum prophylaxis Temperature unstable since birth T 35.9 °C · HR 176/min · respiratory rate 74/min → Blood culture and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever and no intrapartum prophylaxis, with temperature instability, is early-onset group B streptococcal sepsis. Its film mimics respiratory distress syndrome exactly, so surfactant misses it, and observing without antibiotics leaves the infection untreated: culture and start ampicillin and gentamicin
  4. 1-day-old girl born at term after delayed cord clamping is plethoric jittery and irritable before feeds Feeding well; no hepatomegaly; normal genitalia Afebrile · venous hematocrit 70% · glucose 35 mg/dL · HR 150/min → Red cells consume glucose → delayed cord clamping adds blood, and the expanded red cell mass takes up glucose, giving hypoglycemia and hypocalcemia; breakdown of the cells adds hyperbilirubinemia. Liver congestion is not the mechanism ⚠︎, and salt-wasting congenital adrenal hyperplasia brings ambiguous genitalia in girls, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, days later
  5. Term newborn boy has severe respiratory distress at delivery scaphoid abdomen heart sounds displaced to the right chest x-ray shows bowel gas in the left hemithorax T 36.6 °C · HR 92/min · oxygen saturation 64% → Intubate with limited peak pressures and decompress the stomach → a scaphoid abdomen with displaced heart sounds and bowel in the chest is a diaphragmatic hernia. Bag-mask ventilation inflates bowel inside the chest, so intubate, ventilate with limited pressures (the hypoplastic lung is at risk of barotrauma ⚠︎) and decompress with a nasogastric tube. Needle decompression is for a tension pneumothorax: a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax in a deteriorating infant
  6. 4-day-old boy born at 29 weeks in neonatal intensive care several 20-second breathing pauses today, bradycardia and desaturation ends with stimulation; pink, active, feeding well between Cultures negative; antibiotics stopped T 36.9 °C, stable · glucose, electrolytes, hemoglobin, ultrasound normal → Begin caffeine → a central pause from an immature brainstem, starting on day 2 to 3 in an infant who is well between spells, with the mimics checked (infection, anemia, intraventricular hemorrhage, glucose, electrolytes), is apnea of prematurity. Caffeine is a methylxanthine brainstem stimulant; add CPAP or high-flow nasal cannula if spells continue. Antibiotics answer the infant who is ill between spells; dexamethasone and albuterol are used for bronchopulmonary dysplasia, not for apnea
  7. 2-hour-old boy born at 29 weeks is grunting and retracting chest x-ray shows low lung volumes diffuse ground-glass opacity with air bronchograms Membranes ruptured at delivery T 36.8 °C · respiratory rate 72/min · oxygen saturation 86% on room air → Respiratory distress syndrome → surfactant deficiency in a preterm infant (under 34 weeks) gives distress at birth, worsening over 48 to 72 hours, with low volumes, ground glass and air bronchograms: give surfactant and CPAP. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures in a term infant; group B streptococcal pneumonia mimics this film exactly but needs risk factors (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) this stem does not supply
  8. 2-day-old boy born at term is plethoric, lethargic and feeding poorly venous hematocrit 72% no better after 12 hours of intravenous fluids Born after delayed cord clamping Afebrile · glucose 48 mg/dL · HR 156/min → Partial exchange transfusion → most polycythemic infants are ruddy and asymptomatic; hyperviscosity brings lethargy, irritability and jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, respiratory distress, poor feeding and cyanosis. Hydration by feeds or glucose-containing intravenous fluids comes first; symptomatic hyperviscosity despite it needs a partial exchange transfusion, which swaps blood for saline to lower viscosity. A double-volume exchange swaps blood for blood and leaves the hematocrit high, and furosemide removes plasma water and concentrates the blood ⚠︎; true dehydration is rare in the first 2 days, while the neonate still carries excess extracellular fluid
  9. 8-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks is cyanotic preductal saturation 88%, postductal 76% minimal improvement on 100% oxygen chest x-ray nearly clear Delivered through meconium-stained fluid Afebrile · HR 168/min · BP 62/38 mm Hg → Obtain an echocardiogram → a pre- to postductal gap above 10% that barely responds to oxygen is right-to-left ductal shunting: persistent pulmonary hypertension, a failed transition often after asphyxia or aspiration. Echocardiography shows high pulmonary pressure in a structurally normal heart and excludes cyanotic heart disease. Surfactant treats alveolar disease, which corrects on oxygen, and reassurance misses a can't-miss diagnosis
  10. 12-day-old girl born at 26 weeks has abdominal distension bloody stools on day 10 of enteral feeds abdominal x-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis T 35.9 °C · HR 182/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Necrotizing enterocolitis → a preterm infant on enteral feeds with distension, bloody stools and pneumatosis intestinalis has bacterial invasion of the bowel wall: keep nil by mouth, give intravenous antibiotics and consult surgery. Allergic proctocolitis is the well infant with bloody stool; pneumatosis intestinalis is the tell that names this can't-miss diagnosis over it and over malrotation with volvulus
  11. 1-hour-old boy born at 39 weeks by cesarean without labor is breathing fast chest x-ray shows fluid in the fissures with perihilar streaking Mother asks to breastfeed now Afebrile · respiratory rate 80/min · oxygen saturation 93% on oxygen → Keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and supplemental oxygen → neonatal tachypnea is a respiratory rate above 60 per minute, and feeding at a rate of 80 risks aspiration: keep nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and oxygen. Intubation and surfactant are for the preterm surfactant-deficient lung, not retained fluid in a term infant
  12. 24-year-old woman, gravida 1, is in preterm labor at 29 weeks cervix dilated 5 cm delivery expected within 48 hours T 37.0 °C · BP 118/72 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 140/min → Antenatal betamethasone → antenatal betamethasone gives the fetal lung the cortisol signal that drives surfactant maturation (the signal fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes); steroids before delivery, with surfactant after birth, converted bronchopulmonary dysplasia from fibrotic injury to developmental arrest; postnatal surfactant gives up the antenatal dose, and tocolysis only buys time for the steroid course; it does not mature the lung ⚠︎
  13. 1-hour-old boy born at 37 weeks has grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled diabetes chest x-ray shows diffuse ground glass with air bronchograms Afebrile · birth weight 4300 g · oxygen saturation 85% on room air → Fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol, delaying surfactant maturation → fetal hyperinsulinism antagonizes cortisol and suppresses phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylglycerol production, delaying surfactant maturation; the pneumocytes are not directly injured, and placental insufficiency is not the mechanism here ⚠︎
  14. 5-day-old girl born at 30 weeks has new apnea and bradycardia since this morning lethargic and mottled between episodes abdominal distension and feeding intolerance No antibiotics so far T 35.8 °C, unstable · HR 188/min · capillary refill 4 seconds → Blood culture and empiric antibiotics → an infant who is ill between spells (temperature instability, feeding intolerance or poor perfusion) has suspected sepsis, not simple apnea of prematurity: culture and treat. Caffeine is for the infant well between spells; anemia of prematurity comes weeks later, pale with a low hemoglobin; this tachycardia is sepsis
  15. 2-day-old girl was diagnosed with a left congenital diaphragmatic hernia at birth intubated; saturations now falling echocardiogram shows suprasystemic pulmonary pressures right hand saturation 92% · foot saturation 78% · HR 170/min → Inhaled nitric oxide → a hand-foot gap above 10% is right-to-left ductal shunting from pulmonary hypertension of the hypoplastic lung. Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) is the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but this cyanosis is not a closing duct; a chest tube treats a pneumothorax, not shunting. The lungs stay small after repair, and the pulmonary hypertension persists; the gap itself shows the duct is already open, so the target is pulmonary vasodilation
  16. 3-day-old boy born at 27 weeks has abrupt hypoxia on high-pressure mechanical ventilation since birth chest x-ray shows unilateral perivascular cystic lucencies No distended, hyperresonant hemithorax Afebrile · HR 172/min · oxygen saturation 78% → Pulmonary interstitial emphysema → air dissects into the interstitium on high ventilator pressures in the first days: cystic lucencies and abrupt decompensation; reduce ventilator pressures. Tension pneumothorax gives a distended, hyperresonant hemithorax needing needle decompression, and respiratory distress syndrome, though it worsens over 48 to 72 hours, shows ground glass with air bronchograms
  17. 10-hour-old girl born at 29 weeks has needed CPAP since birth rising oxygen requirement, now 60% worsening retractions chest x-ray shows ground glass with air bronchograms T 36.8 °C · oxygen saturation 86% on CPAP → Intubate and give surfactant → worsening surfactant deficiency despite CPAP means CPAP has failed: intubate and give surfactant. Closer observation leaves the failure untreated, and antibiotics alone do not replace surfactant
  18. 6-hour-old boy born at term is ruddy and jittery breathing fast with no retractions chest x-ray is clear; no hepatomegaly; normal heart sounds Mother had preeclampsia Afebrile · glucose 32 mg/dL · respiratory rate 70/min · HR 150/min → Polycythemia → plethora with hypoglycemia and a clear film is polycythemia. Intrauterine hypoxia drives erythropoietin (preeclampsia, maternal diabetes or hypertension, smoking, growth restriction), or placental transfusion adds blood (delayed cord clamping, twin-twin transfusion); hyperviscosity brings jitteriness, and in severe cases tachypnea, and the expanded red cell mass takes up glucose; check a venous hematocrit (above 65%). Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, glycogen storage disease type I brings hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis, and cyanotic heart disease is excluded by a normal heart and exam
  19. 14-month-old boy born at 30 weeks is seen at a well visit has bronchopulmonary dysplasia, on diuretics until 3 months ago his second RSV season starts next month Afebrile · respiratory rate 36/min · oxygen saturation 96% on room air → Nirsevimab prophylaxis → chronic lung disease of prematurity that needed medical support (supplemental oxygen, diuretics or chronic corticosteroids) in the 6 months before the second season qualifies for a second-season dose, and nirsevimab is the product recommended; palivizumab is no longer available from December 31, 2025, and the prophylaxis is an antibody, not an infant vaccine ⚠︎
  20. Term newborn girl has severe cyanosis at 12 hours no improvement on 100% oxygen no retractions; comfortable tachypnea chest radiograph structurally normal Afebrile · oxygen saturation 68% on 100% oxygen · HR 160/min → Prostaglandin E1 infusion → cyanosis that does not correct on oxygen in a comfortable infant with a normal film is a shunt (the hyperoxia test, still keyed on exams though largely abandoned clinically): suspect cyanotic congenital heart disease and start prostaglandin E1 pending echocardiography. Surfactant treats alveolar disease that corrects on oxygen; inhaled nitric oxide treats pulmonary hypertension, whose tell is a ductal saturation gap above 10%
  21. 3-week-old boy born at 28 weeks is given caffeine for central apneic spells well between spells His parents ask when the spells should stop Afebrile · HR 150/min · oxygen saturation 97% on room air → By about his expected due date → the brainstem breathing center matures by term corrected age, so spells resolve by about the expected due date; 28 days is the bronchopulmonary dysplasia clock, not the apnea clock
  22. 1-hour-old boy born at 41 weeks has tachypnea and retractions delivered through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress chest x-ray shows coarse, patchy, asymmetric infiltrates with hyperinflation Afebrile · respiratory rate 84/min · oxygen saturation 87% → Meconium aspiration syndrome → term or post-term delivery through meconium-stained fluid after fetal distress, with coarse patchy asymmetric infiltrates and hyperinflation; watch for pneumothorax and pulmonary hypertension. Transient tachypnea shows fluid in the fissures, and for congenital pneumonia nothing in this stem points to infection (rupture 18 hours or more, maternal fever, no intrapartum prophylaxis) ⚠︎
  23. 2-hour-old girl born at 36 weeks has central cyanosis, grunting and retractions mother has poorly controlled type 2 diabetes chest x-ray shows bilateral ground-glass opacities Afebrile · saturation 64% rising to 82% on oxygen · pre- and postductal readings equal → Surfactant → maternal diabetes delays surfactant maturation, so an infant of a diabetic mother can develop respiratory distress syndrome at a gestational age that would otherwise be safe. Ground glass with equal pre- and postductal readings and a partial oxygen response is lung disease, not a ductal shunt, so prostaglandin E1 is not the answer; steroids for the lung are the antenatal betamethasone given before delivery
  24. 4-month-old boy born at 28 weeks has poor weight gain needed supplemental oxygen until 3 months of age loud P2 liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin Afebrile · respiratory rate 56/min · oxygen saturation 93% on room air → Pulmonary artery hypertension → pulmonary hypertension is a complication of bronchopulmonary dysplasia that arrives months later, with a loud P2 and poor growth: obtain an echocardiogram. Systemic hypertension and recurrent respiratory infections are also complications, but a loud P2 is the pulmonic sound, and chronic aspiration does not explain it ⚠︎; the enlarged liver is right heart failure
  25. 4-day-old girl born at term was diagnosed with transient tachypnea on day 1 still breathing fast at 96 hours of life Feeding by nasogastric tube Afebrile · respiratory rate 74/min · oxygen saturation 94% on room air → Re-evaluate for another diagnosis → transient is a diagnostic criterion, not a description: it resolves within 24 to 72 hours, so tachypnea beyond 72 hours means the diagnosis was wrong; look again. Continued observation and discharge both keep the wrong label
Common wrong answers Refeeding syndrome: feeds introduced today suggest it, but appropriate weight gain on total parenteral nutrition excludes prior malnutrition. Pulmonary interstitial emphysema at 28 days: real ventilator pathology, but it belongs to the first days. RDS in a term infant: the right category, a preterm member. Group B streptococcal pneumonia: needs risk factors the stem must supply. Prostaglandin in a diaphragmatic hernia: the right class for a cyanotic newborn, but the cyanosis comes from hypoplastic lungs and pulmonary hypertension, not a closing duct. Diaphragmatic hernia at an hour with fissural fluid: it presents at delivery with a scaphoid abdomen.
Pairs with Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant: the well infant with bloody stool; here, the ill preterm infant. Ask: is the infant preterm, distended and unwell? Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant: intraventricular hemorrhage and anemia of prematurity, the mimics to exclude before calling a spell apnea of prematurity. Ask: is the infant well between episodes? Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the same distress in the first hours. Ask: is this fluid in normal lungs, or lungs that never developed? Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn: the step before, where work of breathing, the oxygen response and the limb gradient sort lung from heart. Part I Hypoxemia: the physiology under the oxygen response.
Transferable rule

Match the clock before the findings. Birth: RDS or transient tachypnea, sorted by gestational age, labor, onset and the film. Ventilator days: air leak. Day 2 to 3 spells in a well infant: apnea of prematurity. Oxygen at 28 days: BPD. Months: pulmonary hypertension. When the history states a diagnostic criterion exactly, make that diagnosis directly.

Pregnancy is a setting, not a diagnosis — and gestational age is the assassin that fires three times.

Liver Disease in Pregnancy

Abnormal liver tests in pregnancy: check the trimester first

The decision point

Acute fatty liver of pregnancy, intrahepatic cholestasis and preeclampsia/HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) are all third-trimester diseases. A patient at 14 weeks with elevated transaminases, obesity, and diabetes has metabolic liver disease unrelated to pregnancy.

Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
AST, ALT, bilirubin and alkaline phosphataseFirstAlkaline phosphatase raised alone, all else normalPlacental isoenzyme: physiologic, reassure
Serum bile acidsConfirmsRaised bile acids with itching of palms and solesIntrahepatic cholestasis: ursodeoxycholic acid, deliver at 36 to 37 weeks
Blood pressure, urine protein, CBC with smearConfirmsSchistocytes, low platelets, raised LFTs, hypertensionHELLP syndrome: delivery
Glucose, PT/INR, ammonia and creatinineBy branchHypoglycemia with coagulopathy and a rising creatinineAcute fatty liver of pregnancy: emergent delivery
Hepatitis serologies and liver ultrasoundBy branchRaised ALT before 20 weeks, echogenic liverNot pregnancy-specific: MASLD or viral hepatitis
Right upper quadrant ultrasound or bile acidsSkipAdds nothing when AST, ALT and bilirubin are normalIsolated alkaline phosphatase in late pregnancy needs no workup
Mnemonic HELLP — Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
Scenario bank
  1. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intense palmar pruritus, raised bile acids and no rash → Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy → ursodeoxycholic acid
  2. 26 yo F at 36 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy and raised transaminases → Acute fatty liver of pregnancy → urgent delivery
  3. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with hypertension, hemolysis, high LFTs and platelets 68,000 → HELLP syndrome → delivery
  4. 26 yo F at 9 weeks with intractable vomiting, ketonuria and mildly raised transaminases → Hyperemesis gravidarum
  5. 26 yo F at 14 weeks, obese with diabetes and raised transaminases → Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease — the third-trimester diseases do not fit at 14 weeks
  6. 26 yo F at 30 weeks with an isolated alkaline phosphatase twice normal, all else normal → Placental alkaline phosphatase — physiologic → reassurance
  7. 26 yo F at 34 weeks with intractable palmar pruritus and raised bile acids, taking ursodeoxycholic acid → Delivery at 36 to 37 weeks → intrahepatic cholestasis carries stillbirth risk
  8. 29 yo F at 35 weeks with hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, raised ammonia and rising creatinine → Emergent delivery → acute fatty liver of pregnancy is treated by delivering
  9. 28 yo F at 32 weeks with alkaline phosphatase three times normal on routine labs; AST, ALT and bilirubin normal; no symptoms → Reassurance → the placenta makes alkaline phosphatase
Alkaline phosphatase in pregnancy Alkaline phosphatase normally rises in pregnancy because the placenta makes its own isoenzyme; levels run 2–4× normal. AST (aspartate aminotransferase), ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and bilirubin do not rise physiologically; any elevation is pathologic.
Liver labs in normal pregnancy
Rises physiologicallyFalls physiologicallyShould stay normal
Alkaline phosphatase (placental), WBC (to ~15,000), ESR, fibrinogen and factors VII/VIII/X, total T4 and TBG, cholesterol, GFRHemoglobin (dilutional), platelets (mild gestational), creatinine and BUN, PaCO₂, TSH in the first trimesterAST, ALT, bilirubin
Liver disease in pregnancy — by trimester
ConditionTimingThe tellManagement
Hyperemesis gravidarum1stVomiting, ketonuria, >5% weight lossSupportive
Intrahepatic cholestasis2nd–3rdPruritus of palms and soles, worse at night; ↑bile acids, ↑bilirubin; stillbirth riskUrsodeoxycholic acid; deliver 36–37 wk
Preeclampsia / HELLP Emergency>20 wkHTN + proteinuria; Hemolysis, Elevated LFTs, Low Platelets, RUQ pain, schistocytesDelivery
Acute fatty liver Emergency3rdHypoglycemia, ↑ammonia, coagulopathy, ↑Cr, encephalopathy; LCHAD deficiency linkEmergent delivery
AFLP vs. HELLP Hypoglycemia, coagulopathy, high ammonia and renal failure indicate AFLP (acute fatty liver of pregnancy). Hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and more hypertension indicate HELLP (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) syndrome. Both are treated by delivering. Cholecystectomy in pregnancy is safest in the second trimester.
Transferable rule Before diagnosing a pregnancy-specific liver disease, check that the gestational age fits it.
Salient decoy

Fatty Liver Disease

Formerly NAFLD (nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) · a diagnosis of exclusion

The decision point

Metabolic syndrome (obesity, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia) + transaminase elevation + hyperechoic liver on ultrasound. AST (aspartate aminotransferase) is below ALT (alanine aminotransferase), an AST/ALT ratio <1. Alcohol gives the opposite ratio: AST:ALT ≥2 ("t-oAST").

  • Most common chronic liver disease in the US; progression is steatosis → MASH → fibrosis → cirrhosis → HCC, and HCC can occur without cirrhosis
  • Exclude first: alcohol, hepatitis B/C, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, autoimmune hepatitis, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, and drugs (steroids, amiodarone, methotrexate, tamoxifen)
  • Stage fibrosis with FIB-4 or transient elastography
  • Treatment: 7–10% weight loss reverses steatohepatitis; bariatric surgery if BMI ≥35; GLP-1 agonists; resmetirom for MASH with fibrosis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
AST and ALTFirstALT higher, AST:ALT under 1Metabolic; a ratio of 2 or more points to alcohol
Liver ultrasoundFirstHyperechoic liverSteatosis
Hepatitis B and C serology, iron studies, ceruloplasminConfirmsAll normal, alcohol under the thresholdMASLD is a diagnosis of exclusion; also exclude autoimmune hepatitis, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, drugs
FIB-4 scoreStagingHigh scorePossible advanced fibrosis: elastography next
Transient elastographyStagingStiff liverAdvanced fibrosis or cirrhosis: hepatology, HCC surveillance if cirrhotic
Liver biopsy in every patientSkipInvasive; noninvasive staging comes firstReserved for an uncertain diagnosis or discordant staging
Scenario bank
  1. 48 yo M, BMI 34, type 2 diabetes, ALT 70, AST 45, hyperechoic liver → MASLD
  2. 48 yo M with AST 180 and ALT 70 and a history of heavy drinking → Alcohol-associated liver disease → AST:ALT of 2 or more
  3. 48 yo M with MASLD asking what most improves liver histology → 7 To 10% weight loss
  4. 48 yo M with MASLD and a high FIB-4 score → Assess fibrosis with elastography
  5. 48 yo M with MASLD and LDL 160 → Statins are safe and indicated
  6. 32 yo M with fatty liver, low ceruloplasmin and Kayser-Fleischer rings → Wilson disease
Pearls Significant alcohol intake threshold: >21 drinks/week (men), >14 (women) · gallstones in pregnancy are common (progesterone → gallbladder stasis) and usually incidental without wall thickening, fever, or pain · young patient with steatosis + tremor + Kayser-Fleischer rings → Wilson disease.
Pairs with Part II Wilson Disease covers the copper exclusion: is the patient under about 40, with a tremor, psychiatric change or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

Abnormal Liver Tests

Classify, localize, then test for causes

The decision point

Classify the pattern before testing for causes. Alk phos ↑↑ with normal AST (aspartate aminotransferase)/ALT (alanine aminotransferase) and a direct hyperbilirubinemia is cholestasis. Next, order an abdominal ultrasound to see whether the ducts are dilated. Nondilated ducts (intrahepatic) lead to an antibody test; dilated ducts (extrahepatic) lead to cross-sectional imaging.

Step 1.5: confirm that the alk phos is hepatic with a GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase) or 5′-nucleotidase. Alkaline phosphatase also comes from bone, placenta, and intestine.

LFT patternshepatocellular vs cholestatic
PatternLabsCausesTargeted testsConfirms, then
HepatocellularAST/ALT ↑↑, alk phos normal or mildViral hepatitis, MASLD, alcohol (AST:ALT ≥2), autoimmune hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson, α1-antitrypsin, drugsASMA / anti-LKM1, iron studies, ceruloplasminViral serologies first; liver biopsy when the cause stays unclear
CholestaticAlk phos ↑↑ + direct bilirubin ↑PBC, PSC, choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head cancer, stricture, drugs, infiltrative diseaseUltrasound first, then AMA or MRCP/CTNormal ducts: AMA for PBC, biopsy if negative; dilated ducts: MRCP or CT, ERCP only to intervene
Isolated hyperbilirubinemiaBilirubin ↑ aloneIndirect: Gilbert, hemolysis, Crigler-Najjar · Direct: Dubin-Johnson, RotorFractionate, smear, reticulocytesIndirect, normal smear and reticulocytes, rises with fasting: Gilbert, no further testing
Alk phos ↑ with normal GGT—Not liver at all — bone (Paget, metastases, vitamin D deficiency, healing fracture, growing child) or placentaBone-specific workupGGT normal confirms a non-hepatic source; then calcium, phosphate, vitamin D and bone imaging
After the ultrasound
  • Ducts NOT dilated → intrahepatic → AMA (antimitochondrial antibody) for PBC; MRCP and biopsy if suspicion persists
  • Ducts dilated → extrahepatic → MRCP (biliary tree) or CT (pancreatic mass) → ERCP only when intervention is needed
Primary biliary cholangitis vs primary sclerosing cholangitis
PBCPSC
PatientMiddle-aged womenYoung men
AntibodyAMAp-ANCA
AssociationSjögren, Hashimoto, RA, celiacUlcerative colitis (~70–80%)

Scenario bank
  1. Ultrasound shows a dilated CBD and a pancreatic head mass → CT abdomen → pancreatic adenocarcinoma
  2. Normal ducts + AMA positive in a woman with pruritus → Primary biliary cholangitis → ursodiol
  3. Young man with ulcerative colitis and a cholestatic pattern → MRCP → beads on a string → PSC
  4. Alk phos elevated with a normal GGT → Bone source or pregnancy → not liver disease at all
  5. Charcot triad (fever + RUQ pain + jaundice) → Ascending cholangitis → urgent ERCP
  6. Painless jaundice + weight loss + palpable nontender gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) → Pancreatic head malignancy → not stones
  7. Isolated indirect hyperbilirubinemia appearing with fasting or illness, all else normal → Gilbert syndrome → reassurance
  8. Cholestatic pattern after amoxicillin-clavulanate, anabolic steroids, OCPs, or chlorpromazine → Stop the drug, then monitor
  9. Cholestasis + hilar lymphadenopathy + hypercalcemia → Sarcoidosis
Distractors ASMA (anti-smooth muscle antibody) and iron studies test for autoimmune and metabolic liver disease. These cause hepatocellular injury, the wrong pattern here. ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) is premature at this step. It is invasive and carries a risk of post-ERCP pancreatitis, and no lesion has yet been shown to need intervention. Repeat LFTs (liver function tests) in 3 months is appropriate only when a reversible cause has been identified and removed. Here the alk phos is 7× normal with no cause found.
Transferable rule Use the LFT (liver function test) pattern as a triage instrument to choose tests. Tests are pattern-specific. An autoimmune hepatitis antibody looks for hepatocellular disease and does not belong in the workup of a cholestatic pattern.
Sequencing trap

Zenker Diverticulum

Regurgitation of undigested food in an old man · the swallow study comes before any scope or tube

Source vignette Pt — 74 yo M, months of dysphagia, regurgitates undigested food hours after meals, halitosis, gurgling in the neck on swallowing, weight stable · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Zenker diverticulum, achalasia and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
The decision point

An elderly man with dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, and a gurgling sound in the neck has a Zenker diverticulum. It is a pulsion pouch through the weak posterior hypopharyngeal wall that forms because the cricopharyngeus fails to relax. Order a barium esophagram first. A blind endoscope or nasogastric tube can enter the pouch and perforate it.

Once the esophagram shows the pouch, treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy (with or without diverticulectomy). The main complication is aspiration pneumonia.

Dysphagia in an adult — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Zenker diverticulumElderly man; cricopharyngeal dysfunction; food pools in a posterior pharyngeal pouchRegurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, neck gurgling; esophagram before scope
AchalasiaLoss of myenteric inhibitory neurons; middle age; dysphagia to solids and liquids from the startBird's beak on esophagram; manometry confirms absent peristalsis and a non-relaxing LES
Esophageal cancer Can't missSmoker or drinker (SCC) or long-standing reflux (adenocarcinoma); progressive solid then liquid dysphagiaWeight loss with progressive solid-food dysphagia; endoscopy with biopsy
Schatzki ring / peptic strictureDistal mucosal ring or reflux scar; intermittent solid-food dysphagiaEpisodic impaction with meat or bread, no weight loss; dilation
Oropharyngeal (neurologic) dysphagiaStroke, Parkinson disease, myasthenia; trouble initiating the swallowCoughing or choking at the start of the swallow, nasal regurgitation; videofluoroscopy and speech therapy
