TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Barium esophagramFirstPosterior pouch above the cricopharyngeusZenker diverticulum, confirmed; cricopharyngeal myotomy next
Dilated esophagus tapering to a bird's beakAchalasia: manometry next
Esophageal manometryConfirmsAbsent peristalsis, LES fails to relaxAchalasia
Upper endoscopy with biopsyConfirmsMalignant tissueEsophageal cancer; goes first only with alarm features and no neck finding
Videofluoroscopic swallow studyBy branchTrouble initiating the swallow, aspirationOropharyngeal neurologic dysphagia: speech therapy
Upper endoscopy or blind nasogastric tubeSkipCan enter the pouch and perforate itImage before instrumenting
Scenario bank
  1. 74 yo M, months of dysphagia, regurgitates undigested food hours after meals, halitosis, gurgling in the neck when he swallows, weight stable → Zenker diverticulum → barium esophagram
  2. 79 yo M with regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis and a gurgling neck → Barium esophagram → a blind scope or tube risks perforating the pouch
  3. 81 yo M with suspected Zenker diverticulum and poor oral intake; the intervention to avoid → Blind nasogastric tube placement → the tube enters the pouch and perforates it
  4. 72 yo M whose esophagram shows a posterior pharyngoesophageal outpouching above the cricopharyngeus → Cricopharyngeal myotomy with or without diverticulectomy → the pouch is the symptom, the non-relaxing muscle is the cause
  5. 76 yo M with known Zenker diverticulum, 3 days of fever, productive cough and a right lower lobe infiltrate → Aspiration pneumonia → pooled contents aspirate at night
  6. 46 yo F, dysphagia to solids and liquids from the outset, regurgitation of undigested food, 5 kg weight loss, esophagram with a dilated esophagus tapering to a bird's beak → Achalasia → manometry, then pneumatic dilation or myotomy
  7. 63 yo M, 40 pack-years and daily alcohol, 3 months of progressive solid-food dysphagia now with liquids, 8 kg weight loss → Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma → endoscopy with biopsy
Undigested regurgitation Regurgitated undigested food never reached the stomach; a pouch or a non-emptying esophagus held it. With a neck finding it is a Zenker pouch; with dysphagia to liquids from day one it is achalasia. In both, the first study is the esophagram. Endoscopy comes first only with an alarm feature for cancer (weight loss, smoking, progressive solid dysphagia) and no neck finding.
Pearls Zenker is a false (pulsion) diverticulum: mucosa and submucosa herniate through the posterior wall between the inferior pharyngeal constrictor and the cricopharyngeus · the mechanism is cricopharyngeal motor dysfunction (diminished relaxation), not structural weakness alone · halitosis comes from food decaying in the pouch · the main complication is aspiration pneumonia · treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy, with diverticulectomy for larger pouches
Pairs with Ask: is the regurgitated food undigested, and is the finding in the neck or in the chest?
Transferable rule When the diagnosis implies a blind pouch or cavity the instrument cannot see, image it before instrumenting it: esophagram before endoscopy in Zenker, as with ultrasound before the needle in a hip effusion.
Sequencing trapUpper endoscopy is ordered too early; a blind scope can perforate the pouch that the esophagram would have shown.
Salient decoyWeight loss and age suggest cancer, but undigested regurgitation with a neck gurgle indicates a pouch, and the esophagram evaluates both.
Class-vs-memberManometry evaluates motility disorders such as achalasia, not a pharyngeal pouch.

Stool Changes in a Well Infant

Well-appearing infant with a stool complaint · reassure, eliminate, or work up

Source vignette Pt — 4 mo M, thriving, screams and strains for 10 minutes several times daily then passes a soft yellow stool, normal examination · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned reassurance and parental education, a glycerin suppository and switching to an extensively hydrolyzed formula
The decision point

Three benign stool complaints occur in a thriving, well-appearing infant or child whose parents are worried. Straining and screaming for minutes, followed by a normal soft stool in an infant under 9 months, is infant dyschezia → reassurance only. Painless blood-streaked stools in a well infant under 6 months are food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis. Treat it by removing cow's milk and soy from the maternal diet, or by using an extensively hydrolyzed formula. Watery diarrhea and bloating after dairy is reintroduced following gastroenteritis are secondary lactase deficiency → temporary lactose avoidance, with no workup.

Two mimics present with an ill-appearing infant. FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome) causes profuse vomiting and lethargy 1–4 h after the trigger; it is non-IgE and needs fluids. IgE-mediated allergy causes urticaria, wheeze or anaphylaxis within minutes and needs epinephrine. Reassure the parents; a thriving infant needs no formula change, suppository or stool workup.

Defining criteria Infant dyschezia — under 9 months, strains and cries for minutes, then passes a normal soft stool, thriving; hard stool means constipation instead · Food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis — well-appearing infant under 6 months, painless blood-streaked stools, insidious onset; non-IgE · Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome — under 12 months, profuse vomiting with diarrhea, dehydration and lethargy within hours (1–4 h) of the trigger, ill-appearing; non-IgE · IgE-mediated food allergy — urticaria, vomiting, wheeze, angioedema or hypotension within minutes (under 1 h), any age · Osmotic diarrhea — stops with fasting, raised stool osmotic gap, acidic stool pH
The well-appearing infant with a stool complaint — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Infant dyscheziaUnder 9 months; cannot coordinate a Valsalva with pelvic-floor relaxation; resolves spontaneouslyScreams and strains, then a normal soft stool; reassurance, nothing else
Functional constipationInfrequent, hard or pellet stools, often at a diet transitionHard stool — the one word that converts dyschezia into constipation
FPIAPUnder 6 months, breastfed or formula-fed; cow's milk or soy protein; resolves by about 1 yearPainless blood streaks in a well infant; eliminate cow's milk and soy, no scope
FPIESUnder 12 months; non-IgE; classic triggers include cow's milk and soyProfuse vomiting, lethargy, dehydration 1–4 h after feeding, ill-appearing; fluids, not epinephrine
IgE-mediated food allergyAny age; minutes after exposure; may progress to anaphylaxisUrticaria or wheeze within an hour; epinephrine, strict avoidance, allergist
Secondary lactase deficiencyBrush-border lactase lost after gastroenteritis or with IBD; osmotic diarrheaDiarrhea and bloating when dairy is reintroduced after a resolving gastroenteritis; no fever, no vomiting
Necrotizing enterocolitis Can't miss PreemiePreterm infant on enteral feeds; bacterial invasion of an ischemic bowel wallDistension, bloody stools, pneumatosis intestinalis in a preemie — never a well-infant diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 4 mo M, thriving, screams and strains for 10 minutes several times a day, then passes a soft yellow stool, normal exam → Reassurance and parental education → infant dyschezia resolves by about 9 months
  2. 5 mo F, passed meconium on day 1, now hard pellet stools every 3 days with straining since starting solids, thriving → Functional constipation → dietary change, then an osmotic laxative
  3. 6 wk F, exclusively breastfed, thriving, blood-streaked soft stools for a week, comfortable and well → Eliminate cow's milk and soy from the maternal diet → food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis
  4. 3 mo M on cow's milk formula, well-appearing, gaining weight, blood streaks and mucus in soft stools → Extensively hydrolyzed formula → soy cross-reacts, so it is not the substitute
  5. 2 mo F, breastfed, with food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis; the recommendation to avoid → Stop breastfeeding and start a soy-based formula → soy protein triggers the same reaction and breastfeeding need not stop
  6. 7 mo M, 2 hours after his first cow's-milk formula, repetitive profuse vomiting, pale, limp and lethargic, no urticaria or wheeze → Intravenous fluid resuscitation → food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome is non-IgE, so epinephrine does nothing
  7. 9 mo F, hives and wheezing within 15 minutes of her first scrambled egg → Intramuscular epinephrine → IgE-mediated food allergy, strict avoidance and allergist referral
  8. 6 yo M, viral gastroenteritis 10 days ago that was improving, now watery diarrhea and bloating since milk was reintroduced, afebrile, no vomiting → Temporary lactose avoidance, then reintroduce → secondary lactase deficiency needs no workup
  9. 5 yo F, diarrhea after a resolving gastroenteritis that stops when she fasts, acidic stool pH, raised stool osmotic gap → Transient loss of brush-border lactase → colonic bacteria ferment the unabsorbed lactose
  10. 5-day-old born at 32 weeks, bilious and coffee-grounds emesis, distended tender abdomen, pneumatosis intestinalis on abdominal x-ray → Blood cultures and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics with bowel rest → necrotizing enterocolitis
Exceptions Reassurance or trigger elimination before testing applies only to an infant who is well-appearing and thriving. Lethargy, dehydration, or profuse vomiting is FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome). Urticaria or wheeze is IgE-mediated allergy. A preterm infant with distension and bloody stools has necrotizing enterocolitis. A child with fever, vomiting, or weight loss after gastroenteritis does not fit secondary lactase deficiency and needs a workup. Formula changes, rectal stimulation, and laxatives are wrong for dyschezia; a laxative is right only when the stool is hard.
Pearls Dyschezia is a coordination failure: raised intra-abdominal pressure without pelvic-floor relaxation, and inadequate abdominal tone for an effective Valsalva · FPIAP (food protein-induced allergic proctocolitis) is non-IgE and self-limited. The mother eliminates both cow's milk and soy, and FPIAP resolves by about 1 year · FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome) is also non-IgE but ill-appearing: onset hours after the trigger, no urticaria, treated with fluids · Only IgE-mediated disease gets epinephrine · Secondary lactase deficiency is osmotic (stops with fasting, acidic stool, no fever); IBD (inflammatory bowel disease) also causes brush-border loss
Pairs with Part II Feeding an Infant or Toddler covers the age for starting cow's milk; this brief covers the stool effects of cow's-milk protein before that age. Part I Lung Disease in the Newborn and Preterm Infant has the necrotizing enterocolitis item: bloody stool in an ill preemie is not proctocolitis. Ask: is the infant well-appearing, and is the stool soft? Part I Constipation in a Child covers the same complaint in toddlers, where the withholding cycle, not milk protein, is the cause.
Transferable rule In a thriving child with worried parents, base management on the stool, the timing after the trigger, and the child's appearance. Reassure or eliminate the trigger before testing.
Uniform-answer doubtReassurance feels like doing nothing, but for dyschezia every active option is a named wrong answer.
Class-vs-memberSoy formula removes cow's milk, but soy protein cross-reacts.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpinephrine treats IgE-mediated food allergy; FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome) vomiting hours later is non-IgE and needs fluids.
Sequencing trapA stool workup is the tier above dietary change in a well child whose diarrhea followed dairy.

Hereditary Polyposis Syndromes

adenomas or hamartomas: count the polyps, find the pigment · when a known carrier is scoped and operated on · lip macules that redirect an anemia workupHow many polyps, is there an adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) mutation, and where exactly is the pigment?

Which syndromeScreen and operatePigment plus anemiaPractice
Bottom line
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP): an autosomal dominant APC mutation; hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomas, and colon cancer in nearly 100% before age 40.
  • Screening gate: annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy from puberty, age 10 to 12, not the first-degree-relative or average-risk schedule.
  • Colectomy gate: prophylactic proctocolectomy in the teens to early 20s, or at any age with gastrointestinal bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps or high-grade dysplasia.
  • Upper tract: upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas, continued after colectomy.
  • Gardner syndrome: FAP plus osteomas and desmoid tumors.
  • Turcot syndrome: FAP plus central nervous system (CNS) tumors.
  • Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: autosomal dominant, a tumor-suppressor mutation, with mucocutaneous pigmented macules and two or more gastrointestinal hamartomatous polyps.
  • Peutz-Jeghers macules: lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles.
Which syndrome
Hereditary colon cancer syndromes: the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe tell
FAPAPC, autosomal dominant; adenomas carpet the colon from adolescenceHundreds of polyps; scope from puberty, colectomy in the teens to 20s
Gardner syndromeFAP variantPolyposis plus osteomas and desmoid tumors
Turcot syndromeFAP variantPolyposis plus CNS tumors
Lynch syndrome, or hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC)Mismatch-repair mutation; few polyps, early right-sided cancer; endometrial and other cancers in the familyEarly colon cancer with few polyps and an endometrial cancer in the pedigree
Peutz-Jeghers syndromeHamartomatous polyps that intussuscept or bleedMucocutaneous pigmentation of lips and buccal mucosa
Exceptions Sporadic family history – a first-degree relative with sporadic colon cancer follows a different schedule: colonoscopy at 40, or 10 years before the relative's cancer; earlier than average-risk screening, but not annual scoping from puberty · Lynch pedigree – few polyps and endometrial cancer in the family follow a third schedule
FAP: when to scope, when to operate
The ladder Testing unavailable – screen the child as affected · Why puberty – adenomas appear in adolescence and cancer follows within decades · Polyposis develops – plan surgery; any colectomy trigger means operating now, at any age, rather than in the teens to early 20s · The operation – proctocolectomy, or colectomy with ileorectal anastomosis; a retained rectum keeps its own endoscopic surveillance · After colectomy – upper endoscopy continues, because the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk
Peutz-Jeghers: pigment plus anemia
Pigmentation plus anemia: where the pigment is decides
DiagnosisThe pigmentThe anemiaWhat to do
Peutz-JeghersDiscrete brown macules on lips, buccal mucosa, palms and solesMicrocytic, from occult polyp bleedingUpper and lower endoscopy; genetic testing
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)Diffuse, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areasUsually normocytic if presentACTH stimulation test
Lead poisoningBlue gingival line at the tooth marginMicrocytic with basophilic stipplingBlood lead level
Menstrual iron deficiencyNoneMicrocytic, from heavy or prolonged mensesIron; hormonal control if bleeding is heavy
Marrow failure or malignancyNoneUsually normocytic, with other cytopeniasBone marrow evaluation
Gates Not automatically menstrual – microcytic anemia in an adolescent girl: check the mouth, palms and family history · Polyp complications – obstruction or intussusception, anemia from bleeding, rectal prolapse · Intussusception – in an older child it has a lead point until proven otherwise; a hamartoma can be one; perioral pigmentation with intussusception in a child is the classic presentation · Normal platelets and leukocytes – argue against marrow failure
Cancer and family Cancer risk – gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast and genital tract (ovary, cervix) cancers, plus testicular Sertoli cell tumors, so surveillance is lifelong · Why broader – the syndrome is an inherited STK11 variant, and its risk reaches past the gut: pancreas, breast, ovary, cervix, and Sertoli cell tumors of the testis; colorectal and gastric cancers can arise from adenomas common in Peutz-Jeghers · Faded macules – the macules can fade in adulthood but the polyp risk persists, so a normal skin examination in a parent does not exclude the family history
Practice
  1. 12-year-old boy is seen for a well visit His father has familial adenomatous polyposis genetic testing shows the family APC mutation Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL · abdomen soft and nontender → Annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy starting now → the screening gate opens at puberty, age 10 to 12, so a known APC carrier starts annual sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy now. Colonoscopy at 40 is the sporadic family-history schedule and does not apply to a carrier; prophylactic colectomy is planned for the teens to early 20s, or sooner only for bleeding, polyps over 1 cm, innumerable polyps or high-grade dysplasia, and none is present
  2. 13-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue Regular menses lasting 6 days; no medications pale conjunctivae; brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.4 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 70 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal → Upper and lower endoscopy → six-day menses with a microcytic anemia suggest menstrual iron deficiency, but brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa mark Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, so the anemia is occult bleeding from hamartomatous polyps: scope above and below. Iron with an oral contraceptive treats the anemia but leaves the syndrome undiagnosed; lead gives a blue gingival line, not mucosal macules
  3. 28-year-old man has a firm mass in the abdominal wall biopsy shows a desmoid tumor radiograph shows a mandibular osteoma colonoscopy shows hundreds of colonic adenomas No headaches or neurologic deficits Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL → Gardner syndrome → polyposis plus osteomas and desmoid tumors is Gardner syndrome, an FAP variant managed on the same pathway with the same colectomy rules. Turcot syndrome adds central nervous system tumors, and there are no neurologic findings; Peutz-Jeghers polyps are hamartomas that come with lip and buccal pigmentation
  4. 19-year-old man is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis Annual colonoscopy since age 11 2 weeks of rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL · low ferritin consistent with iron deficiency → Colectomy now → bleeding is an any-age indication, so the operation planned for the teens to early 20s happens now. Polypectomy with iron treats the symptom and leaves a colon that adenomas carpet, and repeating colonoscopy in a year delays a trigger that is already met
  5. 15-year-old boy has 3 months of fatigue, anorexia and weight loss diffuse hyperpigmentation, darkest over the elbows, knees and sun-exposed skin No lip macules; gums normal BP 106/64 mm Hg · hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 88 fL → Addison disease → diffuse pigmentation, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areas, is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), with an anemia that is usually normocytic if present; the adrenocorticotropic hormone stimulation test answers it. Peutz-Jeghers gives discrete brown macules on the lips, buccal mucosa, palms and soles, and lead a blue gingival line with a microcytic anemia
  6. 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit Her mother has familial adenomatous polyposis the girl has never had genetic testing Asymptomatic; no rectal bleeding Afebrile · growth at the 50th percentile · hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL → APC genetic testing → APC is autosomal dominant, so each child of an affected parent has a one-in-two risk and is tested rather than presumed: a positive result starts annual endoscopic screening, and a negative result for the known family mutation means average-risk screening. Average-risk screening presumes she is not a carrier, and annual fecal immunochemical testing is the wrong pathway for a carrier
  7. 16-year-old girl has 4 months of fatigue dark brown macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms Regular menses lasting 5 days; intermittent cramping abdominal pain Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.1 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 68 fL · platelets and leukocytes normal → Occult polyp bleeding → the macules mark Peutz-Jeghers, whose hamartomatous polyps bleed slowly and cause iron deficiency. The low MCV separates the bleeding causes from the marrow causes, and normal platelet and leukocyte counts argue against marrow failure, which is usually normocytic; microcytic anemia in an adolescent girl is not automatically menstrual once the macules are seen
  8. 14-year-old boy is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis annual colonoscopy shows a few small adenomas, all under 1 cm biopsies show no dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 13.6 g/dL → Continue annual colonoscopy and plan colectomy for the late teens to early 20s → no immediate trigger is present: no bleeding, no polyp over 1 cm, the polyps are few rather than innumerable, and there is no high-grade dysplasia, so annual surveillance continues toward a planned prophylactic proctocolectomy. Operating now is for a met trigger, and a 5-year interval is not the annual schedule a carrier needs
  9. 15-year-old boy has recurrent cramping abdominal pain ultrasound shows a small-bowel intussusception pigmented macules on the lips, buccal mucosa and palms No vomiting; stools without visible blood Afebrile · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → mucocutaneous macules with hamartomatous polyps that intussuscept is Peutz-Jeghers, autosomal dominant; intussusception in an older child has a lead point until proven otherwise, and a hamartoma can be one. The tell of FAP is hundreds of colonic adenomas, and Addison pigmentation is diffuse, worst on pressure and sun-exposed areas, not discrete macules
  10. 23-year-old woman is seen for follow-up Total proctocolectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis 2 years ago Asymptomatic; eating well; no abdominal mass Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 72/min · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL → Upper endoscopy for duodenal and ampullary adenomas → colectomy does not address duodenal and ampullary adenomas, so upper endoscopy surveillance continues; the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk, so stopping surveillance is wrong. A desmoid tumor marks Gardner syndrome, a feature of the variant rather than the surveillance that continues after colectomy, which is upper endoscopy
  11. 14-year-old girl has 2 months of fatigue a blue line along the gingival margin at the teeth No lip or buccal macules; regular 4-day menses Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.0 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 66 fL · basophilic stippling on the smear → Lead poisoning → a blue gingival line at the tooth margin with a microcytic anemia and basophilic stippling is lead poisoning: check a blood lead level. Peutz-Jeghers pigment is discrete macules on the lips and buccal mucosa, and menstrual iron deficiency brings no pigment and needs heavy or prolonged menses
  12. 17-year-old girl is seen for follow-up of familial adenomatous polyposis colonoscopy shows innumerable polyps, several over 1 cm biopsy of one polyp shows high-grade dysplasia No rectal bleeding Afebrile · hemoglobin 12.9 g/dL → Total proctocolectomy → innumerable polyps, polyps over 1 cm and high-grade dysplasia are each an any-age colectomy trigger. Polypectomy of the largest lesions is not enough once innumerable polyps or dysplasia indicate colectomy, and a segmental resection leaves the rest of a colon that adenomas carpet
  13. 15-year-old girl has fatigue Regular menses every 28 days, lasting 6 days brown macules on the lips and buccal mucosa No medications; no visible blood in stool Afebrile · hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 72 fL · platelets normal → Iron and an oral contraceptive → iron and an oral contraceptive treat the anemia but leave the syndrome undiagnosed. Upper and lower endoscopy finds the bleeding hamartomas, the source of the anemia, and adding STK11 testing confirms the syndrome, after which first-degree relatives are tested because inheritance is autosomal dominant
  14. 36-year-old woman has a right-sided colon cancer on colonoscopy 12 polyps elsewhere in the colon Her mother had endometrial cancer at 45; her brother had colon cancer at 42 Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL · no mucocutaneous pigmentation → Lynch syndrome → early right-sided colon cancer with few polyps and an endometrial cancer in the pedigree is Lynch syndrome, a mismatch-repair mutation: test the tumor for mismatch repair. FAP brings hundreds to thousands of adenomas, and Peutz-Jeghers brings hamartomas with lip and buccal pigmentation
  15. 20-year-old woman is seen for follow-up of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome STK11 mutation confirmed at age 14 Asymptomatic; her lip macules have faded Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min · hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL → Annual hemoglobin with periodic upper and lower endoscopy → surveillance is lifelong, annual hemoglobin ⚠︎ with upper and lower endoscopy and small-bowel examination, plus breast and genital tract cancer screening, because the risk includes gastrointestinal, pancreatic, breast and genital tract (ovary, cervix) cancers, plus testicular Sertoli cell tumors; faded macules do not end the polyp risk. Prophylactic proctocolectomy is the FAP pathway, and the age-40 schedule belongs to sporadic family history
Common wrong answers Colonoscopy at 40: the sporadic family-history schedule; an APC carrier is scoped annually from puberty. Polypectomy of the largest lesions: not enough once innumerable polyps or dysplasia indicate colectomy. Stopping surveillance after colectomy: the duodenum and ampulla remain at risk. Iron with an oral contraceptive: an adolescent girl with menses and microcytic anemia looks like menstrual iron deficiency until the oral macules are noted. ACTH stimulation or a lead level: Addison disease and lead also cause pigmentation, but in a different distribution.
Pairs with Part I Postmenopausal Bleeding lists Lynch syndrome among the endometrial cancer risk factors; Lynch syndrome and its colorectal screening intervals are not covered on this page.
Transferable rule

Identify the hereditary syndrome first: start age, interval and operation all depend on it, and sporadic family-history numbers do not apply to a known carrier. When one finding does not fit an otherwise ordinary explanation, that finding usually determines the diagnosis.

Feeding an Infant or Toddler

the feeding ladder by age · the toddler who refuses food · eosinophilic esophagitisIs the child well and due for the next age-gated step, or refusing a texture, a food group, or eating altogether?

Feeding by ageFood refusalManagementPractice
Bottom line

A well infant: read the age first; each feeding step has an age gate.

A child who refuses food: name the pattern before choosing a test.

  • Texture: every solid refused, purees only past 12 months. The esophagus (dysphagia).
  • Food group (bread and pasta: gluten): celiac disease or IgE (immunoglobulin E) allergy.
  • Appetite changed (lost, or increased with poor gain): systemic or metabolic disease.

Atopic toddler, purees only, normal swallow study: endoscopy with esophageal biopsy.

Feeding by age
The feeding ladder
AgeFeedAdvance when
0 to 6 monthsExclusive breast milk or formula; if breastfed or partially breastfed, vitamin D 400 IU (international units) daily; if breastfed, iron 1 mg/kg daily from 4 monthsAbout 6 months, readiness signs
About 6 monthsIron first (fortified cereal, pureed meats), then pureed vegetables and fruit, one new food every 3 to 5 days; stop supplemental iron once iron-rich foods are establishedSits independently; pincer grasp at 8 to 9 months
8 to 9 monthsSoft finger foods, lumpier textures, self-feeding, a cupTurns 12 months
12 monthsWhole cow's milk, limited to about 16 to 24 oz daily; table foods; off the bottleAge 2: reduced-fat milk
Defining criteria Readiness – sits with support, head control, no extrusion reflex, interest in food · Why 6 months – fetal iron stores deplete at 4 to 6 months; breast milk no longer meets iron and zinc needs · Pincer grasp – emerges at 8 to 9 months; the gate for finger foods · Vitamin D – continues through the first year · Whole milk to age 2 – fat is required for myelination in the second year
Not before 12 months Whole cow's milk – iron deficiency (low content, occult blood loss, poor absorption); later, cap at 16 to 24 oz · Honey – infant botulism · Fruit juice – none · Allergens – no delay; severe eczema or egg allergy: peanut at 4 to 6 months after evaluation
The toddler who refuses food
Defining findings Eosinophilic esophagitis – T helper type 2 (Th2) response to food antigen; most are atopic; 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, other causes, such as achalasia and infection, excluded · By age – toddler: refuses solids; school age: pain and vomiting; adolescent: dysphagia, impaction · Normal swallow study – excludes oropharyngeal dysfunction and aspiration
The toddler who stops advancing his diet
CauseThe tell
Celiac diseaseDiarrhea or constipation, pain, distension; avoids gluten foods only
Oropharyngeal dysphagiaCoughing and choking with feeds; abnormal video swallow study
Anatomic obstruction (stricture, ring, vascular ring ⚠︎)Abrupt onset, or a caustic or reflux history; esophagram or endoscopy shows it
Behavioral feeding disorderDevelopmental delay or autism spectrum; a normal endoscopy
Hyperthyroidism; abdominal massBig appetite, tachycardia, goiter; anorexia, palpable mass
Management
By diagnosis Eosinophilic esophagitis – a proton pump inhibitor, a swallowed topical glucocorticoid or dietary elimination are first-line options; feeding therapy for learned avoidance · Food impaction – urgent endoscopy · Allergy testing – only after biopsy confirms the diagnosis, to guide the elimination diet; tests may have limited accuracy for food triggers · Normal endoscopy – feeding therapy
Practice
  1. 18-month-old boy takes only purees and refuses every solid food weight fell from the 25th to the 5th percentile height steady at the 30th Eczema; always a picky eater; development normal Afebrile · stools soft and daily · swallow study normal → Endoscopy with esophageal biopsy → a texture refusal in an atopic toddler with a normal swallow study points below the pharynx: biopsy, where 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field is diagnostic
  2. 2-year-old boy was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis last week biopsy showed 30 eosinophils per high-power field takes purees, refuses solids Eczema; parents ask about first-line treatment Afebrile · weight at the 10th percentile · examination normal → Dietary elimination → a proton pump inhibitor, a swallowed topical glucocorticoid or dietary elimination are first-line options; systemic prednisone and dilation are not
  3. 16-year-old boy has had meat stuck in his chest for 3 hours now drooling, cannot swallow saliva was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis at age 12 Breathing comfortably, no stridor HR 104/min · oxygen saturation 98% · afebrile → Urgent endoscopy → food impaction is the adolescent presentation of eosinophilic esophagitis: urgent endoscopy
  4. 8-year-old girl has had abdominal pain and vomiting for 6 months asthma and allergic rhinitis esophageal biopsies show 25 eosinophils per high-power field No diarrhea or weight loss Afebrile · abdomen soft and nontender → Eosinophilic esophagitis → abdominal pain and vomiting in an atopic child is the school-age presentation; 15 or more eosinophils per high-power field, with other causes excluded, makes the diagnosis
  5. 3-year-old girl has poor weight gain and chronic diarrhea abdomen distended refuses bread and pasta but eats other solids Weight fell from the 50th to the 10th percentile Afebrile · development normal → Tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total IgA level → a food-group refusal with diarrhea and distension points to gluten: celiac serology, sent with a total IgA level
  6. 14-month-old boy coughs and chokes during most feeds two prior pneumonias weight at the 10th percentile No eczema, asthma or diarrhea T 37.0 °C · respiratory rate 30/min · lungs clear · abdomen soft → Video swallow study → coughing and choking with feeds and aspiration pneumonias are oropharyngeal dysfunction: a video swallow study
  7. 20-month-old girl takes only purees and gags on solids eczema and asthma weight down to the 5th percentile Normal swallow study; eosinophilic inflammation of the esophagus is suspected Afebrile · development normal · stools soft → Allergy skin testing → skin testing shows IgE sensitization only; it diagnoses IgE-mediated allergy, not this, and guides the elimination diet after biopsy
  8. 2-year-old boy has poor weight gain and eats only a few soft foods development normal, no eczema or asthma swallow study normal Endoscopy and esophageal biopsies normal Afebrile · stools soft and daily · weight at the 5th percentile → Feeding therapy for a behavioral feeding disorder → the scope has excluded the organ: a behavioral feeding disorder, treated with feeding therapy
  9. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis after months of vomiting eczema, allergic rhinitis and a peanut allergy biopsy: 40 eosinophils per high-power field Parents ask what drives the inflammation Afebrile · growth normal → A Th2-mediated response to food antigen → a T helper type 2 response to food antigen; comorbid atopy is the clinical correlate; the peanut allergy is IgE-mediated, the esophageal lesion is not
  10. 6-year-old girl was diagnosed with eosinophilic esophagitis by biopsy last month eczema and seasonal allergic rhinitis starting dietary elimination Parents ask whether allergy skin testing still has a role Afebrile · growth at the 40th percentile → To guide dietary elimination given frequent concomitant IgE sensitivities → after the diagnosis, never instead of it: skin testing may guide which foods to eliminate, though its accuracy for food triggers is limited
  11. 6-month-old girl is seen for a well visit born at term takes breast milk, formula and iron-fortified cereal Weight 75th, length 60th percentile Afebrile · examination normal · good head control · sits with support → Begin pureed vegetables and fruit, one new food every few days → the iron source is already in: next comes variety, one new single-ingredient food every 3 to 5 days
  12. 9-month-old boy is seen for a well visit sits independently, brings food to his mouth pincer grasp emerging Tolerating purees of cereal, meats, vegetables and fruit Afebrile · weight 50th percentile · examination normal → Offer soft finger foods → an emerging pincer grasp at 8 to 9 months is the gate for soft finger foods and self-feeding
  13. 12-month-old girl is seen for a well visit healthy, tracking the 50th percentile still taking formula from a bottle Eats table foods with the family Afebrile · hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL · examination normal → Whole cow's milk, about 16 to 24 oz daily → at 12 months, whole cow's milk capped at 16 to 24 oz daily and a move from bottle to cup; reduced-fat milk waits until age 2
  14. 14-month-old boy is pale and irritable drinks 40 oz of whole milk daily eats little else No bleeding, no dark stools Afebrile · HR 128/min · hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 68 fL → Limit milk under 24 oz daily and start oral iron → excess cow's milk causes iron deficiency (low iron content, occult blood loss, impaired absorption): cap the milk and give oral iron
  15. 6-month-old girl is seen for a well visit parents ask about giving fruit juice takes breast milk and iron-fortified cereal Started pureed vegetables last week Afebrile · weight 50th percentile · examination normal → Give no fruit juice before 12 months → no fruit juice before 12 months; offer water in a cup with meals
  16. 4-month-old boy is seen for a well visit exclusively breastfed, born at term already receiving vitamin D No complementary foods started yet; parents ask about supplements Afebrile · weight 50th percentile · examination normal → Oral iron 1 mg/kg daily → a breastfed infant gets iron 1 mg/kg daily from 4 months until iron-rich complementary foods are established
  17. 3-day-old girl is seen for her first newborn visit exclusively breastfed, latching well born at term after an uncomplicated delivery Parents ask which supplements she needs Afebrile · weight 4% below birth weight · examination normal → Vitamin D 400 IU daily → every breastfed or partially breastfed infant gets vitamin D 400 IU daily from the first days through the first year
  18. 5-month-old boy is seen for a well visit severe eczema since 2 months known egg allergy Parents ask when peanut can safely be started Afebrile · weight 40th percentile · examination otherwise normal → Introduce peanut-containing food early, after evaluation → delaying allergens is obsolete: with severe eczema or egg allergy, introduce peanut at 4 to 6 months after evaluation
  19. 8-month-old girl is seen for a well visit grandmother asks which foods to hold until the first birthday eats purees of cereal, meat and vegetables Started soft finger foods this week Afebrile · examination normal → Honey → honey before 12 months risks infant botulism; peanut is introduced early and iron-fortified cereal is a first food
Decoys Always a picky eater: suggests a behavioral cause, but development is normal. Eczema in the past history: easy to overlook. Allergy skin testing: diagnoses IgE-mediated allergy (acute urticaria, angioedema). Finger foods, whole milk: right steps, wrong age; exclusive breastfeeding runs through 6 months, not beyond.
Pairs with Abnormal Growth in a Child: refusing food, or simply failing to grow? Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth: is the curve crossing lines? Stool Changes in a Well Infant: cow's-milk protein before 12 months.
Transferable rule

When the child is well and every option is reasonable, choose by age. When the child refuses food, name the pattern (texture, food group, appetite) before choosing a test.

Right Lower Quadrant Pain

appendix, ileocecum, or neither · Is there profuse mucoid diarrhea, and is there a sick contact?

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo, migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, sibling with the same illness · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Campylobacter infection, acute appendicitis and Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection
The decision point

Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness, and a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis occur in both appendicitis and ileocecitis and do not discriminate. Two findings that appendicitis does not explain are twelve mucus-containing loose stools in 24 hours and a brother with the same illness. Both fit infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) from organisms with an ileocecal predilection, Campylobacter jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica. The migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain also fits: Campylobacter may infect the jejunum first and then spread to the ileum and cecum.

Defining criteria Infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) — right lower quadrant pain from acute ileocecitis caused by organisms with an ileocecal predilection, specifically Yersinia enterocolitica and Campylobacter jejuni · The discriminating symptom — profuse watery or mucoid diarrhea, which acute appendicitis is not classically associated with · The imaging tell — ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with sparing of the appendix · When Campylobacter earns antibiotics — duration beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fevers, or a patient who is pregnant, immunocompromised, or elderly
Pertinent positives & negatives Twelve mucus-containing stools in 24 hours — profuse mucoid diarrhea, not a feature of appendicitis · A brother with the same illness, now improving — a shared exposure, which appendicitis does not explain; the sibling's course fits a self-limited enteritis · Migratory periumbilical → right lower quadrant pain — classic for appendicitis, but also explained by jejunal-then-ileocecal spread of Campylobacter · Right lower quadrant tenderness without rebound or rigidity — no peritonitis; this argues against an advanced or perforated appendix without excluding an early one · Fever 38.8 °C with WBC (white blood cell count) 13,700 and 80% neutrophils — present in both diagnoses; does not discriminate · Mucus in the stool — argues against norovirus, whose stools are watery without mucus · No hematochezia in the patient, with fever above 38.5 °C — argues against E. coli O157:H7, which usually brings hematochezia within 1–3 days and rarely high fever · Age 17 — diverticulitis is exceedingly rare at this age
Right lower quadrant pain in a young patient — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Infectious ileocecitis — Campylobacter, YersiniaUndercooked poultry or a sick contact; ileocecal predilection; fever with mucoid or bloody diarrheaProfuse mucoid diarrhea with right lower quadrant pain; imaging spares the appendix— (the answer)
Acute appendicitisLuminal obstruction; migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, anorexia, vomitingLittle or no diarrhea, progressive localized peritonitis, no sick contactsTwelve mucoid stools and an affected sibling
E. coli O157:H7Shiga toxin colitis; undercooked beef or a point-source outbreakHematochezia within 1–3 days and fever above 38.5 °C is rareThe patient has no bloody stools and a temperature of 38.8 °C
NorovirusCommon-source outbreak; prominent vomitingWatery stools without mucus, normal white blood cell countMucoid stools with a neutrophilic leukocytosis
Cecal diverticulitisRight-sided diverticular inflammationRight lower quadrant pain and fever in an adult; mild or no diarrheaExceedingly rare at 17; profuse mucoid diarrhea
Crohn ileitis ⚠︎Chronic transmural ileal inflammationWeeks to months of pain, weight loss, perianal diseaseThree days of illness with a sick contact
Management, in one line Campylobacter is treated supportively because it is usually self-limited within seven days. Antibiotics are reserved for the severe or high-risk cases listed above. In infectious ileocecitis, surgery is not required.
Decision spine Is there diarrhea, and how much? — Twelve mucoid stools → argues against appendicitis · Is there a sick contact? — A brother with the same illness → an infectious exposure, not a luminal obstruction · Are there peritoneal signs? — No rebound, no rigidity → not a surgical abdomen at this moment · What is the stool like? — Mucoid, with or without blood → invasive bacterial rather than viral · Which organisms live at the ileocecum? — Campylobacter and Yersinia
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBCFirstNeutrophil-predominant leukocytosisShared by appendicitis and ileocecitis; decides nothing
Ultrasound or CT of the abdomenBy branchIleocecal inflammation with a spared appendixInfectious ileocecitis: supportive care, no surgery
Inflamed appendixAcute appendicitis: surgical consultation
Stool culture or PCRConfirmsCampylobacter or YersiniaNames the organism; a susceptibility panel alone is not a reason to treat
Colonoscopy with ileal intubationBy branchChronic ileal inflammation on biopsyCrohn ileitis: months of pain, weight loss, perianal disease
Diagnostic laparoscopySkipInvasive when imaging can decideImage first when the examination leaves the diagnosis unclear
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo with migratory periumbilical to right lower quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness → Campylobacter infection → Infectious ileocecitis
  2. A hemodynamically stable 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness has had 3 days of symptoms without bloody stools. → Supportive care with stool studies → Usually self-limited within 7 days
  3. A 17-year-old with migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, 12 mucoid stools in 24 hours, fever, and a sibling with the same illness now presents on day 9 with bloody stools and fever to 39.5 °C. → Start antimicrobial therapy → A high-risk criterion is met
  4. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain, anorexia and vomiting but no diarrhea, with rebound tenderness → Surgical consultation for appendectomy → The classic script without the stool
  5. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain and diarrhea in whom the diagnosis remains unclear after examination → Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen → Ileocecal inflammation with a spared appendix
  6. 16 yo with months of right lower quadrant pain, weight loss and a perianal fistula → Colonoscopy with ileal intubation → Crohn ileitis
  7. 6 yo with severe crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody stools, temperature 37.6 C, after a family cookout → Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection → Hematochezia early, high fever rare
  8. That 6 year old with suspected Shiga toxin producing E coli; which intervention should be withheld → Empiric antibiotics → Risk of precipitating hemolytic uremic syndrome
  9. Three weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia → Guillain-Barre syndrome → The classic post-infectious sequela
  10. Two weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis → The second named sequela
  11. 5 yo M, 4 days of mucoid diarrhea after a low-grade fever that has resolved, still 5 or 6 stools a day, well hydrated, afebrile, guaiac negative; stool culture grows Campylobacter coli, ciprofloxacin resistant, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Symptomatic care only → mild and self-limited; the susceptibility panel is not an indication
  12. 6 yo with Campylobacter coli enteritis now on day 9 with bloody stools; ciprofloxacin resistant, erythromycin intermediate, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Amoxicillin → sensitive, and safe under 8
  13. 4 yo in day care with high fever, bloody diarrhea and a brief generalized seizure; stool grows Shigella → Azithromycin → treating shortens illness and spread
Decoy note The brother's illness supports an infectious cause, but his bloody stools may prompt a diagnosis of Shiga toxin E. coli in a patient with no blood in his own stool. A contact's findings describe the exposure, not this patient's phenotype. The migratory pain is also explained by Campylobacter spread, so it does not confirm appendicitis.
Bacterial diarrhea: who gets antibiotics Campylobacter — self-limited within about a week; supportive care. Treat only for symptoms beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fever, or pregnancy, immunocompromise or old age; choose by susceptibility · Stool culture — a positive culture with a susceptibility panel is not an indication. Culture is for protracted or severe illness and for outbreak control in day care and nursing homes · Shiga toxin-producing E. coli — bloody diarrhea with little fever; never give antibiotics, which raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome · Shigella — high fever, bloody diarrhea, sometimes a febrile seizure; antibiotics (azithromycin) shorten illness and spread · Nontyphoidal Salmonella — supportive in a healthy child; treat infants under 3 months, sickle cell disease, immunocompromise or bacteremia, because treatment otherwise prolongs carriage · Yersinia — pseudoappendicitis like Campylobacter; supportive unless bacteremic or immunocompromised · Clostridioides difficile — recent antibiotics; oral vancomycin or fidaximicin · Doxycycline under 8 — avoided when another agent covers the organism, because of tooth staining
Pearls Appendicitis does not cause twelve mucoid stools or a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia explains both. · Profuse watery-then-mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact alone should prompt reconsideration of appendicitis before surgery. · Campylobacter and Yersinia have an ileocecal predilection and mimic appendicitis; imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric adenopathy with a normal appendix. · Campylobacter may infect the jejunum before the ileum and cecum, so the pain can migrate as in appendicitis. · The two tested sequelae of Campylobacter are Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis. · Antibiotics are for illness beyond seven days, bloody stools, high fevers, or pregnancy, immunocompromise, or advanced age; otherwise the treatment is supportive. · Antibiotics are withheld for Shiga toxin E. coli ⚠︎, so invasive bacterial diarrheas do not share one management rule.
Pairs with Part II Acute Kidney Injury in a Child has the Shiga toxin and hemolytic uremic syndrome row from the renal side, where the E. coli O157:H7 branch of this differential ends. Ask: whose stool was bloody, and how many days into the illness? Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers hemolytic uremic syndrome, which follows Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, not Campylobacter. Part II Infectious Diarrhea covers the organism by exposure: what did the patient eat, and when?
Transferable rule When a presentation fits a textbook script, look for the finding the script cannot explain, such as a symptom the disease does not produce or an exposure it cannot have.
Salient decoyAcute appendicitis is not associated with profuse watery then mucoid diarrhea and cannot explain a sibling with the same illness. There are no peritoneal signs.
True-fact-wrong-slotE. coli O157:H7 causes hematochezia in the patient within 1–3 days, and fever above 38.5 °C rarely occurs. The bloody stools are the brother's, not this patient's.
Class-vs-memberNorovirus gives watery stools without mucus, a normal white blood cell count, and prominent vomiting
Unchecked attributeCecal diverticulitis is exceedingly rare in children and adolescents and does not produce profuse mucoid diarrhea.
Test-overrides-findingsA susceptibility panel invites treatment, but a mild, improving, afebrile child is treated by the clinical picture, not the culture report.

Constipation in a Child

Exclude alarm signs, then start an oral laxative before any rectal treatment · Is growth normal and the examination benign, and is there stool in the rectum?

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo M, hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, nontender abdomen, anal fissure · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned an oral osmotic laxative, a rectal enema and abdominal radiography
The decision point

Stools were daily and soft until toilet training began, and the pain came before the hardness worsened. This is the withholding cycle: a painful stool leads the child to hold, the rectum desiccates the retained stool, and the next stool hurts more. The anal fissure results from the cycle and worsens it. Growth on the 75th percentile, a nontender abdomen and a normal perineum mean no alarm signs, so treat rather than investigate. Give an oral osmotic laxative to make the next stool painless.

Defining criteria Alarm signs — delayed passage of meconium, fever or vomiting, ribbon stools, poor growth, severe abdominal distension, and abnormal examination findings such as a displaced anus or a tuft at the gluteal cleft · Cow's-milk limit — under 24 oz per day; this child's 24 oz is at the limit, not above it · Complications that are not alarm signs — anal fissure, hemorrhoids, enuresis and urinary tract infections; each argues for the functional diagnosis rather than against it
Pertinent positives & negatives Onset coincides with toilet training — the commonest trigger, with solid-food and cow's-milk introduction and school entry; points to a behavioral rather than anatomic cause · Previously daily soft stools — normal baseline function excludes a congenital motility defect, which would have presented earlier · Cries and screams with defecation — pain drives withholding and is what the laxative treats · Growth tracking at the 75th percentile — no growth alarm sign; effectively excludes Hirschsprung disease, hypothyroidism and celiac disease · Anal fissure — a complication of hard stools and the reason to avoid a rectal enema · Abdomen firm and mildly distended but nontender — stool load without obstruction; severe distension or tenderness would be an alarm sign · 24 oz of milk, refuses fruit — diet contributes and should be modified, not eliminated · Urinates in the toilet without difficulty — normal bladder function argues against a neurologic cause
Constipation in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Functional constipationToddler at a transition — toilet training, school entry, cow's milk; painful stool leads to withholding, which hardens the next stoolNormal growth and examination, onset tied to a transition, anal fissure as a complication— (the answer)
Hirschsprung disease Can't missAganglionic distal segment; usually declares in the neonatal periodDelayed meconium beyond 48 hours ⚠︎, ribbon stools, distension, poor growth; anal fissures are uncommonPassed meconium normally, thriving, fissure present
Congenital hypothyroidismSlowed transit with systemic featuresPoor linear growth, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia, large fontanelle ⚠︎Height and weight both on the 75th percentile
Tethered cord or spinal dysraphismOccult dysraphism impairing sacral outflowSacral dimple, hair tuft or displaced anus, with urinary symptoms and lower-limb findingsNormal perineal examination; urinates without difficulty
Celiac diseaseGluten enteropathy; constipation is a recognised presentation ⚠︎Falling weight percentile, distension with irritability, iron deficiencyGrowth tracking, well nourished
Excessive cow's-milk intakeFat and protein without fiber; slow transit and satiety that crowds out fiberMilk volume well above 24 oz per day, often with iron deficiency24 oz is within the recommended range
Classify first — constipation in a child
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence for management
Any alarm sign?"Height and weight have been tracking along the 75th percentiles… remainder of the examination is unremarkable"No — treat rather than investigate; the film and the manometry both die here
Impacted or not?"abdomen is firm, mildly distended, and nontender"; no stool ball describedNot impacted — maintenance therapy without a disimpaction step
Is the rectum safe to instrument?"An anal fissure is present"The rectal route causes further trauma; if disimpaction were needed, go oral
Is the diet the driver?"drinks 24 oz of milk… eats vegetables, meats, and grains"Within limits — modify fiber and water rather than withdraw milk
Tier fingerprint done: nothing has been tried yet · normal: growth, perineum and urinary function, and a nontender abdomen · bothered: the child cries with every stool, so treat today rather than counsel and wait.
Management ladder — constipation in a child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Oral osmotic laxative such as polyethylene glycol, plus increased dietary fiber and water, cow's milk kept under 24 oz per day, and age-appropriate toileting guidance — sitting after meals with the feet supported ⚠︎A stool ball on examination or overflow soiling means disimpaction is needed first
2Disimpaction — high-dose oral polyethylene glycol, or an enema; enemas are limited when an anal fissure is present because they cause further rectal trauma. Follow with long-term maintenance so the dilated rectum can return to normal sizeFailure to clear, or vomiting and severe pain suggesting obstruction, earns an abdominal x-ray
3Constipation persisting despite standard therapy — anorectal manometry; suction rectal biopsy is the confirmatory test for Hirschsprung disease ⚠︎Manometry abnormal or alarm signs emerging means paediatric gastroenterology and an anatomic workup
MaintenanceContinue the laxative for months rather than days ⚠︎ — the goal is a painless stool often enough that the child unlearns withholdingRelapse on weaning means resuming and re-addressing the behavioural side
Numbers that gate & exit ramps Delayed meconium with ribbon stools and poor growth → Hirschsprung disease, manometry then rectal biopsy ⚠︎ · sacral dimple, hair tuft or a displaced anus → spinal imaging for occult dysraphism · vomiting or severe distension with pain → abdominal x-ray, because severe impaction mimics obstruction · overflow soiling in an older child → impaction with encopresis, so disimpact before maintenance and tell the parents the soiling is not deliberate · milk intake well above 24 oz with pallor → reduce milk and check for iron deficiency ⚠︎.
Decision spine Any alarm sign? — Growth normal, examination benign, meconium normal → no, so do not investigate · Is there an impaction? — Nontender abdomen with no stool ball → no, so no disimpaction · Is the rectum instrumentable? — There is a fissure → no rectal route even if one were needed · Is the diet outside limits? — 24 oz of milk is at the ceiling rather than over it → modify rather than withdraw · What breaks the cycle? — Make the next stool painless → an oral osmotic laxative

Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M with hard painful stools since toilet training began, normal growth, a nontender abdomen and an anal fissure → Initiate an oral osmotic laxative → Functional constipation
  2. 6 yo M with involuntary soiling of his underwear and a palpable suprapubic stool mass, without an anal fissure → Disimpaction followed by maintenance laxative therapy → Impaction with overflow incontinence
  3. 4 yo F with fecal impaction requiring disimpaction who has a painful anal fissure on examination → High-dose oral polyethylene glycol → Enemas cause further rectal trauma
  4. 2 yo M with constipation and pallor who drinks 40 oz of cow's milk daily and eats little else → Reduce cow's milk intake and start a laxative → Milk volume above the recommended limit
  5. 3 yo F with constipation, daytime urinary incontinence and a tuft of hair over the sacrum → Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine → Occult spinal dysraphism
  6. 5 yo M whose constipation persists after 3 months of adequate laxative and dietary therapy, with normal growth and examination → Anorectal manometry → Refractory to standard therapy
  7. Newborn who first passed meconium at 60 hours, now with ribbon-like stools, abdominal distension and poor weight gain → Hirschsprung disease → Manometry, then rectal biopsy
  8. 8-month-old with constipation, prolonged jaundice, hypotonia and a large anterior fontanelle → Congenital hypothyroidism → Check the TSH
  9. Why one painful bowel movement can produce weeks of worsening constipation in a toddler → Withholding desiccates stool in the rectum→ so the next defecation hurts more, which reinforces withholding; The cycle is the disease
  10. 3 yo M with functional constipation who drinks 24 oz of cow's milk daily; which management is inappropriate → Discontinuing cow's milk entirely → It removes calcium and vitamin D without benefit
  11. 15-month-old with constipation since infancy refractory to dietary changes, thin caliber stools, distended abdomen, explosive stool and gas on rectal exam → Contrast enema → Hirschsprung disease
Decoy note Refusing to eat fruit and the milk volume suggest a dietary cause, but the milk is at the limit, not above it, so diet is a contributor to adjust. Finding a firm, mildly distended abdomen is not an alarm sign; the alarm signs are severe distension and tenderness, and neither is present. The anal fissure is an expected complication of functional constipation, not evidence of another diagnosis; its only effect on management is to rule out the rectal route.
Pearls A growing child with painful hard stools and a normal examination gets an oral osmotic laxative, not a rectal procedure or imaging. · Childhood constipation is a behavioural cycle with a mechanical consequence. The laxative makes stools painless so the child stops withholding; continue it for months rather than days ⚠︎. · The three common triggers are solid food and cow's milk, toilet training, and school entry; onset at one of them supports the diagnosis. · An anal fissure is a complication of constipation, not a competing diagnosis, and is the reason to disimpact by mouth rather than by rectum. · Hirschsprung disease presents with delayed meconium and poor growth, and fissures are uncommon in it; normal growth with a fissure indicates functional disease. · Growth is the most informative alarm sign; a child tracking a percentile has essentially excluded hypothyroidism, celiac disease and Hirschsprung disease. · Enuresis and urinary tract infections are complications of constipation, so in a child with both, treat the bowel first.
Pairs with Part II Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult is the adult counterpart of tier 2: there the rectal vault is full and an enema is first-line; here the vault is not full and the fissure rules out the rectal route. Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers infants, and Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the dysraphism the perineal examination screens for. Ask: is growth normal, and is there stool in the rectum?
Transferable rule With no alarm signs and a normal examination, treat; investigate only when an alarm sign is present. A complication of the diagnosis supports it but can still change management, as an anal fissure rules out the rectal route.
Unchecked attributeDiscontinue milk: 24 oz is within the recommended 16 to 24 oz range; stopping it removes calcium and vitamin D with no benefit
Sequencing trapObtain abdominal radiograph: The film is for severe impaction that mimics obstruction, with pain and vomiting; this abdomen is nontender and benign
Salient decoyAdminister rectal enema: There is no impaction to disimpact, and the anal fissure makes the rectal route actively harmful here
Sequencing trapObtain anorectal manometry: Reserved for constipation that persists despite standard therapy; no therapy has been tried and no alarm sign is present

Recurrent Vomiting in a Child

Stereotyped episodes, well in between · the pattern is the diagnosis

Source vignette Pt — 9-year-old girl, 8 months of nausea, vomiting and diffuse abdominal pain for several days each month; episodes begin early morning, recur 10–15 times daily for 2 days, nonbloody and nonbilious; more frequent at the start of the school year; two admissions for intravenous hydration · Between episodes — active, eating well, growth at the 25th percentile and unchanged · Exam — well hydrated, erosive maxillary caries, soft nontender abdomen, normal neurologic examination · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned bulimia, chronic pancreatitis, cyclic vomiting, factitious disorder imposed on another, reflux and inflammatory bowel disease
The decision point

Three features together indicate cyclic vomiting syndrome: stereotyped episodes, each self-limited over 1 to 2 days, and complete wellness between them with normal growth. Stress at the start of term is the trigger. Most patients have a personal or family history of migraine. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, supported by wellness between episodes.

The erosive caries are evidence that the vomiting is real and recurrent, not evidence of purging. There is no bingeing, no restriction and no preoccupation with shape.

Defining criteria Stereotyped episodes — the same acute nausea, abdominal pain, headache and vomiting each time · Duration — self-limited over 1 to 2 days · Interval — often regular, around 2 to 4 weeks, and asymptomatic between · Association — personal or family history of migraine · Triggers — infection or stress
Recurrent vomiting in a child — the differentialwhat happens between the episodes
DiagnosisBetween episodesKey discriminatorWhat to do
Cyclic vomiting syndromeEntirely well, growing normallyStereotyped, self-limited, regular intervals; migraine historyRehydration and antiemetics; triptans may abort
Bulimia nervosaPreoccupied with shape and weightBingeing with compensatory behaviourPsychiatric assessment
Chronic pancreatitisPoor growth, diarrhoeaEpigastric tenderness on examinationPancreatic imaging and enzyme studies
Inflammatory bowel diseaseWeight loss, fever, ongoing symptomsDiarrhoea with abdominal tendernessInflammatory markers and endoscopy
Gastroesophageal refluxOngoing low-grade symptomsRegurgitation and substernal pain, not episodic burstsTrial of acid suppression
Factitious disorder imposed on anotherInconsistent history, symptoms unwitnessedNo objective corroboration of the illnessCareful documentation; child protection
