Bacterial stool cultureBacterial colitisBloody diarrhea with crampy pain and feverFormed stool, afebrile, no pain
Anal examAnal fissureBright red streaks on a hard stool, painful passageVisible on exam; none here
Abdominal CTBowel and mass lesionsAbdominal trauma, abscess or tumorCannot reliably tell the diverticulum from other bowel loops
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBC and stool occult bloodFirstMicrocytic anemia, occult blood positiveOccult GI bleeding
Upper endoscopy and colonoscopyNextUnremarkable, biopsies cleanSource is in the small bowel
Technetium 99m pertechnetate scanConfirmsEctopic gastric mucosaMeckel diverticulum, the child's small-bowel branch
Capsule endoscopyBy branchAngiodysplasia, neoplasia or ulcerAdult branch; then CT or MR enterography
Tissue transglutaminase IgABy branchPositive, with occult blood negativeCeliac disease: iron deficiency from malabsorption, not bleeding
CT angiographySkipNeeds brisk active bleedingOccult bleeding is too slow to show
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchTarget signIntussusception, when there is intermittent severe pain; air enema confirms and reduces it
Abdominal CTSkipCannot separate the diverticulum from bowel loopsThe pertechnetate scan answers the Meckel question
Scenario bank
  1. 10 year old with 2 months of exertional fatigue, pallor, hemoglobin 9.4 with MCV 74, stool positive for occult blood; upper endoscopy and colonoscopy with biopsies are unremarkable → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel scan — it images ectopic gastric mucosa
  2. How a Meckel diverticulum causes occult bleeding → Ectopic gastric mucosa secreting acid → Ulcerating adjacent small bowel
  3. Child with iron deficiency anemia and a positive fecal occult blood test; the first step → Upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Localize before reaching for small-bowel studies
  4. Adult with occult gastrointestinal bleeding and a negative upper endoscopy and colonoscopy → Capsule endoscopy → Angiodysplasia, neoplasia and ulcers — the adult small-bowel causes
  5. Child with painless hematochezia and no abdominal pain, age under 2 → Meckel diverticulum → Failed closure of the vitelline duct
  6. Child with slow occult blood loss and stable vital signs; which study is least likely to help → CT angiography → It needs brisk active bleeding to see anything
  7. Child with microcytic anemia, chronic diarrhea and a negative fecal occult blood test → Celiac disease → Malabsorption, not blood loss — the occult blood is negative
  8. 2-year-old boy with dark red, formed stool in his diaper; eating and drinking well but more tired than usual; lives on a ranch with cattle and goats; afebrile and pale; abdomen soft, nondistended and nontender without masses; no anal fissures or hemorrhoids; stool positive for occult blood; hematocrit 27%, leukocytes 8,000/mm3, platelets 320,000/mm3 → Technetium 99m pertechnetate scan → Meckel diverticulum: ectopic gastric mucosa takes up the tracer; painless small-bowel bleeding in a toddler, and dark red stool without hematemesis or melena is not an upper GI bleed
  9. 10-week-old boy fed cow's milk-based formula with several days of mucus and streaks of blood in otherwise soft stools; feeding well, gaining weight, afebrile and playful; mild eczema on the cheeks; abdomen soft and nontender; no anal fissure on exam → Switch to an extensively hydrolyzed formula → milk protein proctocolitis: a non-IgE reaction in infants; bleeding clears once cow's milk protein is removed, and it resolves by age 1
  10. 2-year-old boy with 12 hours of sudden episodes of severe crying with his legs drawn up, quiet and sleepy between episodes; vomited twice; one stool of dark red blood and mucus (currant jelly); afebrile; a sausage-shaped mass in the right upper quadrant → Abdominal ultrasound → intussusception: pain is the tell; target sign on ultrasound, then air enema to confirm and reduce; a Meckel diverticulum can be the lead point
  11. 3-year-old girl with two episodes of painless maroon stool over the past month; pale, hematocrit 28%, vital signs normal; abdomen soft and nontender; technetium-99m pertechnetate scan shows a focus of uptake in the right lower quadrant → Surgical resection → a symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is removed to stop the bleeding and prevent intussusception, diverticulitis and obstruction; iron treats the anemia, not the source
Stool color and bleeding source Stool color follows transit time, not only where the blood started. Dark red or maroon stool in a toddler is a lower source, usually the small bowel, because the blood passes quickly. The upper GI (gastrointestinal) picture is hematemesis with black, sticky melena, and it is more common in adults. This child had neither, so upper endoscopy is not the first test.
Gates Visible bleeding with instability — hematemesis, melena or hematochezia goes to CT (computed tomography) angiography, not a Meckel scan · Scope first for occult bleeding — small-bowel studies are for after a clean upper endoscopy and colonoscopy; a toddler with visible, painless dark red stool goes straight to the pertechnetate scan · Meckel is classically under 2 but presents into adolescence, so age does not exclude it · Balloon-assisted enteroscopy is the fallback when the source stays hidden
Pearls The Meckel scan detects gastric mucosa, not blood, so it works when the lesion is not actively bleeding · Occult bleeding is too slow for angiography · Celiac gives iron deficiency without occult blood; the FOBT (fecal occult blood test) separates them · Here, small bowel means the segment the two scopes cannot reach · Painless hematochezia in a toddler is Meckel until proven otherwise · Rule of 2s: often presents by age 2, usually under 2 inches long, within 2 feet of the ileocecal valve · The bleed is painless; pain comes from complications: intussusception with the diverticulum as lead point, diverticulitis that mimics appendicitis, obstruction or perforation · A symptomatic Meckel diverticulum is surgically resected to stop the bleeding and prevent those complications
Pairs with Part I The Distended Abdomen in a Newborn or Infant covers the obstructed and acutely bleeding infant gut. Part I Microcytic Anemia covers the iron-versus-thalassemia fork that precedes this workup. Ask: is the bleeding visible, and have both ends been scoped?
Transferable rule When an algorithm branches on age, the same negative workup can send a child and an adult to different tests.
Class-vs-memberCapsule endoscopy is the adult small-bowel study; a child gets the pertechnetate scan.
Sequencing trapOrdering a small-bowel study before upper endoscopy and colonoscopy are done.
Salient decoyMicrocytic anemia in a child pulls toward celiac serology, which the positive FOBT (fecal occult blood test) excludes.
Unchecked attributeMilk elimination fits painless blood in an infant, but milk protein proctocolitis resolves by age 1; a 2-year-old is past it.
Salient decoyRanch animals pull toward bacterial colitis, which needs bloody diarrhea, crampy pain and fever.
True-fact-wrong-slotEndoscopy is right for hematemesis and black melena; dark red stool without either points below.
7 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Gastroenterology & Hepatology

Constipation and Fecal Impaction in an Adult

Firm stool on rectal exam confirms impaction

Source vignette Pt — 77 yo F taking oxybutynin; last bowel movement 5 days ago, and it was loose stool; colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities; no hematochezia · Exam — afebrile, warm dry skin, soft abdomen without distension, diffuse tenderness, firm stool in the rectal vault · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned fecal impaction, adhesions, colon cancer, diverticulitis, ischemic bowel and volvulus
The decision point

Rectal examination shows firm stool in the rectal vault. This confirms fecal impaction and is incompatible with adhesive small bowel obstruction, which gives an empty rectum, a distended abdomen, and high-pitched or absent bowel sounds.

The last bowel movement, 5 days ago, was loose stool. Loose stool in a constipated patient is overflow diarrhea: liquid stool passing around a hard impaction. It is near-pathognomonic.

Stem findings → options ruled out
OptionThe sentence that kills it
AdhesionsFirm stool in the rectal vault (SBO empties the rectum); soft, undistended abdomen
Colon cancer"Colonoscopy 3 years ago showed no abnormalities"
DiverticulitisNo fever; diffuse, not focal LLQ, tenderness
Ischemic bowelNo hematochezia; no AF or atherosclerotic risk factors
VolvulusSoft abdomen without distension; no coffee-bean film
Details that change management Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic that slows colonic transit and is the cause here, so treatment includes addressing it. The patient's warm, dry skin is an anticholinergic sign. Constipating drugs: anticholinergics (oxybutynin, TCAs [tricyclic antidepressants], antihistamines, antipsychotics), opioids, verapamil, iron, calcium, aluminum antacids, ondansetron.
Management ladder — fecal impaction
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Enema (in-context: first-line)Fails to clear
2Manual disimpactionEnema unsuccessful
3Treat the cause — stop or reduce the oxybutynin; then maintenance PEG, fluids, mobilityAlways, after clearing
Scenario bank
  1. 77 yo F, 5 days without a BM, empty rectal vault, distended abdomen, high-pitched bowel sounds, prior laparotomy → Adhesive small bowel obstruction → NG decompression + imaging
  2. 77 yo F, sudden severe pain, distended tympanitic abdomen, coffee-bean sign → Sigmoid volvulus → endoscopic decompression
  3. 68 yo M, LLQ pain with fever 38.5 and focal tenderness → Diverticulitis → CT
  4. 72 yo F with atrial fibrillation, crampy pain and hematochezia → Ischemic colitis
  5. 60 yo M, progressive constipation with iron deficiency anemia and weight loss, no recent colonoscopy → Colon cancer → colonoscopy
  6. 77 yo F, impaction cleared by enema, still constipated → Stop the oxybutynin, start PEG
  7. 80 yo M on chronic opioids, 6 days without a BM, hard stool in the vault → Disimpaction + methylnaltrexone or naloxegol
Exceptions Impaction can sit distal to a second lesion, such as a slow-growing tumor or partial obstruction. Here, a normal colonoscopy 3 years ago and no weight loss or anemia mean no further workup is needed. If any one of these is missing, relieve the impaction and also investigate.
Pairs with Part I Constipation in a Child covers the paediatric case, where the rectal vault is empty and an anal fissure rules out the rectal route that is first-line here.
Transferable rule Change an answer only when a new detail makes the current choice impossible, not when another option merely becomes plausible. Check whether the stem contains a finding that excludes the new option. Here, firm stool in the rectal vault excludes small bowel obstruction.
Salient decoy

Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia

Choking on the first feed · pass a tube before you order a picture

Source vignette Pt — 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned nasogastric tube placement, lateral neck radiography and echocardiography
The decision point

Formula mixed with saliva means the milk filled a blind proximal pouch and overflowed without reaching the stomach. With choking on the very first feed and coarse lungs from aspiration, this is esophageal atresia with a distal tracheoesophageal fistula.

The first step is to pass a nasogastric tube at the bedside. It meets resistance at the pouch, and the film shows it coiled. The murmur, maternal drug history and absent prenatal care do not call for imaging or drug treatment first.

Defining criteria Type C — proximal pouch with a distal fistula, about 85% of cases · Gas in the abdomen — a distal fistula is present · Gasless abdomen — pure atresia with no distal fistula · H-type — no atresia, presenting months later with recurrent pneumonia
Neonatal choking and vomiting — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
EA with distal TEFChoking on the first feed, copious frothy secretions, polyhydramnios in uteroFormula mixed with saliva; tube will not pass
Congenital diaphragmatic herniaSevere distress at deliveryScaphoid abdomen, bowel gas in the chest, shifted heart sounds
Congenital heart diseaseFeeding difficulty with cyanosisCyanosis and diaphoresis with feeds, no excess secretions
EpiglottitisFebrile stridor with droolingSchool-aged child, never a newborn
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosisNonbilious projectile vomitingAge 3 to 6 weeks, hungry after vomiting, olive mass
Respiratory distress syndromePreterm surfactant deficiencyGround-glass with air bronchograms, low lung volumes
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid useOnset at or beyond 24 hours, hypertonia and irritability
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Nasogastric tube passageFirstMeets resistance at the pouchEsophageal atresia likely: film with the tube in place
Chest and abdominal x-ray with the tubeConfirmsTube coiled in the upper chestEsophageal atresia
Gas below the diaphragmDistal fistula present (type C)
Gasless abdomenPure atresia, no distal fistula
Echocardiogram and renal ultrasoundNextVACTERL anomaliesScreen after the diagnosis, before repair
Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagramBy branchH-type fistulaTube passes; months of cough with feeds and recurrent pneumonia
Barium esophagram or endoscopySkipContrast can aspirate from the blind pouchThe coiled tube on film already confirms atresia
Scenario bank
  1. 3 h old term boy born at home, coughs and vomits on his first breastfeed, formula mixed with saliva in his mouth, coarse breath sounds with retractions, soft systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border → Nasogastric tube placement → Esophageal atresia with distal tracheoesophageal fistula
  2. 2 h old term girl drooling frothy secretions who choked on her first feed; a nasogastric tube meets firm resistance and will not advance → Chest x-ray with the tube in place → A coiled tube confirms atresia; gas below the diaphragm means a distal fistula
  3. Term newborn girl, maternal polyhydramnios, drooling; the feeding tube coils in the upper chest on x-ray and the abdomen is completely gasless → Esophageal atresia without a fistula → No tracheal connection, so no air reaches the stomach
  4. 8 mo old boy with three right upper lobe pneumonias and coughing and choking with liquid feeds since birth; a feeding tube passes easily into the stomach → H-type tracheoesophageal fistula → Bronchoscopy or prone contrast esophagram
  5. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, before surgical repair → Echocardiogram and renal ultrasound → VACTERL association
  6. 4 wk old boy with a week of nonbilious projectile vomiting, hungry after each episode, ultrasound showing a thickened elongated pylorus, low chloride and high bicarbonate → IV fluids and electrolyte repletion → Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis; pyloromyotomy once the alkalosis corrects
  7. Newborn girl with upslanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, maternal polyhydramnios, bilious vomiting on day 1, abdominal x-ray with a double bubble and no distal gas → Nasogastric decompression and IV fluids → Duodenal atresia; repair after stabilization and an echocardiogram
  8. 30 wk preterm boy grunting and retracting at 1 h of life, x-ray with diffuse ground-glass opacities, air bronchograms and low lung volumes → Respiratory distress syndrome → CPAP, then surfactant if the oxygen requirement rises
  9. 36 h old girl, irritable and tremulous with a high-pitched cry, sneezing and feeding poorly; mother maintained on methadone → Swaddling, low stimulation and rooming-in → Neonatal abstinence syndrome; morphine only if nonpharmacologic care fails
  10. Term newborn boy with esophageal atresia and a distal fistula confirmed on x-ray, saturating 96% in room air, awaiting surgical repair → NPO, head elevated, continuous pouch suction → Keeps pooled saliva out of the lungs and gastric acid out of the fistula
Age at presentation Age at presentation narrows the differential. Minutes to hours: TEF (tracheoesophageal fistula) with EA (esophageal atresia), choanal atresia, diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, Potter sequence. Beyond 24 hours: neonatal abstinence, sepsis, ductal-dependent lesions as the PDA (patent ductus arteriosus) closes, bilious vomiting and malrotation. 3 to 6 weeks: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. Months: H-type fistula, laryngomalacia.
Pearls Polyhydramnios in utero, because the fetus cannot swallow amniotic fluid · Diagnosis is made by passing the tube: resistance at roughly 9 to 11 cm, confirmed on film · The abdominal gas pattern shows the anatomic type without endoscopy · VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after diagnosis: echocardiogram and renal ultrasound at minimum · A soft systolic murmur on day one is usually a closing ductus, not structural disease
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves shares the mechanism in reverse: a fetus that cannot make urine has oligohydramnios and Potter sequence, and a fetus that cannot swallow has polyhydramnios and foregut or duodenal atresia. Part I Cyanosis in the Newborn covers cyanosis that worsens with feeding and improves with crying, which is choanal atresia, not a fistula. Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) alongside the syndromes it is mistaken for and what excludes each.
Transferable rule When a newborn chokes or vomits with the first feed, first check whether a nasogastric tube reaches the stomach, before any imaging or drug. Imaging only confirms what the tube found.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpiglottitis is a febrile school-age disease; a 3-hour-old cannot have it.
Sequencing trapEchocardiography is indicated for VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb anomalies) screening after the diagnosis, not before it.
True-fact-wrong-slotPyloric stenosis needs 3 to 6 weeks for the muscle to hypertrophy, and it gives projectile vomiting, not coughing with saliva-mixed formula at 3 hours.
True-fact-wrong-slotSurfactant treats respiratory distress syndrome in the preterm lung; this is a term newborn whose retractions come from aspirated secretions, which surfactant does not fix.
Salient decoyThe maternal drug history points at neonatal abstinence syndrome, but withdrawal typically begins at 24 hours or later, never pools saliva or causes coughing with feeds, and is treated first without drugs.

Umbilical Findings in a Newborn

Skin-covered and reducible · is there skin over it, and how big and how old is it?

Source vignette Pt — 4-hour-old boy, 38 wk, 3.6 kg, mother 18 with no prenatal care, normal vitals; soft, nontender, skin-covered 1.4 cm bulge just below the umbilical stump that enlarges with crying and reduces with gentle pressure · Q — the most appropriate next step for the mass; options spanned observation, abdominal ultrasound, karyotype, immediate surgery and topical silver nitrate
The decision point

A skin-covered, soft, reducible bulge that grows with crying is a congenital umbilical hernia: the fascial ring around the umbilicus has not closed yet. It is common in healthy newborns, and incarceration is very rare. Small hernias usually close on their own, so a well infant needs observation only. The diagnosis is clinical; no imaging or genetic test is needed.

A defect over 1.5 cm is less likely to close. Persistence to about age 5 calls for elective repair, and incarceration calls for repair at any age. Bowel with no skin over it, either in a membranous sac (omphalocele) or bare beside the cord (gastroschisis), goes to surgery right after birth.

Decision cutoffs Skin-covered, soft, reducible: observe · Defect over 1.5 cm: spontaneous closure less likely; keep following · Still present at about age 5: elective surgical repair · Incarcerated (firm, tender, irreducible or discolored, with vomiting): urgent repair at any age · No skin over the bowel: gastroschisis or omphalocele, surgery at birth
Umbilical findings in a newborn: the differential
FindingIllness scriptThe NBME tellNext step
Umbilical herniaUnclosed fascial ring; more frequent with Down syndrome, hypothyroidism, Beckwith-Wiedemann and Ehlers-DanlosSkin-covered, soft, reducible, grows with cryingObserve; repair about age 5 if persistent, sooner if incarcerated
Umbilical granulomaExcess granulation tissue at the base after the cord separatesMoist, red, friable nub that appears after the cord falls offTopical silver nitrate
Patent urachus or omphalomesenteric ductPersistent tract to the bladder (urachus) or the ileum (omphalomesenteric duct)Drainage: urine-like fluid from a urachus, stool or mucus from the ductUltrasound, then surgical excision
OmphaloceleMidline defect at the umbilical ring; bowel, often liver, herniates into the base of the cordMembranous sac with the cord inserting on itSurgery at birth; karyotype and echocardiogram for associated anomalies
GastroschisisFull-thickness wall defect, usually right of the umbilicus; usually isolatedBare bowel, no sac, beside a normally inserted cordCover the bowel, decompress, immediate surgery
Scenario bank
  1. 4-hour-old boy born at 38 weeks to a mother without prenatal care, well-appearing, with a soft, nontender, skin-covered 1.4 cm bulge just below the umbilical stump that enlarges with crying and reduces with gentle pressure → Observation only → Congenital umbilical hernia
  2. 5-year-old girl, well, with a soft, reducible, skin-covered umbilical bulge present since birth that has not decreased in size; defect about 2 cm; no pain or vomiting → Elective surgical repair → Persistent umbilical hernia
  3. 8-month-old boy with a known umbilical hernia that is now firm, tender, discolored and cannot be reduced; he has vomited three times → Urgent surgical repair → Incarcerated umbilical hernia
  4. 12-day-old girl whose cord fell off 4 days ago, now with a 4 mm moist, red, friable, pedunculated nub at the umbilical base with slight serous drainage; afebrile, no surrounding erythema → Topical silver nitrate → Umbilical granuloma
  5. 3-week-old boy with clear, urine-like fluid leaking from the umbilicus that increases when he cries or strains; the skin around the umbilicus is normal → Patent urachus → Ultrasound, then surgical excision
  6. Term newborn with loops of bare, edematous bowel protruding through a defect to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, with no covering membrane; vital signs stable → Cover the bowel and arrange immediate surgery → Gastroschisis
  7. Term newborn with a 5 cm midline membrane-covered sac containing bowel and liver at the base of the umbilical cord, with the cord inserting on the sac → Karyotype and echocardiogram → Omphalocele
  8. 7-week-old girl born at home without newborn screening, with a reducible skin-covered umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice, a large tongue, poor tone, constipation and a wide posterior fontanelle → Serum TSH and free T4 → Congenital hypothyroidism
Abdominal wall defect at delivery Exposed bowel loses heat and fluid. Cover it with a sterile moist dressing or bowel bag, place a nasogastric tube, give IV (intravenous) fluids and keep the infant warm. Then proceed to immediate surgery. An omphalocele also needs a karyotype and echocardiogram because it is associated with trisomy 13 and 18, Beckwith-Wiedemann and heart defects. Gastroschisis is usually isolated.
Pearls An umbilical hernia with prolonged jaundice, macroglossia, hypotonia, constipation or a large fontanelle is a reason to check TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), because congenital hypothyroidism is the treatable association · Karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, never for an isolated hernia in a normal infant · Silver nitrate is the treatment for a granuloma; an umbilical lesion that keeps draining urine or stool is a remnant tract and needs imaging and excision
Pairs with Congenital Hypothyroidism: an umbilical hernia is one of its soft signs; ask: is there jaundice, macroglossia or a large fontanelle beside the hernia? Tracheoesophageal Fistula and Esophageal Atresia: after any structural defect, screen for the anomalies that occur with it. For esophageal atresia that means VACTERL (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal and limb) anomalies; for an omphalocele, a karyotype and echocardiogram.
How NBME framed it A sleepy 2-month-old at his first visit, with an umbilical hernia, persistent jaundice and cool extremities, needed thyroid function tests, not karyotype, sweat chloride or head or liver computed tomography.
Transferable rule For a newborn umbilical finding, ask first whether skin covers it. Observe a skin-covered, reducible bulge, and repair it if still present at about age 5 or incarcerated at any age. Bowel without skin goes to surgery at birth.
Redundant workupAbdominal ultrasound adds nothing to a clinical diagnosis; it is for an acquired hernia in an older child or adult.
True-fact-wrong-slotImmediate surgery belongs to gastroschisis and omphalocele, where no skin covers the bowel.
Salient decoyA young mother without prenatal care invites a genetic workup, but karyotype is for Down features or an omphalocele, and this infant has neither.
Mirror twinSilver nitrate treats an umbilical granuloma, the moist red nub that appears after the cord falls off, not a skin-covered bulge at 4 hours.

Wilson Disease

A teen with hepatitis, a tremor and brown corneal rings · is the patient young, with brain, eye or red-cell findings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

Source vignette Pt — adolescent with liver disease (hepatitis, possibly progressing to cirrhosis) plus neuropsychiatric change: tremor, slurred speech and altered behavior · Exam — Kayser-Fleischer rings at the corneal margin · Labs — elevated transaminases · Q — the most likely underlying mechanism of the disease
The decision point

Think of Wilson disease in any patient under about 40 ⚠︎ with unexplained liver disease. Think of it especially when liver disease comes with neuropsychiatric signs (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, depression, personality change, psychosis), Kayser-Fleischer rings, or a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia. Screen with serum ceruloplasmin (low) and a slit-lamp exam. A high 24-hour urine copper confirms the diagnosis, and liver biopsy copper settles cases where the tests disagree.

Wilson disease is autosomal recessive loss of ATP7B, the hepatocyte transporter that loads copper onto ceruloplasmin and excretes the excess into bile. Copper builds up in the liver (hepatitis, cirrhosis, sometimes acute liver failure). It then spills into the blood and deposits in the basal ganglia, the cornea and red cells. Ceruloplasmin is low because it is unstable without its copper. In patients with liver disease alone, Kayser-Fleischer rings are often absent. Ceruloplasmin can also read normal in these patients because it rises with inflammation. The urine copper or the liver biopsy then makes the diagnosis.

Liver disease in a young patient: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellWhy less likely here
Wilson diseaseAutosomal recessive; child, teen or young adult; hepatitis, cirrhosis or acute liver failure, with movement or psychiatric changeKayser-Fleischer rings, low ceruloplasmin, Coombs-negative hemolysisThe key: the only one that adds brain, eye and red-cell findings to the liver
Autoimmune hepatitisYoung woman, often with another autoimmune disease; acute or chronic hepatitisANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody (anti-LKM1 in children), high IgGNo neurologic signs or corneal rings; Wilson can mimic it, so check ceruloplasmin
Hereditary hemochromatosisAutosomal recessive HFE; iron builds for decades, so middle-aged men and women after menopauseHigh transferrin saturation and ferritin; diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy, cardiomyopathy, hypogonadismToo young; iron does not cause tremor or corneal rings
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiencyMisfolded protein retained in hepatocytes; neonatal cholestasis in infants, cirrhosis in adults, early basal emphysemaLow serum alpha-1 antitrypsin; lung disease in a young smokerIts second organ is the lung, not the brain or eye
Viral hepatitisMost common cause; risk factors for hepatitis B or C, or an acute illness with hepatitis APositive serologiesNo neuropsychiatric signs or corneal rings; hemolysis is not a feature
MASLDObesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia; mild ALT-predominant riseMetabolic syndrome with a hyperechoic liver; a diagnosis of exclusionNothing outside the liver
Antipsychotic-induced parkinsonismTremor, rigidity or dystonia after starting a dopamine blockerMovement signs follow the drug; liver tests normalDoes not explain the liver disease
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Liver tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin, INR)FirstHepatocellular rise, from mild to acute liver failureLiver injury; the pattern alone does not name the cause
Hepatitis serologies, iron studies, ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody, alpha-1 antitrypsin levelFirstNormalExcludes the common mimics
Serum ceruloplasminScreenLow, under 20 mg/dL ⚠︎Wilson disease; a normal value does not exclude it in active hepatitis, because ceruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant
Slit-lamp examinationNextKayser-Fleischer ringsCorneal copper; almost always present with neurologic disease, often absent with liver disease alone
24-hour urine copperConfirmsHigh, over 100 mcg per day ⚠︎Copper overflow from an overloaded liver; also used to monitor chelation
Liver biopsy with copper measurementBy branchHigh hepatic copperWhen ceruloplasmin, urine copper and the slit-lamp exam disagree
CBC, reticulocytes, direct Coombs testSupportsAnemia, high reticulocytes, Coombs negativeCopper damages red cells; with acute liver failure, fulminant Wilson disease
Brain MRISupportsBasal ganglia signal changeNeurologic involvement; not needed for the diagnosis
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M with several months of fatigue and mild jaundice, a new hand tremor, slurred speech and irritability with falling grades; elevated AST and ALT; golden-brown rings at the corneal margins on slit-lamp exam → Defective copper transport in hepatocytes → Wilson disease: ATP7B failure blocks biliary copper excretion and copper loading onto ceruloplasmin, so copper deposits in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea
  2. 19 yo F with 3 months of fatigue and a fine hand tremor; ALT 240, AST 190, bilirubin normal; hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody negative; normal BMI and no alcohol use → Serum ceruloplasmin → screen for Wilson disease in a young patient with unexplained hepatitis and a tremor; slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper follow
  3. 17 yo F with Hashimoto thyroiditis and 6 weeks of fatigue, joint aches and jaundice; ALT 850, AST 700; serum IgG high; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positive; ceruloplasmin normal; no Kayser-Fleischer rings; normal neurologic exam → Autoimmune hepatitis → corticosteroids, with azathioprine to spare steroids
  4. 21 yo M with 1 year of hand tremor and dysarthria; compensated cirrhosis on imaging, INR 1.3, no ascites or encephalopathy; ceruloplasmin low, 24-hour urine copper high, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam → Oral penicillamine → symptomatic Wilson disease: lifelong chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc later for maintenance
  5. 18 yo F with 1 week of jaundice, now confused; INR 3.2; hemoglobin 7.8 with high reticulocytes and a negative direct Coombs test; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam; no acetaminophen ingestion → Urgent liver transplantation → fulminant Wilson disease: acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis does not recover with chelation alone
  6. 14 yo M, asymptomatic, whose 17-year-old sister was just diagnosed with Wilson disease; normal growth and development; normal physical and neurologic exam → Serum ceruloplasmin and liver tests → siblings carry a 1 in 4 risk; add a slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper, and treat presymptomatic disease with zinc
  7. 24 yo M with Wilson disease treated with penicillamine for 3 years; tremor resolved, liver tests now normal, urine copper at target; asks about coming off medication → Stopping copper-lowering therapy → treatment is lifelong; stopping can precipitate acute liver failure
Management Symptomatic disease — copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine, lifelong, with a low-copper diet (avoid shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate and mushrooms) · Maintenance or presymptomatic disease — zinc, which blocks intestinal copper absorption · Fulminant liver failure — urgent liver transplantation, which corrects the liver defect · Family — screen first-degree relatives, siblings above all (a 1 in 4 chance of disease, since it is autosomal recessive), with ceruloplasmin, liver tests and a slit-lamp exam · Never stop — stopping therapy can precipitate acute liver failure
Pearls Psychiatric change or falling school performance can precede the liver findings. A young patient with new psychiatric illness and abnormal liver tests needs a ceruloplasmin · Acute liver failure with a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia in a teen or young adult is fulminant Wilson disease. It needs a transplant center, not chelation alone · A presumed autoimmune hepatitis in a young patient should have ceruloplasmin checked before steroids · Serum total copper is usually low; urine copper is high
Pairs with Part I Fatty Liver Disease lists Wilson disease among the exclusions: is the patient under about 40, with tremor or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low? Part I Abnormal Liver Tests places Wilson in the hepatocellular pattern: are the transaminases, not the alkaline phosphatase, leading? Part II Hereditary Spherocytosis covers the other Coombs-negative hemolysis of the young: are there spherocytes and an affected parent, or liver disease with corneal rings? Part I Tick-Borne Illness holds the acute mimic: did confusion with transaminitis arrive over hours with fever and a rash, or over months with a tremor?
Transferable rule When liver disease in a patient under about 40 comes with a finding outside the liver, identify the organ. Brain, cornea or red cells point to copper, and the lung points to alpha-1 antitrypsin. The pancreas, skin, joints and heart in an older patient point to iron.
Class-vs-memberIncreased intestinal iron absorption: the right class, an inherited metal overload of the liver, but the wrong metal; HFE hemochromatosis presents in middle age with diabetes, skin and joint findings, never tremor or corneal rings.
Unchecked attributeHepatocyte retention of a misfolded protease inhibitor: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited liver disease of the young, but its second organ is the lung; it does not explain neuropsychiatric signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings.

Renal & Genitourinary 11 topics + 2 board-style + 1 Aquifer

Two recurring lessons: normal values are eliminations, and a single discordant test component never overturns a convergent picture.

Pyelonephritis

home or admit · imaging gates · organism from the urine · complicated vs uncomplicatedCan the patient take oral therapy safely, and what does the urine say about the organism?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Fever, chills, dysuria and costovertebral angle tenderness make pyelonephritis a clinical diagnosis; with a benign abdomen, treat without imaging.

Admit for intravenous (IV) antibiotics when any of these holds:

  • Cannot take oral therapy: vomiting, or only clear fluids for days.
  • Unstable: sepsis or hypotension, read against the baseline (104/68 is low in long-standing hypertension).
  • Anatomy or host: pregnancy, obstruction, stones or a catheter; immunocompromise or extremes of age.
  • Failed outpatient therapy, or no oral agent the organism is sensitive to.

Otherwise a healthy, stable patient tolerating oral intake goes home on oral therapy. Nitrofurantoin treats cystitis, not the kidney.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Pyelonephritis – fever and chills with flank or costovertebral angle tenderness and urinary symptoms · Complicated UTI (urinary tract infection) – infection beyond the bladder: systemic signs such as fever or bacteremia, a catheter-related infection, or pyelonephritis (IDSA (Infectious Diseases Society of America) 2025); men can have uncomplicated cystitis. Older teaching called every UTI in a man complicated ⚠︎ · Duration – every pyelonephritis is a complicated UTI: typically 7 days, oral or IV, switching to oral as soon as the patient improves (IDSA 2025; older teaching 7 to 14 days ⚠︎)
Which enzyme Nitrate reductase – nitrate to nitrite: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter; not Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Enterococcus or Pseudomonas · Urease – urea to ammonia, alkaline urine, struvite staghorn stones: Proteus, Klebsiella, S. saprophyticus · Catheter, instrumentation, prior antibiotics or hospital – Enterococcus and Pseudomonas (nitrite-negative), Citrobacter, Serratia, Enterobacter; the stem supplies the exposure
Management and treatment
Management ladder: pyelonephritis
TierInterventionEscalate when
OutpatientOral therapy chosen by local resistance: in adults, a fluoroquinolone, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) if the organism is sensitive; in a well child, an oral third-generation cephalosporin; avoid fluoroquinolones in childrenAny admission criterion, or failure of outpatient therapy
AdmitIV antibiotics; switch to oral as soon as the patient improvesNo improvement at 48 to 72 hours: CT for abscess or obstruction
Source controlDrain an abscess or relieve an obstruction; urgent urology for emphysematous pyelonephritisTop rung
By diagnosis Cystitis – no fever, no flank tenderness: nitrofurantoin · Pyelonephritis in pregnancy – admit for IV antibiotics · Benign prostatic hyperplasia – incomplete emptying causes stasis and ascending infection · Struvite stones – a urease organism, usually Proteus
Practice
  1. 28-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, chills and dysuria right costovertebral angle tenderness eating and drinking normally Healthy; not pregnant T 38.6 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 96/min · abdomen benign → Outpatient oral therapy → a healthy, stable patient who tolerates oral intake is treated at home with oral therapy; nitrofurantoin does not reach the kidney
  2. 28-year-old woman has fever, flank pain and dysuria has taken only clear fluids for 2 days vomits everything, including her tablets Healthy; not pregnant T 39.0 °C · BP 110/70 mm Hg · left costovertebral angle tenderness → Admit for IV antibiotics → a patient who cannot keep oral therapy down is admitted for IV antibiotics; one intramuscular dose does not finish the course
  3. 28-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation has fever and flank pain dysuria for 3 days right costovertebral angle tenderness Tolerating fluids; no contractions T 38.8 °C · BP 112/68 mm Hg · fetal heart rate 150/min → Admit for IV antibiotics → pregnancy is on the admission list by itself, even with oral intake intact; nitrofurantoin does not treat the kidney
  4. 28-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency suprapubic discomfort no flank pain or costovertebral angle tenderness Not pregnant; no vaginal discharge Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Treat as cystitis with nitrofurantoin → no fever and no flank tenderness is cystitis: nitrofurantoin; it does not treat pyelonephritis; a fluoroquinolone is not first line for cystitis, and 14 days is a pyelonephritis-length course
  5. 28-year-old woman admitted with fever and flank pain is still febrile 72 hours of IV antibiotics matched to the culture flank pain unchanged Blood cultures negative T 39.1 °C · BP 108/70 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → CT for abscess or obstruction → no improvement at 48 to 72 hours on correct antibiotics: CT for an abscess or obstruction, not broader antibiotics
  6. 28-year-old woman has fever, flank pain and dysuria eating and drinking a past culture grew an organism resistant to every oral agent Not pregnant T 38.7 °C · BP 120/76 mm Hg · left costovertebral angle tenderness → Admit for IV therapy → no oral option means IV therapy, so she is admitted; nitrofurantoin does not reach the kidney
  7. 9-month-old girl has 2 days of fever and fussiness feeding poorly but still drinking well no cough, rash or diarrhea Catheterized urine culture sent; no drug allergies T 39.0 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive → Cefixime → a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefixime covers the gram-negative uropathogens; ciprofloxacin is avoided in children, and clindamycin misses them
  8. 11-month-old boy has a first febrile urinary infection well-appearing, taking fluids pediatrician prescribes cefixime, not trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate Parents ask why the two older drugs were not used T 38.9 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Rising Escherichia coli resistance → rising Escherichia coli resistance; the local resistance pattern drives the empiric choice
  9. 9-month-old girl has a first febrile urinary infection well-appearing, tolerating oral intake culture sensitivities pending No drug allergies; parents ask which drugs are options T 38.8 °C · urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte esterase positive → Ciprofloxacin → fluoroquinolones are avoided in children (cartilage toxicity) and kept for organisms such as Pseudomonas with no alternative; an oral cephalosporin fits
  10. 72-year-old man with an indwelling urinary catheter has fever right flank pain catheter in place for 6 weeks Several antibiotic courses this year T 38.9 °C · BP 128/80 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites negative, pyuria → Pseudomonas aeruginosa → a catheter, instrumentation or prior antibiotics widen the organism list beyond Escherichia coli to Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Serratia and Candida
  11. 58-year-old woman has a third urinary infection this year urine pH 8.5 on every recent urinalysis CT: staghorn calculus filling the left renal pelvis No catheter Afebrile · BP 124/80 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites positive → Proteus mirabilis → urease splits urea to ammonia, alkalinizes the urine and builds struvite staghorn stones: Proteus mirabilis; Klebsiella also has urease but is a far less common cause
  12. 22-year-old woman has 2 days of dysuria and frequency sexually active, with a new partner this month culture: gram-positive cocci, coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant No flank pain Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrites negative → Staphylococcus saprophyticus → Staphylococcus saprophyticus: young sexually active women, coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant, and nitrite-negative because it lacks nitrate reductase
  13. 26-year-old woman has 1 week of dysuria sexually active, inconsistent condom use pyuria, but the urine culture is sterile No flank pain Afebrile · BP 114/70 mm Hg · urinalysis: nitrites negative → Chlamydial urethritis → sterile pyuria in a sexually active patient is chlamydial urethritis until shown otherwise: nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT)
  14. 64-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has fever and flank pain worse despite 2 days of antibiotics CT: gas within the left renal parenchyma Glucose 420 mg/dL T 39.4 °C · BP 96/60 mm Hg · HR 118/min → Emphysematous pyelonephritis → gas in the kidney of a diabetic is emphysematous pyelonephritis: IV antibiotics, glucose control and urgent urology
  15. 45-year-old man has his fourth urinary infection in 2 years every culture grows Proteus mirabilis urine pH 8.0 Imaging shows a large branching calculus in the right renal pelvis Afebrile · BP 126/82 mm Hg → Struvite stones → a urease-splitting organism alkalinizes the urine and precipitates struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate)
Pairs with Urinary Tract Infection in a Child covers febrile infection in children, the imaging that follows it and afebrile recurrences. Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention covers the obstruction behind infection in an older man. Ask: is the infection in the bladder or beyond it?
Transferable rule

Treat a clinical diagnosis without imaging, and image only for a named reason. When an organism is ruled out by an enzyme, name the enzyme: urease and nitrate reductase are independent.

Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia and Urinary Retention

Prostatic obstruction presenting as a three-stage history

The decision point

The underlying cause is the primary process that produces the other findings, not one of its complications. Six months of hesitancy and dribbling came first. Five days of frequency and incomplete emptying followed, then one day of anuria with suprapubic pain. The retention, the UTI (urinary tract infection) and the creatinine of 3.4 all result from prostatic obstruction.

Why 1+ blood does not change the diagnosis Trace-to-1+ hematuria is expected with UTI (urinary tract infection), bladder distension and BPH (benign prostatic hyperplasia) itself. Nephrolithiasis needs the pain syndrome of colicky flank pain radiating to the groin. It also does not explain six months of hesitancy. A single nonspecific dipstick finding does not outweigh a six-month history.
Scenario bank
  1. 72 yo M with 6 months of hesitancy, now anuric for a day with suprapubic fullness → Acute urinary retention from BPH → catheterize
  2. 72 yo M in retention; the question asks the underlying cause → Benign prostatic hyperplasia
  3. 72 yo M after catheter relief; first-line medical therapy → Alpha-blocker
  4. 72 yo M with a very large prostate seeking long-term volume reduction → Add a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor
  5. 72 yo M with BPH started on oxybutynin for urgency, now in retention → Anticholinergic-induced retention → stop the drug
  6. 72 yo M in retention with a hard nodular prostate and PSA 40 → Prostate cancer → biopsy
The management sequel Acute retention → bladder catheterization first (suprapubic if the urethra is impassable). Then treat the UTI (urinary tract infection) and watch for post-obstructive diuresis. Expect the creatinine to fall; the fall proves the AKI (acute kidney injury) was post-renal. Renal ultrasound shows hydronephrosis if confirmation is needed. Long-term, give tamsulosin ± finasteride, with TURP (transurethral resection of the prostate) if refractory.
Transferable rule A single lab value should change the diagnosis only if it is incompatible with it, not merely compatible with another diagnosis.
Treat-the-number

Diabetic Nephropathy Screening

Screening test chosen by detection threshold rather than accuracy

The decision point

The most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold. UACR (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) detects 30–300 mg/g, the reversible window. Dipstick needs ~≥300 mg/day and is concentration-dependent. Early nephropathy causes hyperfiltration, so creatinine can be normal or low while glomeruli are being destroyed.

Defining criteria UACR window — detects 30–300 mg/g, the reversible stage · Dipstick threshold — ~≥300 mg/day, concentration-dependent · Early disease — hyperfiltration; creatinine normal or low while glomeruli are lost

  1. 56 yo M with type 2 diabetes diagnosed today → At diagnosis
  2. 24 yo F with type 1 diabetes diagnosed at 16 → 5 Years after diagnosis

Buzzword → Step 2 phrasing "Microalbuminuria" → "UACR 85 mg/g" (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) · "hyperfiltration" → "creatinine 0.7" in a diabetic · "Kimmelstiel-Wilson" → "nodular glomerulosclerosis on biopsy" · "transient albuminuria" → "he ran a 10K yesterday."
Transferable rule The most sensitive test has the lowest detection threshold. The most specific or confirmatory test is the least likely to give a false positive. Normal creatinine never excludes early diabetic kidney disease.
Test-overrides-findings

Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome

glomerular or not, then symptomatic or not · nephritis weeks after strep: complement and volumeIs it glomerular, how long since the infection, is complement low, and is the child overloaded?

Glomerular or notNephritic syndromePractice
Bottom line

With dysuria, leukocyte esterase and pyuria, the blood is part of the cystitis, not a separate workup. Otherwise ask in order: is it glomerular, and if not, does a symptom name the cause?

  • Glomerular hematuria: any of brown, tea or cola urine, red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, protein, edema or hypertension; check creatinine, complement levels and a complete blood count (CBC).
  • Non-glomerular hematuria: bright red urine or clots, normal red cell shape, no protein. With no symptom to name the cause: renal and bladder ultrasound, the first image for painless gross hematuria, since a young child's kidney stone is often painless; urine culture; and urine calcium/creatinine ratio, high in asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross.
  • Nephritic syndrome: hematuria with red cell casts or dysmorphic red cells, hypertension, edema, oliguria and a rising creatinine; protein present but usually below the nephrotic range.
  • Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN): about 2 to 4 weeks after pharyngitis and up to about 6 weeks after impetigo. Hematuria during or within days of an upper respiratory infection is immunoglobulin A (IgA) nephropathy.
  • Complement clock: C3 (complement component 3) low at onset, back to normal within about 6 to 8 weeks; still low after 8 weeks means a different lesion.
Glomerular or not
Glomerular vs non-glomerular hematuria
GlomerularNon-glomerular
ColorBrown, tea or colaBright red, clots
SedimentRed cell casts, dysmorphic red cellsNormal red cell shape
ProteinPresentAbsent
