Nephritic syndrome after strep
Acute nephritis in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness script and tellAgainst it 2 weeks after a sore throat
PSGNImmune complexes after group A strep pharyngitis or impetigo; edema, hypertension, cola urine; weeks later, low C3, normal by 6 to 8 weeks; positive ASO or anti-DNase B; children recover over weeksThe answer
IgA nephropathyMesangial IgA; recurrent gross hematuria in an older child or young adult, during or within days of an infection; normal C3Two-week gap; edema and hypertension, not isolated episodes
IgA vasculitis nephritisSmall-vessel IgA vasculitis; kidney disease can follow the rash by weeks; palpable purpura on legs and buttocks, arthritis, abdominal pain; normal C3No rash, joint or abdominal pain
Lupus nephritis or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)Immune-complex nephritis that does not resolve; lupus mostly in adolescent girls; persistently low complement; lupus lowers C3 and C4 (complement component 4), with a positive antinuclear antibody (ANA)Decided at 8 weeks: an unrecovered C3 earns a biopsy
Alport syndromeType IV collagen defect, usually X-linked; persistent hematuria with sensorineural hearing loss and family kidney failure; slow progressionAcute onset after an infection; no deafness or family history
Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS)Shiga toxin after bloody diarrhea; microangiopathy; hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, low platelets plus acute kidney injury (AKI)Normal blood count; sore throat, not diarrhea
Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy has bright red urine since yesterday No dysuria, trauma or recent infection no edema or flank tenderness BP 100/65 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts; leukocyte esterase and nitrite negative → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → bright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension is nonglomerular, and no symptom names a cause. In a young child a kidney stone is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone; the ultrasound finds many stones and any obstruction with no radiation and also excludes a renal mass such as Wilms tumor. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Noncontrast CT is more sensitive for small stones but carries radiation, so in a child it follows a nondiagnostic ultrasound
  2. 8-year-old boy has 2 days of tea-colored urine Sore throat 2 weeks ago, resolved without treatment puffy eyelids; mild pretibial edema urine: red cell casts, 2+ protein BP 140/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.1 mg/dL → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → a latent period of weeks, not days, with red cell casts, protein and hypertension: expect a low C3 that normalizes by 6 to 8 weeks and a positive ASO or anti-DNase B. IgA nephropathy bleeds during or within days of an upper respiratory infection with a normal C3. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is the nephritis that does not resolve, with a persistently low complement; it is raised only when the C3 is still low at 8 weeks
  3. 8-year-old girl was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis yesterday periorbital and pedal edema Her physician considers drugs for her blood pressure BP 150/96 mm Hg · creatinine 1.7 mg/dL · potassium 6.0 mEq/L → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors raise potassium and can lower the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in AKI, and this potassium is already high. Furosemide treats the overload that drives the edema and pressure, and nifedipine follows if pressure stays high after diuresis
  4. 14-year-old boy receiving cyclophosphamide has 2 days of bright red urine with clots suprapubic discomfort; no flank pain Urine culture shows no growth Afebrile · BP 110/70 mm Hg · urine: protein negative, no casts → Hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein → bright red urine with clots on cyclophosphamide is a hemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein: give mesna and hydration. After a transplant, think of BK (a polyomavirus) or adenovirus. A bacterial cystitis grows on culture ⚠︎, and bladder cancer is very rare in children
  5. 7-year-old girl has microscopic hematuria on two routine urinalyses Well, with no dysuria, flank pain or edema urine: no protein, no casts, normal red cell shape BP 98/60 mm Hg · urine culture negative · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL → Urine calcium/creatinine ratio → hypercalciuria is the most common cause of asymptomatic hematuria, microscopic or gross, in a well child and the main risk factor for a stone; a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio finds it. A biopsy is a glomerular test, and this urine has no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, very rare in children
  6. 16-year-old boy has a third episode of cola-colored urine each began 1 to 2 days into a sore throat Between episodes he feels well urine: red cells, 1+ protein BP 118/74 mm Hg · C3 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → IgA nephropathy → synpharyngitic hematuria, within 1 to 2 days of the sore throat, recurrent, with a normal C3: mesangial IgA, typical in an older child or young adult. Poststreptococcal disease comes weeks after the infection with a low C3. Thin basement membrane disease causes persistent, often familial, microscopic hematuria, not recurrent gross bleeds with each sore throat ⚠︎
  7. 9-year-old boy has headache, lethargy and 2 days of low urine output Sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital, scrotal and pedal edema; no rash BP 170/102 mm Hg, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL, normal blood count · urine: moderate blood, 2+ protein → Furosemide → hematuria with protein, hypertension, edema and a rising creatinine two weeks after a sore throat is poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. Inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water, and the edema and hypertension both come from that volume: the first drug is a loop diuretic, with sodium and fluid restriction. Saline answers the low urine output and raised creatinine, but this child is overloaded, not dry. Plasmapheresis treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane (GBM) disease; this disease is immune-complex and self-limited. Headache and lethargy at this pressure are signs of hypertensive encephalopathy, so a calcium channel blocker is added alongside the diuretic now rather than after diuresis; it is not among these options
  8. 68-year-old man has two episodes of painless bright red urine Smokes one pack daily for 45 years no dysuria or flank pain Afebrile · BP 136/84 mm Hg · urine: over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein, casts or leukocyte esterase → Cystoscopy + CT urography → painless gross hematuria in an older adult or smoker earns CT urography and cystoscopy, which find a mass or stone; bladder cancer is the concern at this age. A repeat urinalysis in weeks delays that, and a renal ultrasound images only the kidneys and misses urothelial tumors that cystoscopy and CT urography find ⚠︎
  9. 10-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 3 months ago Seen at a scheduled follow-up visit edema has resolved microscopic hematuria persists on urinalysis BP 108/68 mm Hg · C3 still low · creatinine 0.7 mg/dL → Renal biopsy → a C3 that has not recovered by 8 weeks triggers a biopsy to look for membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis or lupus nephritis. Microscopic hematuria may linger for months after recovery, but the low C3 does not; waiting 3 more months delays the biopsy, and a repeat ASO shows only that strep came before, not why the C3 stays low ⚠︎
  10. 8-year-old boy has had 3 days of tea-colored urine He had a sore throat 2 weeks ago periorbital edema urine: red cell casts, 1+ protein Afebrile · BP 138/92 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Serum C3 level → nephritis weeks after pharyngitis: a low C3 with a normal or mildly low C4 supports it; a normal C3 means IgA nephropathy or IgA vasculitis, and a low C3 and C4 suggest lupus. A biopsy is only for an atypical course (C3 still low after 8 weeks or worsening), and an ultrasound shows size and structure, not immune complexes
  11. 10-year-old boy has microscopic hematuria on every urinalysis since age 4 sensorineural hearing loss on audiometry His maternal uncle had kidney failure at 30 BP 112/70 mm Hg · urine: 1+ protein · C3 normal → Alport syndrome → persistent hematuria with sensorineural hearing loss and a family history of kidney failure is a type IV collagen defect, usually X-linked, progressing slowly to kidney failure. Thin basement membrane disease does not bring deafness ⚠︎. IgA nephropathy bleeds in recurrent gross episodes during or within days of an upper respiratory infection
  12. 11-year-old boy fell onto bicycle handlebars 3 hours ago left flank pain, bruising; bright red urine alert; abdomen soft, left flank tender HR 96/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · large blood, over 100 red cells/hpf, no protein or casts → Contrast CT of the abdomen → hematuria after abdominal or flank trauma: CT shows and stages the renal injury. The ultrasound is the first image for painless gross hematuria or flank pain without trauma, and waiting a week to repeat the urinalysis leaves the injury unstaged ⚠︎
  13. 9-year-old boy was diagnosed with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis 2 days ago headache After 24 hours of furosemide with sodium and fluid restriction alert, no respiratory distress BP 165/102 mm Hg · potassium 4.8 mEq/L → Add nifedipine → pressure that stays high after 24 hours of diuresis is the indication for a calcium channel blocker, so waiting another day is not the step. Watch for hypertensive encephalopathy: headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures. Dialysis is for refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia, none of which is present
  14. 17-year-old girl has 5 days of dysuria Sexually active with a new partner; no fever or flank pain urine: leukocyte esterase positive, 20 white cells/hpf, a few red cells urine culture: no growth Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT → sterile pyuria with dysuria in a sexually active adolescent: test for chlamydia and gonorrhea with a nucleic acid amplification test. Other causes of sterile pyuria are renal tuberculosis, interstitial nephritis, a partially treated urinary tract infection and appendicitis. Repeating the culture for bacterial cystitis repeats a negative test ⚠︎, and a renal ultrasound answers flank pain with crystals or painless gross hematuria
  15. 6-year-old girl has cola-colored urine and puffy eyelids Crusted sores on her legs 4 weeks ago red cell casts; no rash or joint pain BP 138/90 mm Hg · C3 low · C4 normal · creatinine 0.9 mg/dL → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → nephritis up to about 6 weeks after impetigo with a low C3 and normal C4, expected to normalize within 8 weeks; anti-DNase B is the better strep marker after impetigo. IgA nephropathy bleeds within days of an infection with a normal C3, and IgA vasculitis brings palpable purpura, arthritis and abdominal pain with a normal C3
  16. 9-year-old girl has 2 days of brown urine puffy eyelids each morning mild pretibial edema BP 132/86 mm Hg · urine: blood 3+, protein 2+, red cell casts · no leukocyte esterase or nitrite → Serum creatinine, complement levels and CBC → brown urine with protein, casts, edema and hypertension is glomerular hematuria: check creatinine, complement levels and a CBC. A low C3 after a recent strep infection points to postinfectious glomerulonephritis. The ultrasound and calcium/creatinine ratio belong to the nonglomerular branch
How NBME framed it: question 1

8-year-old girl with 6 days of intermittent headache, tiredness and little appetite, then 2 days of brown urine Vomited yesterday morning; no abdominal pain, diarrhea or dysuria Sore throat and fever 2 weeks ago that cleared without treatment; previously healthy, no medications; normal growth and development mildly pale, not distressed; height 50th percentile, weight 75th T 36.7 °C · HR 108/min · respiratory rate 16/min · BP 138/88 mm Hg large, mildly red tonsils without exudate; lungs clear grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur, no rub or gallop; abdomen normal; warm extremities with 1+ edema serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL · urea nitrogen 42 mg/dL · sodium 132 mEq/L · potassium 5.2 mEq/L · chloride 100 mEq/L · bicarbonate 15 mEq/L urine: blood 2+ · protein 1+ · red cell casts too numerous to count · pH 5 · specific gravity 1.020 · Gram stain: no organisms

Most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Antinuclear antibody assay: pulls toward lupus nephritis; but it is neither sensitive nor specific here, and lupus lowers both C3 and C4.
  • Urine culture: the urine is abnormal; but a culture answers a urinary tract infection; there is no dysuria and the Gram stain shows no organisms.
  • Renal ultrasonography: the creatinine is rising; but immune-complex deposits are microscopic, not visible on ultrasound.

Down to two: serum C3 or echocardiography. Serum C3: brown urine with casts, protein, hypertension and edema 2 weeks after a sore throat; deposited immune complexes consume C3, so the serum level falls. The soft ejection murmur after the sore throat baits rheumatic carditis, but the lungs are clear, so heart failure is unlikely.

Management ladder for PSGN Volume overload – inflamed glomeruli filter less, so the kidney retains salt and water; edema and hypertension both come from that volume; headache, vomiting, confusion or seizures mean hypertensive encephalopathy · Every child – supportive care with sodium and fluid restriction · Loop diuretic – furosemide first, for edema or hypertension from volume overload; saline for the oliguria would worsen it · Calcium channel blocker – nifedipine when pressure stays high after diuresis or encephalopathy appears; ACE inhibitors only with caution in AKI because of hyperkalemia · Dialysis – refractory overload, hyperkalemia or uremia · No role – plasmapheresis, since the disease is self-limited · Antibiotics – treat a still-active strep infection but do not change the renal course
Nitrite is only about 50% sensitive It needs a nitrate-reducing organism (Enterococcus, S. saprophyticus and Pseudomonas are not) and adequate bladder dwell time. A negative nitrite never excludes a urinary tract infection when leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms agree.
Painless gross hematuria in a child A kidney stone in a young child is often painless and sitting in the kidney, so it presents as gross hematuria alone, and crystals are not always seen. Hypercalciuria is the main risk factor: look for earlier microscopic hematuria and a high spot urine calcium/creatinine ratio. The renal and bladder ultrasound comes first; noncontrast CT only if it is nondiagnostic. Cystoscopy looks for adult bladder cancer, which is very rare in children. Meatal irritation is painful and visible on exam: reassure.
Course Nephritis days after an upper respiratory infection is IgA nephropathy; weeks after pharyngitis or impetigo, PSGN. Treating strep pharyngitis promptly prevents rheumatic fever but does not reliably prevent PSGN. Children usually recover fully within weeks, although microscopic hematuria may linger for months; adults are more likely to develop chronic kidney disease.
Common wrong answers A negative nitrite overruling leukocyte esterase, pyuria and symptoms. Cystoscopy in a child: right for an older adult, but bladder cancer is very rare in a 6-year-old, so the ultrasound comes first. Noncontrast CT before the ultrasound: more sensitive for small stones, but radiation. A 24-hour urine protein or kidney biopsy for bright red urine with no protein, casts, edema or hypertension. Normal saline for a low urine output in an overloaded child. Plasmapheresis: treats antibody-mediated anti-glomerular basement membrane disease; PSGN is immune-complex and self-limited. Lisinopril first: risks hyperkalemia in AKI; diuresis first, then a calcium channel blocker. Protein restriction: for chronic kidney disease, not a self-limited acute nephritis.
Pairs with Part I Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child: protein without red cells, with normal pressure and creatinine; there a normotensive 3-year-old with periorbital edema is treated on presentation rather than biopsied. Ask: does the urine show red cells and casts, or protein alone? Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes starts one step earlier: is the swelling local to the eye? Part I Acute Kidney Injury in a Child: the AKI that does need fluids. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child sends the renal involvement of IgA vasculitis here. Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia: HUS. Part II Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child: protein on a routine dipstick in a child with no symptoms.
Transferable rule

With a full lab panel, base the diagnosis on the pattern of the panel, not the most alarming single value; a discordant component reflects a test's limited sensitivity and does not overrule the pattern. In a child with AKI, decide whether the kidney needs volume given or removed before choosing a drug: edema with hypertension means overload, so the loop diuretic comes first and saline is harmful.

Scrotal Pain and Masses

Painful acute scrotum and painless scrotal mass follow separate workups

The decision point

Separate torsion from epididymitis by timeline, location and infection signs. Torsion is sudden and maximal within minutes to hours. A 3-day escalating course with fever, dysuria and posterior tenderness is epididymitis, a clinical diagnosis. Ultrasound and urology are torsion steps; a clinical picture of epididymitis like this one does not need them.

The acute scrotum — the differential
ConditionOnsetThe tellCremastericNext step
Testicular torsion EmergencySudden, minutesHigh-riding transverse testis, N/V, no feverAbsentEmergent urology — salvage window ~6 h
EpididymitisGradual, daysPosterior tenderness, dysuria, fever; Prehn sign +IntactAntibiotics (clinical dx) + NAAT + UA
OrchitisDaysMumps history, unvaccinatedIntactSupportive
Torsion of appendix testisGradual, prepubertalBlue dot sign, superior poleIntactSupportive
Fournier gangrene EmergencyHoursToxic, crepitus, necrosis; diabetic—Emergent debridement
Scrotal mass (painless tree)
FindingDiagnosis
Bag of worms, ↑ standing/Valsalva, ↓ supineVaricocele — ~90% left-sided (left spermatic vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle)
Right-sided, sudden onset, or fails to decompress supineRetroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal imaging
Transilluminates, uniform, testis palpable withinHydrocele
Enlarges with Valsalva, reducible, doesn't transilluminateInguinal hernia
Firm, fixed, painless, on the testis, no transilluminationTumor → ultrasound + AFP/β-hCG/LDH → inguinal orchiectomy, never transscrotal biopsy
Testicular mass with gynecomastia, ↓ libido, or precocious puberty in a boy; markers normalLeydig cell tumor — a sex cord–stromal tumor secreting testosterone or estrogen. Reinke crystals on histology. Mostly benign; the hormonal syndrome is the tell, and AFP/β-hCG are negative
Testicular mass, heterogeneous with calcification and cystic areas on ultrasound; AFP and/or β-hCG elevatedTeratoma (nonseminomatous). In adults, malignant regardless of maturity; in prepubertal boys, benign — the one tumor whose behavior flips with age. Chemoresistant → resect residual masses after chemotherapy
Tumor marker logic AFP elevated → never a seminoma (AFP, alpha-fetoprotein; it indicates a yolk sac or embryonal/teratoma component) · β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) can rise in seminoma and nonseminoma; only AFP is exclusionary · both markers normal with a solid mass → pure seminoma or a sex cord–stromal tumor (Leydig, Sertoli); a hormonal syndrome separates them · LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) tracks tumor burden, not histology · Sertoli cell tumor is, like Leydig, stromal and usually benign, but is typically hormonally silent.
Pearls Epididymitis treatment splits by age · <35 / sexually active → ceftriaxone + doxycycline · >35 / low STI risk (STI, sexually transmitted infection) → levofloxacin or TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) · varicocele is the most common correctable cause of male infertility; testicular size discrepancy in an adolescent is the surgical indication · seminoma never makes AFP (alpha-fetoprotein).
The two hard pairs
  • Varicocele vs. indirect inguinal hernia — both non-transilluminating, both enlarge with Valsalva. Separators: a hernia is reducible, feels like soft tissue or bowel, and you cannot palpate above it (it descends through the canal). A varicocele feels like worms, isn't reducible, and is confined to the scrotum.
  • Varicocele vs. spermatocele — both sit above and separate from the testis. Separators: the spermatocele transilluminates and does not change with position or Valsalva.
  • Femoral hernia presents below the inguinal ligament in the upper thigh, in older women, and anatomically cannot reach the scrotum — high incarceration risk.
Varicocele mechanism ~90% left-sided: the left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle · possible "nutcracker" compression between the aorta and the SMA (superior mesenteric artery) · the right gonadal vein drains obliquely into the IVC (inferior vena cava) · subfertility comes from increased scrotal temperature impairing spermatogenesis; a varicocele may also cause ipsilateral atrophy · treatment: observation if asymptomatic · gonadal vein ligation or embolization for pain, >20% testicular volume discrepancy in adolescents, or abnormal semen analysis · scrotal support and NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs) for older men not seeking fertility · a varicocele in a prepubertal child, right-sided, or persistent when supine is secondary until proven otherwise · in children think Wilms (with hypertension from renin secretion); in adults think RCC (renal cell carcinoma) invading the renal vein
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Exam with cremasteric reflexFirstAbsent reflex, high-riding transverse testis, sudden painTorsion: emergent urology; do not wait for imaging
Scrotal Doppler ultrasoundBy branchAbsent blood flow to the testisTorsion, used only when the exam is equivocal
Urinalysis and NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrheaSupportsPyuria or a positive NAATEpididymitis, a clinical diagnosis: treat without waiting on results
Transillumination of a painless massFirstMass glows, testis palpable within or separateHydrocele or spermatocele; a solid, dark mass needs ultrasound
Scrotal ultrasound with AFP, beta-hCG and LDHBy branchSolid intratesticular massTesticular tumor; an elevated AFP excludes pure seminoma
Radical inguinal orchiectomyConfirmsHistology names the tumorDiagnostic and therapeutic; never transscrotal biopsy
Ultrasound in gradual, febrile, posterior painSkipWould add delay, not a decisionEpididymitis is clinical; imaging is a torsion answer
Scenario bank
  1. Right-sided varicocele, sudden onset, or one that fails to decompress supine → Retroperitoneal mass or RCC invading the renal vein → abdominal CT
  2. Mass transilluminates with the testis palpable within → Hydrocele → observe (infantile hydroceles usually close by age 1)
  3. Reducible mass extending from the inguinal canal, can't get above it → Indirect inguinal hernia → repair
  4. Firm, fixed, on the testis, no positional change → Ultrasound + AFP, β-hCG, LDH → radical inguinal orchiectomy (never transscrotal — it seeds lymphatics). Cryptorchidism is the biggest risk factor, for both testes
  5. Small transilluminating cyst at the superior pole, unchanging → Spermatocele → reassurance
  6. Adolescent with a varicocele and >20% testicular volume discrepancy → Refer for ligation
  7. Groin bulge below the inguinal ligament in an older woman → Femoral hernia → prompt repair
  8. Sudden severe pain, high-riding transverse testis, absent cremasteric reflex → Testicular torsion → emergent surgery
  9. 4 yo M, painless soft scrotal mass superior to the right testicle that does not decompress supine, blood pressure 160/96 → Secondary varicocele from an abdominal mass → abdominal ultrasonography
Transferable rules A 3-day timeline of scrotal pain excludes torsion. When the clinical findings confirm infection well enough, treat rather than image. Also, read the grammatical form of the answer choices before the stem. If every choice is an anatomic process, the question asks for mechanism; if every choice is a test, the next diagnostic step; if every choice is a drug, treatment.

Hypercalcemia

Check PTH (parathyroid hormone) first in every case of hypercalcemia

The decision point

Calcium high + phosphorus low = PTH-driven until proven otherwise. The first step in any confirmed hypercalcemia is PTH (parathyroid hormone), because it splits the entire differential before anything else is ordered.

  • PTH high or inappropriately normal → primary hyperparathyroidism (most likely) or familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (separate with urine calcium)
  • PTH suppressed → then hunt: malignancy (PTHrP, bone mets), vitamin D excess or granulomatous disease, milk-alkali, thiazides, hyperthyroidism, immobilization
Calcium and phosphorus patterns Ca↑ / Phos↓ = PTH (parathyroid hormone) or PTHrP (parathyroid hormone-related protein) · Ca↑ / Phos↑ = vitamin D–mediated · Ca↓ / Phos↑ = renal failure or hypoparathyroidism · Ca↓ / Phos↓ = vitamin D deficiency. Symptoms: "stones, bones, groans, thrones, psychiatric overtones." In hypercalcemia, polyuria with a dilute urine is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Serum calcium with albumin and phosphorusScreenCalcium high, albumin normalTrue hypercalcemia; no correction needed
PTHFirstPTH high or inappropriately normalPTH-dependent: primary hyperparathyroidism or FHH
PTH suppressedPTH-independent: PTHrP and vitamin D levels next
24-hour urine calciumConfirmsCalcium/creatinine clearance ratio under 0.01FHH, no surgery; a higher ratio fits primary hyperparathyroidism
PTHrPBy branchPTHrP highMalignancy: imaging next
25-OH and 1,25-OH vitamin DBy branch1,25-OH vitamin D highGranulomatous disease or lymphoma; high 25-OH means vitamin D excess
Sestamibi scan to make the diagnosisSkipA negative scan does not exclude itDiagnosis is biochemical; imaging only localizes before surgery
Scenario bank
  1. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and phosphorus 2.1, found incidentally → Check PTH first
  2. 58 yo F with calcium 11.6 and an elevated PTH → Primary hyperparathyroidism
  3. 58 yo F with calcium 13.4, suppressed PTH and weight loss → Malignancy → PTHrP and imaging
  4. 24 yo M with lifelong mild hypercalcemia, normal PTH and a urine calcium-creatinine clearance ratio under 0.01 → Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia → no surgery
  5. 58 yo F with hypercalcemia, suppressed PTH, high 1,25-OH vitamin D and hilar adenopathy → Granulomatous disease
  6. 58 yo F with calcium 14.5, confusion and dehydration → Isotonic saline first, then calcitonin and a bisphosphonate
Normal labs that rule out alternatives A normal albumin means the calcium is truly elevated, with no correction needed · a specific gravity of 1.005 rules out diabetes mellitus, because glucosuria raises the specific gravity · low phosphorus argues against vitamin D excess, which raises both calcium and phosphorus · enalapril rather than a thiazide removes the drug confounder.
Pairs with Part I Polyuria covers the polyuria hypercalcaemia causes. It results from an acquired, reversible resistance to vasopressin at the collecting duct, which corrects when the calcium does. Ask: does the kidney concentrate after desmopressin?

Urinary Tract Infection in a Child

assign the tract, then name the risk factor · reflux grade sets treatment and outcomeIs this infection febrile or afebrile, does the bladder empty, and what grade did the cystourethrogram show?

WorkupRisk factorsRefluxPractice
Bottom line

Assign the tract before the cause. The anatomic causes of recurrent urinary tract infection (UTI) in a child, reflux above all, produce recurrent pyelonephritis rather than recurrent cystitis; emptying problems produce lower-tract disease. Afebrile recurrent cystitis in a constipated child is urinary stasis: a loaded rectum compresses the bladder and urethra so it never empties, and the lasting treatment is a long-term laxative.

  • Lower tract (cystitis): dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, afebrile, without flank or back pain.
  • Upper tract (pyelonephritis): fever, flank or back pain, vomiting and an ill appearance; the pattern reflux produces.
  • Reinfection, not relapse: a 6-week symptom-free gap after an adequate short course (3 days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a lower-tract infection) makes relapse unlikely.
  • Vesicoureteral reflux: retrograde urine flow through a congenitally short intravesical ureter.
  • Reflux grade: mild I to II, dilating III to V. Grade I stays in the ureter and II reaches the pelvis without dilation; grade III dilates the ureter and pelvis with little or no blunting, IV obliterates the fornices, and V adds gross dilation and a tortuous ureter.
  • Reflux nephropathy: recurrent febrile infection leaves focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis; enough scarring is chronic kidney disease, which in a child presents as secondary hypertension, proteinuria and failure to thrive.
Workup
Imaging after a febrile UTI First, under age 2 – renal and bladder ultrasound; VCUG only if it shows hydronephrosis, scarring or other signs of high-grade reflux or obstruction, or the course is atypical or complex · First, age 2 or older – no imaging; observe · Recurrent febrile UTI – ultrasound and VCUG at any age, even when the ultrasound is normal again: ultrasound shows dilation and scarring but cannot show reflux · Other VCUG indications – fever of 39 °C or higher with an organism other than Escherichia coli; signs of chronic kidney disease such as poor growth or hypertension · Timing – ultrasound after treatment, to avoid false-positive findings from the acute infection; sooner only if the child is not improving
Recurrent infection: the risk factors
Which tract, then which risk factor
Risk factorThe tellNot it when
Urinary stasis from constipationRecurrent afebrile cystitis in a constipated child, hard stool in the vault, midline anal fissuresFever or flank pain
Dysfunctional voidingHolds urine all day, holding maneuvers, soft stoolsConstipation explains the emptying
Vesicoureteral refluxRecurrent febrile infection or pyelonephritis in an infant; hydronephrosis on ultrasoundAfebrile, suprapubic, no flank pain
Posterior urethral valvesMale infant, weak stream, palpable bladder, bilateral hydronephrosisFemale, normal stream, no distended bladder
Primary immunodeficiencySevere, multi-site infections, pyelonephritis rather than cystitis, failure to thriveSimple cystitis only; history otherwise unremarkable
Sexual abuseGenital injury or bleeding, behavioral change, disclosure; real but rareNormal genitalia; fissures explained by constipation
Inadequate treatmentNever resolved, or recurrence within days of finishing; same organism6-week symptom-free gap after an adequate course
Reflux: the grade sets the plan
Read the grade off the VCUG Ultrasound – shows hydronephrosis; mild there describes the dilation, not the reflux · VCUG – shows ureteral filling with or without a dilated collecting system, and is what assigns the grade · Mild – ureter or pelvis without dilation: usually disappears as the intravesical ureter lengthens with growth · Dilating – dilated ureter and pelvis, often blunted calices: less likely to resolve, more likely to recur and scar · Secondary – a boy with hydronephrosis and a weak stream has outlet obstruction causing the reflux, a different pathway
Management ladder: primary reflux
TierInterventionEscalate when
Mild (I to II)Observation, with or without prophylactic antibiotics (the rules below decide); expect spontaneous resolutionA breakthrough febrile UTI
Dilating (III to V)Prophylactic antibiotics (recommended under 1 year, and with bladder-bowel dysfunction while it is present and being treated; may be considered over 1 year with prior UTI and no dysfunction), with surgery as the next optionFebrile breakthrough on prophylaxis: consider ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic bulking injection
Established scarringLong-term blood pressure, urine protein and growth ⚠︎Hypertension, proteinuria or declining function: chronic kidney disease care
Who gets continuous prophylaxis: American Urological Association (AUA) Under 1 year, after a febrile UTI – recommended, at any grade · Under 1 year, found by screening – recommended for grades III to V; may be offered for I to II · Bladder-bowel dysfunction – recommended while it is present and being treated; treat the dysfunction, preferably before any surgery, at every grade · Over 1 year, with prior UTI, no dysfunction – may be considered · The trial – in the Randomized Intervention for Children with Vesicoureteral Reflux (RIVUR) trial (age 2 to 72 months, grades I to IV, after a first or second symptomatic UTI), trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis halved recurrent UTIs, with no significant difference in renal scarring
Practice
  1. 4-year-old girl has her third afebrile cystitis this year functional constipation since day care suprapubic tenderness, no back pain hard stool in the rectal vault Last episode 6 weeks ago, after 3 days of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole T 37.2 °C · normal genitalia → Urinary stasis → afebrile, suprapubic and no back pain is the lower tract, so the cause is incomplete emptying: a loaded rectum compresses the bladder and urethra, and ascending Escherichia coli colonizes the residual urine. Reflux produces recurrent upper-tract, febrile disease, and a child with reflux would likely have had at least one febrile episode by now. Three days is an adequate course for a lower-tract infection, and a 6-week symptom-free gap means reinfection, not relapse
  2. 6-month-old girl was treated for her first febrile urinary tract infection ultrasound: hydronephrosis cystourethrogram: dilated ureter with blunting of the calices Feeding well; growing along the 50th percentile Afebrile · BP 88/54 mm Hg → Prophylactic antibiotics → under 1 year with reflux and a febrile infection, continuous prophylaxis is recommended at any grade, and dilating reflux is less likely to resolve and more likely to recur and scar, so observation alone is not an option. Surgery is the next rung, considered after a febrile breakthrough infection on prophylaxis, not immediately
  3. 22-month-old girl had afebrile cystitis 3 months ago soft daily stools then 2 days of fever to 39 °C and irritability; vomited once, now drinking well right costovertebral angle tenderness afebrile within 48 hours of oral cefixime · culture: Escherichia coli → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → fever, vomiting and flank tenderness put this infection in the upper tract, and once treated, a first febrile urinary tract infection (UTI) under age 2 gets a renal and bladder ultrasound. Soft daily stools leave nothing for a laxative to treat, and reassurance with a repeat culture ignores the febrile imaging rule
  4. 4-year-old girl with recurrent cystitis has hard stools every 5 days hard stool fills the rectal vault post-void residual urine is increased No fever with any episode; no back pain Afebrile · rectal tone normal → The dilated rectum compresses the bladder and urethra, preventing complete voiding → residual urine is colonized by organisms ascending from the perineum. Reflux of urine to the kidney is the upper-tract, febrile mechanism, which this afebrile child lacks, and the organism ascends from the perineum rather than crossing the bowel wall
  5. 6-month-old boy had his first febrile urinary tract infection afebrile within 48 hours of oral cefixime Ultrasound after treatment: bilateral hydronephrosis normal urinary stream T 37.1 °C now · catheter culture: 100,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli → Voiding cystourethrogram → after a first febrile infection under age 2, an abnormal renal and bladder ultrasound (hydronephrosis, scarring, or findings of high-grade reflux or obstruction) is the indication for a voiding cystourethrogram, which shows and grades the reflux. No further imaging fits only a normal ultrasound, and prophylaxis waits for the cystourethrogram result
  6. 5-year-old girl has dysuria and frequency for 2 days bruising of the labia small amount of vaginal bleeding normal rectal examination; soft stools Mother noticed blood on her underwear yesterday Afebrile · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase, nitrite → Evaluate for sexual abuse and involve child protective services → genital injury or bleeding is the tell of sexual abuse, a real cause of urinary infection in children though rare: evaluate and involve child protective services. A normal rectal examination with soft stools leaves no constipation for a laxative, and an afebrile infection needs no voiding cystourethrogram
  7. 6-month-old boy had his first febrile urinary tract infection reflux left untreated cystourethrogram: dilated ureter with blunted calices Mother reports no recurrence; examination normal T 37.0 °C · BP 90/56 mm Hg → Focal interstitial fibrosis from recurrent parenchymal infection → blunted calices place him in the dilating group, which scars: recurrent febrile infection puts bacteria in the parenchyma, and inflammation and ischemia leave focal wedges of interstitial fibrosis, which in enough quantity is chronic kidney disease. Glomerular inflammation follows group A streptococcal skin or throat infection, and acquired renal cysts belong to children on dialysis; a quiet interval and a normal examination do not rule out future scarring
  8. 4-year-old girl is seen after treatment of her third cystitis this year hard stools every 4 days since starting day care hard stool in the rectal vault Symptom free now; normal genitalia Afebrile · urine culture after treatment not sent → Long-term laxative therapy → treat the risk factor: a long-term laxative softens stools, stops the withholding and lets the dilated rectum shrink, which relieves the bladder; treating the infection alone guarantees another episode. Prophylaxis belongs to reflux, which this lower-tract pattern does not suggest, and an afebrile infection needs no voiding cystourethrogram
  9. 3-year-old boy given daily prophylaxis since grade IV reflux was diagnosed at 8 months now his second febrile infection on prophylaxis left flank tenderness T 39.0 °C · urine culture: Escherichia coli → Surgical correction of the reflux → a febrile breakthrough infection on prophylaxis means prophylaxis has failed: consider open ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic injection of a bulking agent, with curative intent. Changing the agent keeps a failed strategy, and removing the kidney is not one of the curative options ⚠︎
  10. 18-month-old girl had 2 days of fever to 39.2 °C and irritability first urinary tract infection afebrile within 24 hours of oral cefixime ultrasound after treatment is normal catheter urinalysis: leukocyte esterase, nitrite, pyuria · culture: 80,000 CFU/mL Escherichia coli → No further imaging → a first febrile infection under age 2 gets a renal and bladder ultrasound, and a voiding cystourethrogram only if it is abnormal or a febrile infection recurs. Prophylaxis waits for the cystourethrogram result, so neither distractor applies yet. A fever of 39.2 °C with Escherichia coli does not meet the other-organism indication
  11. 6-year-old boy with reflux has had three Proteus urinary infections intermittent flank pain for 2 months branching staghorn calculus on imaging Urine pH 8.5; no family history of stones Afebrile · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL → A struvite stone from urease-producing bacteria → an alkaline pH above 8 with Proteus means urease, and urease-producing organisms make struvite. Reflux makes calcium stones through stasis, but recurrent Proteus points to urease. Reflux never makes uric acid stones, which come from overproduction, as in tumor lysis
  12. 5-year-old girl has her fourth cystitis in a year soft daily stools holds her urine all day at school crosses her legs and squats on her heel when urgent Afebrile · normal rectal examination → Timed voiding with behavioral therapy → holding urine all day with holding maneuvers is an emptying problem of the bladder itself, and emptying problems cause lower-tract disease: timed voiding with behavioral therapy (voiding habits are part of prevention). Soft daily stools leave nothing for a laxative to treat, and an afebrile infection needs no voiding cystourethrogram
  13. 2-month-old boy has his second febrile urinary tract infection weak urinary stream palpable bladder above the pubis Uncircumcised; feeding less than usual for 2 days Afebrile on intravenous antibiotics · ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis → Voiding cystourethrogram → a male infant with a weak stream, a palpable bladder and bilateral hydronephrosis has outlet obstruction until shown otherwise: the voiding cystourethrogram shows the dilated posterior urethra. Ultrasound shows dilation but cannot show reflux or confirm valves, and circumcision does not relieve an outlet obstruction ⚠︎
  14. 3-year-old boy has had two episodes of pyelonephritis pneumonia three times two skin abscesses drained weight has fallen from the 50th to the 5th percentile T 38.2 °C · normal stream → Primary immunodeficiency → severe infections (pyelonephritis rather than cystitis) at several sites with failure to thrive mean defective clearance across sites and organisms. Constipation-driven stasis gives simple cystitis in one tract, and reflux explains febrile kidney infections but not pneumonia, abscesses or poor growth
  15. 5-year-old girl whose grade II reflux was diagnosed at age 2 hard stools every 4 days daytime wetting most days Taking daily antibiotic prophylaxis; no infection this year Afebrile · urinalysis normal today → Treat the bladder and bowel dysfunction → bladder-bowel dysfunction is screened and treated alongside reflux at every grade, preferably before any surgery, and prophylaxis is recommended while the dysfunction is present and being treated. Surgery comes after that treatment, and nothing in the guideline raises the dose ⚠︎
  16. 3-year-old girl was started on oral cefdinir for a febrile urinary tract infection 72 hours ago left flank tenderness drinking; not vomiting Culture: Escherichia coli susceptible to cefdinir T 39.4 °C → Renal and bladder ultrasonography → no improvement by 48 to 72 hours on a drug the organism is susceptible to means looking for an abscess or obstruction: renal and bladder ultrasound, a repeat culture, intravenous antibiotics and admission. Switching drugs answers a resistant organism, and this one is susceptible; a voiding cystourethrogram does not look for an abscess ⚠︎
  17. 7-year-old boy has dilating reflux treated since infancy renal scarring on imaging no infection in 2 years Height at the 25th percentile; parents ask what to check at each visit BP 104/66 mm Hg · creatinine 0.5 mg/dL → Blood pressure and urinalysis for proteinuria → established scarring can progress to chronic kidney disease, which in a child shows as secondary hypertension, proteinuria and failure to thrive: blood pressure, urine protein and growth ⚠︎. An ultrasound alone does not show those, and uric acid has no role in reflux
  18. 4-year-old girl has her third cystitis this year untreated constipation with hard stools each episode cleared with a short antibiotic course Symptom free between episodes Afebrile · hard stool in the rectal vault → Lengthening the antibiotic course → the risk factor is mechanical, and a short course is adequate for a lower-tract infection, so a longer course treats the episode, not the disease. A laxative, and fiber with water, both target the constipation that keeps the bladder from emptying ⚠︎
  19. 8-month-old boy had a febrile urinary tract infection last month cystourethrogram: grade IV reflux weak, dribbling urinary stream palpable bladder Straining to void; urine dribbles between feeds Afebrile · BP 94/58 mm Hg · creatinine 0.6 mg/dL → Evaluate for bladder outlet obstruction → a boy with a weak stream and a palpable bladder has outlet obstruction causing secondary reflux, a different pathway: here the reflux is the consequence, not the disease, so look for posterior urethral valves on urethral views. Prophylaxis alone or a ureteral reimplantation treats primary reflux and leaves the obstruction in place ⚠︎
  20. 8-year-old girl has had febrile urinary tract infections since infancy headaches proteinuria small, scarred kidneys on ultrasound; no cysts Takes no medications; no recent sore throat or rash BP 128/84 mm Hg · height below the 5th percentile → Reflux nephropathy with chronic kidney disease → recurrent febrile infection scars the interstitium in wedges, and widespread scarring presents as secondary hypertension, proteinuria and failure to thrive, the endpoint prophylaxis prevents. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis follows group A streptococcal skin or throat infection and injures the glomerulus; the kidneys here are small and scarred, with no cysts
  21. 4-year-old boy has his second febrile urinary tract infection, fever to 39.1 °C First at 13 months; ultrasound then normal right costovertebral angle tenderness afebrile within 24 hours of antibiotics repeat renal and bladder ultrasound normal urine culture: Escherichia coli → Voiding cystourethrogram → a second febrile infection needs a voiding cystourethrogram at any age, even when the ultrasound is normal again, because ultrasound cannot show reflux. No further management is right only for a first febrile infection, and daily prophylaxis waits for the cystourethrogram result, since reflux is not yet known
  22. 2-year-old girl had reflux into the ureter only at 6 months no infections since repeat cystourethrogram now shows no reflux No surgery or injection was done Afebrile · BP 92/58 mm Hg → The intravesical ureter lengthens as the child grows → mild reflux disappears on its own as the intravesical ureter lengthens with growth; the anatomy corrects itself, not a muscle change or a pressure change ⚠︎
Reading the urine Specimen – catheter if not toilet trained, clean catch if trained · Leukocyte esterase – from lysed neutrophils; marks pyuria (more than 5 white cells per high-power field) · Nitrite – nitrate reductase of Escherichia coli, Klebsiella and Proteus; a negative result does not exclude a UTI, especially with frequent voiding in infants · pH above 8 – urease; think Proteus mirabilis · Culture – 100,000 CFU/mL or more by clean catch, 50,000 or more by catheter, of one uropathogen · Hematuria alone – not a UTI · Pyuria without bacteriuria in an adolescent – nucleic acid amplification testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea
Febrile UTI: treat before the culture returns Empiric – after the urinalysis, chosen by local sensitivity patterns and adjusted to the culture: oral options include cefixime, cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole · Route – oral is preferred, pyelonephritis included; intravenous (IV) ceftriaxone for age under 2 months, vomiting, an unstable or ill child, or failure of oral therapy · Blood tests – complete blood count, blood culture and procalcitonin only if ill-appearing, unvaccinated or under 2 months · No better by 48 to 72 hours – resistant: switch to a susceptible drug; susceptible: ultrasound for abscess or obstruction, repeat culture, intravenous antibiotics and admission · After a good response – no routine repeat culture · Prevention – treat constipation, prophylaxis for reflux per the AUA rules, voiding habits, front-to-back wiping
The constipated child Constipation is the commonest modifiable risk factor for recurrent cystitis in a young child, and the mechanism is purely mechanical. Functional constipation that dates to day-care entry is the stressor-driven withholding trigger. Hard stool with normal rectal tone argues against both a neurologic cause and anal trauma. Midline anal fissures are a complication of chronic constipation; alongside normal genitalia, they argue against injury, while a fissure off the midline may have another cause, such as Crohn disease. Treating the infection without the constipation treats the episode, not the disease; the laxative runs for months so the rectum can shrink ⚠︎.
Scarring and stones Reflux scarring is tubulointerstitial: bacteria in the parenchyma cause inflammation and ischemia, which lead to wedge-shaped fibrosis, and the glomeruli are lost secondarily. Only the grade predicts the long-term outcome, and the course if untreated follows the severity in this patient: never carry a severity adjective from one study to another. Reflux makes calcium stones through stasis and struvite stones through urease-producing organisms.
Pairs with Part II Posterior Urethral Valves: the obstructive counterpart, with the same cystourethrogram and hydronephrosis but reflux secondary to outlet obstruction; is there a weak stream or a palpable bladder, and is the reflux the disease or its consequence? Part II Pyelonephritis: oral versus intravenous route in adults. Part I Constipation in a Child: the upstream cycle whose urinary complication this is. Aquifer Fever in an Infant: the first febrile UTI in an infant, with the catheter specimen, oral or intravenous treatment, the drug and the dose.
Transferable rule

A disease name strongly associated with a complaint comes to mind before the finding that discriminates it, and recently learned associations come fastest. Convert each into a question: here, which tract is infected, and what grade did the cystourethrogram show?

Enuresis

1° vs 2° · mono- vs nonmonosymptomatic · urinalysis and exam · alarm vs desmopressinHas the urine been tested, and what has been tried, for how long?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Involuntary bedwetting at least twice weekly from age 5 is enuresis. Every child gets an examination and a urinalysis first, primary or secondary; a stressor never replaces them.

Classify on two axes:

  • Primary: never dry for 6 months; usually maturational.
  • Secondary: dry 6 months or more, now wetting; look for a cause.
  • Monosymptomatic: bedwetting only.
  • Nonmonosymptomatic: daytime urgency or holding; treat constipation and daytime symptoms first. A weak stream or dribbling in a boy points to urethral valves.

Normal workup, nothing tried: education, reassurance and motivational therapy. Then an alarm for a durable cure, or desmopressin for a fast, event-driven effect.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Enuresis – involuntary bedwetting at least twice weekly at age 5 or older · Secondary – 6 months or more of continuous dryness, then wetting again · Nonmonosymptomatic – daytime lower urinary tract symptoms with the bedwetting
Management and treatment
Management ladder: monosymptomatic enuresis, no cause found
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Education, reassurance, motivational therapy (reward effort and routine, not dry nights); treat constipation; void every 3 hours while awake and before bed; no drinks 1 to 2 hours before bed, drink well in the morning3 to 6 months without improvement, and the child or family is bothered
2Alarm: best long-term cure; needs a motivated family; usually offered over age 6; consider stopping after 14 consecutive dry nights, restart on relapse.
Or desmopressin: works fast, for camp or sleepovers; relapses more; limit evening fluids, none from 1 hour before the dose until 8 hours after (with oral dosing, hyponatremia is rare)		Alarm without improvement after 6 weeks: add or switch. Failure of both: tier 3
3Imipramine rarely (cardiotoxic in overdose); oxybutynin only with desmopressin or imipramine, not alone; urology referralTop rung
By diagnosis Under 5 – reassure; below the diagnostic age · Secondary – treat the cause; with no cause found, use the ladder · Desmopressin toxicity – headache, vomiting, seizure: hyponatremia; stop the drug; any neurologic symptoms: hypertonic saline; no symptoms: strict water restriction · Why the alarm lasts – conditioning survives stopping it; desmopressin's effect does not
Practice
  1. 7-year-old boy wets the bed nightly has never had a dry night dry by day since age 4, no urgency or dribbling Nothing tried yet; three siblings were dry by age 3 Afebrile · examination normal · urinalysis normal · glucose 82 mg/dL → Education, reassurance and motivational therapy → primary and monosymptomatic with a normal workup and nothing tried: start on the first rung; desmopressin skips a tier, and 2 pm is the wrong hour (limit the evening, drink well in the morning); siblings dry by 3 is a parental comparison, not a clue, while a family history of enuresis would support a maturational cause
  2. 7-year-old girl has started wetting the bed nightly was dry at night for 2 years no daytime urgency, dysuria or dribbling Otherwise healthy Afebrile · BP 98/60 mm Hg · examination normal → Secondary enuresis → 6 months or more of dryness before the wetting makes it secondary; a cause is sought, and the urinalysis comes first
  3. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for 3 weeks was dry at night for a year began after her parents separated Parents ask for counseling only Afebrile · BP 100/62 mm Hg · examination normal → Obtain the urinalysis first → a plausible stressor never replaces the urinalysis; one cheap test screens the organic causes, then address the stressor
  4. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for 2 weeks after a year dry drinking far more than usual tired, with 2 kg of weight loss No dysuria Afebrile · urinalysis: glucose 3+, ketones 1+, specific gravity 1.030 → New-onset diabetes mellitus → glucosuria with ketones in new wetting is type 1 diabetes until proven otherwise: serum glucose and HbA1c (hemoglobin A1c)
  5. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for a week after a year dry also has new daytime accidents No complaint of burning, and no stressor at home T 37.8 °C · urinalysis: leukocyte esterase positive, nitrites positive, no glucose → Urinary tract infection → a urinary infection can present as new wetting without dysuria in a child: urine culture, then treat
  6. 7-year-old girl has wet the bed for a month after a year dry drinks water through the night large pale voids No dysuria Afebrile · urinalysis: specific gravity 1.002, no glucose, no leukocytes → Diabetes insipidus → a very low specific gravity in new wetting points to diabetes insipidus: a water deprivation test, then the desmopressin response
  7. 6-year-old girl wets the bed nightly has daytime urgency and squats on her heel to hold urine stools hard, every 4 days Never dry at night Afebrile · examination: stool palpable in the left lower quadrant → Nonmonosymptomatic enuresis → daytime symptoms make it nonmonosymptomatic: bladder diary, and treat the constipation first, which is often curative
  8. 7-year-old girl still wets the bed most nights 8 months of reward charts and a voiding routine family distressed and keen to keep trying Dry by day; no constipation Afebrile · examination and urinalysis normal → Enuresis alarm → tier 1 has failed past 3 to 6 months in a bothered, motivated family: the alarm gives the most durable cure
  9. 6-year-old girl who has never been dry at night goes to sleepaway camp next week 4 months of reward charts have helped only a little Dry by day; no constipation; parents want a quick fix Afebrile · examination and urinalysis normal → Desmopressin → event-driven beats durable: desmopressin works within days; the alarm needs weeks; oxybutynin is not used alone
  10. 6-year-old girl taking desmopressin for wetting the bed has headache and vomiting had a seizure an hour ago drank several cups of juice at a party tonight Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg · serum sodium pending → Hyponatremia → desmopressin is an ADH (antidiuretic hormone) analog; free-water retention gives both its effect and its hyponatremic seizures: stop it; a seizure needs hypertonic saline
  11. 7-year-old boy wets the bed nightly and dribbles by day weak urinary stream dribbling after voiding Never dry at night; no constipation or urgency Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg · examination otherwise normal → Posterior urethral valves → a weak stream or dribbling in a boy is posterior urethral valves until proven otherwise: renal ultrasound and VCUG (voiding cystourethrogram)
  12. 6-year-old girl wets the bed nightly and now has daytime accidents a tuft of hair over the sacrum brisk lower-extremity reflexes Dry by day from age 3 until this year; no constipation Afebrile · BP 100/60 mm Hg · urinalysis normal → Spinal MRI → a sacral tuft with abnormal neurology is spinal dysraphism: spinal MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), not reassurance
  13. 4-year-old boy wets the bed most nights dry during the day, no urgency or constipation Parents are worried because his cousin was dry at 3 and ask about medicine Afebrile · growth normal · examination normal → Reassurance → enuresis is not diagnosed before age 5: reassure, since many children become dry without treatment
Pairs with Polyuria covers the next step once a very low specific gravity points to diabetes insipidus: the water deprivation test, what its result means, and the one child in whom it must not be done. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule

Set the tier by what has been done and for how long: a normal workup means no further testing, and no treatment yet means no escalation. Pick the lowest rung not yet exhausted.

Polyuria

the urine osmolality sorts it before any hormone is named · when the water deprivation test is indicated, and when it has already been answered

Source vignette Pt — 8 yo M, 2 months of excessive urination, drinking large volumes, irritable and restless; normal growth and milestones; no medications · Vitals — normal · Exam — physical and neurologic examination normal · Labs — Na 142, K 4.2, Cl 100, HCO₃ 24, BUN 30, creatinine 1.0, Ca 9.2, glucose 100 · Urine — specific gravity 1.001, no protein, blood, glucose or ketones; osmolality 120 mOsm/kg; 24-hour output 3.7 L · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned chest radiography, fractional excretion of sodium, brain MRI, an oral glucose tolerance test, renal ultrasonography and the water deprivation test
The decision point

Urine osmolality 120 is a water diuresis. The kidney is failing to concentrate, so solute diuresis and every test for it are excluded before any hormone is named. Then serum sodium 142, a normal value, makes the deprivation test necessary rather than redundant. A patient who drinks enough to hold his sodium normal has not yet shown the cause of the dilute urine. It may be a failure to make or to respond to vasopressin, or simply a normal kidney excreting a large water intake. Water deprivation is the manoeuvre that forces that distinction. It drives serum osmolality to the point where vasopressin secretion must be maximal, then shows whether the urine concentrates.

The two imaging studies are right tests in the wrong order. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) localises an established deficiency, and renal ultrasonography localises an established resistance. Both wait on a diagnosis that has not yet been made.

Defining criteria Polyuria — urine output above 3 L/day in an adult, above 2 L/day/m² in a child · Dilute urine — urine osmolality under 300 mOsm/kg, specific gravity under 1.006 · Concentrated urine — 600 mOsm/kg or above, meaning the kidney can concentrate and the diuresis is driven by solute · Deprivation endpoint — water withheld until serum sodium exceeds 145 and serum osmolality exceeds 295, the point at which vasopressin secretion should be maximal · Deprivation result — urine above 600 is primary polydipsia, urine still under 300 is an AVP disorder · Desmopressin result — urine osmolality rises in deficiency and stays low in resistance
FigureWhen water deprivation testing is indicatedshow

Redrawn from the published indications flowchart. Two deliberate changes: the concentrated-urine branch is labelled with what it means — solute diuresis — rather than only with what not to do, and the indicated branch carries its own interpretation, because the exam asks what the deprivation test showed about as often as it asks whether to order it.

Polyuria with dilute urine — the differentialand the two mimics that never need the test
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Primary polydipsiaDrinking drives the urine; psychiatric illness, or a drug that creates thirstSerum sodium low or low-normal; urine concentrates above 600 after deprivationNot excluded — this is one of the two the test is between
AVP deficiency (central DI)Impaired production or release: trauma, neurosurgery, craniopharyngioma or germinoma, hypophysitis, sarcoid or histiocytosis, a familial AVP mutation, pregnancyUrine stays dilute after deprivation, then rises with desmopressinNot excluded — the desmopressin step is what names it
AVP resistance (nephrogenic DI)The kidney ignores the hormone: AVPR2 or AQP2 mutation, hypercalcaemia, severe hypokalaemia, lithium, chronic tubulointerstitial diseaseUrine stays dilute after desmopressin too; in a child, usually hereditaryNot excluded — complete resistance leaves the osmolality unchanged, partial raises it slightly
Solute (osmotic) diuresisGlucosuria in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, or an osmotic diuretic such as mannitolPolyuria with a urine osmolality above 600; no deprivation test neededUrine osmolality 120, serum glucose 100, urine glucose negative
SIADHThe mirror image — water retained rather than lost; malignancy, CNS and pulmonary disease, drugsConcentrated urine with hyponatraemia, and no polyuriaDilute urine and a normal sodium — the opposite of the finding
Treatment, and the one child who must not be tested AVP deficiency — desmopressin in nearly all patients, oral, intranasal or parenteral; other agents are rarely needed · AVP resistance — remove the cause first (stop the lithium, correct the calcium and the potassium), then a thiazide with a low-sodium diet as first line; a low-protein diet cuts the solute load further; indomethacin is adjunct; amiloride is the one for lithium, because it blocks lithium entry into the collecting duct · Supervision — the deprivation test is performed in hospital in older children and adults, and is not performed in very young children, because the hypernatraemia it deliberately produces is dangerous in a child who cannot ask for water
Decision spine

1. Is the urine dilute or concentrated? Urine osmolality of 600 or above means the kidney concentrates, so look for solute, not for a hormone. 2. Is there glucose in the urine? Glucosuria explains the whole picture without a hormone. 3. Is the sodium above 145 with osmolality above 295? Then the AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder is already proven; go straight to desmopressin. 4. Is the sodium frankly low? Polyuria with hyponatraemia is primary polydipsia and needs no deprivation test. 5. Is the sodium normal? That is the only value that calls for the test. 6. After deprivation, did desmopressin raise the urine osmolality? If yes, it is deficiency, so image the brain. If no, it is resistance, so look at the kidney and the drug list.

Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo M, 2 months of polyuria and polydipsia, normal growth and neurologic examination, Na 142, glucose 100, urine specific gravity 1.001 and osmolality 120, output 3.7 L/day → Water deprivation test → a normal sodium is what leaves the diagnosis open
  2. 10 yo M with polyuria, serum Na 149 and serum osmolality 302, urine osmolality 110 → Desmopressin challenge → the deprivation endpoint has already been reached spontaneously
  3. 12 yo F whose urine osmolality stayed at 150 through deprivation and then rose to 620 after desmopressin → MRI of the brain → AVP deficiency needs its cause localized
  4. 9 yo M whose urine osmolality is 140 after deprivation and unchanged after desmopressin, with normal calcium, potassium and no medications → A thiazide with a low-sodium diet → first line once resistance is established and reversible causes are excluded
  5. 8 yo M for whom water deprivation testing has been chosen → Admit for supervised inpatient testing → the test works by producing hypernatremia deliberately
  6. 20-month-old with polyuria and a serum sodium of 148 → Water deprivation testing → severe hypernatremia in a child who cannot obtain water
  7. 14 yo M with polyuria and weight loss, urine osmolality 650, serum glucose 420, urine glucose 4+ → Osmotic diuresis → a concentrating kidney moves the problem to solute
  8. 30 yo F on an antipsychotic with polyuria, urine osmolality 90 and serum sodium 128 → Primary polydipsia → polyuria with hyponatremia needs no deprivation test
  9. Child with polyuria whose urine remains dilute when fluids are withheld → Desmopressin after water deprivation → the hormone itself is too unstable in a sample to measure routinely; serial urine osmolality is what is read
  10. 17 yo F with polyuria, constipation and a serum calcium of 12.8 → Hypercalcemia blunts the response to vasopressin → an acquired, reversible AVP resistance; at the collecting duct
Pearls A sodium above 145 makes the test redundant. A sodium below normal already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test. · Serum vasopressin is not measured: its half-life is short and it is unstable in the sample, so the desmopressin response is the assay · AVP deficiency — the current name for central diabetes insipidus · AVP resistance — the current name for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus · Hypothalamic injury kills the magnocellular cell bodies and the deficiency is permanent; injury below the infundibulum is usually transient, because those cell bodies survive · Pregnancy can produce a transient deficiency through placental vasopressinase; it resolves with delivery and returns in the next pregnancy · Lithium causes resistance by inhibiting aquaporin-2, and amiloride is the agent that blocks lithium's entry into the cell
Pairs with Part I Enuresis already links a very low specific gravity to diabetes insipidus and to this test. This brief covers what happens after the test is ordered. Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers the causes of AVP (arginine vasopressin) deficiency and the post-operative case where the diagnosis is not in doubt. Hypercalcemia covers the commonest acquired resistance. Ask: is the serum sodium high, low, or normal?
Transferable rule When the kidney is making dilute urine, the serum sodium shows whether a water deprivation test is still needed. A high sodium already confirms an AVP (arginine vasopressin) disorder; a low sodium already means primary polydipsia. Only a normal sodium calls for the test.
Sequencing trapMRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of the brain: the right study once a deficiency is proven, and nothing has been proven yet.
Sequencing trapRenal ultrasonography: it images the kidney, which is implicated only if desmopressin fails.
Salient decoyA BUN (blood urea nitrogen) of 30 pulls toward renal disease, but the creatinine is 1.0 and the defect is concentration, not filtration.
True-fact-wrong-slotFractional excretion of sodium: it measures perfusion, and perfusion is not in question here.
Salient decoyChest radiography: it looks for SIADH (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion), which produces concentrated urine and hyponatraemia, both opposite to the findings here.

Acute Kidney Injury in a Child

Gastroenteritis + ibuprofen · the labs assign the compartment

Source vignette Pt — 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea, taking ibuprofen · Labs — BUN/creatinine ratio 32:1, specific gravity 1.028, bland urinalysis · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned isotonic fluids with stopping the ibuprofen, furosemide and renal ultrasonography
The decision point

In any AKI (acute kidney injury), use the laboratory data to assign the injury compartment before using the drug to assign the mechanism. BUN/Cr >20:1 + specific gravity >1.020 + bland sediment = prerenal (BUN/Cr, blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio). In prerenal injury the kidneys are hypoperfused but intact and still concentrating. Ibuprofen acts hemodynamically. Hypovolemia makes GFR (glomerular filtration rate) prostaglandin-dependent, and COX (cyclooxygenase) inhibition constricts the afferent arteriole. The sediment and the 3-day timeline exclude drug-induced interstitial nephritis.

Defining criteria Prerenal pattern — BUN/Cr >20:1, specific gravity >1.020, bland urine sediment · ATN pattern — muddy brown casts, specific gravity ≈1.010, BUN/Cr <20:1 · Mechanism here — volume depletion makes GFR prostaglandin-dependent; NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole
Pediatric oliguria — cause by compartment
CauseIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Prerenal (NSAID + hypovolemia)vomiting/diarrhea; NSAID constricts the afferent arterioleBUN/Cr >20:1 + SG >1.020 + bland sediment
AINacute interstitial nephritisdrug hypersensitivity — NSAIDs after weeks, β-lactams, PPIsfever, rash, eosinophilia; WBCs/WBC casts
ATNacute tubular necrosisischemia or direct toxins (aminoglycosides, contrast)muddy brown casts; SG ≈1.010
HUS Can't missShiga toxin E coli, 5–10 days after bloody diarrheaschistocytes + thrombocytopenia + hematuria/proteinuria
Immune-complex GNPSGN, IgA nephropathypost-streptococcal (2–4 wk) or gross hematuria with URIhematuria + proteinuria ± low C3

TestOrderResultWhat it points to
BUN and creatinineFirstBUN/Cr ratio over 20:1Prerenal pattern
Urinalysis with specific gravityNextSpecific gravity over 1.020, bland sedimentIntact tubules still concentrating: prerenal
Urine microscopyBy branchMuddy brown casts, specific gravity about 1.010Acute tubular necrosis

Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo M, 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea on ibuprofen, BUN/Cr 32:1, SG 1.028, bland urinalysis → Isotonic fluids and stop the ibuprofen
  2. 5 yo F, bloody diarrhea 6 days ago, now pallor, petechiae, oliguria, schistocytes on smear → Hemolytic uremic syndrome → supportive care; avoid antibiotics and antimotility agents
  3. 68 yo F on naproxen for 3 weeks, fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts → Acute interstitial nephritis → stop the NSAID
  4. 60 yo M after septic hypotension, SG 1.010, muddy brown granular casts, BUN/Cr 14:1 → Ischemic acute tubular necrosis
  5. 74 yo M on lisinopril and furosemide who starts ibuprofen, creatinine rising from 1.1 to 2.0 → Discontinue the ibuprofen and give fluids → the "triple whammy" of ACE inhibitor, diuretic and NSAID
  6. 16 yo M, gross hematuria 2 days into a URI, normal C3 → IgA nephropathy → timing with the URI and normal complement decide
  7. 7 yo M, cola-colored urine and periorbital edema 2 weeks after pharyngitis, low C3 → Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis → supportive care
Pearls Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole. An NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug) and an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor drop GFR (glomerular filtration rate) from opposite ends. An NSAID plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin II receptor blocker) plus a diuretic is the "triple whammy" · FENa (fractional excretion of sodium) <1% supports prerenal but is unreliable after diuretics · the AIN (acute interstitial nephritis) triad is present in a minority; WBC (white blood cell) casts carry the diagnosis · PSGN (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis) vs IgA nephropathy is timing plus complement. PSGN comes 2–4 weeks after the infection with low C3; IgA nephropathy comes during the URI (upper respiratory infection) with normal C3.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers sorting by smear and coagulation studies when renal failure comes with a falling platelet count.
Transferable rule Read the ratio, then the specific gravity, then the sediment, and only then the drug. When a full chemistry panel is given, read it before answering.
Salient decoyDrug-induced interstitial nephritis: the named drug draws attention to it, but the timeline and the sediment are wrong.
True-fact-wrong-slotHUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome): gastroenteritis cues it, but it needs bloody diarrhea, schistocytes and an active sediment.

Proteinuria and Nephrotic Syndrome in a Child

protein on a routine dipstick in a well child · nephrotic or nephritic · the lesion, and the age-directed search for its causeIs the protein still there in a first-morning urine, are there red cells and casts, and how old is the patient?

Routine dipstickWhich lesionMembranousPractice
Bottom line
  • Orthostatic proteinuria: protein in urine made while upright, with a normal first-morning sample after lying down all night; most common in adolescent boys.
  • Transient proteinuria: protein during fever, exercise, stress, cold or dehydration that is gone on a repeat once the trigger passes.
  • Persistent proteinuria: a first-morning protein-to-creatinine ratio above 0.2 mg/mg (above 0.5 at 6 to 24 months), or protein with an abnormal urinalysis; it needs a renal workup.
  • Nephrotic syndrome: proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema and hyperlipidemia; blood pressure and glomerular filtration rate (GFR) usually normal, which is what separates it from nephritic disease.
  • Minimal change disease: about 80% of nephrotic syndrome in children, and the default in a young child.
  • Membranous nephropathy: subepithelial immune deposits with granular immunoglobulin G (IgG) and complement component 3 (C3) along the capillary loops; usually primary in adults, rare and usually secondary in children.
Protein on a routine dipstick in a well child

A well child with protein on a routine dipstick most likely has transient or orthostatic proteinuria; both are benign, so the first step is to repeat the urinalysis, before any imaging, steroids or biopsy. Protein with blood, hypertension or edema points to glomerular disease from the start: that child goes straight to the renal workup.

Management ladder: incidental proteinuria in a well child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Repeat the urine on a first-morning sample, after any fever or hard exercise has passed: dipstick, microscopy and protein-to-creatinine ratio; a bedtime sample alongside shows the orthostatic patternFirst-morning ratio above 0.2 mg/mg, or blood, casts, hypertension or edema
StopNormal first-morning sample (ratio 0.2 mg/mg or less, or 0.5 or less at 6 to 24 months, with a normal urinalysis): reassure and repeat a first-morning dipstick in 1 yearProtein returns on a first-morning sample
2Persistent proteinuria: complete blood count, electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen and creatinine; add albumin, complement or renal ultrasound as the history and exam directHematuria, hypertension, low complement, falling kidney function or signs of vasculitis
3Pediatric nephrology referral; renal biopsy is considered for those featuresTop rung

Orthostatic proteinuriaBenign upright leak; protein at bedtime, none on wakingCommon in adolescent boys; the timed repeat confirms it

Nephrotic syndromeMinimal change disease in a young child; edema, 3+ to 4+ protein, ratio above 2 mg/mg, low albuminNormal examination, no edema
