Scenario bank
  1. 32 yo F with low TSH, high T4, a diffuse goiter with a bruit and proptosis → Graves disease → high radioiodine uptake
  2. 68 yo F with low TSH, a multinodular gland and patchy uptake → Toxic multinodular goiter
  3. 40 yo F with a painful tender thyroid after a viral illness, low uptake and high ESR → Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
  4. 30 yo F, 3 months postpartum, painless thyrotoxicosis with low uptake → Postpartum thyroiditis
  5. 45 yo F with high TSH, low T4, positive TPO antibodies and a firm goiter → Hashimoto thyroiditis → levothyroxine
  6. 28 yo F, thyrotoxic with low uptake and a suppressed thyroglobulin → Factitious thyrotoxicosis
  7. 55 yo F, thyrotoxic with fever 40, agitation and atrial fibrillation → Thyroid storm → beta-blocker, thionamide, then iodine
  8. 32 yo F with low TSH, high T4, a small nontender goiter and no eye signs → Radioactive iodine uptake → splits a gland making hormone from one leaking it
  9. 55 yo F with Graves disease, fever 40, delirium and atrial fibrillation the day after surgery → Beta-blocker → then PTU, then iodine at least 1 hour later, then steroids
  10. 28 yo F with newly diagnosed Graves disease at 8 weeks of pregnancy → Propylthiouracil → PTU in the first trimester, methimazole after, radioactive iodine never
  11. 30 yo F, 3 months postpartum, with palpitations, a painless small goiter, positive TPO antibodies and low radioactive iodine uptake → Beta-blocker alone → nothing is being made, so antithyroid drugs are useless
Paired pearls Lid lag and stare occur in any thyrotoxicosis (sympathetic); proptosis and pretibial myxedema occur in Graves only · a hot nodule is almost never cancer; a cold nodule needs FNA (fine-needle aspiration) · in pregnancy, give PTU (propylthiouracil) in the first trimester and methimazole after; never give RAI (radioactive iodine) · nodule workup starts with TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone); if low, get an uptake scan; if normal or high, get an ultrasound, then FNA.
Pairs with Part I Congenital Hypothyroidism is the neonatal version, where the TSH direction and the neck locate the defect.

Levothyroxine Titration

Recheck timing after a dose change, and its exceptions

The decision point

TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) lags dose changes by 6–8 weeks. At 8 weeks, the TSH is reliable. A TSH of 9.5 at that point means the dose is genuinely inadequate, so increase it.

Defining criteria Recheck interval — TSH lags dose changes by 6–8 weeks; earlier values are untrustworthy · Subclinical hypothyroidism, treat if — TSH >10, TPO-positive, pregnant, or symptomatic · Pregnancy — requirement rises 30–50% immediately
The real trick set
  • Rechecked too soon (<6 wks after a change) → answer is "recheck in 6 weeks," not a dose change
  • TSH stays high despite escalating doses → adherence, then absorption: empty stomach; iron, calcium, PPIs, cholestyramine bind it; consider celiac disease
  • Pregnancy → requirement rises 30–50% immediately; increase as soon as pregnancy is confirmed
  • Elderly or CAD → start low, go slow (25–50 µg) to avoid angina or arrhythmia
  • Central hypothyroidism → titrate to free T4; TSH is the broken variable
  • Subclinical hypothyroidism (high TSH, normal T4) → treat if TSH >10, TPO+, pregnant, or symptomatic
Scenario bank
  1. 44 yo F on levothyroxine for 8 weeks with a TSH of 9.5 → Increase the dose
  2. 44 yo F rechecked at 3 weeks with a TSH of 8 → Make no change — TSH lags 6 to 8 weeks behind the dose
  3. 44 yo F on levothyroxine with a TSH of 0.05 and palpitations → Decrease the dose
  4. 44 yo F on levothyroxine who is newly pregnant → Increase the dose by about 30% and recheck
  5. 44 yo F taking levothyroxine together with her calcium supplement → Separate them by 4 hours
  6. 78 yo F with coronary disease starting levothyroxine → Start low and titrate slowly
Pairs with Part I Levothyroxine in Pregnancy covers the one setting where you adjust the dose before the TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) moves. Ask: is she pregnant right now?
Transferable rule Apply an exception to the standard titration rule only when its trigger condition is actually present. Otherwise, follow the standard rule.

Male Breast Enlargement

A known condition raises the prior probability but does not make the diagnosis

The decision point

A unilateral, firm, progressive, nontender subareolar mass has only features of cancer. Klinefelter syndrome is the risk factor, not the explanation. It increases male breast cancer risk 20–50× through a chronically elevated estrogen/androgen ratio. Always image first.

Gynecomastia vs male breast cancer
GynecomastiaCancer
LateralityUsually bilateralUnilateral
PositionConcentric to the nippleEccentric, off-center
TextureRubbery, mobileFirm, fixed
TendernessOften tender earlyNontender
MarginsBlends into fatWell-defined or spiculated, ± calcifications
Skin / nippleNormalDimpling, retraction, ulceration, discharge
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Diagnostic mammography, with or without ultrasoundFirstEccentric mass, spiculated or with calcificationsSuspicious for cancer: core biopsy; concentric subareolar tissue is gynecomastia
Core needle biopsyConfirmsInvasive ductal carcinoma, usually ER-positiveMale breast cancer, even with known Klinefelter syndrome
Genetic testingCauseBRCA2 variantOffered to every man with breast cancer
Testicular exam and scrotal ultrasoundBy branchTesticular mass in a man with gynecomastiaGerm cell or Leydig cell tumor
Serum hCG and AFPBy branchHigh hCGhCG-secreting germ cell tumor
Hormone levels before imaging a unilateral hard massSkipKlinefelter labs do not explain the massImage and biopsy first; Klinefelter is the risk factor
Scenario bank
  1. 62 yo M with a unilateral firm nontender subareolar mass and nipple retraction → Male breast cancer → mammography and biopsy
  2. 16 yo M with bilateral tender subareolar discs → Pubertal gynecomastia → reassurance
  3. 62 yo M with a breast mass and known Klinefelter syndrome → Klinefelter is the risk factor, not the explanation → biopsy anyway
  4. 55 yo M on spironolactone with bilateral tender gynecomastia → Drug-induced gynecomastia → change the agent
  5. 30 yo M with gynecomastia and a testicular mass → HCG-secreting germ cell tumor → ultrasound and tumor markers
  6. 62 yo M with soft symmetric fatty enlargement and no discrete mass → Pseudogynecomastia
Male breast cancer Risk factors: Klinefelter, BRCA2 (>BRCA1), family history, cirrhosis, obesity, chest radiation, exogenous estrogen · workup: mammography ± ultrasound → core biopsy · usually invasive ductal, >90% ER-positive → mastectomy + tamoxifen · every man with breast cancer gets genetic testing.
When it really is gynecomastia
  • Physiologic — three windows only: newborn, puberty (13–14, resolves in 1–2 yrs), elderly. Prepubertal gynecomastia is always pathologic.
  • Drugs (largest category): spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, finasteride, antipsychotics, digoxin, protease inhibitors, anabolic steroids, marijuana, alcohol
  • Cirrhosis · hyperthyroidism (↑SHBG → ↓free testosterone) · CKD · refeeding · hypogonadism
  • Tumors: hCG-secreting germ cell, Leydig/Sertoli, adrenal — gynecomastia + testicular mass → testicular ultrasound, hCG, AFP
Klinefelter 47,XXY; most common cause of primary hypogonadism and male infertility; tall with long limbs, small firm testes, sparse body hair; ↑FSH, ↑LH, ↓testosterone, ↑estradiol; seminiferous tubule hyalinization; also associated with mediastinal germ cell tumors, SLE, osteoporosis. Testosterone replacement does not restore fertility.
Transferable rule A known condition in the past medical history raises the prior probability but does not make the diagnosis. If the lesion behaves differently from the known disease, the known disease is the risk factor and something else is the diagnosis.
True-fact-wrong-slot

Hyperprolactinemia

Infer the drug from the illness; the prolactin level separates drug effect from prolactinoma

The decision point

When a patient with a known illness remains on an unnamed medication, identify the drug by two-step inference. First identify the drug class the illness requires. Then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. In psychosis, the class is an antipsychotic, and the member is the one with the highest prolactin liability.

The prolactin level separates drug-induced hyperprolactinemia from prolactinoma. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. In this patient, a level of 70 is in the drug-induced range and excludes prolactinoma without any imaging.

Mechanism & the antipsychotic ranking Dopamine is prolactin-inhibiting factor. D2 blockade in the tuberoinfundibular pathway removes that inhibition. Highest prolactin effect: risperidone and paliperidone, plus high-potency typicals such as haloperidol. Lowest: aripiprazole (a D2 partial agonist that can lower prolactin), quetiapine and clozapine. Aripiprazole is therefore the antipsychotic least likely to cause hyperprolactinemia and the one to switch to.
Hyperprolactinemia — causes by category
CategoryExamplesDiscriminator
PhysiologicPregnancy, nipple stimulation, stress, exercise, sleepPregnancy test first
DrugsAntipsychotics, metoclopramide, methyldopa, verapamil, SSRIs, opioids, estrogens, H2 blockersLevel 25–100
ProlactinomaMicro- or macroadenomaLevel >200; macroadenoma adds headache and bitemporal hemianopsia
Stalk effectAny sellar mass compressing the stalkModest elevation (<100) with a large mass on MRI
Hypothyroidism↑TRH stimulates lactotrophsTSH elevated
CKD, cirrhosisReduced clearance—
Workup order & two pituitary pearls For elevated prolactin, first get a pregnancy test, TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), medication review and renal function. Order an MRI pituitary only if all are negative. Do not image before excluding the cheap causes. Hook effect: a very large prolactinoma can saturate the assay and give a falsely low value; repeat with dilution. Prolactinoma is the pituitary tumor you treat medically. First-line treatment is dopamine agonists (cabergoline > bromocriptine), even for macroadenomas, because they shrink the tumor. Surgery is for medical failure, intolerance, or apoplexy.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Serum prolactinFirstOver 200, or 25 to 100Over 200 suggests prolactinoma; 25 to 100 fits drugs or other causes
Pregnancy testNextPositivePhysiologic hyperprolactinemia
TSHNextHigh TSHPrimary hypothyroidism: TRH drives prolactin; treat with levothyroxine
Medication review and renal functionNextAntipsychotic, metoclopramide or other culprit; or CKDDrug-induced or reduced clearance; no imaging needed
Pituitary MRIConfirmsAdenoma once the cheap causes are excludedProlactinoma if level over 200; large mass with level under 100 is stalk effect
Prolactin repeated on a diluted sampleBy branchLevel much higher after dilutionHook effect in a giant prolactinoma
Serum FSH and LHSkipLow from suppression, does not name the causeProlactin, pregnancy test and TSH come first
Scenario bank
  1. Prolactin >200 with bitemporal hemianopsia → Macroprolactinoma → MRI → cabergoline
  2. Patient needs continued antipsychotic coverage → Switch to aripiprazole or quetiapine
  3. Prolactin 60 + TSH 25 + fatigue and cold intolerance → Hypothyroidism → levothyroxine
  4. Prolactin 45 on metoclopramide for gastroparesis → Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia
  5. Large sellar mass with prolactin only 45 → Stalk effect → a non-functioning mass, not a prolactinoma
  6. Huge pituitary mass with a normal-looking prolactin → Hook effect → dilute and repeat
  7. Amenorrhea + galactorrhea + negative pregnancy test → Prolactin and TSH before imaging
  8. Years of untreated hyperprolactinemia → Hypogonadism → infertility and osteoporosis
  9. Woman on an SSRI with new galactorrhea → Modest drug-induced elevation
Pairs with Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers the localization once the trophic-hormone pattern points to the region.
Transferable rule When a lab value has a well-known range that separates two candidate causes, use the value rather than the history to decide between them.

Osteoporosis Screening and Treatment

who is screened early · T-score vs Z-score · when to treat · drug cautionsHas every risk factor been counted, and does each one point the way you assume?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Screen every woman at 65 with DEXA (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry). Run the risk-factor list before applying that default:

  • Exam shorthand (question banks): any one risk factor (prior fragility fracture, family history of hip fracture, smoking, low body weight, chronic glucocorticoids) means DEXA now; when DEXA now is an option, it is the scored answer. ⚠︎ The task force rule differs (next line).
  • USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) 2025: postmenopausal and under 65 with a risk factor such as low body weight, parental hip fracture, smoking or excess alcohol (the USPSTF also lists menopausal status), use a clinical risk tool such as FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool), then DEXA if the risk is raised; no fixed threshold. Men: evidence insufficient (not a recommendation against). Androgen deprivation therapy: the exam keys DEXA ⚠︎.

Obesity protects bone; low body weight (under 58 kg) is the risk factor. A hip or vertebral fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis without a scan.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria T-score – against a young adult peak; postmenopausal women and men 50 or older: -1.0 or above normal, -1.0 to -2.5 osteopenia, -2.5 or below osteoporosis · Z-score – against age- and sex-matched peers; premenopausal women, men under 50, children: -2.0 or below is below expected and needs a secondary-cause search · Clinical osteoporosis – a hip or vertebral fragility fracture, regardless of T-score
Risk factors Nonmodifiable – advanced age, postmenopausal (the entry condition for screening under 65, not a trigger by itself), low body weight, White or Asian, malabsorption, hypercortisolism, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic liver or kidney disease · Modifiable – smoking, excess alcohol, inactivity, glucocorticoids, anticonvulsants, proton pump inhibitors, low vitamin D or calcium, estrogen deficiency (premature menopause, oophorectomy), aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation therapy · Family history – FRAX asks about a parental hip fracture, not a sibling's; a sibling fracture counts only in the exam shorthand
Management and treatment
Management ladder: osteoporosis
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Smoking cessation, calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention; always concurrent, never enough alone once a risk factor existsAge 65: DEXA. Risk factor: DEXA now (exam) or risk tool first (USPSTF) ⚠︎
2Check calcium, 25-hydroxyvitamin D and creatinine; correct low vitamin D firstT-score -2.5 or below, hip or vertebral fragility fracture, or osteopenia with FRAX 20% major or 3% hip ⚠︎
3Bisphosphonate: upright with water, stay upright 30 minutes; drug holiday after about 5 years oral or 3 years intravenous if low riskVery high risk: an anabolic agent (teriparatide or abaloparatide)
Drug cautions Bisphosphonate – esophagitis; long-term osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture · Denosumab – rebound vertebral fractures if stopped abruptly; never simply discontinue · Romosozumab – cardiovascular boxed warning · Raloxifene – lowers breast cancer risk but raises venous thromboembolism · Height loss or kyphosis – vertebral imaging
Practice
  1. 55-year-old woman asks when to check her bones menopause at 50 body mass index 31 Never smoked; no fractures; no parental hip fracture BP 126/80 mm Hg · no glucocorticoid use → DEXA at 65 → no trigger on either list; menopause at a normal age with no risk factor waits until 65 (the USPSTF lists menopausal status; read here as the entry condition ⚠︎): DEXA at 65; obesity protects bone
  2. 56-year-old woman, postmenopausal, asks about bone screening weighs 52 kg smokes a pack a day; her mother fractured a hip No fractures of her own; no glucocorticoids BP 122/76 mm Hg · body mass index 19 → Run FRAX now → DEXA now (the exam shorthand) is not offered; of these, the USPSTF step is a clinical risk tool such as FRAX, then DEXA if risk is raised; no drug before a diagnosis
  3. 48-year-old woman has taken prednisone 10 mg daily for 4 months for sarcoidosis expects to continue for a year Still menstruating; no fractures BP 132/84 mm Hg · body mass index 26 → DEXA now, regardless of age → chronic glucocorticoids call for DEXA now, regardless of age
  4. 68-year-old woman has never had bone density testing feels well and walks daily no fractures, no falls Takes no medications; never smoked; asks whether she needs a scan BP 136/82 mm Hg · body mass index 24 → DEXA now → every woman 65 or older is screened with DEXA; a risk tool alone does not replace it
  5. 60-year-old woman has a DEXA T-score of -1.8 at the hip no fractures of her own her father fractured a hip at 78 Nonsmoker BP 128/80 mm Hg · calcium and vitamin D normal → Run FRAX → osteopenia: run FRAX and treat if the 10-year risk is 20% or more for a major fracture or 3% or more for a hip fracture
  6. 32-year-old woman has a fragility fracture of the wrist fell from standing height on a sidewalk regular periods; no glucocorticoids DEXA ordered to evaluate her bones BP 108/68 mm Hg · body mass index 18 · Z-score -2.3 → Z-score; secondary-cause workup → a premenopausal patient is read by the Z-score, and a score of -2.0 or below sends you after secondary causes: celiac disease, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, an eating disorder, amenorrhea (her regular periods argue against it)
  7. 57-year-old woman with a T-score of -2.7 is about to start alendronate rarely goes outdoors in winter drinks no milk No calcium or vitamin D level on file; no kidney disease BP 124/78 mm Hg · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → Check vitamin D and calcium first → check calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D first: an untreated vitamin D deficiency turns a bisphosphonate into hypocalcemia
  8. 64-year-old man starts androgen deprivation therapy for prostate cancer no fractures, no falls no glucocorticoids Asks whether his bones need checking BP 138/84 mm Hg · body mass index 27 · testosterone castrate level → Screen with DEXA now → androgen deprivation therapy (and an aromatase inhibitor in a woman) is a specific cause of bone loss; the exam keys baseline DEXA at its start, although USPSTF finds the evidence for screening men in general insufficient ⚠︎
  9. 57-year-old woman has back pain after bending to lift a laundry basket radiograph: vertebral compression fracture no trauma No DEXA on file BP 130/80 mm Hg · calcium, vitamin D and creatinine normal → Start a bisphosphonate now → a vertebral or hip fragility fracture diagnoses osteoporosis by itself: start a bisphosphonate now
  10. 57-year-old woman who smokes asks for hormone therapy to protect her bones T-score -2.6 no hot flashes or night sweats Smokes a pack a day BP 134/86 mm Hg · calcium, vitamin D and creatinine normal → Decline estrogen; start alendronate → avoid estrogen: smoking adds to its venous thromboembolism risk, and hormone therapy is not first-line for bone; raloxifene also raises venous thromboembolism risk and is not first-line; a bisphosphonate treats a T-score of -2.6
  11. 70-year-old woman on alendronate for 8 years has thigh pain aching for weeks, worse with walking no fall Radiograph: cortical thickening with a transverse line in the lateral femoral shaft Afebrile · calcium normal → Atypical femoral fracture → thigh pain after years of bisphosphonate is an atypical femoral fracture: image both femurs
Transferable rule

Run the risk-factor list first and apply the age default only when it comes back empty. Check that each variable points the way you assume: obesity raises cardiovascular, endometrial and sleep apnea risk but lowers osteoporosis risk.

Levothyroxine in Pregnancy

Hypothyroidism · the 30% rule · pregnancy-specific norms

The decision point

Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin. β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) shares an alpha subunit with TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and stimulates the TSH receptor. As a result, a normal pregnancy makes more thyroxine on its own. A patient with pre-existing hypothyroidism cannot up-regulate, so increase levothyroxine ~30% as soon as pregnancy is detected, even with a currently normal TSH. Do not wait for the TSH to rise.

Defining criteria Dose rule — increase levothyroxine ~30% at the time pregnancy is detected · Monitoring — TSH every 4 weeks using pregnancy-specific norms; follow total T4 within pregnancy norms · Mechanism — estrogen raises TBG, more hormone is needed to saturate binding sites; β-hCG cross-stimulates the TSH receptor
Thyroid labs in normal first-trimester pregnancy
HormoneChangeInterpretation
Total T4IncreasedPhysiologic — TBG excess binds more hormone
Free T4Unchanged or mildly increasedThe value to trust
TSHDecreasedβ-hCG cross-reactivity — not hyperthyroidism
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F on a stable levothyroxine dose, positive home pregnancy test, TSH 1.8 → Increase the dose ~30% now → recheck TSH in 4 weeks
  2. 30 yo G1P0 at 9 weeks, asymptomatic, total T4 elevated, free T4 high-normal, TSH 0.3 → Normal pregnancy physiology → no treatment
  3. 31 yo F, hypothyroid, dose increased at 6 weeks; when to reassess → TSH in 4 weeks → pregnancy-specific norms
  4. 27 yo F with hypothyroidism taking liothyronine, planning pregnancy → Switch to levothyroxine before conception → T3 has a short half-life with wide level swings
  5. Mechanism: why does the levothyroxine requirement rise in pregnancy → Estrogen-induced rise in thyroxine-binding globulin → more hormone needed to saturate binding sites
Pearls Untreated maternal hypothyroidism risks impaired fetal neurodevelopment, because the fetus depends on maternal T4 (thyroxine) early · a low TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) with high total T4 in the first trimester is physiology, not Graves; free T4 distinguishes the two · T3 (triiodothyronine), given as liothyronine, is never the right drug in pregnancy.
Pairs with Part I Levothyroxine Titration covers the same drug outside pregnancy, where you wait 6–8 weeks for the TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) to be trustworthy. At conception, act before the TSH moves. Ask: "is she pregnant right now?"
Transferable rule When physiology predictably outruns a fixed drug dose, adjust the dose pre-emptively. Do not recheck and react, although that approach is correct in every other setting.
Treat-the-numberAntithyroid workup for TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) 0.3 in early pregnancy: β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) cross-reactivity explains the low TSH.
True-fact-wrong-slot"Recheck in 6–8 weeks": correct as a titration rule, but pregnancy is the one setting where acting first is right.

Congenital Hypothyroidism

read TSH direction and the neck to locate the defect · is TSH high or low, and is there a goiter?

Source vignette Pt — 1 mo old, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since the first week, large tongue; no goiter described, maternal diet balanced with prenatal vitamins · Labs — TSH 110, T4 0.6 · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, iodine deficiency, panhypopituitarism and neonatal Graves disease
The decision point

TSH 110 with T4 0.6 (TSH, thyroid-stimulating hormone; T4, thyroxine) puts the lesion below the pituitary. The feedback loop is intact, so panhypopituitarism is excluded outright. Neonatal Graves gives a suppressed TSH with high T4, so it is excluded in the opposite direction. Among the primary causes, the exam is silent on goiter and the maternal history is clean (balanced diet, prenatal vitamins). This removes the tell of the two goitrous causes, dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency. The default remains: dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland arrested along the thyroglossal tract). The home birth is not a cause. It explains only why a screen-detected, asymptomatic diagnosis instead presented at one month, as maternal T4 washed out.

Defining criteria Primary congenital hypothyroidism — elevated TSH with low T4 (in-context: "increased TSH and decreased T4"); the diagnosis is made by newborn screening, not by symptoms · Prolonged (pathologic) neonatal jaundice — unconjugated jaundice persisting beyond age 2 weeks; it is the finding that converts a sleepy feeder into a thyroid workup
Pertinent positives & negatives TSH 110 with T4 0.6 — primary (glandular) failure; excludes panhypopituitarism and any central cause · Macroglossia + hoarse cry — mucopolysaccharide deposition in tongue and larynx; the specific soft-tissue signature of thyroid hormone deficiency, not of sepsis or a storage disease at this age · Direct bilirubin 0.7 of 8 — unconjugated; excludes biliary atresia and the cholestatic causes of the sick jaundiced neonate, and points at slowed gut motility plus reduced hepatic conjugating enzyme activity · No goiter described — argues against dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency, both of which enlarge the gland under TSH drive · Mother ate well and took prenatal vitamins; infant is formula-fed — iodine deficiency is excluded (formula is iodine-supplemented) · Normal tone with decreased activity — hypometabolism, not a neuromuscular disease; hypotonia may appear later and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis · Symptomatic at 1 month, not at birth — maternal T4 crossed the placenta and masked the deficit; this timing is characteristic of the disease
Congenital hypothyroidism — locating the defect
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Thyroid dysgenesis (agenesis/hypoplasia/ectopy)Failed formation or descent of the thyroid diverticulum from the pharyngeal floor along the thyroglossal duct; sporadic, no family historyHigh TSH, low T4, NO goiter, unremarkable maternal history; ectopic lingual tissue on scintigraphy— (the answer)
Dyshormonogenesis (thyroid peroxidase defect)Autosomal recessive enzyme block in organification; gland present but cannot make hormone, so TSH drive enlarges itGoiter in a hypothyroid newborn; consanguinity or affected sibling; deafness if Pendred ⚠︎No goiter, no family history; <15% of cases
Iodine deficiencyMaternal dietary lack in an endemic region; substrate, not machinery, is missing; goitrousMaternal diet/geography stated; goiter in mother and infantBalanced diet + prenatal vitamins; all formula contains iodine
Central (panhypopituitarism)Pituitary/hypothalamic failure; TSH is the deficient hormoneLOW or inappropriately normal TSH with low T4; midline defects (cleft lip/palate, single central incisor ⚠︎), micropenis, hypoglycemiaTSH 110 — the axis is intact and driving
Transplacental TSH-receptor stimulating antibodyMaternal Graves IgG crosses to the fetus → neonatal Graves, transient for weeks–months as antibody clears ⚠︎Low TSH, high T4, tachycardia, irritability, hyperphagia with poor weight gainDirection is inverted: TSH 110, T4 0.6, poor feeding and lethargy
Management, in one line A maternal blocking antibody against the TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) receptor is the rare counterpart of the stimulating antibody. It causes transient primary hypothyroidism with high TSH, indistinguishable from dysgenesis until it resolves ⚠︎.
Decision spine Is TSH high or low? — High → primary; the pituitary causes are excluded · Is T4 low? — Yes → hypothyroid, not a compensated or antibody-stimulated state · Is there a goiter? — No → not dyshormonogenesis, not iodine deficiency · Is there a maternal story? — Diet fine, no Graves → no acquired/transplacental cause · What's left is the default — dysgenesis, the most common cause; the home birth explains the delay in detection, not the disease

Newborn screen (heel prick at 24 to 48 hours)ScreenHigh TSH (some programs measure T4 first)Recall the infant for serum tests the same day
Serum TSH and free T4ConfirmsHigh TSH, low free T4; or low or normal TSH with low free T4Primary: start levothyroxine now. Central: cortisol before levothyroxine, then pituitary MRI
Thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide scanCause, optionalAbsent or ectopic gland; or an enlarged gland in placeDysgenesis; or dyshormonogenesis. Never delays treatment
Maternal TSH-receptor antibodiesBy branchPositive in a mother with autoimmune thyroid diseaseTransient hypothyroidism from blocking antibody
Serum thyroglobulin aloneSkipCannot stand in for imagingDoes not name the cause by itself
Scenario bank
  1. 3 wk M, home birth with no newborn screen, sleepy and feeding poorly, jaundiced since week 1, large tongue; TSH 140, T4 0.5 → Start levothyroxine now → Congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis
  2. 2 wk F with lethargy and poor feeding, firm anterior neck mass, older brother on levothyroxine, consanguineous parents; TSH 120, T4 0.4 → Dyshormonogenesis from a thyroid peroxidase defect → Levothyroxine; ultrasound shows an enlarged gland in place
  3. 5 d M with cleft palate, micropenis and fasting hypoglycemia; T4 low with TSH 0.8 → Central hypothyroidism from panhypopituitarism → Cortisol replacement before levothyroxine, then pituitary MRI
  4. 6 d F whose mother had Graves disease treated by thyroidectomy; infant tachycardic, irritable, poor weight gain despite hyperphagia; TSH undetectable, T4 elevated → Start a beta blocker and methimazole → Neonatal Graves disease from transplacental TSH receptor stimulating antibody
  5. Newborn screen at 48 hours returns TSH 60 with low T4; the infant is asymptomatic and feeding well on examination → Start levothyroxine without waiting for imaging → Congenital hypothyroidism
  6. 3 wk M with poor feeding and prolonged jaundice, TSH 90 and T4 0.6, no palpable goiter → Thyroid ultrasound or radionuclide uptake scan → An absent or ectopic gland confirms dysgenesis
  7. 4 wk F starting levothyroxine for congenital hypothyroidism; the parent asks how to administer the crushed tablet → Mixing the dose into soy formula or an iron containing supplement → Crush and give in a small volume of water or breast milk
  8. 5 wk M with congenital hypothyroidism, total bilirubin 9 with direct 0.6, stools normally pigmented → Slowed gastrointestinal motility with reduced hepatic bilirubin conjugating enzyme activity → Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that resolves with levothyroxine
  9. 2 mo M diagnosed at 6 weeks and on levothyroxine for 4 weeks; TSH 45 with low normal free T4, parents confirm daily dosing → Increase the levothyroxine dose and recheck in 4 weeks → Under replacement
  10. 3 mo F born where newborn screening is unavailable, never treated, now with developmental delay, poor linear growth and constipation; TSH 180, T4 0.3 → Start levothyroxine immediately → Untreated congenital hypothyroidism
Decoy note The home birth is not a cause. It explains the missed newborn screen and therefore the unusual symptomatic presentation. The balanced maternal diet with prenatal vitamins excludes iodine deficiency. Primigravida, age 24, unremarkable family history: none of these points to a cause, although the absent family history modestly argues against a recessive enzyme defect.
Pearls High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), low T4 (thyroxine) and no goiter mean dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. · Symptom onset at weeks to months, not at birth, is characteristic of congenital hypothyroidism. Placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. · Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age calls for considering thyroid disease and galactosemia; conjugated jaundice at any age calls for considering a biliary cause. · Macroglossia plus hoarse cry is mucopolysaccharide deposition in hypothyroid soft tissue. It is distinct from Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia ⚠︎). · Treat on the screening result. Imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks. There are no deficits when treatment begins in the neonatal period. · A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn points to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem; dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge. · In central hypothyroidism, give cortisol before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis ⚠︎.
Pairs with Jaundice in a Newborn shares the complaint of a jaundiced newborn with an abnormal screen. Ask: is the hyperbilirubinemia conjugated, and is the infant ill or merely slow? Thyroid Disease in an Adult and Levothyroxine Titration cover the adult version of the same TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) direction logic. They also cover the dosing loop that this brief only points at. Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the other causes of low tone in infancy and the yearly TSH in Down syndrome.
Transferable rule In any hormone deficiency, the trophic hormone's direction locates the lesion. High TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) puts it in the gland; low TSH puts it in the pituitary. Within the gland, the presence or absence of an organ (goiter or none) separates a machinery defect from a formation defect.
Class-vs-memberDefective thyroid peroxidase activity: Under 15% of cases and it almost always produces a goiter, which this exam does not describe; no family history in a recessive condition
True-fact-wrong-slotTransplacental TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) receptor–stimulating antibody: It causes neonatal Graves, with suppressed TSH, high T4 (thyroxine), tachycardia and hyperphagia. Every value and symptom here is inverted
Salient decoyIodine deficiency, endemic goiter: The balanced diet plus prenatal vitamins excludes it, and all formula contains iodine
Test-overrides-findingsPanhypopituitarism: TSH 110 proves the pituitary is working; central disease gives a low or inappropriately normal TSH plus midline defects and micropenis

Inherited Tumor Syndromes

Identify the syndrome from the visible lesion and the organ pattern · What exactly is the retinal lesion, and what color is the skin patch?

Source vignette Pt — 16 yo M, bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, mother had an adrenal tumor resected, one light brown facial patch without freckling · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis type 1 and Sturge-Weber syndrome
The decision point

Bilateral retinal hemangioblastoma points to von Hippel-Lindau, because no other listed syndrome produces one. NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) gives optic gliomas and Lisch nodules. MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) gives conjunctival and corneal neuromas. Sturge-Weber gives a leptomeningeal and choroidal vascular malformation. Li-Fraumeni gives sarcomas with no characteristic eye finding. The mother's resected adrenal tumor reads as a pheochromocytoma transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion. Hemangioblastoma plus adrenal medullary tumor is the von Hippel-Lindau organ pattern, with clear cell renal carcinoma the third member. A single light brown facial macule is a normal café-au-lait spot. It is not the multiple macules of NF1 and not a red-purple port-wine stain.

Consider a teenager found confused after an unwitnessed fall. A fibroma growing from under a toenail and calcified nodules lining the lateral ventricles on CT (computed tomography) indicate tuberous sclerosis complex. The fall was a seizure, and the nodules are subependymal hamartomas. The nail lesion is a periungual fibroma, which appears in adolescence. NF1 puts neurofibromas on the trunk and a glioma on the optic nerve. Ataxia-telangiectasia starts with ataxia in early childhood. The nail-bed sign of endocarditis is a splinter hemorrhage, not a fibroma.

Defining criteria The VHL testing gate — any patient with a retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma undergoes VHL gene testing, family history or not · The café-au-lait gate — an isolated macule is normal; six or more with regular borders plus axillary freckling is NF1 (each macule over 5 mm before puberty or over 15 mm after puberty); a few large macules with irregular borders, often segmental and respecting the midline, without freckling is McCune-Albright ⚠︎. Count, border, distribution and freckling are four separate criteria, and the exam varies whichever one is not being checked · Patch color as a criterion — Sturge-Weber's lesion is a red-purple vascular port-wine stain; a light brown patch is pigmented and belongs to a different family
Pertinent positives & negatives Bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas — essentially syndrome-defining; retinal hemangioblastoma may be the first neoplasm of VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) and by itself triggers gene testing · Mother's adrenal tumor removed — pheochromocytoma in a first-degree relative; autosomal dominant transmission, and the second organ of the VHL pattern · A single light brown 4-cm patch — one café-au-lait macule, a normal finding, lacking the multiplicity of NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and the color of Sturge-Weber · Age 16 with painless progressive blurring — VHL can present at any age but usually presents in early adulthood. Vision falls from retinal edema and distortion · BP 110/72 and an otherwise normal examination — no clinically active pheochromocytoma today, which does not exclude one and is why surveillance is needed
Inherited tumor syndromes — the differential
SyndromeIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Von Hippel-LindauAutosomal dominant loss of the VHL tumor suppressor on chromosome 3; tumors of retina, CNS, adrenal medulla and kidneyRetinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pheochromocytoma, clear cell renal carcinoma— (the answer)
Neurofibromatosis type 1Autosomal dominant neurocutaneous disorder of skin, nerve and eyeMultiple café-au-lait macules with axillary freckling; cutaneous neurofibromas on the trunk; optic glioma and Lisch nodules; seizures in someOne macule only, which is normal; the retinal lesion is a hemangioblastoma
Sturge-Weber syndromeLeptomeningeal and ocular capillary-venous malformationRed-purple port-wine stain, seizures, glaucoma ⚠︎The patch is light brown and pigmented, not vascular
Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2BRET proto-oncogene; medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytomaConjunctival or corneal neuromas, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus ⚠︎Eye lesion is a hemangioblastoma; no thyroid disease
Li-Fraumeni syndromeAutosomal dominant TP53 loss; many tumor types across a young familySoft tissue sarcoma, early breast cancer, adrenocortical carcinoma ⚠︎; no characteristic eye or skin lesionNo hemangioblastoma belongs to it
Tuberous sclerosis complexAutosomal dominant TSC1 or TSC2 mutation, inherited or new; benign hamartomas of brain, eye, skin, heart and kidney; epilepsy in most, intellectual disability and autismAsh-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas; calcified subependymal nodules on CT; cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipomaNo skin hamartoma here, and its brain lesions are nodules and tubers, not hemangioblastomas
Neurofibromatosis type 2Autosomal dominant tumors of nerve sheath and meningesBilateral vestibular schwannomas ⚠︎The eighth nerve, not the retina
Management, in one line Confirm with VHL gene testing (VHL: von Hippel-Lindau). Then begin lifelong surveillance: retinal examination, plasma or urine metanephrines, MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen. Resect tumors as they appear. For the retinal lesions, laser therapy is the preferred treatment.
Tuberous sclerosis complex Skin — hypopigmented ash-leaf macules, facial angiofibromas over the cheeks and nose, a shagreen patch (orange-peel plaque on the lower back), and periungual fibromas, which appear in adolescence or adulthood · Brain — subependymal nodules, calcified on CT along the ventricles; cortical tubers, best seen on MRI; a nodule can grow into a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma that obstructs CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) flow and causes hydrocephalus, which needs resection · Seizures — epilepsy in most, often infantile spasms, but the first seizure can come at any age, adolescence included; intellectual disability, autism and behavior disorders · Heart and kidney — cardiac rhabdomyoma; renal angiomyolipoma · Surveillance — skin and eye exams, serial MRI of brain and kidneys, baseline echocardiogram and serial ECGs (electrocardiograms), baseline EEG (electroencephalogram), and neuropsychiatric screening · Not tuberous sclerosis — NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1): café-au-lait macules, trunk neurofibromas, optic glioma; VHL (von Hippel-Lindau): cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas; ataxia-telangiectasia: ataxia from early childhood, poorly coordinated eye movements, conjunctival telangiectasias; endocarditis: fever, murmur and splinter hemorrhages
Neurofibromatosis type 1: tumor risk Optic nerve glioma — the most common brain tumor in neurofibromatosis type 1; usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma of one or both optic nerves or the chiasm · Presentation — insidious vision loss, proptosis and optic atrophy · Eye surveillance — children with neurofibromatosis type 1 need an eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18 · Pheochromocytoma — risk also raised · No established link — medulloblastoma, craniopharyngioma, and arteriovenous malformation, which belongs to Wyburn-Mason syndrome
Decision spine Name the retinal lesion exactly. — Hemangioblastoma → VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) · If it is a different eye lesion: — optic glioma or Lisch nodules point to NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1). Conjunctival neuromas point to MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B). Glaucoma with a choroidal malformation points to Sturge-Weber · Read the skin patch's color. — Light brown pigmented = café-au-lait; red-purple vascular = port-wine · Count the skin lesions. — One café-au-lait macule is normal; multiple plus axillary freckling is NF1 · Read the family's tumor for its organ. — Adrenal medulla with kidney and CNS (central nervous system) points to VHL. Adrenal medulla with thyroid points to MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2)
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Dilated retinal examinationFirstRetinal hemangioblastomaVon Hippel-Lindau suspected, with or without a family history
VHL gene testingConfirmsPathogenic VHL variantVHL disease; offer testing to first-degree relatives now
Plasma or urine metanephrinesStagingElevated metanephrinesPheochromocytoma: alpha blockade before beta blockade, then resection
MRI of brain and spineStagingCerebellar or spinal hemangioblastomaCNS tumors of VHL
MRI of abdomenStagingEnhancing renal massClear cell carcinoma: nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy
Noncontrast head CT after a first seizureBy branchCalcified subependymal nodules along the ventriclesTuberous sclerosis complex; brain MRI shows cortical tubers
Whole-body PET imagingSkipAdds nothing to gene testing and targeted MRIVHL testing follows the lesion; surveillance covers the four organs
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M with bilateral retinal hemangioblastomas, a mother who had an adrenal tumor resected, and one light brown facial patch → Von Hippel-Lindau disease → The eye lesion names the syndrome
  2. 34 yo M with a solitary cerebellar hemangioblastoma and no family history of tumors → VHL gene testing → Testing follows the lesion, not the pedigree
  3. Patient with newly confirmed von Hippel-Lindau disease → Retinal, adrenal, neuraxis and abdominal surveillance→ retinal examination, plasma metanephrines, MRI of brain and spine, and MRI of abdomen; The four organs the syndrome occupies
  4. 22 yo F newly diagnosed with von Hippel-Lindau disease who has an asymptomatic 15-year-old brother → Offer him VHL gene testing now → each first-degree relative carries a 50% risk, and surveillance starts in childhood
  5. 40 yo M with von Hippel-Lindau disease and a 3 cm enhancing renal mass → Nephron-sparing partial nephrectomy → Clear cell carcinoma, with more lesions expected
  6. 28 yo F with von Hippel-Lindau disease, an adrenal mass and elevated metanephrines, scheduled for resection → Alpha blockade started before any beta blockade → Unopposed alpha stimulation otherwise
  7. 4-month-old with a red-purple patch over the V1 distribution and a focal seizure → Brain MRI and ophthalmology referral→ for a leptomeningeal angioma and for glaucoma screening; Sturge-Weber syndrome
  8. 7-year-old with 8 cafe-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, Lisch nodules and an optic glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1 → Multiplicity is the criterion, not presence
  9. 24-year-old with medullary thyroid carcinoma, a pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas of the lips and a marfanoid habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B → Neuromas rather than hemangioblastomas
  10. The molecular defect underlying von Hippel-Lindau disease → Loss of a tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3 → Autosomal dominant inheritance
  11. 9 year old with painless firm rubbery tongue nodules, marfanoid habitus and long fingers → Medullary thyroid carcinoma → MEN2B — aggressive and early; prophylactic thyroidectomy often in infancy
  12. Child with newly diagnosed MEN2B; what else must be evaluated → Plasma fractionated metanephrines → About half have pheochromocytoma
  13. Adult with primary hyperparathyroidism, a prolactinoma and a gastrinoma → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 → No marfanoid habitus and no mucosal neuromas
  14. Patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia, with a normal habitus → Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A → Parathyroid rather than neuromas separates 2A from 2B
  15. Child with perioral pigmented macules and recurrent intussusception → Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → Pigmented macules, not neuromas — the risk is polyps and cancer
  16. Adult with recurrent epistaxis and ruby mucosal papules that blanch with pressure → Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia → Telangiectasias blanch; neuromas do not
  17. Newborn with bilateral absence of the iris, hypospadias and an undescended left testis → Wilms tumor → WAGR — serial abdominal ultrasonography from infancy
  18. Newborn with aniridia and genitourinary anomalies; the underlying lesion → An 11p13 deletion → WAGR: Wilms, Aniridia, Genitourinary, Range of developmental delay
  19. Why Wilms tumor in WAGR differs from isolated Wilms tumor → It is often bilateral and presents earlier → Isolated disease is usually unilateral at age 2 to 5
  20. Macrosomic newborn with macroglossia and hemihyperplasia at risk for embryonal tumors → Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome → Overgrowth rather than aniridia
  21. 17 yo M found confused at the bottom of the stairs after an unwitnessed fall, most likely a seizure; 2-cm forehead contusion; a firm flesh-colored fibroma growing from beneath a toenail; head CT shows calcified nodules along the walls of the lateral ventricles → Tuberous sclerosis complex → Periungual fibroma plus calcified subependymal nodules; surveillance of brain, kidney, heart, eyes and skin
  22. 8 yo F newly diagnosed with tuberous sclerosis complex after a first seizure, with ash-leaf macules and facial angiofibromas; normal blood pressure and development so far → Brain and kidney MRI, echocardiogram and ECG, EEG, and skin and eye exams → Surveillance follows the organs the hamartomas occupy, plus neuropsychiatric screening
  23. Asymptomatic 17 yo M at a sports physical with about 10 light brown macules 0.6 to 2 cm across the trunk and limbs and freckling in both axillae → Optic nerve glioma → Neurofibromatosis type 1; eye examination yearly until age 8, then every 2 years until 18
  24. 6-year-old with 7 café-au-lait macules over 5 mm, inguinal freckling, normal vision and a normal examination otherwise → Yearly eye examination → Neurofibromatosis type 1; screens for optic nerve glioma
  25. 9-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 and months of painless vision loss in one eye, mild proptosis and a pale optic disc → Optic nerve glioma → Usually a low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma
Decoy note The skin patch drew nearly two in five readers: 20% chose NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) and 18% chose Sturge-Weber. A solitary café-au-lait macule is normal, so this most conspicuous physical finding does not discriminate. The mother's adrenal tumor supplies both the inheritance pattern and the second organ. The normal blood pressure does not help the diagnosis, but it indicates that no pheochromocytoma is active yet.
Pearls Retinal hemangioblastoma is von Hippel-Lindau until gene testing says otherwise; the pheochromocytoma and clear cell renal carcinoma follow. · A retinal or cerebellar hemangioblastoma by itself warrants referral to genetics. VHL (von Hippel-Lindau) testing follows the lesion, with or without a family history. · Eye lesions by syndrome: hemangioblastoma → VHL · optic glioma with Lisch nodules → NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1) · conjunctival and corneal neuromas → MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B) · choroidal malformation with glaucoma → Sturge-Weber. · Read a patch's color, not merely its presence. Light brown pigmented is café-au-lait, red-purple vascular is port-wine, and they belong to different syndromes. · VHL surveillance covers its organs: retina, brain and spine, adrenal medulla and kidney. The follow-up is therefore an eye exam, metanephrines, and two MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans. · Any pheochromocytoma in a young patient or with a family history is syndromic until proven otherwise. The syndromes are VHL, MEN2 (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2), NF1, or a hereditary paraganglioma gene ⚠︎. · Before resecting a pheochromocytoma, alpha blockade precedes beta blockade; reversing the order leaves alpha stimulation unopposed ⚠︎. · How NBME framed it: a well 17-year-old at a sports physical has about 10 light brown macules and axillary freckling, and the syndrome is never named. After puberty only macules over 15 mm count, so the axillary freckling supplies the second criterion. The lead-in asks which lesion carries a raised risk compared with the general population.
Pairs with Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers pheochromocytoma from the blood-pressure side, reaching the same tumor from a different complaint. Ask: is the pheochromocytoma isolated, or is it one organ of a syndrome? Related conditions without their own brief: the neurocutaneous syndromes as a set, namely NF1 (neurofibromatosis type 1), NF2 (neurofibromatosis type 2), tuberous sclerosis and Sturge-Weber. Part I Puberty covers the border and distribution attributes of café-au-lait macules. Part II Abdominal Mass in a Young Child covers the mass itself. Ask: is it within the kidney, and is the child older than 2? Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers ataxia-telangiectasia and its infections. Ask: is the skin lesion vascular, or a fibrous tumor? Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers optic pathway glioma and craniopharyngioma as masses. Ask: does the visual field loss come from the optic nerve or from the sella?
Transferable rule When a visible lesion identifies a syndrome, the lesion's category is shared across syndromes, but its identity is not. Name the tissue and the color before matching. The most conspicuous physical finding may be the one that does not discriminate.
Unchecked attributeNeurofibromatosis type 1, for two café-au-lait macules: Two macules sit between the isolated-is-normal rule and the six of NF1. A count rule alone therefore lands on NF1. The border, the segmental distribution and the absent freckling all argue against it.
Salient decoyNeurofibromatosis type 1: One macule is normal; NF1 requires multiple with axillary freckling, and its eye lesions are optic glioma and Lisch nodules, never a hemangioblastoma
Unchecked attributeSturge-Weber syndrome: The patch is the wrong kind; port-wine stains are red-purple vascular malformations, and this one is light brown and pigmented
True-fact-wrong-slotLi-Fraumeni syndrome: TP53 disease is sarcomas, early breast and adrenocortical carcinoma, with no characteristic eye or skin lesion and no hemangioblastoma
Class-vs-memberMultiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B: Its eye findings are conjunctival and corneal neuromas, and it brings medullary thyroid carcinoma, which nobody in this stem has
Class-vs-memberNeurofibromatosis type 1, for the teenager with the toenail fibroma: Also autosomal dominant with seizures, but its skin tumors are neurofibromas on the trunk and its brain tumor is an optic glioma; calcified subependymal nodules belong to tuberous sclerosis
Unchecked attributeAtaxia-telangiectasia: Autosomal recessive, with ataxia from early childhood and vascular telangiectasias rather than a fibrous nail tumor, and no ventricular nodules
Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: The nail finding pulls toward it, but endocarditis gives splinter hemorrhages with fever and a murmur, not a firm periungual fibroma
Salient decoyMedulloblastoma, for the teenager with 10 café-au-lait macules: The most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, with raised intracranial pressure and ataxia, but neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotCraniopharyngioma: A Rathke pouch remnant that causes bitemporal field loss; neurofibromatosis type 1 does not raise its risk
True-fact-wrong-slotArteriovenous malformation: Retinal and midbrain arteriovenous malformations belong to Wyburn-Mason syndrome, not neurofibromatosis type 1
True-fact-wrong-slotCerebral aneurysm: An adult cause of intracranial hemorrhage; the tumor this skin pattern predicts is an optic nerve glioma

Puberty

normal staging: sexual maturity rating (SMR) · early puberty: central or peripheral · virilization in a girlIs the stage right for the age, and if not, which hormones are on board, from where?

StagingEarly pubertyVirilizationPractice
Bottom line

Stage breast and hair separately; a stage wrong for the age needs a workup.

  • Precocious puberty: secondary sexual characteristics before 8 in girls or 9 in boys.
  • Delayed puberty: no breast development by 13, or no testicular enlargement by 14.
  • Central, GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) dependent: the whole axis turns on; consonant, progressive, LH (luteinizing hormone) pubertal.
  • Peripheral, GnRH-independent: sex hormone from gonad, adrenal or an exogenous source.
  • Virilization: clitoral enlargement in a girl; normal adrenarche never causes it.

Breast tissue means estrogen; an androgen-only source gives hair, acne and odor without breasts.

Staging and normal timing
Sexual maturity rating: the phrase that decides each stage
StageBreastPubic hair
1Papilla elevation onlyNone, or vellus only
2Bud: small mound under a widening areolaSparse, straight, lightly pigmented
3Beyond the areola, one contourDarker, coarser, curled; sparse over the pubis
4Areola and papilla form a second moundAdult quality across the pubis, sparing the medial thighs
5Areola recedes; papilla projects aloneAdult quantity, spreads to the medial thighs
Defining criteria One number – only when breast and hair agree · Discordant stages – a finding; hair well ahead of breast suggests an adrenal source · First sign – thelarche in girls; testes 4 mL or more in boys · Peak height velocity – SMR 2 to 3 in girls, SMR 4 in boys · Menarche – SMR 4, about 2 to 3 years after thelarche, about 6 months after peak velocity
Early puberty
McCune-Albright syndrome Triad – peripheral precocious puberty, irregular café-au-lait macules, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (recurrent fractures) · Mechanism – a somatic mosaic activating GNAS (the G protein alpha-s gene) mutation keeps a G protein switched on; any tissue carrying it secretes autonomously, so thyrotoxicosis, acromegaly or Cushing syndrome can accompany or replace the precocity · Family history – silent; postzygotic, not inherited; no recurrence risk ⚠︎
Read a pigmented patch: number, border, distribution, color
SyndromeThe skin
McCune-AlbrightFew, large, irregular; often segmental, respecting the midline ⚠︎; no freckling
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)Six or more, smooth, axillary freckling; precocity via optic glioma
Tuberous sclerosisHypopigmented ash-leaf macules, shagreen patch; seizures ⚠︎
Sturge-Weber; Peutz-JeghersRed-purple port-wine stain; 1 to 5 mm perioral macules; no precocity
Management Central – GnRH agonist, because the axis drives it ⚠︎ · Peripheral – treat the source; a GnRH agonist does nothing · McCune-Albright – aromatase inhibitor or estrogen-receptor blockade ⚠︎
Virilization in a girl: which source?
The markers DHEAS – almost only from the adrenal zona reticularis; urine 17-ketosteroids rise with it · Testosterone – mostly ovarian in a girl · High DHEAS, normal testosterone, normal pelvic ultrasound – adrenal; far above range in a child is a tumor until proven otherwise; many pediatric virilizing adrenal tumors are carcinomas · High 17-hydroxyprogesterone – nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the commoner adrenal cause
Practice
  1. 6-year-old girl is evaluated for breast budding and pubic hair two large hyperpigmented macules with irregular borders confined to the left chest and back, without freckling Long-bone fractures at ages 4 and 5 Afebrile · no headache, emesis or visual change → McCune-Albright syndrome → peripheral precocity, few irregular segmental macules and recurrent fractures (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia) are the triad; only two macules, irregular borders and no freckling argue against neurofibromatosis type 1 (six or more smooth macules, usually with freckling), and breast budding excludes an androgen-only adrenal tumor
  2. 6-year-old girl has breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced to 9 years Skin entirely normal; no headache, emesis or visual change Afebrile · BP 100/62 mm Hg → Measure basal LH with GnRH-stimulation testing if not diagnostic → consonant, progressive puberty with an advanced bone age suggests the axis is on, and normal skin argues against McCune-Albright: a pubertal basal LH confirms it, and a GnRH stimulation test settles a nondiagnostic level; waiting misses progressive puberty, and brain imaging follows confirmation
  3. 5-year-old girl was diagnosed with central precocious puberty this week LH rose after GnRH stimulation bone age advanced No headache, emesis or visual change; parents ask about next steps Afebrile · neurologic examination normal → Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain → younger onset raises the risk of a central nervous system lesion: image the brain for confirmed central puberty, especially in young girls and most boys, before treating or reassuring
  4. 2-year-old girl has breast budding noticed 3 months ago no pubic or axillary hair growth velocity normal Bone age matches her chronological age Afebrile · height and weight at the 50th percentile → Reassurance and observation → isolated breast development with normal growth velocity and a bone age matching age is premature thelarche: observe, without hormone testing or imaging
  5. 7-year-old girl has 6 months of pubic and axillary hair and body odor no breast development growth velocity normal No clitoral enlargement; bone age matches age Afebrile · height at the 60th percentile → Reassurance with interval follow-up → isolated hair and odor with normal growth and bone age is premature adrenarche: reassure and follow; nothing points to the axis or the brain, and clitoral enlargement or fast growth would change that
  6. 6-year-old girl has 5 months of pubic hair and severe acne clitoral enlargement linear growth rapidly accelerating No breast budding; no hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 102/64 mm Hg → Measure 17-hydroxyprogesterone → clitoral enlargement is virilization, which normal adrenarche never causes; it points to an adrenal source, not the axis, so neither a GnRH agonist nor reassurance fits; congenital adrenal hyperplasia shows a high 17-hydroxyprogesterone
  7. 7-year-old boy has pubic hair and acne testes remain prepubertal in size growing faster than his classmates No headache or visual change; no hormone creams at home Afebrile · BP 104/66 mm Hg → Evaluate for a peripheral androgen source → androgen signs with small testes mean the testes are not being driven: a peripheral source, which a GnRH agonist cannot suppress; bilateral testicular enlargement would indicate a central cause
  8. 4-year-old girl is evaluated after a femoral fracture one large hyperpigmented macule with an irregular border free thyroxine high, thyroid-stimulating hormone suppressed No goiter or eye findings noted Afebrile · HR 128/min → McCune-Albright syndrome → the mutation is organ-agnostic: any endocrine organ carrying it can secrete autonomously, here the thyroid; Graves disease would not explain the irregular macule and fracture, and neurofibromatosis macules are six or more and smooth, usually with freckling
  9. 7-year-old girl has 6 months of breast development and pubic hair height crossing percentiles upward bone age advanced Skin normal; no headache or visual change Afebrile · BP 100/60 mm Hg → LH response to GnRH stimulation → a rise in LH after GnRH stimulation means the axis is driving it (central); a flat LH points to a peripheral source; estradiol alone cannot tell which axis, and bone age shows progression, not its source
  10. 7-year-old girl was diagnosed with McCune-Albright syndrome last year breast development progressing basal LH prepubertal; one large irregular macule over the right flank Parents ask about treatment for the early puberty Afebrile · bone age advanced → GnRH agonist → the axis is not the driver, so a GnRH agonist does nothing; treat the source, here with aromatase inhibitors or estrogen-receptor blockade ⚠︎
  11. 6-year-old girl has 4 months of pubic hair, acne and clitoral enlargement no breast development 17-hydroxyprogesterone normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate markedly high, testosterone normal No hormone creams or medications at home Afebrile · BP 108/70 mm Hg → Computed tomography of the adrenal glands → a markedly high adrenal androgen with normal testosterone is an adrenal tumor until proven otherwise: image the adrenals, not the brain; normal testosterone points away from the ovary; histology, not labs, separates adenoma from carcinoma
  12. 12-year-old girl is seen for a well visit breast tissue extends beyond the areola without a separate contour pubic hair curled, spread partially across the pubis Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile → Stage 3 → one contour is 3, a second mound is 4; curled hair is past 2, partial spread is below 4; both agree, so one number is acceptable, and it is normal for age
  13. 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit areola and papilla form a secondary mound above the breast contour adult-type pubic hair that spares the medial thighs Afebrile · height at the 40th percentile → Stage 4 → a second mound is the stage 4 tell; stage 5 needs the areola to recede and hair on the thighs; menarche typically occurs at this stage
  14. 10-year-old girl is seen for a well visit small mound of breast beneath a widened areola a few straight, lightly pigmented hairs along the labia Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile → Stage 2 → a bud and straight hair are stage 2: thelarche, the first sign in girls, at a normal age; curled hair would make it 3
  15. 13-year-old girl is seen for a well visit her first menstrual period began last month breast development began about 2 years ago Her mother asks how much taller she will grow Afebrile · height at the 50th percentile → SMR 4 → menarche comes at SMR 4, about 6 months after peak height velocity (SMR 2 to 3 in girls), so little growth is left
  16. 14-year-old boy is brought in because he is the shortest in his class no testicular enlargement height at the 3rd percentile His father entered puberty late Afebrile · examination otherwise normal → Obtain a bone age → no testicular enlargement by 14 is delayed puberty; the bone age comes before treatment or reassurance; delayed, with a late-blooming parent, it fits constitutional delay of growth and puberty
  17. 13-year-old girl is brought in because she has no breast development short stature webbed neck and widely spaced nipples No headaches or visual change Afebrile · height below the 3rd percentile → Obtain a karyotype → no breast development by 13 is delayed puberty, and the dysmorphic features point to Turner syndrome: a karyotype, which a bone age or waiting would miss
  18. 13-year-old boy has tender lumps beneath both nipples 2 cm of subareolar breast tissue on each side sexual maturity rating 3 pubic hair and genitals Examination otherwise normal Afebrile · growing fast this year → Reassurance and follow-up → pubertal gynecomastia is normal at SMR 3 to 4 and coincides with peak height velocity; it resolves within 1 to 2 years, so reassure rather than image
How NBME framed it: question 1

10-year-old girl with 6 months of increased facial hair growth and facial acne At the 50th percentile for height and weight T 37 °C · pulse 64/min · respirations 12/min · BP 110/60 mm Hg mild clitoral enlargement; early male pubic hair pattern serum testosterone 0.2 nmol/L (normal 0.17 to 0.7) dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate 9 μg/mL (normal 0.5 to 5.4); urine 17-ketosteroids 20 mg/24 h (normal 6 to 15) pelvic ultrasonography: no abnormalities

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Androgen insensitivity syndrome: an androgen disorder in a genital-examination stem; but it is a receptor defect in a genetically male child with no androgen effect, so it cannot virilize.
  • Pituitary adenoma: the third adenoma, and a pituitary cause of early puberty; but there is no headache or visual field loss, and pituitary adenomas rarely virilize.
  • Polycystic ovarian syndrome: hirsutism and acne; but testosterone and ovaries are normal, weight is at the 50th percentile, and it does not enlarge the clitoris.

Down to two: adrenal adenoma or ovarian adenoma. Adrenal adenoma: DHEAS comes almost only from the adrenal, and testosterone in a girl mostly from the ovary; a high DHEAS and 17-ketosteroids with normal testosterone and a normal pelvic ultrasound localize the source to the adrenal. An ovarian tumor would raise testosterone. Three options are adenomas at different glands, so it is a location question; at 10, pubic hair alone would be ordinary, and the clitoral enlargement is what makes it virilization.

Decoys Precocity is a complaint, not a diagnosis: sort central from peripheral, then look outside the endocrine system. Fractures in a preschooler: not incidental, one of the triad. No headache, emesis or visual change: nothing intracranial. Stage 4: the adjacent stage the stem negates (no second mound). Enlarged areola: in stage 2, but stage 2 hair is straight.
Pairs with Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth: is bone age ahead of, matching, or behind the age? Inherited Tumor Syndromes: café-au-lait macules from the tumor side.
Transferable rule

When staging, find the phrase that fits exactly one level. When every option is a syndrome sharing the complaint, find the finding only one produces.

Tall Stature and Marfanoid Habitus

A tall, thin child with a clot or learning problems, especially with fair skin, needs a homocysteine level before Marfan is called

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

A Marfanoid child: look for what Marfan does not do.

  • Intellectual disability, a thrombotic stroke or clot, fair skin and hair, lens dislocated down: homocystinuria. Plasma homocysteine and methionine are both high.
  • Normal intellect, lens up and out, aortic root dilation: Marfan syndrome. Echocardiographic surveillance and a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker.
  • Stretchy skin, easy bruising and lax joints with normal proportions: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, not a Marfanoid disorder.

Treat homocystinuria with pyridoxine (B6) first (about half respond), plus folate and vitamin B12 (cobalamin); nonresponders need methionine restriction and betaine. Never nitrous oxide.

Diagnosis
Marfanoid child: which one?
FeatureMarfan syndromeHomocystinuria
InheritanceAutosomal dominant; fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1)Autosomal recessive (cystathionine beta-synthase)
LensUp and outDown
IntellectNormalOften impaired
VesselsAortic root dilation, dissectionClots: stroke, DVT (deep vein thrombosis), PE (pulmonary embolism)
Skin, hair, jointsUsual coloring; joints often laxFair, fine hair; joints often stiff, not lax
Decoys Ehlers-Danlos – lax joints, hyperextensible skin, fragile tissue; vascular EDS (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome) ruptures arteries rather than clotting them; no Marfanoid build or learning problems · Phenylketonuria – fair skin and intellectual disability, with a musty odor and eczema; no Marfanoid build or clots
Management and treatment
By situation Homocystinuria – pyridoxine trial; folate and B12; methionine restriction and betaine if B6 fails · Surgery – avoid nitrous oxide: it inhibits methionine synthase, raises homocysteine and invites thrombosis · Marfan – echocardiographic surveillance of the aortic root; beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker
Practice
  1. 5-year-old girl with sudden weakness of the right arm and leg developmental delay; fair skin long, thin limbs; low upper-to-lower segment ratio Joint hyperlaxity T 37.0 °C · MRI: left middle cerebral artery infarct → Homocystinuria → a Marfanoid child with a stroke, developmental delay and fair skin has homocystinuria; joint laxity fits Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos and is atypical for homocystinuria (joints usually stiff), but neither explains the stroke, delay or fair skin; check plasma homocysteine and methionine
  2. 18-year-old man, 195 cm tall, with pectus excavatum both lenses subluxed upward normal intellect; no clots ever Arm span exceeds height; father also very tall BP 124/70 mm Hg · echocardiogram: aortic root 4.8 cm → Marfan syndrome → tall with pectus, upward lens subluxation, normal intellect and a dilated aortic root is Marfan syndrome (autosomal dominant, FBN1): echocardiographic surveillance and a beta-blocker or angiotensin receptor blocker
  3. 12-year-old girl with recurrent shoulder and knee dislocations since age 8 velvety, hyperextensible skin bruises easily; wide, thin scars Normal height and proportions; normal school performance T 36.9 °C · lenses in place → Ehlers-Danlos syndrome → joint laxity with stretchy, fragile skin and normal proportions and intellect is Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: genetic testing for the collagen defect
  4. 8-year-old boy was diagnosed with homocystinuria last week plasma homocysteine and methionine both high downward lens dislocation; tall, thin; learning support at school No clot so far T 37.0 °C · B12 and folate normal → Pyridoxine with assessment for B6 responsiveness → first try pyridoxine and test the response (about half respond), with folate and B12; nonresponders need methionine restriction and betaine
  5. 16-year-old boy, tall and thin with long fingers both lenses subluxed struggles in school; repeated a grade No family history of sudden death BP 118/72 mm Hg · slit lamp: direction unclear → Serum homocysteine level → a Marfanoid build with lens subluxation fits Marfan and homocystinuria; serum (plasma) homocysteine separates them, and it comes before echocardiography or FBN1 testing when learning problems or clots are present
  6. 10-year-old girl was diagnosed with homocystinuria at 4 on pyridoxine, folate and B12 scheduled for dental surgery under general anesthesia Parents ask what the anesthesiologist must avoid T 37.0 °C · homocysteine near target → Nitrous oxide anesthesia → nitrous oxide inhibits methionine synthase (a B12 enzyme), raises homocysteine and invites perioperative thrombosis; avoid it
Pairs with Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies: acquired high homocysteine (methylmalonic acid high in B12 deficiency, normal in folate). Inherited Tumor Syndromes: the Marfanoid habitus of MEN2B (multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B).
Transferable rule

When a lookalike syndrome is on the table, list what the classic one cannot do; any such finding moves the answer.

3 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Endocrine & Bone

Diabetes: the Annual Care Bundle

Morbidity versus mortality in diabetes care

Source vignette Pt — 28 yo F, type 2 diabetes diagnosed 1 month ago, asymptomatic · Labs — A1c 6.1% · Q — the measure most likely to prevent disease-related morbidity; options spanned annual dilated eye examination, pneumococcal vaccination and monthly A1c measurement
The decision point

Morbidity is disease burden: complications and disability. Mortality is death. In a patient with diabetes, preventing disease-related morbidity means preventing the complications of diabetes. The annual dilated eye exam detects retinopathy, the most common preventable complication. Retinopathy is asymptomatic until advanced and is the leading cause of new blindness in working-age adults.

Defining criteria A1c interval — every 3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change; every 6 months when stable at goal · Pneumococcal vaccination — diabetes is itself an ACIP indication in adults 19–64
Outcome word → intervention selected
The stem asksIt meansIt selects
"prevent morbidity"Complications, disabilityScreening for the complication
"reduce mortality"DeathInterventions with survival data (COPD → LTOT)
"reduce hospitalization"AdmissionsThe driver of decompensation (CHF → BP control)
"most beneficial"Magnitude, any outcomeUsually smoking cessation
The annual bundle Dilated eye exam annually · foot exam with monofilament annually · UACR (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) + serum creatinine annually · blood pressure at every visit · lipids at least every 5 years · depression screening · weight and tobacco counseling.
⚠︎ Two problems with the vendor explanation 1. The pneumococcal rationale is wrong. It says vaccination "is recommended for patients over the age of 65 or for patients who are asplenic". However, diabetes is itself an ACIP indication in adults 19–64 (ACIP: Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices), so she is a candidate. The eye exam is preferred because it targets a diabetes-specific complication; vaccination addresses infection risk downstream of diabetes.
2. The attribution is off. The annual bundle and A1c intervals come from the ADA Standards of Care (American Diabetes Association), not the USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force).
Why monthly A1c is wrong A1c reflects glycation across the 90–120 day RBC (red blood cell) lifespan, so consecutive monthly values measure heavily overlapping windows. Check the A1c q3 months if not at goal or after a therapy change, and q6 months if stable and at goal. At A1c 6.1% she is at goal, so she needs the 6-month schedule. Monthly testing is six times more often than that schedule.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Dilated eye examinationScreenRetinopathyOphthalmology; start at diagnosis in type 2, 5 years after in type 1
Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio with serum creatinineScreenUACR 30 mg/g or moreRepeat before labeling albuminuria
Repeat UACR over 3 to 6 monthsConfirms2 of 3 samples elevatedAlbuminuria: ACE inhibitor or ARB plus SGLT2 inhibitor
Monofilament foot examinationScreenLoss of protective sensationNeuropathy: foot care education, podiatry, inspect feet each visit
A1cNextAt goal and stableEvery 6 months; every 3 months if not at goal or therapy changed
Monthly A1cSkipMeasures overlapping 3-month windowsAdds no information and does not prevent complications
Scenario bank
  1. 28 yo F, T2DM ×1 month, A1c 6.1%, asymptomatic → Annual dilated eye exam (plus foot exam, UACR)
  2. 28 yo F, T2DM at goal, asks about A1c frequency → Check the A1c every 6 months
  3. 28 yo F, T2DM, A1c 9.4% after adding a second agent → Check the A1c every 3 months
  4. 32 yo F, type 1 diabetes diagnosed at age 8 → 5 Years after diagnosis → in type 2 diabetes screening starts at diagnosis
  5. 55 yo M, T2DM, question asks what reduces mortality → Smoking cessation, then BP and statin → not the eye exam
  6. 60 yo F, T2DM, UACR 85 mg/g → ACE inhibitor or ARB + SGLT2 inhibitor
  7. 45 yo M, T2DM, painless plantar ulcer over the first metatarsal head → Neuropathic ulcer → off-loading + glycemic control
  8. 28 yo F with type 2 diabetes due for vaccines → Pneumococcal vaccination → diabetes is itself an ACIP indication at 19–64
Pairs with Part I Diabetic Nephropathy Screening covers the renal limb of the same bundle. Ask: is the outcome morbidity, mortality, hospitalization or benefit?
Transferable rule Read the outcome noun before the options. Morbidity, mortality, hospitalization, and benefit are four different targets. A distractor can be the right intervention for the wrong target.

Abnormal Growth in a Child

short stature and growth velocity · faltering weight · normal variants, endocrine, nutritional and genetic causesIs velocity normal, which parameter fell first, and what is the bone age?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Velocity matters more than the percentile. A low, steady channel is a normal variant; height crossing 2 or more major percentile lines downward is growth failure.

Then ask which parameter fell first:

  • Weight first, length and head preserved: inadequate intake (up to 80%, mostly psychosocial), malabsorption or increased demand.
  • Height first, weight preserved or rising: endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, glucocorticoid excess).
  • All three from birth: genetic, congenital infection or intrauterine insult.

Bone age comes first among tests: delayed means growth potential remains; advanced means sex steroid exposure.

Choose a rare organic cause over inadequate intake only when a symptom, sign or admission supports it.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Short stature – height at or below the 2nd percentile for age and sex · Faltering weight – weight below the 2nd percentile, or crossing 2 or more major percentile lines downward · Not pathologic – catch-up growth in a preterm infant; shifts toward genetic potential in the first 2 years · Midparental height – average of the parents' heights, plus 6.5 cm for a boy or minus 6.5 cm for a girl
Short stature: the differential
CauseVelocityWeightBone ageThe tell
Familial or idiopathicNormal, low channelProportionateNormalShort parents; puberty on time
Constitutional delayNormal, low channelProportionateDelayedLate puberty; a parent who bloomed late; normal adult height
Hypothyroidism (usually Hashimoto)FallsPreservedDelayedFatigue, bradycardia, constipation, cold intolerance, goiter; no breasts but pubic hair
Growth hormone deficiencyFallsPreserved, chubbyDelayedLow IGF-1; neonatal hypoglycemia or micropenis; midline defects, cranial irradiation, sellar mass
Glucocorticoid excessFallsRisesDelayedOral steroids for asthma or nephrotic syndrome; central obesity, striae, hypertension
Malnutrition, celiac, IBD (inflammatory bowel disease), chronic illnessFalls after weightFalls firstDelayedPoor intake, diarrhea, abdominal pain, iron deficiency, raised ESR
Turner syndromeSlows through childhoodProportionateNormal to mildly delayed ⚠︎Any short girl, even without features; webbed neck, broad chest, absent breasts with pubic hair
Skeletal dysplasia (achondroplasia), Down syndromeLow from early childhoodDysplasia: short limbsNot the deciding testDysmorphic features: genetic diagnosis before endocrine tests
Precocious puberty or adrenal tumorAccelerated: tall now, short adultProportionateAdvancedEarly breasts or testes, or virilization (clitoromegaly, acne, voice change)
