Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M with 2 wk of fatigue, 1 wk of leg pain and 1 day of fever with petechiae, pale, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, cervical and axillary adenopathy → Complete blood count with differential and peripheral smear → bone marrow confirms afterwards
  2. 5 yo M whose complete blood count shows hemoglobin 7, platelets 22,000 and WBC 3,100 → Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy → greater than 20% lymphoblasts
  3. 4 yo M, 3 wk fever, pallor, petechiae, nontender diffuse adenopathy, splenomegaly, midshaft femoral tenderness, WBC 2,800 and platelets 18,000 → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone marrow aspirate and biopsy
  4. 4 yo M with fever, limp and pancytopenia in whom a colleague proposes empiric prednisone for presumed systemic JIA → Obtain bone marrow before any corticosteroid → steroids partially treat ALL and destroy the specimen
  5. 5 yo M with 4 wk of fatigue and pallor, pancytopenia, no adenopathy, no organomegaly and no bone pain → Aplastic anemia → bone marrow biopsy showing a hypocellular marrow
  6. 6 yo F, 5 wk of daily spiking fever, evanescent salmon rash, WBC 24,000 and platelets 700,000 → Systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis
  7. 4 yo M with petechiae and bruising 2 wk after a viral illness, well-appearing and afebrile, platelets 12,000 with normal hemoglobin and WBC → Immune thrombocytopenia → observation
  8. 8 yo M with sickle cell disease, hemoglobin 4.2, reticulocytes 0.2%, normal platelets and WBC → Parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis → transfuse and supportive care
  9. 3 yo M with fever, refusal to walk, pancytopenia, periorbital ecchymoses and proptosis, and an abdominal mass crossing the midline → Neuroblastoma → urine HVA and VMA
  10. 16 yo M, 3 wk fever, sore throat, tender posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and atypical lymphocytes → Infectious mononucleosis → avoid contact sports for 3 to 4 weeks
  11. 6 yo F with petechiae and gum bleeding, platelets 9,000, PT and PTT normal, otherwise well → No further coagulation testing is needed → petechiae are a platelet problem
  12. 5 yo M with pancytopenia and adenopathy in whom a normal white count on an earlier CBC is offered as reassurance → Accepting a normal white count as excluding leukemia → some ALL presents with under 1% circulating blasts
  13. 7 yo M, day 3 of ALL induction, potassium 6.8, phosphate 8.1, uric acid 14, calcium 6.8 and creatinine 2.1 → Tumor lysis syndrome → intravenous hydration and urate-lowering therapy
  14. 7 yo M on day 3 of ALL induction with rising potassium, phosphate and uric acid, a low calcium and a rising creatinine → IV hydration and urate-lowering therapy → tumor lysis syndrome
  15. 14 yo M with pancytopenia, marrow lymphoblasts and an anterior mediastinal mass on chest film → T-cell lineage → a mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL
  16. 5 yo F brought by her mother and the mother's boyfriend a week after a fall from the couch, now leg pain worse at night and refusing to walk; a month of dry cough, temperature 38.3 C, pale, liver 3 cm below the costal margin, bilateral proximal tibial tenderness, scattered bruises on the chest and back; hemoglobin 8, platelets 30,000, WBC 3,000 → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia → bone pain plus pancytopenia
  17. 2 yo with bruises of different ages on the ears, neck and trunk, a history that changes between caregivers, and a normal CBC and coagulation profile → Nonaccidental trauma → normal counts; bruises away from injury-prone areas
  18. 5 yo with ALL and scattered truncal bruises whose family links them to a recent fall → Marrow replacement by blasts → thrombocytopenia, not trauma
  19. 4 yo M with 1 month of bruises on the chest, back and legs, more fatigue and longer naps, poor appetite, and 1 week of gum bleeding with brushing; tonsillectomy last year without complications; a paternal uncle has hemophilia; normal vital signs; pale; buccal mucosal hematomas; bruises and petechiae on the shins, chest and back; nontender bilateral anterior cervical nodes; hepatosplenomegaly; no joint swelling → Platelet production → Acute lymphoblastic leukemia replacing the marrow
  20. 3 yo M with a warm, swollen, painful knee after a minor fall; prolonged bleeding after circumcision as a newborn; a maternal uncle has hemophilia; no pallor, adenopathy or organomegaly; hemoglobin, platelets and WBC normal; PT normal, PTT prolonged → Hemophilia A → Factor VIII activity level
Never steroids before the marrow Corticosteroids partially treat ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia). They transiently improve the child while destroying the diagnostic specimen and degrading risk stratification. Separate systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) from ALL before treatment, not after. A normal white count does not exclude ALL; the cytopenias are the clue, not the blasts.
Leukemic bone pain blamed on a fall The story — families often date leukemic bone pain to a fall; the pain is dull, in the long-bone shafts, worse at night, and the child limps or refuses to walk · What makes it systemic — fever, hepatomegaly, bilateral tibial tenderness and two or more cytopenias · The bruises — thrombocytopenia explains truncal bruising; trauma cannot depress three cell lines · When to think abuse — a vague history with bruising away from injury-prone areas, and normal counts · The white count — often low early, since normal production falls; later high as blasts spill into the blood · Versus aplastic anemia — pancytopenia from a hypocellular marrow, so no bone pain and rarely hepatomegaly · Versus immune thrombocytopenia — hemoglobin and white count normal, no bone pain or organomegaly · Workup — marrow biopsy with flow cytometry (20% or more blasts), then lumbar puncture for CNS (central nervous system) disease · Prognosis — 5-year survival above 85% in children with multidrug chemotherapy
A paternal family history of hemophilia Paternal uncle with hemophilia — hemophilia A is X-linked recessive, so a boy inherits it through his mother; his father's brother cannot pass it to him · Uneventful tonsillectomy last year — a surgical challenge passed without bleeding argues against any inherited bleeding disorder · New bleeding plus pallor, nodes and hepatosplenomegaly — an acquired marrow problem: blasts crowd out megakaryocytes, so platelet production fails · Hemophilia — joint and muscle bleeds after trauma, prolonged PTT (partial thromboplastin time), normal counts and no organomegaly · Von Willebrand disease — lifelong mucosal bleeding with a normal platelet count and a normal exam
Pearls Leukemia lowers blood counts; systemic JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) raises them, with ferritin, platelets and WBC (white blood cell count) all rising · Neuroblastoma and ALL (acute lymphoblastic leukemia) are confirmed by the same test; periorbital ecchymoses and a midline-crossing mass separate them · A mediastinal mass points to T-cell ALL and can compress the airway or cause superior vena cava syndrome; a normal chest film does not exclude B-cell ALL · About half of children with ALL present with bleeding (petechiae, bruising, gum oozing) from thrombocytopenia · Extramedullary spread also shows as testicular enlargement and as leptomeningeal disease with cranial nerve deficits or meningismus, which is why a lumbar puncture is part of the workup · Inflammatory markers monitor disease; they do not distinguish between diagnoses that all raise them · Tumor lysis: potassium up, phosphate up, uric acid up, calcium down, with acute kidney injury
Pairs with Part I Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis is the mirror twin, and Part I The Limping Child shares the presenting complaint. Ask: are the counts up or down? Part I Leg Pain in a Child covers the benign nocturnal limb pain whose normal examination excludes this diagnosis. Aquifer Bruising and Purpura in a Child places leukemia among the other causes of bruising in a child. Part I Hemophilia covers the bleeding-pattern-to-lab table: is the PT (prothrombin time) or the PTT (partial thromboplastin time) long, and are the platelets normal?
How NBME framed it A systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis diagnosis made 2 months earlier, partly improved on ibuprofen, was the anchor; new pancytopenia with hepatosplenomegaly still meant bone marrow aspiration, not imaging or liver biopsy.
Transferable rule Choose laboratory tests by what a result could change, not by their sophistication. A test that is abnormal in every diagnosis on the differential discriminates nothing. A test of an uninvolved compartment does not address the clinical question.
Salient decoyEthnicity and travel are epidemiologic priors, not findings, and cannot outrank the blood count.
True-fact-wrong-slotSplenomegaly and generalised adenopathy are not features of Kawasaki or of leukemia's mimics in the way offered.
Class-vs-memberPTT is the right class of haematologic test on the wrong compartment.
Salient decoyThe fall and the mother's boyfriend pull toward abuse, but trauma cannot explain fever, hepatomegaly or three low cell lines.

Hereditary Spherocytosis

Spherocytes with a negative Coombs · map the disease to its assay

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo M, months of jaundice and splenomegaly; father affected · Labs — MCHC 38%, direct Coombs negative · Smear — spherocytes · Q — the most appropriate confirmatory test; options spanned eosin-5-maleimide binding, flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59, and hemoglobin electrophoresis
The decision point

On a board smear, spherocytes have exactly two causes: hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia. A negative Coombs test separates them: it excludes antibody-coated cells, so the spherocytes reflect a membrane defect. MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) 38% and the affected father support the diagnosis, but neither decides it.

Confirm hereditary spherocytosis with eosin-5-maleimide binding; osmotic fragility is the older equivalent. Do not choose CD55/CD59 testing just because the hemolysis is Coombs negative. That test is for PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria), and three findings here do not fit PNH: normal white cells and platelets, spherocytes, and an affected father.

Defining criteria MCHC in HS — above 36%, because membrane loss dehydrates the cell and concentrates hemoglobin; the one common anemia in which MCHC is high · Confirmatory test — eosin-5-maleimide binding by flow cytometry showing reduced fluorescence, or increased osmotic fragility · The HS triad — Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia with jaundice and splenomegaly
Coombs-negative hemolysis in a child - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Hereditary spherocytosisAutosomal dominant ankyrin, spectrin or band 3 defect; extravascular splenic hemolysis, pigment stonesSpherocytes with a negative Coombs and MCHC above 36%
Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemiaIgG against red cells; lupus, CLL, methyldopa or penicillins; subacuteDirect Coombs positive — the only line separating it from HS
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuriaAcquired PIGA clone, complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis, adultsHemolysis with cytopenias and thrombosis at odd sites, bland smear
G6PD deficiencyX-linked, so mostly boys; normal between episodes; hemolysis 2 to 3 days after an oxidant stress: infection (activated leukocytes release oxidants), drugs such as TMP-SMX or nitrofurantoin, or fava beans; common with African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern and Asian ancestryBite cells, with Heinz bodies on a crystal violet stain, after a trigger; sudden dark urine with back or abdominal pain; MCHC normal
HemoglobinopathySickle or thalassemia, chronic inherited hemolysis with splenomegalyTarget cells or sickled forms with a low MCV
Production failureIron, B12 or folate deficiency, or marrow disease; pallor without jaundiceLow reticulocytes, with the MCV pointing the way

TestOrderResultWhat it points to

Peripheral smearFirstSpherocytesHereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolysis; in a newborn, ABO disease too

Smear clues in hemolysis
Smear findingWhat made itPoints to
Sickle cellsCrescent cells from polymerized hemoglobin SSickle cell disease; a crisis brings severe pain
Target cellsToo much membrane for the hemoglobin insideThalassemia, microcytic and chronic rather than acute; also hemoglobin C and liver disease
SpherocytesMembrane lost, leaving small round cells without central pallorHereditary spherocytosis or warm autoimmune hemolysis; ABO disease in a newborn

Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M, months of jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes, MCHC 38%, Coombs negative, father affected → Eosin-5-maleimide binding test → hereditary spherocytosis
  2. 24 yo F with lupus, 2 wk of fatigue and jaundice, spherocytes, direct Coombs positive → Prednisone → warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia
  3. 5 yo M with dark urine 3 days after TMP-SMX, bite cells and Heinz bodies, still actively hemolysing → Measuring G6PD activity during the acute episode → young surviving cells read falsely normal
  4. 30 yo M, dark morning urine, pancytopenia, new hepatic vein thrombosis, Coombs negative, bland smear → Flow cytometry for CD55 and CD59 → paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria
  5. 10 yo F with known hereditary spherocytosis, hemoglobin 12 falling to 5 over a week, reticulocytes 0.1%, slapped-cheek rash at school → Transfusion → parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis
  6. 14 yo M with hereditary spherocytosis and colicky right upper quadrant pain after meals → Right upper quadrant ultrasound → pigment gallstones
  7. 8 yo M, splenectomy a year ago for hereditary spherocytosis, temperature 39.5 C, ill-appearing → Blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone now → overwhelming post-splenectomy infection
  8. 18-hour-old newborn with jaundice, mother blood group O positive, infant A positive, spherocytes on smear, direct antiglobulin weakly positive → Phototherapy → ABO hemolytic disease of the newborn
  9. 7 yo M with jaundice, splenomegaly, spherocytes, Coombs negative and MCHC 37%, with no family history → Hereditary spherocytosis → a meaningful fraction are de novo or recessive
  10. 16 yo F with hereditary spherocytosis, hemoglobin 8, fatigue limiting sport, gallstones on ultrasound, planned for splenectomy → Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib vaccination before surgery → moderate disease, splenectomy deferred to age 6 or older
  11. 12 yo Black M with back pain, abdominal pain and dark urine since this morning, his first such episode; 2 days earlier he had fever, rhinorrhea and cough and took ibuprofen; now afebrile, HR 100, scleral icterus, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness, no rash; hemoglobin 8.2; smear shows bite cells, and a crystal violet stain shows red-cell inclusions → G6PD deficiency → oxidant stress from the infection denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies
  12. 8 yo M with known G6PD deficiency develops pallor, jaundice and dark urine on day 2 of a febrile pneumonia, before any antibiotic was given; direct antiglobulin test negative; bite cells on smear → Oxidants from activated leukocytes denature hemoglobin → red cells short of NADPH cannot regenerate glutathione
  13. 5 yo M from a Greek family with pallor, jaundice and dark urine 2 days after eating fava beans; hemoglobin 7.9, reticulocytes raised, direct antiglobulin test negative → Bite cells → G6PD deficiency; Heinz bodies need a supravital stain
Management, and what splenectomy does not fix Give folic acid for chronic reticulocytosis and transfusion for aplastic or hemolytic crisis. Management also includes splenectomy for moderate to severe disease deferred until age 6 or older ⚠, preceded by pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) vaccination. Add cholecystectomy if pigment stones are present. Splenectomy stops the hemolysis but not the defect: spherocytes persist and Howell-Jolly bodies appear. Treat every post-splenectomy fever as sepsis until proven otherwise.
Pearls Spherocytes have two causes, hereditary spherocytosis and warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and the Coombs test alone separates them; in a newborn, add ABO incompatibility as a third · The MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) is the only red-cell index that rises in a common anemia, and the RDW (red cell distribution width) rises with it · Hemolysis in HS (hereditary spherocytosis) is extravascular, with indirect bilirubin, splenomegaly and pigment stones · Hemolysis in PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria) and in severe G6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency is intravascular, with hemoglobinuria, low haptoglobin and high LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) · A falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count in any chronic hemolytic patient is parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis until proven otherwise · Do not assay G6PD during acute hemolysis, because the surviving young cells carry near-normal enzyme and read falsely normal; repeat weeks later · A normal MCV (mean corpuscular volume) does not exclude hemolysis, because a 10% reticulocytosis inflates it
Pairs with Related conditions without their own brief: warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (ask: is the direct Coombs positive?) and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (ask: are the white cells and platelets normal?). Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia shares jaundice, anemia and spherocytes with this disease. Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers the boundary: an isolated hemolytic anemia is one process, and a hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia is another. Part I Drug-Induced Immune Hemolysis is the Coombs-positive mirror of this brief's Coombs-negative spherocytic anemia.
Transferable rule When two diagnoses share a morphologic finding, the next step is the test that separates them, not the finding they share. Name the disease from the smear plus that one separating test, then map the disease to its confirmatory assay.
True-fact-wrong-slotPNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria) is the other famous Coombs-negative hemolysis, but it means cytopenias, a bland smear and acquired disease.
Salient decoyG6PD (glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase) deficiency: a boy with jaundice and hemolysis suggests it, but it needs an oxidant trigger and is not passed father to son.
Class-vs-memberHemoglobinopathy is the right class of inherited red-cell disorder but gives targets or sickles, never spherocytes.

Hematology

Bruising and Purpura in a Child

vessel, platelets, clotting factors, or trauma

Source case Pt — 6 yo with new bruising, Aquifer Pediatrics 21; the case works through purpura and petechiae to IgA vasculitis · Q — build the differential for purpura in a school-age child, then narrow it by history, examination and a first set of tests
The approach

Bruising is a finding, not a diagnosis. Ask what failed: the vessel wall (IgA vasculitis), the platelets (immune thrombocytopenia, leukemia, von Willebrand disease), the clotting factors (hemophilia), or the story (accidental or nonaccidental trauma). Each leaves a different bruise, history and first test. First check whether the child needs intervention now. Then use the history, the examination and the platelet count to remove whole branches at a time. Order the confirmatory test last, once one branch is left.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Altered mental status, labored breathing, slow capillary refillUnstable: circulation, airway, breathing first

Pallor, fatigue, bone pain, big spleen or nodesMarrow disease: CBC and smear today
Headache or confusion with low plateletsIntracranial bleeding
Sudden severe belly pain, vomiting, bloody stoolIntussusception

Finalists

IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schönlein purpura) What it is — the commonest vasculitis of childhood, about half of cases; an IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis of the skin, gut, joints and kidneys that usually settles in about a month · Who — 4 to 6 years (range 2 to 17), boys about twice as often; about half follow a URI · Mechanism — an IgA-dominated immune response, often to an infection, inflames small vessels; biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits · Features — palpable purpura with a normal platelet count, symmetric and gravity-dependent, sometimes starting as macules or hives; arthritis of the knees and ankles; colicky belly pain, sometimes before the rash; hematuria; no big spleen · Diagnosis — clinical; the urinalysis is the one test it needs, with BUN and creatinine if the urine or blood pressure is abnormal · Treatment — acetaminophen or an NSAID unless there is GI bleeding or nephritis; steroids are debated, used for severe belly pain, and have not been shown to protect the kidney · Complications — kidney disease in about a third (about 5% chronic renal failure, under 1% end-stage); GI bleeding, with occult blood in about half; intussusception, usually ileoileal, so an enema cannot reduce it · Follow-up — urinalysis and blood pressure every 1 to 2 weeks for 1 to 2 months, then monthly to every other month for a year; about 30% recur, weeks to months later · Return for — severe belly pain, blood in the stool, vomiting that stops fluids, puffy face, hands or feet, severe headache, blurred vision or confusion
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
ITPPlatelets normal, and the purpura is raised
LeukemiaA well child with normal counts and no big spleen
Hemolytic uremic syndromeNo anemia or schistocytes; platelets normal
AbuseRaised, symmetric, dependent lesions with joint, belly or kidney findings
Scenario bank
  1. 6 yo boy, a week after a cold, with raised, nonblanching red-purple spots on the backs of both legs and the buttocks, swollen tender ankles and crampy periumbilical pain; platelets 280,000 → IgA vasculitis → urinalysis next
  2. 6 yo with 3 days of new bruises and pinpoint red spots on the legs and trunk; afebrile, alert, normal vital signs, no history of injury → CBC with smear → the platelet count sorts every branch
  3. 4 yo, well-appearing, flat petechiae everywhere and a nosebleed two weeks after a viral illness; platelets 12,000, hemoglobin and white count normal, no organomegaly → Immune thrombocytopenia → low platelets and nothing else
  4. 5 yo with petechiae and platelets of 20,000 who otherwise looks like ITP, except that the spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin → Bone marrow examination → a spleen this size is not ITP
  5. 8 yo girl with frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising and bleeding for a day after a tooth extraction; platelet count normal; her mother has heavy periods → Von Willebrand disease → platelets that do not stick, at a normal count
  6. 7 yo boy, afebrile, with a warm, tense, swollen knee after a minor fall, a deep thigh hematoma last year, and an uncle who bled after surgery; platelet count normal → Hemophilia → deep bleeding means a clotting factor
  7. 7 yo boy with a swollen knee after a minor fall; platelet count and PT normal, aPTT prolonged → Factor VIII and IX activity → names the missing factor
  8. 9-month-old who cannot yet crawl, with a bruise on the ear and another on the upper back; the parent says he bruises easily; CBC and coagulation studies are normal → Skeletal survey → a child who cannot crawl cannot bruise his back by accident
  9. 5 yo with purpura on the legs, abdominal pain and hematuria a week after bloody diarrhea; hemoglobin 7, platelets 40,000, schistocytes on the smear → Hemolytic uremic syndrome → low platelets and hemolysis; IgA vasculitis keeps both normal
  10. 6 yo diagnosed with IgA vasculitis on examination, platelet count normal → Urinalysis → the only test the diagnosis itself requires
  11. 6 yo with raised purpura on both legs, ankle pain and a normal platelet count, whose serum IgA level comes back normal → It does not exclude IgA vasculitis → serum IgA is high in only about half
  12. 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria → BUN and creatinine → measures the extent of renal disease
  13. 5 yo with IgA vasculitis who develops sudden severe colicky abdominal pain with vomiting → Abdominal ultrasound → looking for intussusception
  14. 5 yo with IgA vasculitis and an ileoileal intussusception that is still present on repeat ultrasound hours later, with ongoing pain → Surgical reduction → an enema cannot reach the small bowel
  15. 6 yo with IgA vasculitis whose purpura has faded; urinalysis and blood pressure were normal at diagnosis → Serial urine and BP checks → kidney disease can come after the rash
  16. 4 yo with ITP, platelets 15,000, skin petechiae only, no mucosal or other bleeding → Observation → with activity limits; the count alone does not call for treatment
  17. 4 yo with ITP and a painful sprained ankle → Ibuprofen → impairs platelet function
  18. Previously healthy 4 yo boy with 3 days of bruising that started on the arms and legs and has spread to the trunk; no injury recalled, and his parents call him very active; afebrile, normal vital signs; scattered petechiae and bruises of different ages, most on the limbs; hemoglobin 12 g/dL, white count 6,000, platelets 1,000, PT and aPTT normal → Increased platelet destruction → immune thrombocytopenia; antibody-coated platelets are cleared in the spleen
  19. 5 yo with 2 weeks of bruising, pallor, fever and leg pain; liver and spleen enlarged; hemoglobin 7 g/dL, white count 2,000, platelets 15,000; PT and aPTT normal → Decreased platelet production → marrow replacement, as in leukemia; peripheral smear next, and bone marrow examination confirms
Bleeding by mechanism Normal PT (prothrombin time) and aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) argue against a clotting factor deficiency and against DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). A low platelet count with a normal hemoglobin and white count in a well child means increased platelet destruction. In ITP (immune thrombocytopenia), antibodies coat platelets and splenic macrophages clear them; the antibodies also reduce platelet production. Decreased production from leukemia or aplastic anemia usually lowers two or more cell lines. Abnormal platelet function (von Willebrand disease, Glanzmann thrombasthenia) causes bleeding at a normal or near-normal count.
How NBME framed it The key was a mechanism class, increased platelet destruction, not the name ITP (immune thrombocytopenia). Child abuse was the decoy, planted as an active boy with bruises in several stages of healing. Widespread petechiae, a platelet count of 1,000 and a normal PT (prothrombin time) and aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) explain the bruising.
Pairs with Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers the child with two cell lines down. Part II Acute Leukemia in a Child covers the marrow branch and its confirmatory biopsy. Part I Hematuria and Nephritic Syndrome covers the glomerular workup that renal IgA vasculitis enters. Part II Suspected Child Abuse covers the fracture branch of nonaccidental trauma. Ask: does the fracture need a pull or a twist, and does the film show a bone disease?
Transferable rule For bruising in a child, decide whether the vessel, the platelets, the clotting factors or the story failed. The feel of the lesion, the platelet count and the spleen each remove a branch. Order the confirmatory test only after one branch is left.
Salient decoyThe recent cold is shared by ITP and IgA vasculitis and cannot separate them.
Unchecked attributePurpura read as a platelet problem without checking whether it is raised.
Mirror twinA child who looks like ITP but has a spleen more than 2 cm down is not ITP.
Test-overrides-findingsA normal serum IgA offered as exclusion, when it is high in only about half.
Salient decoyChild abuse: bruises of different colors on an active boy invite it, but bruise color cannot reliably date a bruise. Widespread petechiae, a platelet count of 1,000 and normal clotting times explain the bleeding; a platelet count and coagulation studies belong in most bruising workups for suspected abuse.
Unchecked attributeAbnormal platelet function: von Willebrand disease and Glanzmann thrombasthenia cause bleeding at a normal or near-normal count; this count is 1,000.
Unchecked attributeDecreased platelet production: leukemia and aplastic anemia usually lower more than one cell line; a hemoglobin of 12 and a white count of 6,000 are normal.
True-fact-wrong-slotDisseminated intravascular coagulation: it occurs in an ill patient and prolongs the clotting times, with low fibrinogen and high D-dimer; this boy is well and his clotting times are normal.

Infectious Disease 10 topics + 8 board-style + 2 Aquifer

Screening thresholds, drug toxicities, and sequencing. Isolation precedes medication; aspiration precedes antibiotics.

Tuberculosis

Screen → sort → treat

The decision point

No test distinguishes latent from active TB (tuberculosis); the CXR (chest X-ray) and symptoms do. A positive test with a normal CXR and no symptoms means latent TB → monotherapy. A positive test with symptoms or an abnormal CXR means active TB. For active TB, isolate first, then give four drugs.

PPD positivity thresholds by risk group
PPD is positive at…Group
≥5 mmHIV+ · recent TB contact · fibrotic changes on CXR · transplant, TNF-α inhibitor, prednisone ≥15 mg/day
≥10 mmHealthcare workers · immigrants <5 yrs from endemic areas · prisoners · homeless · IVDU · diabetes · CKD · children <4
≥15 mmNo risk factors
Test mechanics BCG-vaccinated → IGRA: use an IGRA (interferon-gamma release assay), which BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination does not affect · anergy is a false-negative PPD (purified protein derivative) in HIV (human immunodeficiency virus), steroid use or sarcoid · PPD is a type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
RIPE drug toxicities
RIPE drugToxicity
RifampinOrange secretions (benign — counsel, don't stop) · potent CYP inducer → OCP failure, warfarin; use rifabutin with HIV protease inhibitors
IsoniazidPeripheral neuropathy → give B6 · hepatitis · drug-induced lupus · sideroblastic anemia
PyrazinamideHyperuricemia / gout · hepatitis
EthambutolOptic neuritis — red-green vision lost first. "Eye-thambutol"
The costumes — how the same question keeps showing up
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
PPD or IGRA (IGRA if BCG-vaccinated)ScreenPositive at the risk-group thresholdInfection, latent or active; the test cannot tell which
Symptom review and chest radiographNextNormal radiograph, no symptomsLatent TB: single-drug regimen; abnormal: airborne isolation, then sputum

Sputum AFB smear, three samplesBy branchAcid-fast bacilliActive, infectious pulmonary TB
Sputum nucleic acid amplification testSupportsM. tuberculosis DNA, with rifampin resistance resultRapid diagnosis and first resistance check
Sputum mycobacterial cultureConfirmsGrowth of M. tuberculosisActive TB, with drug susceptibility
Repeat PPD or IGRA to judge activitySkipCannot separate latent from activeThe radiograph and symptoms decide
  1. Booster / two-step: HCW with a negative first PPD, positive on repeat 1–3 weeks later = old memory, not conversion → Treat as latent
  2. Window period: contact of an active case → PPD now and at 8–10 weeks → the only time "repeat later" is correct
  3. Before biologics: starting a TNF-α inhibitor (RA or IBD stem) → Screen for latent TB first
  4. Sequencing trap: coughing + cavitary CXR → Airborne isolation → before any medication is started
Reference notes
  • HIV co-infection: PPD ≥5 mm = treat · TB drugs first, ART at 2–8 weeks (immediate risks IRIS) · rifabutin with protease inhibitors
  • Extrapulmonary: Pott (spine) · scrofula (cervical node) · meningitis (↑protein, ↓glucose, basilar) · sterile pyuria · miliary CXR · adrenal insufficiency
  • Location logic: primary = lower/mid lobe (Ghon complex); reactivation = apices (highest pO₂)
Treatment Latent: rifampin ×4 mo (preferred) · INH ×9 mo + B6 · INH + rifapentine weekly ×3 mo. Active: RIPE ×2 mo → INH + rifampin ×4 mo; reportable; DOT if nonadherent.
Sequencing trap

Bacterial Meningitis

The CSF 2×2

The decision point

Read the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) as a 2×2: cell type on one axis, glucose on the other.

CSF interpretation — the 2×2
Glucose LOWGlucose NORMAL
NeutrophilsBacterialEarly viral · parameningeal focus
LymphocytesTB · fungal (± partially treated bacterial)Viral
Organism by host
  • Neonate: GBS · E. coli (K1 capsule) · Listeria  |  Unvaccinated toddler: Hib
  • Teen / dorm / military: N. meningitidis  |  Adult (most common): S. pneumoniae
  • >50, pregnant, immunosuppressed: + Listeria → add ampicillin
  • VP shunt: S. epidermidis  |  Basilar skull fracture / CSF rhinorrhea: S. pneumoniae  |  HIV CD4 <100: Cryptococcus
Mechanism pearls Encapsulated organisms need opsonization, so they hit hardest in asplenia/sickle cell (lost filter), cirrhosis (lost complement synthesis) and complement deficiency. Complement deficiency means a lost MAC (membrane attack complex), which causes recurrent Neisseria infection; screen with CH50 (total hemolytic complement) · lipid A of LOS (lipooligosaccharide) triggers TNF (tumor necrosis factor) and IL-1 (interleukin-1) release → shock, DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation), Waterhouse-Friderichsen · Listeria escapes the phagosome with listeriolysin O and spreads via ActA-driven host actin polymerization; it has intrinsic cephalosporin resistance · conjugate vaccines convert T-independent polysaccharide into a T-dependent response, which is why they work under age 2.

Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo M with fever and neck stiffness; CSF 3,000 neutrophils, glucose 25, protein 180 → Bacterial meningitis → dexamethasone with ceftriaxone and vancomycin
  2. 22 yo M with CSF 200 lymphocytes, normal glucose and mildly raised protein → Viral meningitis
  3. 35 yo M with HIV; CSF lymphocytes, very low glucose, high protein, basilar involvement → Tuberculous meningitis
  4. 22 yo M with suspected meningitis and papilledema on fundoscopy → CT head before lumbar puncture
  5. 22 yo M with suspected bacterial meningitis and a delayed CT scanner → Blood cultures and antibiotics before imaging
  6. 68 yo M with bacterial meningitis; what coverage must be added → Ampicillin for Listeria
  7. 8 yo M in summer, headache, fever, stiff neck, CSF with 200 WBCs and 85% lymphocytes, protein 60, glucose 55, Gram stain negative → Enteroviral meningitis → supportive care
  8. 5 yo F with fever and meningismus, CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein, well appearing → Supportive care and observation → viral meningitis
  9. The most common cause of aseptic meningitis in a child presenting during summer → Enterovirus → supportive care is sufficient
  10. 2 yo with fever, hypotension, lethargy and a purpuric rash on the legs; cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci → Serum fibrinogen → purpura signals disseminated intravascular coagulation
  11. When complement testing is indicated in a patient with meningococcal disease → After recovery, for recurrent or unusual-serogroup infection → terminal complement deficiency is C5 to C9, a predisposition rather than an acute study
  12. 1 year old with meningococcemia who develops large purpuric lesions and sudden vasomotor collapse and dies; the autopsy finding → Bilateral adrenal hemorrhage → Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
  13. Infant with fever, nuchal rigidity, spreading purpura and abrupt hypotension → Fulminant meningococcemia → 10 to 20% of infected infants; mortality approaches 100%
  14. 16 yo M, 8 hours of abrupt high fever and sore throat with severe diffuse leg pain, says he has never felt this terrible; pale, nonexudative pharyngitis, supple neck, mottled tender legs; rapid strep and influenza negative; CBC and blood culture drawn → Lumbar puncture → early meningococcal disease; no seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise, so no CT first, and ceftriaxone does not wait
  15. Adolescent 10 hours into an abrupt febrile illness with severe leg pain, cold hands and feet and mottled skin, no rash yet → Meningococcemia → poor perfusion and severe myalgia arrive before the petechiae
Sequencing Get CT before LP (computed tomography before lumbar puncture) only if there is papilledema, focal deficit, seizure, immunocompromise, depressed consciousness or age >60. However, an open fontanelle in an infant generally removes the requirement, since it acts as a pop-off valve. Never delay antibiotics; draw cultures and treat. Empiric therapy is vancomycin + ceftriaxone (+ ampicillin for Listeria). Neonates get cefotaxime, not ceftriaxone (biliary sludging, bilirubin displacement). Dexamethasone before or with the first antibiotic dose: give it to blunt the cytokine burst from bacterial lysis.
Early meningococcal disease Onset — nonspecific fever, headache, vomiting, myalgia or sore throat, easily mistaken for a viral or streptococcal pharyngitis · Red flags — severe myalgia such as leg pain, poor perfusion with pallor, mottling or cold hands and feet, and the worst illness the patient has ever felt · Tempo — petechiae, meningeal signs and altered mental status follow within 12 to 24 hours · Workup — blood cultures and lumbar puncture, with ceftriaxone given without waiting for either · CT first only for — recent seizure, obtundation, focal deficit, papilledema or immunocompromise · Complications — shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, adrenal haemorrhage · Prevention — droplet precautions and chemoprophylaxis for close contacts
Follow-up facts The classic triad is present in only 44% (van de Beek, NEJM 2004; n=696) · the most common sequela is sensorineural hearing loss; check hearing in every survivor · prophylaxis for meningococcus is rifampin, cipro or ceftriaxone; for Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) it is rifampin · eculizumab blocks C5, so meningococcal vaccination is mandatory first.
Pairs with Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child covers the decision to obtain the fluid; this brief covers interpreting it.
Salient decoyHeterophile antibody test: mononucleosis gives exudate and posterior cervical nodes, not leg pain, mottling and a collapse measured in hours.
Salient decoyCT scan of the neck: deep neck infection brings trismus, uvular deviation or a bulging pharyngeal wall.
Salient decoyThroat culture for diphtheria: needs a gray, adherent pharyngeal pseudomembrane.
Salient decoyHIV antigen/antibody test: acute HIV adds diffuse lymphadenopathy, rash and diarrhoea.

Vaccines in Special Populations

HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) and the CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count gate for live vaccines · cirrhosis, asplenia, complement deficiency, cochlear implant and pregnancy · hepatitis B serologyIs the vaccine live, and what has the condition taken away?

EligibilitySchedulePractice
Bottom line

Two questions: is the vaccine live, and what has the condition taken away?

  • HIV: check the CD4 count before a live vaccine; HIV alone does not exclude every live vaccine.
  • CD4 200 or higher: varicella, MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) and yellow fever (with caution) are permitted; MMR needs that count, with a CD4 percentage of 15% or higher, for at least 6 months.
  • CD4 under 200: these live vaccines are contraindicated.
  • Never at any CD4: LAIV (live attenuated influenza vaccine; use inactivated influenza), BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin), oral polio.
  • Pregnancy: no live vaccines (MMR, varicella, LAIV).

Cirrhosis loses opsonins and asplenia loses the filter, so their vaccine lists differ.

Eligibility by condition
Adult vaccine special populations
ConditionExtra vaccinesWhy
Chronic liver disease or cirrhosisPneumococcal, hepatitis A, hepatitis BThe liver makes complement, so cirrhosis means lost opsonins; portosystemic shunting bypasses Kupffer cells; hepatitis A on a cirrhotic liver is fulminant
Asplenia, splenectomy or sickle cellPneumococcal, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) and meningococcalLost filter: encapsulated organisms need splenic clearance
Complement deficiency or eculizumabMeningococcalComplement components 5 through 9 kill Neisseria

HIV additions to the adult schedule Meningococcal ACWY (serogroups A, C, W and Y) – 2-dose primary series at least 8 weeks apart, a booster 5 years later, then every 5 years while risk remains; a schedule unique to HIV, asplenia, complement deficiency and complement-inhibitor use · Pneumococcal – regardless of age and CD4 count · Hepatitis A and B – unless immune · HPV (human papillomavirus) – through 26, consider to 45 · Recombinant zoster – from age 19 rather than waiting until 50; not live, so permitted even at a low CD4 count · Influenza – annually, inactivated

Transferable rule

For an enlarged organ, ask what the enlargement means hemodynamically before equating it with an absent organ: a congested spleen is not an absent spleen.

Practice
  1. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care CD4 count 320/mm³ on antiretroviral therapy varicella antibody negative No history of chickenpox or varicella vaccination T 36.8 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg → Give the varicella vaccine → varicella is permitted once the CD4 count is 200 or above; HIV alone does not exclude every live vaccine
  2. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care CD4 count 120/mm³ measles antibody negative Started antiretroviral therapy 1 month ago T 36.9 °C · BP 120/76 mm Hg → Withhold MMR until CD4 is at least 200 and 15% for 6 months → MMR is live: contraindicated under a CD4 count of 200; given once the count is 200 or higher, with a CD4 percentage of 15% or higher, for at least 6 months
  3. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care in influenza season CD4 count 450/mm³ asks for the nasal spray vaccine Takes antiretroviral therapy daily T 37.0 °C · BP 122/78 mm Hg → Inactivated influenza vaccine → the live attenuated influenza vaccine is never given in HIV, at any CD4 count: use inactivated influenza, annually
  4. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care CD4 count 400/mm³ on antiretroviral therapy traveling to a yellow fever zone next month Never vaccinated against yellow fever T 36.7 °C · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Give yellow fever vaccine with caution → a CD4 count of 200 or higher permits yellow fever vaccine, with caution
  5. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care asks about pneumococcal vaccination CD4 count 160/mm³ Has never received a pneumococcal vaccine T 36.8 °C · BP 124/80 mm Hg → Give pneumococcal vaccine regardless of CD4 count → pneumococcal vaccine is not live: in HIV it is given regardless of age and CD4 count
  6. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care asks about shingles vaccination CD4 count 90/mm³ Had chickenpox as a child T 36.9 °C · BP 118/76 mm Hg → Recombinant zoster vaccine → recombinant zoster is not live, so it is permitted even at a low CD4 count, from age 19 in HIV rather than waiting until 50
  7. 36-year-old man with HIV comes for a vaccine review hepatitis B surface antigen negative core antibody negative; surface antibody positive Completed a hepatitis B vaccine series years ago CD4 count 450/mm³ · Afebrile → No hepatitis B vaccination needed → surface antibody alone, with negative surface antigen and core antibody, is immunity from vaccination
  8. 48-year-old man with cirrhosis from alcohol use comes for a checkup no vaccine records ascites controlled on diuretics Not immune to hepatitis A or B albumin 3.0 g/dL · platelets 98,000/mm³ → Pneumococcal, hepatitis A and hepatitis B → cirrhosis loses opsonins (the liver makes complement) and hepatitis A on a cirrhotic liver is fulminant: pneumococcal, hepatitis A and B
  9. 48-year-old man is seen 2 weeks after a splenectomy spleen removed after a car crash recovering well Vaccine records are up to date for his age T 36.8 °C · platelets 520,000/mm³ → Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib → without a spleen the filter is lost and encapsulated organisms need splenic clearance: pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib
  10. 48-year-old man is about to start eculizumab blocks the terminal complement pathway no prior meningococcal vaccine Vaccine records otherwise up to date T 36.9 °C · BP 122/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL → Meningococcal vaccination is mandatory → complement components 5 through 9 kill Neisseria: blocking them makes meningococcal vaccination mandatory
  11. 48-year-old man is scheduled to receive a cochlear implant for profound hearing loss no prior pneumococcal vaccine Vaccine records otherwise up to date T 36.7 °C · BP 124/80 mm Hg → Pneumococcal vaccination → a cochlear implant, like a cerebrospinal fluid leak, gives direct meningeal access: pneumococcal vaccination
  12. 26-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation asks which vaccines she needs it is influenza season not immune to rubella Last tetanus booster 3 years ago BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile → Tdap and inactivated influenza → Tdap in every pregnancy (27 to 36 weeks) and inactivated influenza; no live vaccines in pregnancy (MMR, varicella, LAIV)

DTaP: Contraindication vs. Precaution

Three false contraindications to DTaP

The decision point

Classify each history as a contraindication (never give), a precaution (weigh risk vs. benefit) or neither. A brief self-limited seizure hours after a prior dose is technically a precaution. Precautions are overcome when benefit is high, as in an outbreak. Family history of epilepsy is neither a contraindication nor a precaution.

DTaP — contraindications vs precautions
CategoryItems
Contraindication
(all pertussis-containing)		Anaphylaxis to the vaccine or a component · Encephalopathy (coma, decreased consciousness, prolonged seizures) within 7 days of a prior dose → give DT instead
Precaution
(defer or weigh)		Progressive/unstable neurologic disorder — infantile spasms, uncontrolled epilepsy · seizure ≤3 days after a prior dose · temp ≥40.5 °C within 48 h · hypotonic-hyporesponsive episode within 48 h · inconsolable crying ≥3 h · Guillain-Barré within 6 weeks of prior tetanus toxoid · Arthus reaction · moderate-severe acute illness
Not a contraindicationFamily history of seizures or epilepsy · personal febrile seizure · mild illness · recent exposure

  2. 2 mo M with a brief self-limited seizure hours after a previous dose → Precaution — weigh risk against benefit
  3. 2 mo M with a family history of seizures → Not a contraindication
  4. 2 mo M with a mild febrile upper respiratory infection on the day of the visit → Not a contraindication — vaccinate
  5. 2 mo M with anaphylaxis after a previous dose → Contraindication
  6. 2 mo M with a temperature of 41 °C within 48 hours of a previous dose → Precaution

Schedule & timing DTaP at 2, 4, 6 months; 15–18 months; 4–6 years · Tdap at 11–12 and every pregnancy at 27–36 weeks · pertussis post-exposure prophylaxis only useful within 21 days · live vaccines same day or ≥28 days apart · after IVIG or blood products, defer MMR/varicella 3–11 months.
Transferable rule Vaccinate unless you can name the criterion that makes the patient ineligible; a history that only sounds disqualifying is not one.

Acute Cervicitis

Chlamydia & gonorrhea · treat before the test returns

The decision point

Mucopurulent cervical discharge + a friable cervix that bleeds on contact is a clinical diagnosis of cervicitis. Cervicitis is most prevalent in women under 25. NAAT (nucleic acid amplification testing) for both organisms is sent, and empiric ceftriaxone plus doxycycline is given before results return. The aim is to interrupt transmission and prevent PID (pelvic inflammatory disease), ectopic pregnancy and infertility. Absent CMT (cervical motion tenderness) does not reassure. CMT marks ascent, and early or low-burden infection lacks it.

Defining criteria Clinical diagnosis — mucopurulent cervical discharge + friable cervix · Empiric regimen — ceftriaxone (covers N gonorrhoeae) + doxycycline (covers C trachomatis); azithromycin replaces doxycycline in pregnancy · Testing — NAAT for both organisms; treatment does not wait for it
Chlamydia & gonorrhea in women
AxisFindings
Risk factorsAge <25, high-risk sexual behavior
ScreeningEvery sexually active woman under 25, even when asymptomatic with a normal exam; test for both organisms, which often coinfect
ManifestationsAsymptomatic most commonly; cervicitis, urethritis, perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh–Curtis)
DiagnosisNucleic acid amplification testing
TreatmentEmpiric ceftriaxone + doxycycline; confirmed chlamydia alone → doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy)
ComplicationsPID, ectopic pregnancy, infertility
Diagnostic workup

Bimanual examNextCervical motion, uterine or adnexal tendernessAscent to PID; its absence does not exclude cervicitis
Urine pregnancy testNextPositiveAzithromycin replaces doxycycline
Urinalysis, if dysuriaBy branchLeukocyte esterase positive, nitrite negativeChlamydial urethritis rather than cystitis

Scenario bank
  1. 22 yo F, mucopurulent discharge, cervix bleeds on swab contact → Ceftriaxone + doxycycline now → empiric dual therapy precedes the NAAT result
  2. 24 yo G1 at 12 weeks with NAAT-confirmed chlamydia → Azithromycin → doxycycline is avoided in pregnancy
  3. 23 yo F with mucopurulent discharge, now uterine and adnexal tenderness with cervical motion tenderness → Pelvic inflammatory disease → the infection has ascended
  4. 25 yo F, fever and uterine tenderness 3 days after vaginal delivery → Clindamycin plus gentamicin → polymicrobial ascent of vaginal flora, not an STI regimen
  5. 21 yo F, dysuria, leukocyte esterase positive but nitrite negative, mucopurulent cervical discharge on exam → Chlamydial urethritis with cervicitis → NAAT; the pelvic exam reframes the "UTI"
  6. 16 yo F at a health maintenance visit, sexually active with one male partner for a year without condoms, no discharge and a normal genital exam, BMI 25, mother had breast cancer at 40 → Chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT → every sexually active woman under 25 is screened because infection is often silent
  7. 19 yo F with no symptoms whose routine screening NAAT is positive for chlamydia and negative for gonorrhea; normal pelvic exam, negative pregnancy test → Doxycycline alone → confirmed chlamydia alone in a nonpregnant patient needs no ceftriaxone; treat partners
Pearls Azithromycin + doxycycline doubles atypical coverage and leaves N gonorrhoeae untreated; it is the classic wrong pairing · gonococcus is multidrug-resistant, including to sulfonamides, so TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) never treats an STI (sexually transmitted infection) syndrome · sterile pyuria in a sexually active woman (leukocyte esterase-positive, nitrite-negative) is chlamydia until the pelvic exam shows otherwise · treat partners.
Screening USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) recommends screening every sexually active woman under 25 for chlamydia and gonorrhea · the screening test is NAAT (nucleic acid amplification testing) for both organisms, even with no discharge and a normal exam · most infections are silent, and treating them prevents PID (pelvic inflammatory disease) and its sequelae. How NBME framed it: each decoy option had a planted cue, such as the mother's breast cancer at 40, and the key named the test in full.
Pairs with Part II Cervical Screening: the Age-21 Floor: is she 21 or older, or is she due only for chlamydia and gonorrhea screening?
Transferable rule When a clinical diagnosis is sufficient and the sequelae are irreversible, treat at the visit. Send tests at the same time; never wait for results before treating.
Class-vs-memberAzithromycin + doxycycline looks like dual therapy but both cover the same organism.
Test-overrides-findingsA negative nitrite cannot rule out infection that nitrite was never sensitive for, because atypicals do not reduce nitrate.
True-fact-wrong-slotPap smear: cervical cytology starts at 21 whatever the sexual history, so a sexually active 16-year-old gets chlamydia and gonorrhea screening instead
Salient decoyMammography: the mother's breast cancer at 40 is a planted cue; routine mammography starts at 40, not in adolescence
Unchecked attributeFasting serum glucose: a body mass index of 25 alone does not meet the adolescent diabetes screening bar, which needs overweight plus risk factors such as insulin resistance
Salient decoyHemoglobin concentration: irregular menses are a planted cue; the US Preventive Services Task Force does not recommend routine screening for iron deficiency anemia

Antibody Deficiencies

which antibody defect, and what it predicts · Are B cells present, and which isotype is preserved or elevated?

Source vignette Pt — toddler with ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic membrane perforation with otorrhea, weight below the 3rd percentile · Labs — IgM 450, IgG 250, IgA 24; neutropenia (15% of 9,000) · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned CD40 ligand deficiency, X-linked agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV
The decision point

ICU-level pneumococcal pneumonia, tympanic perforation with otorrhea, and weight below the 3rd percentile establish a primary immunodeficiency rather than ordinary toddler illness. The infection history does not show which one. The panel shows IgM 450 against IgG 250 and IgA 24. XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) requires IgM to be low, and CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) requires it to be low or normal. Selective IgA deficiency and Job syndrome require a normal IgM. Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) require a non-immunologic finding this child does not have: microthrombocytopenia and an inverted CD4/CD8, respectively. An isolated elevation of IgM with everything downstream absent is class-switch failure. CD40 ligand on the T cell cannot engage CD40 on the B cell, so the B cell stays locked on its native isotype. The neutropenia (15% of 9,000) is a confirmatory detail: it accompanies CD40 ligand deficiency and does not belong to XLA or CVID.

Defining criteria Class switching (isotype switch recombination) — the CD40L(T cell)–CD40(B cell) interaction that lets an IgM-committed B cell rearrange to IgG, IgA, or IgE; when it fails, IgM is preserved or elevated and every other isotype falls · The CD40L signature — B cells normal, IgM ↑, IgG ↓, IgA ↓, IgE ↓. B and T cell counts are normal; they are dysfunctional, not absent · The B-cell count is the first gate — low or absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia; normal B cells → the block is downstream of B-cell development, and the isotype pattern names it
Pertinent positives & negatives IgM 450 with IgG 250 and IgA 24 — class-switch failure; simultaneously excludes XLA (all isotypes low) and CVID (IgM low or normal, never elevated) and selective IgA deficiency (requires normal IgG and IgM) · Neutropenia (ANC ≈1,350) — common in CD40L deficiency; not a feature of XLA or CVID · Lymphocytes 75%, CD4/CD8 2.2 — normal lymphocyte compartment; excludes HIV, where leukopenia and an inverted ratio are expected · Platelets 260,000 — excludes Wiskott-Aldrich, which requires small, low platelets · Age 14 months with disease since early infancy — argues against CVID, which surfaces in adolescents and young adults · Vaccinations up to date, yet invasive pneumococcal disease — vaccine failure from absent opsonizing IgG, not from missed doses; it also raises a live-vaccine safety question ⚠︎ · Lymphadenopathy — separates HIV from SCID: HIV causes generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly from chronic immune activation, while SCID has absent or tiny lymph nodes because there are no lymphocytes to populate them
Antibody deficiencies — reading the isotype panel
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency)X-linked recessive boy, infancy; recurrent AOM/sinusitis/pneumonia from encapsulated bacteria, plus opportunistic infection (Pneumocystis) because the T-cell–APC limb is also brokenIgM high, IgG/IgA/IgE low, B cells normal — plus neutropenia— (the answer)
X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinemiaBoy, infections begin ~6 months as maternal IgG wanes ⚠︎; recurrent sinopulmonary and enteroviral diseaseB cells absent/low with ALL isotypes low; scant tonsils and lymph nodes ⚠︎IgM 450 (high) with a normal lymphocyte compartment
Common variable immunodeficiencyNormal early childhood, then onset at puberty or age 20 to 40; sinopulmonary infections with encapsulated bacteria → bronchiectasis; chronic lung disease including asthma and fibrosis; GI infection (Giardia, Salmonella, Campylobacter) with low IgA, and chronic diarrhea; failure to thrive in children; atopic and autoimmune associations, granulomas, and lymphoma risk ⚠︎Low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, low vaccine titers, with a NORMAL B-cell count: B cells fail to become plasma cellsIgM 450 (high); age 14 months
Selective IgA deficiencyOften asymptomatic; otherwise recurrent respiratory/GI (giardiasis) or urogenital infection; anaphylaxis to IgA-containing blood products ⚠︎IgA alone low; IgG and IgM normalIgG 250 — the deficiency is not isolated
Syndromic defects with an Ig signature (Wiskott-Aldrich · Job/hyper-IgE)WAS: eczema + microthrombocytopenia + infection, X-linked. Job: cold staphylococcal abscesses, retained primary teeth, pneumatoceles ⚠︎The non-immunologic finding makes the diagnosis, not the panel — small platelets; IgE markedly highPlatelets 260,000 and normal-sized; no eczema or abscess history
Secondary immune defects (HIV; protein-losing states ⚠︎)Opportunistic infection, thrush, diarrhea, failure to thrive; in perinatal HIV, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and a mother with an AIDS-suggestive illnessHIV: inverted CD4/CD8 with leukopenia and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG and IgA high, IgM normal or high); protein loss: low IgG ⚠︎IgG 250 (low); CD4/CD8 2.2, WBC 9,000
CVID or XLA Onset — XLA: boys at 4 to 6 months as maternal IgG wanes; CVID: after a normal childhood, at puberty or age 20 to 40 · B-cell count — XLA: absent; CVID: normal, but they fail to mature into plasma cells · Immunoglobulins — XLA: all isotypes and vaccine titers absent; CVID: low IgG plus low IgA and/or IgM, low vaccine titers · Family history — XLA: affected maternal male relatives; CVID: usually none · A few toddler ear infections that cleared promptly — ordinary childhood illness, not the start of XLA
Infection pattern → immune compartmentwhich arm of immunity is broken
Infection patternOnsetLabsCompartment and examples

Viral, fungal (Candida, Pneumocystis) and bacterial infection with failure to thriveBefore 4 to 6 monthsLow lymphocytes, ± low immunoglobulinsT cell or combined: DiGeorge syndrome, SCID, Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia

B cellsIgGIgAIgMIgEDefect
NormalNormalLowNormalNormalSelective IgA deficiency
NormalNormalNormalNormalHighHyper-IgE (Job) syndrome
NormalLowLowHighLowHyper-IgM syndrome (CD40 ligand deficiency)
NormalLowLowLow or normalLowCommon variable immunodeficiency

SCID: the newborn screen and the cure Defect — gene defects stop T-cell development; B cells fail without T-cell help, so antibody is low too; X-linked or autosomal recessive · Presentation — in the first months: severe viral, fungal (thrush) and opportunistic (Pneumocystis) infection, chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive · Labs and exam — lymphopenia with low CD4 and CD8 counts, hypogammaglobulinemia, no palpable nodes or tonsils · Newborn screen — part of US newborn screening: absent T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on the dried blood spot; lymphocyte flow cytometry confirms · Treatment — hematopoietic stem cell transplant as early as possible; no live vaccines · Not SCID — Bruton agammaglobulinemia has absent B cells but normal T cells and bacterial rather than fungal or opportunistic infection; CVID starts later with normal T- and B-cell counts; CGD has normal lymphocytes and immunoglobulins
Syndromic immunodeficiencies: the tell off the panel Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome — WATER: Wiskott-Aldrich, Thrombocytopenia with small platelets, Eczema, Recurrent infections; X-linked; bleeding at circumcision or from the umbilical stump in early infancy; T-cell dysfunction and low immunoglobulins worsen with age; stem cell transplant · Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome — FATED: coarse Facies (broad nose, prominent forehead), cold staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, high IgE with eosinophilia, Dermatologic eczema; autosomal dominant; impaired Th17 signaling; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis · Ataxia-telangiectasia — autosomal recessive defect in DNA break repair; early childhood progressive cerebellar ataxia and poorly coordinated eye and head movements, then telangiectasias of the conjunctivae and face; recurrent sinopulmonary infection; high malignancy risk; genetic testing confirms · Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis with polyendocrinopathy — AIRE deficiency breaks thymic negative selection, giving a T-cell defect against Candida plus autoimmunity; chronic Candida of skin, mouth and nails with hypoparathyroidism (hypocalcemia, seizure), adrenal insufficiency, type 1 diabetes and thyroiditis
Management, in one line Management is to replace what is missing and cover what the defect exposes. Give immunoglobulin replacement for any low-IgG defect, plus antibiotic prophylaxis with TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) ⚠︎. Give no live vaccines ⚠︎. In selective IgA deficiency, use washed or IgA-depleted products instead of IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) ⚠︎. Allogeneic HSCT (hematopoietic stem cell transplantation) is the only cure for CD40 ligand deficiency ⚠︎.
Long-term treatment: match it to the defect CVID and XLA — lifelong IVIG: the B cells cannot make antibody, so it is supplied; infections fall, but the autoimmune and malignancy risk of CVID remains · SCID — hematopoietic stem cell transplant, as early as possible · Complete DiGeorge syndrome (no thymus) — cultured thymus tissue transplant · CGD — interferon gamma, the immunomodulator, plus TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis · Cellular (T-cell) defects — antiviral and antifungal prophylaxis · Antibody defect with normal T cells — needs antibody replacement, not a transplant or an immunomodulator, although each is right for some other defect
Decision spine Is this beyond normal childhood illness? — ICU pneumonia, perforated TMs, weight <3rd percentile → yes, work it up as primary immunodeficiency · Are B cells / lymphocytes present? — Normal → not XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia) · Is IgM high, normal, or low? — High with everything else low → class-switch failure → CD40L deficiency · Is any isotype normal or high? — IgG normal with IgA alone low → selective IgA deficiency; IgE very high → Job · Is every isotype high? — IgG, IgA and IgM all high is polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. The primary antibody deficiencies all lower IgG or IgA. With thrush, adenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly, test for HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) · Any finding off the panel? — Small low platelets → Wiskott-Aldrich; inverted CD4/CD8 → HIV · Now use the pattern: — which organisms and which treatment does this specific block predict?
