  1. 11 mo M with newly diagnosed CD40 ligand deficiency, started on monthly immunoglobulin replacement → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis → Hyper-IgM syndrome
  2. 12 mo M with X-linked agammaglobulinemia on immunoglobulin replacement, presenting for the 12-month visit → Measles-mumps-rubella vaccine → X-linked agammaglobulinemia
  3. 23 yo F, sinopulmonary infections since age 16, bronchiectasis on CT, IgG/IgA/IgM all low, normal CD19+ B cells → Immunoglobulin replacement therapy → Common variable immunodeficiency
  4. 24 yo M with known selective IgA deficiency, upper GI bleed, hemoglobin 6.5, requires transfusion → Transfuse washed red blood cells → Selective IgA deficiency
  5. 9 yo M, recurrent nontender staphylococcal skin abscesses, chronic eczema, retained primary teeth, lung cyst after pneumonia, IgE 4,200 → Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome → Antistaphylococcal prophylaxis and skin care
  6. 3 yo M, eczema, recurrent otitis media, bloody diarrhea, platelets 38,000 and small on smear → Refer for allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation → Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome
  7. 18 mo M with hyper-IgM syndrome, 2 weeks of dry cough, hypoxemia, diffuse interstitial infiltrates, elevated LDH → Pneumocystis jirovecii → Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treatment
  8. 10 mo M, recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections, IgG, IgA and IgM all markedly low → Flow cytometry for CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia if B cells are absent
  9. 4 yo M with CD40 ligand deficiency on immunoglobulin replacement → Boiled or filtered drinking water → Cryptosporidium and sclerosing cholangitis
  10. 7 mo M, third otitis media, thriving, IgG mildly low with normal IgA and IgM, normal B cells, protective tetanus titers → Reassurance and repeat immunoglobulin levels → Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
  11. 7 mo M with two otitis media episodes and prior bronchiolitis, growing at the 65th percentile, facial eczema, IgG low for age with normal IgA and IgM, normal leukocytes, and elevated tetanus- and diphtheria-specific IgG → Transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy → a normal vaccine response is the discriminator
  12. 7 mo M with transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy, thriving, with two otitis media episodes → Observation with repeat immunoglobulin levels → it self-resolves by early childhood
  13. 4-month-old foster child with oral thrush, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly → Perinatal HIV infection → HIV DNA PCR
  14. 3-month-old with failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, absent thymic shadow on chest x-ray, absent T cells on flow cytometry → Severe combined immunodeficiency → hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  15. 6-month-old born to a mother with unknown prenatal care, recurrent oral candidiasis, bilateral otitis media, CD4 count 180 → Perinatal HIV infection → start antiretroviral therapy
  16. 12 mo M, two prior pneumonias, chronic thrush, tympanostomy tubes, 2nd percentile height and weight, now intubated; lymphocytes 5%, CD3+ absent, CD19+ low, IgG 220, HIV antibody negative → Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation → the only definitive therapy in SCID
  17. 10 mo M with newly diagnosed severe combined immunodeficiency presenting for catch-up immunizations → The live attenuated rotavirus vaccine → live vaccines can cause fatal disseminated disease
  18. 14 yo boy with severe left ear pain and a bulging, erythematous tympanic membrane; a few ear infections as a toddler cleared promptly, but over the past 3 years he has had recurrent otitis media, often with sinusitis, and pneumonia last year; fully vaccinated; IgG 258 mg/dL (768 to 1,728) and IgA 28 mg/dL (99 to 396) are low, IgM 40 mg/dL (38 to 266) is low-normal; tetanus, diphtheria and pneumococcal antibody titers are low → Impaired B-cell differentiation into plasma cells → Common variable immunodeficiency; B-cell count is normal
  19. 16 yo boy, healthy through early childhood, with recurrent sinusitis and two pneumonias over the past 3 years and a recent episode of giardiasis; IgG and IgA low, IgM low-normal, CD19+ B cells normal in number, poor antibody response to tetanus and pneumococcal vaccines; no affected relatives → Common variable immunodeficiency → Immunoglobulin replacement therapy
  20. 17 yo boy admitted with his second episode of meningococcal meningitis; no history of sinopulmonary, skin or opportunistic infections; CBC with differential and serum immunoglobulins are normal → Total hemolytic complement (CH50) → Terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9)
  21. 5 mo M with 2 days of fussiness and fever; earlier otitis media, oral candidiasis and rotavirus gastroenteritis; weight at the 3rd percentile; T 39.3; bulging red right tympanic membrane; no palpable lymph nodes and tonsils not visible; platelets 240,000; WBC 7,500 with 5% lymphocytes; IgG 210, IgA 35 and IgM 14 mg/dL, all low; CD4 80 and CD8 70 cells/µL, both low → Severe combined immunodeficiency → absent TRECs on the newborn screen; hematopoietic stem cell transplant
  22. 5 yo boy who walked on time but over the past 2 years has developed a progressively unsteady, wide-based gait and poorly coordinated eye and head movements; dilated small vessels on both bulbar conjunctivae; three pneumonias and recurrent sinusitis; platelets normal in number and size; no eczema → Ataxia-telangiectasia → DNA break repair defect; high malignancy risk
  23. 9 yo girl with oral thrush and thick, discolored fingernails since age 3 despite repeated antifungal courses, now brought in after a seizure; serum calcium 6.8 mg/dL with a low parathyroid hormone; normal facies, no heart murmur, and no skin abscesses → Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 → AIRE deficiency; watch for adrenal insufficiency and type 1 diabetes
  24. 12 yo F with 2 weeks of nasal congestion, now thick green discharge, fever today and maxillary tenderness; two prolonged sinusitis episodes this year, a recent Giardia infection and Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteremia last year; asthma since age 3; normal milestones and fully immunized; height and weight at the 5th percentile; Hb 12 g/dL, platelets 180,000, WBC 7,500 → Intravenous immunoglobulin infusion → Common variable immunodeficiency; low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and a normal B-cell count
  25. 4 mo F with truncus arteriosus repaired as a newborn, hypocalcemic seizures, recurrent oral thrush and no thymic shadow on chest x-ray; flow cytometry shows almost no CD3+ T cells; 22q11.2 deletion confirmed → Cultured thymus tissue transplant → Complete DiGeorge syndrome: without a thymus, T cells cannot mature
  26. 2 yo girl admitted with pneumococcal bacteremia; in the past year three otitis media episodes, two bacterial pneumonias and recurrent thrush; mother has persistent oral candidiasis, chronic diarrhea and a 9-kg weight loss; weight 5th percentile, height 50th percentile; white oral plaques, 2-cm nontender axillary nodes, spleen 2 cm and liver 3 cm below the costal margins; WBC 5,000, platelets 95,000; IgG 2,200, IgA 420 and IgM 400 mg/dL, all above normal → HIV infection → Perinatally acquired; confirm with an HIV viral load, then start antiretroviral therapy
  27. 20 mo boy with recurrent otitis media, two bacterial pneumonias and chronic diarrhea; generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly; IgG, IgA and IgM all high; CD4/CD8 ratio inverted → Perinatal HIV infection → Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia with an inverted CD4/CD8 ratio
  28. 14 mo boy with Pneumocystis pneumonia after two pneumococcal pneumonias; IgM high, IgG and IgA low; normal lymphocyte count and CD4/CD8 ratio → CD40 ligand deficiency → Class-switch failure; low IgG and a normal CD4/CD8 ratio separate it from HIV
Decoy note Lymphocytes at 75% look alarming but are expected. Lymphocytosis accompanies active infection. It also confirms that lymphocyte numbers are intact, which excludes XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). The three bronchiolitis episodes read as ordinary infant viral illness but support CD40 ligand deficiency, which impairs viral defense as well as opsonization. Up-to-date vaccination converts the pneumococcal ICU admission into vaccine failure, an immunodeficiency finding rather than a gap in care.
Pearls High IgM with low IgG/IgA is class-switch failure. Absent B cells is XLA (X-linked agammaglobulinemia). Low IgG with low IgA and/or IgM and B cells present is CVID (common variable immunodeficiency). · Read the panel in a fixed order: B cells, then IgM, then IgG/IgA/IgE. · The missing isotype predicts the organism. No opsonizing IgG → encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae). A broken CD40 ligand–CD40 axis also breaks T-cell licensing of macrophages → Pneumocystis and Cryptosporidium ⚠︎. · Neutropenia alongside hypogammaglobulinemia points at CD40L deficiency rather than XLA. · Selective IgA deficiency is the defect whose management is what you withhold: no IVIG, and washed or IgA-deficient blood products for transfusion ⚠︎. · Any patient on immunoglobulin replacement or with a defective T-cell limb gets no live vaccines ⚠︎; and replacement IgG makes serologic testing uninterpretable afterward. · A mildly low IgG at 6–9 months in a thriving infant with normal IgM, normal B cells, and protective vaccine titers is transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy — recheck, don't treat ⚠︎. · How NBME framed it: the lead-in asks for a mechanism but lists diseases, and the mother's thrush, chronic diarrhea and weight loss hold the deciding clue.
The physiologic IgG nadir The nadir — maternally derived IgG wanes after birth and troughs at 3 to 6 months, when the infant's own synthesis takes over · Transient hypogammaglobulinemia — that synthesis is delayed and the nadir is prolonged beyond 6 months, with recurrent respiratory infection and atopy · Vaccine response is the most discriminating line on the panel — a normal response excludes common variable immunodeficiency and X-linked agammaglobulinemia at once, whatever the isotype levels say
Pairs with Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease shares the complaint of recurrent otitis media and pneumonia in a child. Ask: does the immunoglobulin panel explain it, or does the anatomy? When the panel is normal, that brief covers the structural and mucociliary axis; when an isotype is out of step, this one does. Part I Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function covers the phagocyte defects: chronic granulomatous disease, leukocyte adhesion deficiency and Chédiak-Higashi. Ask: are the immunoglobulins normal, and is there pus? Part I 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome covers the thymic T-cell defect with hypocalcemia (CATCH-22); ask: is there a conotruncal heart lesion? Part II Infectious Diarrhea follows a patient with common variable immunodeficiency on immunoglobulin replacement who develops Salmonella gastroenteritis. Ask: does the organism point to the immune defect, or to the food it came from?
Transferable rule With recurrent sinopulmonary infection and an immunoglobulin panel, read the pattern rather than recall a disease. Count the B cells, then ask which isotype is preserved. The preserved isotype names the block, and the missing isotypes name the organisms you must cover.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: eczema plus recurrent infection fits its pattern, but it requires small, low platelets. A normal count excludes it, and atopy is itself a feature of transient hypogammaglobulinemia.
Class-vs-memberBruton agammaglobulinemia: That member of the class requires absent B cells and low IgM; IgM is 450 and the lymphocyte compartment is intact
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: CVID leaves IgM low or normal but never high, and presents in adolescence or later, not at 14 months
Salient decoyHIV infection: HIV would show leukopenia and a low CD4/CD8 ratio; here the ratio is 2.2 and WBC 9,000. HIV raises IgG in a polyclonal rise, while this panel has IgG 250.
True-fact-wrong-slotIgA deficiency: Isolated IgA deficiency requires normal IgG and IgM; IgG 250 makes the deficiency global-with-a-block, not selective
Class-vs-memberWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: The syndromic member is defined by microthrombocytopenia; platelets are 260,000 and normal-sized, and there is no eczema
Class-vs-memberSevere combined immunodeficiency: It presents in early infancy with lymphopenia, low immunoglobulins and no palpable nodes. A 2-year-old with every isotype high and 2-cm axillary nodes does not fit.
Unchecked attributeWiskott-Aldrich syndrome: Platelets of 95,000 are the lure. It classically has eczema and small platelets, and it is X-linked, while this patient with every isotype high is a girl.
True-fact-wrong-slotCommon variable immunodeficiency: It lowers IgG along with IgA and/or IgM, and it usually starts after puberty. Here every isotype is high at age 2.
True-fact-wrong-slotChronic granulomatous disease: It causes catalase-positive abscesses and granulomas with an abnormal DHR (dihydrorhodamine) test. Immunoglobulins are normal or high in it, so this panel does not exclude it; the thrush, the adenopathy and the mother's illness point to HIV.
Unchecked attributeChédiak-Higashi syndrome: It needs oculocutaneous albinism and neuropathy, and neither is described in the girl with every isotype high.
True-fact-wrong-slotTerminal complement deficiency: It causes recurrent Neisseria infection, not pneumococcal disease with thrush and every isotype high.
Salient decoyCystic fibrosis: Recurrent pneumonia and low weight fit. It causes lung and pancreatic disease, without thrush, adenopathy or a mother with an AIDS-suggestive illness.

Tick-Borne Illness

treat suspected rickettsiosis before confirming it · where the rash started, and what the platelets did

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, abdominal pain, body aches and headache with an unremarkable ED workup, now back with confusion and worse pain; lives by a lake surrounded by woods · Exam — T 39, BP 90/60, HR 120; new maculopapular rash on arms and legs, generalised abdominal tenderness without rebound, no neck stiffness, nonfocal neurologically · Labs — leukocytes 4,600, platelets 46,000, ALT 158, AST 202, creatinine 1.1 · Imaging — abdominal CT normal · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned amoxicillin, doxycycline, laparoscopy, prednisone, serum ceruloplasmin and stool ova and parasites
Source vignette · NBME Pediatrics CMS Pt — 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of persistent fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area and is often bitten by mosquitoes; took corticosteroids for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill · Exam — T 39 C, HR 110, RR 22; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned dengue fever, erysipelas, erythema infectiosum, exanthema subitum, Kawasaki disease, measles, meningococcemia, Rocky Mountain spotted fever and typhoid fever
The decision point

The picture is three to four days of undifferentiated fever, headache and myalgia, then a rash on the extremities, in a child with wooded exposure. With the laboratory triad of thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and hyponatremia, this is Rocky Mountain spotted fever. The management is empiric doxycycline started now. Diagnosis is made retrospectively by serology, and the disease progresses to vascular collapse and death if you wait for it. The abdominal pain is not a second problem: severe abdominal pain is part of RMSF in children. It is the specific reason this boy got a CT rather than an antibiotic on his first visit.

Defining criteria Rocky Mountain spotted fever — Rickettsia rickettsii, a gram-negative obligate intracellular organism transmitted by tick bite, peaking in late spring and summer, most often in the southeastern and south-central United States despite the name; incubation 2 to 14 days; many patients never recall the bite, so its absence proves nothing · The rash — begins maculopapular on the wrists and ankles, spreads centrally, involves palms and soles, and evolves to petechiae · The laboratory triad — thrombocytopenia from intravascular platelet destruction, hyponatremia, and raised AST and ALT from hepatic endothelial injury · Treatment gate — doxycycline empirically on suspicion, in all patients including young children; staining risk is minimal over the 5 to 7 day course used ⚠︎
Pertinent positives & negatives Three days of nonspecific fever then a rash — the rickettsial tempo; the rash appears late, which is why the first visit was unremarkable · Rash on arms and legs — extremity onset, spreading centrally · Platelets 46,000 with raised transaminases — the vascular-injury signature, belonging to no isolated abdominal process · Lives near woods — the exposure; no recalled bite is typical, not exculpatory · Severe abdominal pain with a normal CT — the paediatric RMSF mimic of appendicitis; the negative scan closes the surgical option rather than opening a new one · Confusion with a nonfocal examination and no neck stiffness — early encephalitic involvement, not meningitis · BP 90/60 with HR 120 — early vascular compromise, and the reason waiting is dangerous · No adenopathy, clear oropharynx — argues against the viral exanthems and mononucleosis
Fever and rash after outdoor exposure — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Rocky Mountain spotted fever Can't missSummer, wooded exposure; R. rickettsiiExtremity rash spreading centrally, palms and soles; low platelets, low sodium, high transaminases— (the answer)
Lyme diseaseSame season and habitat; Borrelia burgdorferiErythema migrans — a single expanding annular lesion with central clearingMaculopapular extremity rash; cytopenias and transaminitis atypical
Ehrlichiosis / anaplasmosisSame tick exposure, similar prodromeSame labs, usually no rash; morulae in leukocytesA prominent rash is present
Dengue feverAedes mosquito; travel to or residence in the tropicsRetro-orbital pain, severe bone and muscle pain; leukopenia, low platelets; bleeding in severe casesNo tropical travel; mosquito bites at home in the US do not transmit it
MeningococcemiaNeisseria meningitidis; any seasonHours from fever to petechiae, purpura, shock and DIC; meningismus in someDays of fever before the rash; rash began distally and spread inward
Kawasaki diseaseVasculitis of young childrenFever for 5 days or more plus 4 of 5: nonexudative conjunctivitis, cracked lips or strawberry tongue, polymorphous rash, hand and foot redness or swelling, cervical node; platelets risePetechial palm rash, low platelets; conjunctival injection alone does not make it
MeaslesUnvaccinated child; paramyxovirusCough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots; rash starts at the hairline and spreads down, sparing palms and solesRash began on the hands and wrists; no cough or coryza
Roseola (exanthema subitum)HHV-6; under age 2Days of high fever in a well infant, then a blanching truncal rash as the fever breaksIll school-age child; petechial rash during the fever
Immune thrombocytopeniaPost-viral, otherwise well childIsolated thrombocytopenia, normal liver, afebrileFever, rash, transaminitis and hypotension
Wilson diseaseGenetic copper transport defectKayser-Fleischer rings; hepatic and neuropsychiatric disease over monthsAn acute febrile illness with a rash over days
AmebiasisFever, abdominal pain, liver abscessBloody diarrhea; abscess on imagingCT normal, no diarrhea, rash unexplained
Decision spine How long has the fever run and when did the rash appear? — Three to four days, then rash, the rickettsial tempo · Where did the rash start? — Wrists and ankles, spreading inward · What did the platelets, sodium and transaminases do? — Low, low, high, the triad · Any outdoor or wooded exposure? — Yes, and a recalled bite is not required · Is there abdominal pain? — In a child that is part of the disease, not a second one · So when do you treat? — Now; serology is retrospective and untreated disease kills
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBCFirstPlatelets low, white count normal or lowEndothelial injury; fits RMSF, not a surgical abdomen
Basic metabolic panel and liver enzymesFirstHyponatremia with raised AST and ALTCompletes the rickettsial triad; start doxycycline now
Peripheral smearBy branchMorulae in leukocytes, usually no rashEhrlichiosis or anaplasmosis; doxycycline treats it too

Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 3 days of fever, headache and abdominal pain, now confused with a maculopapular rash on the arms and legs; platelets 46,000, AST 202, ALT 158; lives near woods; abdominal CT normal → Doxycycline → empiric treatment for Rocky Mountain spotted fever
  2. 4 yo with suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever whose parents decline doxycycline over concerns about dental staining → Give doxycycline → staining risk is minimal with a 5 to 7 day course
  3. 10 yo with fever, an extremity rash, thrombocytopenia and transaminitis after wooded exposure; serology has been sent → Withholding antibiotics until serology returns → untreated disease progresses to vascular collapse
  4. 9 yo seen 10 days after a hike with a single expanding annular lesion showing central clearing and mild fatigue → Lyme disease → erythema migrans
  5. 40 yo with summer tick exposure, fever, headache, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and raised transaminases, with no rash → Ehrlichiosis → doxycycline treats it as well
  6. The mechanism of thrombocytopenia in Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Intravascular platelet destruction from infection of vascular endothelium → small-vessel vasculitis
  7. 12 yo with severe abdominal pain and fever, a maculopapular rash on the wrists and ankles, and a normal abdominal CT → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → abdominal pain in children mimics appendicitis
  8. Child already started on doxycycline for suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever → Rickettsia serology → confirmation is retrospective and never delays therapy
  9. 6 yo F, previously healthy, seen in June with 4 days of high fever and severe headache and 1 day of a rash on the hands; lives in a rural area, often bitten by mosquitoes; finished a steroid course for poison ivy a month ago; appears ill; T 39 C; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; scattered petechiae on the palms and distal arms → Rocky Mountain spotted fever → doxycycline now, without waiting for serology
  10. 10 yo F, 5 days after returning from 2 weeks in the Dominican Republic, with fever to 39.5 C, severe headache with pain behind the eyes, and severe bone and muscle pain; diffuse macular rash on the trunk; no outdoor or wooded exposure in the US; WBC 2,800, platelets 90,000, sodium normal → Dengue fever → supportive care with fluids; avoid NSAIDs
  11. 4 yo M on a farm in Tennessee, seen in July with 4 days of fever and headache; bilateral conjunctival injection without discharge; blanching macules on the wrists and ankles that became petechial and now reach the palms, soles and trunk; no cracked lips or hand swelling; platelets 85,000, sodium 130, AST 140 → Start doxycycline → Rocky Mountain spotted fever; any age, treat on suspicion
Decoy note Two details suggest abdominal and hepatic causes. Worsening abdominal pain with a normal CT is the classic paediatric RMSF (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) presentation that gets children taken to theatre. Once the scan is negative, stop pursuing an abdominal cause. Confusion with transaminitis suggests Wilson disease, but confusion in RMSF is early encephalitis arriving over hours, not over months.
Decoy note: no tick in the stem No tick — most RMSF stems never mention one; the clue is season (late spring to summer), rural or outdoor life, days of fever and severe headache, then a rash that starts on the wrists, ankles, palms or soles and spreads inward, turning petechial · Mosquito bites — point to dengue only with tropical travel, and dengue brings retro-orbital pain and severe bone and muscle pain · Conjunctival injection — occurs in RMSF too; Kawasaki disease needs 5 days of fever plus its criteria, and measles needs cough, coryza and a rash from the hairline down · Steroids for poison ivy a month ago — irrelevant; they explain none of the fever, headache or petechiae
Pearls Treat on suspicion, confirm retrospectively — doxycycline treats the patient; serology only documents the diagnosis · Doxycycline is given to children of any age for RMSF — the staining concern applies to prolonged courses, and withholding it is the dangerous choice · Low platelets plus transaminitis plus hyponatremia after outdoor exposure — a rickettsial fingerprint the viral exanthems do not produce · The rash moves inward — extremity onset spreading centrally with palms and soles is a short differential: RMSF, secondary syphilis, coxsackie hand-foot-and-mouth · No recalled tick bite — does not lower suspicion; the exposure history is habitat, not bite · Abdominal pain in a febrile child with a rash is part of the illness — a normal CT should redirect you to a systemic diagnosis, not a more invasive abdominal one
Pairs with Part I Skin and Soft Tissue Infection covers the febrile-rash differential. Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and roseola, and Kawasaki Disease covers the 5-day fever with red eyes. Related conditions without their own brief: Lyme disease and ehrlichiosis. Ask: where did the rash start, and what did the platelets and transaminases do?
How NBME framed it Kawasaki disease appeared under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome, as a decoy for a child with 4 days of fever, red eyes and a petechial rash on the palms.
Transferable rule When the confirmatory test is retrospective and the untreated disease is lethal, treat on the clinical picture. Let the serology arrive whenever it arrives. A pending test is not a reason to wait; treatment should already have started.
Salient decoyStool for ova and parasites: fever with abdominal pain and liver enzymes fits amebiasis, but that causes bloody diarrhea and a liver abscess and explains no rash.
Treat-the-numberPrednisone: platelets of 46,000 invite ITP, but ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia in a well child, not fever with rash, transaminitis and hypotension.
True-fact-wrong-slotAmoxicillin: correct for Lyme, same season and habitat, but Lyme rash is a single expanding annular lesion and it spares the platelets and liver.
Salient decoySerum ceruloplasmin: liver enzymes plus confusion reads as Wilson disease, a chronic disorder with Kayser-Fleischer rings, not four days of fever with a rash.
Sequencing trapLaparoscopy: the abdominal CT is already normal, which answers the surgical question.
Salient decoyDengue fever: mosquito bites suggest it, but without tropical travel dengue is not on the table. It brings retro-orbital and bone pain rather than a rash spreading in from the wrists.
Unchecked attributeKawasaki disease: red eyes fit, but fever has run 4 days, not 5, and the rash is petechial on the palms, not polymorphous with swollen hands.
Salient decoyMeasles: conjunctivitis tempts, but measles rash starts at the hairline, spares the palms and soles, and follows cough and coryza.

Lymphadenopathy

acute and unilateral is bacterial · tempo and laterality sort every neck node

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo M, lump on the right neck noticed yesterday, today red, painful and larger; cough, rhinorrhea and low-grade fever a week ago, resolved; family reunion in eastern Arkansas with several cousins also coryzal · Exam — T 38.6, HR 98; 5 cm tender, warm, poorly mobile anterior cervical node with overlying erythema; no hepatosplenomegaly · Q — the most appropriate treatment; options spanned azithromycin, cefdinir, clindamycin, itraconazole, oseltamivir and supportive care only
The decision point

Sort the node by tempo and laterality. A node that appeared yesterday and is bigger, red and tender today is acute. A single inflamed node on one side is unilateral. Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis in a child under five is a bacterial infection of the node itself. The organisms are Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, with anaerobes when there is periodontal disease. Empiric therapy has to cover gram-positives including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) plus anaerobes. Among the offered agents, only clindamycin does all three. The preceding viral illness is the portal of entry, not the cause, and it has already resolved.

Defining criteria Acute unilateral cervical lymphadenitis — child under 5; a 3 to 6 cm node, markedly tender, warm and erythematous, with or without fever; the child is usually well-appearing and the diagnosis is clinical · Empiric coverage required — S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes, and anaerobes, which is clindamycin; amoxicillin-clavulanate is reasonable where community MRSA is low, a first-generation cephalosporin where periodontal disease is unlikely · Suppuration — fluctuance on examination signals abscess and adds incision and drainage · Observation gate — supportive care alone is defensible only in an afebrile child with minimal tenderness and minimal enlargement
Pertinent positives & negatives Onset yesterday, larger today — acute; excludes cat-scratch disease and nontuberculous mycobacterial disease, both of which build over weeks · Unilateral — a node infection, not reactive adenopathy, which is bilateral · Tender, warm, erythematous — inflammatory; mycobacterial nodes are nontender and violaceous · T 38.6 — opens the antibiotic gate that observation would otherwise satisfy · 5 cm — large enough to risk suppuration; size is part of the treatment gate · Poorly mobile with overlying erythema — tethering from inflammation; malignancy is painless and not erythematous · URI a week ago, now resolved — the portal of entry, not the active illness · No hepatosplenomegaly or diffuse adenopathy — excludes disseminated histoplasmosis and mononucleosis
The inflamed cervical node — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Acute bacterial lymphadenitisUnder 5, after a URI; S. aureus and S. pyogenesAcute, unilateral, tender, warm, erythematous, with or without fever— (the answer)
Cat-scratch diseaseCat or kitten scratch or bite, or flea bite; Bartonella henselae; the inoculation papule is often small and not reportedTender regional node proximal to the scratch, arising over weeks, sometimes suppurative; fails antibiotics aimed at S. aureus and S. pyogenes; fever in someOnset yesterday; no animal exposure
Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitisAlso under 5, indolent courseChronic, violaceous, nontender; treated by excision ⚠︎Acute, tender, erythematous and febrile
Reactive viral adenopathyConcurrent URI or influenzaBilateral, small, mobile, mildly tenderUnilateral and 5 cm; the URI has resolved
Disseminated histoplasmosisMississippi and Ohio River ValleysPulmonary disease with mediastinal adenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly with diffuse adenopathyIsolated neck node; no organomegaly or lung findings
Infected branchial cleft cystCongenital second-arch remnant that declares itself after a URI, often in later childhoodCystic lateral mass with a draining pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoidA solid tender node with no pit or sinus tract
The node pattern names the cause Acute, unilateral, tender, warm node — pyogenic: S. aureus or S. pyogenes; clindamycin · Tender regional node proximal to a scratch, failing antistaphylococcal antibiotics — Bartonella henselae (cat-scratch disease): ask about cats and kittens, send Bartonella serology; azithromycin speeds recovery · Chronic, single, nontender cervical node — mycobacterial: tuberculosis in an adolescent or adult with TB risk (interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test, then biopsy); nontuberculous mycobacteria in a child under 5, violaceous, excised · Generalized, painless adenopathy — systemic: HIV (antigen/antibody test), EBV with pharyngitis and splenomegaly, disseminated histoplasmosis in the immunosuppressed · Bilateral, symmetric, nontender nodes with cat exposure — toxoplasmosis; Toxoplasma serology · Bilateral, small, mildly tender nodes with a current URI — reactive viral adenopathy; supportive care
Decision spine Acute or chronic? — Days means bacterial; weeks means Bartonella or mycobacterial · Unilateral or bilateral? — Unilateral is a node infection; bilateral is reactive · Tender and erythematous, or violaceous and painless? — Tender means pyogenic · Febrile? Large? — Both means antibiotics, not observation · Fluctuant? — If yes, drain as well · Which agent covers S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes? — Clindamycin

Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M with a 5 cm tender, warm, erythematous, poorly mobile right anterior cervical node appearing over 2 days, T 38.6, with a resolved upper respiratory illness a week earlier → Clindamycin → covers MRSA, S. pyogenes and anaerobes
  2. 4 yo with a 2 cm mildly tender unilateral cervical node, afebrile, well-appearing, no overlying erythema → Supportive care with reassessment → observation is appropriate below the treatment gate
  3. 3 yo who has taken clindamycin for 48 hours whose node is now fluctuant with spreading erythema → Incision and drainage with continued antibiotics → suppuration has developed
  4. 8 yo with a 3-week history of a slowly enlarging tender axillary node and a papule where a kitten scratched him → Cat-scratch disease → azithromycin
  5. 3 yo with a 6-week painless violaceous submandibular node, afebrile and otherwise well → Nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis → surgical excision
  6. 3 yo with acute unilateral bacterial cervical lymphadenitis in a community with high MRSA prevalence → Cefdinir → no coverage of Staphylococcus aureus or anaerobes
  7. 5 yo from the Mississippi River Valley with cough, mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and diffuse adenopathy → Disseminated histoplasmosis → itraconazole
  8. 2 yo with fever, cough and rhinorrhea with bilateral small mobile mildly tender cervical nodes → Reactive viral adenopathy → supportive care
  9. 4 year old with 1 day of fever and a red, tender, fluctuant 2 cm anterior cervical node; normal dentition, no animal contact, no rash → Staphylococcus aureus → With Streptococcus pyogenes — acute, unilateral, suppurative
  10. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis and extensive dental caries → Anaerobic oral flora → Prevotella and relatives follow periodontal disease
  11. Child with acute unilateral cervical adenitis after skinning a rabbit → Francisella tularensis → The exposure names the organism
  12. Child with bilateral tender cervical nodes, coryza and pharyngitis for 3 days → Acute viral adenitis → Bilateral and acute points at adenovirus and its relatives
  13. 3 yo with cough and rhinorrhea last week, now resolved, and a single neck node noticed yesterday that is 4 cm, tender, warm and red today; T 38.5 → Acute bacterial lymphadenitis → empiric clindamycin
  14. 12 yo M with a painful left neck lump a week after a febrile URI, now cystic, with a small pit anterior to the sternocleidomastoid draining mucopurulent fluid → Branchial cleft cyst → second-arch remnant infected after a URI; resect cyst and tract
  15. 8 yo with a tender midline neck cyst after a cold that rises when she sticks out her tongue → Thyroglossal duct cyst → follows the path of thyroid descent from the foramen cecum
  16. Adult trumpet player with a soft lateral neck swelling that enlarges when he bears down → Laryngocele → laryngeal mucosa pouching through the thyrohyoid membrane, inflated by pressure
  17. 16 yo F with a tender red lump at the left elbow 5 days ago, diagnosed as lymphadenitis and treated with clindamycin taken as prescribed; now fever and increasing swelling in the left armpit; T 38.3; a 1 cm tender mobile epitrochlear node and several 2 to 3 cm tender left axillary nodes; no other enlarged nodes → Bartonella henselae serology → cat-scratch disease; ask about cats; azithromycin speeds recovery
  18. 24 yo F who adopted a stray cat 2 months ago, with 3 weeks of fatigue and low-grade fever; 1 to 2 cm nontender, mobile posterior cervical nodes on both sides, symmetric; no pharyngitis, no splenomegaly, no skin lesions; heterophile antibody test negative → Toxoplasmosis → Toxoplasma serology; self-limited in an immunocompetent adult
  19. 26 yo M who moved from the Philippines 2 years ago, with a single firm, nontender, 3 cm right cervical node that has enlarged slowly over 2 months; no pain, no overlying warmth, no animal exposure; other node regions normal → Tuberculous lymphadenitis → interferon-gamma release assay, then node biopsy with acid-fast culture
Decoy note The location, eastern Arkansas, is genuinely endemic for histoplasmosis. Mentioned beside the sick contacts, it reads as an exposure history. It is not one: the cousins explain the resolved URI (upper respiratory infection). The location explains nothing, because histoplasmosis does not present as a single hot node.
Congenital neck masses, sorted by location Midline, moves with swallowing or tongue protrusion — thyroglossal duct cyst, often found after a URI · Midline, does not move with the tongue — dermoid cyst, along an embryologic fusion plane · Lateral, anterior to the sternocleidomastoid, below the mandible — branchial cleft cyst, usually second arch, between the internal and external carotids; cured by resecting the cyst and its tract · Lateral, necrotic node with violaceous skin and a fistula — nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis · Posterior triangle, from birth or on prenatal ultrasound — cystic hygroma · Lateral, enlarges with Valsalva — laryngocele, through the thyrohyoid membrane; glassblowers and trumpet players · Submandibular sinus draining sulfur granules — actinomyces, after dental infection or trauma
Pearls Tempo and laterality sort neck nodes before anything else — acute and unilateral is bacterial, chronic and unilateral is Bartonella or mycobacterial, acute and bilateral is viral · Clindamycin is chosen for its spectrum, not its class — a cephalosporin that misses staphylococci fails · Violaceous and nontender is mycobacterial, and its treatment is surgical excision rather than antibiotics ⚠︎ · Fluctuance adds drainage — the drug stays the same · A resolved URI a week earlier is a portal of entry, not a competing diagnosis; a concurrent URI would point at reactive adenopathy instead
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the reactive-adenopathy end of this spectrum and the exudative pharyngitis fork. Ask: how fast did it appear, and is it one node or many?
How NBME framed it Scratches from a pet cat were planted beside a cat-scratch disease option, but acute midline pain that worsens with swallowing or tongue protrusion names an infected thyroglossal duct cyst.
Transferable rule When every option is a drug, name the organisms you must cover, then find the single agent that covers all of them. A geographic detail matters only when the syndrome matches the endemic disease, not merely the location.
Unchecked attributeSupportive care only: the observation gate requires an afebrile child with a small, minimally tender node; this is 38.6 with a 5 cm inflamed node at risk of abscess.
Unchecked attributeAzithromycin: correct for cat-scratch and part of mycobacterial therapy, but both are chronic and indolent; this appeared yesterday.
Class-vs-memberCefdinir: covers S. pyogenes but not S. aureus or anaerobes, and the two are clinically indistinguishable here.
Salient decoyItraconazole: eastern Arkansas is histoplasmosis country, but histoplasmosis presents with pulmonary or disseminated disease, not an isolated hot node.
True-fact-wrong-slotOseltamivir: influenza adenopathy is bilateral and accompanies active respiratory symptoms, which have resolved.

Oral Lesions in a Child

lesion location identifies the virus · front of the mouth or back

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with 2 days of throat pain and poor intake; T 38.3, HR 108 · Exam — scattered 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars with grey shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula; tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared; no rash · Q — the most likely associated pathogen; options spanned adenovirus, coxsackievirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus and Streptococcus pyogenes
The decision point

The lesions are vesicles and ulcers, not exudate. This removes every bacterial and mononucleosis-type pharyngitis. Adenovirus, EBV (Epstein-Barr virus) and S. pyogenes all produce tonsillar exudate, and none produces oral vesicles. The lesions are posterior (soft palate, uvula, anterior palatine pillars), with the tongue, lips and buccal mucosa explicitly spared. Herpangina, from coxsackievirus A, affects the back of the mouth. In herpetic gingivostomatitis, lesions affect the front, with red swollen gums. The spared structures are exactly those HSV (herpes simplex virus) would involve.

Defining criteria Herpangina — coxsackievirus A; ages 3 to 10; late summer and early fall; fever and pharyngitis with grey vesicles progressing to fibrin-coated ulcers on the posterior oropharynx, and no rash; treatment is supportive · Herpetic gingivostomatitis — HSV-1; 6 months to 5 years; no seasonality; clusters of vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa and lips with erythematous, edematous gingiva; treated with oral acyclovir · Hand-foot-and-mouth disease — also coxsackievirus, but anterior oral lesions plus vesicles on palms and soles; herpangina's defining negative is the absent rash
Pertinent positives & negatives Vesicles and ulcers, not exudate — excludes adenovirus, EBV and group A streptococcus in one move · Soft palate, uvula and palatine pillars involved — the posterior distribution, herpangina territory · Tongue, lips and buccal mucosa spared — a stated negative that excludes HSV gingivostomatitis, whose distribution is precisely those structures · No rash — separates herpangina from hand-foot-and-mouth disease · No gingival erythema or edema described — a second strike against HSV, whose gingivitis is near-universal · Age 5, starting the fall term in 2 weeks — age 3 to 10 and late summer, both epidemiological features; the school detail is dating the season, not flagging exposure · No adenopathy or splenomegaly — nothing to support mononucleosis
Oral lesions in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Herpangina (coxsackievirus A)3 to 10 yrs, late summer and early fall, abrupt high feverPosterior grey vesicles becoming ulcers: soft palate, uvula, pillars; no rash— (the answer)
Herpetic gingivostomatitis (HSV-1)6 months to 5 years, any season; drooling, refuses to drinkAnterior clusters on buccal mucosa, tongue and lips; swollen red gingivaThose exact sites are stated as spared
Hand-foot-and-mouth diseaseSame virus family, same seasonAnterior oral lesions plus palms and solesThe skin has no rash
Streptococcal pharyngitisFever, sore throat, no coughTonsillar exudate, tender anterior nodes, palatal petechiaeVesicles and ulcers rather than exudate
Infectious mononucleosisAdolescent with prolonged fatigueExudate plus posterior cervical nodes plus splenomegalyNo exudate, no adenopathy, no splenomegaly
Adenoviral tonsillitisFever, cough, sore throat, sometimes conjunctivitisExudate without vesiclesVesicular lesions are not its picture
Decision spine Vesicles and ulcers, or exudate? — Vesicles means a viral enanthem, and the bacterial and EBV options fall · Front of the mouth or back? — Back means herpangina · Are the gums red and swollen? — Not described, which argues against HSV · Is there a rash on palms and soles? — No, so not hand-foot-and-mouth · Age and season? — Five years in late summer corroborates · So what is the management? — Supportive; it self-resolves within a week
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo M, 3 days of fever with throat pain, 1 mm vesicles on the anterior palatine pillars and gray shallow ulcers on the soft palate and uvula, tongue and lips and buccal mucosa spared, no rash → Coxsackievirus A → herpangina
  2. 2 yo with fever, drooling and refusal to drink; clusters of vesicles on the gingiva, tongue and lips with erythematous edematous gums → Herpetic gingivostomatitis → oral acyclovir
  3. 3 yo with fever, oral ulcers and vesicles on the palms and soles → Hand-foot-and-mouth disease → supportive care
  4. 5 yo with posterior oral vesicles and ulcers, drinking less but with moist mucous membranes and normal vital signs → Cold non-acidic fluids with analgesia → herpangina resolves within a week
  5. 8 yo with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender anterior cervical nodes, without cough or oral vesicles → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → rapid antigen testing before treating
  6. 16 yo with 2 weeks of fatigue, exudative pharyngitis, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly → Epstein-Barr virus infection → avoid contact sports
  7. 5 yo with gray vesicles and ulcers confined to the soft palate and uvula, no rash, well hydrated → Oral acyclovir → herpangina is an enteroviral illness, not a herpesvirus one
  8. 4 yo with herpangina now refusing all fluids, with dry mucous membranes and no urine output for 10 hours → Intravenous rehydration → dehydration is the principal complication
  9. 5 yo in late summer with abrupt fever and sore throat; gray vesicles and shallow ulcers on the soft palate, uvula and anterior pillars; gums, lips and tongue normal; no rash → Herpangina → coxsackievirus A; supportive care
Pearls Anterior is herpes, posterior is coxsackie — both diseases otherwise present with fever, sore throat and a miserable child · Vesicles and ulcers exclude exudate-producing pathogens wholesale: strep, EBV and adenovirus make exudate, not blisters · Herpangina has no rash; hand-foot-and-mouth does — same virus family, separated by the skin · Red swollen gingiva is the HSV signature, and its absence is as informative as any positive finding · Starting the fall term in two weeks is dating the season, not describing an exposure · shedding continues in stool for weeks after recovery ⚠︎, so hand hygiene rather than exclusion is the public-health answer
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the exudative pharyngitis fork and the Centor rule; this brief covers vesicular lesions. Ask: are the lesions exudate or vesicles, and are they front or back? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child sorts hand-foot-and-mouth disease among the other rashes with fever.
Transferable rule When two diseases share a lesion type, the discriminating attribute is usually anatomical, not clinical. Ask where the lesions are before asking what they are. Treat a stated spared structure as an active exclusion, not as background.
Unchecked attributeHerpes simplex virus: oral vesicles in a child retrieves HSV automatically, but HSV is anterior and those sites are explicitly spared, with no gingival swelling.
Class-vs-memberAdenovirus: a common cause of paediatric fever with sore throat, but it produces exudative tonsillitis, not vesicles or ulcers.
Class-vs-memberStreptococcus pyogenes: exudate with tender anterior nodes; vesicles and ulcers argue against it.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus: exudate, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly and adolescent age; none present.

Neutrophil Disorders: Number and Function

the organism list identifies the diagnosis · Are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?

Source vignette Pt — 2 yo M, 3 days of fever, cough and irritability; perirectal abscess drained at 9 months; T 38.9, bilateral lower-lobe crackles · Imaging — bilateral pneumonia on chest film; after 3 days of antibiotics still febrile, CT shows a small left effusion with paratracheal and hilar lymphadenopathy · Labs — lymph node and lung biopsy shows granuloma formation; culture grows Burkholderia (Pseudomonas) cepacia · Q — the mechanism responsible; options spanned decreased immunoglobulin production, decreased superoxide production, defective opsonization, impaired clearing of airway secretions and impaired neutrophil chemotaxis
Source vignette · NBME Pediatrics CMS Pt — 2 yo M, 2 days of fever and mouth sores, fussy and refusing food, now improving; a year of similar episodes about every 3 weeks, each lasting 3 to 5 days; normal growth and development · Exam — T 38.4 C, HR 120; scattered aphthous ulcers; skin clear; no lymphadenopathy · Labs — Hb 11.5; WBC 4,000 with 4% segmented neutrophils, 84% lymphocytes, 12% monocytes; platelets 250,000 · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, cyclic neutropenia, dyskeratosis congenita, Fanconi syndrome, hypersplenism, leukemia, severe congenital neutropenia, viral illness and vitamin B12 deficiency
The decision point

The pneumonia does not name the defect. Granulomas on biopsy and a Burkholderia cepacia culture together point at one disease: chronic granulomatous disease. It is a disorder of NADPH oxidase, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms. The enzyme drives the neutrophil respiratory burst, so its loss means decreased superoxide production. Phagocytes migrate normally and ingest normally, but have impaired intracellular killing. Neutrophils can borrow hydrogen peroxide made by the pathogen itself. Susceptibility therefore particularly involves characteristic catalase-positive organisms that destroy their own peroxide; this is not an exclusive organism list. The granulomas are the same defect seen histologically: phagocytes arrive but clear pathogens poorly, contributing to granuloma formation.

Defining criteria Chronic granulomatous disease — NADPH oxidase disorder, commonly X-linked with autosomal recessive forms; impaired respiratory burst and reduced reactive oxygen species, so intracellular killing is impaired · The organism pattern — particular susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive bacteria and fungi, because catalase degrades the pathogen's own hydrogen peroxide and denies the neutrophil a borrowed oxidant: S aureus, B cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus · Sites — lungs, skin, liver and lymph nodes; perirectal abscess is characteristic, with diffuse granulomas in the gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts · Diagnosis — measure neutrophil superoxide production: dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry preferred, nitroblue tetrazolium the older equivalent · Treatment — prophylaxis with TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma; haematopoietic cell transplant is curative
Recurrent infection — reading the mechanismwhich defect, by organism and by histology
MechanismDiseaseThe NBME tellExcluded here by
↓ superoxide productionChronic granulomatous diseaseCatalase-positive organisms + granulomas + abscesses (perirectal, liver)— (the answer)
Impaired airway clearanceCystic fibrosisNasal polyps, clubbing, steatorrhoea; also gets B cepaciaNo granulomas; infections confined to the sinopulmonary tract
↓ immunoglobulin productionX-linked agammaglobulinaemiaEncapsulated organisms; all isotypes low, absent B cellsNo granulomas, no abscesses, wrong organism
Defective opsonisationComplement (C3) deficiencyEncapsulated organisms, recurrent pyogenic infectionSame — and B cepacia is not the pattern
Impaired neutrophil chemotaxisLeukocyte adhesion deficiencyDelayed umbilical cord separation (over 3 weeks), skin and mucosal infections without pus (cellulitis, periodontitis), poor wound healing, marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia; CD18 integrin defectPus was present (abscess drained); no granulomas
Impaired Th17 signalling (JAK-STAT)Hyper-IgE (Job) syndromeCold staphylococcal and Candida abscesses, severe eczema, eosinophilia with a normal white countNo eczema or eosinophilia; granulomas and Burkholderia point to the oxidative burst
Pertinent positives & negatives Granulomas on biopsy — the most specific finding; excludes CF, XLA, complement deficiency and leukocyte adhesion deficiency, none of which form them · Burkholderia cepacia — catalase-positive, and shared with cystic fibrosis, which is exactly why it is not sufficient alone · Perirectal abscess at 9 months — extrapulmonary abscess; CF does not do this, and it is the finding that separates the two · Persistent fever after 3 days of appropriate antibiotics — killing is defective, not coverage · Hilar and paratracheal lymphadenopathy — node involvement, part of the CGD site pattern · Male, age 2 — consistent with the common X-linked form presenting in early childhood; autosomal recessive forms also occur · Normal ear, nose and throat examination — no chronic rhinosinusitis, arguing further against CF
Decision spine Are there granulomas? — Yes → CGD, essentially alone among the immunodeficiencies · What grew? — A catalase-positive organism → confirms · Where are the infections? — Lung and perirectal → extrapulmonary, so not CF · Was there pus? — Yes → chemotaxis and adhesion intact, so not leukocyte adhesion deficiency · What is the mechanism of that defect? — NADPH oxidase → decreased superoxide · How is it confirmed? — Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBC with differentialFirstNeutrophils present, count normal or highThe defect is killing, not number; marked leukocytosis without pus suggests LAD; an absolute neutrophil count under 500 is a number problem instead
Biopsy and culture of abscess or nodeNextGranulomas with a catalase-positive organismCGD pattern; B. cepacia alone also fits cystic fibrosis
Dihydrorhodamine 123 flow cytometryConfirmsAbsent or reduced oxidative burstChronic granulomatous disease
Nitroblue tetrazolium testConfirmsNeutrophils fail to turn the dye blueCGD; the older equivalent of the DHR test
Neutrophil counts 2 to 3 times a week for 6 weeks, if the count is lowBy branchNadirs about every 21 days, normal between; or persistently lowCyclic neutropenia if periodic; severe congenital neutropenia if persistent
Sweat chloride, if no granulomasBy branch60 mmol/L or moreCystic fibrosis, which also grows B. cepacia
Genetic testing of NADPH oxidase genesCauseX-linked or autosomal recessive variantInheritance and family counseling
Quantitative serum immunoglobulinsSkipNormal or high in CGDAntibody production is intact
First fork: neutrophil number or function Number — the neutrophil count is low; infections are bacterial, with fever, mouth ulcers, gingivitis and skin, lung or gut infection when the count is lowest · Function — the count is normal or high and the cells fail at a step: adhesion (leukocyte adhesion deficiency), killing (chronic granulomatous disease), granule traffic (Chédiak-Higashi syndrome, which also lowers the count) · Absolute neutrophil count — WBC × (segmented neutrophils + bands); 4,000 × 4% is about 160; under 1,500 is neutropenia and under 500 is severe · Name trap — Fanconi syndrome is proximal renal tubule wasting of glucose, phosphate, bicarbonate and amino acids; Fanconi anemia is inherited marrow failure
Low neutrophil count in a child: the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe tellExcluded in the periodic-fever child by
Cyclic neutropeniaInherited, neutrophil elastase (ELANE) mutation; well between episodesEvery 21 days, lasting 3 to 6 days: fever, oral ulcers, pharyngitis; periodontal disease and early tooth loss; ANC often under 200 at the nadir— (the answer)
Severe congenital neutropeniaInherited, often ELANE; presents in the first months of lifePersistent severe neutropenia with omphalitis, pneumonia, abscesses; high risk of AMLPeriodic episodes with health between; first symptoms after infancy
Viral marrow suppressionParvovirus B19, EBV, CMV, HIV, other virusesTransient dip with the illness and its other symptomsA year of regular 3-week episodes; a virus does not keep a calendar
Acute leukemiaMalaise, weight loss, bone painAnemia and thrombocytopenia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, blastsNormal platelets, no nodes or spleen, well between episodes
HypersplenismSplenic sequestrationSplenomegaly with all three cell lines lowNo splenomegaly; hemoglobin and platelets preserved
Fanconi anemiaInherited marrow failurePancytopenia with short stature, thumb or radial anomalies, microcephaly, café au lait spots, developmental delayNormal growth, only one line low
Dyskeratosis congenitaInherited marrow failureReticular hyperpigmentation, dystrophic nails, oral leukoplakia; pancytopeniaSkin and nails normal; only one line low
Chédiak-Higashi syndromeLysosomal trafficking defect (LYST)Oculocutaneous albinism, giant granules, neuropathy; frequent bacterial infectionsNormal pigment and neurologic examination
Vitamin B12 deficiencyDiet, malabsorptionMacrocytic anemia, hypersegmented neutrophilsNo macrocytic anemia; not periodic
Cyclic neutropenia: confirm and treat Confirm — one normal count between episodes proves nothing; check neutrophil counts 2 to 3 times a week for at least 6 weeks to catch the nadirs; genetic testing for the elastase mutation supports it · During an episode — treat any infection, keep up oral and dental hygiene · Long term — G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) keeps the count up and prevents episodes; the same drug treats severe congenital neutropenia
Scenario bank
  1. 2 yo M with a perirectal abscess drained at 9 months, now with bilateral pneumonia still febrile after 3 days of antibiotics; biopsy shows granulomas and culture grows Burkholderia cepacia → Decreased superoxide production → NADPH oxidase defect in chronic granulomatous disease
  2. 3 yo M with recurrent Serratia marcescens skin abscesses and hepatic granulomas on imaging → Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry → measures the neutrophil respiratory burst
  3. Why are characteristic catalase-positive organisms associated with chronic granulomatous disease? → Catalase degrades the organism's own hydrogen peroxide → the neutrophil cannot borrow the pathogen's oxidant
  4. 2 yo newly diagnosed with chronic granulomatous disease, currently well between infections → TMP-SMX, itraconazole and interferon gamma prophylaxis → bacterial, fungal and immunomodulatory cover
  5. 5 yo with chronic granulomatous disease and repeated life-threatening infections despite full prophylaxis → Hematopoietic cell transplantation → the only curative therapy
  6. Newborn with delayed umbilical cord separation and a soft tissue infection producing no pus, with a leukocyte count of 38,000 → Leukocyte adhesion deficiency → impaired chemotaxis and adhesion
  7. 4 yo with nasal polyps, digital clubbing, steatorrhea and Burkholderia cepacia pneumonia; biopsy shows no granulomas → Cystic fibrosis → sweat chloride testing
  8. 9 mo M with recurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae infections, all immunoglobulin isotypes low and absent CD19+ B cells → X-linked agammaglobulinemia → immunoglobulin replacement therapy
  9. 3 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus liver abscess, a perirectal abscess drained in infancy and granulomas on biopsy → Chronic granulomatous disease → confirm with dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry
  10. 3 yo M with eczema since infancy and recurrent Staphylococcus aureus and Candida abscesses, now a nontender fluctuant buttock abscess, afebrile; leukocytes 9,000 with 30% neutrophils and 40% eosinophils → Hyper-IgE syndrome → impaired Th17 signaling blunts neutrophil recruitment
  11. 2 yo with recurrent staphylococcal skin infections, silvery hair, pale skin and neutropenia → Chédiak-Higashi syndrome → lysosomal trafficking defect
  12. Why the abscesses of hyper-IgE syndrome are cold, without erythema or tenderness → Th17 defect blunts neutrophil recruitment → few neutrophils arrive, so little inflammation
  13. 2 yo M with a Staphylococcus aureus perianal abscess drained at 2 months after failed oral antibiotics, left inguinal lymphadenitis at 7 months, and now a fluctuant right arm abscess that grows Serratia marcescens; leukocyte and platelet counts normal, B and T cells normal; dihydrorhodamine test abnormal → Itraconazole → antifungal prophylaxis in chronic granulomatous disease
  14. 3 yo M with chronic granulomatous disease on TMP-SMX and itraconazole prophylaxis, due for vaccines before his family moves to a country where tuberculosis is common → BCG vaccine → live bacterial vaccine; live viral and inactivated vaccines are safe
  15. 2 yo M with 2 days of fever and painful mouth sores, now improving; a year of similar episodes about every 3 weeks, each lasting 3 to 5 days, well and growing normally between them; T 38.4 C, scattered aphthous ulcers, no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly; Hb 11.5, WBC 4,000 with 4% segmented neutrophils, platelets 250,000 → Cyclic neutropenia → neutrophil elastase (ELANE) mutation; confirm with serial counts, treat with G-CSF
  16. 4 yo F with fever, mouth ulcers and sore throat that recur about every 3 weeks and last 4 to 5 days, for 10 months; well between episodes with normal growth; today, on a well day, the examination is normal and a CBC shows WBC 7,200 with 45% neutrophils, normal hemoglobin and platelets → Neutrophil counts twice weekly for 6 weeks → cyclic neutropenia; a single count between episodes can be normal
  17. 5 yo M with cyclic neutropenia confirmed by serial counts and an ELANE mutation; despite good dental care he has painful mouth ulcers every 3 weeks, early periodontal disease and two pneumonias this year, each during a nadir → Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor → keeps the count up and prevents episodes
  18. 2-month-old boy with omphalitis at 3 weeks and now a perianal abscess; the umbilical cord separated at 10 days and the wound drains pus; absolute neutrophil count under 200 on every CBC over 4 weeks, with normal hemoglobin and platelets → Severe congenital neutropenia → G-CSF; lifelong risk of myelodysplasia and AML
Separating chronic granulomatous disease from cystic fibrosis Burkholderia cepacia belongs to two diseases: cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease. It therefore identifies neither alone. Granulomas and extrapulmonary abscesses are what split them. In the vignette, a perirectal abscess in an infant is the single most specific clue to chronic granulomatous disease. It sits in the past medical history, where it is easy to skim.
Reading the CBC in recurrent abscesses Eosinophilia, normal white count — hyper-IgE syndrome · Marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia — leukocyte adhesion deficiency · Neutropenia with oculocutaneous albinism — Chédiak-Higashi syndrome: giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils on the smear, recurrent bacterial infection, progressive neurodegeneration with peripheral neuropathy; autosomal recessive lysosomal trafficking defect · Small platelets with bruising — Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome · Lymphopenia — DiGeorge syndrome, whose infections are invasive viral, fungal and bacterial rather than cold abscesses · Unremarkable CBC with Candida infections — myeloperoxidase deficiency · Job syndrome, the rest — autosomal dominant; eczema from the first weeks of life, recurrent sinopulmonary infection, broad nose and prominent forehead, retained primary teeth; genetic testing confirms; skin care and antibiotic prophylaxis
Pearls Granulomas plus abscesses plus a catalase-positive organism is CGD, and no other immunodeficiency assembles that trio · Catalase-positive is a mechanism, not a list — the neutrophil can use the organism's own peroxide, helping explain susceptibility to characteristic catalase-positive organisms; other organisms are not excluded · Dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry has replaced nitroblue tetrazolium as the preferred test; both measure the same respiratory burst · Prophylaxis — TMP-SMX for bacteria plus itraconazole for fungi such as Aspergillus, with interferon gamma added for severe disease; transplant is the only cure · Not CGD prophylaxis — G-CSF, because the neutrophil count is normal; IVIG, because immunoglobulins are normal (it treats antibody deficiency such as XLA); valacyclovir, which belongs to T-cell defects · Vaccines — avoid BCG and other live bacterial vaccines; live viral and inactivated vaccines are safe · Phagocytes in CGD migrate and ingest normally; the failure is intracellular killing, which is why pus forms and chemotaxis-defect diseases look different
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers the antibody deficiencies, and this brief covers the phagocyte defects. Together the two cover the common primary immunodeficiencies. Ask: are there granulomas, and is the infection outside the chest?
How NBME framed it No organism or granuloma was named; the clue was a maternal uncle who died of fungal pneumonia, which points to X-linked disease. Four of the five options were steps in leukocyte function, and the key named the killing defect as impaired microbicidal activity.
Transferable rule When an organism belongs to two diseases, it cannot separate them; find the finding that belongs to only one. Here the shared organism is B cepacia, and the findings that belong to only one disease are the granuloma and the perirectal abscess.
Unchecked attributeImpaired clearing of airway secretions: cystic fibrosis makes no granulomas, and its infections stay sinopulmonary; a perirectal abscess is outside its territory.
Class-vs-memberDefective opsonization: complement deficiency gives encapsulated-organism infection without granulomas.
Class-vs-memberImpaired neutrophil chemotaxis: leukocyte adhesion deficiency gives pus-free infections with delayed cord separation; pus was drained here.
True-fact-wrong-slotDecreased immunoglobulin production: XLA gives encapsulated sinopulmonary infection; no granulomas, wrong organism.
Unchecked attributeSevere congenital neutropenia: the right category and often the same gene, but it is persistent from the first months with severe infections; this child is well between regular 3-week episodes.
Salient decoyViral illness: fever and mouth sores look viral, and viruses do lower the count, but once, not every 3 weeks for a year.
True-fact-wrong-slotFanconi syndrome: a proximal tubule disorder, not a marrow one; the marrow disease is Fanconi anemia, which lowers all three lines and brings short stature and thumb anomalies.
9 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Infectious Disease

Deep Neck Infections

Trismus with a deviated uvula · no imaging needed

Source vignette Pt — 14 yo M, a week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned peritonsillar abscess, retropharyngeal abscess and infectious mononucleosis
The decision point

A week of worsening unilateral sore throat with trismus, a muffled voice and a uvula deviated away from the swelling is a peritonsillar abscess. It is a clinical diagnosis, so imaging adds nothing. The next step is needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics.

The deep neck spaces sort by age and by what the child cannot do. Trismus and uvular deviation are peritonsillar; pain on neck extension with a bulging posterior wall is retropharyngeal; tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx is epiglottitis.

Defining criteria Peritonsillar abscess — trismus, muffled hot-potato voice, uvula deviated to the contralateral side, unilateral tonsillar bulge · Retropharyngeal abscess — pain on neck extension, bulging posterior pharyngeal wall, typically under 5 years · Epiglottitis — toxic, tripoding, drooling, stridor, with a deceptively normal oropharynx
The child or adolescent with a severe sore throat - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Peritonsillar abscessAdolescent or young adult, days of worsening unilateral painTrismus with uvular deviation; no imaging required
Retropharyngeal abscessUnder 5 years, often after a pharyngeal infectionPain on neck extension, bulging posterior wall; CT neck with contrast
EpiglottitisUnvaccinated child, hours not daysTripoding with stridor and a normal pharynx; secure the airway in theatre
Infectious mononucleosisBilateral exudates, posterior cervical nodesSplenomegaly; avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
Ludwig anginaDental source, floor of mouthTongue elevation and submental induration; airway first
Lemierre syndrome Can't missAfter oropharyngeal infectionPersistent fever with nodular lung opacities; internal jugular thrombophlebitis
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Oropharyngeal examFirstTrismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated away from the swellingPeritonsillar abscess; a clinical diagnosis, no imaging needed
Needle aspirationConfirmsPus aspiratedAbscess, drained in the same step; send for culture
Intraoral ultrasoundBy branchPhlegmon versus abscess unclear: fluid collectionAbscess to drain

Scenario bank
  1. 14 yo M, week of worsening unilateral sore throat, trismus, muffled voice, uvula deviated left → Peritonsillar abscess → no imaging - needle aspiration or incision and drainage plus antibiotics
  2. 14 yo M with a peritonsillar abscess, what must the antibiotics cover → Group A Streptococcus and respiratory anaerobes
  3. 4 yo M, fever and drooling with pain on neck extension and a bulging posterior pharyngeal wall → Retropharyngeal abscess → CT neck with contrast
  4. 5 yo M, unvaccinated, toxic and tripoding with stridor and a normal-looking pharynx → Epiglottitis → secure the airway in the operating room
  5. 17 yo F back from camp, bilateral exudative tonsils, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly → Infectious mononucleosis → heterophile antibody, avoid amoxicillin and contact sports
  6. 14 yo M whose drained abscess is followed by persistent fever, pleuritic chest pain and nodular lung opacities → Lemierre syndrome → contrast CT and anaerobic coverage
  7. 50 yo M with a dental infection, floor-of-mouth induration and tongue elevation → Ludwig angina → airway first
  8. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling where phlegmon versus abscess is uncertain → Intraoral ultrasound
  9. 14 yo M with tonsillar swelling who develops new neck swelling and torticollis → Parapharyngeal extension → CT neck with contrast
  10. 14 yo M with a third peritonsillar abscess this year → Tonsillectomy
  11. 6 yo F with bilateral exudates, no trismus, no uvular deviation, positive rapid strep → Group A streptococcal pharyngitis → penicillin or amoxicillin
Airway before anything In Ludwig angina and epiglottitis, the airway is the emergency. Examination can precipitate obstruction, so do not depress the tongue or instrument the pharynx of a tripoding child outside the operating theatre. Recurrent peritonsillar abscess, three or more in a year, is an indication for tonsillectomy.
Pearls Peritonsillar abscess is diagnosed clinically; intraoral ultrasound only helps when phlegmon versus abscess is genuinely uncertain · Retropharyngeal abscess hurts on extension; meningitis hurts on flexion · Amoxicillin in undiagnosed mononucleosis produces a florid morbilliform rash · Lemierre syndrome is Fusobacterium necrophorum with septic pulmonary emboli after an oropharyngeal infection
Pairs with Part I Respiratory Infection in a Child covers the uncomplicated end of this spectrum. Ask: is anything unilateral?
Transferable rule When a diagnosis is clinical and the complication is airway compromise, imaging is almost always the wrong next step. It cannot change what is already known, and it costs time the airway may not have.
Sequencing trapImaging before drainage in a clinically obvious abscess.
Mirror twinRetropharyngeal abscess is the younger child's version, separated by extension versus trismus.

Congenital Infections (TORCH)

Periventricular calcifications · organism first, then its signature sequela

Source vignette Pt — 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly · Imaging — periventricular calcifications · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned congenital cytomegalovirus, congenital toxoplasmosis and congenital rubella
The decision point

Identify the organism, then its signature sequela.

Calcifications along the ventricular margin (periventricular) indicate CMV (cytomegalovirus). Calcifications scattered through the parenchyma indicate toxoplasmosis. An indoor cat suggests toxoplasmosis but is compatible with congenital CMV.

Defining criteria Periventricular calcifications — CMV · Diffuse parenchymal calcifications — toxoplasmosis, with chorioretinitis · Subcortical calcifications with arthrogryposis — Zika · Diagnostic window — urine or saliva PCR within the first 3 weeks of life, after which congenital and perinatal acquisition cannot be separated
Congenital infection — the differential
InfectionIllness scriptThe NBME tell
CMVMost common congenital infection; hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, microcephalyPeriventricular calcifications with microcephaly; sequela is sensorineural hearing loss
ToxoplasmosisCat litter, undercooked meatDiffuse parenchymal calcifications and chorioretinitis; sequela is obstructive hydrocephalus
RubellaUnvaccinated motherCataracts and a continuous machine-like PDA murmur
SyphilisUntreated maternal infectionSnuffles, palm-and-sole rash, periostitis; no CNS calcifications
HSV Can't missIntrapartum acquisitionDays 5 to 21, vesicles, seizures, temporal lobe; without vesicles, cerebrospinal fluid with lymphocytes and red cells and normal glucose
ZikaMaternal travelSevere microcephaly with subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis
Parvovirus B19Maternal febrile illness with arthralgia; risk highest before 20 weeksHydrops fetalis or fetal loss; congenital anomalies are rare in survivors
Listeria monocytogenes Can't missNonspecific maternal febrile illness, often foodborneSevere neonatal sepsis with disseminated abscesses in liver, spleen, lung, kidney and brain
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Head ultrasound or CTFirstPeriventricular calcificationsCMV; diffuse parenchymal: toxoplasmosis; subcortical with arthrogryposis: Zika
Saliva CMV PCR, first 3 weeksScreenPositiveNeeds urine PCR to confirm; saliva gives false positives
Urine CMV PCR, first 3 weeksConfirmsPositiveCongenital CMV; after 3 weeks, perinatal acquisition cannot be excluded

Infant rubella IgMBy branchPositiveCongenital rubella syndrome; serology, not PCR
Cerebrospinal fluid herpes simplex virus PCRBy branchPositiveNeonatal herpes encephalitis; start intravenous acyclovir before the result
