Infant CMV IgGSkipMaternal IgG crosses the placentaCannot separate infant from maternal antibody
Mnemonic TORCH: Toxoplasmosis, Other (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, HIV), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex virus
Scenario bank
  1. 2 mo F, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, microcephaly, periventricular calcifications → Congenital CMV → valganciclovir
  2. 2 mo F with symptomatic congenital CMV, greatest long-term risk → Sensorineural hearing loss
  3. Newborn with diffuse parenchymal calcifications, chorioretinitis and ventriculomegaly → Congenital toxoplasmosis
  4. Newborn with cataracts and a continuous machine-like murmur → Congenital rubella
  5. Newborn with snuffles, a palm-and-sole rash and long-bone periostitis → Congenital syphilis → penicillin
  6. 7 yo with notched incisors, saddle nose and interstitial keratitis → Late congenital syphilis
  7. Neonate on day 10 with vesicles, seizures and temporal-lobe changes → Neonatal HSV → intravenous acyclovir
  8. Newborn with severe microcephaly, subcortical calcifications and arthrogryposis after maternal travel → Congenital Zika
  9. Newborn with suspected congenital CMV → Urine or saliva PCR in the first 3 weeks of life
  10. Newborn with a positive saliva CMV PCR → Confirm with urine PCR → saliva gives false positives
  11. Newborn with symptomatic congenital CMV, treatment duration → 6 Months of valganciclovir
  12. Newborn with congenital CMV who passes the newborn hearing screen → Serial audiology through childhood → the loss is often late-onset
  13. Infant with congenital CMV and enlarged ventricles → Hydrocephalus ex vacuo → parenchymal volume loss
  14. 2-day-old, failed hearing screen bilaterally, absent red reflex, continuous murmur at the left second interspace, hepatosplenomegaly, growth below the 5th percentile, mother with a first-trimester febrile illness and arthralgia → Congenital rubella syndrome → hearing loss, cataracts and patent ductus arteriosus
  15. Why the first trimester is rubella's dangerous window → Transplacental infection during organogenesis → spontaneous abortion or congenital rubella syndrome
  16. Newborn with suspected congenital rubella syndrome; establishing the diagnosis → Infant rubella IgM serology → serology rather than PCR, because the PCR window belongs to cytomegalovirus
  17. Pregnant woman with fever and arthralgia at 16 weeks whose fetus develops ascites, effusions and skin edema → Parvovirus B19 with hydrops fetalis → anomalies are rare in survivors
  18. 29 yo woman at 18 weeks' gestation, an elementary school teacher, exposed during a school outbreak of slapped-cheek rash; she has mild arthralgia; parvovirus B19 IgM positive, IgG negative; ultrasound today shows a normally grown fetus without hydrops → Serial ultrasound with MCA Doppler → Acute maternal parvovirus B19 infection; watch for fetal anemia and hydrops
  19. 26 yo woman at 14 weeks' gestation whose 5-year-old has a slapped-cheek facial rash and lacy rash on the arms; she has had fatigue and aching wrists and knees for 3 days → Parvovirus B19 IgM → Acute maternal infection; then serial fetal ultrasonography
  20. 31 yo woman at 23 weeks' gestation with confirmed acute parvovirus B19 infection 4 weeks ago, followed with serial ultrasonography; middle cerebral artery Doppler now indicates severe fetal anemia, and there is new fetal ascites and skin edema → Intrauterine transfusion → Hydrops fetalis from parvovirus B19 fetal anemia
  21. 8-day-old girl with apnea during a feed, then a focal seizure with bicycling leg movements and eye deviation; lethargic and hypotonic with brisk reflexes and bilateral Babinski signs; cerebrospinal fluid glucose 55 mg/dL, protein 65 mg/dL, 350 erythrocytes/mm3, 70 leukocytes/mm3 with 80% lymphocytes; empiric antibiotics started → Herpes simplex virus → confirm with cerebrospinal fluid PCR and add intravenous acyclovir
  22. 10-day-old boy with lethargy and a focal seizure and no skin lesions; cerebrospinal fluid shows normal glucose, mildly raised protein, 90 leukocytes/mm3 that are mostly lymphocytes, and many erythrocytes; empiric antibiotics are running → Add intravenous acyclovir now → empiric antiviral therapy before the PCR result
  23. 12-day-old with poor feeding, lethargy and focal seizures; cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with many erythrocytes and normal glucose → CSF HSV PCR → neonatal herpes simplex encephalitis
Shared sequela Rubella also causes sensorineural hearing loss. Hearing loss therefore does not separate rubella from CMV (cytomegalovirus); the calcification pattern does.
The rubella triad Sensorineural hearing loss — a failed newborn hearing screen · Cataracts — an absent red reflex, or leukocoria · Patent ductus arteriosus — a continuous machine-like murmur at the left second interspace · Plus — growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly and a purpuric blueberry-muffin rash · Maternal arthralgia after a febrile illness in pregnancy — rubella causes organ malformation from first-trimester organogenesis; parvovirus B19 causes hydrops and no malformation
Parvovirus B19 in pregnancy Exposure — a child with slapped cheeks at home, school or day care; a child with the rash is no longer contagious, so exposure happened earlier; most maternal infections are asymptomatic, others flu-like with rash or symmetric arthralgia · Maternal serology — B19 IgM positive means acute infection; IgG positive with IgM negative means past infection and immunity; B19 DNA testing if immunocompromised · Fetal risk — the virus infects erythroid progenitors, so the danger is fetal anemia, then hydrops or fetal death, not malformation · Acute infection — serial ultrasonography with middle cerebral artery Doppler to detect fetal anemia and hydrops · Severe fetal anemia — intrauterine transfusion
Neonatal herpes without vesicles Timing — seizures, lethargy or apnea in the second or third week of life; vesicles are often absent · Cerebrospinal fluid — normal or mildly low glucose, mildly raised protein, a modest pleocytosis that is mostly lymphocytes, and many red cells · Bacterial meningitis — low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant leukocyte count, often over 1,000/mm3 · Confirm — herpes simplex virus PCR (polymerase chain reaction) of the cerebrospinal fluid · Treat — add intravenous acyclovir to empiric antibiotics without waiting for the PCR · How NBME framed it: no vesicles are given and antibiotics are already begun, so the day of life and the lymphocytic, bloody cerebrospinal fluid identify the virus.
Pearls CMV (cytomegalovirus) is the most common congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss · Only about 10% are symptomatic at birth, and that group carries up to 50% hearing-loss risk untreated · Six months of valganciclovir is better than six weeks: 8% versus 13% hearing worsening at one year · Hearing loss is progressive and can be late-onset, so passing the newborn screen does not discharge the child from audiology · CMV — ventricles enlarge ex vacuo from volume loss · Toxoplasmosis — ventricles enlarge from obstruction
Pairs with Part I Hearing Loss & Otosclerosis covers the childhood sensorineural causes. Part I Cerebral Palsy covers the same imaging; the calcification pattern and the white-matter injury each point to a different cause. Part II Neonatal Sepsis and Its Mimics: does the cerebrospinal fluid show low glucose with over 1,000 neutrophil-predominant leukocytes, or lymphocytes and red cells with normal glucose?
Transferable rule Identifying the complication of a syndrome takes two independent steps: name the syndrome, then its complication. When anatomic distribution and exposure history are both given, always rely on anatomic distribution.
Unchecked attributeCytomegalovirus and toxoplasmosis both follow a mild maternal flu-like illness, but neither produces cataracts or a cardiac defect. The maternal history is shared; the fetal organ pattern separates them.
Salient decoyToxoplasmosis: the indoor cat suggests it, but a cat is also compatible with cytomegalovirus.
True-fact-wrong-slotRubella: it causes cataracts, but not periventricular calcifications.
Salient decoyGroup B streptococcus: the antibiotics already begun point toward it, but neonatal bacterial meningitis gives low glucose and a neutrophil-predominant count, often over 1,000/mm3.
Unchecked attributeEscherichia coli: a common cause of neonatal meningitis, but a count of 70 that is mostly lymphocytes, with normal glucose, does not fit a bacterial cause.
True-fact-wrong-slotCytomegalovirus: symptomatic congenital infection shows at birth with periventricular calcifications and hearing loss, not as an acute encephalitis in the second week.
True-fact-wrong-slotToxoplasma gondii: congenital infection shows chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and diffuse calcifications, not a new encephalitis on day 8.

Neonatal Sepsis and Its Mimics

Afebrile neonate with leukopenia · the WBC decides when the temperature does not

Source vignette Pt — 3 do F, irritable and refusing feeds, HR 180, normothermic · Labs — WBC 3,000, glucose normal · Q — the most appropriate pharmacotherapy; options spanned ampicillin plus gentamicin, intravenous dextrose and morphine sulfate
The decision point

An afebrile 3-day-old has irritability, feeding refusal and tachycardia. NAS (neonatal abstinence syndrome), hypoglycemia and neonatal thyrotoxicosis share this entire behavioral pattern. The single value that separates sepsis from all three is a WBC (white blood cell count) of 3,000, which is leukopenia. NAS produces tremor with a normal WBC; a normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia; thyrotoxicosis requires a maternal Graves history. Leukopenia in a neonate reflects marrow depletion by overwhelming infection and is more ominous than leukocytosis. The empiric regimen is ampicillin plus gentamicin. Ampicillin covers GBS (group B Streptococcus) and Listeria, and gentamicin gives gram-negative coverage.

Defining criteria Early-onset neonatal sepsis — onset within 72 hours; organisms from the maternal genital tract (GBS, E. coli, Listeria) · Late-onset neonatal sepsis — onset 72 hours to 90 days; nosocomial organisms join (coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus) · Neonatal empiric coverage — ampicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime); ceftriaxone is avoided because it displaces bilirubin from albumin and causes biliary sludging
The irritable neonate — what decides the diagnosisleukopenia separates sepsis from the behavioral mimics
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Neonatal sepsis Can't missDay 0–7, maternal GBS or chorioamnionitis; subtle — poor feeding, temp instability, apnea, tachycardiaLeukopenia or leukocytosis with left shift; the neonate who “doesn’t look right”— (the answer)
Neonatal abstinence syndromeMaternal opioid use, onset 24–72 hHigh-pitched cry, tremor, sneezing, hyperactive Moro; normal WBCNo maternal drug history; leukopenia
Neonatal hypoglycemiaIDM, LGA, SGA, pretermJitteriness, lethargy, seizures; glucose <40–45Glucose normal
Neonatal thyrotoxicosisMaternal Graves diseaseTachycardia, irritability, exophthalmos, goiterNo maternal thyroid history; leukopenia
Inborn error of metabolismPoor feeding after protein or galactose, day 2–5Metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia, specific dietary triggerNo metabolic derangement described
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
CBC with differentialFirstLeukopenia, or leukocytosis with left shiftSepsis over the behavioral mimics; a low count is more ominous
Point-of-care glucoseFirstNormalExcludes hypoglycemia
Blood cultureConfirmsGrowth of GBS, E. coli or ListeriaSepsis and its organism; draw it, but do not delay antibiotics
Lumbar punctureNextCSF pleocytosisMeningitis; changes the length of treatment
Catheterized urine culture, after 72 hours of lifeBy branchGrowthUrinary source in late-onset sepsis
Ammonia and blood gasBy branchHyperammonemia with metabolic acidosisInborn error of metabolism

Scenario bank
  1. 3 do F, irritable, refusing feeds, HR 180, normothermic, WBC 3,000, glucose normal → Ampicillin and gentamicin → early-onset neonatal sepsis
  2. 2 do M, jittery, high-pitched cry, sneezing, hyperactive Moro reflex, maternal heroin use, WBC 12,000, glucose normal → Neonatal abstinence syndrome → supportive care, consider morphine if severe
  3. 1 do F, jittery, lethargic, glucose 28, mother with gestational diabetes → Intravenous dextrose infusion → neonatal hypoglycemia
  4. 4 do F, tachycardia, tremor, poor weight gain, exophthalmos, maternal Graves disease → Neonatal thyrotoxicosis → propranolol and methimazole
  5. 5 do M with confirmed neonatal sepsis; which antibiotic to avoid → Ceftriaxone → displaces bilirubin from albumin and causes biliary sludging
  6. 6 hr old M born to mother with chorioamnionitis, grunting with nasal flaring, HR 170 → Blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → early-onset GBS sepsis
  7. Most common organism causing early-onset neonatal sepsis in a term infant → Group B Streptococcus → intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
  8. 21 do M, fever 38.8, irritability, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle → Lumbar puncture with blood cultures and empiric ampicillin plus gentamicin → late-onset neonatal meningitis
Age-based empiric regimens Neonate (0–28 days) — ampicillin plus gentamicin (or cefotaxime), covering GBS (group B Streptococcus), E. coli and Listeria · Infant >28 days — ceftriaxone plus vancomycin; the neonatal organisms recede and ceftriaxone’s biliary risk becomes acceptable · Never ceftriaxone in a neonate — it displaces unconjugated bilirubin from albumin (kernicterus risk) and precipitates in the biliary tract. The under-28-day rule also means a well appearance does not reassure: full evaluation, admission and empiric antibiotics regardless of clinical impression.
Pearls Neonates with sepsis may be afebrile or hypothermic; fever is unreliable in the first month. Leukopenia is more ominous than leukocytosis because it signals marrow exhaustion · Early-onset organisms come from the maternal genital tract: GBS (group B Streptococcus), E. coli (K1 capsule), Listeria · Late-onset organisms add nosocomial flora: coagulase-negative staphylococci, S. aureus, Candida in VLBW (very low birth weight) infants · GBS prophylaxis (intrapartum penicillin) reduced early-onset GBS disease but did not change E. coli rates; E. coli now predominates among preterm and VLBW neonates · 5% weight loss at day 3 is physiologic (up to 7–10% in breastfed newborns)
Pairs with Part II The Febrile Infant — Finding the Source covers the source-identification algorithm and the under-28-day rule. Ask: is the neonate febrile, or is the lab the only sign? Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the cerebrospinal fluid grid and the neonatal organism-by-host list.
Transferable rule In a neonate, the absence of fever does not exclude sepsis. Without fever, the laboratory results decide, and leukopenia in a newborn is sepsis until proven otherwise. With no fever and no maternal drug history, the WBC (white blood cell count) decides, not the behavioral pattern.
Salient decoyNAS (neonatal abstinence syndrome) or hypoglycemia: irritability and poor feeding fit either, but leukopenia fits neither.
Class-vs-memberCeftriaxone and vancomycin: the right class of empiric coverage at the wrong age; neonates get ampicillin plus gentamicin.
True-fact-wrong-slotPropranolol: it treats neonatal thyrotoxicosis, but thyrotoxicosis does not produce leukopenia.

Fever, Rash and Joint Pain: Name the Rash, Then Date the Exposure

Hives mid-course of an antibiotic, or a face-first pink rash in the unvaccinated

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line
  • Itchy hives, low fever, nodes and tender but unswollen joints 5 to 14 days into a drug (penicillins, cefaclor, TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole)): serum sickness-like reaction. Stop the drug; it resolves. More common in children than serum sickness, and milder.
  • Same timing after a foreign protein (antivenom, antitoxin, monoclonal antibody), with high fever and low complement: serum sickness.
  • Fine pink rash from face to feet within 24 hours, palms and soles spared, posterior auricular and suboccipital nodes, unvaccinated and well: rubella. In teenage girls and women, finger and wrist pain may last up to a month.
  • Swollen, hot, migratory joints, carditis or erythema marginatum 2 to 4 weeks after an untreated sore throat: rheumatic fever (extremely rare after prompt penicillin).

Sexual history decides two rashes: pustules with tenosynovitis (gonococcus) and a rash on the palms and soles (secondary syphilis).

Diagnosis
Name the rash
DiagnosisRashTell
Serum sickness-like reactionItchy hives lasting over 24 hours; mucosa sparedTender, unswollen joints; nodes; mild proteinuria possible
RubellaFine pink maculopapular, face to feet within 24 hours; palms, soles sparedLow fever; posterior auricular, suboccipital nodes
MeaslesFace first, spreads over days, confluentFever 40 °C or more; cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; ill; no joint pain
VaricellaItchy vesicles in cropsNo joint pain
EBV (Epstein-Barr virus)Mainly after a beta-lactamExudative pharyngitis; posterior nodes
Disseminated gonococcal infectionA few painless vesiculopustules on distal limbs, rarely the faceTenosynovitis and migratory joint pain, or one hot, swollen knee; sexually active
Secondary syphilisMaculopapular, including palms and solesGeneralized nodes, condylomata lata
Acute rheumatic feverErythema marginatum: faint, non-itchy pink rings with clear centers, trunkSwollen, hot, migratory large joints; carditis
Scarlet feverSandpaper papules, flexural linesWith the sore throat; strawberry tongue
IgA (immunoglobulin A) vasculitisPalpable purpura, buttocks and legsNormal platelets; abdominal pain; hematuria
Stevens-Johnson syndromePainful dusky macules that blister, days to weeks into a drugHemorrhagic oral erosions; skin hurts rather than itches
Management and treatment
By situation Serum sickness-like reaction – stop the drug if still taken; antihistamine and NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); avoid the drug afterward; epinephrine only for airway, breathing or blood-pressure compromise · Rubella – supportive care, NSAIDs for the joints; keep away from pregnant contacts (miscarriage, stillbirth, congenital rubella syndrome)
Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy, 2 days of fever, itchy spreading rash sore wrists and ankles strep throat 9 days ago; oral penicillin ends tomorrow Hives on arms and back T 38.8 °C · nodes: neck, axillae, groin · joints tender, not swollen or red → Serum sickness-like reaction → hives with tender, unswollen joints and nodes 5 to 14 days into a drug is a serum sickness-like reaction: stop the penicillin; rheumatic fever has swollen migratory joints and is extremely rare after treated strep, and scarlet fever has no hives or joint pain
  2. 16-year-old girl, unvaccinated, pink maculopapular rash since yesterday face first, now trunk, limbs; palms, soles spared finger, wrist pain since this morning; tired; no stiff neck inconsistent condom use Postauricular, suboccipital nodes; clear throat T 38.2 °C · well · rash blanches → Rubella virus → a fine rash from face to limbs within a day, sparing palms and soles, with posterior auricular and suboccipital nodes and finger arthralgia in an unvaccinated, well teenager is rubella; gonococcal pustules rarely reach the face, and measles makes the patient ill with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, without joint pain
  3. 14-year-old boy, 10 days after antivenom for a rattlesnake bite urticarial rash for 2 days knee and wrist pain, worse with movement Feels unwell; no wheeze or lip swelling T 39.5 °C · urine protein 2+ · serum complement low → Serum sickness → high fever, hives, joint pain and low complement 5 to 14 days after a foreign protein is serum sickness: immune complexes against the antivenom
  4. 7-year-old girl on day 8 of amoxicillin for otitis media 1 day of itchy wheals on trunk, limbs ankle and wrist pain, worse with movement; joints not swollen No wheeze; lips and tongue normal T 38.1 °C · blood pressure normal → Stop amoxicillin and give an oral antihistamine → a serum sickness-like reaction: stop the amoxicillin and give an oral antihistamine; epinephrine only for airway, breathing or blood-pressure compromise
  5. 11-year-old boy with 5 days of fever hot, swollen right knee, then left elbow as the knee settles sore throat 3 weeks ago, not treated Faint, non-itchy pink rings with clear centers on trunk T 38.6 °C · ASO titer elevated → Acute rheumatic fever → migratory polyarthritis and erythema marginatum 2 to 4 weeks after untreated pharyngitis, with strep evidence, is acute rheumatic fever; Lyme arthritis is a single large joint months after erythema migrans
  6. 17-year-old girl, 3 days of fever pain over the backs of both wrists and hands with finger extension painful, swollen right knee Five small pustules on forearms and ankles T 38.4 °C · sexually active, no condoms · vaccinations up to date → Disseminated gonococcal infection → tenosynovitis, a few pustules and a swollen knee in a sexually active teen is disseminated gonococcal infection: aspirate the knee, NAAT of genital, pharyngeal and rectal sites, blood cultures, then ceftriaxone
  7. 15-year-old girl, never vaccinated, with a fine pink rash began on the face; reached the legs within a day palms and soles spared; sore finger joints Suboccipital nodes; oropharynx clear T 38.0 °C · no conjunctivitis or cough → Rubella IgM serology → a face-to-feet rash within a day with suboccipital nodes and finger arthralgia in an unvaccinated teen is rubella: confirm with rubella IgM
  8. 5-year-old boy who finished amoxicillin for otitis media 6 days ago raised, nonblanching purple spots on buttocks and legs painful, swollen ankles Colicky abdominal pain T 37.9 °C · platelet count normal → IgA vasculitis → palpable purpura on the buttocks and legs with normal platelets, joint pain and colicky abdominal pain is IgA vasculitis, not a drug reaction: check a urinalysis
Pairs with Acute Rheumatic Fever: Jones criteria, the strep clock, and Lyme arthritis among its mimics. Bruising and Purpura in a Child: IgA vasculitis. Tick-Borne Illness: erythema migrans. Fever and Rash in a Child: rash and fever without joint pain. Genital Ulcers: the chancre before secondary syphilis. Anaphylaxis: the minutes-not-days reaction.
Transferable rule

When a triad is shared, classify the most specific finding first (here the rash), then put it on a clock against the exposure.

Fever and Rash in a Child

Itchy vesicles in crops at different stages · what is the lesion, where did it start, and how did it relate to the fever?

Source vignette Pt — 3 yo M, 2 days of fever and poor appetite; a maculopapular rash on the trunk and face yesterday turned vesicular, and a new small group of vesicles appeared on the arms and legs this morning; intensely itchy; playful and drinking; vaccines up to date; attends day care; recent 2-week trip to South Africa · Exam — T 38.2; mild diffuse maculopapular rash with scattered vesicles on the face and hands; mucous membranes normal · Q — the most likely explanation for the findings; options spanned eczema herpeticum, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, roseola, rubella, scabies and varicella
The decision point

Name the lesion first, then ask where it started and how it related to the fever. Itchy macules, papules and vesicles arriving in successive crops show several stages side by side. When they start on the trunk and face and spread to the limbs after a short febrile prodrome, the diagnosis is varicella. The other common exanthems are not vesicular. Measles and rubella are maculopapular and spread head to toe; roseola appears as the fever breaks. Erythema infectiosum is slapped cheeks then a lacy rash, and scarlet fever is sandpaper with a sore throat.

Being up to date on vaccines does not exclude varicella at age 3. The child has had only the first of two doses (ages 1 and 4). This child's lower fever and fewer lesions fit breakthrough varicella, which is milder.

Rash with fever in a child: the differential
DiagnosisLesion and spreadProdrome and appearanceThe NBME tell
Varicella (VZV)Itchy macules, papules, vesicles, then crusts, in successive crops; trunk and face, then limbsFever and malaise for about 2 days, or rash first; well-appearingVesicles at different stages at the same time
Measles (paramyxovirus)Maculopapular, face to trunk, spares palms and soles; confluentHigh fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis; ill-appearing; unvaccinatedKoplik spots: gray-white spots on a red buccal base
RubellaMaculopapular, face first, head to toe, spares palms and soles; discrete pink spotsMild fever; well-appearing; unvaccinated; arthralgia in adolescents and adultsPosterior auricular and suboccipital nodes
Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19)Slapped cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, then a lacy reticular rash on trunk and limbsMild cold-like prodrome that has passed; well-appearingRash comes and goes with sun, heat or stress
Roseola (HHV-6)Maculopapular, trunk first, then face and limbs3 to 4 days of high fever in an infant or toddler; well-appearingRash appears as the fever breaks; febrile seizures
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease (coxsackievirus)Macules, papules and vesicles on palms and soles, sometimes buttocks and limbsFever; painful mouth, poor drinkingOral ulcers with palm and sole lesions
Scarlet fever (group A Streptococcus, the one bacterial exanthem here)Fine, rough sandpaper papules on the neck and trunk, worst in skin folds (axillae, groin); circumoral pallor; peels as it fadesSchool age; fever and sore throat with exudative tonsils and palatal petechiae; tender anterior cervical nodesStrawberry tongue with pharyngitis; confirm with a rapid strep antigen test or throat culture; penicillin or amoxicillin
Kawasaki diseasePolymorphous rash; red, swollen hands and feet, then fingertip peelingFever for 5 days or more plus 4 of 5: conjunctivitis, lip and oral changes, rash, extremity changes, a cervical node over 1.5 cm; usually under 5Nonexudative conjunctivitis and the fever count; strep testing negative
Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)Maculopapular rash, classically after amoxicillinExudative pharyngitis, fatigue, splenomegaly; adolescentPosterior cervical nodes; heterophile antibody positive

Eczema herpeticum (HSV)Painful, uniform vesicles and punched-out erosionsFever; illClustered on atopic dermatitis

Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo M, 2 days of fever and poor appetite; a maculopapular rash on the trunk and face yesterday became vesicular, and a new small group of vesicles appeared on the arms and legs today; intensely itchy; playful and drinking; vaccines up to date; attends day care; recent trip to South Africa; T 38.2; scattered vesicles on the face and hands among maculopapular lesions; mouth normal → Varicella → breakthrough disease after one vaccine dose; supportive care
  2. 6 yo F, well-appearing and afebrile, had a runny nose and low-grade fever last week; now bright red cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds and a lacy, net-like pink rash on the arms and thighs that brightens after a warm bath; no sore throat; vaccines up to date → Erythema infectiosum → parvovirus B19; no longer contagious
  3. 7 yo M with erythema infectiosum: slapped cheeks 3 days ago, now a lacy rash on the limbs; afebrile and playful; no chronic illness; his mother asks when he can return to school → Return to school now → parvovirus is not contagious once the rash appears
  4. 4 yo F whose parents declined vaccines, 3 days of fever to 40 C with cough, runny nose and red watery eyes, then a maculopapular rash that began at the hairline and spread down to the trunk; ill-appearing; small gray-white spots on a red base on the buccal mucosa → Measles → airborne precautions; vitamin A if severe
  5. 8 yo healthy boy whose family declined vaccines and who has never had chickenpox; a classmate developed chickenpox 3 days ago; afebrile, no rash → Varicella vaccine now → within 5 days of exposure it can prevent or soften the illness
  6. 6 yo F with acute lymphoblastic leukemia on chemotherapy, varicella IgG negative; her brother developed chickenpox 7 days ago; she is afebrile with no rash → Varicella-zoster immune globulin now → immunocompromised and within the 10-day window
  7. 4 yo M with chickenpox, rash began 4 days ago; afebrile and eating well; most lesions crusted, but two new vesicles appeared on the trunk this morning; his parents ask when he can return to day care → Keep him home until every lesion has crusted → contagious until all lesions crust
  8. 3 yo healthy girl with 2 days of low-grade fever and itchy vesicles in crops on the trunk, face and scalp, some crusted; playful and drinking well; no chronic illness → Supportive care with an oral antihistamine → acyclovir is for high-risk or complicated varicella
  9. 10 yo M, immunized, with 2 days of fever, headache and sore throat, then since yesterday a rough, fine, blanching papular rash on the anterior trunk that is most intense in the axillae and groin; T 38.3 C, HR 108; tired but playful; tender anterior cervical nodes; red pharynx with tonsillar exudates and palatal petechiae; several classmates had the same illness and are now peeling → Scarlet fever → Group A strep; rapid strep antigen test or throat culture, then penicillin or amoxicillin
  10. 3 yo M, vaccines up to date, with 6 days of fever to 39.8 C, bilateral red eyes without discharge, cracked red lips, a strawberry tongue, swollen red hands and feet, a polymorphous truncal rash and a single 2-cm anterior cervical node; tonsils without exudate; rapid strep antigen test negative → Kawasaki disease → IVIG and high-dose aspirin, then echocardiography
  11. 10 yo F who recently immigrated from Central America, vaccine history not given; 5 days of low-grade fever, fatigue, mild itching and a mild runny nose, then 1 day of a rash that began on the face and now covers the body; no abdominal pain or diarrhea; T 37.8 C; discrete maculopapular lesions on the face, trunk, back and limbs; no eye or mouth lesions → Measles-mumps-rubella → it prevents both measles and rubella; the low fever, discrete spots and absent conjunctivitis fit rubella better than measles
  12. 7 yo F who recently moved from abroad with no vaccine records; 2 days of low-grade fever and a mild runny nose, then pink, discrete maculopapular spots that began on the face and spread to the trunk and limbs within a day; well-appearing; T 37.9 C; tender posterior auricular and suboccipital nodes; eyes and buccal mucosa normal → Rubella → mild illness with posterior nodes; the MMR vaccine prevents it
Varicella postexposure Immune — prior chickenpox or 2 vaccine doses: observe only · Not immune, immunocompetent — age 1 or older and not pregnant: varicella vaccine within 5 days of exposure; after day 5 give it anyway for future protection, but it no longer prevents this infection · Not immune and high risk — immunocompromised, pregnant, or a newborn whose mother's rash began 5 days before to 2 days after delivery: VariZIG within 10 days; the live vaccine is contraindicated in the first two
Varicella management Diagnosis — clinical; VZV PCR of a vesicle only when the picture is atypical · Treatment — supportive with antihistamines for a healthy child; acyclovir for high-risk patients (adolescents, adults, immunocompromised, newborns, pregnant) or complicated disease · Contagious — from the prodrome until every lesion has crusted; airborne and contact precautions until then · Complications — secondary bacterial skin infection, pneumonia, encephalitis
Pearls Varicella vaccine is 2 doses, at ages 1 and 4; a vaccinated preschooler has had one, so breakthrough disease is still on the list · Parvovirus B19 is no longer contagious once the rash appears, because the rash is immune mediated; the child can stay in school · Parvovirus infects red cell precursors, so a child with sickle cell disease or hereditary spherocytosis can develop transient aplastic crisis: falling hemoglobin with a low reticulocyte count · Measles needs airborne precautions (N95 and an isolation room); give vitamin A in severe cases · Diagnosis of the viral exanthems is clinical; serology or PCR is for severe or atypical cases · Scarlet fever is the bacterial exception: a sandpaper rash with pharyngitis needs a rapid strep test or throat culture and then penicillin or amoxicillin; the rash itself needs no separate treatment · Peeling does not make it scalded skin syndrome: scarlet fever desquamates as it fades, while SSSS begins with flaccid bullae in a young child
Which vaccine prevents it Face-first maculopapular rash that spreads down — measles or rubella; the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine prevents both · Schedule — MMR is a live attenuated vaccine given in 2 doses, at 12 to 15 months and at 4 to 6 years · Itching — mild itching does not make a rash varicella; varicella needs vesicles in crops
How NBME framed it The lead-in asked which vaccine would have prevented the rash, so MMR was the answer whether the illness was measles or rubella. The options listed the routine childhood vaccines plus one travel vaccine, typhoid.
Pairs with Part I Oral Lesions in a Child covers hand-foot-and-mouth disease and the oral vesicles. Ask: are the lesions in the mouth, and front or back? Part II Fever, Rash and Joint Pain: Name the Rash, Then Date the Exposure covers rubella with arthralgia. Ask: are there posterior auricular nodes in an unvaccinated patient? Part II Congenital Infections (TORCH) covers parvovirus in pregnancy (hydrops) and congenital rubella. Vaccines in Pregnancy covers varicella exposure in a pregnant patient. Seizure with Fever in a Child covers the seizure that roseola can bring. Atopic Dermatitis covers eczema herpeticum, and Scabies covers the afebrile itchy mimic. Part I Kawasaki Disease covers the fever-for-5-days criteria that separate it from scarlet fever. Ask: how many days of fever, and is the throat exudative?
Transferable rule For a child with fever and rash, classify the lesion (vesicles in crops, maculopapular, lacy, sandpaper). Then check where it began and whether it came with or after the fever. For a varicella exposure, check immunity, then risk group, then the days since exposure (5 for vaccine, 10 for VariZIG).
Unchecked attributeHand-foot-and-mouth disease: vesicles on the hands fit, but the mouth is normal and the lesions are on the trunk, face and limbs in crops rather than centered on palms and soles.
Unchecked attributeRoseola: fever then rash in a toddler, but its rash is maculopapular, never vesicular, and appears after the fever breaks rather than during it.
Class-vs-memberEczema herpeticum: a vesicular viral rash, but it needs underlying atopic dermatitis and its vesicles are painful and uniform, not itchy crops.
Unchecked attributeRubella: face-first spread in a febrile child, but it is maculopapular without vesicles, and this child is vaccinated.
True-fact-wrong-slotScabies: intensely itchy, but no fever, and it favors finger webs, wrists and the periumbilical skin.
Salient decoyThe trip to South Africa suggests a travel infection, but day care and a single vaccine dose explain all the findings.
True-fact-wrong-slotDiphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis vaccine: a routine childhood vaccine that a recent immigrant may have missed; diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis do not cause a spreading maculopapular rash.
True-fact-wrong-slotHaemophilus influenzae type b vaccine: another routine vaccine she may have missed; this organism causes epiglottitis, meningitis and pneumonia, not a face-first rash.
True-fact-wrong-slotHepatitis B vaccine: a routine infant vaccine she may have missed; acute hepatitis B brings right upper quadrant pain and nausea, and she has no abdominal symptoms.
True-fact-wrong-slotInactivated poliovirus vaccine: a routine vaccine she may have missed abroad; polio causes flaccid paralysis, not a rash.
True-fact-wrong-slotPneumococcal vaccine: a routine childhood vaccine she may have missed; pneumococcus causes otitis media, pneumonia and meningitis, not a viral exanthem.
Unchecked attributeInfluenza vaccine: fever, fatigue and a runny nose fit influenza; influenza does not typically cause a rash.
Salient decoyTyphoid vaccine: fever and a rash in a child from Central America suggest typhoid rose spots; she has no abdominal pain or diarrhea, and her rash began on the face and covers the whole body.
Unchecked attributeVaricella vaccine: itching and a whole-body rash suggest chickenpox; her lesions are discrete maculopapules with no vesicles.

Anaphylaxis

Swollen eyes, a tight throat and cramps half an hour after a new amoxicillin prescription · how many organ systems, and how soon after the exposure?

Source vignette Pt — 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; seen earlier the same day for several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies · Exam — T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk · Q — the pathogenesis of his symptoms; options spanned Epstein-Barr virus infection, immune complex formation, impaired bradykinin degradation, mast cell activation and systemic vasculitis
The decision point

Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis based on the number of organ systems involved and the time since exposure; hypotension is not required. Within minutes to hours of a likely allergen, skin or mucosal findings plus one more system (respiratory, gastrointestinal or cardiovascular) meet criteria. This boy has wheals and periorbital swelling (skin), throat tightness (respiratory) and cramps (gut) 30 minutes after amoxicillin. He therefore has anaphylaxis despite a normal blood pressure. The mechanism is IgE-mediated mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, prostaglandins and leukotrienes. A history of no known drug allergies does not argue against it. An earlier exposure sensitized him without a reaction, and re-exposure triggers the release.

The exception is angioedema without hives. Swelling of the lips, tongue, face or bowel wall with no wheals and no itch from an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or hereditary angioedema is bradykinin-mediated. It builds over hours and responds poorly to epinephrine and antihistamines. Rashes that arrive days into a drug or an infection are delayed reactions, not anaphylaxis.

Defining criteria Anaphylaxis is likely with acute onset (minutes to hours) and any 1 of: · 1 — skin or mucosal involvement (hives, flushing, swollen lips, tongue or eyes) plus respiratory compromise or hypotension · 2 — 2 or more systems after a likely allergen: skin or mucosa, respiratory, cardiovascular, persistent gastrointestinal symptoms · 3 — hypotension alone after a known allergen for that patient
Anaphylaxis and its mimics — the differential
DiagnosisTiming after exposureMechanismThe NBME tell
AnaphylaxisMinutes to a few hoursIgE-mediated mast cell activation (type I)Skin plus a second system: wheeze, stridor, throat tightness, vomiting or cramps, hypotension
Acute urticaria aloneMinutes to hoursMast cell activation, often IgEHives and itch with no second system; normal airway, gut and blood pressure
Bradykinin angioedema (ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema)Hours; ACE inhibitor reactions can start months or years into therapyImpaired bradykinin degradation (ACE inhibitor); C1 inhibitor deficiency (hereditary, low C4)Lip, tongue or bowel-wall swelling with no hives or itch; little response to epinephrine or antihistamines
Serum sickness-like reaction5 to 14 days into a drugDelayed drug hypersensitivity; true serum sickness is immune complexUrticarial rash with fever, arthralgia and nodes
Epstein-Barr virus with an aminopenicillinDays into amoxicillinVirus-driven drug rash, not IgEMaculopapular rash with fever, exudative pharyngitis, posterior nodes, LUQ pain
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritisDays to weeks after pharyngitisImmune complex (type III)Edema building over days with hypertension and cola-colored urine
Systemic vasculitis (IgA vasculitis)DaysImmune complex vessel inflammationPalpable purpura, fever, arthralgia, colicky abdominal pain
Vasovagal syncopeSeconds, with pain or fear (needles)Vagal surgeBradycardia, pallor and sweating; no hives, no wheeze
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo M, 30 minutes of burning, swollen eyes, a scratchy, tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; earlier today diagnosed with pharyngitis after several days of sore throat and started on amoxicillin; no known drug allergies; T 37.2, BP 116/68, HR 92; bilateral periorbital swelling, mild conjunctival redness, scattered wheals on the trunk → Mast cell activation → anaphylaxis: skin, respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement within 30 minutes of amoxicillin, after sensitization by an earlier course; IM epinephrine
  2. 7 yo F at a birthday party, 10 minutes after eating a cookie made with peanut butter, develops hives on the face and trunk, wheezing and 2 episodes of vomiting; no previous reactions to food; T 37.0, BP 98/60, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 94% on room air; diffuse expiratory wheezes → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylaxis by skin plus respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement; blood pressure need not fall
  3. 9 yo M, itchy raised wheals on the trunk and arms 1 hour after eating strawberries for the first time this season; no lip or tongue swelling, throat symptoms, cough, vomiting or abdominal pain; BP 104/66, HR 90, SpO2 99%; lungs clear; blanching urticarial plaques → Oral cetirizine → acute urticaria alone: one system, so criteria for anaphylaxis are not met
  4. 15 yo M treated in the emergency department for hives, throat tightness and wheezing 20 minutes after eating cashews, his first reaction to food; one dose of intramuscular epinephrine was given, and after 6 hours of observation he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs and clear lungs → Epinephrine autoinjector prescription → anaphylaxis, observed for a biphasic reaction; discharge with self-injectable epinephrine, an action plan, avoidance and allergy referral
  5. 58 yo M with hypertension and diabetes, 6 hours of progressive swelling of the lips and tongue; no itching, hives, wheezing or abdominal pain; takes lisinopril, which he started 2 years ago, and metformin; no new foods or medications; swelling did not improve after intramuscular epinephrine and diphenhydramine → Impaired bradykinin degradation → ACE inhibitor angioedema: no urticaria and little response to epinephrine; stop the ACE inhibitor permanently
  6. 16 yo F with recurrent episodes over 3 years of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the hands, face and once the throat, each lasting 2 to 3 days, and separate episodes of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes no medications; her mother has similar episodes; antihistamines and epinephrine have not helped; examination between episodes is normal → Serum C4 level → hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency; low C4, bradykinin-mediated, so epinephrine disappoints
  7. 17 yo F, 5 days of fever, sore throat and fatigue, treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep pharyngitis; 4 days later, a diffuse, mildly itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs; T 38.4, BP 112/70; tonsillar exudates, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, left upper quadrant tenderness; no wheals, no lip swelling, lungs clear → Infectious mononucleosis → an aminopenicillin rash during Epstein-Barr virus infection; not an IgE-mediated penicillin allergy
  8. 34 yo F with a known severe shellfish allergy becomes lightheaded 15 minutes after eating a dish she later learns contained shrimp; no rash, flushing, lip swelling, wheeze or vomiting; BP 76/44, HR 132, warm extremities; lungs clear → Anaphylaxis → hypotension alone after a known allergen meets criteria; give IM epinephrine
  9. 22 yo F with recurrent episodes since adolescence of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the lips and one hand lasting 2 to 3 days, the latest starting the day after a dental extraction; separate bouts of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes a combined oral contraceptive and no other medications; her father has similar episodes; epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the emergency department did not help; serum C4 low → C1 inhibitor deficiency → hereditary angioedema: bradykinin-mediated swelling without urticaria; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function
  10. 19 yo M with known hereditary angioedema, 4 hours of progressive swelling of the face and tongue with a hoarse voice after a facial injury in a basketball game; no stridor; SpO2 98% on room air; no hives; no improvement after intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous diphenhydramine → Intravenous C1 inhibitor concentrate → acute HAE attack with laryngeal involvement: give specific therapy and be ready to secure the airway
  11. 45 yo F with hereditary angioedema, low C4 and a family history, now with blood pressure 152/96 on three separate visits; no diabetes or kidney disease → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown and provoke attacks
Management First — IM epinephrine in the anterolateral thigh, 0.01 mg/kg of the 1 mg/mL solution (max 0.5 mg adult, 0.3 mg child); lie the patient flat with legs raised · Repeat — every 5 to 15 minutes if symptoms persist; persistent hypotension gets isotonic fluid boluses and then an epinephrine infusion; glucagon if the patient takes a beta-blocker · Adjuncts only — H1 and H2 antihistamines for itch and hives, albuterol for residual wheeze, glucocorticoids; none of them treats airway obstruction or shock, and none replaces or delays epinephrine · Observe — for a biphasic reaction, symptoms returning hours later without re-exposure; typically 4 to 6 hours ⚠︎, longer after a severe reaction · Discharge — epinephrine autoinjector with training and an action plan, avoidance of the trigger, and allergy referral
Hereditary angioedema Mechanism — autosomal dominant C1 inhibitor deficiency; unchecked kallikrein makes excess bradykinin · The tell — recurrent nonpitting swelling of the face, lips, limbs or bowel wall (colicky abdominal attacks) with no urticaria and no itch, often with a family history · Triggers — dental work, trauma, stress, estrogen (oral contraceptives, pregnancy) · Avoid — ACE inhibitors, which block bradykinin breakdown and worsen attacks · Tests — screen with C4 (low), confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function · Acute attack — secure the airway if the larynx is involved; give C1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor blocker) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor); epinephrine, antihistamines and steroids do not work
Pearls Waiting for hypotension is a deadly delay; in children hypotension is a late sign. Throat tightness or wheeze with hives is enough to give epinephrine · Diagnosis is clinical; a serum tryptase drawn early can support mast cell activation afterward but never delays treatment · Bradykinin swelling is the one angioedema in which epinephrine works poorly. Stop the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor for life, and check C4 when swelling recurs without a drug · Most childhood anaphylaxis is from food (peanut, tree nuts, milk, egg); insect stings and drugs such as beta-lactams follow
Pairs with Part II Fever, Rash and Joint Pain: Name the Rash, Then Date the Exposure covers the serum sickness-like reaction: did the hives start 5 to 14 days into the drug, with joint pain? Part I Transfusion Reactions covers anaphylaxis during transfusion: is the recipient IgA deficient? Aquifer Shock in Children covers anaphylactic shock as a distributive subtype: is perfusion abnormal? Part I Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome), the non-IgE mimic: is it hours of vomiting without hives? Part I DTaP: Contraindication vs. Precaution covers anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose as a contraindication. Aquifer Child with Puffy Eyes places the acute allergic reaction among the other causes of swollen eyelids: is it one eye or both, and does the urine contain protein?
Transferable rule Skin or mucosal involvement plus any second system within minutes to hours of an exposure is anaphylaxis. Treat it with IM (intramuscular) epinephrine first. Swelling with no hives points to bradykinin. A rash that arrives days later points to a delayed drug or immune complex reaction.
Unchecked attributeImpaired bradykinin degradation: the swollen eyes suggest angioedema, but bradykinin swelling has no wheals or itch; he has wheals on the trunk plus throat and gut symptoms, which is mast cell release.
Unchecked attributeImmune complex formation: the sore throat invites poststreptococcal disease or serum sickness, but immune complexes take days to form; this began 30 minutes after the drug.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus infection: mononucleosis really does cause a rash after amoxicillin, but that rash is maculopapular, comes days later and brings fever and nodes; he is afebrile with wheals.
Salient decoySystemic vasculitis: crampy abdominal pain recalls IgA vasculitis, but vasculitis develops over days with fever and palpable purpura, not wheals within minutes.

Isolation Precautions

Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF of a shocked infant · how big is the particle, and who is being protected from whom?

Source vignette Pt — 8 mo M with fever and lethargy; BP 70/40; antibiotics started and admitted to the pediatric ICU · Labs — CSF Gram stain: gram-negative diplococci · Q — which isolation precautions to institute; options spanned airborne, contact, droplet, neutropenic and standard
The decision point

Choose the precaution by how the organism travels. Droplets are 5 microns or larger and fall within 3 to 6 feet, so a surgical mask within that range is enough. Droplet organisms include N. meningitidis, H. influenzae type b, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, influenza, adenovirus and pertussis. Airborne particles are under 5 microns and stay suspended, so they need an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room. Airborne organisms include tuberculosis, measles, varicella and SARS (severe acute respiratory syndrome). Contact organisms spread by hands and surfaces and need a gown and gloves. They include MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), C. difficile, E. coli O157:H7, scabies and RSV (respiratory syncytial virus). Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) are meningococcus. This infant therefore needs droplet precautions until 24 hours of effective antibiotics.

Standard precautions apply to every patient, so they are never the added precaution. Neutropenic precautions protect the patient from the environment rather than others from the patient.

Defining criteria Droplet — particles 5 microns or larger, fall within 3 to 6 feet · Airborne — particles under 5 microns, remain suspended and travel on air currents · Contact — spread by direct touch or contaminated surfaces · Neutropenic (protective) — shields an immunocompromised patient, usually severe neutropenia (ANC under 500)
Isolation precautions — the differential
PrecautionOrganismsGear and roomEnds when
StandardEvery patientHand hygiene; gloves, gown, mask or eye protection when contact with blood or body fluids is expectedNever; always in effect
DropletN. meningitidis, Hib, Mycoplasma, influenza, adenovirus, pertussis, mumps, rubellaSurgical mask within 3 to 6 feet; private roomMeningococcus and Hib: 24 hours of effective antibiotics; pertussis: 5 days of azithromycin ⚠︎
AirborneTuberculosis, measles, SARSN95 respirator and a negative-pressure single room; nonimmune staff stay out of measles roomsTB: 3 negative sputum AFB smears on therapy; measles: 4 days after rash onset ⚠︎
Airborne plus contactVaricella, disseminated zosterN95 and negative-pressure room, plus gown and glovesAll lesions crusted
ContactMRSA, VRE, C. difficile, E. coli O157:H7, scabies, RSVGown and gloves; dedicated equipment; soap and water for C. difficile because alcohol does not kill sporesSymptoms resolve (diarrhea stops for C. difficile)
NeutropenicProtects a patient with severe neutropenia (chemotherapy, stem cell transplant)Hand hygiene, private room with filtered air; no fresh flowers, plants or animals; no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositoriesNeutrophil count recovers
Scenario bank

  2. 2 yo M, unvaccinated, 4 days of fever to 40 C, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, then a maculopapular rash that began at the hairline and spread to the trunk; small gray-white spots on the buccal mucosa; admitted for dehydration → Airborne precautions → measles: N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room
  3. 3 yo F admitted with cellulitis of the thigh complicating chickenpox that began 3 days ago; several vesicles on the trunk and scalp have not yet crusted; T 38.9 → Airborne and contact precautions → varicella: N95, negative-pressure room, gown and gloves until every lesion has crusted
  4. 4 mo F admitted with 3 days of cough, rhinorrhea and increased work of breathing, SpO2 88% on room air; diffuse crackles and wheezes; nasal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus → Contact precautions → RSV spreads mainly by hands and contaminated surfaces: gown and gloves
  5. 8 yo M on clindamycin for an abscess develops 6 watery stools a day and cramping; stool PCR positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin; admitted for dehydration → Contact precautions with soap-and-water hand washing → alcohol-based rubs do not kill C. difficile spores
  6. 48 yo M with 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss, admitted with an upper lobe cavity on chest radiograph; sputum smear positive for acid-fast bacilli; four-drug therapy and airborne isolation were started 3 days ago → Three negative sputum AFB smears → active pulmonary TB: airborne isolation ends when three sputum smears are negative on effective therapy
  7. 6 yo F with acute lymphoblastic leukemia admitted during induction chemotherapy; afebrile; absolute neutrophil count 200/mm3; placed in a private room under neutropenic precautions → Rectal temperature measurement → neutropenic precautions protect the patient: no rectal thermometers, enemas or suppositories, no fresh flowers or plants
Management Meningococcal disease — droplet precautions for the first 24 hours of effective antibiotics, plus chemoprophylaxis (rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone) for close contacts: household, day care, and anyone exposed to oral secretions; staff need it only after unprotected exposure such as intubation without a mask · Suspected TB or measles — airborne isolation before the workup or treatment; a patient who must leave the room wears a surgical mask
Pearls Many respiratory viruses need contact plus droplet precautions, because they spread by both hands and large droplets; RSV (respiratory syncytial virus) is classically contact · For C. difficile, the hand-hygiene method matters: alcohol rub fails against spores · The 24-hour rule applies to meningococcus and Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b). TB (tuberculosis) isolation ends with negative smears, and varicella isolation ends with crusting · A patient with a rash and fever of unknown cause gets airborne and contact precautions until measles and varicella are excluded
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid, the organism by age and chemoprophylaxis: who counts as a close contact? Part II Fever and Rash in a Child covers measles and varicella, including postexposure prophylaxis: is the contact immune, and how long since exposure? Part I Tuberculosis covers the latent-versus-active distinction: is the radiograph abnormal or are there symptoms? Part II Scabies covers the contact-spread rash whose treatment includes the household.
Transferable rule Pick the precaution by the particle and the route. Large droplets that fall within 6 feet need a surgical mask. Small particles that hang in the air need an N95 and a negative-pressure room. Organisms on skin, stool or surfaces need a gown and gloves. Neutropenic precautions protect the patient rather than the staff.
Unchecked attributeAirborne precautions: the right idea, a respiratory route, with the wrong particle size; meningococcus travels in large droplets that fall within 3 to 6 feet, and airborne isolation is for TB, measles and varicella.
Salient decoyContact precautions: a septic, possibly petechial infant in the ICU feels like a gown-and-gloves patient, but meningococcus spreads by respiratory droplets, not by skin or surfaces.
True-fact-wrong-slotStandard precautions: they apply to every patient, including this one, but they are the baseline, not the transmission-based precaution the organism requires.
Unchecked attributeNeutropenic precautions: the direction is reversed; they protect an immunocompromised patient, and this infant is the source of infection.

Infectious Diarrhea

Fever and bloody stools after camp food · what did the patient eat, and does that organism need a blood culture or an antibiotic?

Source vignette Pt — 14-year-old girl with 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, today with fever and blood in the stool; home from a week-long summer camp, well while there; CVID on immunoglobulin replacement; sinusitis a month ago treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate · Exam — T 38.2 C, HR 102; mild diffuse tenderness, no peritoneal signs · Labs — stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella · Q — the most likely underlying cause of her illness; options spanned food handling, seafood, contaminated infusions, antibiotic disruption of gut flora and typhoid vaccine failure
The decision point

Identify the organism from the exposure. Nontyphoidal Salmonella comes from undercooked poultry and eggs. Food left unrefrigerated lets it multiply. Symptoms start within 3 days with fever, vomiting, cramps and diarrhea, which can be bloody in children. Camp food fits this source, and her stool culture confirms Salmonella.

The organism then determines the workup and treatment. Invasive diarrhea needs a stool culture. A fever-first illness after travel is typhoid and needs a blood culture. Most bacterial diarrhea needs only rehydration.

Timing gates 1 to 6 hours, vomiting first, no fever — preformed toxin: S aureus or B cereus · Within about 3 days, fever and diarrhea — invasive bacteria: nontyphoidal Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella; Shiga toxin E coli with little fever · Fever for days to weeks after travel, diarrhea minor — typhoid · During or after antibiotics, watery — C difficile
Diarrhea by source: the differential
OrganismSource and settingThe NBME tellTest and treatment
Nontyphoidal SalmonellaUndercooked poultry and eggs, poor refrigeration; reptiles and backyard poultryFever, vomiting, cramps; bloody stools possible in childrenStool culture; supportive; antibiotics only for infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia
Typhoid (S Typhi)Travel to areas with poor sanitation; contaminated food or waterFever and bacteremia first; abdominal pain, rose spots, relative bradycardia; later splenomegaly, intestinal perforationBlood culture; ceftriaxone; the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains
CampylobacterUndercooked poultry, unpasteurized milkFever, bloody diarrhea, pain that can mimic appendicitis; Guillain-Barre weeks laterStool culture; supportive unless severe or prolonged
Shiga toxin E coli (O157:H7)Undercooked ground beef, petting zoosBloody diarrhea with little fever; HUS about a week laterStool culture and Shiga toxin test; no antibiotics, no antimotility drugs
ShigellaDay care; spreads person to person from a very small inoculumHigh fever, bloody diarrhea, seizures in young childrenStool culture; azithromycin shortens illness and spread
Vibrio parahaemolyticusRaw or undercooked seafood, shellfishWatery diarrhea and cramps after raw oystersSupportive
S aureus and B cereus toxinToxin already in the food: S aureus in ham, mayonnaise or custard; B cereus in reheated riceVomiting within 1 to 6 hours, no fever, several diners illClinical; supportive
C difficileRecent antibioticsWatery diarrhea at onset, cramps, leukocytosisStool toxin or PCR; oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Stool culture, with Shiga toxin testing if bloodyFirstNames the organismFor fever with bloody diarrhea, immunocompromise, severe or prolonged illness, or an outbreak
Blood cultureBy branchS Typhi or other bacteremiaFever-first illness after travel, infants under 3 months, immunocompromise
C difficile toxin or PCRBy branchPositiveWatery diarrhea during or after antibiotics
Stool ova and parasites or Giardia antigenBy branchGiardiaProlonged watery, greasy diarrhea after untreated water; common in CVID and IgA deficiency
Stool studies for brief watery diarrhea without fever or bloodSkip Self-limited; rehydrate
Scenario bank
  1. 14-year-old girl with CVID on immunoglobulin replacement has 2 days of cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, and today fever and bloody stools; she just returned from a week-long summer camp; she took amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis a month ago; T 38.2 C, HR 102, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs; stool ova and parasites negative; stool culture grows Salmonella → Inadequate cooking and refrigeration of chicken and eggs → nontyphoidal Salmonella from undercooked poultry or eggs starts within 3 days, and warmth lets it multiply; bloody stools are common in children
  2. 10-year-old boy and his sister begin vomiting repeatedly 2 hours after a lunch of fried rice left out overnight from a takeout meal and reheated; mild cramps, no fever, no diarrhea yet; normal vital signs apart from mild tachycardia → Bacillus cereus food poisoning → vomiting within hours from a toxin already in the food; reheated rice is the classic source; supportive care
  3. 16-year-old boy develops watery diarrhea and abdominal cramps 18 hours after eating raw oysters at a coastal cookout; temperature 37.9 C; no blood in the stool; he ate no poultry or eggs → Vibrio parahaemolyticus infection → raw or undercooked shellfish; self-limited, supportive care
  4. 6-year-old girl has 2 days of crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody diarrhea 3 days after eating an undercooked hamburger at a barbecue; temperature 37.4 C; mildly dry mucous membranes; stool testing for Shiga toxin is pending → Oral azithromycin → antibiotics and antimotility drugs raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome in Shiga toxin E coli infection; rehydrate and watch hemoglobin, platelets and creatinine
  5. 17-year-old girl returned 12 days ago from visiting family in rural South Asia; for 6 days she has had fever rising to 39.8 C, headache, abdominal pain and constipation; heart rate 82 at that temperature; faint pink macules on the upper abdomen; she is alert and hemodynamically stable → Blood cultures → typhoid presents as fever and bacteremia; the blood culture confirms it before empiric ceftriaxone
  6. 6-week-old boy has 1 day of fever to 38.4 C and loose stools with streaks of blood; both parents had fever and diarrhea after a family picnic with undercooked chicken; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella; he feeds well and is well hydrated → Blood culture and antibiotic therapy → infants under 3 months with Salmonella are at risk of bacteremia and meningitis, so they are treated
  7. 11-year-old girl has 3 days of fever, cramps and loose stools with some blood after a summer barbecue where chicken was undercooked; she is otherwise healthy; today she is afebrile, drinking well, and her stools are fewer; stool culture grows nontyphoidal Salmonella → Oral rehydration and supportive care → antibiotics do not shorten uncomplicated nontyphoidal Salmonella in a healthy child and prolong carriage
Management Rehydrate first — oral rehydration for nearly everyone · Antibiotics only for — typhoid; Shigella; C difficile; nontyphoidal Salmonella in infants under 3 months, immunocompromise, sickle cell disease or bacteremia, since treating others prolongs carriage · Suspected Shiga toxin E coli — never antibiotics or antimotility drugs, which raise the risk of HUS
Pearls Exposures to know: a pet turtle, reheated rice, raw oysters, a hamburger · Humoral immunodeficiency such as CVID (common variable immunodeficiency) raises the risk of Salmonella, Campylobacter and Giardia infection; it does not change which food carries which organism · A vaccine exists for typhoid, not for nontyphoidal Salmonella · In sickle cell disease, Salmonella is the organism of osteomyelitis, which is why these children are treated
Pairs with Part I Antibody Deficiencies covers CVID (common variable immunodeficiency): are IgG and at least one other isotype low, with poor vaccine responses? Part I Right Lower Quadrant Pain covers Campylobacter and Yersinia pseudoappendicitis and its list of who gets antibiotics: is the pain from the appendix or the ileocecum? Part I Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers HUS (hemolytic uremic syndrome), which follows Shiga toxin E coli infection: is a second cell line down a week after bloody diarrhea? Part II Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers Salmonella osteomyelitis: is it trait or disease?
Transferable rule In infectious diarrhea, name the organism from the exposure and the timing. That organism then determines the culture and whether to treat. A risk factor for a different organism is not the exposure.
Salient decoyAntibiotic disruption of gut flora: the recent amoxicillin-clavulanate is real, but it predisposes to C difficile, which starts watery; the culture grew Salmonella.
Class-vs-memberTyphoid vaccine failure: the vaccine covers only typhoidal strains, and there is no vaccine for nontyphoidal Salmonella; CVID blunting the response does not matter here.
True-fact-wrong-slotRaw or unrefrigerated seafood: a real foodborne source, but of Vibrio parahaemolyticus, not Salmonella.
Salient decoyContaminated immunoglobulin infusions: rare, and they cause bacteremia with high fever and chills found on blood culture, not gastroenteritis with a positive stool culture.
2 briefsAquifer · Case-Based Briefs

Infectious Disease

The Febrile Infant — Finding the Source

Paradoxical irritability · every stem negative is an eliminated source

Source vignette Pt — 7 mo M, fever 39.5 C, lies quietly when undisturbed and cries violently when picked up · Labs — WBC 16,000 with 83% neutrophils; urine dipstick negative on a concentrated specimen · Q — the most appropriate test; options spanned lumbar puncture, abdominal ultrasonography and stool PCR
The decision point

On examination, he is calm when left alone and screams when picked up. This is paradoxical irritability: handling stretches inflamed meninges, so being comforted makes an infant worse. It is the meningeal sign of infancy because nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable under roughly 12 to 18 months.

No cough or rhinorrhea closes the respiratory branch. A negative leukocyte esterase and nitrite in urine concentrated to a specific gravity of 1.030 closes the urinary branch. The concentration is what makes the negative trustworthy. When the sources are eliminated one by one and a meningeal sign remains, do a lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Paradoxical irritability — quiet when undisturbed, crying on being picked up or moved · Fever without a source — documented fever with no localising findings after history and examination · Dipstick sensitivity — leukocyte esterase about 83%, nitrite about 53%; both negative in concentrated urine is genuinely reassuring
The toxic febrile infant — where is the source
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Bacterial meningitisAny age; infants show no neck signsParadoxical irritability, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry
Intussusception6 to 36 months, ileocolic, often post-viralParoxysmal crying with pain-free intervals, sausage mass, currant-jelly stool
Urinary tract infectionThe commonest serious bacterial infection in febrile infantsPositive leukocyte esterase or nitrite with pyuria
Bacterial gastroenteritisHigh fever with crampingBloody or mucoid stools, many per day, sick contacts
Viral respiratory infectionCough, congestion, coryzaRhinorrhea and cough, both explicitly absent here
Occult bacteremia or pneumoniaFever with leukocytosis, no localising signTachypnea with hypoxia or focal crackles, not fever-driven tachypnea alone
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Catheterized urinalysisFirstLeukocyte esterase and nitrite negative in concentrated urineUrinary source unlikely; positive: urine culture and antibiotics
CBC and blood cultureFirstLeukocytosis with neutrophil predominanceBacterial infection likely; does not locate the source
Head CTBy branchFocal deficit or papilledema: image first, after antibioticsAn open fontanelle usually permits a tap without imaging
Lumbar puncture: cell count, glucose, Gram stain, cultureConfirmsNeutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, positive cultureBacterial meningitis; give antibiotics first if the tap is delayed
Abdominal ultrasoundBy branchParoxysmal crying with a sausage mass: target signIntussusception
Stool PCR for enteric pathogensSkipLoose stools are nonspecific in a septic infantNot a localizing source
Scenario bank
  1. 7 mo M, fever 39.5, lies quietly when undisturbed and cries violently when picked up, WBC 16,000 with 83% neutrophils, urine dipstick negative in concentrated urine → Lumbar puncture for Gram stain and culture → bacterial meningitis
  2. 9 mo M with paroxysmal crying and legs drawn up, calm between episodes, lethargic, sausage-shaped right upper quadrant mass → Abdominal ultrasound → intussusception
  3. 8 mo F, fever 39.2, no localizing findings, urine dipstick positive for leukocyte esterase → Urine culture and empiric antibiotics → urinary tract infection
  4. 6 mo M with suspected meningitis in whom lumbar puncture will be delayed an hour → Give empiric antibiotics now and perform the lumbar puncture after → a sterilized Gram stain is an acceptable trade
  5. 3 wk old F with a temperature of 38.4 C, well-appearing, with no identified source → Full evaluation including lumbar puncture, admission and empiric antibiotics → under 28 days, well appearance does not reassure
  6. 10 mo M with fever, irritability, a bulging anterior fontanelle and a high-pitched cry → Bacterial meningitis → neuroimaging only if focal signs are present
  7. 7 mo M with 3 days of fever to 39 C, then defervescence followed by a blanching rose-pink truncal rash → Roseola infantum → human herpesvirus 6, no testing needed
  8. 12 mo F with suspected meningitis, papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit → Head CT before lumbar puncture → antibiotics first, then CT, then LP
  9. 8 mo M with fever, petechiae and hypotension → Delaying antibiotics to complete the lumbar puncture → treat first, tap after
Sequence and its exceptions Head CT (computed tomography) precedes lumbar puncture only for focal deficits, papilledema, altered consciousness or immunocompromise. In that case, antibiotics precede the CT, not the other way round. In an infant with an open fontanelle the requirement is generally suspended. The fontanelle decompresses rising pressure, so tap without imaging first. Under 28 days, a well appearance does not reassure; full evaluation, admission and empiric antibiotics are needed regardless. Empiric coverage beyond the neonatal period is ceftriaxone plus vancomycin. Neonates get ampicillin plus cefotaxime or gentamicin to cover Listeria.
Pearls Nuchal rigidity, Kernig and Brudzinski are unreliable in infants; look for paradoxical irritability, a bulging fontanelle and a high-pitched cry · A dipstick is a screen, not a rule-out; nitrite is insensitive because infant bladder transit is too short for nitrate reduction · Loose stools and mild tachypnea are nonspecific systemic responses in a septic infant, not localising findings · Dexamethasone with or before the first antibiotic dose reduces hearing loss in Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis
Pairs with Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) grid, so this brief stops at the decision to tap. Ask: am I deciding whether to tap, or reading the fluid? Part I Seizure with Fever in a Child covers what a seizure adds to the decision to tap. Part II Neonatal Sepsis and Its Mimics covers the afebrile neonate whose lab result is the only sign. Ask: is the infant febrile, or is the WBC (white blood cell count) the only sign? Aquifer Fever in an Infant covers the workup before a source is found. It covers which tests the age, appearance and vaccines call for, and the febrile UTI (urinary tract infection) that is most often found.
Transferable rule Name the disease first, then choose the test that follows from it. In a febrile infant, reach the diagnosis by elimination: each reliable negative finding closes a source, and the diagnosis is the source that remains.
Mirror twinIntussusception is the other inconsolable-infant diagnosis, but its crying is paroxysmal with calm intervals.
Class-vs-memberUrine culture is the right class of test on the wrong fluid.
Salient decoyThree loose stools cannot produce a fever of 39.5 with 83% neutrophils.

Fever in an Infant

urine, blood, meninges, lungs, or a virus

Source case Pt — 6-month-old with fever, Aquifer Pediatrics 10; the case works a fever without a source through the serious bacterial infection workup to a first febrile urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) · Q — decide which tests the infant’s age, appearance and vaccines call for, read the urine, CBC and CSF, then choose the setting, the antibiotic, the dose and the imaging
The approach

Fever without a source means a complete history and examination found no focus. Most of these infants have a virus (roseola, other viral syndromes). A small minority have a serious bacterial infection. The urine is the commonest source: a UTI (urinary tract infection). Other sources are the blood (occult bacteremia, sepsis), the meninges (bacterial meningitis), the lungs (pneumonia), or rarely bone, joint or gut. Look at the child first: an ill-appearing infant gets the full workup. In a well infant, age and vaccine status decide how much testing is needed. The catheter urine culture, blood culture or CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) culture confirms the infection.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to
Slow capillary refill, low blood pressure, altered mental statusSeptic shock: circulation, airway, breathing first
Fast heart or breathing rate in an ill childEarly sepsis: cultures and antibiotics now
Hypothermia in a young infantSepsis; fever may be absent
Bulging fontanelle, lethargy, seizureMeningitis: lumbar puncture
Workup by age, appearance and vaccines
InfantWorkup
21 days or youngerFull workup with lumbar puncture, whatever the appearance
22 to 60 days, ill-appearingFull workup with lumbar puncture
22 to 60 days, well-appearingLumbar puncture only if inflammatory markers are abnormal
Over 2 months, ill-appearingUrine, CBC, blood culture; consider lumbar puncture
3 to 36 months, well, fully immunizedUrine if at risk; nothing else
3 to 36 months, well, underimmunizedUrine, CBC and blood culture

DiagnosisSourceWhat it looks likeFirst clue
