Febrile urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis) in an infant What it is — bacterial infection of the kidney; the commonest serious bacterial infection behind fever without a source · Who — girls under 2, uncircumcised boys under 1, circumcised boys under 6 months; prior UTI or a urinary tract anomaly · Mechanism — bowel flora ascend the urethra to the bladder and kidney; E. coli in 85 to 90% of first episodes, the rest Klebsiella, Proteus or enterococcus · Features — fever with no focus, fussiness and poor appetite; an infant cannot report dysuria or flank pain · Diagnosis — catheterized urinalysis: pyuria over 5 WBC/hpf, and esterase and nitrite positive, strongly suggest it; the catheter culture confirms. Collect by catheter in a child not toilet trained; suprapubic aspiration only if catheterization fails; a bag specimen is never cultured · Setting — most are treated orally at home; IV and admission for a toxic child, one who cannot keep oral medicine down, or doubtful adherence · Treatment — oral cephalexin or another cephalosporin by local resistance; TMP-SMX and amoxicillin-clavulanate work but are not first choices; IV ceftriaxone after the first month (it displaces bilirubin in neonates; no calcium in the same line); ampicillin plus gentamicin also works, and ampicillin covers enterococcus, which ceftriaxone misses; nitrofurantoin reaches only the urine, so it treats cystitis, not pyelonephritis · Dosing — mg/kg per day times weight, divided by doses per day; prefer fewer daily doses and a whole-number volume · Follow-up — improvement expected in 48 to 72 hours; renal and bladder ultrasound after a first febrile UTI under age 2, usually after the course; VCUG if the ultrasound is abnormal, fever of 39 C or more with an organism other than E. coli, or a second febrile UTI · Complications — renal scarring; vesicoureteral reflux behind recurrences · Return for — fever or fussiness after 2 to 3 days of antibiotics, vomiting that stops the medicine, lethargy, any new fever later
What sets it apart
VersusWhat separates it
Occult bacteremiaA positive urine names the source
Bacterial meningitisWell child, normal fontanelle: no lumbar puncture needed
RoseolaRoseola has a normal urine and a rash as fever ends
CystitisFever puts the infection in the kidney
Scenario bank
  1. 6-month-old girl with 2 days of fever to 39.4 C, fussier than usual and taking less formula; no cough, runny nose, vomiting or diarrhea; vaccines up to date; well-appearing with a normal examination, including a flat fontanelle, clear lungs and normal eardrums; catheterized urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite with many white cells → Pyelonephritis → a febrile UTI in an infant is an upper-tract infection; catheter culture next
  2. 7-month-old girl with 2 days of fever to 39.2 C and no other symptoms; vaccines up to date; playful and well hydrated, with a normal fontanelle, clear lungs, normal eardrums and no rash → Urinalysis by catheter → UTI is the commonest serious bacterial infection behind a fever without a source
  3. 10-month-old circumcised boy with 1 day of fever to 38.9 C; vaccines up to date; no prior urinary infection or known urinary tract anomaly; playful and drinking well, with a normal examination → Clinical follow-up alone → low UTI risk and well-appearing: no testing needed
  4. 9-month-old boy whose parents declined all vaccines, with 1 day of fever to 39.6 C and no other symptoms; alert and playful, with a flat fontanelle, supple neck and normal examination → CBC, blood culture, and urine → underimmunized: bacteremia is more likely, so blood tests join the urine
  5. 12-month-old unvaccinated boy with fever to 39.8 C and no source on examination; a blood culture drawn in clinic grows gram-positive diplococci the next day, when he is afebrile, playful and eating well, with a normal fontanelle and no rash → Occult bacteremia → a positive blood culture in a well-appearing child; recall and reexamine
  6. 5-month-old boy with 1 day of fever, irritability and poor feeding; neck supple; Kernig and Brudzinski signs absent → Does not exclude meningitis → these signs are usually absent in infants with meningitis
  7. 7-month-old girl with fever to 39.3 C, no source on examination and a normal fontanelle; vaccines up to date; catheterized urinalysis shows pyuria with positive leukocyte esterase and nitrite → Urine culture → the catheter culture confirms the UTI and names the organism
  8. 8-month-old girl with 2 days of fever, lethargy and vomiting and a bulging fontanelle; cerebrospinal fluid shows a high white cell count, mostly neutrophils, low glucose and high protein; Gram stain shows no organisms → Bacterial meningitis → a negative Gram stain does not exclude it; the culture confirms
  9. 10-month-old boy with 4 days of fever to 40 C who stayed playful and fed well throughout; the fever stopped yesterday and today he has a pink, blanching rash on the trunk; examination otherwise normal → Reassurance → roseola (HHV-6): no tests or treatment needed
  10. 9-month-old fully immunized girl with fever to 39 C for 1 day; well-appearing and playful, with a normal examination; a CBC obtained at urgent care shows a white count of 17,000 with a mild left shift → Probably a false positive → bacteremia is rare in a well, immunized child, so the count predicts little
  11. 6-month-old girl with fever and no source on examination, not toilet trained; a urine specimen is needed to rule out infection → Culture of a bag specimen → high contamination rate; a bag specimen is for screening only
  12. 6-month-old girl with pyelonephritis on catheterized urinalysis, culture pending; well-appearing, taking formula and keeping it down; reliable parents with a phone and transportation → Oral cephalexin at home → most febrile UTIs are treated orally
  13. 6-month-old girl started on oral cephalexin for pyelonephritis 1 day ago now vomits every dose, is sleepier and has cool hands with a capillary refill of 3 seconds → Admit for IV ceftriaxone → toxic, or unable to keep oral medicine down
  14. 7-month-old boy with fever to 39.5 C and a catheter urine culture growing E. coli susceptible to all oral agents tested; well-appearing and ready to go home on oral therapy → Nitrofurantoin → therapeutic levels in the urine only, not the kidney
  15. 5-month-old girl admitted on IV ceftriaxone for pyelonephritis is still febrile after 48 hours; the catheter urine culture grows Enterococcus faecalis susceptible to ampicillin → Switch to ampicillin → ceftriaxone does not cover enterococcus
  16. 8-kg infant is prescribed an oral antibiotic at 50 mg/kg/day divided every 12 hours; the suspension contains 250 mg per 5 mL → 4 mL twice daily → 400 mg a day, 200 mg a dose, at 50 mg per mL
  17. 6-month-old girl with her first febrile UTI, E. coli on catheter culture, afebrile within 48 hours on oral therapy and now finishing the course; normal growth and blood pressure → Renal and bladder ultrasound → first febrile UTI under age 2; VCUG only if abnormal or recurrent
  18. 9-month-old boy with 2 days of fever to 39.6 C, no cough, fussy with feeds and a mildly uncomfortable belly; vaccines up to date; well-appearing, breathing comfortably, lungs clear; catheterized urinalysis normal; white count 22,000 → Chest x-ray → occult pneumonia: high fever and a white count of 20,000 or more with no other source

Salient decoyFussiness and poor feeding come with UTI, meningitis and viral illness alike and cannot separate them.

Neurology & HEENT 12 topics + 3 board-style + 2 Aquifer

Three questions triage every red eye. Two tuning forks triage every hearing loss.

Hearing Loss & Otosclerosis

Start with the Rinne and Weber tests

The decision point

Conductive loss: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, and Rinne shows BC > AC (bone conduction greater than air conduction) in that ear. Sensorineural loss: Weber lateralizes away from the affected ear, and Rinne stays AC > BC bilaterally. A conductive loss with a normal otoscopic exam in a young adult is otosclerosis.

Otosclerosis pathophysiology Otosclerosis is a genetic bone-remodeling disorder of the otic capsule at the fissula ante fenestram. An otospongiotic (hypervascular, resorptive) phase is followed by a sclerotic phase that fixes the stapes footplate. Inheritance: Autosomal dominant with ~40% penetrance, so family history is often absent. Onset is in the 20s–40s, with a 2:1 female predominance. Estrogen and progesterone accelerate it, so it is classically unmasked in pregnancy. Measles virus RNA has been found in otosclerotic foci.
Exam & audiogram Paracusis of Willis — hears better in noisy environments · Carhart notch — dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz, an artifact of ossicular fixation · Schwartze sign — reddish blush from hypervascularity · treatment: amplification or stapedectomy · van der Hoeve syndrome = osteogenesis imperfecta + otosclerosis + blue sclerae (both type I collagen disorders).
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
OtoscopyFirstDrum normal, or effusion, perforation or retraction pocketNormal drum with conductive loss suggests otosclerosis; an abnormal drum names the middle-ear cause
Weber and Rinne tuning forksFirstWeber toward the affected ear, bone conduction over airConductive loss; Weber away with air over bone is sensorineural
Pure-tone audiometryConfirmsAir-bone gap, often with a Carhart notch at 2000 HzConductive loss and its degree; otosclerosis when the drum is normal
MRI with gadolinium, internal auditory canalsBy branchEnhancing mass in the internal auditory canalVestibular schwannoma; ordered for unilateral sensorineural loss with tinnitus
Temporal bone CTBy branchBone erosion by a middle-ear massCholesteatoma extent before surgery
Head CT for unilateral sensorineural lossSkipCan miss a small schwannomaMRI with gadolinium is the study
Scenario bank
  1. 35 yo F with progressive conductive loss, Weber lateralizing to the affected ear, normal drum → Otosclerosis
  2. 35 yo F with Weber lateralizing away from the affected ear and Rinne AC over BC bilaterally → Sensorineural hearing loss
  3. 35 yo F with conductive loss, foul discharge and a retraction pocket → Cholesteatoma
  4. 68 yo M with symmetric high-frequency sensorineural loss and poor speech discrimination → Presbycusis
  5. 45 yo F with unilateral sensorineural loss, tinnitus and imbalance → Vestibular schwannoma → MRI
  6. 50 yo M with sudden unilateral sensorineural loss over hours → Sudden sensorineural hearing loss → urgent corticosteroids
  7. 5 yo M, progressive hearing difficulty over a year, born small for gestational age at 36 weeks, Weber lateralizes to the unaffected ear with air conduction better than bone conduction bilaterally → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → delayed-onset sensorineural hearing loss
  8. 3 yo F with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, an older brother in hearing aids since infancy, normal development → Connexin 26 mutation → the commonest cause of hereditary sensorineural loss
  9. The most common cause of nonhereditary sensorineural hearing loss in children → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → often asymptomatic at birth, with hearing loss that may be delayed
The sensorineural mimics Aminoglycosides cause sensorineural loss (hair cell damage), never conductive · Ménière = episodic vertigo + fluctuating hearing loss + tinnitus · presbycusis = gradual, high-frequency, elderly · vestibular schwannoma = unilateral SNHL (sensorineural hearing loss) + tinnitus → MRI. All have normal otoscopy. The tuning forks separate them from otosclerosis.
Pairs with Part I Cholesteatoma and Chronic Ear Drainage expands the cholesteatoma line of this brief into its own topic.

The Red Eye

Three questions triage every red eye

The decision point

1. Is visual acuity affected? 2. Is there true deep pain (not gritty or itchy)? 3. Is the pupil, cornea, or globe abnormal? Any "yes" means this is not simple conjunctivitis and points toward urgent ophthalmology.

Conjunctivitis types
TypeDiscriminatorTreatment
Viral (adenovirus)Watery, follicular tarsal conjunctiva, preauricular node, URI prodromeSupportive — cool compresses, artificial tears
BacterialPurulent, lids stuck shut on waking, papillaryErythromycin ointment or polymyxin-trimethoprim
Contact lens wearerAny red eye → think PseudomonasFluoroquinolone; remove lens; urgent ophtho if infiltrate
AllergicITCHING is the hallmark; bilateral, cobblestone papillaeOlopatadine, ketotifen
Gonococcal EmergencyHyperacute (<24 h), copious purulence — can perforate the corneaIM ceftriaxone + irrigation + urgent ophtho
ChlamydialChronic >3 weeks, follicular, sexually active adultOral azithromycin/doxycycline + treat partners
The can't-miss red eyes
DiagnosisThe tellAnswer
Acute angle-closure glaucomaSevere pain, halos, vomiting, mid-dilated fixed pupil, hard globe; triggered by dark rooms or anticholinergicsTimolol + apraclonidine + pilocarpine + IV acetazolamide → laser peripheral iridotomy
HSV keratitisDendritic ulcer on fluorescein, ↓ corneal sensationTopical trifluridine or oral acyclovir — never steroids
Herpes zoster ophthalmicusV1 vesicles + Hutchinson signOral antivirals + ophtho
Anterior uveitisCiliary flush, cell and flare, consensual photophobia; HLA-B27, JIA, sarcoidTopical steroid + cycloplegic — the one place prednisolone is right
ScleritisBoring pain that wakes from sleep, does not blanch with phenylephrine; RA, GPASystemic NSAIDs/steroids
EpiscleritisSectoral, minimal pain, blanches with phenylephrineSupportive
EndophthalmitisPost-op or post-injection, pain + ↓VA + hypopyonIntravitreal antibiotics — emergency
Orbital cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegiaCT orbits + IV antibiotics (preseptal has none of those)
Scenario bank
  1. 24 yo M with bilateral watery red eyes, a preauricular node, recent URI and normal vision → Viral conjunctivitis → supportive care
  2. 24 yo M contact lens wearer with pain, photophobia and a corneal infiltrate → Bacterial keratitis → urgent ophthalmology, never patch
  3. 62 yo F with severe pain, halos, a mid-dilated fixed pupil and vomiting → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → topical agents plus acetazolamide
  4. 24 yo M with a dendritic corneal ulcer on fluorescein staining → HSV keratitis → topical antiviral, never steroids
  5. 30 yo M with ankylosing spondylitis, photophobia, ciliary flush and anterior chamber cells → Anterior uveitis → topical steroid plus cycloplegic
  6. 55 yo F with rheumatoid arthritis and severe boring eye pain that wakes her at night → Scleritis
  7. Newborn with purulent conjunctivitis on day 3 of life → Gonococcal conjunctivitis → parenteral ceftriaxone
  8. 9 yo M with bilateral eye itching, watery discharge, cobblestone papillae under the upper eyelids, nasal congestion each spring → Allergic conjunctivitis → olopatadine or ketotifen drops
  9. 5 yo F, 3 days of photophobia with lids crusted shut on waking, diffuse bulbar and palpebral erythema, mucopurulent discharge, acuity unchanged → Bacterial conjunctivitis → Mucopurulent discharge with normal acuity
  10. School-age child with mucopurulent conjunctivitis and no contact lens use; the likeliest organism → Haemophilus influenzae → With S pneumoniae and Moraxella catarrhalis
  11. Child with an undifferentiated red eye and mucopurulent discharge; which is contraindicated before slit-lamp examination → Topical corticosteroid drops → Steroid on an unrecognized HSV keratitis worsens it
Neonatal conjunctivitis by day of onset Day 0–1 chemical · day 2–5 gonococcal → IM/IV ceftriaxone + irrigation · day 5–14 chlamydial → oral erythromycin, or oral azithromycin as the alternative (counsel on pyloric stenosis with either) · day 6–14 HSV (herpes simplex virus) → IV acyclovir. Birth prophylaxis (erythromycin ointment) prevents gonococcal but not chlamydial disease.
How NBME framed it A home birth delivered by the father stood in for missing eye prophylaxis, and Kawasaki disease was listed under its formal name, mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the red eye that comes from a tender lump on the lid margin, and its lid-swelling mimics. Ask: is there a lump on the lid?
The steroid rule Steroids are indicated in anterior uveitis (topical) and scleritis (systemic). Topical steroids are catastrophic in HSV (herpes simplex virus) keratitis, bacterial/fungal keratitis, and undifferentiated red eye. If you cannot name the diagnosis with certainty, do not give steroids.

Primary Headache in an Adult

Migraine · cluster · tension · the autonomic tell

Source vignette Pt — 27 yo M, nightly 90-minute attacks of stabbing left periorbital pain with tearing, ptosis and rhinorrhea · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned cluster headache, trigeminal neuralgia and acute angle-closure glaucoma
The decision point

Acute unilateral periorbital pain with ipsilateral autonomic signs (ptosis, miosis, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection) is a cluster headache. Attacks wake the patient from sleep, peak fast, last ~90 minutes, and recur several times daily for weeks before remitting. Acute treatment is 100% oxygen; sumatriptan aborts attacks but is second-line (slower onset, side effects). Vision stays intact in cluster headache; vision change or a fixed mid-dilated pupil moves the diagnosis to angle-closure glaucoma.

Defining criteria Cluster attack — excruciating periorbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signs, often nocturnal onset · Pattern — several attacks daily for 6–8 weeks, then remission lasting months to years · Abortive — 100% oxygen first-line; sumatriptan second · Prophylaxis — verapamil
Headache types — the differential
MigraineClusterTension
SexF > MM > FF > M
OnsetVariableDuring sleep, similar timing dailyUnder stress
LocationOften unilateralBehind one eyeBand-like, bilateral
CharacterPulsatile, throbbingExcruciating, sharp, steadyDull, tight, persistent
Duration4–72 h15–180 min30 min to months
AssociatedPhotophobia, phonophobia, nausea, ± auraIpsilateral autonomic signs — tearing, ptosis, miosis, rhinorrhea, flushingPericranial muscle tenderness
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
History and neurologic exam, including pupilsFirstAttacks of 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral autonomic signsCluster headache; attacks lasting seconds point to trigeminal neuralgia
Visual acuity and intraocular pressureBy branchRaised pressure, fixed mid-dilated pupil, halosAcute angle-closure glaucoma, an eye emergency
CT or MR angiography of the neckBy branchCarotid dissectionHorner syndrome that persists between attacks, or neck pain
MRI of the brainBy branchA structural lesion, such as a pituitary massExcludes a secondary cause when the exam is abnormal or attacks are atypical
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsNo test confirms cluster headacheTests only exclude mimics; relief with 100% oxygen supports it
Sinus CTSkipRhinorrhea here is autonomic, not infectiveEpisodic attacks without fever or congestion are not sinusitis
Scenario bank
  1. 27 yo M, nightly 90-minute attacks of stabbing left periorbital pain with tearing, ptosis, and rhinorrhea → Cluster headache → abort with 100% oxygen
  2. 27 yo M with cluster headaches recurring nightly for 3 weeks; best prophylaxis → Verapamil
  3. 24 yo F, 8 hours of unilateral throbbing pain with nausea and photophobia, prior similar episodes → Migraine → NSAID or triptan early
  4. 35 yo F under work stress, band-like bilateral head tightness with neck muscle tenderness, normal exam → Tension headache
  5. 55 yo M, seconds-long electric shocks over the cheek and jaw triggered by chewing and brushing → Trigeminal neuralgia → carbamazepine
  6. 63 yo F, acute eye pain with halos around lights, decreased vision, fixed mid-dilated pupil → Acute angle-closure glaucoma → pressure-lowering drops, then laser iridotomy
Pearls Autonomic signs are nearly universal in cluster headache; their absence should force a second look · agitation during the attack points to cluster (migraineurs lie still) · rhinorrhea plus facial pain suggests sinusitis, but sinusitis pain is not episodic and brings congestion and fever, not ptosis · trigeminal neuralgia lasts seconds; cluster lasts an hour and a half.
Pairs with Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment covers the pediatric red-flag check that comes before this headache-type differential.
Transferable rule Classify headache by duration and associated features: seconds = neuralgia; minutes-to-hours with autonomic signs = cluster; hours-to-days with nausea/photophobia = migraine. Establish the duration before the character of the pain.
Salient decoySinusitis: rhinorrhea suggests it, but the episodic pattern and the autonomic signs point away from it.
Class-vs-memberSumatriptan: it aborts cluster attacks, but oxygen is the first-line abortive.

Sellar and Suprasellar Masses

Endocrine signs localize the tumor, and imaging confirms it · Does the endocrine axis point at the stalk rather than the gland, and is the chiasm involved?

Source vignette Pt — 13 yo F, a year of headaches, now worse; height fell from the 50th to the 5th percentile between ages 11 and 13 while weight held at the 75th; Tanner 1 · Exam — afebrile, normal blood pressure, supple neck, optic disc edema; normal finger-nose-finger, gait and skin; no focal deficit · Q — the most likely finding on MRI of the brain; options spanned a cystic, calcified suprasellar mass, subependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles, a tumor in the cerebellar vermis, a parietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim, and an enhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal
The decision point

The neurologic examination is normal: no dysmetria, no gait abnormality, no focal weakness, no skin findings. Three findings remain: linear growth arrested at age 11 while weight held, Tanner 1 at 13, and papilledema. Growth failure with preserved weight is a hormonal deceleration, not a nutritional one. Arrest of puberty with it means more than one anterior pituitary axis has failed. Multiple axes failing together point to the stalk, not the gland. With headache and disc edema from obstructive hydrocephalus, the mass is midline and suprasellar. It is cystic and calcified on MRI, a craniopharyngioma from Rathke pouch remnants.

Defining criteria Growth failure — downward crossing of height percentiles after a previously stable channel (50th to 5th between ages 11 and 13 here), with weight preserved. Pituitary or hypothalamic causes lose height before weight; nutritional and gastrointestinal causes lose weight before height ⚠︎ · Pubertal delay — one teaching source gates it at no breast development by age 12 in girls; the threshold conventionally taught is age 13 ⚠︎. Tanner 1 at 13 clears either gate, so the discrepancy does not change this answer, but note which figure you are being scored on · Stalk pattern vs gland pattern — multiple anterior axes down plus posterior failure (diabetes insipidus) localizes to the stalk; a single hypersecreting axis with intact others localizes to the gland (in-context: stalk compression causes panhypopituitarism, most commonly manifesting as growth failure from TSH or GH deficiency)
Pertinent positives & negatives Height 50th → 5th, weight 75th and steady — endocrine growth failure; excludes malabsorption, inflammatory bowel disease, and undernutrition, which cost weight first · Tanner 1 at 13 — gonadotropin deficiency; a second failed axis, which indicates hypopituitarism rather than short stature alone. · Optic disc edema with a supple neck and no fever — raised intracranial pressure without meningitis; here from obstructive hydrocephalus at the third ventricle · Normal finger-nose-finger and normal gait — excludes the cerebellar compartment and with it medulloblastoma, the posterior fossa candidate · Normal skin — excludes tuberous sclerosis (ash-leaf macules, angiofibromas) and neurofibromatosis type 1 (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling), the two phakomatoses whose intracranial lesions are on option lists · No focal deficit, no fever — excludes brain abscess, which comes with focal findings and usually fever · Headaches for a year before worsening — a slow-growing lesion; craniopharyngiomas are subtle for years before diagnosis
The sellar/suprasellar mass — the differential
DiagnosisIllness script + buzzwordsThe NBME tellExcluded here by
CraniopharyngiomaRathke pouch epithelial remnants in the stalk; bimodal peaks at 5–14 and 50–75; years of subtle symptomsCystic and calcified suprasellar mass; growth failure + pubertal delay + bitemporal hemianopsia— (the answer)
Suprasellar germinoma — can't missAdolescent, often male; midline germ cell tumor of the suprasellar or pineal regionDiabetes insipidus arrives first, before the anterior axes; non-calcified; CSF/serum β-hCG or AFP elevated; radiosensitiveNo polyuria or polydipsia; the anterior axes failed first
Prolactinoma / pituitary adenomaAdolescent or adult with galactorrhea and amenorrhea, or acromegalic featuresIntrasellar, non-calcified; one axis hypersecreting with the others intactTwo axes down, no galactorrhea, and the mass would not obstruct CSF flow (covered in Posterior Fossa Localization)
Optic pathway gliomaYoung child, often NF1; pilocytic astrocytoma of the chiasm or nerveCafé-au-lait macules and axillary freckling; visual loss and afferent pupillary defect precede endocrine failure; may cause diencephalic syndrome (emaciation with normal appetite)Normal skin, normal pupils, and weight preserved
Rathke cleft cystSame embryologic origin, benign, frequently incidentalNon-enhancing, non-calcified cyst; usually asymptomatic or mild headacheProgressive panhypopituitarism with raised pressure is too much disease for a simple cyst
Langerhans cell histiocytosisYoung child; infiltrates the stalkCentral diabetes insipidus with a thickened stalk, plus lytic skull lesions and a seborrheic scalp rashNormal skin, no polyuria, no bone pain
Management Once the mass is found, glucocorticoid replacement goes in before levothyroxine. Thyroid hormone raises metabolic demand and can precipitate adrenal crisis in an unrecognized cortisol deficiency ⚠︎. Treat post-operative hypotonic polyuria with desmopressin, not fluid restriction.
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination focal? — No → the lesion is not hemispheric or in the posterior fossa · Plot the growth chart. — Height falling, weight holding → endocrine · Count failed axes. — Growth and puberty → panhypopituitarism, which localizes to the stalk · Is there posterior pituitary failure? — Polyuria present → germinoma or histiocytosis become more likely. Polyuria is absent here · Is there raised pressure or a field cut? — Papilledema, bitemporal hemianopsia → the mass is midline and suprasellar, and the MRI descriptor is calcified and cystic
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Growth chart: height and weight percentilesFirstHeight falling while weight holdsEndocrine growth failure, not nutritional
MRI of the brain with contrast, sellar viewsNextCystic and calcified suprasellar massCraniopharyngioma; intrasellar and non-calcified suggests an adenoma
Morning cortisol, free T4 and TSH, IGF-1NextLow in more than one axisStalk compression; replace cortisol before thyroxine, before surgery
Serum sodium and urine osmolalityBy branchDilute urine with a high sodiumCentral diabetes insipidus; if it came first, think germinoma or histiocytosis
Serum and CSF beta-hCG and AFPBy branchElevated markersGerminoma, especially non-calcified with diabetes insipidus
Resection with histologyConfirmsAdamantinomatous epithelium with calcificationCraniopharyngioma
Hand radiograph for bone ageSkipDelayed bone age is nonspecificDelays the MRI when papilledema is present
Scenario bank
  1. 12 yo F, 6 months of morning headaches, height crossed 75th to 10th percentile with weight at 60th, Tanner 1, papilledema → MRI of the brain with contrast → Suspected suprasellar mass
  2. 9 yo M, MRI shows a cystic calcified suprasellar mass, resection planned → Measure morning cortisol, free T4/TSH, and IGF-1 before surgery → Craniopharyngioma
  3. 14 yo M, 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia, urine osmolality 90, non-calcified suprasellar mass, CSF beta-hCG elevated → Suprasellar germinoma → Radiation therapy
  4. 10 yo F, POD 1 from suprasellar tumor resection, urine output 350 mL/h, serum Na 152, urine osmolality 85 → Desmopressin → Central diabetes insipidus
  5. 8 yo M with a new suprasellar mass, BP 84/50, Na 128, glucose 52 → Levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement → Adrenal crisis
  6. 15 yo F, amenorrhea and galactorrhea, normal growth, Tanner 4, MRI shows a 6 mm intrasellar lesion without calcification → Prolactinoma → Cabergoline
  7. 6 yo M, declining vision with nystagmus, cafe-au-lait macules and axillary freckling, thin despite a good appetite → MRI of the brain and orbits → Optic pathway glioma in NF1
  8. 11 yo F with a known suprasellar mass, now vomiting with a depressed level of consciousness, dilated lateral and third ventricles → Neurosurgical CSF diversion → Obstructive hydrocephalus
  9. 10 yo M, 1 year after resection and radiation of a craniopharyngioma, currently asymptomatic → Serial growth velocity with annual pituitary hormone panel and formal visual fields → Lifelong endocrine and visual surveillance
  10. 13 yo F with a suprasellar mass and loss of both temporal visual fields → Compression of decussating nasal retinal fibers at the optic chiasm → Bitemporal hemianopsia
Decoy note The one-year duration is not reassuring; it is the classic tempo of a slow-growing suprasellar tumor. The normal blood pressure and temperature exclude infection and crisis but say nothing about the pituitary; a morning cortisol would.
Pearls Height falling away from a stable weight with Tanner arrest and headache is a suprasellar mass until MRI says otherwise; calcified and cystic indicates craniopharyngioma. · Plot the growth chart before you order the headache imaging. A height percentile crossing is a localizing sign, and it remains detectable when the neurologic examination is normal. · Height lost with weight preserved is endocrine; weight lost before height is nutritional or gastrointestinal. The exception is the diencephalic syndrome of a hypothalamic glioma: emaciation with a normal appetite ⚠︎. · Diabetes insipidus first, anterior axes later makes germinoma or Langerhans cell histiocytosis more likely than craniopharyngioma. Send CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) and serum β-hCG (beta human chorionic gonadotropin) and AFP (alpha-fetoprotein) before assuming craniopharyngioma. · Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone in any new panhypopituitarism ⚠︎. Expect the post-operative sodium to rise, not fall, when the stalk has been handled. · Boundary: untreated acquired primary hypothyroidism reproduces this growth pattern exactly: height arrest, preserved or rising weight, delayed puberty. It does not produce papilledema. Check TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free T4; disc edema separates the two.
Pairs with Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment covers the same complaint, a 13-year-old girl with worsening headaches, with the red-flag gate answered in opposite directions. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? If yes, image and look at the sella; if no, explain the change in pattern. Posterior Fossa Localization covers the other compartment. When the abnormality is on the neurologic examination rather than the growth chart, the mass is in the posterior fossa, not the sella. Hyperprolactinemia covers the intrasellar adenoma in the adult. Part I Polyuria covers the step before this one: whether the polyuria is water or solute, and whether the deprivation test is still needed.
Transferable rule When a mass sits on a midline structure, the localizing finding may be endocrine rather than neurologic. A growth chart and a Tanner stage are examination findings. In the sellar region they appear years before the field cut and the papilledema.
True-fact-wrong-slotSubependymal nodules in the lateral ventricles: Tuberous sclerosis is a skin-first diagnosis; the stem states the skin examination is normal, and TSC (tuberous sclerosis complex) does not arrest linear growth
Class-vs-memberTumor in the cerebellar vermis: Vermian tumors present with truncal ataxia and dysmetria; this examination is explicitly clean, and they do not touch the pituitary
Sequencing trapParietal lesion with air-fluid levels and a hyperdense rim: Abscess is acute, febrile, and focal; a year of headaches with growth arrest is not an infection
Salient decoyEnhancing lesion in the internal auditory canal: Acoustic neuroma is an adult disease of hearing loss and tinnitus, with no endocrine consequence

Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment

When pediatric headache needs neuroimaging, and when it does not · Is anything abnormal outside the headache history — the examination, the fundus, the growth chart, the vitals?

Source vignette Pt — 13 yo F, 2 years of similar headaches: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worse with activity, with nausea; now monthly instead of every other month, same characteristics; menarche at 12, periods now regular; this one began after a sleepover, she vomited twice and could not finish her homework; intermittent acetaminophen only · Exam — temperature 37 °C, alert and oriented, pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal, no papilledema described · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned no additional testing, CT of the head, a urine toxicology screen, serum electrolytes and lumbar puncture
The decision point

This headache is already diagnosable: unilateral, pulsatile, hours long, worsened by activity, with nausea and vomiting, in an adolescent girl with a two-year history of the same thing. Image only if a feature meets an imaging indication. None of the following three features meets one. Vomiting is a diagnostic criterion of migraine, not a pressure sign. The disability ("could not finish her homework") measures severity, and no guideline images for severity. The increase in frequency is a change in rate, not in character. The headaches "have the same characteristics" and remain monthly. The change tracks the arrival of regular menses since menarche. The examination is normal, including the pupils, and no papilledema is described. No additional testing is needed. Imaging is reserved for an abnormal neurologic examination, signs of raised intracranial pressure, or a dramatic change in headache characteristics.

When papilledema is present, imaging is indicated. Then find why the pressure is high; the medication list often answers it. An adolescent on isotretinoin with a month of morning headache and vomiting, brief blurring of vision, bilateral disc edema and full visual fields has drug-induced intracranial hypertension. A mass at the optic chiasm would cut the fields. Optic neuritis is painful, acute and usually affects one eye.

Defining criteria Indications for neuroimaging in pediatric headache — — (1) abnormal neurologic examination findings, such as weakness or ataxia; (2) signs of raised intracranial pressure, such as papilledema; (3) a dramatic change in headache characteristics. None is present here · Not an indication — — a modest rise in frequency when the headaches keep the same character, remain relatively infrequent, and have a physiologic explanation for the change · Migraine, diagnostic features — — pulsatile, unilateral (may be bilateral in children), hours to days; photophobia and phonophobia; nausea or vomiting; ± aura; normal neurologic examination. Formal criteria add ≥5 prior attacks lasting 2–72 hours in patients under 18 (4–72 in adults); beyond 72 hours is status migrainosus (ICHD-3)
Pertinent positives & negatives Two years of similar headaches — recurrent and stereotyped; excludes "first and worst," which is the thunderclap gate · Vomited twice — a migraine criterion; it becomes a pressure sign only when it is morning vomiting, projectile, or paired with papilledema · Pupils equal and reactive, remainder of the neurologic examination normal — closes indication (1) and, in the absence of described disc edema, indication (2) · Menarche at 12, now regular cycles — the physiologic explanation for the change in rate, so the change is explained · Afebrile, alert and oriented — excludes meningitis, so lumbar puncture is not indicated · Began after a sleepover — sleep deprivation is a named migraine trigger, not evidence of ingestion
Classify first — headache in a child
AxisThe stem sentence that settles itConsequence for management
Examination and fundus normal?"Pupils equal and reactive... remainder of neurologic examination normal"; no papilledemaCloses both of the first two imaging indications, and the IIH branch with them (in-context: papilledema would be expected)
Character or only rate?"Similar headaches over the past 2 years"; "every other month… now monthly," same featuresRecurrent, not first-and-worst; a rate change only, which does not meet "dramatic change in characteristics"
Explanation for the change?"Menarche at age 12; menstrual periods now regular"A physiologic cause is identified, so the change is accounted for
Systemic signs?"Temperature 37 C," alert, normal vitalsNo infection, no toxidrome
Tier fingerprint done: nothing but intermittent acetaminophen · failed: 2 years of attacks with inadequate abortive dosing and timing, the actual unmet need · bothered: missed schoolwork, which justifies better treatment, not more testing.
Management ladder — headache in a child
TierInterventionEscalate when
1Clinical diagnosis; trigger diary (sleep, meals, menses, screens); sleep-hygiene and hydration counseling; no laboratory or imagingAny red-flag gate is breached, or attacks recur despite trigger control
2Abortive therapy at first symptom, at full weight-based dose — ibuprofen or acetaminophen, rest in a dark quiet room, antiemetic if vomiting blocks oral dosingAn early, adequately dosed NSAID fails on 2 consecutive attacks ⚠︎
3Triptan for refractory attacks, then daily prevention (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate ⚠︎) if attacks reach ≥4 headache days per month ⚠︎Reassess prevention at 2–3 months ⚠︎
Exit / de-escalationMedication-overuse headache — withdraw the offending analgesicSimple analgesics on ≥15 days/month, or triptans/combination analgesics on ≥10 days/month ⚠︎
Numbers that gate & exit ramps Diagnostic: up to 3 days per attack; ≥5 prior attacks of 2–72 hours ⚠︎. Escalation: 2 adequately dosed failures ⚠︎, ≥4 headache days/month ⚠︎, and the overuse thresholds above ⚠︎. The exam answer versus clinical practice: the exam keys the preventive rung, though pediatric trials found amitriptyline and topiramate no better than placebo ⚠︎. That trial result does not change the keyed rung. · Papilledema → MRI with MR (magnetic resonance) venography, then LP (lumbar puncture) with an opening pressure; a normal MRI with a high opening pressure means intracranial hypertension, idiopathic or drug-induced. · Fever with meningismus → lumbar puncture. A thunderclap headache → noncontrast CT, then LP if negative ⚠︎. · Wakes from sleep, worse on waking or with Valsalva → MRI, however migrainous the rest sounds. · Focal deficit or ataxia → Posterior Fossa Localization. A falling height percentile or arrested puberty → MRI with sellar views; see Sellar and Suprasellar Masses. · Household all symptomatic → carboxyhemoglobin. Image any child who is immunocompromised, shunted, or anticoagulated.
Intracranial hypertension: check the drug list Who — women of childbearing age, obesity or recent weight gain, and drugs: retinoids and vitamin A (isotretinoin for acne), tetracyclines (minocycline, doxycycline) and growth hormone · Symptoms — daily headache worse lying flat and in the morning, better standing, with nausea and vomiting; transient visual obscurations; pulsatile tinnitus; diplopia from a CN VI palsy · Signs — bilateral papilledema with enlarged blind spots and full visual fields, otherwise a normal neurologic exam; a lesion at the chiasm would cut the fields (bitemporal hemianopia) · Workup — MRI with MR venography first, to exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis; then LP (lumbar puncture): opening pressure over 250 mm H2O with normal CSF · Treatment — stop the offending drug, which usually resolves it; weight loss; acetazolamide
Decision spine Is the neurologic examination normal, including the fundus? — Yes → the strongest two indications are closed · First and worst, or recurrent and familiar? — Recurrent → no urgent pathway · Did the character change, or only the rate? — Rate only → not a dramatic change · Is there a physiologic explanation for the change? — Menarche and regular cycles → yes · Any systemic signal: fever, altered sensorium, abnormal vitals, growth failure? — None → make a diagnosis and a treatment plan, not a test
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Neurologic exam, fundi and growth chartFirstNormal exam, no papilledema, growth on trackPrimary headache, usually migraine: no testing
None: clinical diagnosis of migraineConfirmsNo test confirms migraineDiagnosis rests on the history and a normal exam
MRI of the brain, for a red flagBy branchMass or hydrocephalusRed flags: focal deficit, papilledema, waking from sleep, change in character
Noncontrast head CTBy branchBlood in a thunderclap headacheSubarachnoid hemorrhage; LP if the CT is negative
MRI of the brain with MR venography, for papilledemaBy branchNormal: no mass, hydrocephalus or venous sinus thrombosisRaised pressure without a structural cause; proceed to LP
Lumbar puncture with opening pressureBy branchOpening pressure over 250 mm H2O with normal CSF, after a normal MRI and MR venographyIntracranial hypertension, idiopathic or drug-induced; with fever and meningismus, LP for meningitis
CarboxyhemoglobinBy branchElevated, with the household affectedCarbon monoxide exposure
Head CT for recurrent headache, normal examSkipStable character, normal examNo imaging needed; chronic headache that earns imaging gets MRI
Scenario bank
  1. 10 yo M, 1 year of bilateral throbbing headaches with photophobia and vomiting, relieved by sleep, normal examination → Reassurance, trigger diary, and early-dose ibuprofen → Pediatric migraine
  2. 13 yo F with 2 years of migraines, now with papilledema and vomiting on waking → MRI of the brain → Suspected intracranial mass
  3. 16 yo F, obese, daily headache with pulsatile tinnitus and papilledema, MRI of the brain normal → Lumbar puncture with opening pressure → Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
  4. 15 yo M, sudden headache maximal within seconds while lifting weights, worst of his life, normal examination → Noncontrast CT of the head → Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage
  5. 4 yo M, 12 h of headache with T 39.2, nuchal rigidity, irritable, no focal deficit or papilledema → Lumbar puncture → Bacterial meningitis
  6. 8 yo F, 6 months of headaches with a normal neurologic examination, height crossed from 50th to 5th percentile with weight held → MRI of the brain with sellar views → Suprasellar mass
  7. 12 yo M with morning headaches and nausea on winter weekdays; mother and brother affected, all better away from home → Carboxyhemoglobin level → Carbon monoxide exposure
  8. 6 yo F, frontal headaches only on school afternoons, squints at the board, normal neurologic examination → Ophthalmologic examination with refraction → Uncorrected refractive error
  9. 13 yo F, 3 years of episodic headaches now monthly and predictable in the 2 days before each period, unchanged in character → Menstrual migraine → Trigger counseling and timed NSAIDs
  10. 15 yo M using ibuprofen or acetaminophen on 20 days per month for a headache that is now daily and dull → Continuing the daily as-needed analgesic → Medication-overuse headache
  11. 16 yo M taking oral isotretinoin for severe acne, with 1 month of daily throbbing frontal headache that is worse in the morning, occasional nausea and vomiting, partial relief from acetaminophen, and brief blurring of the left eye at sports practice; BP 130/80; pupils equal and reactive; bilateral optic disc edema with decreased visual acuity and full visual fields; no meningismus; normal strength, reflexes and sensation → Drug-induced intracranial hypertension → Isotretinoin (a retinoid) impairs CSF resorption; MRI with MR venography, then LP; stop the drug
  12. 15 yo M taking minocycline for acne for 3 months, with daily morning headache and pulsatile tinnitus; bilateral papilledema with full visual fields; MRI of the brain with MR venography is normal; lumbar puncture opening pressure is 340 mm H2O with normal CSF → Discontinue minocycline → Tetracycline-induced intracranial hypertension; it usually resolves off the drug, with acetazolamide added for persistent symptoms
  13. 11 yo M started on growth hormone 4 months ago for growth hormone deficiency, with 3 weeks of headache that is worse lying down and on waking, brief episodes of graying vision, and bilateral papilledema; full visual fields and an otherwise normal neurologic exam → MRI of the brain with MR venography → Exclude a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis before LP; growth hormone-induced intracranial hypertension
Decoy note Awakening from sleep would indicate imaging, and it is absent here. The homework detail measures disability, which sets the treatment tier and never the imaging threshold. The near-doubling of frequency is real but explained.
Pearls A change in frequency needs an explanation; a change in character, an examination finding or a pressure sign needs a scan. · Reassurance is defensible only when you can name the criteria you cleared. · Change in rate ≠ change in character. Ask what changed. If the only change is "more often," look for the physiologic cause (menarche, a new schedule, a new medication) before you look at the brain. · MRI for chronic and progressive; CT for acute and hemorrhagic. The right decision to image still needs the right modality. · Boundary: nocturnal awakening, morning vomiting, and headache worsened by Valsalva are pressure signs even when the rest is textbook migraine. They take precedence over the migraine features. · Migraine onset and changes in frequency cluster around menarche. Through the same estrogen link, menstrual migraine is the commonest cause of headaches that got worse this year in an adolescent.
Pairs with Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers the same complaint at the same age and sex, on the opposite side of the imaging gate. There, the headache came with papilledema, a height percentile crossing, and Tanner 1. Here it comes with a normal examination and an explained change in frequency. Ask: is anything abnormal outside the headache history (the fundus, the growth chart, the Tanner stage, the neurologic examination)? Primary Headache in an Adult covers the headache-type differential once imaging has been excluded. Low Back Pain in an Adult uses the same gating logic in a different region. The pain's severity never opens the gate, and a specific finding always does. Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin A excess as a cause of pseudotumor cerebri. Ask: is the patient taking a retinoid or a vitamin A supplement? Part I Headache in a School-Age Child covers the whole workup once the gate opens, through the posterior fossa tumor it most often finds. Ask: does the exam show ataxia as well as papilledema?
Transferable rule Findings, not suffering, cross an imaging threshold. The examination, the fundus, the tempo of change in character, and the systemic signs decide imaging. Frequency, duration, and disability decide only the treatment tier. When a pattern changes and you can name why, the change is explained and is not a red flag.
Mirror twinCT scan of the head: Imaging requires examination findings, pressure signs, or a change in character, and none is present; even where imaging is indicated for a chronic pediatric headache, the modality is MRI
Salient decoyUrine toxicology screen: Toxic ingestion presents with altered sensorium, pupillary abnormality, respiratory depression, or seizure; she is alert with reactive pupils, and the sleepover is a sleep-deprivation trigger
Sequencing trapSerum electrolyte measurement: Two episodes in a well-hydrated, alert adolescent change no management decision; the clinical findings already answer the question electrolytes would ask
True-fact-wrong-slotLumbar puncture: She is afebrile with a normal examination, and IIH (idiopathic intracranial hypertension) would show papilledema; lumbar puncture before imaging in a patient with pressure signs is also out of order
Unchecked attributeCluster headache, for the adolescent on isotretinoin: Unilateral periorbital or temporal attacks in men aged 20 to 50, with no papilledema; this headache is daily, frontal, worse in the morning and comes with bilateral disc edema
Salient decoyOptic chiasm glioma: The blurred vision pulls toward the visual pathway, but a chiasm lesion causes bitemporal field loss, and his fields are full
True-fact-wrong-slotOptic neuritis: Disc swelling with blurred vision is real there, but it brings acute vision loss and eye pain, usually in one eye, without morning headache and vomiting
Salient decoyViral encephalitis: Headache and vomiting fit, but encephalitis needs fever and altered mental status; he is afebrile and alert with no meningismus

Cholesteatoma and Chronic Ear Drainage

the mass behind an intact drum · Is the drum intact, is the mass on it, and is the loss conductive?

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo M, a month of purulent ear drainage unimproved by topical and oral antibiotics; intact immobile tympanic membrane with a superior retraction pocket and a pearly white mass, conductive hearing loss; cleft palate, prior effusions and tympanostomy tubes · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned cholesteatoma, acute otitis media with perforation and otitis externa
The decision point

The drum is intact, so the drainage is not coming through a perforation, which otitis media with discharge requires. The drum is immobile with a superior retraction pocket containing a pearly white mass. The lesion is therefore of the tympanic membrane rather than of the canal, which excludes otitis externa and a foreign body. The loss is conductive, so the ossicles are affected rather than the nerve, which excludes the schwannoma. The three named risk factors are cleft palate, chronic middle-ear effusions and tympanostomy tubes. Each is a mechanism for the chronic middle-ear disease that pulls a retraction pocket into the attic. The pocket traps desquamated epithelium, keratin accumulates, and the mass erodes toward the ossicles. This is a cholesteatoma, treated by surgical excision.

Defining criteria Cholesteatoma — a benign growth of squamous epithelium with accumulation of keratin debris within the middle ear; most cases are acquired and unilateral · Pathogenesis — chronic middle-ear disease creates a retraction pocket, an invagination of the tympanic membrane, which traps epithelium and debris · The two consequences it is tested on — chronic otorrhea when the trapped debris becomes infected, and conductive hearing loss when growth reaches the ossicles · Risk factors — recurrent acute otitis media, chronic middle-ear effusion, tympanostomy tube placement, and cleft palate through its association with middle-ear disease · Examination — a pearly white mass or a visible retraction pocket with draining debris behind an intact drum, placed in the anterosuperior quadrant in-context. The two locations are not in conflict — they name different entities: congenital disease sits behind an intact drum (classically anterosuperior, though surgical series find it variable), while acquired disease arises from pars flaccida or posterosuperior retraction. Read the drum first, then the quadrant
Pertinent positives & negatives Drainage for a month, unimproved on topical and oral antibiotics — refractory to antibiotics; infection alone would have improved · Tympanic membrane intact — excludes acute otitis media with perforation, which is what produces discharge in that disease · Immobile on insufflation — the drum is tethered by the retraction pocket, and there is middle-ear disease behind it · Superior retraction with a pearly white mass — the lesion is on the drum rather than in the canal, and this finding is specific · Conductive hearing loss — ossicular involvement; a sensorineural loss would point at the nerve and a different disease entirely · Cleft palate, prior effusions, prior tympanostomy tubes — all three risk factors, which explain why this child is affected · No pain and no fever — argues against acute otitis media and against otitis externa, both of which hurt · No dizziness with a normal gait — no labyrinthine fistula yet, and their absence is what makes this elective rather than urgent ⚠︎
Chronic ear drainage — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
CholesteatomaChronic middle-ear disease creates a retraction pocket that traps squamous epithelium and keratin, expanding toward the ossiclesPearly white mass behind an intact drum with painless refractory otorrhea and conductive loss— (the answer)
Acute otitis media with perforationMiddle-ear infection under pressure ruptures the drum and drainsBulging, erythematous or perforated drum, with pain and fever preceding the dischargeDrum intact, non-bulging, uninflamed, painless
Otitis externaCanal maceration and inflammation, usually infectious, classically in swimmersTragal tenderness with a swollen tender canal, responding to topical dropsFailed appropriate topical therapy, and the mass is on the drum
Necrotising otitis externa Can't missPseudomonas osteomyelitis of the skull base in diabetics and the immunocompromised ⚠︎Severe pain with granulation tissue at the bony–cartilaginous junction and cranial neuropathiesA child, painless, without granulation tissue
Foreign body in the canalOften asymptomatic, but may cause pain, discharge and decreased hearingObject visible in the canal, with abrasions from prior removal attemptsThe mass is within the drum rather than the canal, and there were no removal attempts
Vestibular schwannomaCerebellopontine angle tumour compressing the cochlear nerve; NF2 in the youngSensorineural loss with tinnitus, adult onset, NF2 stigmataConductive loss, no tinnitus, age 5, no NF2 findings
Management, in one line Cholesteatoma is treated by surgical excision. No further topical or oral antibiotic will resolve it, because antibiotics treat the superinfected debris rather than the epithelium generating it.
Decision spine Is the drum intact? — Yes → the discharge is not coming through a perforation, so acute otitis media is out · Where is the mass? — On the drum in a retraction pocket → not the canal, so otitis externa and foreign body are out · Which kind of hearing loss? — Conductive → ossicles rather than nerve, so the schwannoma is out · Did adequate antibiotics fail? — A month of topical and oral therapy → this is not primarily an infection · Do the options name diseases or processes? — Processes → translate the diagnosis into epithelium and keratin, then pick
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Otoscopy with pneumatic insufflationFirstIntact, immobile drum with a pearly white mass in a retraction pocketCholesteatoma; a bulging or perforated drum points to otitis media
Tuning forks and audiometryNextConductive lossOssicular erosion; a sensorineural loss points to the nerve
Temporal bone CTStagingBone erosion of the ossicles or attic wallExtent of disease before surgery
MRI of the brain and temporal boneBy branchIntracranial extension or abscessFacial palsy, vertigo on canal pressure, or neurologic signs: urgent surgery
Excision with histologyConfirmsKeratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle earCholesteatoma; excision is also the treatment
Culture of the drainageSkipGrows only the superinfecting organismsAntibiotics quiet the drainage but leave the lesion
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo boy with a month of purulent ear drainage unimproved by topical and oral antibiotics, an intact immobile tympanic membrane with a superior retraction pocket and a pearly white mass, and conductive hearing loss → Cholesteatoma → Trapped squamous epithelium and keratin debris
  2. 5 yo boy with cholesteatoma of the right middle ear and conductive hearing loss; definitive management → Surgical excision → Antibiotics do not remove the epithelium
  3. Child with a known cholesteatoma who develops acute unilateral facial droop on the affected side → Urgent imaging and surgical referral → Facial nerve erosion
  4. Child with a cholesteatoma who develops vertigo when pressure is applied to the external auditory canal → Urgent surgical referral → Labyrinthine fistula
  5. 3 yo with 2 days of fever and ear pain, a bulging erythematous tympanic membrane, now with sudden drainage and relief of pain → Oral antibiotic therapy → Acute otitis media with perforation
  6. 12 yo competitive swimmer with ear pain, tenderness on tragal traction, a macerated erythematous canal and a normal tympanic membrane → Topical antibiotic drops → Otitis externa; water exposure is the risk factor, and the drum is what sorts the risk lists
  7. 68 yo man with diabetes, severe otalgia, granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the canal and a new facial nerve palsy → Computed tomography with intravenous antipseudomonal therapy → Necrotizing otitis externa
  8. 4 yo with unilateral conductive hearing loss and a white mass behind an intact tympanic membrane, with no history of ear infection, effusion or tube placement → Congenital cholesteatoma → No retraction pocket was required
  9. Why a cholesteatoma produces conductive rather than sensorineural hearing loss → The expanding keratin mass erodes and immobilizes the ossicular chain → Sound never reaches an intact cochlea
  10. 5 yo with a cholesteatoma and persistent malodorous drainage; which management will not resolve the condition → Another course of topical and oral antibiotics → It treats the superinfection rather than the lesion
Decoy note The purulent drainage over a month suggests infection. The drainage is real: it is the cholesteatoma's trapped debris becoming superinfected. This is why antibiotics produce only partial, temporary responses. The tubes were removed three years ago, when audiometry was normal. The conductive loss is therefore new, so something in the ear has changed. No dizziness and a normal gait confirm that no labyrinthine complication has occurred yet.
Pearls A retraction pocket traps keratin and squamous epithelium behind an intact drum, causing painless otorrhea and conductive loss; treatment is surgical excision. · Discharge with an intact drum is not otitis media. Middle-ear infection drains only through a perforation, so otorrhea with an intact drum comes from the drum itself or the canal. · A cholesteatoma is not a tumour and not an infection; it is skin in the wrong place, growing and shedding keratin. Treatment is therefore surgical, and antibiotics only quiet the smell. · The risk-factor triad is recurrent acute otitis media, chronic effusion, and tympanostomy tubes, and cleft palate multiplies all three through eustachian tube dysfunction. · Conductive loss localises to the ossicles, so a cholesteatoma that causes hearing loss is already eroding the ossicles. · Complications come from erosion into neighbouring structures: facial nerve palsy, labyrinthine fistula with vertigo on canal pressure, and intracranial extension ⚠︎. Each converts an elective operation into an urgent one. · A white mass behind an intact drum in a child with no history of ear disease at all is congenital, which needs no retraction pocket to explain it ⚠︎.
Canal and middle-ear risk factors External canal risks — water exposure, trauma from swabs or ear candling, foreign material such as hearing aids and headphones, and dermatologic conditions such as eczema · Middle ear risks, which are not canal risks — sick contacts, incomplete immunization, tobacco smoke exposure, prior tympanostomy tubes and recurrent acute otitis media · Why water does it — it strips antibacterial cerumen, raises the canal pH, macerates the skin barrier and introduces organisms, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa grows in water · The boundary — the tympanic membrane separates the two compartments, which is why a middle-ear risk factor transfers no risk to the canal
Pairs with Part I Hearing Loss & Otosclerosis covers the tuning-fork sort that assigns any hearing loss to conductive or sensorineural. Part II Sinusitis and Its Complications applies the same logic to the neighbouring air-filled space. There, a chronic infection of a bony cavity is dangerous because of what it erodes into. Ask: is the drum intact, and is the mass on it or in the canal?
Transferable rule When the options describe processes rather than diseases, translate the diagnosis into its mechanism before reading them. Discharge that fails adequate antibiotics is a symptom of something structural rather than the disease itself.
Salient decoyAcute middle ear effusion with tympanic membrane inflammation: That disease requires a bulging or inflamed drum, and drainage in it implies perforation; this drum is intact, non-bulging and uninflamed
True-fact-wrong-slotChronic foreign body impaction with canal abrasion: The mass is within the tympanic membrane rather than the canal, and there were no prior removal attempts to abrade anything
Class-vs-memberExternal ear canal epithelial maceration and inflammation: Appropriate topical therapy failed, and a discrete mass on the drum is not a canal finding
Unchecked attributeSchwannoma formation with cochlear nerve injury: Schwannomas give sensorineural loss with tinnitus, occur in adulthood, and would need NF2 stigmata in a child

Seizure with Fever in a Child

Benign only inside the age window and without intracranial signs · Is this child inside the febrile-seizure age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?

Source vignette Pt — 10 wk F, fever and vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsy an hour later, open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck, decreased tone · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned lumbar puncture, neuroimaging and reassurance with discharge
The decision point

At 10 weeks old, febrile seizure is excluded by age. Simple febrile seizures are defined between 6 months and 5 years. A child outside that window with fever and a seizure needs a meningitis workup by definition, before any other finding is weighed. Three other findings independently indicate the same step. A full anterior fontanelle and vomiting are signs of raised intracranial pressure. The drowsiness persisting an hour is a postictal period far beyond the ten minutes a simple febrile seizure allows. A supple neck is not reassuring, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants; read the fontanelle and the tone instead. Perform a lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Simple febrile seizure — age 6 months to 5 years, generalized, lasting under 15 minutes, with a brief postictal period under 10 minutes and rapid return to baseline, in a child with no signs of intracranial infection; the diagnosis is clinical and needs no laboratory studies or imaging · Findings that mandate urgent lumbar puncture — age outside 6 months to 5 years, signs of intracranial infection such as headache, vomiting, a bulging or full fontanelle or nuchal rigidity, prolonged altered mental status meaning a postictal period beyond 10 minutes, and a petechial rash concerning for meningococcal disease · Additional considerations for tapping — current antibiotic therapy, which masks meningitis, and an incomplete immunization history · The open-fontanelle exemption — signs of raised intracranial pressure usually require imaging before lumbar puncture, but an open fontanelle acts as a pop-off valve, limiting herniation risk and generally negating the need for a head CT first
Pertinent positives & negatives Age 10 weeks — outside the febrile-seizure window entirely; this alone rules out discharge · Full anterior fontanelle — a sign of intracranial infection and raised pressure, and an indication to tap rather than a reason to image · Fontanelle open — acts as a pop-off valve, so CT is not needed first · Drowsy one hour after a 4-minute seizure — a postictal period beyond 10 minutes. This is prolonged altered mental status and an indication on its own · Weak suck and decreased tone — altered mental status in an infant, whose neurologic examination is feeding and tone rather than orientation · Neck supple — excludes nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable under about 12 to 18 months ⚠︎ · Seizure generalized, single, 4 minutes, now stopped — no benzodiazepine, since she is not seizing and it was under 5 minutes. No EEG (electroencephalography), since it was not focal, prolonged or recurrent · Skin normal — no petechiae, so meningococcemia is not the presentation; four other findings already indicate the tap · Vaccinations up to date — the incomplete-immunization consideration no longer applies, but the indication for the tap remains
Seizure with fever in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Bacterial meningitis Can't missAny age, and infants localise poorly, so systemic and pressure signs substitute for neck signsSeizure with fever plus a full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia or prolonged altered mental status, with CSF culture deciding— (the answer to pursue)
Simple febrile seizureViral fever triggers a generalized seizure in a neurologically normal childAge 6 months to 5 years, under 15 minutes, back to baseline within 10 minutes, otherwise normal examinationAge 10 weeks, postictal drowsiness at 1 hour, full fontanelle
Complex febrile seizureThe same trigger, but focal, prolonged, or recurrent within 24 hoursFocal features, longer than 15 minutes, or recurrence in the same illness, earning EEG and often imaging ⚠︎The seizure was single, generalized and 4 minutes
Herpes simplex encephalitis Can't missNeonatal or later, and parenchymal rather than meningealProlonged altered mental status with focal or temporal findings and CSF lymphocytes with red cells ⚠︎Not excluded — it is found by the same tap, and acyclovir is added ⚠︎
Meningococcemia Can't missN. meningitidis sepsis with rapid decompensationPetechial or purpuric rash with fever and shock, where antibiotics precede the tapSkin examination normal, normotensive
Abusive head trauma Can't missInfant with subdural collections, and may be afebrileSeizure with a bulging fontanelle, retinal hemorrhages and no fever, with unexplained irritability ⚠︎Fever 39.3 with a viral prodrome — but this is the case where imaging is the answer
Decision spine How old? — Ten weeks → outside the window, so this is not a febrile seizure and discharge is ruled out · Is she seizing now? — No, it stopped in 4 minutes → no benzodiazepine · Was it focal, prolonged or recurrent? — No → no EEG (electroencephalography) · Any sign of intracranial infection? — Full fontanelle, vomiting, hypotonia, still drowsy → yes · Does she need a CT first? — The fontanelle is open → no, so perform the lumbar puncture
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Age, exam and time to return to baselineFirstAge 6 months to 5 years, back to baseline within 10 minutesSimple febrile seizure: no tests needed
Lumbar punctureBy branchCSF pleocytosis; lymphocytes with red cells in HSVMeningitis or encephalitis; tap for age under 6 months, full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness
Serum electrolytes and glucoseBy branchLow sodium or glucoseProvoked seizure; order with vomiting or diarrhea
