Scenario bank
  1. 10-week-old girl with fever, vomiting, a 4-minute generalized seizure, drowsiness persisting an hour later, an open and full anterior fontanelle, weak suck and decreased tone → Lumbar puncture → Age outside the window plus signs of intracranial infection
  2. 18-month-old boy with temperature 39.1 C and a single 3-minute generalized seizure who is alert with a normal examination 20 minutes later → Reassurance and discharge → Simple febrile seizure
  3. 2-year-old girl with fever who is still convulsing 8 minutes after the seizure began → Intravenous lorazepam → Duration gates the benzodiazepine
  4. 3-year-old boy with fever, a generalized seizure, a spreading petechial rash and hypotension → Give empiric intravenous antibiotics immediately and perform the lumbar puncture afterward → Meningococcemia
  5. 12-month-old girl with fever and a seizure who has papilledema and a new focal neurologic deficit, with a closed anterior fontanelle → Antibiotics, then head CT, then lumbar puncture → The imaging exception
  6. 6-week-old boy, afebrile, with a seizure, a bulging fontanelle and retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy → Neuroimaging → Abusive head trauma
  7. 4-year-old boy having his third seizure of this febrile illness, this one left-sided and lasting 20 minutes → Electroencephalography → Complex febrile seizure
  8. 2-year-old with fever, seizure and persistently altered mental status whose cerebrospinal fluid shows lymphocytic pleocytosis with red blood cells → Herpes simplex encephalitis → Add acyclovir to empiric therapy
  9. Why an open anterior fontanelle removes the usual requirement for head CT before lumbar puncture → It acts as a pop-off valve that decompresses rising intracranial pressure, limiting herniation risk → The anatomy suspends the rule
  10. Infant with fever, petechiae and hypotension in whom the lumbar puncture will be delayed; which action is inappropriate → Delaying antibiotics until the lumbar puncture is completed → Treat first, tap after
  11. 2 yo M, 2 days of rhinorrhea, fever 39.2 C this morning, a 3-minute generalized seizure, sleepy and confused when paramedics arrived, now alert and playful with a normal examination; uncle has epilepsy; immunizations current → Reassurance and discharge home → simple febrile seizure; the postictal drowsiness has resolved and an uncle's epilepsy changes nothing
  12. Parents of a 2 yo after a first simple febrile seizure ask what to expect → About 30% have another; epilepsy risk stays near 1% → antipyretics do not prevent the next one
  13. 2 yo back to baseline after a brief generalized febrile seizure, but with 2 days of profuse vomiting and diarrhea and dry mucous membranes → Serum electrolytes and glucose → hypoglycemia or hyponatremia can provoke a seizure
  14. 11-month-old back to baseline after a first simple febrile seizure, with no pneumococcal or Hib vaccine doses → Lumbar puncture → incomplete immunization at 6 to 12 months lowers the bar to tap
Decoy note A supple neck excludes nothing, because nuchal rigidity is unreliable in infants. The criteria list substitutes the fontanelle, the tone and the feeding. The rest of the examination is normal: tympanic membranes, oropharynx, lungs, abdomen and skin. With no source found, this strengthens the case for tapping rather than weakening it. When every peripheral source is excluded in a febrile infant with neurologic signs, the meninges are what is left. Up-to-date vaccinations remove one of the modifiers on the list but leave the four indications already present.
Counselling, and what each test is for Recurrence — about 30% have another febrile seizure · Epilepsy — risk slightly raised, about 1% overall · Antipyretics — treat discomfort, do not prevent the next seizure · Course — resolves by school age, with no effect on development · Risk factors — fever of 39.5 °C or higher, a viral illness such as roseola or influenza, recent immunisation, a family history of febrile seizures or epilepsy · Timing — usually the first day of the illness, sometimes before the viral symptoms appear · Brain imaging — focal neurologic signs · EEG — recurrent unprovoked seizures, not a simple febrile seizure · Admission — not back to neurologic baseline · Electrolytes and glucose — vomiting or diarrhoea, since hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia can provoke a seizure · Lumbar puncture — also at 6 to 12 months with incomplete pneumococcal or Hib immunisation, or when already on antibiotics
Pearls Fever with seizure under 6 months, or with a full fontanelle or prolonged drowsiness, needs a lumbar puncture. An open fontanelle needs no CT. · The febrile-seizure diagnosis has an age gate on both ends, 6 months and 5 years. It is the fastest disqualifier, so check it before anything else. · An open fontanelle is a pop-off valve, so infants tolerate rising intracranial pressure that would herniate an older child. The CT-before-tap rule therefore generally does not apply to them. · The same finding can be both the indication and the apparent contraindication. Then ask what the rule is protecting against, and whether that risk exists in this patient. · Infants do not have neck signs; read the fontanelle, the tone, the suck and the cry instead. A supple neck excludes nothing under about 18 months ⚠︎. · A postictal period beyond 10 minutes is altered mental status, not a long febrile seizure, and it indicates a tap on its own. · With petechiae and hypotension, reverse the order: antibiotics first, tap after. A sterilised Gram stain is an acceptable price.
Pairs with Part II The Febrile Infant — Finding the Source covers the workup when there is no seizure, up to the decision to tap. This brief covers what a seizure adds to that decision. Part I Bacterial Meningitis covers the cerebrospinal fluid grid that interprets the fluid once it is obtained. Ask: is this child inside the age window, and is any sign of intracranial infection present?
Transferable rule For a benign diagnosis defined by an age range, check the age before weighing the findings, because age disqualifies it first. When a rule and a finding point in opposite directions, ask what the rule was built to prevent. If the anatomy has already prevented it, the rule does not apply.
True-fact-wrong-slotNeuroimaging: The rule exists to prevent herniation, and an open fontanelle decompresses the pressure, so the risk it guards against is not present and CT is generally unnecessary
Mirror twinReassurance and discharge: Requires age 6 months to 5 years; at 10 weeks this was never a febrile seizure, and the postictal drowsiness and full fontanelle each independently disqualify it
Salient decoyElectroencephalography: EEG is for seizures that are prolonged, recurrent or focal, and this was single, generalized and four minutes
True-fact-wrong-slotIntravenous lorazepam: Given for generalized convulsions lasting over 5 minutes, and she stopped at four and is no longer seizing

Cerebral Palsy

the MRI pattern names the cause · What does the MRI actually describe, and are the findings unilateral or global?

Source vignette Pt — 7 mo, born at 31 weeks, left-sided spasticity · Imaging — MRI shows white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity, transplacental Toxoplasma infection and inherited thrombophilia with perinatal stroke
The decision point

White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia. It is ischemia and necrosis in the poorly perfused zone beside the ventricles, and the signature injury of prematurity. The examination independently confirms a unilateral injury. Increased tone, 3+ reflexes and ankle clonus on the left only, with a right-sided lesion, is spastic hemiplegia. A congenital infection produces global deficits, not one-sided spasticity.

Defining criteria Cerebral palsy — nonprogressive motor dysfunction caused by a neurologic injury; the etiology is often multifactorial and may never be identified · Periventricular leukomalacia — ischemia and necrosis of the poorly perfused white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles, seen as white matter injury on MRI; premature infants are at greatest risk, and their friable germinal matrix vessels also predispose to intraventricular hemorrhage · Early signs that should raise suspicion — motor delay (not rolling by 4 months corrected), early hand preference before age 1, persistent neonatal reflexes (tonic neck beyond 6 months), abnormal tone · The tone evolution — infants may be hypotonic initially, with spasticity developing over time, accompanied by hyperreflexia and often clonus
Pertinent positives & negatives White matter injury adjacent to the lateral ventricle — periventricular leukomalacia, which points to prematurity; each other cause has a different imaging signature · Born at 31 weeks — the commonest setting for cerebral palsy; premature infants carry the greatest risk · Left-sided findings with a right-sided lesion — spastic hemiplegia matching a unilateral injury; intrauterine infection produces global, not one-sided, deficits · Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, sustained clonus — upper motor neuron; excludes spinal dysraphism, where lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased · Early hand preference at 7 months — abnormal before age 1, and one of the earliest signs · Not rolling over — motor delay, judged against corrected age in a 31-weeker · Head circumference at the 50th percentile — no microcephaly, which argues further against congenital infection · Babinski present bilaterally — normal at this age ⚠︎; the abnormal sign is the asymmetry of tone and reflexes, not the plantar response · Veterinary office, inconsistent prenatal care — suggest toxoplasmosis, but the MRI pattern refutes it
Cerebral palsy — the MRI pattern names the cause
EtiologyIllness scriptThe NBME tell — imagingExcluded here by
Prematurity / low birth weightIschemia in the watershed white matter beside the ventricles; friable germinal matrix vesselsPeriventricular leukomalacia; intraventricular hemorrhage— (the answer)
Hypoxic-ischemic injuryPerinatal asphyxia in a term infant; low Apgars, encephalopathy, seizuresWatershed injury; basal ganglia and thalamic lesionsBorn preterm; no depressed Apgars or neonatal encephalopathy described
Perinatal stroke (± inherited thrombophilia)Arterial infarct around the time of birth; hemiplegia emerging in infancyInfarct in a vascular distribution, most often the middle cerebral arteryThe lesion is periventricular white matter, not a territory
Intrauterine infectionCMV, toxoplasmosis; transplacental transmissionIntracranial calcifications; microcephaly; global deficitsPeriventricular white matter injury, normocephaly, unilateral findings
Neural tube defect (folate deficiency)Spinal dysraphismA spinal lesion — and the examination is lower motor neuron: decreased lower-extremity tone and reflexesHypertonia with hyperreflexia and clonus
Magnesium sulfate exposureGiven to the mother for preterm laborTransient neonatal hypotonia only; no long-lasting effectFindings at 7 months, and they are hypertonic
Management, in one line Cerebral palsy is managed supportively and lifelong. Care includes early intervention and physical therapy, tone management, and surveillance of hips, feeding and growth, seizures, vision and hearing ⚠︎. No treatment reverses the static injury itself.
Decision spine Upper or lower motor neuron? — Increased tone, 3+ reflexes, clonus → upper · Unilateral or global? — Left side only → a single-sided lesion, so global insults are excluded · What does the MRI actually say? — Periventricular white matter → leukomalacia · What produces that pattern? — Prematurity; she was born at 31 weeks · Does any exposure in the history produce it? — No: infection calcifies, thrombophilia infarcts a territory, magnesium is transient, folate affects the spine
Diagnostic workup

Brain MRICauseThe lesion pattern names the insultPeriventricular white matter: prematurity; a territory: stroke; calcifications: infection
Thrombophilia and stroke risk evaluationBy branchArterial infarct on MRIPerinatal stroke

Scenario bank
  1. 7 mo born at 31 weeks with left-sided spasticity and MRI showing white matter injury beside the right lateral ventricle → Ischemic injury of the periventricular white matter of prematurity → Periventricular leukomalacia
  2. Term infant with Apgars 2 and 4, neonatal encephalopathy and seizures; MRI shows watershed and basal ganglia lesions → Hypoxic-ischemic injury → The term-infant pattern
  3. 4 mo term infant with new left arm weakness; MRI shows infarct in the right middle cerebral artery territory → Evaluate for perinatal stroke risk factors including thrombophilia → A vascular distribution, not leukomalacia
  4. Newborn with microcephaly, periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss and petechiae → Congenital cytomegalovirus infection → Calcifications rather than white matter injury
  5. 7 mo infant with early hand preference and asymmetric tone, growing normally → Refer for brain MRI and early intervention therapy → Suspected cerebral palsy
  6. 3 yo with spastic diplegia, toe-walking and tight hamstrings, ambulating with difficulty → Physical therapy with orthoses and focal tone management → The commonest cerebral palsy subtype
  7. 7 mo infant born at 31 weeks who is not yet rolling; parents ask whether she is delayed → Assess milestones against her corrected age of about 5 months → Correct the age before judging delay
  8. 6 mo infant with decreased lower-extremity tone, absent reflexes and a sacral dimple → Spinal imaging → Closed spinal dysraphism
  9. 4 yo with known cerebral palsy who has lost independent ambulation over 6 months → Attributing the regression to the cerebral palsy → Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive
  10. 5 yo with spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy at a routine health maintenance visit → Hip surveillance imaging with feeding, growth, vision, hearing and seizure review → The comorbidities of a static injury
  11. 2 yo M, term, hypotonic at 4 months and sitting only at 10 months; over the past 3 months has developed spasticity and dystonia with involuntary hand and foot movements, and for the past month bites his fingers and hands, pinches himself and bangs his limbs; family history unremarkable; nonverbal; hypertonia, hyperreflexia and bilateral extensor plantar responses; new and healing abrasions on the fingers and hands → Lesch-Nyhan syndrome → HGPRT deficiency; check serum uric acid
  12. 2 yo F who babbled, reached for toys and said a few words by 12 months, then over 6 months stopped speaking and using her hands purposefully; now makes constant hand-wringing movements; head growth has slowed from the 50th to the 10th percentile → Rett syndrome → MECP2 testing; regression is never cerebral palsy
Decoy note The veterinary office evokes cat litter, and the inconsistent prenatal care reinforces it, but the MRI refutes it. Of the three maternal drugs named, the antenatal corticosteroids actually lowered this infant's risk rather than raising it. The bilateral Babinski is a normal finding at 7 months ⚠︎ and should not be over-read. The asymmetry of tone and reflexes is the abnormal sign.
Pearls White matter injury beside the lateral ventricle is periventricular leukomalacia, and prematurity is what causes it. · The imaging pattern maps to the insult: periventricular white matter → prematurity · watershed or basal ganglia → hypoxic-ischemic injury · a vascular territory → perinatal stroke · calcifications → congenital infection. · Distribution defines the subtype: both legs is spastic diplegia, the commonest; one side is spastic hemiplegia, which should match a unilateral lesion. · Hand preference before age 1 is abnormal, and it is often the earliest sign a parent reports. · Cerebral palsy is nonprogressive; losing an acquired milestone is a different disease and reopens the workup ⚠︎. · Infants with cerebral palsy may begin hypotonic and become spastic later, so normal early tone never excludes it. · Magnesium sulfate given before preterm birth is neuroprotective and reduces cerebral palsy risk ⚠︎.
When it is not cerebral palsy Lesch-Nyhan syndrome — a boy who is hypotonic and delayed in infancy, then by about age 3 develops new dystonia, spasticity and hyperreflexia and self-mutilation (biting fingers and hands, banging limbs); X-linked recessive HGPRT deficiency (hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase) with high uric acid, and gouty arthritis and obstructive nephropathy later if untreated · Rett syndrome — a girl with normal early development who regresses after about 6 months, losing speech and purposeful hand use, with hand wringing · Autism spectrum disorder — social and language deficits, sometimes self-injury, but no spasticity, dystonia or pyramidal signs · Progression — cerebral palsy is nonprogressive, so new movement signs or self-injury after a hypotonic infancy mean a progressive or metabolic disease
Pairs with Part II Follow-Up of the Preterm Infant covers periventricular leukomalacia and intraventricular hemorrhage as prematurity outcomes, and the corrected-age arithmetic this brief uses. Part II Congenital Infections (TORCH) covers the calcification pattern and the global-deficit picture, which is where toxoplasmosis belongs. Part II Spinal Dysraphism covers the upper-versus-lower motor neuron examination that separates a brain lesion from a spinal one. Part I Tics and Tic Disorders covers Tourette syndrome, and Part I Developmental Milestones and Normal Growth covers the regression red flags. Ask: what does the imaging actually describe, and are the deficits one-sided or global? Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the floppy infant before any spasticity appears: is the problem in the brain or the motor unit? Part II Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi separates Rett syndrome from Angelman syndrome. Ask: did the child lose skills, or never gain them?
Transferable rule An exposure in the history suggests a cause; only a described imaging pattern decides it. When a stem gives both, read the imaging first.
Salient decoyTransplacental Toxoplasma gondii: Congenital infection produces intracranial calcifications and global deficits; this MRI describes periventricular white matter and the findings are strictly one-sided, in a normocephalic infant
True-fact-wrong-slotLack of maternal folic acid: Folate deficiency causes neural tube defects, in which lower-extremity tone and reflexes are decreased, the opposite of this examination
Unchecked attributeMaternal magnesium sulfate: It causes transient hypotonia in the immediate newborn period, not lasting spasticity at 7 months
Class-vs-memberInherited thrombophilia: Stroke shows an infarct in a vascular distribution, usually the middle cerebral artery, not periventricular leukomalacia

Sinusitis and Its Complications

A normal neuro exam is a low-sensitivity test

Source vignette Pt — child with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in a double-worsening pattern, now with focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness; neurologic examination nonfocal · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned oral antibiotics, lumbar puncture and urgent neuroimaging
The decision point

A double worsening course indicates acute bacterial rhinosinusitis. Focal headache, early-morning vomiting and drowsiness are intracranial extension flags. Vomiting is worst in the early morning because ICP (intracranial pressure) rises in recumbency. These flags call for urgent imaging rather than oral antibiotics.

"Neurologic examination is nonfocal" does not exclude a brain abscess; frontal lobe abscesses are neurologically silent until late. When raised ICP is suspected, image before LP (lumbar puncture).

Sinusitis complications — features → next step
ComplicationFeaturesNext step
Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitisEyelid swelling; normal EOM, normal vision, no proptosis; often from a skin break such as an insect bite, eczema or traumaOral antibiotics
Orbital (postseptal) cellulitisProptosis, pain with EOM, ophthalmoplegia, ↓ acuity; usual source is ethmoid or maxillary sinusitis (cheek tenderness), less often a maxillary dental infection or orbital traumaCT orbits and sinuses + IV antibiotics; surgical drainage for an abscess
Pott puffy tumorFrontal bone osteomyelitis with subperiosteal abscess — doughy forehead swellingCT/MRI + IV antibiotics + surgery
Brain abscess EmergencyFocal headache, early-morning vomiting, drowsiness, ± focal deficitCT/MRI → ring-enhancing lesion; IV antibiotics + drainage
MeningitisDiffuse headache, nuchal rigidity, photophobiaImage first if ICP signs, then LP
Cavernous sinus thrombosisCN III, IV, V1–V2, VI palsies, proptosis, spreads bilaterallyMRI/MRV + IV antibiotics
Where orbital cellulitis comes from Sinusitis — the most common source; ethmoid or maxillary, spreading contiguously into the orbit (streptococci, S aureus); cheek tenderness points to the maxillary sinus · Dental infection — only maxillary (upper) teeth sit near the sinus and orbit; a mandibular abscess, especially on the opposite side, does not explain it · Skin break (eczema, insect bite, trauma) — causes preseptal cellulitis, anterior to the orbital septum, without proptosis, vision change or painful eye movements · Otitis media — spreads to the mastoid or meninges, not the orbit
Signs of raised ICP & abscess essentials Early-morning headache and vomiting (recumbent CO₂ retention → cerebral vasodilation) · papilledema · altered mental status · late, the Cushing triad. Contiguous sinus spread means Streptococcus anginosus/milleri group and anaerobes; CT with contrast shows a ring-enhancing lesion, and MRI with restricted diffusion on DWI separates abscess from tumor. Treat with vancomycin + ceftriaxone + metronidazole plus drainage. Ring-enhancing differential: abscess, glioblastoma, metastasis, toxoplasmosis, tuberculoma, lymphoma.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Clinical course and neurologic historyFirstDouble worsening with no red flagsUncomplicated sinusitis: oral antibiotics, no imaging
Eye exam: movements, acuity, proptosisBy branchPain with eye movement or proptosisOrbital cellulitis: CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast, which shows the source sinus and any abscess to drain
CT or MRI of the head with contrastNextRing-enhancing lesionBrain abscess; order for morning vomiting or drowsiness, even with a nonfocal exam
MRI with diffusion-weighted imagingSupportsRestricted diffusion in the lesionAbscess rather than tumor
MRI with MR venographyBy branchCavernous sinus thrombosisCranial nerve palsies with proptosis, becoming bilateral
Drainage with Gram stain and cultureConfirmsStreptococcus anginosus group or anaerobesNames the organism; drainage is also treatment
Lumbar puncture before imagingSkipRisk of herniation with raised pressureImage first; LP without CT only when no pressure signs
Scenario bank
  1. Eyelid swelling but normal EOM and vision → Preseptal cellulitis → oral antibiotics
  2. Proptosis and painful eye movement → Orbital cellulitis → CT orbits + IV antibiotics
  3. Doughy swelling over the forehead → Pott puffy tumor → imaging + IV antibiotics + drainage
  4. CN VI palsy with proptosis becoming bilateral → Cavernous sinus thrombosis → MRV
  5. Fever + nuchal rigidity with no ICP signs → Lumbar puncture without prior CT
  6. A child has rhinosinusitis with a double-worsening course, focal headache, and 12 days of symptoms. The neurologic examination is nonfocal, and there is no vomiting or drowsiness. → Uncomplicated acute bacterial rhinosinusitis → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Ring-enhancing lesions in an HIV patient with CD4 <100 → Toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma → multiple basal ganglia lesions favor toxoplasmosis
  8. Child with morning headache and vomiting plus ataxia, no infection → Posterior fossa tumor → same ICP syndrome, non-infectious cause
  9. Adult with a ring-enhancing lesion and recent dental infection → Brain abscess by contiguous spread
  10. 5 yo M, right eye pain since morning with blurred vision for several hours; history of frequent ear infections, recurrent sinusitis, many dental caries, atopic dermatitis and hives after mosquito bites; T 39.4, HR 120; right eye acuity 20/70 with proptosis, conjunctival injection, periorbital swelling and redness, and pain with limited adduction; normal fundus; right cheek tenderness; a large foul-smelling cavity in the left lower second molar → Bacterial sinusitis → Orbital cellulitis from contiguous ethmoid or maxillary spread
  11. 6 yo with a week of purulent rhinorrhea, now fever, proptosis, painful and limited eye movements, and falling visual acuity despite 2 days of IV antibiotics; CT shows ethmoid sinusitis with a large subperiosteal orbital abscess → Surgical drainage with continued IV antibiotics → Orbital abscess
  12. 7 yo with a week of nasal congestion and cough, now fever, a swollen red upper eyelid, proptosis and pain with eye movement; normal mental status and no neck stiffness → CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast → Orbital cellulitis; start IV antibiotics
Pairs with Part II Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child covers the hordeolum and dacryocystitis that can spread into preseptal cellulitis. Ask: is the swelling a focal lump or the whole lid?
Transferable rule A normal neurologic exam is a low-sensitivity test for intracranial pathology. When the symptom pattern is positional and progressive (morning headache, morning vomiting, declining alertness), symptoms of raised ICP (intracranial pressure) outweigh a reassuring exam.
Test-overrides-findingsSequencing trap

Hydrocephalus and Shunt Complications

Neurology · shunt in situ changes the entire ICP workup · image first, never LP

The decision point

A child with a VP (ventriculoperitoneal) shunt presents with vomiting, irritability, lethargy, and hypertension, four signs of increased intracranial pressure. Raised ICP (intracranial pressure) calls for neuroimaging. The specific concern is shunt malfunction causing recurrent obstructive hydrocephalus. CT of the head is the first step; it shows whether the ventricles have re-dilated.

Do not choose LP (lumbar puncture). LP is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus; the pressure gradient between the ventricles and the lumbar subarachnoid space can cause transtentorial herniation. In a shunt patient, obtain CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) by tapping the shunt reservoir, never by lumbar puncture.

Defining criteria Signs of increased ICP in children — headache, vomiting (especially morning), irritability, lethargy, hypertension with bradycardia (Cushing response), papilledema, sunset sign, bulging fontanelle · Shunt malfunction — any ICP sign in a patient with a VP shunt · VP shunt tap — CSF is obtained percutaneously from the shunt reservoir, not by lumbar puncture
Management ladder — VP shunt with raised ICPCT first, shunt tap for CSF
TierInterventionEscalate when
1CT head: compare ventricle size to baselineVentricles enlarged → shunt malfunction confirmed
2Shunt series (skull, chest, abdomen x-rays): trace catheter for disconnection, migration, kinkingDiscontinuity or migration visible
3Shunt tap (percutaneous reservoir aspiration): cell count, Gram stain, culture; measure opening pressureElevated pressure → obstruction; elevated WBC or positive culture → infection
4Surgical shunt revision or externalizationClinical deterioration despite medical management
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Head CT, compared with baselineFirstVentricles larger than on prior imagingShunt malfunction
Shunt series: skull, chest and abdomen filmsNextCatheter discontinuity, kinking or migrationMechanical failure: urgent neurosurgical revision
Shunt tap with opening pressureBy branchHigh opening pressureProximal or distal obstruction
Shunt tap CSF: cell count, Gram stain, cultureConfirmsPositive culture with neutrophilsShunt infection, often S. epidermidis; tap if febrile even with stable ventricles
Head CT showing small ventriclesBy branchSlit ventricles unchanged from priorSlit ventricle syndrome or another cause of headache
Lumbar punctureSkipHerniation risk in obstructive hydrocephalusCSF comes from the shunt reservoir
Before the shunt: the first presentation in an infant Macrocephaly — head circumference above the 97th percentile · Growth velocity — a head that crosses percentiles upward is abnormal even before it passes the 97th; plot weight and length beside it · Infant signs — full or bulging fontanelle, split sutures, prominent scalp veins, irritability and poorer feeding, developmental delay or loss of skills, leg spasticity, sunsetting eyes · Absent classic signs — papilledema, vomiting and the Cushing response may be missing while the fontanelle is open · Imaging — head ultrasound if the fontanelle is open, or fast MRI; MRI shows the posterior fossa best and uses no radiation; CT only with signs of acutely raised ICP
The big infant head: mimics Benign familial macrocephaly — large head that tracks its own percentile, normal development, soft flat fontanelle, often a parent with a large head: reassure and recheck · Craniosynostosis — abnormal head shape with a palpable ridged suture; the fontanelle is not full: skull film or CT · Congenital hypothyroidism — a large but soft fontanelle, with no rapid head growth; lethargy, constipation, jaundice, umbilical hernia · Hydrocephalus — head crossing percentiles plus a full fontanelle, split sutures or delay: image now, no lumbar puncture
Scenario bank
  1. 4 yo F with a VP shunt, 24 hours of vomiting, irritability and lethargy, BP 125/75, afebrile → CT scan of the head → evaluate for shunt malfunction
  2. 6 yo M with a VP shunt, CT showing dilated ventricles compared to baseline → Shunt series radiographs to evaluate catheter integrity → shunt malfunction confirmed
  3. 3 yo M with a VP shunt placed 3 months ago, fever 38.8, irritability, CT showing stable ventricles → Shunt tap for CSF cell count, Gram stain and culture → possible shunt infection despite normal ventricles
  4. 5 yo F with a VP shunt, CT showing dilated ventricles and shunt series showing catheter discontinuity at the neck → Urgent neurosurgical shunt revision → shunt malfunction from catheter fracture
  5. Why lumbar puncture is contraindicated in a child with a VP shunt and signs of increased intracranial pressure → Obstructive hydrocephalus creates a pressure gradient between the ventricles and the lumbar space, risking transtentorial herniation
  6. 2 yo M with a VP shunt placed 2 weeks ago, low-grade fever, poor feeding, CSF from shunt tap showing 250 WBCs with 80% neutrophils and positive Gram stain for cocci in clusters → Shunt infection with Staphylococcus epidermidis → externalize shunt and start IV vancomycin
  7. 8 yo F with a VP shunt, acute headache and vomiting, CT shows slit ventricles with no change from prior → Evaluate for slit ventricle syndrome or alternate causes of headache → slit ventricle syndrome
  8. 6 mo F, term, several weeks of fussiness and less interest in feeding that the parents blame on teething; afebrile with normal vital signs; anterior fontanelle full and sutures widely split; normal tone, babbles and transfers objects but cannot roll over or sit with support; weight and length at the 30th percentile, head circumference crossing percentiles upward → MRI of the brain → Hydrocephalus; head ultrasound is the alternative while the fontanelle is open
  9. 9 mo M at a well visit, head circumference at the 98th percentile, which it has followed since birth; weight and length at the 60th percentile; sitting, babbling and pulling to stand; anterior fontanelle soft and flat; his father has a large head → Routine follow-up → Benign familial macrocephaly: large but growing parallel to the curve with normal development
  10. 4 mo F, head circumference risen from the 50th to above the 97th percentile over 2 months, full anterior fontanelle, split sutures, prominent scalp veins; alert, feeding, afebrile, normal vital signs → Head ultrasound → Suspected hydrocephalus with an open fontanelle; no radiation, no sedation
  11. 5 mo M with a head circumference crossing percentiles over several weeks, now with repeated vomiting, lethargy, a tense bulging fontanelle, downward deviation of both eyes, heart rate 80/min and blood pressure 118/74 → Noncontrast head CT → Acutely raised ICP from hydrocephalus; speed outweighs radiation, then neurosurgery
Exit ramps Normal CT + fever → still tap the shunt (ventriculitis) · Normal CT + no fever + no recent surgery → GI, metabolic, or other cause · Peritoneal signs → distal catheter complication (pseudocyst, peritonitis)
Pearls S. epidermidis — most common shunt infection organism; a skin commensal that colonizes the hardware; S. aureus second; Gram-negatives in neonates · The shunt series is three plain films (skull, chest, abdomen) that trace the catheter from ventricle to peritoneum, looking for fracture, disconnection, or migration · Slit ventricle syndrome — chronic overdrainage collapses the ventricles, causing intermittent obstruction and headache with small or normal ventricles on CT · Shunt infection risk is highest in the first 6 months after placement or revision · The open fontanelle in infants acts as a pressure pop-off valve, so papilledema and Cushing response may be absent; instead look for bulging fontanelle and increasing head circumference
Pairs with Posterior Fossa Localization — shared finding: raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus; discriminator: is a shunt present? · Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant covers craniosynostosis; discriminator: an abnormal head shape with a ridged suture rather than a full fontanelle and a head crossing percentiles
Transferable rule A VP (ventriculoperitoneal) shunt changes the entire workup for raised intracranial pressure. Imaging replaces LP (lumbar puncture) as the first step. The shunt reservoir replaces the lumbar space as the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) source. The catheter itself becomes a possible cause and must be traced on plain films.
Sequencing trapLumbar puncture: it looks like the standard workup for altered mental status, but it is contraindicated in obstructive hydrocephalus because of herniation risk.
Sequencing trapEmpiric antibiotics tempt when infection is the concern, but the patient is afebrile, and antibiotics should follow culture (shunt tap), not precede it.
True-fact-wrong-slotIV acetazolamide decreases CSF (cerebrospinal fluid) production but treats idiopathic intracranial hypertension, not obstructive hydrocephalus from shunt failure.
True-fact-wrong-slotLP (lumbar puncture) diagnoses meningitis, but this infant is afebrile with a subacute course, and opening pressure does not diagnose hydrocephalus.
Unchecked attributeReassurance fits a large head only when it grows along its own percentile with normal development; this head is crossing percentiles in a delayed infant.
Mirror twinA skull film looks for craniosynostosis, which gives an abnormal head shape and ridged sutures, not a full fontanelle with split sutures.
Salient decoyA large fontanelle suggests hypothyroidism, but that fontanelle is wide and soft, not full, and the head does not grow fast.

Night Blindness

Night blindness: the fundus exam identifies the cause · pale disc or cupped disc, and is the front of the eye normal

Source vignette Pt — 17 yo F, 2 months of progressive difficulty seeing at night while driving, with a near-collision; strict vegan eating a variety of plant products · Exam — visual acuity 20/20 bilaterally; lashes, conjunctivae and cornea unremarkable; pupils equal and reactive, extraocular muscles intact, red reflex equal; midperipheral visual field defect both eyes · Fundus — optic disc pallor, attenuation of retinal vessels and focal areas of discoloration, bilateral · Q — the most likely cause; options spanned cataract, open-angle glaucoma, retinal detachment, retinitis pigmentosa and vitamin A deficiency
The decision point

Night blindness has a short differential, and the fundus exam settles it. Optic disc pallor with attenuated retinal vessels and patchy pigmentary change is the triad of retinitis pigmentosa. Rods degenerate first; they are densest in the midperiphery and serve dim-light vision. So the first symptom is night blindness, and the first field defect is midperipheral. Acuity stays 20/20 until cones are lost late. A normal red reflex and 20/20 vision exclude cataract. A pale rather than cupped disc excludes glaucoma. A two-month progressive course with no tear excludes detachment. The normal cornea and conjunctivae exclude vitamin A deficiency, whose ocular disease is xerophthalmia.

Defining criteria Retinitis pigmentosa, funduscopic triad — retinal vessel attenuation from reduced metabolic demand, waxy optic disc pallor from nerve gliosis and atrophy, and abnormal retinal pigmentation in a bone-spicule pattern, which is a late finding · Symptom sequence — night blindness first, then progressive midperipheral field loss, then decreased acuity late when cones are involved; onset from age 10 into adulthood · Xerophthalmia — the mimic's gate: dryness of the cornea and conjunctivae with night blindness, which is what vitamin A deficiency looks like in the eye · Glaucomatous disc — an increased cup-to-disc ratio; the retinitis pigmentosa disc is pale and not cupped
Pertinent positives & negatives Two months, progressive — a degeneration, not an event; excludes retinal detachment · Visual acuity 20/20 — cones intact, so early disease, and inconsistent with cataract · Red reflex equal bilaterally — no lens opacity, closing cataract independently · Cornea and conjunctivae unremarkable — no xerophthalmia, closing vitamin A deficiency on examination rather than on diet · Midperipheral field defect — the rod-dense zone, the signature distribution of early disease · Optic disc pallor, not cupping — the single most efficient discriminator · Vessel attenuation with focal discoloration — the pigmentary retinopathy itself · Age 17 — open-angle glaucoma is a disease of late adulthood
Night blindness — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Retinitis pigmentosaInherited photoreceptor degeneration, rods first; most legally blind by 40Disc pallor plus vessel attenuation plus bone-spicule pigment; night blindness then midperipheral field loss— (the answer)
Vitamin A deficiencyMalabsorption, restrictive diet or povertyXerophthalmia — dry cornea and conjunctivae, Bitot spots, corneal ulcerationCornea and conjunctivae normal; varied plant diet
Open-angle glaucomaPainless gradual peripheral field loss in late adulthoodIncreased cup-to-disc ratio with raised intraocular pressureAge 17, and the disc is pale rather than cupped
Retinal detachment Can't missAcute; myopia, trauma or prior surgeryFloaters, flashes, a curtain; tear or elevation on fundusTwo-month progressive course, no tear or elevation
CataractAge, steroids, diabetes; glare from headlights at nightDecreased acuity plus diminished red reflex plus lens opacity20/20 acuity with an equal red reflex
Management, in one line Refer for formal visual fields and electroretinography, with genetic counselling. Treatment slows rather than reverses the disease, and most patients are legally blind by age 40. Care therefore focuses on prognosis, low-vision support and family screening rather than cure.
Decision spine Is the acuity normal? — Yes, so the problem is not the lens or the macula · Is the red reflex intact? — Yes, so cataract is out · Acute or progressive? — Two months and worsening, so not a detachment · Pale disc or cupped disc? — Pale means retinitis pigmentosa, not glaucoma · Is the front of the eye normal? — Yes, so no xerophthalmia and not vitamin A · Where is the field defect? — Midperipheral, which is the rods
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Visual acuity and red reflexFirst20/20 with a normal red reflexExcludes cataract; cones are spared early
Slit-lamp exam of cornea and conjunctivaeFirstNo xerosis or Bitot spotsExcludes vitamin A deficiency
Dilated fundus examNextDisc pallor, attenuated vessels, bone-spicule pigmentRetinitis pigmentosa; a cupped disc is glaucoma
Formal visual fieldsSupportsMidperipheral field lossRod loss
ElectroretinographyConfirmsReduced or absent rod responsesRetinitis pigmentosa
Genetic testing, exam of relativesCausePathogenic variant identifiedInheritance pattern; screen first-degree relatives
Serum vitamin A for a vegan dietSkipNot needed with a normal cornea and conjunctivaeThe fundus, not the diet, names the cause
Scenario bank
  1. 17 yo F, 2 months of progressive night blindness, visual acuity 20/20, midperipheral field defect both eyes, funduscopy shows optic disc pallor with attenuated vessels and focal pigmentary change, cornea and conjunctivae normal → Retinitis pigmentosa → rods degenerate before cones
  2. 4 yo recently resettled refugee with night blindness, dry conjunctivae with Bitot spots and corneal xerosis → Vitamin A deficiency → oral vitamin A supplementation
  3. 17 yo F with night blindness, midperipheral field loss and a fundus showing disc pallor with vessel attenuation → Electroretinography with formal visual fields and genetic counseling → confirming retinitis pigmentosa
  4. 68 yo M with painless gradual peripheral field loss, intraocular pressure 26 and a cup-to-disc ratio of 0.8 → Open-angle glaucoma → topical prostaglandin analog
  5. 55 yo M with sudden floaters and flashes followed by a curtain across the temporal field → Same-day ophthalmology referral → retinal detachment
  6. 72 yo F troubled by glare from oncoming headlights at night, visual acuity 20/60, diminished red reflex → Cataract → lens opacification
  7. Why night blindness is the earliest symptom of retinitis pigmentosa → Rod photoreceptors degenerate before cones → rods serve dim-light vision and the midperiphery
  8. Newly diagnosed 17 yo F with retinitis pigmentosa who has an asymptomatic 12 yo brother → Ophthalmologic examination with genetic counseling for first-degree relatives → most cases are inherited
Decoy note Strict vegan is the decoy. She also eats a variety of plant products, which counters that risk factor. When a risk factor is qualified straight away, the qualifier takes precedence.
Pearls Examination versus history — diet, occupation and travel raise hypotheses, and the examination settles them; when the two disagree, trust the fundus · Pale disc is retinitis pigmentosa; cupped disc is glaucoma — one descriptive word separates a teenager's genetic degeneration from an older adult's pressure disease · vitamin A deficiency and retinitis pigmentosa share night blindness and differ at the front of the eye · Acuity is preserved until late because rods go first, so 20/20 vision argues for the diagnosis in a patient with field loss, not against it · night driving trouble in an older adult is cataract glare; in a teenager with a normal red reflex it is retinal
Pairs with Part I The Red Eye covers everything anterior to the lens, the territory of xerophthalmia. Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers what a plant-only diet actually requires supplementing; that brief's answer is B12, not vitamin A. Ask: is the front of the eye normal, and is the disc pale or cupped? Part II Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies covers vitamin A deficiency itself (ask: is fat being malabsorbed, and are there Bitot spots?).
Transferable rule A demographic or lifestyle detail is a prior, not a finding. If a diet, job or country of origin is the only thing still supporting an option, that option is the decoy. Switch only when a stated finding is incompatible with your current answer.
Salient decoyVitamin A deficiency: strict vegan plus night blindness is a taught pairing and it outpolled the key, but ocular vitamin A deficiency is xerophthalmia and the front of the eye is explicitly normal.
Unchecked attributeOpen-angle glaucoma: painless peripheral field loss is genuinely its presentation, but it is a disease of late adulthood and the disc is cupped, not pale.
Unchecked attributeRetinal detachment: a retinal cause of field loss, but acute with floaters, flashes and a visible tear; this is two months of steady progression.
True-fact-wrong-slotCataract: difficulty driving at night from headlight glare is a real cataract complaint, but it requires reduced acuity and a diminished red reflex, both normal here.

Tics and Tic Disorders

Classify the movement first · is the behaviour involuntary, or is it neutralising an obsession

Source vignette Pt — 7 yo M, behavioural concerns at school; repeats exactly what other children say, and last year raised his hand repeatedly then said he was just stretching when called on; plays alone to avoid bullying, prefers books and jigsaw puzzles; says he tries not to be bad but sometimes cannot help it · History — father has obsessive-compulsive disorder; growth tracking at the 60th percentile · Exam — frequent head turning and shoulder shrugging; remorseful and anxious on mental status examination · Q — the most appropriate next step in management; options spanned atomoxetine, exposure and response prevention, fluoxetine, methylphenidate, parent management training and risperidone
The decision point

Three of the described behaviours are tics. Head turning and shoulder shrugging are motor tics. Repeating exactly what other children say is echolalia, a vocal tic. The hand-raising, explained away afterward, is a motor tic he covered for; this is how school-age children manage tics. Multiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic, present over a year with onset before 18, is Tourette syndrome. Among the offered options, the therapy that targets tics is the antidopaminergic risperidone. It is a second-generation antipsychotic, preferred over first-generation agents for its adverse-effect profile.

Defining criteria Tourette syndrome — multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, not necessarily concurrent, present over 1 year, with onset before age 18; more common in boys, typically presenting age 6 to 15 · Motor tics — facial grimacing, blinking, head or neck jerking, shoulder shrugging, tongue protrusion · Vocal tics — grunting, sniffing, snorting, throat clearing, barking, yelling, echolalia, coprolalia · Compulsion — the mimic's gate: a repetitive behaviour performed in response to an obsession to reduce anxiety; absent an obsession, a repetitive movement is a tic · Treatment tiers — habit reversal training is behavioural and first-line; antidopaminergic agents when tics impair function, meaning second-generation antipsychotics, dopamine depleters such as tetrabenazine, or alpha-2 agonists such as guanfacine and clonidine
Pertinent positives & negatives Head turning and shoulder shrugging — two motor tics, the examination finding that names the disorder · Echolalia — the required vocal tic; without it this is a chronic motor tic disorder, not Tourette · Symptoms over more than a year — meets the duration criterion, and the waxing and waning course is itself characteristic · Reads books, completes jigsaw puzzles, plays alone quietly — sustained attention, which argues against ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) despite the classroom referral · Remorseful, says he cannot help it — insight and distress consistent with tics, not oppositional defiance · No obsessional thoughts described — closes OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and with it both exposure therapy and fluoxetine · Bullied and avoiding peers — functional impairment, the gate that licenses pharmacotherapy · Father with OCD — a family-history decoy; OCD and Tourette are comorbid and heritable together, which is why it is plausible and why it is not diagnostic
Repetitive behaviour in a school-age child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tourette syndromeBoys 6 to 15; waxing and waning; comorbid ADHD and OCDMultiple motor tics plus at least one vocal tic over 1 year— (the answer)
Obsessive-compulsive disorderObsessions driving compulsions that relieve anxietyA named obsession; the behaviour neutralises itNo obsessional thought anywhere in the stem
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorderInattention or hyperactivity across settingsFidgetiness, cannot sustain attention, impairment in two or more settingsReads and completes puzzles alone; behaviour is school-confined
Oppositional defiant disorderAngry mood, defiance and vindictiveness toward authorityDeliberate defiance without remorseHe is remorseful and distressed by the behaviour
Provisional tic disorderTics present less than 1 yearSame movements, shorter durationSymptoms span more than a year
Management, and the option list that was not offered Behavioural therapy with habit reversal training is first-line and is the choice whenever it is offered. When tics impair function, add an antidopaminergic or an alpha-2 agonist. Clonidine and guanfacine are both guideline-supported for tics and ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) together. Guanfacine is often preferred first for its milder sedation profile; this is clinical practice, not a guideline ranking. When the guideline first-line treatment is not on the option list, choose the best offered treatment for the diagnosis you made. Do not change the diagnosis to fit an offered drug.
Decision spine Describe the movements. — Head turning, shrugging, hand-raising are motor tics · Is there a sound? — Echolalia is a vocal tic · How long? — Over a year and waxing and waning, so Tourette rather than provisional · Is any behaviour neutralising an obsession? — No, so not OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), and the exposure therapy and fluoxetine options fall · Can he sustain attention? — Books and puzzles, so not ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder), and the stimulants fall · Is function impaired? — Bullied and isolated, so pharmacotherapy is licensed
Scenario bank
  1. 7 yo M with head turning, shoulder shrugging and repetition of classmates' words for over a year, now bullied and socially isolated → Risperidone → Tourette syndrome with functional impairment
  2. 8 yo M with mild motor and vocal tics who is performing well academically and has friends → Habit reversal training → behavioral therapy precedes medication when tics are mild
  3. 9 yo M with motor tics who also describes intrusive thoughts of contamination relieved only by repeated handwashing → Comorbid obsessive-compulsive disorder → exposure and response prevention
  4. 7 yo M with head jerking and eye blinking for 8 months and no vocal tic → Provisional tic disorder → duration under 1 year with no vocal tic
  5. How antipsychotic agents suppress tics in Tourette syndrome → Dopamine receptor blockade → tetrabenazine instead depletes presynaptic dopamine
  6. 8 yo with Tourette syndrome and inattention impairing him at home and at school → A stimulant for the comorbid ADHD → stimulants are not contraindicated in Tourette — methylphenidate reduces ADHD symptoms without worsening tics (AAN 2019)
  7. 7 yo with Tourette syndrome whose parents request medication to reduce the tics → Fluoxetine → an SSRI treats comorbid OCD, not tics
  8. 10 yo with moderate impairing tics whose parents decline an antipsychotic because of weight-gain concerns → Guanfacine → alpha-2 agonists are an accepted alternative
Decoy note Family history of obsessive-compulsive disorder in the father is the strongest decoy. It is true in a way that makes it worse: obsessive-compulsive disorder and Tourette syndrome are comorbid and co-heritable. So this history is consistent with Tourette syndrome while pointing toward obsessive-compulsive disorder. The child's own words describe the involuntariness of a tic, not the anxiety relief of a compulsion.
Pearls Describe the movement before you name the disorder — a family history does not change what a movement is · A compulsion requires an obsession; with no obsessional thought, a repetitive behaviour is a tic and exposure therapy is the wrong tool · Echolalia is a vocal tic, and it upgrades a chronic motor tic disorder to Tourette syndrome. It is the criterion most often missed, because repeating words does not seem like a vocal tic · tics wax and wane, so a behaviour that stopped last year and was replaced by a new one is natural history, not improvement · stimulants for comorbid ADHD (attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) are not contraindicated in Tourette ⚠︎, despite older teaching
Pairs with Part II School Difficulty in a Child is the nearest relative. It shares the same referral route, a school behaviour complaint. The resolution is opposite: there the private interview reveals a learning disorder, and here the examination reveals tics. Ask: what exactly is the child doing, and is it involuntary?
Transferable rule A family history raises the prior probability, but the phenomenology decides. When a relative's diagnosis and a child's behaviour are both given, first describe the behaviour in neutral terms. If the behaviour is involuntary and stereotyped, it is a tic, whatever the family carries.
Salient decoyExposure and response prevention: the father's OCD and the anxious remorseful affect sell it, but exposure therapy treats compulsions driven by obsessions and no obsession is described.
True-fact-wrong-slotFluoxetine: first-line for paediatric OCD and depression, but the same category error, and an SSRI does not suppress tics.
Class-vs-memberParent management training: targets oppositional defiant disorder; he is remorseful rather than defiant, and it does nothing for tics.
Class-vs-memberMethylphenidate and atomoxetine: ADHD is genuinely comorbid with Tourette, but these behaviours are tics and sustained attention on books and puzzles argues against ADHD.

Sleep Problems in a Child

nightmares · sleep terrors · sleepwalking and confusional arousals · obstructive sleep apnea · behavioral insomniaEarly and inconsolable, or late and awake with a dream to tell?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Time the event in the night and test the arousal:

  • Nightmares: mostly the second half of the night; wakes alert and recalls the dream
  • Sleep terrors: usually the first half (most often the first third); may show autonomic arousal; unresponsive to comfort; no memory; most common at ages 3 to 7
  • Sleepwalking: usually the first half; lock doors and windows

Sleep terrors: reassure and keep the child safe; scheduled awakenings, before the expected episode, are another option.

Snoring: screen at every well-child visit; obstructive sleep apnea needs polysomnography, and adenotonsillectomy is first-line.

Repetitive, stereotyped behaviors or posturing at night: investigate for nocturnal seizures.

Diagnosis
Which event Nightmares – REM (rapid eye movement) sleep, mostly the second half of the night, recall on waking · Sleep terrors – NREM (non-rapid eye movement) sleep, usually the first half; may show tachycardia and sweating; does not respond to comfort; amnesia · Obstructive sleep apnea – snoring and attention problems; peaks at 2 to 8 years with adenotonsillar hypertrophy · REM sleep behavior disorder – dream enactment with loss of REM atonia; male predominance in older adults; linked to alpha-synucleinopathies
Management and treatment
Next step by problem
ProblemFirstThen or also
Sleep terrorsReassure and educate; ensure safety; increase total sleepScheduled awakenings before the expected episode
NightmaresCommon at ages 3 to 5Cognitive behavioral therapy; ask about posttraumatic stress disorder (trauma) and mood
SleepwalkingLock windows and outer doors; remove breakable objects–
Obstructive sleep apneaPolysomnography to diagnoseAdenotonsillectomy, first-line
Behavioral insomniaBehavioral interventions, first-lineHypnotics are not recommended
Practice
  1. 6-year-old boy wakes crying most nights in the early morning hours tells his parents a dog was chasing him; settles after a hug happy and busy by day T 36.8 °C · examination normal · no snoring → Nightmares → late in the night, fully awake, recalls the dream and can be comforted: REM nightmares; sleep terrors and confusional arousals come early from NREM sleep with no memory
  2. 4-year-old girl sits up screaming about 90 minutes after falling asleep sweaty and breathing fast; does not respond as her parents try to comfort her no memory of it next morning HR 150/min during an episode · daytime examination normal → Sleep terrors → usually early in the night, autonomic arousal, unresponsive to comfort and amnesia: NREM sleep terrors; nightmares come late with recall, and seizures are stereotyped and repetitive
  3. 5-year-old boy with screaming episodes 1 to 2 hours after bedtime, twice a week inconsolable for minutes, then sleeps; remembers nothing no snoring, no jerking or stiffening afebrile · neurologic examination normal → Reassure and keep him safe → classic sleep terrors at a typical age: reassure, educate and ensure safety; snoring would call for a sleep study and repetitive stereotyped movements for a seizure workup
  4. 6-year-old girl screams, unconsolable, nightly at about 10:30 pm for 2 months parents have reassured her and made the room safe she still has episodes most nights afebrile · no snoring · examination normal → Wake her before the usual time → scheduled awakenings, before the expected episode, are a listed treatment; total sleep should be increased, not shortened; polysomnography is for suspected obstructive sleep apnea, and she does not snore
  5. 5-year-old boy snores loudly every night with pauses and gasps teacher reports poor attention; restless sleep, wakes tired BMI (body mass index) 50th percentile · tonsils nearly touching · BP 98/60 mm Hg → Polysomnography → snoring with attention problems and big tonsils suggests obstructive sleep apnea; polysomnography is required to make the diagnosis, and adenotonsillectomy is first-line treatment; attention problems are a listed feature of the apnea, so test for it before a stimulant
  6. 2-year-old boy will not fall asleep unless a parent lies beside him wakes twice a night and needs the same to fall back asleep healthy, growing well T 36.7 °C · examination normal · no snoring → Behavioral sleep training → sleep-onset association insomnia: behavioral interventions are first-line, and hypnotics are not recommended for behavioral insomnia; with no snoring, polysomnography is not indicated
  7. 9-year-old boy found walking in the dark kitchen an hour after bedtime eyes open, mumbling; back in bed without waking; no memory twice this month afebrile · examination normal · no snoring → Secure doors and windows → sleepwalking is an NREM arousal, usually in the first half of the night; safety measures such as locking windows and outer doors reduce injury; with no snoring or stereotyped movements, neither a sleep study nor a seizure workup is indicated
Pairs with Tics and Tic Disorders: at night, repetitive stereotyped behaviors or posturing call for a nocturnal seizure workup
Transferable rule

Early in the night with no memory usually means a NREM arousal; late, awake and recalling a dream is a nightmare.

3 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Neurology & HEENT

Spinal Dysraphism

Grade the reflexes first · a number outranks a story

Source vignette Pt — 6 yo M, 2 months of progressive gait difficulty and back pain, new incontinence, pes cavus and hammer toes, 1+ lower extremity reflexes · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned tethered cord, Duchenne muscular dystrophy and spastic diplegia
The decision point

1+ reflexes are the key finding. Hyporeflexia is a lower motor neuron sign that localises at or below the anterior horn cell. It eliminates spastic diplegia outright, since cerebral palsy is by definition an upper motor neuron disorder. Three findings then pick the lesion. Bladder involvement counts because muscle and peripheral nerve diseases spare the bladder. Back pain points at a structural spinal lesion. Pes cavus is chronic denervation of the intrinsic foot muscles.

One lesion explains all four findings: a tethered cord from closed spinal dysraphism, stretched by two months of growth.

Defining criteria Reflex grading — 0 absent, 1+ diminished, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ clonus · Lower motor neuron signs — weakness with hypotonia, hyporeflexia and atrophy, localising at or below the anterior horn cell · Upper motor neuron signs — weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski, localising above the anterior horn cell · Secondary incontinence — continence achieved and held, then lost; always pathologic · Low-lying conus — the conus reaches L1 to L2 by about 3 months, so below mid-L2 is low; a filum over 2 mm is thickened
The child with progressive leg weakness - the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Tethered cordCord anchored caudally and stretched by growthLMN signs with bladder dysfunction, pes cavus and back pain together
Duchenne muscular dystrophy3 to 5 yo boy, progressive degenerationProximal weakness, Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, pes planus; no bladder involvement
Spastic diplegiaStatic perinatal insult, often prematurityHypertonia and hyperreflexia, scissoring gait, nonprogressive
Transverse myelitisPost-infectious cord demyelinationAcute over hours to days with a sensory level
Charcot-Marie-ToothHereditary neuropathy, autosomal dominantPes cavus with foot drop and family history; no bladder involvement
Friedreich ataxiaAutosomal recessive, teensPes cavus with ataxia and areflexia with upgoing toes, cardiomyopathy
Spinal cord tumor Can't missAstrocytoma or ependymomaNight-waking back pain with progressive deficits; same MRI answers both
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Reflex grading and neurologic examFirst1+ reflexes with bladder dysfunctionLower motor neuron signs plus bladder: spinal cord
Inspection of the lower backFirstHair tuft, lipoma or dimple above the gluteal cleftClosed dysraphism; a normal back does not exclude it
Spinal ultrasound, infant under about 3 monthsBy branchLow-lying conus or thick filumClosed dysraphism; MRI after the posterior elements ossify
MRI of the lumbosacral spineConfirmsConus below mid-L2, filum over 2 mmTethered cord: surgical detethering; also shows a cord tumor
Creatine kinaseBy branchVery high CKDuchenne: proximal weakness, Gower sign, bladder spared
Brain MRI for suspected spastic diplegiaSkipReflexes are decreased, not briskHyporeflexia localizes below the brain
Scenario bank
  1. 6 yo M, 2 mo of progressive gait difficulty and back pain, new incontinence, pes cavus and hammer toes, 1+ lower extremity reflexes → Tethered cord → MRI of the spine
  2. 5 yo M, difficulty climbing stairs, Gower sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, CK 18,000, continent → Duchenne muscular dystrophy → genetic testing
  3. 3 yo, former 27-week preemie, toe-walking with a scissoring gait, hypertonia, 3+ reflexes, nonprogressive → Spastic diplegic cerebral palsy
  4. 12 yo F, 3 days of leg weakness, a sensory level at T8, urinary retention, 2 wk after a viral illness → Transverse myelitis → MRI and high-dose intravenous steroids
  5. 14 yo M, distal weakness, foot drop with steppage gait, pes cavus, absent ankle reflexes, father has the same feet → Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease
  6. 13 yo M, progressive ataxia and dysarthria, pes cavus, areflexia with upgoing toes, scoliosis, cardiomyopathy → Friedreich ataxia → echocardiogram
  7. Newborn with a lumbosacral hair tuft and a dimple above the gluteal cleft, normal neurologic exam → Closed spinal dysraphism → ultrasound of the spine
  8. 8 yo F, back pain that wakes her at night, progressive leg weakness, bladder dysfunction, normal feet → Spinal cord tumor → MRI of the spine
  9. 7 yo M, bedwetting at night only, never been dry, normal exam and urinalysis → Primary nocturnal enuresis → reassurance
  10. 6 yo M with tethered cord on MRI and progressive symptoms → Surgical detethering
Occulta means hidden A normal-looking back does not exclude dysraphism. Cutaneous stigmata are common but not universal. Look for a hair tuft, lipoma, hemangioma, sacral appendage, or a dimple above the gluteal cleft; a simple dimple within the cleft with a visible base is benign. Image with ultrasound before about 3 months, while the posterior elements are cartilaginous, and MRI after.
Pearls Pes cavus is a neurologic sign, not an orthopedic one: Charcot-Marie-Tooth, Friedreich ataxia, and tethered cord · Secondary enuresis is never assumed functional; consider infection, diabetes, constipation, neurologic disease, stress and sleep apnea · Back pain in a child under 10 is pathologic until proven otherwise · Occulta — skin intact, no herniation · Meningocele — meninges herniate, cord normal · Myelomeningocele — meninges and neural tissue, with Chiari II and hydrocephalus · Folate prevents neural tube defects: 0.4 mg periconceptionally, 4 mg with a prior affected pregnancy
Pairs with Part I Enuresis is the mirror twin: it shares the complaint of a school-age child wetting, and the classification flips from functional to neurologic. Ask: was the child ever dry, and is anything else abnormal? Part I Constipation in a Child screens for this condition on every perineal examination; a sacral dimple or hair tuft converts constipation into imaging.
Transferable rule Grade the reflexes before you name the disease. Hyperreflexia and hyporeflexia split the weakness differential into halves that share no members. That split holds however compelling the history.
Class-vs-memberDuchenne: the right age and sex, with proximal weakness, flat feet and no bladder involvement.
Mirror twinSpastic diplegia: the upper motor neuron version of the same complaint.
True-fact-wrong-slotTransverse myelitis: a real cord syndrome on the wrong timeline.

Encephalopathy and Cerebral Edema in a Child

Cause of the cerebral edema, not of the illness

Source vignette Pt — 5 yo F, viral illness treated with over-the-counter medications; improved, then vomiting and lethargy; hepatomegaly with a normal spleen; no hypertension, no peripheral edema · Vitals — T 36.8 °C, pulse 110, BP 98/60 · Imaging — cerebral edema · Q — the most likely cause of the imaging findings; options spanned hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, uremia, adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism
The decision point

The sequence is a viral prodrome, then "over-the-counter medications" (the aspirin, never named). A biphasic course follows (better, then vomiting and lethargy). Then come hepatomegaly without splenomegaly and cerebral edema. This is Reye syndrome. The cause of the imaging finding lies one level down, at the mechanism.

Hyperammonemia, hypoglycemia, uremia, adrenal insufficiency and hypothyroidism can all cloud consciousness, but only hyperammonemia causes edema. In astrocytes, glutamine synthetase combines ammonia with glutamate to form glutamine. Glutamine is osmotically active and cannot leave. Water follows, and the astrocytes swell, causing cytotoxic cerebral edema. Hypoglycemia, uremia and adrenal crisis produce encephalopathy by other routes and leave the brain the same size.

Option audit — which options cause encephalopathy?
OptionEncephalopathy?Why it fails here
HyperammonemiaYesCorrect — the only one that swells astrocytes
HypoglycemiaYesGenuinely occurs in Reye (failing hepatic gluconeogenesis) but causes no edema — a true fact in the wrong slot
UremiaYesUremic encephalopathy without edema; expect hypertension and peripheral edema, not hepatomegaly
Adrenal insufficiencyYesDysfunction is from hypoperfusion; BP is 98/60 — normal, which kills it outright
HypothyroidismYesMyxedema coma is hypothermic and bradycardic; this child is 36.8 °C with a pulse of 110
The vitals do most of the eliminating BP 98/60 (normal) — excludes adrenal crisis, which is a hypotension diagnosis · pulse 110, temp 36.8 — excludes myxedema coma, which is slow and cold · no hypertension, no peripheral edema — excludes uremia · hepatomegaly with a normal spleen — points to acute hepatic steatosis, not congestion or storage disease.
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathies & precipitants
Toxic-metabolic encephalopathyPrecipitant
Hypoxic-ischemicNear-drowning, choking episode
Diabetic ketoacidosisPoorly controlled diabetes; edema often follows fluid resuscitation
HyponatremiaSIADH; or rapid correction of hypernatremia
Liver failureViral or autoimmune hepatitis; hepatotoxic drugs such as acetaminophen
Reye syndromeAspirin given for a viral illness in a child
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Serum ammonia and liver enzymesFirstHigh ammonia with raised AST and ALTReye syndrome; a neonate with normal liver tests points to a urea cycle defect
Serum glucoseFirstLow glucoseFailing gluconeogenesis; does not cause the edema
PT and INRSupportsProlonged PTHepatic dysfunction
Head CTNextDiffuse cerebral edemaManage intracranial pressure; image before any lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture, when safeBy branchNormal CSF apart from raised pressureExcludes meningitis and encephalitis
Liver biopsyConfirmsMicrovesicular steatosisReye syndrome; supportive, rarely needed
Salicylate levelSkipOften undetectable by the time of encephalopathyA negative level does not exclude Reye; the history does
Scenario bank
  1. 5 yo F, viral URI treated with an OTC medicine, now vomiting and lethargic with hepatomegaly and cerebral edema → Reye syndrome → supportive care and ICP management
  2. 5 yo F with Reye syndrome; the question asks the cause of the imaging finding → Hyperammonemia → astrocyte glutamine draws in water
  3. 5 yo F with Reye syndrome; what was in the over-the-counter medicine → Aspirin
  4. 5 yo F, liver biopsy performed → Microvesicular steatosis → supportive of the diagnosis but not required
  5. Which children may still receive aspirin → Kawasaki disease and rheumatologic disease such as JIA
  6. 6 yo F, altered after an infection, hypotensive with hyperkalemia and hyponatremia → Adrenal crisis → stress-dose hydrocortisone
  7. 12 yo M with type 1 diabetes, glucose 620, becomes obtunded hours into fluid resuscitation → DKA-associated cerebral edema → hypertonic saline or mannitol
  8. 2 yo M with hypernatremic dehydration corrected too rapidly → Cerebral edema from the osmotic shift
  9. 3 yo M pulled from a pool, now unresponsive → Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
  10. 3 day old with hyperammonemia, normal LFTs and no hepatomegaly, after feeds began → Urea cycle defect → ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
Distractors Hypoglycemia: the sharpest trap in the set, because it is true; Reye does cause hypoglycemia through failing hepatic gluconeogenesis. It simply is not what swells the brain. Uremia: a neurotoxin, but nothing here suggests renal failure. Adrenal insufficiency: plausible until you read the blood pressure. Hypothyroidism: the pulse and temperature contradict it.
Paired pearls Aspirin is contraindicated in children except for Kawasaki disease and rheumatologic disease such as JIA (juvenile idiopathic arthritis); Kawasaki is the reason the exception exists · the mechanism is mitochondrial injury → impaired β-oxidation. This causes microvesicular steatosis, which is why the liver is big but not scarred · treatment is supportive; there is no antidote · hyperammonemia without hepatomegaly in a neonate is a urea cycle defect, not Reye; the neurotoxin is the same, but the disease is different.
Pairs with Diabetes: the Annual Care Bundle also turns on reading the outcome noun (morbidity versus mortality). Here this stem says "cause of this patient's imaging findings," not "cause of this patient's presentation." Ask: "which effect am I being asked to explain?"
Transferable rule When a stem names a specific finding and asks what caused it, the answer must explain that finding, not the illness. Options that are true of the disease but cannot produce the named finding are the intended traps. They are the hardest to reject precisely because they are true.
True-fact-wrong-slotSalient decoy

Stroke in a Child or Adolescent

Find the arteriopathy · constitutional symptoms plus unequal pulses make it inflammatory

Source vignette Pt — 15 yo with weeks of constitutional symptoms and episodic light-headedness, now an acute focal neurologic deficit, with asymmetric upper-extremity pulses · Q — the most likely cause of the stroke; options spanned the pediatric stroke categories: vasculitis, bacterial endocarditis, fibromuscular dysplasia and others
The decision point

A stroke in a teenager is never "just a stroke"; find what made the artery fail. Weeks of fever, weight loss and aches indicate systemic inflammation. Unequal pulses or arm pressures indicate that several large arteries are narrowed at once. Inflammation plus multiple fixed large-artery stenoses is a large-vessel vasculitis; in an adolescent, that is Takayasu arteritis.

Endocarditis is the exception. It also brings fever and stroke, but emboli occlude one vessel at a time and never narrow the aorta's branches, so the pulses stay equal. Look for the murmur and the embolic skin findings instead.

Pediatric stroke, by category Cardiac — congenital heart disease with a right-to-left shunt, endocarditis, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia · Vascular, noninflammatory — arterial dissection, moyamoya, fibromuscular dysplasia · Vascular, inflammatory — Takayasu arteritis, lupus, primary CNS vasculitis, post-varicella arteriopathy, meningitis · Hematologic — sickle cell disease, inherited thrombophilia such as factor V Leiden, antiphospholipid antibodies · Takayasu arteritis — granulomatous vasculitis of the aorta and its primary branches in a young patient, most often female; a systemic phase (fever, weight loss, arthralgia) then an occlusive phase (arm claudication, weak or absent pulses, unequal arm pressures, bruits, renovascular hypertension, TIA and stroke)
Stroke in a young patient: the causes and their tells
CauseIllness scriptThe tell
Vasculitis (Takayasu)Adolescent with weeks of fever, weight loss and arthralgia; high ESRUnequal arm pulses or pressures, bruits, long smooth stenoses of the aorta and branches
Bacterial endocarditisFever with a damaged valve or injection drug useNew regurgitant murmur, embolic skin lesions, positive blood cultures; pulses equal
Fibromuscular dysplasiaYoung woman, renovascular hypertension, no inflammationString of beads on angiography, normal ESR
Arterial dissectionNeck trauma, contact sports, neck manipulationNeck pain or headache, Horner syndrome, one tapered vessel
Moyamoya diseaseDown syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1, sickle cell diseaseDeficits provoked by hyperventilation (crying, blowing); puff-of-smoke collaterals
Sickle cell diseaseKnown disease or unexplained anemiaLarge-artery vasculopathy; exchange transfusion for the acute stroke
Factor V LeidenFamily history of clotsVenous thrombosis; arterial stroke only by paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale
AtherosclerosisDiabetes, smoking, hyperlipidemia in adultsRare in adolescents without familial hypercholesterolemia; no systemic inflammation
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Brain MRI with diffusion, or head CTFirstAcute infarct, no hemorrhageArterial stroke; now find what made the artery fail
Pulses and blood pressure in both armsFirstUnequal arm pressures or pulsesSeveral large arteries narrowed: large-vessel vasculitis
ESR and CRPSupportsElevatedInflammatory arteriopathy; normal in fibromuscular dysplasia
CT or MR angiography of the aorta and branchesConfirmsLong smooth stenoses of the aorta and its branchesTakayasu arteritis
Blood cultures and echocardiographyBy branchVegetation with positive culturesEndocarditis: fever with a murmur, pulses equal
Angiography of the head and neckBy branchA single tapered vessel, beading, or puff-of-smoke collateralsDissection, fibromuscular dysplasia or moyamoya
Temporal artery biopsySkipGiant cell arteritis occurs over 50Takayasu is diagnosed by angiography
Scenario bank
  1. 15 yo with weeks of fatigue, weight loss and joint aches and episodes of light-headedness, now an acute focal deficit; the arm pulses are unequal → Vasculitis → Takayasu arteritis narrowing the aorta and its branches
  2. 15 yo with fever, weight loss, a 20 mm Hg difference in arm pressures and a carotid bruit → Aortic angiography → CT or MR angiography of the aorta and branches
  3. 15 yo F whose angiogram shows long smooth stenoses of both subclavian arteries; ESR is high and she is still losing weight → High-dose glucocorticoids → then a steroid-sparing agent
  4. 15 yo with Takayasu arteritis who becomes light-headed whenever she exercises her left arm → Subclavian steal → reversed vertebral flow feeds the arm beyond the stenosis
  5. 16 yo who injects drugs, febrile with a new regurgitant murmur and splinter hemorrhages, then sudden aphasia → Infective endocarditis → septic embolus; draw blood cultures
  6. 14 yo struck in the neck during hockey, with neck pain and a left Horner syndrome, then right arm weakness the next day → Carotid dissection → a single tapered vessel on angiography
  7. Young woman with severe hypertension, an abdominal bruit, a normal ESR and a string of beads on renal angiography, who has a TIA → Fibromuscular dysplasia → noninflammatory; no constitutional symptoms
  8. 7 yo with Down syndrome who develops transient arm weakness when crying hard or blowing out candles → Moyamoya disease → hyperventilation constricts the collateral vessels
Pearls Check both arm pressures and every pulse in any young stroke with constitutional symptoms; the older name is pulseless disease · Takayasu and giant cell arteritis share the granulomatous large-vessel histology and are split by age, with giant cell arteritis over 50 · diagnose with CT or MR angiography of the aorta and its branches, and treat with high-dose glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing agent · renal artery involvement makes it a cause of secondary hypertension in a young patient · light-headedness or syncope comes from carotid, vertebral or subclavian narrowing, including subclavian steal.
Pairs with Part I Polymyalgia Rheumatica has a giant cell arteritis row, the same vasculitis in patients over 50. Part I Hypertension in an Adult covers fibromuscular dysplasia and the abdominal bruit, the noninflammatory twin. Part II Sickle Cell Disease and Trait covers the sickle cell stroke and its exchange transfusion. Part I Tall Stature and Marfanoid Habitus covers thrombotic stroke in a tall, thin child with learning problems: check plasma homocysteine.
Transferable rule When a young patient has a stroke, name what made the artery fail. Systemic inflammation with unequal pulses is vasculitis; fever with a murmur is an embolus; neck strain with Horner syndrome is a dissection; a string of beads with no inflammation is fibromuscular dysplasia.
Salient decoyBacterial endocarditis: fever plus stroke looks embolic, but emboli do not narrow several arteries or unequalize the pulses.
Mirror twinFibromuscular dysplasia: a young woman with arterial stenoses, but no fever, weight loss or raised ESR.
Class-vs-memberThe options name the class (vasculitis), not the member (Takayasu); answer at the level offered.

Imprinting Disorders: Angelman and Prader-Willi

Happy, laughing child with seizures, ataxia and no words · NBME · which parent's chromosome 15 copy is missing?
