Source vignette Pt — 3 yo F with a seizure disorder on valproic acid and strabismus; height and weight at the 25th percentile, head circumference at the 3rd · Exam — happy and excitable, smiles and laughs often; flat back of the head, prominent jaw, widely spaced teeth; repeated hand flapping; stiff-legged gait, needs help on stairs; short attention span; communicates with gestures and sounds, no words · Q — the most likely genetic defect; options spanned chromosome 15 deletions of maternal or paternal origin, a chromosome 7 deletion, an MECP2 mutation, trisomy 15 and trisomy 21
The decision point

A child with no words, seizures, microcephaly, a stiff-legged, ataxic gait and a happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter has Angelman syndrome. Hand flapping, a flat occiput, a prominent jaw, widely spaced teeth and strabismus support it. The usual cause is deletion of the maternally inherited 15q11-q13 region, which contains UBE3A (ubiquitin protein ligase E3A). In neurons, imprinting silences the paternal copy of UBE3A. Losing the maternal copy therefore leaves those neurons with no working gene.

The same region deleted from the paternal chromosome causes Prader-Willi syndrome. Prader-Willi follows loss of the paternally expressed genes of the region. It presents as a floppy newborn with a poor suck, followed by hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism and short stature.

A less common cause of Angelman syndrome is paternal uniparental disomy. Both chromosome 15s come from the father, so no maternal UBE3A copy is present even though nothing is deleted. Maternal uniparental disomy is the mirror cause of Prader-Willi syndrome.

Defining criteria Angelman syndrome — no active maternal copy of UBE3A in neurons, usually from a maternal 15q11-q13 deletion · Prader-Willi syndrome — no active paternal copy of the 15q11-q13 genes, usually from a paternal deletion · Imprinting — silencing of one parent's copy of a gene by DNA methylation · Uniparental disomy — both copies of a chromosome inherited from one parent
Developmental delay with a genetic syndrome: the differential
DiagnosisBrief illness scriptKey discriminatorWhy less likely here
Angelman syndrome: maternal 15q11-q13 deletion; paternal uniparental disomy less oftenSevere delay with little or no speech, seizures usually before age 3, microcephaly, ataxic gaitHappy, excitable manner with frequent laughter; hand flappingThe answer: every finding in this child fits
Prader-Willi syndrome: paternal 15q11-q13 deletion; maternal uniparental disomy in about a quarterFloppy newborn with a poor suck; hyperphagia and obesity in childhood; hypogonadism, short stature, cognitive impairmentHyperphagia and obesity after a hypotonic infancy; hypogonadismHer weight is at the 25th percentile, with no hyperphagia or hypogonadism
Rett syndrome: MECP2 (methyl-CpG binding protein 2) mutation, X-linked, mostly girlsNormal development for 6 to 18 months, then loss of speech and purposeful hand use; head growth slows; seizures, gait problems, scoliosisRegression after normal early development; hand wringingNo loss of skills is described, and her hands flap rather than wring
Williams syndrome: 7q11.23 deletion that includes the elastin geneOverfriendly, usually mild intellectual disability; broad forehead, periorbital fullness, wide mouth with full lips; hypercalcemia in infancyOverfriendliness with supravalvar aortic stenosisNo murmur, typical facies or hypercalcemia is described
Down syndrome: trisomy 21Hypotonia from birth, up-slanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, single palmar crease; heart defects and duodenal atresiaRecognizable at birth by the face, hands and low toneNone of its facial or hand features is described
Scenario bank
  1. 3 yo F with seizures treated with valproic acid and strabismus; head circumference at the 3rd percentile; happy and excitable with frequent laughter; flat occiput, prominent jaw and widely spaced teeth; repeated hand flapping; stiff-legged gait; communicates with gestures and sounds but no words → Chromosome 15 deletion, maternally inherited → Angelman syndrome; neurons express UBE3A only from the maternal copy
  2. 4 yo M who was floppy with a weak suck as a newborn and needed tube feeds; now constantly seeks food and is obese; short stature, small hands and feet, a small penis and undescended testes; mild developmental delay → Chromosome 15 deletion, paternally inherited → Prader-Willi syndrome; maternal uniparental disomy is the next most common cause
  3. 3 yo F with seizures, microcephaly, an ataxic gait, no words and frequent laughter; DNA methylation analysis shows only the paternal pattern at 15q11-q13; SNP (single nucleotide polymorphism) microarray with parental samples shows no deletion and paternal isodisomy of chromosome 15 → Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 15 → Angelman syndrome without a deletion; no maternal UBE3A copy is present
  4. 20 mo F who sat, babbled and picked up small objects by 9 months; over the past 6 months she stopped babbling and using her hands to hold toys; now makes constant hand-wringing movements; head growth has slowed → Mutation of the MECP2 gene → Rett syndrome; X-linked and nearly always de novo
  5. 4 yo F who is overly friendly with strangers and has mild intellectual disability; broad forehead, periorbital fullness and a wide mouth with full lips; a systolic murmur from supravalvar aortic stenosis; high serum calcium as an infant → Chromosome 7 deletion → Williams syndrome; the 7q11.23 deletion includes the elastin gene
  6. 4 yo F with no spoken words, a wide-based jerky gait, seizures since age 2 and a small head; she laughs often and easily, is fascinated by water, and has never lost a skill she had gained → Angelman syndrome → maternal 15q11-q13 deletion in most cases
  7. 3 yo F with seizures, microcephaly, an ataxic gait, no words and a happy, excitable manner with frequent laughter → DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 → detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects; a normal result leads to UBE3A sequencing
Pearls Other Angelman features include a fascination with water and a reduced need for sleep · DNA methylation analysis of 15q11-q13 is the first test. It detects deletion, uniparental disomy and imprinting defects · A normal methylation result does not exclude Angelman syndrome. A UBE3A (ubiquitin protein ligase E3A) mutation accounts for about 1 in 10 cases and needs gene sequencing
How NBME framed it The options named the genetic defect and parent of origin, not the syndrome; the two chromosome 15 deletions differed only by parent.
Pairs with Part I Genetic Syndromes Recognized at Birth covers Down syndrome and the newborn picture of Prader-Willi syndrome. Ask: was the child floppy from birth, or delayed with seizures and laughter later? Part I Hypotonia in an Infant covers the methylation workup for Prader-Willi syndrome in a floppy infant. Part I Cerebral Palsy carries Rett syndrome as a regression mimic. Ask: did the child lose skills, or never gain them?
Transferable rule Identify the syndrome from the phenotype before choosing the genetic defect. For chromosome 15, laughter, seizures and ataxia mean the maternal copy is missing. Hyperphagia after a floppy infancy means the paternal copy is missing.
Unchecked attributeChromosome 15 deletion, paternally inherited: deletion of the same region from the paternal chromosome causes Prader-Willi syndrome, with hypotonic infancy, then hyperphagia, obesity and hypogonadism.
Salient decoyMutation of MECP2 (methyl-CpG binding protein 2): Rett syndrome also affects girls with microcephaly, seizures and repetitive hand movements. It follows normal early development with regression, and the hands wring rather than flap.
Salient decoyChromosome 7 deletion: Williams syndrome also gives a sociable child, but with overfriendliness, elfin facies, supravalvar aortic stenosis and hypercalcemia.
True-fact-wrong-slotTrisomy 15: a complete trisomy 15 is typically lethal before birth. Paternal uniparental disomy, with two paternal chromosome 15s, is the less common route to Angelman syndrome.
Class-vs-memberTrisomy 21: Down syndrome is the most common chromosomal cause of intellectual disability. It shows at birth with hypotonia, up-slanting palpebral fissures and a single palmar crease, none of which is described.

Eyelid Lumps and Swelling in a Child

Tender nodule on the lid margin with a red eye and no fever · NBME · where is the swelling, and does it spread beyond the lump?

Source vignette Pt — 10 yo M, 2 days of redness and mild pain in the left eye; afebrile · Exam — left conjunctiva mildly red, swollen and tender; a 3-mm nodule on the lower lid margin, toward the outer corner; right eye normal · Q — the most appropriate treatment; options spanned nasolacrimal massage, oral amoxicillin, topical prednisolone, topical tetrahydrozoline and warm compresses
The decision point

A tender nodule on the eyelid margin, with local redness and no fever, is a hordeolum (stye). It is an acute infection of an eyelid gland, usually by Staphylococcus aureus. First-line treatment is warm compresses with gentle lid massage several times a day. Heat softens the blocked gland contents so the gland can drain. Conjunctival redness and swelling beside the nodule come from surface irritation and do not make this conjunctivitis.

Add oral antibiotics only when redness and swelling spread across the lid, which is preseptal cellulitis. A lesion that has not settled after several weeks of compresses goes to ophthalmology for incision and drainage.

Lump or swelling of the eyelid in a child: the differential
DiagnosisBrief illness scriptKey discriminatorWhy less likely here
Hordeolum (stye)Acute staphylococcal infection of a lash follicle or eyelid gland; warm compresses and lid massageTender, red nodule on the lid margin, sometimes with a yellow pointFits: 2 days, tender 3-mm nodule on the margin, afebrile
ChalazionSterile, chronic inflammation of a blocked meibomian gland, sometimes left behind by a hordeolum; compresses, then steroid injection or incision if it persistsPainless, firm nodule in the body of the lid, away from the margin, present for weeksThis nodule is tender, on the margin and 2 days old
DacryocystitisInfection of the lacrimal sac behind a blocked nasolacrimal duct; oral antibiotics, with warm compresses as supportTender swelling at the inner corner of the eye, beside the nose; pus from the punctum on pressureThe nodule sits on the lid margin toward the outer corner
Preseptal cellulitisInfection of the lid in front of the orbital septum, from a skin break, hordeolum or dacryocystitis; oral amoxicillin-clavulanateDiffuse red, warm, swollen lid; eye movements and vision normal, no proptosisRedness and swelling stay at the nodule, and there is no fever
Orbital cellulitis Can't missInfection behind the septum, usually spread from ethmoid sinusitis; computed tomography of the orbits with contrast and intravenous antibioticsProptosis, pain with eye movement, limited eye movement or reduced visionNone of these is described, and he is afebrile
BlepharitisChronic inflammation of both lid margins, often with seborrheic dermatitis; lid hygiene and warm compressesBoth lids red and crusted along the lash line, worse on waking, with no discrete noduleOne focal nodule in one eye
Management ladder: the tender lid nodule
TierInterventionEscalate when
1. HordeolumWarm compresses several times a day with gentle lid massage; do not squeeze the lesionRedness and swelling spread across the lid; or no improvement after several weeks, when ophthalmology offers incision and drainage
2. Preseptal cellulitisOral antibiotic covering Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci, such as amoxicillin-clavulanate, with close follow-upProptosis, pain with eye movement, limited eye movement or reduced vision; or worsening on oral antibiotics
3. Orbital cellulitisAdmission, computed tomography of the orbits with contrast, intravenous antibiotics and ophthalmology consultationAbscess on imaging or falling vision: surgical drainage
Scenario bank
  1. 10 yo M with 2 days of redness and mild pain in the left eye; afebrile; mildly red, swollen and tender left conjunctiva; a 3-mm nodule on the lower lid margin toward the outer corner; right eye normal → Warm compresses → hordeolum; heat helps the blocked gland drain
  2. 8 yo F with a painless, rubbery 6-mm nodule in the middle of the upper eyelid, away from the margin; it began as a tender red bump 2 months ago and has not shrunk despite warm compresses; no redness, discharge or fever → Ophthalmology referral for incision and curettage → chalazion; an intralesional steroid injection is the alternative
  3. 4 yo F with 2 days of a tender, red swelling just below the inner corner of the right eye, beside the nose; pressing on it brings pus from the lower punctum; afebrile; eye movements full and vision normal → Oral antibiotics with warm compresses → acute dacryocystitis; probing waits until the infection settles
  4. 6 yo M with a stye on the left upper lid 4 days ago, now with diffuse redness, warmth and swelling of both left lids; T 38.2 C; vision normal, eye movements full and painless, no proptosis → Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and close outpatient follow-up → preseptal cellulitis spreading from a hordeolum
  5. 12 yo F with 1 day of a tender, red nodule with a yellow point on the upper lid margin; afebrile; no redness beyond the nodule → Squeezing the nodule to express the pus → squeezing can spread the infection into the lid
  6. 11 yo M with months of burning, itchy eyes that are worse on waking; both lid margins are red and crusted, with flakes on the lashes and no discrete nodule; scaly patches on the scalp → Blepharitis → lid hygiene and warm compresses
Pearls Squeezing a hordeolum can spread the infection into the lid · A lump at the inner corner of the eye is the lacrimal sac, not an eyelid gland · Topical steroid drops treat anterior uveitis and are avoided when infection is possible
How NBME framed it The stem opened with a red, sore eye and conjunctival swelling, and it described the lump on the lid margin without ever naming a stye. Each wrong option was the right treatment for a neighboring eye problem: a blocked tear duct, preseptal cellulitis, uveitis or simple redness.
Pairs with Part I The Red Eye covers conjunctivitis and the can't-miss red eyes, including uveitis, where topical steroids belong. Ask: does the redness come from the conjunctiva, or from a lump on the lid? Part I Sinusitis and Its Complications covers preseptal versus orbital cellulitis and orbital imaging. Ask: are eye movements painful or limited, and is there proptosis?
Transferable rule Locate the swelling before treating it. A tender nodule on the lid margin gets warm compresses. Antibiotics start when redness spreads across the lid, and imaging when the eye protrudes or eye movement hurts.
Unchecked attributeNasolacrimal massage: it sounds like the lid massage that goes with compresses; it treats a blocked tear duct at the inner corner, and this nodule is on the lid margin toward the outer corner.
Sequencing trapOral amoxicillin: the nodule is an infection; there is no fever and no redness spreading across the lid, so there is no cellulitis to treat.
True-fact-wrong-slotTopical prednisolone: the eye is inflamed; steroid drops treat anterior uveitis, and a tender lump on the lid margin is not uveitis; steroids are also avoided when infection is possible.
Salient decoyTopical tetrahydrozoline: it clears the redness the stem opens with; this vasoconstrictor acts at alpha-1 and alpha-2 receptors and does nothing for the blocked gland.

Neurology & HEENT

Posterior Fossa Localization

Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral · side first, then structure

Source vignette Pt — 9 yo M, left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, listing to the left, bilateral papilledema, left facial numbness · Q — the most likely localization; options spanned the left cerebellar hemisphere, the right middle cerebellar peduncle and the left frontal lobe
The decision point

Every cerebellar finding is on the left. He has dysmetria reaching with the left hand, slow rapid alternating movements on the left, and a gait that lists to the left. Cerebellar output decussates twice, so the crossings cancel and cerebellar signs are ipsilateral. This rules out the right middle cerebellar peduncle.

Limb dysmetria is hemispheric. A midline vermian lesion gives truncal and gait ataxia with spared limbs. He has both, so the mass is hemispheric and large enough to disturb midline structures. This fits the left facial numbness, because the trigeminal system serves the face ipsilaterally. It also fits the papilledema from fourth-ventricular compression.

Defining criteria Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral — and the patient falls and lists toward the side of the lesion · Hemisphere — limb ataxia, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, intention tremor · Vermis or midline — truncal and gait ataxia with a wide base and titubation · Central nystagmus — direction-changing and gaze-evoked, versus peripheral which is unidirectional and suppresses with fixation · Raised-pressure headache — daily or progressive, worse on waking or lying flat, poorly analgesia-responsive, with papilledema
Where is the mass - localizing the pediatric brain tumor
LocationIllness scriptThe NBME tell
Cerebellar hemispherePilocytic astrocytoma most classically, cystic with a mural noduleIpsilateral limb dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, falls toward the lesion
Cerebellar vermisMedulloblastoma, early fourth-ventricular obstructionTruncal and gait ataxia with a wide base, relatively spared limbs
Middle cerebellar peduncleCarries pontocerebellar inputAtaxia is still ipsilateral, so a right peduncle gives right-sided signs
Brainstem, ponsDiffuse intrinsic pontine gliomaCrossed findings — cranial nerve palsy one side, long-tract weakness the other
Pineal regionGerminoma, adolescent boysParinaud syndrome — upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation
Frontal lobeSupratentorial gliomaContralateral weakness, personality change, expressive aphasia

Scenario bank
  1. 9 yo M with left-hand dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesia, listing to the left, bilateral papilledema and left facial numbness → A mass in the left cerebellar hemisphere → cerebellar signs are ipsilateral
  2. Why a lesion in one cerebellar hemisphere produces signs on the same side of the body → Cerebellar output decussates twice → the two crossings cancel
  3. 6 yo M with truncal and gait ataxia, a wide-based stance, minimal limb dysmetria and a midline fourth-ventricular mass → Medulloblastoma of the vermis → seeds drop metastases through the CSF
  4. 5 yo F with progressive left sixth and seventh nerve palsies, right hemiparesis and diffuse expansion of the pons → Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma → crossed findings localize to the pons
  5. 12 yo M with an upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation → MRI of the brain with serum and CSF tumor markers → pineal germinoma
  6. 9 yo M with papilledema and cerebellar signs in whom a lumbar puncture is proposed → Obtain MRI of the brain instead → lumbar puncture risks herniation
  7. 9 yo M whose MRI shows a posterior fossa mass with hydrocephalus and who has become drowsy → Dexamethasone and urgent neurosurgical consultation → CSF diversion then resection
  8. 7 yo F with newly confirmed medulloblastoma → MRI of the entire neuraxis with CSF cytology → medulloblastoma seeds the cerebrospinal fluid
  9. 4 yo M with 3 weeks of headache waking him from sleep and morning vomiting, with a normal neurologic examination → MRI of the brain → a normal examination does not exclude a posterior fossa tumor
Papilledema forbids the tap With a posterior fossa mass, lumbar puncture risks herniation. Image first. Posterior fossa tumours are 54 to 70% of childhood brain tumours but only 15 to 20% of adult brain tumours. In a child, ataxia with raised pressure is therefore infratentorial until imaged.
Pearls Cerebellum — ipsilateral · Face — ipsilateral · Body long tracts — contralateral, so crossed findings mean brainstem · Medulloblastoma seeds the CSF (cerebrospinal fluid), so staging requires neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology · Red-flag pediatric headache: wakes from sleep, worse on waking, morning vomiting, progressive over weeks, any focal sign, or a child under six · Peripheral vertigo nystagmus is unidirectional and suppressed by fixation; central nystagmus is direction-changing and unsuppressed
Pairs with Part II Torticollis and Plagiocephaly in an Infant carries posterior fossa tumour as the can't-miss cause of acquired head tilt; this brief supplies the localization that identifies it. Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers the anterior compartment. Ask: which region does the endocrine or visual sign point to? Part I Headache in a School-Age Child covers the workup before localization. Ask: is the headache primary or secondary, and do the fundi show raised pressure?
Transferable rule Localize side first and structure second. The cerebellum is the one place where signs stay on the same side as the lesion.
Class-vs-memberThe right middle cerebellar peduncle is the right region on the wrong side.
True-fact-wrong-slotPineal masses are common in children but produce Parinaud syndrome, which he does not have.

Headache in a School-Age Child

primary headache, or a mass, raised pressure, infection or bleeding

Source case Pt — 7 yo with headache, Aquifer Neurology 10 / Pediatrics 20; the case works from red flags and the fundoscopic exam through cerebellar localization to a posterior fossa brain tumor · Q — separate primary from secondary headache, find raised intracranial pressure at the bedside, localize the lesion by site and time course, and name the likely tumor
The approach

Ask first whether a headache is primary (migraine, tension-type headache) or secondary. Causes of a secondary headache include a mass (posterior fossa or supratentorial tumor) and pressure without a mass (idiopathic intracranial hypertension). The others are blocked CSF flow (cerebrospinal fluid flow, as in hydrocephalus), infection (meningitis, abscess) and bleeding. Primary headaches come and go; secondary headaches progress. Check the vital signs for Cushing triad and fever first. Then use the pattern over time, the fundi and the neurologic exam to sort the causes. MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) finds the lesion. Tissue, CSF or the typical story confirms the diagnosis.

Red flags: act before the full history
FindingWhat it points to

Wakes from sleep; vomits on waking; worse with cough or lying flatRaised intracranial pressure
Weakness, numbness, clumsiness or a new gait changeSpace-occupying lesion
Worst pain at the moment it startsBleeding or a vascular cause
Worse week by week, or a child under 6Secondary headache until proven otherwise

Posterior fossa tumor in a child What it is — brain tumors are the commonest solid tumor of childhood, second to leukemia among childhood cancers, and cause the most childhood cancer deaths; after age 2 and through the first decade most arise below the tentorium · Who — first decade; risk factors are ionizing radiation and genetic syndromes (neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, Li-Fraumeni) · Mechanism — a cerebellar mass compresses the fourth ventricle, causing obstructive hydrocephalus; pressure carried along the optic nerve sheath blocks axoplasmic flow and swells the disc · Features — progressive headache on waking with vomiting, ataxia, papilledema; vermis: truncal ataxia and slurred speech; hemisphere: same-side limb ataxia, falls to that side · Types — medulloblastoma (about 20%): malignant, midline, spreads through the CSF, needs surgery, radiation and chemotherapy; pilocytic astrocytoma (about 20%): often cystic, the best prognosis, about 90% 5-year survival after complete resection, 50 to 70% after partial; ependymoma: fourth ventricle lining, hydrocephalus, surgery then radiation, about 50% 5-year survival; brainstem glioma: cranial nerve and long-tract signs · Diagnosis — MRI; CT sees the posterior fossa poorly; histology names the tumor · Treatment — dexamethasone for edema, CSF diversion for hydrocephalus, resection; radiation and chemotherapy by type · Complications — herniation; late effects mostly from radiation and chemotherapy: neurocognitive deficits, learning disabilities, endocrine deficits, stroke, epilepsy · Follow-up — oncology imaging, growth and endocrine checks, school and neuropsychological support; give the news to both parents together, in private, in plain words · Return for — worse headache, repeated vomiting, drowsiness, double vision, new weakness or gait change

  4. The mechanism by which raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc → Blocked axoplasmic flow in the optic nerve → Pressure travels through the subarachnoid space around the nerve
  5. 9 yo with 3 weeks of new daily headaches that do not wake her; no vomiting, fever or visual complaints; alert with a normal gait, strength and coordination; the fundi have not yet been examined → Fundoscopic examination → Papilledema decides between imaging and a diary
  6. 8 yo with 6 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting, a wide-based unsteady gait and papilledema; a noncontrast head CT in the emergency department is read as normal → It does not exclude a mass → CT sees the posterior fossa poorly; obtain MRI
  7. 7 yo admitted with a cerebellar mass on MRI and dilated ventricles, stable overnight, who suddenly develops severe headache, repeated vomiting and increasing drowsiness → Noncontrast head CT → Fast, needs no sedation; looks for bleeding or worse hydrocephalus
  8. 7 yo with a known posterior fossa mass who becomes drowsy; blood pressure 158/94, pulse 52, and breathing that is slow and irregular → Impending brain herniation → Cushing triad; emergent measures to lower pressure
  9. 10 yo stands steadily with feet together and eyes open but sways and nearly falls when he closes his eyes; vibration and position sense are reduced in the toes; finger-to-nose testing is normal → Dorsal column lesion → A Romberg sign only with eyes closed means lost position sense
  10. 8 yo with 2 months of morning headaches, a clumsy right hand, and falls to the right; MRI shows a cyst in the right cerebellar hemisphere with an enhancing nodule in its wall → Pilocytic astrocytoma → Cystic cerebellar tumor with the best prognosis; resection
  11. 12 yo treated for medulloblastoma with resection, craniospinal radiation and chemotherapy 4 years ago, with no recurrence on imaging; his grades are slipping and his height has fallen from the 50th to the 15th percentile → Neurocognitive and endocrine testing → Late effects of radiation and chemotherapy
  12. 3 yo, well until today, now walks with a wide-based, staggering gait and has nystagmus; she had chickenpox 2 weeks ago; afebrile, alert, no headache, normal fundi; no medicines or alcohol in the home → Acute cerebellar ataxia → Post-infectious; CSF and imaging normal; recovers over weeks to months
  13. 18-month-old with 2 weeks of unsteady walking, jerking of the arms and legs, and rapid, chaotic, darting movements of both eyes; afebrile and alert → Urine catecholamine metabolites → Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome: look for neuroblastoma
  14. 9 yo with fever and a worsening headache for 5 days, 2 weeks after a sinus infection that was not treated; new weakness of the left arm; no neck stiffness → Brain abscess → Spread from the sinuses; MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion
  15. 8 yo with 1 day of fever, headache and a stiff neck, now confused; bilateral papilledema → Blood cultures and IV antibiotics now → Treat first, then image, then lumbar puncture
  16. 14 yo girl with obesity, no medications, and 2 months of daily headache worse lying down with brief graying of vision; bilateral papilledema with full visual fields; MRI with MR venography normal; lumbar puncture opening pressure high with normal CSF → Weight loss and acetazolamide → Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; follow the visual fields
  17. 12 yo who, when asked to stand, sways at the waist and lurches wildly across the room without falling, then sits comfortably; strength, reflexes, finger-to-nose and fundi are normal → Functional gait disorder → Astasia-abasia: the lurching needs good balance
Pairs with Part II Posterior Fossa Localization covers localization by side and structure, and imaging before a lumbar puncture. Ask: which side, and which part of the cerebellum? Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment covers when to image and the drug causes of intracranial hypertension. Part I Sellar and Suprasellar Masses covers the supratentorial midline mass. Ask: is growth or vision failing? Part I Hydrocephalus and Shunt Complications covers hydrocephalus once a shunt is in. Part I Inherited Tumor Syndromes covers neurofibromatosis and tuberous sclerosis. Part I Primary Headache in an Adult covers the adult primary headache types.
Transferable rule For headache in a child, decide first whether it is primary or secondary. A headache that progresses, wakes the child, or comes with papilledema or a focal sign needs an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging). The location of the signs shows where the lesion is.
Salient decoyVomiting fits migraine and raised pressure alike; only vomiting on waking, with a headache that wakes the child, points to pressure.
Test-overrides-findingsA normal head CT offered as reassurance, when CT sees the posterior fossa poorly.
Mirror twinPapilledema with an otherwise normal exam and a normal MRI is intracranial hypertension; papilledema with ataxia is a mass.
Unchecked attributeA positive Romberg read as cerebellar without asking whether the child also sways with eyes open.

Dermatology & Wounds 7 topics + 1 board-style

Morphology and depth decide these. Exposures and risk profiles suggest; the lesion in front of you decides.

Scaly Rashes

Exam findings outweigh the exposure history

The decision point

Nail dystrophy together with extensor-surface scaly plaques indicates psoriasis. An extensor distribution indicates psoriasis; a flexural distribution indicates eczema. An occupational "wet work" history does not override these findings. Psoriasis does show the Koebner phenomenon, so friction can localize it.

Scaly plaques — the differential
DiagnosisDistributionThe tellNails?
PsoriasisExtensor, scalp, trunkSalmon plaques, silvery scale, Auspitz sign, KoebnerYes — pitting, onycholysis
Atopic dermatitisFlexuralPruritus first, rash second; lichenification; atopy triadNo
Nummular eczemaExtremitiesCoin-shaped, intensely pruriticNo
Tinea corporisAnywhereAnnular with central clearing; KOH shows hyphaeSeparate (onychomycosis)
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp, nasolabial, browsGreasy yellow scale; MalasseziaNo
Pityriasis roseaTrunkHerald patch → Christmas-tree patternNo
Lichen planusWrists, ankles, mucosa6 Ps: pruritic purple polygonal planar papules; Wickham striaeCan

TestOrderResultWhat it points to

RPRBy branchReactive with a truncal or palm and sole eruptionSecondary syphilis, the mimic of pityriasis rosea
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsExtensor silvery plaques with nail pittingPsoriasis; the tests only exclude tinea and syphilis

X-ray of the handsBy branchPencil-in-cup erosions at the DIP jointsPsoriatic arthritis in a patient with dactylitis

Scenario bank
  1. 34 yo M with extensor-surface silvery plaques and nail pitting → Psoriasis
  2. 34 yo M with flexural lichenified pruritic patches and a history of asthma → Atopic dermatitis
  3. 34 yo M with an annular scaly patch with central clearing and an active border → Tinea corporis → KOH preparation
  4. 34 yo M with a herald patch followed by a Christmas-tree truncal eruption → Pityriasis rosea
  5. 34 yo M with purple polygonal pruritic papules and oral Wickham striae → Lichen planus
  6. 34 yo M whose plaques bleed at pinpoints when the scale is lifted → Auspitz sign
  7. 34 yo M with psoriasis, dactylitis and DIP joint involvement → Psoriatic arthritis
  8. 34 yo M with a few silvery extensor plaques on the elbows and knees and nail pitting → Topical steroid plus calcipotriene → first rung before phototherapy and systemics
  9. 34 yo M with a single annular scaly trunk plaque with central clearing and an active border → KOH preparation → if tinea, a steroid causes tinea incognito
  10. 34 yo M with severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis about to start a TNF-alpha inhibitor → Test for latent tuberculosis → TNF blockade can reactivate tuberculosis
  11. 34 yo M with extensive plaque psoriasis who was started on oral prednisone for an asthma flare → Abrupt discontinuation of prednisone → abrupt steroid withdrawal can trigger a pustular flare
Psoriasis facts they attach Pathology: parakeratosis, acanthosis, Munro microabscesses, thinned suprapapillary plates (→ Auspitz) · immunology: Th17 / IL-17 / IL-23 (T helper 17 cell / interleukin 17 / interleukin 23) axis · drugs: secukinumab (IL-17), ustekinumab (IL-12/23), TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor alpha) inhibitors after screening for latent TB (tuberculosis) · associations: psoriatic arthritis with DIP (distal interphalangeal) joints, "pencil-in-cup," dactylitis; metabolic syndrome and CV (cardiovascular) risk · ladder: topical steroids + calcipotriene first, then narrowband UVB (ultraviolet B), then systemics · abrupt steroid withdrawal can trigger a pustular flare · for tinea, order a KOH prep (potassium hydroxide preparation), never a steroid (tinea incognito).
Pairs with Part I Hair Loss in a Child is the scalp version, where follicular invasion changes the therapy from topical to oral.
Transferable rule Exposures can suggest a diagnosis, but examination findings determine it. When the history and the exam conflict, rely on the exam.
Salient decoy

Skin and Soft Tissue Infection

Border sharpness reflects the depth of infection

The decision point

A flat border indicates cellulitis; a raised, sharply demarcated border indicates erysipelas. Superficial infection stops at a sharp edge because superficial infection is contained by tissue planes. Deeper infection fades into an indistinct edge because deeper infection diffuses through fat.

Skin & soft-tissue infections by depth
LayerInfectionThe tellOrganism
Epidermis / superficial dermis + lymphaticsErysipelasRaised, sharply demarcated, intense erythema; rapid onset, early feverS. pyogenes
Deep dermis + subcutaneous fatCellulitis (nonpurulent)Flat, poorly demarcated; indolent over days; fever laterBeta-hemolytic strep, MSSA
Same, with drainageCellulitis (purulent) / abscessPurulent drainage; furuncle → carbuncleS. aureus incl. MRSA
FasciaNecrotizing fasciitis EmergencyPain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, necrosis, anesthesia over the lesion, hourly progressionPolymicrobial (type I) or GAS ± Clostridium (type II)
The treatment fork is purulent vs. nonpurulent Nonpurulent infection: cover streptococci with cephalexin or dicloxacillin (penicillin for erysipelas). Purulent infection: incision and drainage, plus coverage of MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) with TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), doxycycline, or clindamycin. Necrotizing infection: emergent surgical exploration, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Never wait for imaging.
Mimics — roughly 30% of "cellulitis" is misdiagnosed
MimicThe tell
Stasis dermatitisBilateral, chronic, hemosiderin staining, afebrile — the single most common misdiagnosis
DVTSwelling without a sharply defined rash; recent surgery or immobility
Contact dermatitisItchy, geometric border, afebrile
Erythema nodosumBilateral tender nodules on anterior shins; sarcoid, IBD, strep
Erythema migransExpanding with central clearing, minimally tender
Ruptured Baker cystPopliteal fossa and posterior calf
The bilateral rule Cellulitis is nearly always unilateral. Bilateral lower-extremity erythema is stasis dermatitis until proven otherwise; treat with compression, not antibiotics.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
None: clinical diagnosisConfirmsUnilateral warm erythema with a flat, indistinct borderCellulitis; tests exclude abscess, DVT and deeper infection
Bedside ultrasoundBy branchFluid collection under the erythemaAbscess: incision and drainage plus MRSA coverage
Culture of drained pusBy branchS. aureus, with susceptibilitiesGuides antibiotic choice in purulent infection
Duplex ultrasound of the legBy branchNoncompressible veinDVT, the swollen-leg mimic

Emergent surgical explorationConfirmsNecrotic fascia, dishwater fluid, little bleedingNecrotizing fasciitis; debride in the same operation

Scenario bank
  1. Raised, sharply demarcated, intensely erythematous, rapid onset with early fever → Erysipelas → penicillin
  2. Purulent drainage or a fluctuant abscess → Incision and drainage plus MRSA coverage
  3. Pain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, hourly progression → Necrotizing fasciitis → emergent surgical exploration
  4. Bilateral, chronic, hemosiderin staining, afebrile → Stasis dermatitis → compression
  5. Saltwater exposure + cirrhosis + hemorrhagic bullae → Vibrio vulnificus → doxycycline + ceftriaxone (high mortality)
  6. Cat bite with cellulitis within 24 hours → Pasteurella multocida → amoxicillin-clavulanate
  7. Dog bite in an asplenic or cirrhotic patient → Capnocytophaga canimorsus → fulminant sepsis risk
  8. Clenched-fist human bite → Eikenella corrodens
  9. Rose gardener with nodules ascending the lymphatics → Sporothrix schenckii → itraconazole
  10. Aquarium exposure with nodular lesions → Mycobacterium marinum
  11. Recurrent cellulitis in the same leg → Find and treat the portal of entry → usually tinea pedis with toe-web maceration, or lymphedema
Transferable rule Terms that describe morphology usually reflect an underlying anatomic fact. A "sharply demarcated" border shows how deep the process is.

Diabetic Foot Ulcer

Exam findings outweigh the risk profile

The decision point

Three findings each independently exclude arterial disease: painless, plantar over a bony prominence, and warm feet. Warm feet are perfused, and dry feet indicate autonomic denervation. These findings indicate a neuropathic ulcer, and the most common cause is diabetes. A culture characterizes the wound, and an ABI (ankle-brachial index) characterizes perfusion. Only the A1c (hemoglobin A1c) identifies the underlying disease.

Foot ulcer typesneuropathic vs arterial vs venous
TypeLocationPainBed & surrounding skinPulsesTest
Neuropathic / diabeticPlantar, over pressure points (1st/5th MT head, heel)Painless"Punched out," necrotic base, surrounding callus; skin warm, dry, fissuredNormalA1c; 10-g monofilament
Arterial / ischemicTips of toes, lateral malleolus, dorsumPainful — worse elevated, better danglingDry, pale, minimal granulation; cool, shiny, hairless, dependent ruborDiminished / absentABI
Venous stasisMedial malleolus (gaiter area)Mild ache, better elevatedShallow, irregular, wet; hemosiderin staining, edemaNormalDuplex ultrasound
Pressure / decubitusSacrum, heel, trochanterVariableStaged by depth; immobile patientNormalClinical
Pyoderma gangrenosumLower legVery painfulViolaceous undermined border, rapid; IBD, RANormalBiopsy — do not debride (pathergy)
Marjolin ulcerChronic wound or scarVariableRolled everted edges, non-healing >3 months—Biopsy
ABI values & neuropathy mechanism >1.4 noncompressible, calcified (diabetes, ESRD (end-stage renal disease)) → use the toe-brachial index (<0.7 abnormal) · 1.0–1.4 normal · 0.5–0.9 claudication · <0.4 critical limb ischemia. Small-fiber neuropathy → pain, burning, autonomic dysfunction. Large-fiber neuropathy → sensory loss, which is what lets injury go unrecognized. Peripheral neuropathy can be present at the time of type 2 diabetes diagnosis.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Pulse exam and ankle-brachial indexFirstNormal pulses, ABI 1.0 to 1.4Perfused foot: neuropathic ulcer; a low ABI points to arterial disease
Toe-brachial indexBy branchUnder 0.7 when the ABI is over 1.4Arterial disease hidden by calcified, noncompressible vessels
10-g monofilamentSupportsLoss of protective sensationLarge-fiber neuropathy lets injury go unnoticed
Hemoglobin A1cCause6.5% or higherDiabetes, the underlying cause of the neuropathic ulcer
Probe-to-bone test, ESR and plain filmsBy branchProbe touches bone; ESR over 70Osteomyelitis likely; plain films are insensitive early
MRI, then bone biopsyConfirmsMarrow edema; bone culture positiveOsteomyelitis; the biopsy names the organism
Superficial wound swabSkipGrows colonizersCulture only a clinically infected ulcer, using deep tissue or bone
Scenario bank
  1. Painful ulcer at the toe tips, cool pale foot, absent pulses → Arterial ischemic ulcer → ABI
  2. ABI 1.5 in a diabetic → Noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
  3. Medial malleolar wet ulcer + hemosiderin + edema → Venous stasis ulcer → duplex + compression
  4. A patient with a diabetic plantar foot ulcer over a bony prominence has a positive probe-to-bone test. → Osteomyelitis → MRI + bone biopsy (plain films insensitive early; ESR >70 supports it)
  5. Warm, swollen, erythematous foot in a diabetic with no ulcer, no fever, normal WBC → Charcot arthropathy → immobilize; "rocker-bottom" deformity
  6. Rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with a violaceous undermined border in a patient with IBD → Pyoderma gangrenosum → steroids, never debride
  7. Chronic non-healing ulcer with rolled edges → Biopsy for Marjolin ulcer
Management once diabetes is confirmed Off-loading (total contact cast) is the single most important intervention · debride callus and necrotic tissue · glycemic control · culture only if clinically infected, and take deep tissue rather than a swab · check the ABI (ankle-brachial index) anyway, since mixed neuroischemic ulcers are common · annual 10-g monofilament exam in every diabetic.
Transferable rule Risk factors set the prior probability; physical findings set the posterior probability. When the exam contradicts the risk profile on three separate axes, rely on the exam.
Salient decoy

Atopic Dermatitis

Atopic dermatitis as the precondition for HSV spread

The decision point

Atopic dermatitis with vesicles is eczema herpeticum until proven otherwise. The atopic dermatitis is the precondition. A disrupted barrier plus local immune dysfunction lets HSV (herpes simplex virus) spread across the skin instead of staying a single cold sore. Treatment is immediate systemic acyclovir, because the infection can disseminate to the liver and brain.

Findings that exclude the mimics "Conjunctiva and oropharynx are clear" excludes the drug reaction. SJS (Stevens-Johnson syndrome) and TEN (toxic epidermal necrolysis) require mucosal involvement (classically ≥2 sites) plus symmetric target lesions. "Progressive worsening on TMP-SMX" (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) excludes impetigo. TMP-SMX covers staph, including MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus). So failure on appropriate antibacterial therapy eliminates the bacterial hypothesis, exactly as a failed antihistamine eliminates upper airway cough syndrome.
Atopic dermatitis complications
Complication of atopic dermatitisPathogenPresentationTreatment
Eczema herpeticum Can't missHSV-1Painful monomorphic vesicles → punched-out erosions, hemorrhagic crusting; fever, lymphadenopathySystemic acyclovir immediately
ImpetigoS. aureus, S. pyogenesHoney-colored adherent crustMupirocin or oral cephalexin
Molluscum contagiosumPoxvirusSkin-colored papules with central umbilicationSelf-limited; curettage/cantharidin
Tinea corporisT. rubrumAnnular, central clearing, raised scaly borderTopical azole or terbinafine
Eczema coxsackiumCoxsackie A6Vesicles concentrated in eczematous skinSupportive
Morphology tell & workup Herpes causes monomorphic vesicles that evolve into "punched-out" erosions with hemorrhagic crust and scalloped coalescing borders. Impetigo causes honey-colored crust, not hemorrhagic crust. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed with HSV PCR of vesicle fluid (herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction). A Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells but is less sensitive. Give IV acyclovir if the eruption is widespread, the patient is ill-appearing, or the patient is a young infant; ophthalmology consult if periocular.
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Exam of the eyes and mouthFirstConjunctiva and oropharynx clearNot SJS or TEN, which needs mucosa at 2 or more sites
HSV PCR of vesicle fluidConfirmsHSV-1 detectedEczema herpeticum; start acyclovir before the result returns
Tzanck smearSupportsMultinucleated giant cellsHSV or VZV; less sensitive than PCR and does not separate them
Ophthalmology slit-lamp examBy branchDendritic corneal lesions with periocular vesiclesHSV keratoconjunctivitis, which threatens vision
Culture of nares, conjunctiva or throatBy branchS. aureus at a distant focusStaphylococcal scalded skin syndrome; the bullae themselves are sterile
Skin swab for bacterial cultureSkipS. aureus colonizes eczematous skinA positive swab does not explain failure on TMP-SMX
Scenario bank
  1. A child with atopic dermatitis and monomorphic vesicles evolving into punched-out erosions has periocular lesions. → Emergent ophthalmology (HSV keratoconjunctivitis threatens vision)
  2. Widespread, ill-appearing, poor oral intake → Admit for IV acyclovir
  3. Honey-colored crust, afebrile, no vesicles → Impetigo → mupirocin
  4. Fever + mucositis at two sites + targetoid lesions after a new drug → Stevens-Johnson syndrome → stop the drug, admit
  5. Nikolsky positive with spared mucosa in a toddler → Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome → IV anti-staph; culture the distant focus, not the skin
  6. Lesions in different stages simultaneously → Varicella
  7. Umbilicated papules in an eczematous child → Molluscum → observe
  8. Eczema + recurrent skin and lung infections + very high IgE + retained primary teeth → Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome
  9. Child with atopic dermatitis, fever and painful monomorphic vesicles evolving into punched-out erosions with hemorrhagic crust, worsening on TMP-SMX; conjunctiva and oropharynx clear → Eczema herpeticum → systemic acyclovir immediately
Transferable rule The past medical history can contain the deciding fact. Sometimes it is a risk factor that overrides a benign reading (prior cancer → spinal mets). Sometimes it is a risk factor masquerading as an explanation (Klinefelter → gynecomastia). Sometimes it is the precondition that makes the right diagnosis possible at all. Read the past medical history as information that enables a diagnosis.
True-fact-wrong-slotTest-overrides-findings

Hair Loss in a Child

The scalp surface and the nodes identify the cause · Is the patch scaly, and are the draining nodes enlarged?

Source vignette Pt — 8 yo, enlarging scaly bald patch with pruritus, tender occipital and postauricular nodes · Q — the most likely diagnosis; options spanned tinea capitis, trichotillomania and alopecia areata
The decision point

Two examination findings, not the history, identify the cause. The patch has overlying scale, which means an inflammatory or infectious process in the skin rather than hair that is simply being pulled or shed. The occipital and posterior auricular nodes are enlarged and tender, which is regional lymphadenopathy draining an infected scalp. Together these findings indicate tinea capitis. Unlike tinea of the body, this dermatophyte invades the hair follicle and shaft. As a result, the hair breaks and the patch expands centrifugally over weeks. The recent school change and the anxiety suggest trichotillomania, but neither scale nor tender nodes occurs in trichotillomania.

Defining criteria Tinea capitis — scaly erythematous patch with hair loss and localized lymphadenopathy, with or without black dots (broken hairs at the follicle) and with or without a tender boggy kerion · Why systemic therapy is required — the organism invades the follicle and shaft, which topical agents penetrate poorly, so oral griseofulvin or terbinafine is needed · Confirmation — the diagnosis is clinical; KOH examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture confirms it
Pertinent positives & negatives Scale over an enlarging bald patch — an inflammatory or infectious scalp process; scale is what separates infection from every non-inflammatory alopecia · Tender occipital and posterior auricular lymphadenopathy — the nodes that drain the scalp; expected in tinea capitis and absent in traction alopecia and trichotillomania · Frequent scratching — pruritus, an inflammatory feature that argues against a purely mechanical cause · Recent school change with anxiety — a psychosocial cue for hair-pulling, which the scale and the nodes exclude · Age 8, previously healthy — the peak age; tinea capitis is predominantly a disease of children and the immunocompromised
Patchy hair loss in a child — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Tinea capitisTrichophyton or Microsporum acquired from a contact or a fomite — shared comb, hat, pillowcase; invades follicle and shaftScaly patch with hair loss plus regional lymphadenopathy; black dots; kerion— (the answer)
Alopecia areata ⚠︎ (not on the option list)Autoimmune, non-scarring; abrupt, sharply circumscribedRound, smooth patch completely devoid of hair, scale-free, no lymphadenopathy; exclamation-point hairs; nail pitting ⚠︎The patch is scaly and the nodes are enlarged
TrichotillomaniaRecurrent pulling the patient cannot stop; most common in children and adolescent girls; loss hidden under hats or wigs; swallowed hair can form a trichobezoarIrregular patch with hairs of varying lengths, often sparse eyebrows or eyelashes; no scale, no erythema, nonscarringScale and tender lymphadenopathy
Traction alopeciaProlonged pulling from bands or braidsGeometric loss along the traction sites, most often frontal and temporal or along braids; no scale, no nodes; never thins the eyebrowsNo hairstyle history; scale and nodes present
Telogen effluviumSynchronized shedding a few months after a stressor such as illness, surgery or childbirthDiffuse thinning over the whole scalp, not a patchThe loss is a single patch with scale and nodes
Seborrheic dermatitisScalp scaling, i.e. dandruff, with pruritusScale without hair lossIt cannot explain the alopecia or the nodes
Discoid lupus erythematosusCutaneous lupus; scarring, well-demarcated inflammatory plaquesAdult women, with face and neck lesions, and the alopecia scarsAge 8 and no facial or neck involvement
Trichotillomania: the tells Irregular patch, hairs of different lengths — hairs pulled and regrowing at different times; alopecia areata leaves a round patch that is completely bald · Sparse eyebrows or eyelashes — pulling reaches other sites; traction and tinea stay on the scalp · Hats or wigs — used to hide the loss; even when another reason for them is given, traction does not explain the eyebrows or a parietal patch · No scale, no erythema, no scarring — excludes tinea capitis and discoid lupus · Treatment — cognitive behavioral therapy with habit reversal · Complication — swallowing the hair (trichophagia) can form a gastric trichobezoar
Management, in one line Treatment requires oral griseofulvin or terbinafine, because topical antifungals do not reach the organism inside the hair follicle.
Decision spine Is there scale on the patch? — Yes → an inflammatory or infectious cause, not a pulling one · Are the draining nodes enlarged? — Yes → infection, which excludes trichotillomania and traction alopecia · Are the remaining hairs broken? — Black dots are shafts snapped at the follicle; the fungus is inside the hair · Any traction history or geometric pattern? — No · Confirm and treat — KOH (potassium hydroxide) of the proximal shafts; oral, never topical alone
Diagnostic workup
TestOrderResultWhat it points to
Scalp exam with a check of the draining nodesFirstScale plus tender occipital and postauricular nodesInfection: tinea capitis; a smooth patch without nodes is not
Close look at the remaining hairsBy branchBroken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular patch, no scale; eyebrows or lashes sparseTrichotillomania; exclamation-point hairs point to alopecia areata
KOH of plucked proximal hair shaftsConfirmsSpores within or around the hair shaftTinea capitis: start oral griseofulvin or terbinafine
Fungal culture of hairs or scaleConfirmsTrichophyton or Microsporum growsTinea capitis; results take weeks, so do not wait to treat
Wood lampSupportsGreen fluorescence only with MicrosporumNegative with Trichophyton tonsurans, the common US cause
Serum fungal antibody titersSkipNo role in dermatophyte infectionKOH or culture of the hair confirms it
Scenario bank
  1. 8 yo with an enlarging scaly bald patch, pruritus, and tender occipital and postauricular nodes → Tinea capitis → Regional lymphadenopathy plus scale
  2. Child with clinically confirmed tinea capitis; appropriate treatment → Oral griseofulvin or terbinafine → Topicals cannot reach the follicle
  3. Child with tinea capitis; which therapy will not clear the infection → Topical antifungal shampoo used alone → Adjunctive at best
  4. 8 yo with a smooth, scale-free, sharply demarcated bald patch, no lymphadenopathy, and nail pitting → Topical or intralesional glucocorticoid → Alopecia areata
  5. 10 yo with irregular patches of broken hairs of varying lengths, no scale, no lymphadenopathy, after a recent stressor → Habit-reversal behavioral therapy → Trichotillomania
  6. 12 yo with symmetric temporal thinning along tightly pulled braids, no scale and no lymphadenopathy → Loosen the hairstyle → Traction alopecia is reversible if caught early
  7. Child on oral antifungal therapy for tinea capitis who develops a boggy tender scalp mass with pustules → Continue systemic antifungal therapy → A kerion is the same infection
  8. Child with a scaly patch of alopecia and regional lymphadenopathy → KOH examination of proximal hair shafts or fungal culture → The diagnosis is otherwise clinical
  9. Why tinea capitis requires oral therapy while tinea corporis responds to topical treatment → It invades the hair follicle and shaft → Body lesions remain in the epidermis
  10. Child newly diagnosed with tinea capitis → Examine close contacts and stop sharing combs, hats and pillowcases → Fomite transmission
  11. 15 yo F cast as the lead in a school play a month ago, wearing hats and wigs to stay in character; her mother noticed bald spots a few days ago; doing well in school, no substance use, regular menses, BMI 22; a 3 x 5 cm irregular right parietal patch of hair loss bordered by hairs of uneven length, sparse eyebrows, no scale or erythema → Trichotillomania → Cognitive behavioral therapy with habit reversal
  12. 9 yo with a round, sharply bordered bald patch that appeared over 2 weeks; the scalp inside is completely smooth with no scale or erythema; a few short hairs at the margin taper toward the scalp; eyebrows normal; no lymphadenopathy → Alopecia areata → Topical or intralesional glucocorticoid
  13. 16 yo F shedding handfuls of hair in the shower for 3 weeks, 3 months after hospitalization for pneumonia; thinning is spread evenly over the whole scalp with no patches, no scale and normal eyebrows → Telogen effluvium → Reassurance; regrowth over months
  14. 15 yo F with long-standing hair pulling who also chews and swallows the hair, now with early satiety, weight loss, halitosis and a firm, mobile epigastric mass → Gastric trichobezoar → Endoscopic or surgical removal
Decoy note A new school and anxiety about teachers and friends make a complete, plausible causal story. The examination refutes it. "Frequently scratches at the area" seems to support it, since scratching sounds like a behavior. However, scratching reflects pruritus, an inflammatory symptom, and it points the other way. The patch is nontender, which is easy to misread as a general absence of tenderness. The nodes are tender, and that tenderness is the key finding.
Pearls A scaly, enlarging bald patch with tender occipital nodes in a child is tinea capitis, and it needs an oral antifungal. · Scale plus regional lymphadenopathy means infection rather than a simple alopecia; the two pulling alopecias, traction and trichotillomania, have neither. · Tinea capitis invades the follicle and shaft, so it needs an oral antifungal, the single most tested management point on the topic. · Black dots are hair shafts broken at the follicular orifice; a boggy tender mass is a kerion, which is the same infection inflamed, not a bacterial abscess to drain. · Alopecia areata causes a smooth, scale-free, sharply circumscribed patch with no lymphadenopathy, sometimes with nail pitting ⚠︎. · Fomites such as combs, hats and pillowcases carry it, so the household is examined rather than treated blindly. · A scaly scalp plaque that scars, in an adult woman with facial lesions, is discoid lupus rather than tinea.
Pairs with Part I Scaly Rashes covers the scaly-plaque differential of the body. It also covers the rule that a scaly annular lesion needs a KOH (potassium hydroxide) preparation rather than a steroid. This brief covers the scalp version, where the follicle changes the therapy. Ask: is there scale, and are the draining nodes enlarged?
Transferable rule In hair loss, the surface of the patch identifies the diagnosis. Scale with regional nodes means infection. A smooth patch means an autoimmune or traction cause. Broken hairs of unequal length mean the hair is being pulled. Examine the scalp before you accept a psychosocial explanation.
Class-vs-memberTraction alopecia: Traction produces geometric loss along the sites of pulling (temporal areas, along braids), with no scale and no lymphadenopathy
Salient decoyTrichotillomania: Hair-pulling leaves broken hairs of varying lengths in an irregular pattern, without scale or nodes
Class-vs-memberCutaneous candidiasis: Candida causes intertrigo in warm moist skinfolds; it does not scale the scalp or take hair
True-fact-wrong-slotSeborrheic dermatitis: It explains only the scale and the pruritus, not the hair loss or the nodes
True-fact-wrong-slotDiscoid lupus erythematosus: It occurs mostly in adult women, involves the face and neck, and scars

Benign Neonatal Rashes

Sort by onset · reassurance vs. removable cause

The decision point

Reassure when a benign, self-limited rash has no modifiable cause. Remove the trigger when a benign rash has an identifiable, removable trigger. Miliaria rubra has its cause in the history: onesies under pajamas under a fleece swaddle. Treat it by unwrapping the baby, not by waiting it out.

Sort by onset age first. At birth: pustular melanosis and milia. Birth to 3 days: erythema toxicum. Any age but never at birth: miliaria rubra. About 3 to 4 weeks: cephalic pustulosis. A rash outside its window, erythema toxicum-like pustules on the palms or soles, vesicles or crusting, or a febrile or irritable infant is not benign until the dangerous mimics below are excluded.

Benign neonatal rashes
RashOnsetAppearance & distributionManagement
Neonatal pustular melanosisAt birthNonerythematous pustules that rupture into hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale; forehead, neck, lower back; may involve palms and soles; more common in darker skin; neutrophilsObserve; pustules clear in days, pigment fades over months
MiliaAt birthFirm white papules on the nose and cheeks, no erythema; retained keratinObserve; resolves within a month; do not extract
Erythema toxicum neonatorumBirth to 3 daysPoorly demarcated erythematous macules and papules that become small firm pustules on an erythematous base; trunk and proximal limbs; spares palms and soles; well infant; eosinophils (smear rarely needed)Reassurance; resolves in about a week
Miliaria rubraAny age, never at birthFine erythematous papules in occluded and intertriginous areas; blocked sweat glandsCool environment, no overbundling, thin cotton; low-potency steroid if severe
Neonatal cephalic pustulosisAbout 3 to 4 weeksErythematous papules and pustules on the face and scalp only; no comedones; linked to MalasseziaObserve (weeks to months); low-potency steroid or ketoconazole if severe; avoid oily emollients
Seborrheic dermatitis2–6 weeksGreasy yellow scale, scalp and foldsEmollient, gentle brushing
Scenario bank
  1. 2 day old M, erythematous macules with central pustules on the trunk and proximal limbs, palms and soles spared, well-appearing → Erythema toxicum neonatorum → reassurance
  2. 2 wk M dressed in a onesie, pyjamas and a fleece swaddle, with tiny clear vesicles → Miliaria rubra → remove the extra layers
  3. Newborn with pustules rupturing to hyperpigmented macules with a collarette of scale → Transient neonatal pustular melanosis → reassurance
  4. 2 wk M with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base and irritability → Neonatal herpes simplex → PCR and IV acyclovir
  5. 6 wk M with greasy yellow scale on the scalp → Seborrheic dermatitis → reassurance with an emollient
  6. Newborn with 1 mm white papules across the nose → Milia → reassurance
  7. 3 wk F bundled in a fleece swaddle in a warm room, with fine erythematous papules in the neck folds and axillae → Lighter, cooler clothing → miliaria rubra has a removable cause: thin cotton and a cool room
  8. 10 day old, afebrile and feeding well, with clustered vesicles on an erythematous base on the scalp → HSV PCR and IV acyclovir → any vesicular rash in a neonate is HSV until proven otherwise
  9. 4 mo with a beefy red diaper rash involving the inguinal creases, with satellite papules → Topical nystatin → candida involves the creases; irritant dermatitis spares them
  10. 4 mo with blue-gray macules over the sacrum and buttocks noted on a well-child exam → Document the finding and reassure → congenital dermal melanocytosis is benign; documenting it prevents confusion with abuse
  11. 2 day old boy born at 40 weeks by vaginal delivery, breastfeeding every 2 to 3 hours and voiding, with a diffuse rash noticed this morning; mother gets occasional cold sores with stress, last one a year ago; normal vital signs; pustules on erythematous bases over the extremities and scattered erythematous papules on the trunk and back, palms and soles spared → Reassurance only → Erythema toxicum neonatorum; resolves in about a week
  12. 3 week old girl, well and feeding, with erythematous papules and pustules on the cheeks, forehead and scalp; no comedones; trunk, palms and soles clear → Neonatal cephalic pustulosis → Observation; ketoconazole or low-potency steroid only if severe
  13. 6 day old boy, afebrile and feeding well, circumcised on day 2, with a few pustules and flaccid blisters around the circumcision site, some ruptured to honey-colored crusts; no other skin findings → Topical mupirocin → Staphylococcal pustulosis
Not benign: red flags and the dangerous mimics Red flags — palms or soles involved in an otherwise erythema toxicum picture, vesicles or crusting, or fever or irritability; any one means the rash is not benign. Pustular melanosis, present at birth and nonerythematous, is the benign rash that may reach the palms and soles · Neonatal HSV — clustered vesicles on an erythematous base, days 5–14 → PCR (polymerase chain reaction) + IV acyclovir. Any vesicular rash in a neonate is HSV (herpes simplex virus) until proven otherwise · Congenital syphilis — maculopapular rash that includes the palms and soles, snuffles, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, no pustules → IV penicillin · Staphylococcal pustulosis — localized pustules, vesicles or bullae that rupture to honey-colored crusts, in the diaper area or at a wound such as a circumcision → topical mupirocin · Blueberry muffin rash — TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex virus) · Langerhans cell histiocytosis — looks seborrheic but is petechial and doesn't resolve · Maternal cold sores — do not diagnose HSV in a well 2-day-old with erythematous pustules and spared palms and soles. Base the diagnosis on the morphology and the infant's well appearance.
Diaper rash rule Candida involves the inguinal creases (beefy red + satellite papules → nystatin). Irritant contact dermatitis spares them (convex surfaces only → barrier cream). · Congenital dermal melanocytosis — blue-grey macules over the sacrum and buttocks, most common in darker-skinned infants, benign and self-resolving by age 3–5 years; document on exam to avoid confusion with non-accidental trauma
Transient color changes Acrocyanosis (symmetric blue-purple hands and feet with crying or cold), cutis marmorata (symmetric lacy violaceous mottling of the limbs that changes with temperature) and harlequin color change (sharply demarcated redness of one side of the body) are clinical diagnoses that need no treatment.
Pairs with Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers the non-cutaneous half of the same principle: transplacental hormone, physiologic, self-limited.
How NBME framed it Erythema toxicum appeared as small yellow papules on a red base; each decoy fits another rash: staphylococcal or herpes culture, potassium hydroxide prep, topical steroid.
Transferable rule Before choosing pure reassurance, scan the history for a modifiable exposure: bundling, a soap, a detergent, a medication, a position. When the history describes the environment, removing that exposure is the treatment.

Diaper Dermatitis

Diaper rash that improved on a barrier, then worsened: superinfection · folds spared or folds involved

Source vignette Pt — 18 mo F, one week of diaper rash that improved on petrolatum and zinc oxide and is now worsening; fussy during changes, eating and sleeping normally; diarrheal illness a week ago, resolved; attends day care, no affected classmates · Exam — afebrile with normal vitals; beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases with satellite papules; remainder normal · Q — the best next step in management; options spanned oral amoxicillin, topical antifungal, topical permethrin, oral zinc and screening for sexual abuse
The decision point

The diagnosis rests on the rash's trajectory, not its morphology. Barrier therapy is the correct and sufficient treatment for irritant contact dermatitis. A rash that got better on it and then got worse has therefore acquired something the barrier does not treat. Two examination findings identify the cause: the rash involves the skinfolds and has satellite lesions. Irritant dermatitis spares the creases because the convex surfaces contact the wet diaper and the depths of the folds are protected. Candida does the opposite and thrives in the warm, occluded crease. Satellite papules beyond the border of the main plaque are the hallmark of Candida. The recent diarrhea explains the mechanism: fecal bacteria raise local pH and compromise the barrier. Candida albicans from the gastrointestinal tract then colonises the skin. Treat with a topical antifungal applied under the barrier ointment, not instead of it.

Defining criteria Candida dermatitis — beefy-red confluent plaques that involve the skinfolds, with satellite lesions; the second most common diaper rash, a yeast superinfection of irritant dermatitis, treated with a topical antifungal · Irritant contact dermatitis — erythematous papules and plaques on convex surfaces that spare the skinfolds; the most common diaper rash, treated with a topical barrier · Satellite lesion — a discrete erythematous papule beyond the border of the main plaque; the finding that separates the two above when both are red and confluent
Pertinent positives & negatives Improved on barrier, now worsening — the trajectory that defines superinfection; a rash failing first-line therapy from the start would instead question the original diagnosis · Involves the inguinal creases — excludes irritant contact dermatitis, which spares them · Satellite papules — rules in Candida; no other diaper rash produces them · Recent resolved diarrhea — the risk factor, not a diagnosis; it raises stool pH and seeds the skin · Rash confined to the diaper area — excludes scabies, which involves trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles · No perioral dermatitis, no alopecia, diarrhea already resolved — excludes acrodermatitis enteropathica, which needs chronic diarrhea plus the other two · No verrucous papules, no genital ulcers, no adenopathy or fever — no finding that would raise a sexually transmitted infection, and therefore none that licenses an abuse evaluation · Afebrile, eating and sleeping normally — not systemically ill; fussiness confined to changes is local pain
Diaper dermatitis — the differential
DiagnosisIllness scriptThe NBME tellExcluded here by
Candida dermatitisYeast superinfection of an irritant rash; after diarrhea, antibiotics, or with thrushBeefy-red plaques in the creases with satellite lesions; worse despite barrier— (the answer)
Irritant contact dermatitisStool and urine breakdown of convex skin; the commonest diaper rashSpares the skinfolds; no satellites; responds to barrierCreases involved, and barrier therapy already failed
Perianal group A streptococcal diseaseBacterial; painful defecation and stool withholdingBright red, sharply demarcated perianal rash with or without anal fissuresThe rash is not perianal or sharply demarcated
ScabiesMite; refractory diaper rash in infants with itchy contactsDiffuse — trunk, axillae, neck, palms and solesConfined to the diaper area; no affected contacts
Acrodermatitis enteropathicaZinc deficiency; rare and refractoryChronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis plus alopeciaDiarrhea resolved; no perioral rash, no alopecia
Sexually transmitted infection Can't missThe concern behind any genital rashVerrucous papules in HPV, or ulcers with fever and adenopathy in HSV, or mucopurulent discharge in gonorrhea and chlamydiaNone of those lesions is present
Management, in one line Apply topical nystatin or clotrimazole beneath a barrier ointment. The antifungal treats the yeast, and the barrier keeps stool and urine off skin that is still broken.
Decision spine Did correct first-line therapy work and then stop working? — Yes means look for a superinfection, not a new diagnosis · Folds spared or folds involved? — Involved means Candida · Any satellite lesions? — Yes confirms it · Does the rash leave the diaper area? — No, so scabies is out · Is the diarrhea chronic, with perioral rash and alopecia? — No, so zinc is out · Any lesion that is itself a sexually transmitted infection? — No, so nothing licenses an abuse workup
Scenario bank
  1. 18 mo F, one week of diaper rash worsening despite petrolatum and zinc oxide, diarrheal illness a week ago now resolved, beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases with satellite papules → Topical nystatin under a barrier ointment → candidal diaper dermatitis
  2. 8 mo M, erythematous papules and plaques over the convex buttocks and thighs with the inguinal creases spared and no satellite lesions → Barrier ointment with more frequent diaper changes → irritant contact dermatitis
  3. 3 yo F, bright red sharply demarcated perianal plaque with an anal fissure and painful defecation → Oral amoxicillin → perianal group A streptococcal disease
  4. 4 mo M receiving amoxicillin for otitis media, now with beefy-red confluent rash in the inguinal creases and white plaques on the buccal mucosa → Topical nystatin to the diaper area plus oral nystatin → candidal dermatitis with thrush
  5. 5 mo M with a refractory diaper rash plus papules on the trunk, axillae, neck, palms and soles; his mother itches at night → Scabies → permethrin for the infant and all household contacts
  6. 7 mo with a refractory perineal rash, perioral dermatitis and diffuse alopecia, and chronic diarrhea → Acrodermatitis enteropathica → oral zinc supplementation
  7. Why a recent diarrheal illness increases the risk of candidal diaper dermatitis → Fecal bacteria raise local pH and compromise the skin barrier → gut Candida albicans then colonizes the broken skin
  8. 10 mo F with beefy-red confluent plaques involving the inguinal creases and satellite lesions → A high-potency topical corticosteroid → occlusion causes atrophy and striae
  9. 5 yo F, 5 days of burning with urination and vulvar redness, afebrile, no medications or serious illness, abuse denied; moderate erythema over the vulva and entire perineum reaching the perianal skin, no vesicles or pustules, scant white discharge at the introitus; vaginal culture pending → Topical nystatin → candidal vulvovaginitis
  10. 4 yo F, toilet-trained, finished amoxicillin for otitis media last week; vulvar itching, erythema over the vulva and perineum extending into the inguinal creases with satellite papules, thick white discharge at the introitus → Candidal vulvovaginitis → topical antifungal such as nystatin
Decoy note The history items "The parents are separated" and "attends day care" raise the abuse and contagion hypotheses, respectively, but neither is an examination finding. No classmate has a rash, which excludes contagion from day care. The initial improvement on barrier therapy is the single most informative detail. It proves the original diagnosis was right and something was added.
Pearls Improvement then deterioration on correct therapy means a second organism, not a wrong diagnosis; the same pattern occurs in otitis with a new fever after day 3, in cellulitis with an abscess forming, and in eczema herpeticum · Folds are the discriminator: irritant dermatitis spares them and Candida involves them · Satellite lesions are near-specific for cutaneous candidiasis · Antifungal under the barrier, not instead of it, because the skin is still broken and still in contact with stool · risk factors that should make you expect Candida before you see it are recent diarrhea, recent antibiotics, and oral thrush · Candidal vulvovaginitis in a toilet-trained girl: dysuria, redness over the vulva and whole perineum reaching the perianal skin, and white discharge at the introitus; treat with topical nystatin, since topical agents are preferred for superficial candidiasis · Risk factors for candidal vulvovaginitis: diabetes mellitus, recent antibiotics and corticosteroids; none is required
How NBME framed it The stem opens on burning with urination and closes on a pending culture, while the diagnosis sits in the white discharge and perineal-to-perianal redness.
Pairs with Part I Benign Neonatal Rashes covers the one-line diaper rule and the newborn rashes that need no treatment at all. Ask: does the rash involve the creases, and are there satellites? Part I Maternal Effects in the Newborn covers vaginal discharge in a newborn girl: is the discharge white with perineal redness, or mucoid in a well newborn?
Transferable rule When a correct treatment works and then stops working, the diagnosis was not wrong; something was added. Ask what the first treatment does not cover, and look for the finding that identifies it.
True-fact-wrong-slotOral amoxicillin: bacterial superinfection is a real cause of refractory diaper rash, but perianal strep is bright red and sharply demarcated around the anus, and this rash is neither.
Unchecked attributeTopical permethrin: scabies genuinely causes refractory diaper rash in infants, but it is diffuse across trunk, axillae, palms and soles, and no contact is affected.
Salient decoyOral zinc: she had a diarrheal illness, but acrodermatitis enteropathica needs chronic diarrhea plus perioral dermatitis and alopecia, and hers resolved in days.
Sequencing trapScreening for sexual abuse: an abuse evaluation is triggered by findings that are themselves sexually transmitted infections; none is present, and a social detail is not a finding.
Unchecked attributeIntramuscular ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin: this treats gonorrhea and chlamydia, which give mucopurulent discharge, not white discharge; in a prepubertal child past the newborn period either infection also prompts a sexual abuse evaluation.
Unchecked attributeOral acyclovir: herpes simplex virus gives painful vesicles on a red base; this perineum has no vesicles or pustules.
Salient decoyOral amoxicillin: burning with urination suggests cystitis, but redness over the vulva and perineum with white discharge points to candidal vulvovaginitis.
True-fact-wrong-slotOral metronidazole: it treats bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis but has no activity against Candida.
