The decision point

Reasonable suspicion → report to Adult Protective Services. You do not need proof, and you do not investigate first. Confounders such as warfarin (easy bruising) and dementia (unreliable historian) are real but irrelevant to the decision to report. Adult Protective Services investigates; you do not adjudicate.

Scenario bank
  1. 82 yo F with bruises in multiple stages of healing and a vague mechanism → Report now, on suspicion alone → proof is not required, and confirming it is not the physician's job
  2. 82 yo F on warfarin with easy bruising and an implausible history → Report to Adult Protective Services → anticoagulation explains bruising, not the implausible history; suspicion alone obligates the report
  3. 82 yo F with dementia who denies abuse while her caregiver is present → Interview her alone
  4. 34 yo F disclosing intimate partner violence, fully competent, who declines reporting → Support and safety planning, respecting her autonomy
  5. 6 yo M with a spiral femur fracture and an inconsistent history → Mandatory report to child protective services
  6. 82 yo F with suspected abuse; who investigates → Adult Protective Services → the physician reports suspicion; APS investigates
The findings that build suspicion Bruises in multiple stages of healing (the single most tested physical finding, as in child abuse) · implausible or vague mechanism · caregiver who cannot explain the injuries · patient who becomes uncomfortable and minimizes when asked alone · risk profile: dementia, dependency, caregiver stress. Interview technique: separate the patient from the caregiver, ask direct nonjudgmental questions, and do not confront the suspected abuser.
Reporting pathways
SituationPath
Elder / dependent adult abuseAPS — report on suspicion, mandated in most states
Child abuseCPS — report on suspicion, no parental consent needed
Intimate partner violence in a competent adultNOT reportable without consent in most states → safety assessment, safety plan, resources, document
Gunshot / stab wounds, certain infectionsReportable regardless
The asymmetry rule Capacity determines whether to report. Report abuse of children and cognitively impaired elders over anyone's objection. For a competent adult experiencing IPV (intimate partner violence), offer support and respect autonomy. Once abuse is suspected, never "document and re-ask at the next visit". Doing so sends a dependent patient back into the home you suspect.

Vitamins and Nutritional Deficiencies

name the vitamin by its sign · fat-soluble: why fat is not absorbed · water-soluble: what the patient drinks, takes or does not eat · the vegan diet: what must be supplementedWhich organ pattern names the vitamin, and why is this patient short of it?

RecognizeWorkupManagementPractice
Bottom line

Name the vitamin by its sign, then ask why this patient is short of it.

  • Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K): absorbed only with bile and pancreatic enzymes, so any fat malabsorption can deplete all four: cystic fibrosis (CF) and other pancreatic insufficiency, cholestasis and biliary atresia, celiac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, gastric bypass or short bowel.
  • Water-soluble (B and C): the body stores little, except B12 (cobalamin), so deficiency follows chronic alcohol use, poor intake, malabsorption (bypass, short bowel, Crohn disease) or a drug.
  • Vitamin K deficiency: the PT (prothrombin time) lengthens first, because factor VII (proconvertin) has the shortest half-life; the aPTT (activated partial thromboplastin time) follows only when deficiency is severe, and platelets stay normal.
  • B12 or folate: both cause a megaloblastic anemia; neurologic signs and a high methylmalonic acid mark B12.
  • Unfortified vegan diet: B12 always, plus vitamin D and calcium, must be supplemented; iron and zinc join the list for children and menstruating women.
  • Order of treatment: thiamine before or with glucose; no folate alone until the B12 level is known, since folate corrects the anemia but not the nerve damage.
Recognize: name it by its sign
Each vitamin: who gets it and the sign that names it
VitaminWho gets itThe sign
AFat malabsorption; poor intake in low-income regionsNight blindness, dry conjunctivae and cornea (xerophthalmia), Bitot spots, dry skin
DFat malabsorption; breastfed infant without supplements; little sun, dark skin; vegan dietChildren: rickets (bowed legs, widened wrists, rachitic rosary). Adults: osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal weakness
ECholestatic liver disease, CF, abetalipoproteinemiaAtaxia with lost vibration and position sense, neuropathy with hyporeflexia, myopathy, hemolytic anemia; mimics Friedreich ataxia
KFat malabsorption; broad-spectrum antibiotics; newborn without prophylaxis; poor intakeBruising, mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding; a long PT that corrects with vitamin K
B1 (thiamine)Alcohol use (most common), malnutrition including anorexia nervosa, hyperemesis gravidarum, bariatric surgery with vomitingWernicke: confusion, ophthalmoplegia (horizontal nystagmus, bilateral abducens palsy), gait ataxia. Dry beriberi: symmetric sensorimotor neuropathy. Wet beriberi: high-output heart failure with edema
B3 (niacin)Alcohol use, anorexia, Crohn disease, Hartnup disease, carcinoid syndrome (tryptophan diverted to serotonin)Pellagra: photosensitive dermatitis of the neck (Casal necklace), hands and face, with diarrhea and dementia
B6 (pyridoxine)Isoniazid, alcohol usePeripheral neuropathy, cheilitis, stomatitis; seizures when severe; microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia
B9 (folate)Alcohol use, pregnancy, hemolysis, poor intake; methotrexate, trimethoprim, triamterene, phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepineMegaloblastic anemia with a normal neurologic exam; neural tube defects in pregnancy
B12Pernicious anemia, atrophic gastritis, vegan diet, metformin, proton pump inhibitors, ileal resection or Crohn disease, fish tapewormMegaloblastic anemia with lost vibration and position sense and spastic weakness (subacute combined degeneration of the dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts), neuropathy, dementia
CNo fruits or vegetables: food-selective child (autism), alcohol use, severe malnutritionSwollen bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, poor wound healing, a limp in children from bleeding under the periosteum; platelets, PT and aPTT normal
Bleeding: which pathway Vitamin K deficiency – PT/INR (international normalized ratio) prolonged first, aPTT normal or prolonged if severe, platelets and factor V normal · Liver failure – PT prolonged with a low factor V (factor V does not need vitamin K) and low albumin; the PT does not correct with vitamin K · Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) – sepsis, trauma or malignancy; a critically ill patient oozing from lines; platelets and fibrinogen low, PT and aPTT prolonged, D-dimer high
Vegan diet (unfortified) Must supplement – B12 (no unfortified plant source), vitamin D (skin synthesis covers only about half the requirement, less in northern latitudes) and calcium (plant calcium, as in spinach, is oxalate-bound and poorly absorbed) · At risk – iron and zinc in children (growth) and menstruating women; non-heme iron absorbs poorly, so pair it with vitamin C · Not deficient – folate (greens, legumes, fruit) and protein with essential amino acids in balanced diets
Workup
Vitamin D Measure – 25-hydroxyvitamin D, made in the liver; skip 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, often normal in deficiency because parathyroid hormone (PTH) drives its production · Rickets labs – alkaline phosphatase and PTH rise, 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls; phosphate is low (less absorbed, more lost in urine); calcium is low or normal, because PTH defends it
Management
By vitamin Vitamin K – parenteral for severe coagulopathy; add fresh frozen plasma for serious bleeding (intracranial, gastrointestinal or at several sites); in CF, restart pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins · Newborn – one intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth · Vitamin D – 50,000 international units (IU) weekly for 8 weeks, then 800 to 1,000 IU daily; recheck 25-hydroxyvitamin D in 3 to 4 months, aiming for 20 ng/mL or more; 400 IU daily for every infant in the first year · Thiamine – IV, before or with any glucose, in Wernicke encephalopathy or any malnourished or alcohol-using patient · B12 – intramuscular or high-dose oral; with neurologic signs, never folate alone · Folate – oral folic acid once the B12 level is known, or with B12 when the cause is unclear; alongside methotrexate; 0.4 mg daily for anyone who could become pregnant, 4 mg after a prior neural tube defect, starting before conception · B6 and C – pyridoxine with isoniazid; oral vitamin C, improving within days to weeks
Practice
  1. 24-year-old woman asks which supplements she needs strict vegan diet of unprocessed, unfortified plant foods Takes no supplements; eats legumes, greens and grains daily No fatigue, numbness or bone pain BP 112/70 mm Hg · hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL → Vitamin B12 → no unfortified plant source of B12 exists, so it must always be supplemented. Legumes, greens and grains supply abundant folate and protein, and balanced vegan diets supply complete protein, so neither folic acid nor protein needs supplementing; folate matters in pregnancy, but vegan diets are folate-rich
  2. 3-day-old boy has oozing from the umbilical stump dark stools since this morning Born at home; exclusively breastfed; parents declined newborn injections Well-appearing · platelets and fibrinogen normal · PT markedly prolonged · aPTT mildly prolonged → Vitamin K deficiency bleeding → a well newborn with no prophylaxis, normal platelets and fibrinogen and a long PT has vitamin K deficiency bleeding: parenteral vitamin K, with fresh frozen plasma if bleeding is serious; breast milk is low in vitamin K. Disseminated intravascular coagulation consumes platelets and fibrinogen in a critically ill patient. Hemophilia A lacks factor VIII (antihemophilic factor), which does not need vitamin K; it prolongs the aPTT and leaves the PT normal
  3. 47-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has 2 months of watery diarrhea worsening forgetfulness sharply bordered, scaly, darkened rash on the backs of the hands, the face and a band around the neck All sun-exposed; no blisters Afebrile → Niacin deficiency → photosensitive dermatitis with diarrhea and dementia is pellagra, the 4 Ds ending in death, and alcohol use is a leading cause. Porphyria cutanea tarda is also photosensitive, but it blisters on the backs of the hands and brings no diarrhea or dementia. Thiamine deficiency strikes the brain, eyes, gait or heart, not the skin
  4. 18-month-old boy walked late, only last month Exclusively breastfed with no supplements; dark skin; rarely outdoors bowed legs and widened wrists beading along the costochondral junctions Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high → Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D → nutritional rickets: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the form measured, and it falls in deficiency; replace vitamin D. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is often normal, because PTH drives its production, and PTH holds calcium low or normal, so neither confirms the cause
  5. 52-year-old man with heavy daily alcohol use is brought in confused and unsteady horizontal nystagmus and weak lateral gaze in both eyes wide-based gait Afebrile · BP 128/80 mm Hg · fingerstick glucose 58 mg/dL → Intravenous thiamine before or with dextrose → confusion, eye findings and ataxia in a drinker is Wernicke encephalopathy: IV thiamine goes in before or with the dextrose, because a glucose load can precipitate or worsen it. The glucose is needed, but not first; oral thiamine at discharge misses the emergency, which needs IV thiamine on suspicion
  6. 16-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 3 days of nosebleeds bruises easily for 2 months Off her prescribed medications; low-grade fever last week no organomegaly; neurologic exam normal Normal vital signs · platelet count normal → Absent coagulation factor activation → in CF the prescribed medications are usually pancreatic enzymes and fat-soluble vitamins; off them, fat is not absorbed, and without vitamin K the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate (activate) factors II, VII, IX (Christmas factor) and X, so the PT lengthens first: give vitamin K. Consumption (disseminated intravascular coagulation) needs a critically ill patient with low platelets; the recent fever is the decoy. Vitamin C is water soluble, so pancreatic insufficiency does not deplete it, and scurvy leaves the PT normal
  7. 15-year-old girl who follows a vegan diet has 3 months of fatigue heavy menstrual periods pale conjunctivae Takes no supplements or medications Afebrile · hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL · mean corpuscular volume 71 fL → Iron deficiency → menstruating vegans are an at-risk group for iron; non-heme plant iron absorbs poorly, so supplement it and pair it with vitamin C. Vitamin B12 deficiency is macrocytic, not microcytic. Vitamin B6 deficiency can cause a microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia, but it follows isoniazid or alcohol use, with neuropathy
  8. 14-year-old girl with cystic fibrosis has 6 months of falls Skips her pancreatic enzymes wide-based gait, positive Romberg, lost vibration and position sense absent ankle reflexes Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL · MCV 88 fL · reticulocytes high · echocardiogram normal → Vitamin E deficiency → fat malabsorption depletes vitamin E: dorsal column and cerebellar damage with hemolysis (normal MCV, high reticulocytes); replace vitamin E. Vitamin B12 deficiency is megaloblastic and adds spastic weakness. Vitamin E deficiency mimics Friedreich ataxia, but here the cause is in sight: cystic fibrosis off enzymes, with hemolysis, and the echocardiogram is normal
  9. 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes on metformin has 2 months of fatigue mild numbness of the feet Hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL · MCV 108 fL · hypersegmented neutrophils · serum B12 240 pg/mL · folate normal → Serum methylmalonic acid → a megaloblastic anemia with a B12 of 200 to 300 pg/mL needs methylmalonic acid, and a high level confirms B12 deficiency; metformin is a cause. Homocysteine is high in both B12 and folate deficiency, so it cannot separate them. Intrinsic factor antibodies look for the cause (pernicious anemia) once the deficiency is shown
  10. 23-year-old woman has daily headaches and blurred vision Took several high-dose vitamin A supplements for acne for 4 months bilateral papilledema Body mass index 22 kg/m2 · brain imaging normal · opening pressure high, fluid normal → Excess vitamin A intake → vitamin A toxicity from supplements or retinoids causes pseudotumor cerebri (headache, papilledema, high opening pressure): stop the supplements and check for pregnancy, since vitamin A is teratogenic. Excess vitamin D causes hypercalcemia, not raised pressure, and a normal body mass index argues against obesity-related intracranial hypertension
  11. 6-year-old boy with autism has refused to walk for 3 weeks, citing leg pain Eats only white bread, crackers and cheese swollen, bleeding gums; perifollicular hemorrhages; coiled hairs Hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL · white cells and platelets normal · PT and aPTT normal → Vitamin C deficiency → scurvy, from impaired collagen hydroxylation: a food-selective child with bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, corkscrew hairs and a limp from bleeding under the periosteum; give oral vitamin C. It mimics acute lymphoblastic leukemia, but normal white cells, platelets and coagulation studies with gum disease point to the diet. Vitamin K deficiency lengthens the PT; scurvy leaves it normal
  12. 26-year-old man who follows a vegan diet has diffuse bone aches proximal muscle weakness Lives in a northern state; takes no supplements Afebrile · calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase high → Vitamin D deficiency → skin synthesis covers only about half the vitamin D requirement, less in northern latitudes, and an unfortified vegan diet adds little: osteomalacia with bone pain and proximal weakness. Vitamin B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis and dorsal-column signs, not bone pain. Primary hyperparathyroidism raises calcium; here calcium is low-normal, held there by PTH
  13. 4-week-old boy has oozing from his circumcision site since yesterday large scalp bruise Born at home; exclusively breastfed; parents declined all newborn injections Well-appearing · platelets normal · PT markedly prolonged · aPTT prolonged → Parenteral vitamin K → vitamin K deficiency bleeding: give parenteral vitamin K, the route for a severe coagulopathy, adding fresh frozen plasma for serious bleeding; oral vitamin K with a recheck in a week is too slow. Factor VIII treats hemophilia A; it does not need vitamin K and is not the missing factor
  14. 61-year-old man with long-standing alcohol use disorder cannot form new memories Hospitalized 3 months ago for confusion, eye-movement weakness and ataxia invents detailed accounts of recent days Steady gait · HR 78/min · alert and attentive · eye movements normal · no asterixis → Korsakoff syndrome → anterograde amnesia with confabulation in an alert drinker marks progression to Korsakoff syndrome (mammillary bodies), often permanent. Wernicke encephalopathy needs confusion, ophthalmoplegia or ataxia, and these have cleared. Hepatic encephalopathy ranges from subtle cognitive change to confusion and coma, with asterixis typically in its intermediate stages; he has no asterixis and is alert and attentive
  15. 58-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has fatigue Takes weekly methotrexate; stopped her folic acid no numbness or gait change Hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL · MCV 112 fL · hypersegmented neutrophils · serum B12 450 pg/mL · neurologic exam normal → Resume folic acid → methotrexate is a folate antagonist (a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor), and folic acid is given alongside it: resume it. A B12 over 300 pg/mL is sufficient and the neurologic exam is normal, so intramuscular B12 replaces nothing missing. The cause is already in sight, so a bone marrow biopsy adds nothing
  16. 47-year-old woman has 5 months of unsteadiness, numb feet Gastric bypass 6 years ago; off supplements 2 years thin, lighter hair; broad-based gait; positive Romberg lost vibration and position sense; brisk knee reflexes Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL · B12, methylmalonic acid normal → Copper deficiency → copper deficiency after bypass mimics B12 deficiency, with ataxia, weakness and neuropathy plus fragile, depigmented hair: check copper when B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal, replace it and resume supplements. Vitamin E deficiency brings hemolysis and a neuropathy with hyporeflexia, not brisk reflexes
  17. 2-year-old boy is raised on the family's unprocessed vegan diet Takes vitamin B12 and vitamin D drops growing along the 50th percentile Eats legumes, greens, grains and fruit Afebrile · hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL → Iron and zinc → rapid growth raises requirements, so iron and zinc join the list for children, as for menstruating women. Greens, legumes and fruit supply folate, and balanced vegan diets supply protein and essential amino acids
  18. 44-year-old woman on phenytoin for epilepsy: 4 months of aching hips, thighs Walks outdoors daily; drinks milk trouble climbing stairs; tender pelvis Calcium low-normal · phosphate low · alkaline phosphatase, PTH high · 25-hydroxyvitamin D 9 ng/mL · creatinine, albumin, liver enzymes normal → Accelerated hepatic breakdown of vitamin D → phenytoin, carbamazepine, isoniazid and rifampin speed the breakdown of vitamin D: drug-induced deficiency with osteomalacia despite sun and milk; replace vitamin D. A normal creatinine argues against chronic kidney disease (impaired renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation), and a normal albumin and liver enzymes against chronic liver disease (impaired hepatic 25-hydroxylation)
  19. 38-year-old woman has 3 weeks of burning and tingling in both feet Taking isoniazid alone for latent tuberculosis for 3 months; no other supplement decreased pinprick sensation in a stocking distribution Afebrile · liver enzymes normal → Add pyridoxine → isoniazid causes a B6 deficiency neuropathy, and pyridoxine is given with isoniazid: add it. Switching to rifampin is not needed, because the neuropathy comes from a missing vitamin that pyridoxine replaces, and gabapentin treats the symptom, not the deficiency
  20. 62-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has new oozing from IV sites Admitted with pneumonia; 10 days of broad-spectrum antibiotics and little oral intake INR 2.6 · aPTT mildly prolonged · platelets 140,000/mm3 → Factor V activity → both causes can lengthen his PT: antibiotics and poor intake cut vitamin K, and cirrhosis cuts synthesis. Factor V does not need vitamin K, so a normal factor V points to vitamin K deficiency and a low one to hepatic synthetic failure. Factor VII depends on vitamin K, so it falls in vitamin K deficiency and cannot clear the liver; a mixing study separates a factor deficiency from an inhibitor, which is not the question
  21. 30-year-old woman who follows a vegan diet has 4 months of numb feet Takes no supplements loss of vibratory sense in both feet Afebrile · hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL · MCV 109 fL → Vitamin B12 deficiency → B12 has no unfortified plant source; macrocytosis plus dorsal-column signs (subacute combined degeneration) is B12 deficiency, and its neurologic signs can appear before the anemia. Folate deficiency causes macrocytosis alone, with a normal neurologic exam, and iron deficiency is microcytic
  22. 1-hour-old boy born at term after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery Mother plans to breastfeed exclusively Parents ask about routine newborn care Well-appearing · Apgar scores 8 and 9 · HR 140/min · T 37.0 °C → Single intramuscular dose of vitamin K → one intramuscular dose of vitamin K at birth prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding, and breast milk is low in vitamin K; the single intramuscular dose, not an oral dose, is the prophylaxis, and waiting for bleeding gives up prevention
  23. 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is confused and unsteady 4 weeks of vomiting, 6 kg lost; intravenous dextrose twice horizontal nystagmus, weak lateral gaze bilaterally BP 104/66 mm Hg · no headache or papilledema · sodium 134 mEq/L, stable → Wernicke encephalopathy → confusion, eye findings and ataxia after weeks of hyperemesis gravidarum and dextrose loads is Wernicke encephalopathy: IV thiamine before further dextrose. Osmotic demyelination follows rapid correction of hyponatremia, and this sodium has not moved. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis brings headache in 80 to 90%, and papilledema may join it when pressure rises significantly; she has neither
  24. 9-year-old boy with cystic fibrosis cannot see well at dusk Skips his pancreatic enzymes and vitamin supplements dry conjunctivae and cornea; Bitot spots on both eyes dry skin Afebrile · gait and reflexes normal → Vitamin A deficiency → cystic fibrosis off enzymes means fat malabsorption, which depletes vitamin A: night blindness, dry conjunctivae and cornea (xerophthalmia), Bitot spots and dry skin; one fat-soluble deficiency means all four need checking or replacing. Vitamin E deficiency brings ataxia and lost vibration sense with hemolysis, and his gait and reflexes are normal. Retinitis pigmentosa also brings night blindness, but the front-of-eye signs here (dry conjunctivae and cornea, Bitot spots) are the vitamin A signs, and the cause is in sight
  25. 22-month-old girl walked late and now waddles Still drinks mostly breast milk; never had vitamin D drops bowed legs; thickened wrists and ankles Afebrile · HR 110/min · weight at the 40th percentile → Phosphorus concentration → vitamin D deficiency rickets: phosphate falls, because less is absorbed and PTH increases its loss in the urine. PTH and alkaline phosphatase both rise; osteoblasts release the enzyme as they lay down bone matrix
  26. 27-year-old woman is planning a pregnancy Her first pregnancy was affected by anencephaly Healthy; takes no medications; eats a varied diet BP 114/72 mm Hg · body mass index 23 kg/m2 → Folic acid 4 mg daily starting before conception → after a prior neural tube defect pregnancy the dose is 4 mg daily, started before conception; 0.4 mg daily is for anyone who could become pregnant, and the first prenatal visit is too late to start
  27. 74-year-old woman in a nursing home has 3 months of aching hips and thighs Rarely goes outside trouble rising from a chair; tender bones Afebrile · 25-hydroxyvitamin D 8 ng/mL · calcium normal · kidney function normal → Vitamin D 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks → osteomalacia from vitamin D deficiency: 50,000 IU weekly for 8 weeks, then 800 to 1,000 IU daily, rechecking the level in 3 to 4 months. A daily 1,000 IU is the maintenance dose, not the load. Calcitriol, a vitamin D analog, treats low calcium and bone disease when the kidneys or parathyroid glands are not working; her kidney function and calcium are normal
How NBME framed it: question 1

5-day-old boy with bleeding from vitamin K deficiency bleeding from the nose, mouth and gastrointestinal tract subdural hemorrhage Vitamin K therapy is being given

In addition to vitamin K, which is the next step?

Competing answers
  • Cryoprecipitate: a blood product for bleeding; but it carries fibrinogen, factors VIII and XIII (fibrin-stabilizing factor) and von Willebrand factor, not II, VII, IX or X.
  • Lactated Ringer solution: he is losing blood from several sites; but it restores volume and carries no clotting factors.
  • Platelets: a bleeding newborn; but vitamin K deficiency leaves the platelet count normal, so they replace nothing missing.

Down to two: fresh frozen plasma or factor VIII concentrate. Fresh frozen plasma replaces factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S at once, while vitamin K restores them over hours. Factor VIII concentrate treats hemophilia A, and factor VIII does not need vitamin K. The lead-in grants vitamin K, so only the blood product is tested; factor VIII concentrate is the bait.

How NBME framed it: question 2

15-month-old girl has not begun to crawl or walk Exclusively breastfed since birth Length at the 50th and weight at the 85th percentile; language and social skills normal for age widened wrists; examination otherwise normal

Which serum finding is most likely to be increased?

Competing answers
  • Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) activity: a liver enzyme beside alkaline phosphatase; but it rises with liver cell injury; a high alkaline phosphatase with normal ALT and GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase) comes from bone.
  • Calcium concentration: a bone mineral; but PTH holds it low or normal; a high calcium points to hyperparathyroidism or vitamin D excess.
  • Magnesium concentration: a mineral tied to calcium balance; but vitamin D deficiency does not raise it; a low magnesium impairs PTH secretion and action.

Down to two: alkaline phosphatase activity or phosphorus concentration. Alkaline phosphatase: osteoblasts make it as they lay down matrix, and it is high in active rickets, often before calcium or phosphate falls. Phosphorus falls instead, because absorption drops and PTH increases urinary loss; a high phosphate points to kidney failure or hypoparathyroidism. The key was an enzyme activity set among minerals and a liver enzyme, and the infant's rickets showed only as late crawling and walking with widened wrists.

Brain and skin Wernicke triad – confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia; often incomplete, so one or two features in a drinker is enough to treat · Korsakoff – anterograde and retrograde amnesia with confabulation and no insight, older long-term memories relatively preserved; it marks progression (mammillary bodies) and is often permanent · Pellagra, the 4 Ds – dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, death · Thiamine level – skip it before treating suspected Wernicke: the result is not back in time, so give IV (intravenous) thiamine on suspicion
Toxicity: only A and D Vitamin A – from excess liver, supplements or retinoids: pseudotumor cerebri (headache, papilledema, high opening pressure), bone pain and fractures, hepatomegaly, dry skin and alopecia, and teratogenicity, the reason isotretinoin needs pregnancy testing and contraception · Vitamin D – hypercalcemia, from massive overdose or from granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis, where macrophages make 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D without PTH control; 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is the level to order for hypercalcemia with suspected sarcoidosis or lymphoma
Vitamin D deficiency: causes Poor intake (milk avoidance, lactose intolerance, unfortified vegan diet); malabsorption (Crohn disease, celiac disease, gastrectomy or bariatric surgery); little sun (high latitude, dark skin, indoor life, nursing home, night work); obesity and older age; chronic kidney and liver disease; phenytoin, carbamazepine, isoniazid and rifampin, which speed its breakdown.
Common wrong answers Increased platelet sequestration: CF liver disease can enlarge the spleen, but sequestration lowers platelets without lengthening the PT. Reduced von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease activity: TTP is acute, with thrombocytopenia, hemolysis and neurologic signs. Homocysteine to separate B12 from folate: high in both; only methylmalonic acid separates them. Folic acid for a megaloblastic anemia with numb feet: the blood improves, but the neurologic signs mark B12, and folate alone lets them progress. Vitamin K for bleeding gums: scurvy leaves the PT normal. Folic acid for a vegan: it matters in pregnancy, but vegan diets are folate-rich. Dextrose first in a confused drinker: needed, but thiamine goes in before or with it.
After gastric bypass Supplements and periodic levels are lifelong, because deficiencies overlap: B12 (macrocytic anemia, neuropathy, cognitive change); A (night blindness), D and calcium (bone loss with secondary hyperparathyroidism), K (coagulopathy); iron (anemia; the duodenum is bypassed); zinc (alopecia, rash, night blindness); copper (ataxia, weakness and neuropathy that mimic B12 deficiency, with fragile, depigmented hair; check copper when B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal); folate (macrocytic anemia); thiamine (Wernicke, especially with intractable vomiting).
Pearls One malabsorption cause usually depletes several fat-soluble vitamins, so a CF or cholestatic patient with one deficiency needs all four checked or replaced. Vitamin A supplementation is standard in severe measles and where deficiency is endemic. Broad-spectrum antibiotics cut gut bacterial production of vitamin K. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (about 6 hours), then IX (Christmas factor), X and II (about 60 hours); protein C is also short (about 8 hours), so starting warfarin lowers it first and briefly makes blood hypercoagulable, the reason for heparin bridging and the cause of warfarin skin necrosis. Without vitamin K, the liver cannot gamma-carboxylate factors II, VII, IX and X. Fresh frozen plasma replaces them and proteins C and S at once; vitamin K restores them over hours. B12 neurologic signs can appear before the anemia. Rarer B vitamins: B2 (riboflavin) causes angular cheilitis, stomatitis, glossitis and a normocytic anemia; B5 (pantothenic acid), rare, distal paresthesias; B7 (biotin), rare, from raw egg whites, alopecia and dermatitis. The vegan diet also lowers glucose and cholesterol and reduces cardiovascular risk; on the exam, a well-planned vegan diet is credited as nutritionally adequate except for B12.
Vitamin D thresholds: current status Checked September 2026. In force: the Institute of Medicine 2011 cutoffs, still used by the National Institutes of Health Office of Dietary Supplements and matched by the 2016 Global Consensus on nutritional rickets: under 12 ng/mL (30 nmol/L) deficient, 12 to under 20 inadequate, 20 or more adequate, over 50 ng/mL a risk of harm. Retired: the Endocrine Society 2011 set (under 20 deficient, 21 to 29 insufficient, 30 to 100 sufficient); its 2024 guideline endorses no cutoff or target of 30 and advises against routine testing in healthy people. In 2024 it advised empiric supplementation above the daily allowance at ages 1 to 18, over 75, in pregnancy and in high-risk prediabetes; adults 19 to 74 take the usual allowance (600 IU, 800 IU over 70). Unchanged: treat symptomatic deficiency (rickets, osteomalacia) whatever the cutoff. On the exam, older questions may use the 20 and 30 cutoffs, so read the level against the symptoms. Most deficiency is silent or causes vague aches and surfaces as low bone density, fracture or osteomalacia. The vitamin D pathway: skin makes it from 7-dehydrocholesterol with ultraviolet light and diet adds more; the kidney 1-alpha-hydroxylase, driven by PTH and suppressed by high calcium, makes the active form, which raises intestinal calcium absorption (its main action) and renal calcium and phosphate reabsorption, mineralizes bone and suppresses PTH.
Pairs with Part I Recurrent Respiratory Infection and Structural Lung Disease: is growth poor with greasy stools, and is the sweat chloride high? Part I Hemophilia: is the PT or the aPTT long, and are platelets normal? Part I Night Blindness: vitamin A against retinitis pigmentosa; is the front of the eye normal? Part I Hypercalcemia: vitamin D excess and sarcoidosis; is the 25-hydroxy or the 1,25-dihydroxy vitamin D high? Feeding an Infant or Toddler: vitamin D 400 IU for breastfed infants. Part II Fever and Rash in a Child: measles. Part I Headache in a Child: Imaging and Treatment: the papilledema workup and the other drugs that raise intracranial pressure; is the papilledema bilateral with full visual fields? Part I Tall Stature and Marfanoid Habitus: inherited high homocysteine, treated with B6, folate and B12. Part I Teratogenic Exposures: folate-antagonist antiepileptics and neural tube defects. Part I Tuberculosis: isoniazid with B6.
Transferable rule

Read the organ pattern first: eye, bone, dorsal columns with hemolysis, bleeding, brain and eyes, sun-exposed skin with diarrhea, megaloblastic blood, or bleeding gums with normal clotting. Then ask what the patient drinks, takes or does not eat, or why fat is not absorbed. For a diet, ask where each nutrient physically comes from: no unfortified plant source means it must be supplemented. Give thiamine before glucose, and settle B12 before folate alone.

2 briefsBoard-Style · Next-Step Questions

Preventive Medicine & Ethics

Adolescent Confidentiality

Ask what would have to be true to break it

Source vignette Pt — 16 yo M, well, discloses weekend marijuana use during the confidential portion of the visit · Q — the most appropriate next step; options spanned confidential counseling with CRAFFT screening, informing his parents and ordering a urine drug screen
The decision point

A minor discloses substance use during a confidential interview. In this case, keep it confidential and counsel him directly. Substance use is a confidential service in essentially every state, and nothing he describes meets an exception. Confidentiality is what makes honest disclosure possible at all; adolescents who don't expect it don't disclose.

Set the frame before he talks by saying "what you tell me stays between us, unless someone's safety is at risk". Then screen with CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble), deliver brief counseling, and encourage him to tell his parents himself. Encouraging voluntary disclosure is not the same as disclosing.

Defining criteria Suicidal or homicidal intent — harm to self or others; break confidentiality · Physical or sexual abuse — including statutory abuse by partner age; break confidentiality and report · Imminent danger — specific and serious; imminence is the word that decides · Not an exception — vagueness, a parent asking, an embarrassing diagnosis, or risky behavior that is not imminently lethal
Adolescent confidentiality — what is protected
Confidential without parental consent
STI diagnosis and treatment (all 50 states)
Contraception
Pregnancy care (abortion varies — many states require notification or consent)
Substance use evaluation and treatment
Mental health services (age and state vary)
Emancipated / mature minors: married, military, parenting, self-supporting, court-declared → consent as adults
Distractors "Inform his parents": parental authority is the higher principle for most care, but the confidential-services carve-outs exist to override it (trump-card inversion) · "Tell him you can't promise confidentiality": this sounds true but is harmful; frame confidentiality as conditional, naming the specific exceptions, not as a blanket refusal · "Refer to a substance-use program": escalating before you have screened severity is a sequencing trap; occasional use gets brief counseling, not a program · "Order a urine drug screen": he already told you. Testing to confirm a disclosure is redundant, and a non-consented screen is its own ethics violation.
Mnemonic HEEADSSS (Home, Education and employment, Eating, Activities, Drugs, Sexuality, Suicide and depression, Safety) is the adolescent psychosocial history, asked privately.
Scenario bank
  1. 16 yo M discloses weekend marijuana use, otherwise well → Confidential counseling, CRAFFT, encourage self-disclosure to parents
  2. 16 yo M discloses use and says he's been thinking about killing himself → Break confidentiality — safety exception
  3. 16 yo M who drives after drinking → Maintain confidentiality and counsel about the driving → escalate only if he describes an imminent plan to drive impaired
  4. 15 yo F requesting contraception, doesn't want her mother told → Provide it confidentially
  5. 15 yo F at 15 weeks, sexual partner is 24 years old → Report it → the age gap converts this to statutory abuse
  6. 17 yo M with chlamydia → Treat confidentially; partner notification is a public-health obligation and does not breach his confidentiality
  7. 17 yo F, married, needs surgery → She is emancipated and consents herself
  8. 16 yo M whose mother calls to ask what was discussed → Decline to disclose; redirect to encouraging the conversation at home
  9. 14 yo M with an appendectomy needed → Parental consent required → surgical care is not a confidential service
  10. 16 yo M, opioid use with withdrawal symptoms and IV track marks → Severity now warrants treatment referral, still discussed with him first
  11. 16 yo M in a state where billing goes to the parent's insurance → Address the practical confidentiality limit up front; this is the real-world failure point
Paired pearls Set the frame before the disclosure; confidentiality cannot be promised retroactively · CRAFFT (Car, Relax, Alone, Forget, Family/Friends, Trouble) is the validated adolescent screen; ≥2 is positive · emergency care never waits for consent · Management almost always includes "encourage him to tell his parents", which preserves confidentiality and the family relationship.
Pairs with Elder Abuse above covers the same axis in the opposite direction. There, impaired capacity forces reporting over the patient's wishes. Here, a minor with a confidential service forces confidentiality over the parent's wishes. Both turn on who holds decisional authority for this specific decision, not on who is older.
Transferable rule Maintain confidentiality unless the disclosure satisfies a named exception (harm to self, harm to others, abuse). Do not weigh how serious the behavior sounds; without a named exception, confidentiality holds no matter how alarming the disclosure.
Trump-card inversionSequencing trap

Vaccines at the Infant Visits

Well infant, vaccines up to date · which vaccine the age allows at this visit

Source vignette Pt — 4-month-old girl at a well-child visit in October; uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery; immunizations up to date; normal growth, development, vital signs and examination · Q — immunization against which disease is most appropriate now; options spanned chickenpox, influenza, measles-mumps-rubella, rotavirus and shingles
The decision point

At 4 months, an infant who is up to date gets the second doses of the 2-month vaccines. These are DTaP (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids and acellular pertussis), Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b), PCV (pneumococcal conjugate vaccine), IPV (inactivated poliovirus vaccine) and oral rotavirus vaccine. Rotavirus vaccine has fixed age limits: the first dose by 14 weeks 6 days and the last dose by 8 months 0 days.

Influenza vaccine starts at 6 months, so an October visit does not make a 4-month-old eligible. MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) and varicella vaccines are live vaccines first given at 12 to 15 months. Zoster vaccine is an adult vaccine, given from age 50.

Defining criteria: age limits Rotavirus — first dose by 14 weeks 6 days, final dose by 8 months 0 days; 2 doses at 2 and 4 months (RV1, monovalent rotavirus vaccine) or 3 doses at 2, 4 and 6 months (RV5, pentavalent rotavirus vaccine) · Influenza — from 6 months, every season; a child aged 6 months to 8 years with fewer than 2 earlier doses gets 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart · MMR and varicella — first doses at 12 to 15 months, second doses at 4 to 6 years · Recombinant zoster — 2 doses 2 to 6 months apart from age 50, or from age 19 with immunocompromise
Vaccines due at each infant visit
VisitVaccines dueAge limit that matters here
2 monthsDTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus, first doses; hepatitis B second dose if not given at 1 monthRotavirus must start by 14 weeks 6 days
4 monthsDTaP, Hib, PCV, IPV and rotavirus, second dosesToo young for influenza (6 months) and for MMR and varicella (12 months)
6 monthsDTaP and PCV third doses; Hib third dose except with the PedvaxHIB product; rotavirus third dose with RV5 only; IPV and hepatitis B third doses (due 6 to 18 months); influenza in seasonRotavirus series ends by 8 months 0 days; the first influenza season needs 2 doses
12 to 15 monthsMMR and varicella first doses; hepatitis A first of 2 doses (12 to 23 months); PCV fourth dose; Hib boosterRoutine MMR and varicella start at 12 months
Scenario bank
  1. 4-month-old girl at a well-child visit in October, immunizations up to date, normal growth, development and examination → Rotavirus → second dose of the 2-month set; influenza waits until 6 months
  2. 17-week-old boy starting his infant vaccines today after moving from another state; he received only the hepatitis B birth dose → Rotavirus vaccine → the first dose must be given by 14 weeks 6 days
  3. 7-month-old girl at a well-child visit in November, up to date on her infant vaccines, who has never received influenza vaccine → Influenza vaccine today and a second dose in 4 weeks → first influenza season under age 9
  4. 12-month-old boy at a well-child visit, up to date on his vaccines, healthy → Measles-mumps-rubella and varicella → first live injected vaccines at 12 to 15 months
Schedule status, September 2026 In January 2026 the CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) moved childhood rotavirus and influenza vaccines from routine to shared clinical decision-making. A federal court stayed that change in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts is the 2025 schedule, which lists both vaccines as routine; check the CDC site for the current schedule. The AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) schedule also keeps both routine, and this NBME item keys rotavirus as a routine 4-month vaccine.
Pearls Rotavirus vaccine is live and oral; do not give it with SCID (severe combined immunodeficiency) or after an intussusception · Up to date at 4 months means the 2-month doses were given, so the second doses are due · Older sources, including this NBME explanation, start zoster vaccine at 60; recombinant zoster vaccine is now given from 50
How NBME framed it The October date is a seasonal cue for influenza, but at 4 months she is below its 6-month age limit. The options form an age ladder of live and inactivated vaccines, from rotavirus at 2 months through MMR and varicella at 12 months to zoster at 50.
Pairs with Aquifer Adolescent Vaccines covers the 11 to 12 year visit and influenza timing by season. Part I DTaP: Contraindication vs. Precaution covers when a DTaP dose is withheld. Ask: has this child reached the vaccine's age window, and has the window closed?
Transferable rule Check the child's age against each vaccine's age window before the season or the disease. A vaccine whose window has not opened, or has closed, is not given at this visit.
Unchecked attributeChickenpox: a routine live childhood vaccine; the first varicella dose is not given until 12 months.
Salient decoyInfluenza: the October visit falls in influenza vaccine season; she is 4 months old, and influenza vaccine starts at 6 months.
Unchecked attributeMeasles-mumps-rubella: routine and live, like rotavirus; the first dose is at 12 months.
Unchecked attributeShingles: the same virus as chickenpox; zoster vaccine is for adults from age 50.
1 briefAquifer · Case-Based Briefs

Preventive Medicine & Ethics

Adolescent Vaccines

Platform, series complete, season · a date buried in line one is data

Source vignette Pt — 11 yo F, up to date on vaccines at age 9, seen in June for a pre-participation evaluation, healthy, no travel · Q — the most appropriate vaccine today; options spanned Tdap, influenza and measles-mumps-rubella
The decision point

Age 11 is the adolescent immunization platform, the only age gate that any of the offered vaccines satisfies. She was up to date at 9, so every infant and early-childhood series is finished: hepatitis B, MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) and pneumococcal conjugate. Tdap (tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid and acellular pertussis) is the one vaccine whose scheduled slot is now.

Influenza vaccine is excluded by timing, not eligibility: she is due for it every year, just not in June. The target window is September or October. July and August are explicitly discouraged for single-dose recipients because immunity wanes before influenza peaks from December through February.

Defining criteria Adolescent platform at 11 to 12 years — Tdap, HPV and MenACWY come due together · Influenza timing — offer in September or October; avoid July and August for anyone needing a single dose · Catch-up principle — every encounter is a vaccination opportunity, including a sports physical
Each option and the gate it fails
VaccineWhen it is actually givenWhy not at this visit
TdapSingle dose at 11 to 12 years— it is the answer
InfluenzaAnnually, ideally September to OctoberIt is June, and July to August is discouraged
MMR12 to 15 months and 4 to 6 yearsSeries complete before age 9
Pneumococcal conjugateInfant series at 2, 4, 6 and 12 to 15 monthsComplete; no routine dose in a healthy 11-year-old
Hepatitis BBirth, 1 to 2 months, 6 to 18 monthsSeries complete in infancy
Scenario bank
  1. 11 yo F, up to date on vaccines at age 9, seen in June for a pre-participation evaluation, healthy, no travel → Tdap → adolescent platform at 11 to 12 years
  2. 11 yo F receiving Tdap today → HPV and MenACWY → the full 11 to 12 year platform
  3. 16 yo M who received MenACWY at age 11 → MenACWY booster dose → MenB by shared decision-making at 16 to 23
  4. 11 yo F, up to date, seen in early October for a pre-participation evaluation → Give Tdap and influenza vaccine at this visit → both are due now
  5. 15 yo F who has never received HPV vaccine → Begin the HPV series today → catch-up is recommended through age 26
  6. 11 yo M with functional asplenia from sickle cell disease, otherwise up to date → MenACWY as a two-dose primary series, plus MenB → asplenia changes the schedule
  7. 11 yo F newly arrived from abroad with no written immunization records → Vaccinate as though unimmunized → written records only
  8. 11 yo F with rhinorrhea and a temperature of 37.8 C, otherwise well → Vaccinate today → mild illness is not a contraindication
  9. Why influenza vaccine is deferred in June for a child who needs only one dose → Immunity wanes before influenza peaks in December to February → target September or October
Schedule status, October 2026 A January 2026 CDC (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) revision recommended a single HPV dose. A federal court stayed that revision in March 2026, and the stay is under appeal. The schedule CDC now posts keeps the 2-dose series when started at 9 to 14, and the AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) also recommends two doses, starting at 9 to 12; check the CDC site for the current schedule. On retired exam items, the classic keyed answer remains two doses if initiated before 15 and three if at 15 or older or immunocompromised. The posted schedule and the exam answer currently agree. The HPV brief covers dose-count mechanics.
Pearls The 11 to 12 platform is three vaccines: Tdap (tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid and acellular pertussis), HPV (human papillomavirus) and MenACWY (meningococcal conjugate vaccine for serogroups A, C, W and Y). · MenACWY gets a booster at 16 when the risk period begins; MenB (serogroup B meningococcal vaccine) is separate, at 16 to 23 by shared decision-making · Asplenia, complement deficiency and eculizumab convert MenACWY into a two-dose primary series with lifelong boosters · Mild illness, low-grade fever, antibiotics and breastfeeding are not contraindications · Undocumented means unvaccinated; verbal report does not count
Pairs with Part I HPV Vaccination & Series Rules covers the series rules, and Part I DTaP: Contraindication vs. Precaution covers pertussis contraindication versus precaution. Ask: is this an age-platform question or a series-mechanics question? Part II Vaccines at the Infant Visits covers the infant schedule and the rotavirus age limits.
Transferable rule When every option is a real vaccine, decide by eligibility. There are only three gates: age platform, series already complete, and season. Check them in that order.
Treat-the-numberTwo years since the last visit baits an interval calculation for a series with no remaining doses.
True-fact-wrong-slotPneumococcal and hepatitis B recommendations feel unsettled enough that something seems owed.

Psychiatry & Behavioral Health 9 topics

Mood, anxiety, psychotic, substance use and behavioral topics.

Psychosis

rule out a cause, then time itHow long, and only during mood episodes?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Hospitalize first if dangerous or unable to meet basic needs.

Then rule out a drug or medical cause:

  • Urine toxicology
  • Chemistry and glucose
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone)

Then time the psychosis against the gates:

  • Brief psychotic disorder 1 day to under 1 month
  • Schizophreniform disorder 1 to under 6 months
  • Schizophrenia 6 months or more

One or more delusions for 1 month or more, with Criterion A never met, is delusional disorder.

Psychosis only during mood episodes is a mood disorder with psychotic features.

Criterion A with a major mood episode, plus delusions or hallucinations 2 weeks or more without one, and mood episodes for most of the illness, is schizoaffective disorder.

Diagnosis
Criterion A (schizophrenia) Symptoms – 2 or more of delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms · Core – at least 1 is delusions, hallucinations or disorganized speech
Schizoaffective disorder types Bipolar type – a manic episode is part of the illness; major depressive episodes may also occur · Depressive type – major depressive episodes only · Either type – a depressive episode must include depressed mood; anhedonia alone does not count, since it is a common negative symptom of schizophrenia
Management and treatment
Management ladder: schizophrenia spectrum
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineAntipsychotic; hospitalize if dangerous or unable to meet basic needsNo response after an adequate trial (4 to 6 weeks)
Second trialA different antipsychotic; long-acting injectable if nonadherent2 or more adequate trials fail, adherence confirmed
Treatment resistantClozapine, with ANC (absolute neutrophil count) monitoringTop rung
By diagnosis Brief psychotic disorder – supervision and support; a short antipsychotic course if needed, and hospitalization by severity · Delusional disorder – antipsychotic plus psychotherapy · Schizoaffective disorder – a second-generation antipsychotic; for bipolar type, a mood stabilizer (lithium or valproate) may be added; for depressive type, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) may be added for persistent depressive symptoms
Practice
  1. 24-year-old man, previously well; for 3 months he has: believed neighbors implanted a tracker in his tooth heard voices commenting on everything he does stopped attending classes No episodes of depressed or elevated mood Urine toxicology negative · flat affect → Schizophreniform disorder → a delusion plus prominent voices for at least 1 month and under 6 months
  2. 26-year-old man; for 9 months he has: heard voices believed television hosts send him coded messages lost his job, rarely speaks, stopped bathing No episodes of depressed or elevated mood Vital signs normal · urine toxicology negative · flat affect → Schizophrenia → Criterion A symptoms with functional decline for 6 months or more
  3. 46-year-old woman; for 4 months she has: written daily letters to a news anchor she has never met been certain he loves her Works full time and runs her household; no hallucinations; mood normal Vital signs normal · laboratory studies normal → Delusional disorder → an erotomanic delusion for at least 1 month, with functioning intact and no other psychotic or mood symptoms
  4. 34-year-old woman with 1 year of insulting voices and belief coworkers are poisoning her two depressive episodes (4 and 3 months): low mood, anhedonia, insomnia, guilt, poor focus voices and belief persist 4 weeks after mood normalized Toxicology negative · euthymic → Schizoaffective disorder → Criterion A concurrent with major depressive episodes, 2 weeks or more of delusions and voices without a mood episode, and mood episodes for most of the illness
  5. 29-year-old man with 1 week of euphoria: 2-hour nights, rapid talk, his savings spent believing God chose him to rule the world Similar week 2 years ago; beliefs stopped when mood settled; none between episodes Vital signs normal · toxicology negative → Bipolar I disorder with psychotic features → the psychosis occurs only during the manic episode
  6. 22-year-old man with 2 days of believing federal agents are following him smoked methamphetamine daily for 3 days barely slept No psychiatric history HR 96/min · BP 128/80 mm Hg · oriented to person, place and time → Substance-induced psychotic disorder → the delusion began during stimulant intoxication; timing ties it to the drug
  7. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of: believing the government hacked her phone hearing whispers at night No psychiatric history; neurologic examination normal T 37.0 C · HR 88/min · chemistry panel and TSH normal → Urine toxicology screen → the first-line test still missing after chemistry and TSH; a negative screen lowers suspicion of a drug cause; imaging needs a neurologic finding or history; lumbar puncture needs fever, meningismus or delirium
  8. 40-year-old man with 10 days of believing his coworkers are poisoning his food yesterday he bought a knife to confront them No psychiatric history Vital signs normal · urine toxicology negative · oriented to person, place and time → Hospitalization and an antipsychotic → likely harm to others: admit first, whatever the duration; involuntarily if he refuses and no less restrictive option is safe
  9. 33-year-old man treated for schizophrenia for 6 years still hears voices daily after adequate trials of risperidone, then olanzapine adherence confirmed by pill counts No suicidal or homicidal ideation Vital signs normal · flat affect → Clozapine → 2 or more failed adequate trials with documented adherence define treatment resistance
  10. 35-year-old man with 5 years of recurring major depressive episodes each episode brings voices and persecutory beliefs voices persisted 3 weeks after his mood recovered depressed for most of those 5 years; never manic Afebrile · urine toxicology negative → Schizoaffective disorder, depressive type → Criterion A with major depressive episodes, voices 2 weeks or more without one, and depression for most of the illness; never manic, so depressive type
  11. 41-year-old woman newly diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder, depressive type hears voices and has felt hopeless for 2 months; denies suicidal ideation no history of manic episodes BP 118/76 mm Hg · urine toxicology negative → Second-generation antipsychotic plus an SSRI → depressive type: an antipsychotic treats the psychosis, and an SSRI may be added for the depression; a mood stabilizer such as lithium is for bipolar type
How NBME framed it: question 1

52-year-old man brought by police for strange behavior after an arrest for disturbing his neighbors for 6 months: aggressively handing out leaflets for the New Age healing business he runs from home claims special abilities to cure all physical and mental ailments very upset; sure the police and the physician are plotting against him and his business “I really have special powers; I can heal everyone in the waiting room” Denies past psychiatric problems, depression, elevated mood or hearing voices; sleeps 6 to 8 hours Examination normal · laboratory studies normal

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Bipolar disorder: grandiose claims; but no low or high mood, and normal sleep.
  • Brief psychotic disorder: an acute presentation after an arrest; but it lasts under 1 month, and his delusion has lasted 6.
  • Schizoaffective disorder: a persecutory delusion; but no mood episode and no second Criterion A symptom.
  • Schizophrenia: a fixed persecutory delusion; but it needs a second Criterion A symptom, and delusions are his only symptom.

Down to two: delusional disorder or schizophrenia. Delusional disorder: delusions alone (grandiose and persecutory) for 6 months; no voices, mood episode or disorganization; sleep and labs normal. (NBME says no hallucinations at all; current criteria allow minor ones tied to the delusion.)

How NBME framed it: question 2

37-year-old man with odd experiences that began 2 weeks ago, after he was fired instead of promoted a guard watched him clear his desk and walked him out six drinks at a bar over 4 hours; felt the patrons knew, were watching and talking about him next morning still felt it; closed the curtains; believed television hosts mocked him over that week a man’s voice called him a failure who would amount to nothing; went out only for food, in dark glasses to avoid recognition everything resolved by the end of the week No serious illness or medications; 2 to 3 beers nightly; marijuana once a month Examination normal · no hallucinations now · logical, goal-directed thinking · alert and oriented to person, place and time

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Adjustment disorder: a clear stressor; but psychotic symptoms would be atypical.
  • Delusional disorder: paranoid beliefs; but it needs 1 month or more, and his lasted a week.
  • Posttraumatic stress disorder: a distressing event; but job loss is not life-threatening, and it needs intrusions and over 1 month.
  • Schizophreniform disorder: delusions and a voice; but it needs 1 to 6 months.
  • Substance-induced psychotic disorder: six drinks and monthly cannabis; but alcohol rarely causes psychosis directly, and his cannabis use is occasional.

Down to two: brief psychotic disorder or delusional disorder. Brief psychotic disorder: paranoid delusions and a voice after a stressor, gone within a week, well under 1 month.

Pairs with Bipolar disorder: psychosis only during mania? Delirium: psychosis with a clouded, fluctuating sensorium?
Transferable rule

Rule out a cause, then ask how long the psychosis has lasted and whether it occurs only during mood episodes.

Bipolar Disorder

rule out a cause, time the episode, then treatMania or hypomania, and what to start or stop?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Hospitalize when needed to prevent harm: mania is an emergency.

Then rule out a drug or medical cause:

  • Urine drug screen
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free thyroxine
  • CBC (complete blood count) and basic metabolic panel

Then time the episode:

  • Manic episode 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalized
  • Hypomanic episode 4 days or more in a row
  • Cyclothymic disorder 2 years or more of swings below episode criteria

One manic episode makes bipolar I disorder; psychosis, marked impairment or hospitalization makes an episode manic, never hypomanic.

Treat: stop any antidepressant; start lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic.

Diagnosis
Manic episode criteria Mood – elevated, expansive or irritable mood plus more energy, most of the day, nearly every day · Duration – 1 week or more, or any length if hospitalization is necessary · Symptoms – 3 or more DIGFAST symptoms, 4 if the mood is only irritable · Severity – marked impairment, hospitalization to prevent harm, or psychotic features · Cause – not a substance or medical condition; an episode that outlasts an antidepressant still counts · Mixed features – 3 or more depressive symptoms on most days of the episode
DIGFAST
  • Distractibility – attention too easily drawn to irrelevant stimuli
  • Indiscretion – painful consequences: buying sprees, sexual behaviours, foolish business investments
  • Grandiosity – inflated self-esteem
  • Flight of ideas – thoughts are racing
  • Activity increased – goal-directed, or psychomotor agitation
  • Sleep decreased – feels rested after only 3 hours
  • Talkativeness – pressure to keep talking
Management and treatment
Management ladder: acute manic episode
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineStop antidepressants; lithium, valproate or a second-generation antipsychotic, alone or an antipsychotic plus lithium or valproateNo better after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses, adherence and substances checked
Add on or switchAnother first-line agent, added or switchedNo improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses
Severe or resistantElectroconvulsive therapyTop rung
By situation Severe agitation or psychosis – sedating second-generation antipsychotic, sometimes lorazepam; lithium takes 4 to 10 days · Could become pregnant – avoid valproate: teratogenic · After remission – continuous maintenance for years; lithium lowers suicide risk · Bipolar depression – suicide risk first; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone; no antidepressant alone
Practice
  1. 31-year-old woman with 5 days of: sleeping 4 hours without fatigue faster speech and three new work projects Coworkers notice; she still meets deadlines; only past episode: major depression 2 years ago Elevated mood · no delusions · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar II disorder → 4 or more days of symptoms others notice, without marked impairment or psychosis, plus a past major depressive episode
  2. 27-year-old man brought in after walking into highway traffic, laughing 3 days without sleep savings spent on a sailboat; talks without pause Admitted for his own safety; no delusions; no earlier mood episodes Expansive mood · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → hospitalization satisfies both the duration and the severity criteria, so 3 days is enough
  3. 29-year-old man with 9 days of: 3-hour nights, rapid speech, new business plans is certain he can heal the sick with his touch Still works daily; major depressive episode 1 year ago Expansive mood · toxicology negative · TSH normal → Bipolar I disorder → psychotic features make the episode manic by definition, even while he keeps working
  4. 38-year-old woman with 10 days of irritable mood and: 2-hour nights, racing thoughts, nonstop talk $9,000 spent online; stopped going to work most days: crying, calling herself a terrible mother, thoughts of death Past admission for elevated mood Toxicology negative → Bipolar I disorder, manic episode with mixed features → irritable mood with 4 symptoms and marked impairment (stopped going to work) for 10 days, plus 3 or more depressive symptoms on most days; the past admission for elevated mood already makes it bipolar I
  5. 26-year-old woman on sertraline 4 weeks for depression; for 8 days she has: slept 3 hours a night, talked rapidly quit her job to launch three businesses; says she is destined for fame Euphoric mood · HR 92/min · pregnancy test negative → Stop sertraline and start quetiapine → a full manic episode on an antidepressant: stop the antidepressant and start a first-line agent
  6. 33-year-old man found on his apartment roof at night announcing that he can fly 9 days of almost no sleep gave away his car; talks nonstop Refuses admission, saying he has never felt better Expansive mood · toxicology negative → Inpatient psychiatric admission → hospitalization is needed to prevent harm to himself; mania is an emergency; involuntarily if he refuses and no less restrictive option is safe
  7. 29-year-old man in the emergency department shouting threats and throwing chairs at staff a week without sleep; pressured speech believes he is a secret agent chosen to save the world Similar hospitalization 2 years ago Irritable, expansive mood · toxicology negative → Sedating antipsychotic and lorazepam → severe manic psychosis compromising safety needs rapid behavioral control; lithium takes 4 to 10 days
  8. 41-year-old woman hospitalized with elevated mood, no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech lithium for 16 days, at therapeutic levels for 14 every dose confirmed She is no better Toxicology negative → Add quetiapine to lithium → no improvement after 2 weeks at therapeutic doses with adherence and substance use checked: add on or switch
  9. 24-year-old woman admitted with 10 days of: little sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, reckless spending Elevated mood; no psychotic symptoms; sexually active with inconsistent condom use Pregnancy test negative · TSH normal · toxicology negative → Divalproex → valproate should not be used in a woman of childbearing potential (fetal malformations, impaired intellectual development)
  10. 35-year-old man admitted 4 months ago for a week of euphoria, no sleep, grandiosity and pressured speech euthymic for 3 months on lithium at therapeutic levels asks to stop it now that he feels well BP 120/78 mm Hg → Continue lithium long term → maintenance for all patients with bipolar I disorder, continuous rather than intermittent
  11. 30-year-old woman with 3 weeks of: depressed mood, loss of interest, oversleeping, fatigue, poor concentration Hospitalized 2 years ago for 10 days of euphoria, no sleep, grandiosity and spending; no suicidal thoughts HR 72/min → Sertraline monotherapy → antidepressant monotherapy is not used in bipolar I depression and risks a switch to mania; quetiapine, lithium, lamotrigine or lurasidone is first line
  12. 45-year-old man on lithium for 6 years after two admissions for euphoria, grandiosity and no sleep 2 weeks of depressed mood, insomnia, poor appetite, slowed movements, hopelessness says his family would be better off without him HR 76/min → Assess suicide risk → most suicide deaths in bipolar disorder occur in the depressive phase, so suicide risk comes first
  13. 36-year-old woman with 8 days of: little sleep, restlessness, rapid speech, irritability 4-kg weight loss over 6 weeks; always feels hot Fine tremor of the outstretched hands HR 118/min · toxicology negative → Serum TSH and free thyroxine → weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia and tremor point to hyperthyroidism, a medical cause of these symptoms
How NBME framed it: question 1

24-year-old receptionist at an accounting firm brought in by police cursed at a rental car agent; grew “out of control” when no luxury sports car was available asks for the physician’s number, winks, promises “a good time” and tries a kiss agitated; feels “absolutely fantastic”; loud, rapid speech says she is obviously very rich and the agents will regret delaying her for a television interview Examination normal · urine toxicology negative

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder): hyperactive and impulsive; but ADHD is chronic and in more than one setting, and this is acute.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed grandiose belief; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and she has it.
  • Histrionic personality disorder: the wink and the attempted kiss; but personality disorders are chronic and pervasive.
  • Schizophrenia: a grandiose delusion; but it sits inside a manic episode (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder or histrionic personality disorder. Bipolar disorder: the seductiveness sits inside an acute episode of euphoric, irritable mood with rapid speech, overspending and grandiosity. (NBME gives no duration; it reads the severity and psychosis as mania.)

How NBME framed it: question 2

43-year-old man admitted with superficial frostbite of the toes police found him 5 hours earlier walking barefoot in a snowstorm says he is a god who can melt snow and purify the heart knows the date and place asked to recall red, penny, train, he playfully laughs: “color, coin, conveyance” rapid, incessant speech; paces with arms raised, both index fingers aimed upward Normal vital signs and laboratory results

Most likely diagnosis?

Competing answers
  • Brief psychotic disorder: an acute delusion; but his psychosis is secondary to mania.
  • Delirium, alcohol withdrawal: found wandering in the cold; but vital signs are normal and he is fully oriented.
  • Delusional disorder: a fixed delusion; but delusional disorder excludes mania, and he has it.
  • Malingering: an odd, dangerous act; but nobody walks into frostbite for gain, and he has none.
  • Schizoid personality disorder: an odd man; but he is playful and talkative, not detached.
  • Schizophrenia: the god delusion and the posture; but the delusion is part of mania (NBME cites missing negative symptoms).

Down to two: bipolar disorder, manic, or schizophrenia. Bipolar disorder, manic: the god delusion rides on playful, euphoric affect, rapid incessant speech and pacing; NBME also cites no negative symptoms.

Pairs with Psychosis: does the psychosis occur only during a mood episode? Lithium Therapy: what does maintenance lithium do to the kidney and thyroid? Delirium: are attention and orientation intact? Part I Thyroid Disease in an Adult: is a thyroid cause driving the energy and weight loss?
Transferable rule

Before naming a psychosis or a personality disorder, rule out a drug or thyroid cause, then ask whether the symptoms sit inside a discrete episode of elevated or irritable mood with DIGFAST symptoms; if they do, it is mania, and any antidepressant stops.

Schizophrenia: Long-Term Care

psychosocial care and relapse preventionWhat is driving this relapse or limiting recovery, and which added treatment answers it?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Danger to himself or others can require hospitalization, involuntary if necessary.

Every patient with schizophrenia stays on an antipsychotic, with psychosocial treatment added to it.

Worse while receiving his doses: find what changed in his life before changing the drug. A family conflict just before the worsening calls for family therapy first; a higher dose or dosing frequency is considered after that.

Then match the added treatment to the problem (table below).

Diagnosis
High expressed emotion in the family Shows – criticism, hostility or overinvolvement · Effect – more frequent relapses than in families less expressive of emotion
Management and treatment
Match the added treatment to the problem
ProblemAddStrength
Danger to himself or othersHospitalize; involuntary admission may be necessary
A family conflict just before the worseningFamily therapy first, as an outpatient (not dangerous; antipsychotic continues); then consider a higher dose or dosing frequency
Ongoing contact with familyFamily intervention: psychoeducation, mutual understanding, communication, coping skillsSuggested
Prefers it, or a history of poor or uncertain adherenceLong-acting injectable antipsychotic; continuous use can lower 1-year relapse to about 30% or lowerSuggested
History of poor engagement with services leading to frequent relapse or social disruption (homelessness, legal trouble)Assertive community treatment: a team gives nearly all care where he livesRecommended
Every patientPsychoeducation; cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis (delusional thoughts, hallucinations, negative symptoms); supported employment (competitive job, on-site coach; the answer when he wants a job)Recommended
Goal of better social functioningSocial skills training: helps him get along with othersSuggested
Improved on an antipsychoticContinue it: without it after a first episode, 65 to 80% relapse within 12 monthsRecommended

Recommended and suggested are the American Psychiatric Association’s two strengths (2020); suggested is the weaker. The first row follows the level-of-care rule; the second follows the NBME explanation.

Not the answer here Lithium – sometimes used for mood symptoms in schizoaffective disorder; unhelpful in schizophrenia · Lorazepam – may ease the anxiety; treats neither the psychosis nor its likely cause · Long-acting injectable, already receiving injections – it is for poor or uncertain adherence, and he has his doses · Partial hospital or clozapine – not necessary at this point when a stressor drives the relapse in a patient who is not dangerous
Prevention of relapse Family intervention – may reduce relapses and hospital admissions and encourage taking medication; the trials were of poor quality, so the effects may be overestimated · Protective factors – strong psychosocial support, well-developed coping skills and antipsychotic medication · Other triggers to ask about – substance use, especially cannabis; becoming unemployed or impoverished; leaving home for college; the end of a romantic relationship; joining the Armed Forces
Practice
  1. 30-year-old man, schizophrenia, monthly aripiprazole injection argued with his parents 1 week ago a voice tells him to stab his father has hidden a kitchen knife in his room Refuses admission T 37.0 °C · HR 92/min · guarded, oriented → Involuntary psychiatric hospitalization → a command to harm his father and a hidden knife are danger to others; he refuses, so admission is involuntary; safety comes before family therapy
  2. 27-year-old man, schizophrenia, haloperidol injection every 3 weeks voices rose after arguments with his parents after 8 weekly family sessions: arguments stopped; parents see an illness voices still more frequent than before Threatens no one vital signs normal · cooperative, oriented → Increase the haloperidol dose or frequency → the stressor has been treated; the next step is a higher dose or dosing frequency, and a switch to clozapine is not necessary at this point
  3. 22-year-old man, schizophrenia, risperidone since a first admission 3 months ago lives with his parents family meeting: mother calls him lazy, says he ruins every holiday father interrupts to list his failures vital signs normal · flat affect · no hallucinations now → Frequent criticism and hostility from his parents → high expressed emotion in the family: criticism, hostility or overinvolvement means more frequent relapses; family intervention answers it
  4. 20-year-old man, schizophrenia, risperidone since a first admission 4 months ago no psychotic symptoms for 6 weeks lives with parents who get along well with him they ask how to prevent another episode vital signs normal · euthymic, oriented, no hallucinations → Psychoeducation sessions for him and his parents → he lives with his family; psychoeducational family interventions can reduce the rate of relapse, and psychoeducation is recommended for every patient
  5. 31-year-old man brought by his sister; schizophrenia oral risperidone 4 years; filled 2 of last 5 monthly prescriptions forgets the pills 2 weeks of voices; believes neighbors spy Lives alone; threatened no one afebrile; toxicology negative · guarded, oriented → Restart risperidone as a long-acting injection → poor adherence, not a failed drug: a long-acting injectable is suggested for poor or uncertain adherence
  6. 38-year-old man, schizophrenia, monthly paliperidone injections missed 3 of last 5 injections 6 months: 2 admissions, 4 emergency visits in a shelter since losing his apartment cannot reach the clinic across town afebrile · calm, oriented · a quiet voice at night → Assertive community treatment → poor engagement with services has led to frequent relapse and homelessness; a team brings nearly all care to where he lives
  7. 29-year-old woman, schizophrenia, aripiprazole for 3 years no psychotic symptoms for 1 year sheltered workshop for 2 years wants a regular paid job at a grocery store Lives with her husband vital signs normal · euthymic, linear thought, no hallucinations → Supported employment with an on-site job coach → she wants competitive work; supported employment places her in a competitive job with a coach and is recommended for every patient
  8. 26-year-old man, schizophrenia, risperidone for 2 years no psychotic symptoms for 8 months part-time job with a coach; takes every dose no friends; avoids conversation at work Goal: getting along with people vital signs normal · blunted affect, linear thought → Social skills training → his stated goal is better social functioning, for which social skills training is suggested; he is already engaged, adherent and working
  9. 34-year-old man, schizophrenia, olanzapine for 2 years every dose taken by pill count still hears a critical voice most days; distressed Lives with a supportive brother; no conflict; no thoughts of harm vital signs normal · toxicology negative · oriented; partial insight → Add cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis → adherent, safe and without a family conflict; this therapy works on hallucinations and delusional thoughts and is recommended for every patient
  10. 36-year-old woman, schizophrenia, risperidone for 5 years still hears voices several times a week never a manic or depressive episode Lives with her parents vital signs normal · euthymic, full affect, oriented → Adding lithium carbonate → no mood episodes: lithium is sometimes used for mood symptoms in schizoaffective disorder but is unhelpful in schizophrenia
  11. 32-year-old woman, schizophrenia, olanzapine since her first episode no psychotic symptoms for 18 months feels well; takes every dose asks to stop the medication Lives with her husband vital signs normal · euthymic, linear thought → Continue olanzapine → symptoms improved on an antipsychotic, so it is continued; without ongoing antipsychotic after a first episode, 65 to 80% relapse within 12 months
How NBME framed it: question 1

27-year-old man with schizophrenia; haloperidol injection every 3 weeks cooperative and friendly, but anxious and jittery 1 week of more frequent voices; job performance suffering Works at a sheltered workshop; lives with his parents argued with them about his illness 10 days ago they repeatedly say that without a regular job he will “never amount to anything” they call the voices an excuse not to meet new people and worry he will never marry

Most appropriate intervention?

Competing answers
  • Partial hospital program: his voices are worse; but it is not necessary now: address the conflict as an outpatient first.
