  • Move to a halfway house: it would separate him from critical parents; but it is not appropriate; the explanation notes he has no criminal history.
  • Add lithium carbonate: an add-on drug for a relapse; but it is sometimes used for mood symptoms in schizoaffective disorder and is unhelpful in schizophrenia.
  • Add lorazepam: he looks anxious and jittery; it may ease anxiety but addresses neither the psychosis nor its likely root, the family conflict.
  • Switch haloperidol to clozapine: the voices are breaking through; but a switch is not necessary at this point; the immediate stressor comes first.
  • Increase the haloperidol dose: it targets the voices; but it is a later step, to consider once the family conflict has been addressed.

Down to two: family therapy or adding lithium. Family therapy: family conflict is a risk factor for worsening psychosis, and the argument came just before the voices increased in a patient receiving his injections. Treat that stressor first, as an outpatient; then consider a higher haloperidol dose or frequency.

Pairs with Psychosis covers which psychotic disorder by duration and the antipsychotic ladder up to clozapine; this brief covers what to add around the drug. Here a higher dose or frequency is considered after a treated stressor in a patient already receiving his doses (NBME); the sibling ladder's switch is for no response after an adequate trial. Ask: is the question which disorder, which drug, or what to add?
Transferable rule

Danger to himself or others comes before every other step. When a patient who is receiving his antipsychotic gets worse, ask what changed in his life before changing the drug, and treat that first.

Delirium

tell it from dementia and psychosis, then find the causeDid attention fail over hours to days, and which drug or illness caused it?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Act first on delirium tremens: sweating, tremor, fever and a fast pulse, usually 48 to 72 hours after the last drink. Give an intravenous (IV) benzodiazepine now; it can be fatal.

Delirium: attention and awareness fail over a short time (usually hours to days) and tend to fluctuate, with one more cognitive change and a cause (criteria below). Dementia starts slowly, with attention spared until it is severe.

Review every drug first: anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines are common causes, and meperidine is one of the most deliriogenic opioids.

Stop the drug, treat the cause, reorient the patient and protect sleep.

Antipsychotics are not shown to shorten delirium; give one only for severe agitation that threatens safety.

Benzodiazepines treat alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium; in every other delirium, avoid them.

Diagnosis
Diagnostic criteria A – attention and awareness disturbed · B – develops over a short time (usually hours to a few days), a change from baseline, and tends to fluctuate during the day · C – one more cognitive disturbance: memory, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception · D – not better explained by a preexisting, established or evolving neurocognitive disorder, and not in severely reduced arousal such as coma · E – evidence of a cause: medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, toxin, or several · Against dementia and psychosis – timing chart
Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
Every patientTreat the cause; stop deliriogenic drugs; reorient; glasses and hearing aids; protect sleep; mobilizeBehavior puts the patient or others at risk
Severe agitationLow-dose antipsychotic (haloperidol, quetiapine or risperidone); baseline ECG for the QTc (rate-corrected interval)Top rung: adjust the dose daily; stop as soon as clinically feasible
By situation Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal – IV benzodiazepine, the drug of choice; in alcohol withdrawal, no haloperidol at first · Any other cause – avoid benzodiazepines: more confusion and sedation · Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia – an atypical antipsychotic preferred · Restraint to prevent harm – trained staff; release at least every 2 hours; stop as soon as possible
Prevention and course Beers criteria – avoid meperidine in older adults; with or at high risk of delirium, also avoid anticholinergics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, corticosteroids, histamine-2 receptor antagonists, zolpidem-type hypnotics and opioids, except in listed situations · Course – usually reversible, but deficits often take weeks or months to clear; decline, institutionalization and death stay more likely for up to 2 years
Practice
  1. 72-year-old man 2 days after hip replacement since last night sees children in his room says staff stole his wallet calm mornings, agitated evenings No psychiatric history vital signs normal · fails days of the week backward · oriented to person only → Delirium → acute, fluctuating inattention with visual hallucinations and disorientation after surgery is delirium
  2. 78-year-old woman, 2 years of worsening forgetfulness repeats questions; misses bills lost driving a familiar route no day-to-day fluctuation alert · days backward correct · 0 of 3 words recalled · disoriented to date only · afebrile; vitals, blood count, chemistry, thyroid normal → Major neurocognitive disorder → slow onset over years, memory lost first, attention spared: dementia, not delirium
  3. 84-year-old woman, pneumonia, hospital day 3 drowsy; one-word answers cannot count backward from 20 son: sharp last week; is she depressed? No history of depression oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L/min · other vital signs normal · oriented to person only → Hypoactive delirium → somnolent and inattentive with an acute change from last week: hypoactive delirium, often mistaken for depression
  4. 81-year-old woman in the hospital for cellulitis given diphenhydramine for sleep last evening, her first dose overnight: confused, picks at the air T 37.4 °C · HR 104/min · BP 136/80 · inattentive · oriented to person only → Anticholinergic effect → first-generation antihistamines are highly anticholinergic, a Beers delirium class
  5. 86-year-old woman from a nursing home with 1 day of confusion that comes and goes at baseline oriented; walks with a cane no new medications Neurologic examination nonfocal T 37.8 °C · HR 98/min · BP 124/70 · inattentive · oriented to person only → CBC, metabolic panel and urinalysis → look for the medical cause first; imaging is not routine without focal signs
  6. 77-year-old man taking warfarin fell at home 2 days ago now drowsy and confused, worse at night new weakness of the right arm Blood count and chemistry normal T 36.9 °C · HR 84/min · BP 164/90 · inattentive · oriented to person only → CT of the head without contrast → a focal sign after head trauma on an anticoagulant: look for a subdural hemorrhage
  7. 69-year-old man 2 days after knee replacement restless; says someone hides in the closet fluctuating meperidine every 4 hours for pain Not dangerous to himself or others vital signs normal · creatinine 2.1 mg/dL · inattentive · oriented to person and place → Replace meperidine with another analgesic → stop the deliriogenic drug; poor kidney clearance lets normeperidine accumulate; untreated pain also precipitates delirium, so give another analgesic
  8. 80-year-old man after bowel surgery yesterday pulls his IV, climbs bed rails, hits a nurse despite reorientation, daughter present Infection, pain treated; sedatives stopped; no alcohol T 37.6 °C · HR 102/min · BP 150/88 · inattentive · oriented to person only · QTc normal → Low-dose haloperidol → severe agitation that threatens safety despite nonpharmacologic care: low-dose antipsychotic after a QTc check
  9. 52-year-old man admitted 2 days ago for femur fracture now confused, sweaty and tremulous picks at insects he sees on sheets drank 10 beers a day until admission T 38.3 °C · HR 128/min · BP 168/98 · inattentive · oriented to person only → Intravenous benzodiazepine → alcohol withdrawal delirium, usually 48 to 72 hours after the last drink: benzodiazepines are the drug of choice
  10. 83-year-old woman on day 2 of ceftriaxone for a urinary tract infection restless and calling out at night; calmer by day not harming herself or others No alcohol or sedative use vital signs normal · inattentive · oriented to person and place → Lorazepam at bedtime → benzodiazepines worsen confusion and sedation outside withdrawal; keep treating the infection
  11. 79-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment admitted for an elective hip replacement tomorrow wears glasses and hearing aids Alert and attentive oriented to person, place and time · vital signs normal → Reorientation, mobilization and sleep protection → targeted nonpharmacologic prevention; antipsychotics are not shown to prevent episodes, and zolpidem is on the Beers delirium list
  12. 81-year-old woman, Alzheimer disease for 3 years baseline: knows family, dresses herself 1 day of drowsiness alternating with shouting cannot follow a conversation; dysuria T 38.4 °C · HR 104/min · BP 118/70 · inattentive · oriented to person only · urine: leukocyte esterase, nitrites → Delirium from a urinary tract infection → an acute change from her baseline with fever and dysuria is delirium, and dementia is a leading risk factor; Lewy body fluctuations usually span days to weeks within a chronic dementia and do not explain fever or dysuria
  13. 68-year-old woman admitted 2 days ago for pyelonephritis nightly alprazolam for years; not ordered here since last night: sleepless, tremulous, hallucinating Antibiotic covers the cultured organism T 37.0 °C · BP 166/94 mm Hg · HR 110/min · oriented to name only → Benzodiazepine withdrawal → a long-term benzodiazepine stopped on admission; withdrawal follows within days, depending on half-life, can be life-threatening and is treated by restarting a benzodiazepine; she is afebrile on an antibiotic that covers the organism
How NBME framed it: question 1

57-year-old woman; tibial fracture fixed (open reduction, internal fixation) 4 days ago now agitated; believes the nurses are experimenting on her and keep her from sleeping says the nurses are trying to poison her appears tremulous Hypertension, systemic lupus erythematosus; no psychiatric illness or substance abuse Medications: chloroquine, hydrochlorothiazide, meperidine, propranolol, thyroxine oriented to person and place, not time

Which drug most likely caused her symptoms?

Competing answers
  • Chloroquine: a daily drug she takes for lupus; but the explanation clears all four non-opioid options: none is linked to delirium or on the Beers list.
  • Hydrochlorothiazide: her antihypertensive; but not linked to delirium in the explanation.
  • Propranolol: a beta blocker that also treats tremor, and she is tremulous; but not linked to delirium in the explanation.
  • Thyroxine: tremor and agitation suggest too much thyroid hormone; but it treats hypothyroidism and is not linked to delirium in the explanation.

Down to two: meperidine or thyroxine. Meperidine: new agitation, disorientation to time and paranoid delusions days after surgery is delirium, and she takes an opioid. The explanation names anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines as common causes and calls meperidine and tramadol highly deliriogenic; no psychiatric or substance history argues against a primary psychosis or withdrawal. Thyroxine treats hypothyroidism and is not linked to delirium in the explanation.

Pairs with Psychosis: exclude a medical cause first; acute onset over hours to days suggests one.
Transferable rule

In a new psychosis or confusion in a hospitalized or older patient, test attention and ask when it began: acute, fluctuating inattention points to delirium. Then read the medication list and stop the anticholinergic, opioid or benzodiazepine that started it.

Substance Intoxication and Withdrawal

PCP (phencyclidine) and stimulants · opioids · alcohol withdrawal · benzodiazepines · cannabisWhich drug do the pupils and vital signs point to, and is it intoxication or withdrawal?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Read the pupils, breathing and vital signs:

  • PCP: violent agitation, psychosis, nystagmus in any direction, hypertension; sedate with a benzodiazepine
  • Cocaine or amphetamine: dilated pupils, sweating, tachycardia, hypertension; benzodiazepines usually first-line
  • Opioid: pinpoint pupils, slow breathing, decreased consciousness; naloxone
  • Opioid withdrawal: dilated pupils, yawning, runny nose, goose flesh, diarrhea; distressing, but not life-threatening when stopping is spontaneous

Alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal can kill: treat with a benzodiazepine.

Flumazenil is not routine; in a chronic benzodiazepine user it can provoke seizures.

Diagnosis
Read the toxidrome
DrugPupils and eyesVital signsBehavior and other
PCPNystagmus: horizontal, vertical or rotaryHypertension, tachycardia; fever from agitationViolence, hallucinations, delusions; rhabdomyolysis, seizures
Cocaine or amphetamineDilatedTachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermiaAgitation, sweating; coronary ischemia, seizures
OpioidPinpoint (not always)Respiratory depressionDecreased consciousness
Opioid withdrawalDilated; tearingAutonomic hyperactivityYawning, runny nose, goose flesh, diarrhea, muscle aches
CannabisConjunctival injection; nystagmusRaised heart rateSlowed concentration and psychomotor function; hyperemesis relieved by warm showers
Benzodiazepine withdrawal Timing – 2 to 10 days after stopping, by half-life and duration of use; can last weeks · Risk – potentially life-threatening, like alcohol withdrawal
Management and treatment
Treat by drug
ProblemFirstAvoid or also
PCP agitationBenzodiazepine (lorazepam or diazepam, intravenous or intramuscular)Urinary acidification is no longer recommended
Cocaine or amphetamineBenzodiazepineSome clinicians avoid beta-blockers (unopposed alpha stimulation)
Opioid overdoseNaloxone–
Opioid withdrawalBuprenorphine or methadoneClonidine for autonomic signs
Alcohol withdrawalBenzodiazepine, symptom-triggered by a withdrawal scaleWith intravenous fluids, thiamine before glucose
Benzodiazepine withdrawalA long-acting benzodiazepine with a slow taper (reported outpatient)–
Benzodiazepine overdoseFlumazenil is not routineSeizure risk in chronic users
Practice
  1. 26-year-old man brought by police after fighting strangers in the street shouting that he cannot be hurt; eyes jerk up and down T 38.4 °C · BP 170/104 mm Hg · HR 118/min · pupils midsize · respirations 18/min → Intravenous lorazepam → violent agitation, vertical nystagmus and hypertension suggest PCP; benzodiazepines are the preferred sedative; urinary acidification is no longer recommended, and normal breathing with midsize pupils is not an opioid picture
  2. 29-year-old woman with chest pain an hour after a party restless, talking fast; skin wet with sweat pupils 7 mm, reactive · BP 182/106 mm Hg · HR 132/min · T 38.0 °C · no nystagmus → Cocaine intoxication → agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, dilated pupils and sweating form the sympathomimetic picture, and cocaine can trigger coronary ischemia; heroin gives small pupils and slow breathing
  3. 34-year-old man with chest pain and agitation after using cocaine ECG (electrocardiogram): sinus tachycardia, no ST-segment elevation; troponin pending BP 176/102 mm Hg · HR 128/min · pupils dilated · diaphoretic · oxygen saturation 98% → An intravenous benzodiazepine → benzodiazepines are first-line for cocaine agitation and cardiovascular toxicity; some clinicians avoid beta-blockers because unopposed alpha stimulation can worsen vasoconstriction
  4. 22-year-old man found unresponsive in a restroom a needle and spoon beside him; shallow, snoring respirations; no response to voice respirations 6/min · oxygen saturation 84% · pupils 1 mm · BP 104/68 mm Hg · T 36.4 °C → Naloxone → pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression and decreased consciousness are the opioid triad; naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist; flumazenil is not routine and can provoke seizures
  5. 55-year-old man admitted for pancreatitis; last drink 60 hours ago now disoriented, says rats run across the floor, drenched in sweat T 38.1 °C · HR 126/min · BP 168/98 mm Hg · coarse tremor → Delirium tremens → disorientation, visual hallucinations, fever, sweating and tachycardia at 48 to 72 hours are delirium tremens, which can be fatal; hallucinosis comes earlier, at 12 to 24 hours, and opioid withdrawal after a spontaneous stop is not life-threatening
  6. 48-year-old woman 20 hours after her last drink tremulous, anxious, sweating; symptom scale score moderate needs intravenous fluids for vomiting HR 112/min · BP 152/94 mm Hg · glucose 92 mg/dL → Benzodiazepine; thiamine before glucose → benzodiazepines are first-line for moderate alcohol withdrawal, and with intravenous fluids thiamine goes before glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy; clonidine is only an adjunct to a benzodiazepine
  7. 31-year-old man who stopped heroin 1 day ago yawning, runny nose, goose flesh, cramps and diarrhea wants to stop using pupils 6 mm · HR 104/min · BP 142/88 mm Hg · T 37.2 °C → Buprenorphine → opioid withdrawal after a spontaneous stop is distressing but not life-threatening; buprenorphine or methadone treats it, and clonidine can help; naloxone, an opioid antagonist, treats overdose, not withdrawal
  8. 24-year-old man with 6 months of repeated bouts of vomiting smokes cannabis daily; feels better only under hot showers normal between bouts HR 96/min · abdomen soft · lipase normal · T 36.9 °C → Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome → cyclical vomiting relieved with warm showers in daily cannabis use, which resolves with cessation; the cannabis use is the clue the other labels ignore
Pairs with Delirium: is a withdrawal driving the confusion? Psychosis: did the psychosis start during or soon after use?
Transferable rule

Pupils and breathing first: small pupils with slow breathing is an opioid; big pupils with sweating and a fast pulse is a stimulant or opioid withdrawal; nystagmus with violence is PCP.

Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety

which anxiety, and how to treatAre the attacks unexpected, and have a substance and a medical cause been excluded?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Exclude a substance and a medical cause first:

  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone), glucose and urine toxicology
  • Consider an ECG (electrocardiogram) for palpitations or chest pain

No test makes the diagnosis.

Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks, then 1 month or more of worry about more attacks or a maladaptive change in behavior.

Attacks only in feared social situations, or with one feared object or situation, are social anxiety disorder or specific phobia.

Treat with CBT (cognitive behavioral therapy) with exposure, an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) or venlafaxine XR (extended release), or both. Start the drug low and titrate slowly.

A benzodiazepine is short term only.

Diagnosis
Panic disorder criteria A – recurrent unexpected panic attacks; each an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort, peaking within minutes, with at least 4 of 13 symptoms (STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's) · B – at least 1 month, after at least 1 attack, of persistent worry about more attacks or their consequences, or a significant maladaptive change in behavior related to the attacks · C – not attributable to a substance or another medical condition · D – not better explained by another mental disorder
STUDENTS FEAR the 3 C's
  • S – sweating
  • T – trembling
  • U – unsteadiness, dizziness
  • D – depersonalization, derealization
  • E – excessive heart rate, palpitations
  • N – nausea
  • T – tingling
  • S – shortness of breath
  • FEAR – of dying, of losing control, of going crazy
  • C – chest pain, chills, choking
Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineCBT with exposure, an SSRI or venlafaxine XR, or bothDrug ineffective after at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range
Second lineClomipramine, imipramine or mirtazapine; a benzodiazepine (short term)Top rung
By situation Starting the SSRI – half the usual depression starting dose; increase about every 7 days (early activation makes patients stop it) · Severe symptoms or co-existing conditions before the SSRI works – a benzodiazepine such as alprazolam until the antidepressant takes effect; short term only · History of substance use – avoid benzodiazepines; gabapentin and mirtazapine are recommended · Not recommended – propranolol; buspirone (helps generalized anxiety; does not appear effective for panic disorder) · Improved – continue the drug for 12 months, then taper
Follow-up Response – with some meaningful improvement at 4 to 6 weeks, allow several months before judging the full effect · Watch for – depression and disability, alcohol and substance use, suicidal ideation, all more common in panic disorder; agoraphobia often co-occurs
Practice
  1. 32-year-old woman, 8 months of episodes racing heart, sweating, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; some at rest 7 months avoiding buses, crowds, lines: no escape or help oriented, anxious about the next · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, toxicology normal → Panic disorder and agoraphobia → unexpected attacks plus fear of 2 or more situations where escape is hard; when criteria for both are met, both are assigned
  2. 41-year-old man, 9 months of worry, more days than not about job, finances, children's safety; cannot switch it off restless, tired, tense; sleeps poorly No sudden episodes of intense fear alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH normal → Generalized anxiety disorder → excessive worry about a number of events, hard to control, more days than not for at least 6 months, with at least 3 of 6 symptoms; the worry is not about attacks
  3. 23-year-old man, 10 months of pounding heart, sweating, shaking only when presenting in class or eating in the cafeteria fears others will see him blush, think him foolish now skips those classes alert, oriented, euthymic · afebrile; vitals, toxicology normal → Social anxiety disorder → the attacks come only in social situations, and the fear is of negative evaluation, not of the attacks
  4. 27-year-old woman, 1 year of intense fear, sweating, racing heart begins within seconds whenever she must ride an elevator climbs 12 flights of stairs to avoid it No episodes at other times alert, oriented, euthymic · vital signs normal → Specific phobia → one situation almost always provokes immediate fear and is avoided; one situation is not the 2 of 5 that agoraphobia needs
  5. 36-year-old woman, 14 months of fear that she has heart disease checks her pulse many times a day has seen three cardiologists No sudden fear episodes; occasional mild chest tightness alert, oriented, anxious, not delusional · afebrile; vitals, ECG, echocardiogram normal → Illness anxiety disorder → persistent preoccupation with a serious illness for at least 6 months with mild or no symptoms; health anxiety in panic disorder is acute and episodic
  6. 29-year-old woman, 3 months of feeling anxious and shaky, with palpitations lost 5 kg (11 lb) without trying feels hot when others are comfortable alert, oriented, restless · HR 112/min · BP 138/70 mm Hg · warm, moist skin · fine hand tremor → Serum TSH → weight loss, heat intolerance and resting tachycardia point to hyperthyroidism; a low TSH screens, and a high free thyroxine confirms
  7. 38-year-old man, 4 months of spells pounding headache, drenching sweats, racing heart each lasts 15 to 30 minutes Alert, oriented, euthymic BP 196/112 mm Hg in a spell, 150/94 between · HR 104/min · TSH 2.1 μU/mL · glucose 96 mg/dL → Plasma free metanephrines → episodes of severe hypertension with headache, sweating and a racing heart point to pheochromocytoma
  8. 22-year-old man, 2 months of sudden episodes racing heart, lightheadedness and fear they start and stop abruptly Alert, oriented, euthymic HR 76/min and BP 122/78 mm Hg between episodes · TSH, glucose and urine toxicology normal → Electrocardiogram → palpitations call for an ECG to look for preexcitation before the episodes are called panic attacks
  9. 26-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, fear of dying peak in minutes; 3 months worrying about the next wants a diagnostic test oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, glucose, ECG, toxicology normal → Sertraline at a low starting dose and CBT → criteria are met and the mimics are excluded; no test makes the diagnosis, and a lactate challenge has no standardized criteria
  10. 34-year-old man, 6 months of recurrent unexpected episodes intense fear with sweating, palpitations, dizziness, trembling stopped driving 5 months ago, fearing another asks for something to stop them alert, oriented, anxious · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → Escitalopram, started low and titrated → an SSRI is first line; a benzodiazepine alone does not improve longer-term outcomes, and propranolol is not recommended
  11. 28-year-old woman, 5 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, chest pain, fear of losing control months of worry started sertraline 50 mg daily 5 days ago now jittery, more anxious; wants to stop oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 88/min → Lower the dose, then raise it slowly → initial activation can be troubling; start at half the usual depression dose and increase about every 7 days
  12. 31-year-old woman, 4 months of unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying months of worry sertraline 25 mg daily for 2 weeks: little change No adverse effects alert, oriented · no suicidal ideation · HR 78/min · BP 116/74 mm Hg → Raise the sertraline dose → a drug is not ineffective until it has been given for at least 4 weeks at the high end of the dose range
  13. 25-year-old man, 2 months of unexpected fear episodes palpitations, choking, sweating, chest pain; many a day housebound 6 weeks; cannot work started sertraline yesterday No substance use history oriented · no suicidal ideation · afebrile; vitals, TSH, ECG, toxicology normal → A benzodiazepine for the first weeks → with severe symptoms, a benzodiazepine such as alprazolam bridges until the antidepressant takes effect; short term only
  14. 40-year-old man with alcohol use disorder, abstinent 2 months 5 months of recurrent unexpected episodes palpitations, sweating, trembling, fear of dying avoids leaving home alone alert, oriented, euthymic · vitals, TSH, ECG normal · urine toxicology negative → Alprazolam → benzodiazepines are avoided with a history of substance use; gabapentin and mirtazapine are recommended
  15. 33-year-old woman treated with sertraline and CBT for recurrent unexpected episodes of fear no episodes for 3 months asks to stop the drug alert, euthymic · HR 70/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg → Continue it for 12 months, then taper → once symptoms improve, continue the drug for 12 months before tapering to limit relapse
How NBME framed it: question 1

25-year-old woman, 2 months of sudden anxiety episodes, several times a week chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations fears losing control and going crazy says they come out of the blue Not depressed; sleep and appetite unchanged 170 cm, 60 kg, BMI (body mass index) 21 kg/m² · pulse 88/min · BP 130/86 mm Hg · physical and mental status examinations normal · laboratory studies normal · urine toxicology negative

Which abnormality is she most likely to have?

Competing answers
  • Abnormal eye tracking: “going crazy” suggests psychosis; but abnormal eye tracking goes with schizophrenia, and her mental status examination is normal.
  • Delayed rapid eye movement (REM) sleep on polysomnography: the stem mentions sleep; but it goes with sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder and some drugs and alcohol, not panic disorder.
  • Enlarged third and lateral ventricles on head CT (computed tomography): a structural brain cause; but aqueductal stenosis, the most common cause of congenital hydrocephalus, is atypical in a healthy young adult and does not explain the attacks.
  • Cortisol not suppressed by 1 mg of dexamethasone: a stress-axis test; but nonsuppression points to Cushing syndrome, not panic disorder.

Down to two: increased sensitivity to lactate infusions or cortisol nonsuppression. Lactate: recurrent attacks that come out of the blue, with a normal workup, point to panic disorder (NBME's key), and patients with it have attacks in response to lactate at an increased rate (the explanation ties this to catastrophic appraisal of body states). Its diagnostic utility is unclear: there are no standardized criteria. The stem never states worry or avoidance, and the lead-in asks for a finding, not the diagnosis.

Pairs with Hypertension in an Adult: is the blood pressure severely high during the episodes? Thyroid Disease in an Adult: constant symptoms with weight loss? SSRI (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor) Adverse Effects: did the restlessness start with the drug? Bipolar Disorder: episodes of elevated mood?
Transferable rule

Exclude a substance and a medical cause first. Then name what the fear is about: the attacks themselves, negative evaluation, one object or situation, difficult escape, a number of events, or a serious illness.

Major Depressive Disorder

criteria · adequate trial · switch, augment or electroconvulsive therapy · continuation and maintenance · drug choice by comorbidityHas the drug had a fair trial, and how long should it continue?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Five or more symptoms for 2 weeks, one of them depressed mood or loss of interest, with impairment, no substance or medical cause and never a manic or hypomanic episode.

Judge a drug only after an adequate trial:

  • 2 weeks: too early; keep the dose
  • 4 weeks at a therapeutic dose (start of an adequate trial): under 20% improvement, raise the dose or switch
  • Adequate trial failed (at least 4 to 6 weeks at a therapeutic dose): switch to another first-line antidepressant

After remission:

  • Continuation: about 6 more months at the same dose (guidelines: 4 to 9 months), then taper gradually if still in remission and not at high relapse risk
  • Maintenance: 2 years or more with higher relapse risk; often indefinite after 3 or more episodes

Bupropion is contraindicated with a seizure disorder or a current or prior diagnosis of bulimia or anorexia nervosa.

Diagnosis
Defining criteria Symptoms – 5 or more of 9, most of the day, nearly every day, for at least 2 weeks; at least one is depressed mood or loss of interest · The 9 – depressed mood, loss of interest, appetite or weight change, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor change, fatigue, worthlessness or guilt, poor concentration, thoughts of death or suicide · Impairment – clinically significant distress or impairment · Exclusions – not due to a substance, a medication or a medical condition (eg, hypothyroidism); never a manic or hypomanic episode
Management and treatment
Antidepressant therapy when the first drug fails
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineAn SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor), SNRI (serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor), bupropion or mirtazapine; similarly effectiveUnder 20% better by 4 weeks at a therapeutic dose, or no response after an adequate trial
NextRaise the dose, or switch to a different SSRI or another first-line class (eg, venlafaxine)Severe and still incomplete after 6 to 12 weeks
AddA second-generation antipsychotic (akathisia, sedation, weight gain), or psychotherapy; lithium as an add-on, not as monotherapySeveral first-line trials fail
LastA TCA (tricyclic antidepressant) or MAOI (monoamine oxidase inhibitor): effective, but toxicity limits use; after fluoxetine, wait at least 5 weeks before an MAOITop rung
By situation ECT (electroconvulsive therapy) – severe depression with catatonia, psychosis, severe suicidality, a need for a rapid response, or poor response to previous treatment · Eating disorder or seizures – no bupropion (also contraindicated during abrupt stopping of alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates or antiepileptic drugs); fluoxetine can reduce binge eating and vomiting · Weight gain or sexual dysfunction a concern – bupropion, if not contraindicated · Mirtazapine – stimulates appetite and causes drowsiness
Practice
  1. 34-year-old man, low mood 3 weeks since losing his job most days: sleeps poorly, lost interest, tired, can't focus, feels worthless stopped looking for work Never had elevated mood no drug or alcohol use · T 36.8 °C · TSH normal → Major depressive disorder → five symptoms including depressed mood and loss of interest, most days for 2 weeks or more, with impairment; no hypomania ever, so not bipolar II; a normal TSH makes a thyroid cause unlikely
  2. 26-year-old man started citalopram at a therapeutic dose 2 weeks ago a final exam is this week; mood dipped again the past 2 days Headache in week 1 resolved; no suicidal ideation HR 72/min · BP 120/74 mm Hg → Keep the current citalopram dose → 2 weeks is not an adequate trial (at least 4 to 6 weeks at a therapeutic dose); a few low days, partly from stress, do not mean failure, and a higher dose only adds adverse effects
  3. 29-year-old woman with depression on maximum-dose fluoxetine for 8 weeks minimal change in mood, energy or concentration; takes it daily Prior anorexia nervosa, now at a healthy weight; no suicidal ideation BP 112/70 mm Hg · potassium 4.1 mEq/L → Switch to venlafaxine → 8 weeks at the maximum dose is already an adequate trial, so switch to another first-line antidepressant; bupropion is contraindicated with a current or prior diagnosis of bulimia or anorexia nervosa
  4. 27-year-old woman with 6 weeks of sadness, hypersomnia and worthlessness eats large amounts in secret, then feels she must undo it hates her body BP 102/66 mm Hg · potassium 3.0 mEq/L · chloride 90 mEq/L · bicarbonate 33 mEq/L → Bupropion → low potassium and chloride point to self-induced vomiting; bupropion is contraindicated with bulimia or anorexia nervosa (seizure risk); fluoxetine can also reduce binge eating and vomiting; mirtazapine is a poor fit (appetite, drowsiness) but not contraindicated
  5. 61-year-old woman with her first depressive episode on paroxetine 20 mg; at 10 weeks every symptom has resolved tolerating it; would like to cut down or stop soon euthymic, full affect · no suicidal ideation · BP 128/80 mm Hg → Continue 20 mg for about 6 more months → continuation at the dose that achieved remission lowers relapse (6 more months: 41% to 12%); afterward, if still in remission, taper gradually
  6. 52-year-old woman in remission 6 months on escitalopram this was her third major depressive episode; each followed stopping treatment wants to know how long to stay on it euthymic · no suicidal ideation · BP 124/78 mm Hg → Continue escitalopram indefinitely → three or more episodes: indefinite maintenance is often recommended; two or more episodes already carry a high risk of relapse
  7. 67-year-old man with severe major depression for 6 weeks barely speaks, eats almost nothing, believes his organs are rotting lost 6 kg; sertraline started 3 weeks ago T 37.0 °C · HR 98/min · dry mucous membranes → Electroconvulsive therapy → psychotic depression with poor intake and weight loss needs a rapid response; both are indications for electroconvulsive therapy
Pairs with Bipolar Disorder: was there ever a manic or hypomanic episode? SSRI Adverse Effects: is the new complaint an adverse effect or discontinuation, not relapse?
Transferable rule

Check the clock before changing the plan: no switch before an adequate trial, and no stop before continuation is complete.

SSRI Adverse Effects

name the effect, then take the next stepOn the drug or after stopping it, and which phase of sexual response is affected?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Sexual dysfunction affects more than half of patients on an SSRI and can reach desire, arousal or orgasm.

Persistent, distressing low desire: lowering the dose is the common first step, especially with the depression in sustained remission. If that fails:

  • one episode in sustained remission: consider tapering off
  • staying on an antidepressant: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine)

Another SSRI carries a similar risk. Sildenafil can help arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire has been shown.

FINISH symptoms typically within 3 days of a stop or a taper are discontinuation syndrome, not relapse: once other serious causes are ruled out, reassure.

Diagnosis
Which effect Sexual dysfunction – decreased desire, arousal problems or anorgasmia during SSRI therapy; increased serotonin likely explains it · Discontinuation syndrome – FINISH symptoms, typically within 3 days of stopping or starting a taper (FINISH) · Serotonin syndrome – mental status changes, autonomic hyperactivity and neuromuscular changes, rapid onset after a medication change
FINISH
  • F – flu-like symptoms: fatigue, lethargy, malaise, muscle aches, headaches, diarrhea
  • I – insomnia
  • N – nausea
  • I – imbalance: gait instability, dizziness or lightheadedness, vertigo
  • S – sensory disturbances: paresthesia, "electric shock" sensations, visual disturbance
  • H – hyperarousal: anxiety, agitation
Management and treatment
Persistent, distressing low desire on an SSRI
TierInterventionEscalate when
Common first stepLower the SSRI doseStill persistent and distressing at the lower dose
ThenOne episode, sustained remission: consider tapering off. Staying on an antidepressant: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine)Top rung
By situation Bulimia or seizure-prone – not bupropion (contraindicated); mirtazapine has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs · Arousal problems or anorgasmia – sildenafil can help; not shown to help desire · Unlikely to help or not recommended – another SSRI (similar risk; unlikely to resolve it); propranolol (unlikely to help sexual dysfunction; not helpful for depression); weekend drug holidays (not commonly used, and they interfere with the antidepressant effect)
Discontinuation syndrome
TierInterventionEscalate when
Other serious causes ruled outReassure: reversible, not serious, runs its course in 1 to 2 weeks; then consider restarting with a slow taper, or support if the patient prefers not to restartSymptoms arose during a taper
During a taperConsider restarting the original dose, then taper more slowlySlow tapering poorly tolerated
Slow taper failsConsider substituting fluoxetine for the short half-life drugTop rung
Prevention Before stopping – forewarn the patient; a supervised taper over 6 to 8 weeks may be required (another source: about 25% of the dose each week) · Choice of drug – fluoxetine, with its long half-life, is less likely than paroxetine to cause discontinuation symptoms · How long – after a first mild or moderate episode, 6 months of treatment, then a taper over 2 months
Practice
  1. 34-year-old man, one depressive episode in remission 7 months on sertraline 150 mg daily low sexual desire since starting it it is straining his marriage no suicidal ideation · euthymic, full affect, linear thought · HR 72/min, BP 124/76 mm Hg → Lower the sertraline dose → persistent, distressing low desire in sustained remission: lowering the dose is the common first step; drug holidays are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect
  2. 31-year-old man, one moderate depressive episode in remission 10 months on sertraline dose cut from 150 to 100 mg 2 months ago for low desire still distressed; would rather stop euthymic, full affect, linear thought · no suicidal ideation · HR 70/min → Taper sertraline off gradually → a lower dose failed, and one episode in sustained remission allows stopping; an SSRI is tapered, not stopped abruptly
  3. 27-year-old woman, one depressive episode, in remission 14 months escitalopram lowered 8 weeks ago for low desire desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant No seizures, eating disorder or heart disease euthymic, reactive affect · HR 68/min → Add bupropion to escitalopram → a lower dose failed and she prefers to stay on medication: reasonable options are adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine); sildenafil has not been shown to affect desire
  4. 45-year-old man, one depressive episode, in remission 9 months sertraline cut 150 to 100 mg 3 months ago wants to stay on it desire intact; erection trouble since starting it; bothers him euthymic · HR 72/min, BP 126/80 mm Hg → Add sildenafil to sertraline → desire is intact and the problem is arousal, which sildenafil can help; propranolol is unlikely to help, and another SSRI carries a similar risk
  5. 24-year-old woman with bulimia nervosa one depressive episode, in remission on fluoxetine after a dose reduction, desire still low and distressing wants to stay on an antidepressant BMI (body mass index) 21 kg/m² · HR 66/min · potassium 3.9 mEq/L · euthymic → Switching to bupropion → bupropion has no sexual adverse effects but is contraindicated in bulimia; mirtazapine has fewer sexual adverse effects than SSRIs
  6. 38-year-old woman ran out of paroxetine 4 days ago after 2 years for remitted depression 2 days of nausea, dizziness, unsteady gait, poor sleep brief electric-shock sensations in arms T 37.0 °C · reflexes normal, no clonus · anxious, irritable; mood fine → SSRI discontinuation syndrome → FINISH symptoms, typically within 3 days of stopping a short half-life drug; relapse comes 2 to 3 weeks or more later, and normal reflexes without clonus argue against serotonin syndrome
  7. 52-year-old man stopped sertraline on his own 3 days ago after 1 year; depression in remission mild nausea, lightheadedness, trouble sleeping wants to stay off T 36.9 °C · reflexes normal, no tremor or clonus · euthymic, mildly irritable · no suicidal ideation → Reassure; it resolves in 1 to 2 weeks → with other serious causes unlikely (afebrile, normal reflexes, no clonus), discontinuation symptoms after an abrupt stop: begin with reassurance that they are reversible and run their course in 1 to 2 weeks; restarting with a slow taper is considered, or support if he prefers not to restart
  8. 35-year-old woman, depression in remission 8 months 2 weeks into a paroxetine taper, 40 mg to 20 mg daily 3 days of dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations irritability keeps her from work T 37.1 °C · no clonus · anxious; mood not depressed → Resume 40 mg and taper more slowly → symptoms during a taper: consider restarting the original dose and tapering more slowly; fluoxetine is for a slow taper that is poorly tolerated
  9. 42-year-old man, depression in remission 1 year two tries to come off paroxetine, each tapered over 8 weeks both times: dizziness, nausea, electric-shock sensations relieved by resuming the full dose euthymic · no suicidal ideation · T 36.8 °C → Switch to fluoxetine, then stop → slow tapering is poorly tolerated: consider substituting fluoxetine, whose longer half-life makes discontinuation symptoms less likely
  10. 58-year-old woman taking sertraline got tramadol for back pain this morning 5 hours later: agitated, sweating, nauseated T 38.4 °C · HR 122/min · BP 162/94 mm Hg · dilated pupils · tremor, hyperreflexia, ankle clonus · hyperactive bowel sounds · oriented to person only → Serotonin syndrome → tramadol added to an SSRI, then clonus, hyperreflexia and mydriasis within hours; neuroleptic malignant syndrome builds over days with lead-pipe rigidity and slow reflexes
How NBME framed it: question 1

23-year-old woman at a follow-up visit first major depressive episode 1 year ago; fluoxetine 40 mg daily since depression well controlled: enjoys social activities more, more productive at work Reports no suicidal ideation new relationship; concerned about her limited sexual desire vital signs normal · smiling, euthymic affect

Most appropriate next step?

Competing answers
  • Initiate propranolol: an add-on that leaves the antidepressant alone; but it is unlikely to help sexual dysfunction and is not helpful for major depressive disorder.
  • Initiate sildenafil: a treatment for sexual dysfunction; but it helps arousal problems and anorgasmia; no effect on desire, her complaint, has been shown.
  • Recommend weekend drug holidays: they seem to spare the relationship; but they are not commonly used and interfere with the antidepressant effect.
  • Replace fluoxetine with citalopram: a switch sounds like progress; but citalopram carries a similar risk of sexual dysfunction.

Down to two: lowering the dose or switching to citalopram. Lower the dose: her low desire is persistent and distressing, and the explanation says initial management commonly involves decreasing the SSRI dose, especially with sustained remission. If that fails: one episode in sustained remission, so stopping can be considered; or, if she prefers to stay on medication, adding bupropion or switching to a lower-risk antidepressant (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine).

Pairs with Bipolar Disorder: did the mood rise, not fall, after the SSRI started? (antidepressant-induced mania is rare) Panic Disorder and Other Anxiety: is the anxiety new within 3 days of a stop, a hyperarousal symptom of discontinuation?
Transferable rule

Name the effect and its timing before changing the drug. During therapy, with persistent, distressing low desire, lowering the dose is the common first step; typically within 3 days of a stop or a taper, think discontinuation, not relapse.

Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

acute dystonia · akathisia · parkinsonism · tardive dyskinesia · neuroleptic malignant syndrome · metabolic and prolactin effectsWhich effect, timed from the start or the last dose increase, and what is the next step?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Time the effect from the start or the last dose increase:

  • Acute dystonia: hours to days; also after antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine; give an anticholinergic
  • Akathisia: within weeks; lower the dose, switch, or add propranolol
  • Parkinsonism: within weeks; lower the dose; amantadine or an anticholinergic
  • Tardive dyskinesia: months to years; stop anticholinergics; a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor if moderate to severe
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: days to weeks, evolving over 1 to 3 days, including with second-generation drugs; stop the drug, cool, give fluids

Serotonin syndrome comes within hours of a serotonergic change, such as an SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor), with clonus and hyperreflexia; neuroleptic malignant syndrome comes over days to weeks with rigidity.

Clozapine and olanzapine carry the greatest metabolic risk; screen at least yearly.

Diagnosis
Which effect Acute dystonia – sustained spasm of the neck, jaw, eyes or tongue · Akathisia – internal restlessness and a compelling urge to move · Parkinsonism – tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, masked face, shuffling gait; reversible · Tardive dyskinesia – repetitive lip smacking, tongue and jaw movements, cheek puffing · Neuroleptic malignant syndrome – mental status change, fever, rigidity, autonomic instability; the creatine kinase (CK) can be very high
Management and treatment
Next step by effect
EffectFirst stepThen or also
Acute dystoniaA parenteral anticholinergic: benztropine or diphenhydramine; relief usually within 10 to 30 minutesLaryngeal spasm: assess the airway; intravenous anticholinergic
AkathisiaLower or stop the dose, or switch (eg, quetiapine, olanzapine)Propranolol
ParkinsonismLower or stop the doseAmantadine or an anticholinergic
Tardive dyskinesiaStop anticholinergics; they may worsen itModerate to severe: valbenazine or deutetrabenazine
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeStop the antipsychotic; aggressive cooling; correct volume and electrolytesBromocriptine or dantrolene are options
By drug Metabolic – greatest with clozapine and olanzapine; lowest with aripiprazole, risperidone, ziprasidone and high-potency first-generation drugs; at least yearly screening · Prolactin – any first-generation drug or risperidone: galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, bone loss · Clozapine – severe neutropenia, myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, seizures, profound hypotension; check the ANC (absolute neutrophil count) before and during treatment
Practice
  1. 23-year-old man given intramuscular haloperidol for agitation 8 hours ago now his neck is twisted to the right and his eyes are fixed upward Alert; speaks clearly; no stridor T 37.1 °C · HR 104/min · BP 138/84 mm Hg → Benztropine → acute dystonia within hours of a dopamine blocker: an anticholinergic such as benztropine gives rapid relief; dantrolene belongs to neuroleptic malignant syndrome and propranolol to akathisia
  2. 19-year-old woman in the emergency department for vomiting 1 hour after intravenous metoclopramide: jaw clenched, tongue pushing out, words slurred Fully alert; no lip or tongue swelling; no wheeze BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 96/min → Diphenhydramine → an antiemetic dopamine blocker caused acute dystonia: a parenteral anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine usually works within 30 minutes; dantrolene belongs to neuroleptic malignant syndrome and propranolol to akathisia
  3. 34-year-old man started haloperidol 2 weeks ago for schizophrenia cannot sit through visits; paces, shifts his legs, says he feels driven to move voices quieter; dose cannot be lowered HR 82/min · no rigidity or tremor → Add propranolol → inner restlessness with a compelling urge to move within 4 weeks of starting is akathisia; propranolol treats it when the dose cannot be lowered; more haloperidol would worsen it, and valbenazine is for tardive dyskinesia
  4. 46-year-old woman whose risperidone dose was doubled 3 weeks ago both hands shake at rest; slower walking with short steps; blank face No lip smacking or tongue movements T 36.9 °C · cogwheel rigidity both arms · alert, oriented → Drug-induced parkinsonism → tremor, rigidity, slow shuffling gait and masked face within weeks of a dose increase; tardive dyskinesia comes months to years later with orofacial movements, and there is no fever or altered mental status
  5. 58-year-old man with schizophrenia on haloperidol for 9 years constant lip smacking and tongue darting that embarrass him and disrupt eating takes benztropine as well BP 128/80 mm Hg · no tremor or rigidity → Stop benztropine and start valbenazine → orofacial movements after years of a dopamine blocker are tardive dyskinesia; anticholinergics may worsen it and should be stopped, and moderate to severe disease is treated with a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor
  6. 52-year-old man started on risperidone for schizophrenia 6 days ago now disoriented, diaphoretic and rigid in all limbs T 40.3 °C · BP 172/100 mm Hg · HR 118/min · reflexes normal, no clonus · creatine kinase 24,000 U/L → Neuroleptic malignant syndrome → fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability and a high CK developing over days, even from a second-generation drug; serotonin syndrome comes within hours with clonus and hyperreflexia; acute dystonia is a localized spasm of the neck, jaw, eyes or tongue
  7. 29-year-old woman started on haloperidol in hospital 4 days ago rigid, confused, febrile; creatine kinase rising No new serotonergic drugs T 39.8 °C · HR 120/min · BP 164/98 mm Hg · urine dark → Stop haloperidol; cool; give fluids → neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stopping the drug is paramount, then aggressive cooling and fluids; another antipsychotic can cause it too, an anticholinergic does not treat it, and bromocriptine or dantrolene are options beyond supportive care
  8. 32-year-old man with schizophrenia stable on olanzapine for 1 year gained 14 kg; new fasting glucose 128 mg/dL Wants to stay on an antipsychotic BMI (body mass index) 33 kg/m² · BP 136/86 mm Hg · triglycerides 260 mg/dL → Aripiprazole → metabolic disturbances are greatest with clozapine and olanzapine, intermediate with quetiapine and lowest with aripiprazole; screen at least yearly
  9. 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia on risperidone for 8 months no periods for 4 months; milky nipple discharge Urine pregnancy test negative; no headaches TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) normal · BP 110/70 mm Hg · visual fields full → Dopamine blockade raising prolactin → risperidone, like any first-generation drug, commonly raises prolactin, causing amenorrhea and galactorrhea; a normal TSH argues against hypothyroidism, and risperidone commonly raises prolactin, so the drug is the likely cause
Pairs with SSRI Adverse Effects: hours after a serotonergic change, with clonus? Schizophrenia: Long-Term Care: monitoring the maintenance drug, with yearly metabolic screening?
Transferable rule

Time the movement from the start or the last dose increase before naming it: hours to days is dystonia, weeks is akathisia or parkinsonism, months to years is tardive dyskinesia.

Lithium Therapy

which complication, and what to doIs this toxicity, diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism or an expected effect?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Act first: in lithium toxicity, decreased consciousness, seizures or a life-threatening dysrhythmia calls for hemodialysis at any level.

New symptoms on lithium: read three pairs together:

  • serum sodium with urine osmolality
  • lithium level with the neurologic examination
  • TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) with free thyroxine

High sodium with dilute urine after years of lithium is nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: replete volume, and stop lithium if possible.

Coarse tremor, slurred speech, ataxia or confusion with a raised level is toxicity (commonly above 1.5 mmol/L; lower in chronic toxicity): stop lithium and give IV isotonic fluids.

High TSH with low free thyroxine is hypothyroidism: add levothyroxine and continue lithium. A mildly high TSH with normal free thyroxine and no symptoms is the routine thyroid change.

Diagnosis
Which complication Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus – little or no response to desmopressin · Adverse effects – LMNOP (mnemonic below)
LMNOP
  • L – lithium
  • M – movement: tremor
  • N – nephrology: kidney injury and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (thirst and urination)
  • O – hypothyroidism
  • P – pregnancy: Ebstein's anomaly
Which one: the stem and the decider
ComplicationThe stem showsDecides it
Chronic lithium toxicityLong-term user; new thiazide, NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug), ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor or ARB (angiotensin receptor blocker); dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, low-sodium diet or kidney injuryLong-term use; neurologic findings lead: coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion; raised level
Acute lithium toxicityRecent large ingestionLarge ingestion; nausea, vomiting, diarrhea often come first
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidusYears of lithium; thirst, polyuria; confusion with dehydrationHigh sodium, dilute urine
HypothyroidismTiredness, cold intolerance, mental fogginess; may have a goiter; middle-aged women at highest riskHigh TSH, low free thyroxine
Routine side effectsFine tremor, polyuria, mildly high TSHSodium, mental status, free thyroxine normal
Management and treatment
Management ladder: lithium toxicity
TierInterventionEscalate when
First lineStop lithium; IV isotonic fluids; serial levelsDecreased consciousness, seizures or life-threatening dysrhythmia; level over 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidneys
EscalationHemodialysisTop rung
By situation Mild toxicity – stopping lithium may be sufficient · Ingestion – activated charcoal does not bind lithium (it may be given for a suspected coingestion); gastric lavage or whole-bowel irrigation may be considered, particularly for sustained-release tablets · Diabetes insipidus, drowsy and volume-depleted – replete volume and check the level; a thiazide can treat the disorder but raises the lithium level · Hypothyroidism – add levothyroxine; thyroid abnormalities are not a reason to stop lithium · Routine thyroid change – continue lithium; recheck TSH in 4 to 6 months · Return – infection, heavy sweating or diarrhea (a dose reduction should be considered), or any new interacting drug
Lithium monitoring
WhenCheck
Before startingCreatinine, BUN (blood urea nitrogen), TSH, calcium with albumin; weight, height, blood pressure
Cardiac risk or age 50 or olderAdd an ECG before starting
After startingLevel every 1 to 2 weeks until two in a row are in range at one dose
Every 6 to 12 monthsLevel, electrolytes, creatinine, BUN, TSH
New ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide or NSAIDLevel and creatinine more often
YearlyCalcium with albumin; PTH (parathyroid hormone) if calcium is high

Level target: a trough about 12 hours after the last dose; 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L for maintenance (some sources use 0.8 as the lower bound).

Practice
  1. 44-year-old man with bipolar disorder, stable lithium 6 years 3 days of vomiting and diarrhea drowsy; oriented to person only coarse tremor, slurred speech, unsteady gait HR 56/min · sodium 138 mEq/L · creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (baseline 0.9) · urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg → Chronic lithium toxicity → dehydration raised the level in a long-term user, and neurologic findings lead; a serum lithium level confirms
  2. 22-year-old woman took 30 immediate-release lithium tablets 2 hours ago started lithium 3 weeks ago vomited 3 times; diarrhea alert, oriented; no tremor HR 96/min · BP 116/70 mm Hg · lithium 3.2 mmol/L · creatinine 0.8 mg/dL → IV isotonic fluids and serial lithium levels → alert, kidneys working and level under 4.0 mmol/L: no dialysis criterion is met; lithium does not bind charcoal
  3. 67-year-old man on lithium for 15 years a week of poor intake; took extra tablets yesterday drowsy, confused; responds only to a loud voice coarse tremor HR 54/min · BP 100/62 mm Hg · lithium 4.4 mmol/L · creatinine 2.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.1) → Urgent hemodialysis → decreased consciousness, or a level over 4.0 mmol/L with impaired kidneys: either one indicates dialysis; lithium does not bind charcoal
  4. 62-year-old woman with bipolar disorder, stable lithium dose for 9 years hydrochlorothiazide started for hypertension 3 weeks ago now coarse tremor, slurred speech, confusion HR 60/min · lithium 2.4 mmol/L · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL → Increased renal reabsorption of lithium → a thiazide increases renal reabsorption of lithium, which is handled like sodium; the kidney is its only real exit
  5. 54-year-old man on lithium for 10 years for bipolar disorder knee osteoarthritis pain; asks what to take for it euthymic, alert and oriented BP 128/80 mm Hg · creatinine 1.0 mg/dL · lithium trough 0.8 mmol/L → Oral naproxen, taken daily → NSAIDs raise the lithium level
  6. 46-year-old man on lithium for 14 years 6 months of thirst passing large volumes of urine day and night euthymic, alert and oriented BP 124/78 mm Hg · sodium 146 mEq/L · glucose 94 mg/dL · urine osmolality 160 mOsm/kg → Collecting duct unresponsive to antidiuretic hormone → lithium blocks the ADH (antidiuretic hormone) signal, so fewer aquaporins reach the membrane; desmopressin changes the urine little or not at all
  7. 58-year-old woman on lithium for 16 years months of thirst and polyuria in bed 2 days after a fall now drowsy and disoriented HR 104/min · BP 102/64 mm Hg · sodium 156 mEq/L · urine osmolality 140 mOsm/kg · creatinine 1.3 mg/dL → IV fluid replacement and a serum lithium level → water and volume loss from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; dehydration also raises the lithium level
  8. 33-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, euthymic on lithium for 18 months 2 months of tiredness and feeling cold small nontender goiter alert and oriented HR 62/min · TSH 12.4 μU/mL · free thyroxine low · sodium 140 mEq/L · lithium trough 0.8 mmol/L → Add levothyroxine and continue lithium → lithium-induced hypothyroidism; thyroid abnormalities are not a reason to stop lithium
  9. 26-year-old man, lithium for 4 months; euthymic mild tremor holding a cup urinating more than before alert, oriented, gait normal HR 72/min · sodium 140 mEq/L · urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg · TSH 5.6 μU/mL · free thyroxine normal · trough 0.9 mmol/L → Expected lithium adverse effects → normal sodium, mental status, level and free thyroxine; a fine tremor, polyuria and a mildly high TSH are routine
  10. 40-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, euthymic on lithium for 3 years takes no other medications routine visit; last laboratory studies 12 months ago alert and oriented BP 118/74 mm Hg · BMI (body mass index) 23 kg/m² → Lithium level, creatinine, TSH and calcium → level, electrolytes, creatinine and TSH every 6 to 12 months; calcium yearly
  11. 59-year-old man with bipolar disorder, on lithium 8 years lisinopril started 2 weeks ago 4 days of nausea and a coarse tremor of both hands alert and oriented HR 64/min · BP 126/80 mm Hg · sodium 139 mEq/L → Serum lithium level and creatinine → an ACE inhibitor raises the lithium level; coarse tremor and nausea suggest toxicity
How NBME framed it: question 1

50-year-old woman brought to the emergency department: trouble speaking, cannot walk mildly agitated, uncooperative, not oriented to place Husband: lithium for 20 years for bipolar disorder; lately more thirst and urination No family history of kidney or endocrine disease 163 cm, 77 kg, BMI 29 kg/m² · T 36.8 °C · pulse 84/min · BP 110/75 mm Hg · speech difficulty, muscle weakness, the cognitive findings; otherwise normal · sodium 150 mEq/L · TSH 5.5 μU/mL · urine specific gravity 1.005 · urine osmolality 200 mOsm/kg

Most likely cause of her symptoms?

Competing answers
  • Acute lithium toxicity: confusion and trouble walking fit toxicity; but acute toxicity follows a large ingestion, and the labs here point to the kidney.
  • Lithium-induced hypothyroidism: the TSH of 5.5 is mildly high; but no free thyroxine is given, and hypothyroidism explains neither the hypernatremia nor the dilute urine.
  • Routine side effects of lithium: polyuria alone is routine; but dehydration, confusion, hypernatremia and dilute urine can be life-threatening.
  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus: a BMI of 29 with polyuria suggests glucose diuresis; but hypernatremia after years of lithium fits the kidney better.

Down to two: lithium-induced diabetes insipidus or hypothyroidism. Diabetes insipidus: 20 years of lithium, thirst and polyuria, then a sodium of 150 with urine osmolality 200; the kidney is losing water it should keep. The stem never names diabetes insipidus or gives a lithium level, so the answer rests on reading the sodium against the urine. Four of the five options are lithium effects, and the one lab placed to tempt, a mildly high TSH, belongs to the wrong one.

Pairs with Polyuria: the renal workup of a dilute urine and the agent used when lithium must continue. Teratogenic Exposures: lithium in pregnancy. Thyroid Disease in an Adult: reading the TSH.
Transferable rule

When a patient on a drug with several known complications presents, choose the complication that explains every abnormal value. On lithium, a high sodium with dilute urine belongs to the kidney, and a mildly high TSH beside it is not the answer.

Intimate Partner Violence

plan for safety, report by who is at riskIs she safe at home, and who decides what happens next?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Suspect IPV (intimate partner violence) when frequent injuries come with explanations that do not fit, and/or when bruises sit in a suspicious distribution: lower abdomen, back or forearms.

Ask her tactfully whether she feels safe at home, alone if possible.

Every patient gets help developing an emergency safety plan, whether or not she discloses abuse or is ready to leave.

Suspected abuse of a child in the home is reported on suspicion; reporting her own abuse varies by state and is not the first step.

Diagnosis
Raise it Injuries – frequent, with explanations that do not fit; forearms may bruise from defensive movements · Risk factors – recent job loss or job or financial instability; substance use · Pregnancy – IPV often begins or increases, especially in unintended pregnancy · No test – the injury pattern and the history raise it
Management and treatment
What every patient gets, then what depends on her answer
StepWho gets itWhy
See her aloneEvery patient, if possibleA partner present can intimidate her
Ask, tactfully and in a nonthreatening manner, whether she feels safeEvery patient with suspicious findingsAsking directly, in private, helps her disclose
Emergency safety planEvery patientMany are not yet willing or able to leave
Assess readiness to actShe says she is abusedShe decides when to leave
ReportSuspected child abuse, or state law requires itA legal duty; for her own abuse, it varies by state

If seeing her alone is not possible or not offered, the safety plan comes first.

The safety plan Include – a place to flee to if needed; signals or code words that tell her children or neighbors to call for help; an emergency kit stored outside the home · Avoid – generally, written materials such as pamphlets, because the abuser can find them · Resources – local shelter and national hotline information in a form safe to carry (wallet card, phone under a code name) · Every later visit – reassess her risk of immediate harm, privately
Who decides, and who must be reported
IfThen
Competent adult, not older or disabled (alert, oriented, judgment intact)She decides what to do and when; reporting her own abuse varies by state, and most states do not require it
Not yet willing and able to leave safelyPolice or a protective order may escalate harm
Prepared to actSupport the step she chooses
Only she is at riskSafety plan with her; no report as the first step
Suspected abuse of a child in the homeReport to child protective services on suspicion
Capacity impaired (older or dependent adult): she cannot decide for herselfReport per state law
An older or disabled adultMost states require a report
Injury from a gun, knife or other weaponReportable in most states
Where the state requires a report for herReport, but not as the first step

Most states require reports of specified injuries and wounds, and very few require reporting domestic violence itself; know your state's law.

Screening and complications Screen – the USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) recommends screening women of reproductive age for IPV, including during pregnancy and after delivery (grade B); screening often uses a brief questionnaire, asked in a private and safe setting · Positive screen – evaluate and, if appropriate, offer or refer for evidence-based interventions with several components and ongoing support · Complications – repeated injury, seen as frequent emergency visits; in pregnancy, miscarriage, preterm labor and low birth weight
Practice
  1. 28-year-old woman in the emergency department cut lip; bruises on lower abdomen and back says she fell down the stairs 1 day ago her boyfriend stays and answers most questions T 37.0 °C · HR 98/min · alert, oriented; anxious → Interview her alone about her safety at home → the boyfriend answers for her, so see her alone first, if possible, to prevent intimidation; the safety plan every patient receives follows
  2. 34-year-old woman seen alone for a 2-day-old wrist sprain husband shoved and slapped her several times this year will not leave him: she has no income bruises on both forearms · HR 84/min · alert, oriented; thought process linear; judgment intact → Build an emergency safety plan with her → a competent adult not yet ready to leave; the plan protects her until she is, and therapy for perpetrators has not conclusively been shown to lower the risk of violence
  3. 31-year-old woman in the emergency department husband slapped and shoved her 2 hours ago wants to go home No psychiatric history HR 96/min · arm and back bruises · slightly disheveled, tearful, anxious · denies suicidal, homicidal ideation · alert, oriented; judgment intact → Develop an emergency safety plan with her → the danger is her home, not a psychiatric condition: judgment intact and no suicidal ideation; a competent adult decides when to leave
  4. 29-year-old woman seen alone in the emergency department bruised cheek; her boyfriend punched her last night asks that the police not be told No children HR 90/min · alert, oriented, calm; judgment intact → Plan for her safety and respect her refusal → a competent adult: reporting her abuse varies by state and most states do not require it; where required, it is still not the first step; Adult Protective Services is for older or dependent adults
  5. 32-year-old woman seen alone at a clinic her husband hits her last week he struck their 6-year-old son with a belt, leaving welts she does not want to leave bruise on her upper arm · HR 80/min · alert, oriented, judgment intact → Report the child's abuse to child protective services → suspected child abuse is reported on suspicion; her own safety plan continues, and reporting her own abuse follows state law
  6. 81-year-old woman with dementia, brought by her husband, her caregiver bruises on both upper arms he says she falls; her gait is steady HR 78/min · oriented to person only; cannot name the year · poor insight and judgment → Report the abuse to Adult Protective Services → she cannot decide for herself, so seeing her alone cannot yield a plan she can carry out; most states require reporting the abuse of older adults, and waiting for a follow-up visit leaves her with the suspected abuser
  7. 27-year-old woman in the emergency department says her husband beats her plans to go home tonight is making a safety plan with the physician bruises on both forearms · HR 88/min · alert, oriented, judgment intact → A printed pamphlet to keep at home → written materials should generally be avoided, because the abuser may find them
  8. 23-year-old woman, 20 weeks, unplanned pregnancy lower-abdominal bruises; says she walked into a table second injury visit in 2 months partner answers for her No alcohol or drug use HR 88/min · platelets 250,000/mm³ · fetal heart rate 145/min · alert, oriented, anxious → Intimate partner violence → lower-abdominal bruises, a story that does not fit and a partner who speaks for her; IPV often begins or increases in pregnancy, especially unintended
  9. 30-year-old woman in the emergency department swollen, tender forearms with bruises along both 1 day after what she calls a trip over a rug third injury visit this year HR 92/min · BP 124/80 mm Hg · alert, oriented; anxious → Raising the arms to shield the face and torso → the forearms may bruise from defensive movements during an attack
  10. 35-year-old woman returns alone for a blood pressure check 1 month ago she said her husband hits her made a safety plan then BP 128/82 mm Hg · HR 76/min · no new injuries · alert, oriented, euthymic → Ask again, privately, about her current safety → assess the risk of immediate harm at every visit
  11. 24-year-old woman at a routine health maintenance visit no complaints; came alone takes an oral contraceptive Never screened for partner violence HR 72/min · BP 112/70 mm Hg · no injuries · alert, oriented, euthymic → A private brief questionnaire on partner violence → the USPSTF recommends screening women of reproductive age (grade B); screening often uses a brief questionnaire, asked in a private and safe setting
How NBME framed it: question 1

26-year-old woman in the emergency department with a broken arm she attributes to a fall third emergency visit in 6 months: earlier a broken ankle and a concussion apologizes and calls herself clumsy Left teaching after her third child's birth 8 months ago; lost income, significant financial strain; husband works two jobs No psychiatric illness or significant medical history alert, slightly disheveled, mildly anxious; often glances at her husband before answering vital signs normal · swollen right forearm · several bruises on upper extremities and stomach, from often bumping into things, she says

Most appropriate first course of action?

Competing answers
  • Admit to an inpatient psychiatric facility: she is in danger; but from her home situation, not a psychiatric condition; admission removes her only for a while.
  • Contact the police: the injuries are serious; some states may require it, but it is not the first step; before she is willing and able to leave safely, it may escalate the violence.
  • Recommend anger management therapy for her husband: he is the source; but therapy has not conclusively been shown to lower the risk of violence.
  • Recommend an order of protection against her husband: it sounds protective; but filed before she is willing and able to leave safely, it may increase the risk of harm.

Down to two: a safety plan or contacting the police. Safety plan: all patients with suspected abuse get help with one, whether or not they disclose abuse. The stem never says abuse: repeated injuries, an apologetic story that does not match the bruises, and a patient who looks at her husband before answering; four options act through the police, the courts, a psychiatric unit or the husband, and only the safety plan acts with her.

Pairs with Elder Abuse: the older adult who cannot protect herself, where suspicion alone leads to a report. Ask: can the injured adult decide for herself? Suspected Child Abuse: the injured child. Ask: is the person being harmed a child?
Transferable rule

When a competent adult is being hurt at home, the first action is one she can use today: ask her alone, then build a safety plan with her, whatever she discloses. Reporting follows who is at risk and state law, and it is not the first step for her own abuse.

Genito-Pelvic Pain/Penetration Disorder

vaginismus · exclude a body cause, then treatIs it pelvic floor tightening with fear of pain, or a cause the examination finds?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Persistent or recurrent difficulty with one or more of vaginal penetration, pain, fear of pain or pelvic floor tightening on attempted penetration, for about 6 months with distress, is genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder (GPPPD), the DSM-5 (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition) diagnosis that took in vaginismus.

Risk factors: a history of abuse, anxiety disorders, relationship conflict, cultural taboos; not every patient has one. It can also follow a vulvar infection such as candidiasis, a gynecologic problem such as endometriosis, or pregnancy.

Examine before labeling it:

  • inspect the vulva
  • map focal pain with a cotton swab
  • palpate the pelvic floor with one finger
  • test a discharge if there is one

Treatment is multimodal: pelvic floor physical therapy, psychotherapy such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and psychoeducation.

Pain deep in the pelvis with painful periods is not an entry problem; it points to endometriosis or a structural cause.

Diagnosis
Criteria A – persistent or recurrent difficulty with one or more of: vaginal penetration during intercourse; marked vulvovaginal or pelvic pain during intercourse or penetration attempts; marked fear or anxiety about that pain before, during or as a result of penetration; marked tensing or tightening of the pelvic floor muscles on attempted penetration · B – about 6 months or longer · C – clinically significant distress · D – not better explained by a nonsexual mental disorder, severe relationship distress such as partner violence, or other significant stressors, and not due to a substance, a medication or another medical condition

Criteria as listed by the University of British Columbia Sexual Health Research group; Merck Manual Professional gives the DSM-5-TR (text revision) version as at least 6 months with significant distress.

What else hurts or blocks penetration
DiagnosisThe stem showsDecides it
VulvodyniaVulvar pain for 3 months or moreNo identifiable cause; the swab maps the pain
Vaginal candidiasisRecent antibiotics, diabetes, immunosuppressionRed, swollen vulva; thick white discharge
Genitourinary syndrome of menopausePostmenopausal burning and drynessOften pale, dry tissue (may look normal in early menopause)
Lichen sclerosusBurning, dryness, itchingVisible skin changes; biopsy if needed
EndometriosisDeep pain; painful periods commonCul-de-sac nodularity
Female sexual interest/arousal disorderLittle interest or arousalAt least 3 of 6 symptoms; 6 months; distress
Major depressive disorderLow mood, lost interestLow mood or anhedonia beyond sex; five symptoms in the same 2 weeks
Generalized anxiety disorderWorry about a range of topics6 months or more of excessive worry, hard to control, plus three more symptoms; anxiety not limited to penetration
Somatic symptom disorderPreoccupied with symptoms; repeated visitsExcessive, persistent thoughts, anxiety or time and energy on symptoms that distress or disrupt daily life, for more than 6 months
Management and treatment
Multimodal treatment: the parts are combined, not stepped Pelvic floor physical therapy – pelvic muscle relaxation; considered an effective intervention · Psychotherapy such as CBT; sex therapy – fear and anxiety about pain; CBT is strongly recommended · Psychoeducation – a primary part of treatment · Sequential vaginal dilators – tight pelvic muscles; part of multidisciplinary care · Topical lidocaine before sex – pain; for a short time only

The sources give no fixed order or failure interval between these parts, so there is no escalation ladder here.

When the examination finds a body cause Postmenopausal, pale, dry tissue – vaginal estrogen, the most effective therapy when symptomatic; lubricants may give temporary relief · Lichen sclerosus – usually topical steroids · Vulvodynia – gentle vulvar care, physical therapy; vestibulectomy may help only after nonsurgical options fail, with pain localized to the vestibule · Endometriosis – options such as nonopioid analgesics, combined oral contraceptives or progestogens; laparoscopic excision
Practice
  1. 26-year-old woman, 8 months of pain at the vaginal opening with every attempt at intercourse fear before each attempt; distressed Never had a pelvic examination T 36.8 °C · HR 78/min · anxious; asks to go slowly → Vulvar inspection, cotton swab testing and a single-digit examination → entry pain is examined first: inspection looks for a body cause, the swab maps vestibular pain and one finger finds a tight pelvic floor
  2. 27-year-old woman, 7 months unable to have intercourse began after a treated yeast infection dreads attempts; pelvic floor clamps down distressed; wants intercourse with her partner afebrile; vulva, vitals normal; no discharge or yeast · anxious · contracts on one-finger examination → Genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder → fear and pelvic floor tightening for about 6 months with distress; it can follow a vulvar infection, and a clear microscopy excludes active infection
  3. 22-year-old woman, 1 year unable to have intercourse or insert a tampon fears the pain; muscles clamp down distressed; wants intercourse with her partner afebrile; vulva, vitals normal · swab test painless · microscopy normal · pelvic floor contracts on one finger · anxious → Pelvic floor physical therapy with cognitive behavioral therapy → genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder: treatment is multimodal, aimed at the pelvic floor and the fear
